You know and you love it; the Borderlands franchise is here with another swing and a hit. Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is a FPS RPG from 2K Australia and Gearbox Software. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
Two words: Laser Guns. The addition of various laser weapons was a phenomenal idea. Personally, I found them to be far more effective (and worth it) than the Eridian and E-Tech weapons from the previous Borderlands installments. Once you get your hands on one of the ones that just shoots a continuous beam of death and destruction, you’ll be in heaven.
The boosting feature while you are airborne is pretty cool. It gives you that extra distance you need to get to areas that would otherwise be unreachable. Additionally, it’s a helluva lot faster than sprinting everywhere.
The new Stinger vehicle was really cool. It reminded me a lot of the Sand Skiffs from Borderlands 2: Captain Scarlett DLC. Sadly, the explosive harpoons weren’t there to continue strengthening the resemblance. That being said, they were still a lot of fun. Very fast, very maneuverable, and they featured a launch boost to boot.
The new characters are all pretty cool. Claptrap is, of course, still hilarious, but my favorite new character to play as was definitely Athena. Lot’s of damage output melee and otherwise.
Did I mention some Lovecraftian themed enemies?
The Bad
B:TPS lacked the the same undefinable charm as it’s predecessors, in my opinion. It’s still fun and it’s still Borderlands, but something just felt missing.
Several of the missions felt highly repetitive. “Go here and turn this on” followed by “then go here and turn this knob” followed by “then go over here and turn this on”. It wasn’t entertaining for very long to say the least. Not to mention the sheer volume of enemy forces placed in your way every time you turn around.
The Meh
Being on Pandora’s moon was cool at first with the whole “you need oxygen when you’re outside” and low gravity, but, after a time, it lost it’s novelty and just became fairly tedious.
The campaign itself is pretty short; especially coming off of Borderlands 2.
Verdict: Yea
Despite a few detractors Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is a fun game and a good addition to the franchise as a whole. If you see it go on sale, pick it up. As always, thanks for reading.

What an excellent game. A 1st person shooter that keeps you coming back for more. The game itself has excellent graphics and mechanics, with a easy-to-understand shop system. Not to mention it's like $1-$2 for the game. The maps you play are different on each server and on some servers you can even be the dinosaur (either human or dinosaur).
The game has a few minor bugs, but nothing like falling through the map or driving though walls type of bugs, only things like a 1 second delay every now and then (but you hardly notice them).  The devs are constantly bringing out updates to fix the minor bugs and the community is very active!
This game is definitely on my top 10 and I encourage any COD/FARCRY/CSGO/INSURGENCY fan to give this game a go and see what all the fuss is about!

Ok, so I just conquered a few of your cities, my army is much larger then yours, and you are declining WHITE PEACE?! They attacked my army, pope excomunicated me (?!)... Spain allied with France, they attack, too... Try to sign peace with them, white peace, me giving tribute, they decline... Conquer 2 of their cities, and offer them all my money to sign peace, they decline...  Went "I don't give a ♥♥♥♥"... started destroying France, and left them with 1 city... Ok, trying to bribe french and spanish small armies, they usually decline, or take enormous amounts of money for a 2-3 units... Not important, anyway...
I attack French last city... My enormous army is crossing the bridge, they are bribed... All of them... Ok, I have another one in vicinity, will attack with them while I gather more troops... They cross the bridge and are bribed... By whom!? How?! What the ♥♥♥♥ is wrong with that river?!
So, this is the most annoying thing that happened... There were more small things... Much more... On the other hand, I understand that people will like the battle parts of this game, and I cannot say too many things about it, because I don't play it...

Remember, "Your Mileage May Vary" in regards to this port, but I believe that this time around performance is way better on launch than Disgaea PC was. Great job NISA!
TL;DR: I wholeheartedly recommend Disgaea 2 PC for $20, especially if you've played Disgaea PC. (Buy it so we can get future Disgaea games on PC :D)
------------------------
Let's get introductions out of the way first, dood:
Disgaea 2 PC is a port of the PSP remake of Disgaea 2: Cursed Memories, called Disgaea 2: Dark Hero Days. (Lots of confusing names thrown around, I apologize! Basically: PS2 - Cursed Memories > PSP - Dark Hero Days > PC - Disgaea 2 PC) Disgaea 2 PC is much more of the gameplay from Disgaea PC, but improved.
From my previous Disgaea PC review: (
)
I'd like to add that Disgaea is perhaps a fully-aware series (in that it KNOWS it's a series of grinding SRPGs, and that the characters are well aware they are part of an entertainment medium), and I personally enjoy fourth-wall leaning/breaking in games. I'm a sucker for being super over-leveled for a stage so this series scratches my "power fantasy itch" well. Also, this series has some crazy over-the-top attack animations that just has to be experienced.
Disgaea 2 remains mostly similar to Disgaea 1. So, instead of just analyzing this title on its own, I'm going to compare and contrast Disgaea 1 (PC) and Disgaea 2 (PC).
Going off this table, you can see I slightly lean towards Disgaea 2 for music and characters, but Disgaea 1 for a story. On their own, I like most of the D2 characters -- heck even Taro and Hanako I don't mind too much -- except for maybe Yukimaru, zam. ...GOD THAT "ZAM" IS ANNO-- *clears throat* I'm joking about not liking Yukimaru :). Anyway... the plot of Disgaea 2 that the characters are placed in is... well, I can't really express it other than "it's just a pretty good story". Whereas D1 has an excellent story
, but most of the characters are all bonkers, if not a little annoying (whether on purpose or otherwise idk; in Disgaea D2 they're much more enjoyable imo). Basically what I'm getting at is D1 has genre-savvy characters in an overall excellent RPG plot and D2 has cliche characters in a rather mediocre RPG plot. Take your pick.
I should probably also say that there's a lot more to do in Disgaea 2, but the added mechanics of Magichange (monster polymorphing into a weapon), "Toss & Pass" (monster "tossing"), Innocent Towns, Mystery Rooms, and the Land of Carnage just adds on to the amount of things to learn (which is already quite mind-numbing for a newbie before these additions). Overall, the game feels slightly faster and smoother, but not as fast or smooth as I would want it to be. Take that statement however you will.
I think that a gamepad is preferable for Disgaea. If you don't own one you'll have to fiddle with key binds, like I did. Or, you can try using the Mouse (I don't use Mouse but I hear it's a bit fiddly, just like Disgaea PC) EDIT: I used an Xbox 360 Controller and I can confirm the gamepad support is solid, if maybe a little unstable (the game crashed when my controller lost connection to the wireless receiver).
With regards to Graphics, neither port/re-make has improved much on/moved beyond the PS2-era graphics (you can only do so much to them). So if you're in the market for a graphically-pleasant SRPG, don't try this one. In terms of music, I didn't think Disgaea 1's soundtrack was bad, but Disgaea 2 has a better OST than D1 in my opinion.
Overall, a better buy than Disgaea PC if you already own that one. Plus, you get an ownership discount for buying Disgaea 2 PC if you own Disgaea PC! Otherwise, if you don't own D1 PC, I'd say try the demo first before getting D1 or D2.

The underlying storyline and quests are interesting. Nice music and graphics. I am looking forward to the final product.

I am a HUGE fan of Final Fantasy Tactics - have many many hours on the gba of that title. I have never played Final Fantasy or any of it's titles; just Tactics.  I love the way the combat works.  I've always wanted a game that incorporated that type of combat on a non-console; and haven't really been able to do one myself.
Hadn't found one, and this looked similar enough - and now that I've played it -
Ok let's just get the part out of the way where the Prinny characters say 'DOOD' (pronounced dude) all the time.  Yes, like I do.  Moreso, but well - just like when I speak "dude" (a dialect of US English.)  That alone makes me love the game.
There's a part of the tactics where you can 'lift' (pick up) a character adjascent to you and _throw_ them.  That means you can move further in one turn.  Which is great for extending your attack range.  And you can toss to another character, who can then toss... so you can move very quickly across the battle.  And then you can pick up someone picking someone else up, which... yeah there's a great deal you can do with that tactic.  (Also the prinnies explode when you toss them.  Which is somewhat a problem as they are then dead, but... it's a tactic.)
I haven't quite mastered the combo attack yet (where a character next to another character will combine for a bigger attack) or figured out some of the special attacks, but - yeah.  This is as good, if not better, than Final Fantasy Tactics.
Yes, it's a PSP port (thanks Shiki Ryougi), but I don't care - the game is great and I hadn't been familiar with it before.  I am hoping the first in the series, and eventually everything up to and including the 5th version (coming for the Nintendo switch) is available, because this is excellent.
I understand it is very grindy, and I'm likely to be playing this for the rest of my life, as I haven't finished the GBA FFT yet and I've been playing that on/off for 10+ or so years.
So - if you like Final Fantasy Tactics - you'll likely love this game; very similar, but with it's own extensions to the combat.

Stellaris is one of those typical Paradox Games in their early stage: You play it and are blown away at the beginning, discovering new elements of the game at every turn (I was extactic when i found out about uplifting). After you play 1 or 2 games, however, you notice the lack of depth and missing polish at every corner. Then you look to EU4 or CK2, and you know the game is gonna be great 2 years down the line, in fact, you can already SEE how good this game is gonna be while still playing this basic framework.
Every big patch is bringing new stuff to table and does not shy away from redesigning core elements, in my opinion so far for the better. While there is still a lot to do (my biggest gripe is still that endgame crises are not formal wars and thus the AI is unable to recognize them as enemies and doesnt do jack against the doomstacks of extragalactic invaders) I'm positive the game is only going to become better as time progresses.

The Night of the Rabbit is phenomenal. A great story, beautiful music, hand drawn art and clever puzzles, and it all works together perfectly. A near perfect point-and-click adventure experience.
Lets start with the music. The first thing you hear when you start the game is a melodious theme that can only be described as the game in music form. It is near indescribable how perfect the main theme is. The rest of the music is also amazing, enhancing the atmosphere of the game, deepening the emotion of various scenes.
The hand drawn art is beautiful, has a unique style, and is a perfect medium in which to tell the story of Jerry and his journey into the realm of magic. Visually, the game is very pretty to look at, but it's the attention to detail that truly brings this fantasy realm to life. In addition, the transition from cut-scene to game is near seamless. You almost can't tell you're watching a video.
The story is just as mystery filled as you'd expect from a journey into the realm of magic. The intro does a great job of setting the tone of the story, and it carries all the way to the end. Jerry's story is told near perfect, the conclusion of his story is satisfying. But the end is so open, with so many questions remaining, so much left to explore. So many avenues for further adventure. I really hope this game gets a sequel. It truly deserves one, crafted with the same love and dedication.
Like all point-and-click adventures, the gameplay is as you would expect. You use the mouse to interact with the environment, the people and objects within. The items you collect are then used to solve a variety of clever puzzles throughout the game. Many of the puzzles are crafty, and even though you can see the solution, there's always another clever obstacle to overcome. The puzzles are very seamless in execution.
You can observe all the objects you can interact with by clicking on a magic coin in the inventory (a clever means of integrating a gameplay element into the story). This is a brilliant addition to point-and-click adventure gameplay as it's sometimes easy to miss key items lying around. The only downside is that the coin only shows the interactive elements for a moment, too short to take in everything. You can continuously observe the interactive objects by holding the shortcut key (holding spacebar), but it would have been nice to have the mouse implementation be given some better functionality.
There is also a minor bug where you sometimes can't open the inventory by clicking on the backpack. There were only two points in the game where I observed this. The first was after exiting the boat, but going to the title menu and then returning to the game fixes this. The second one is more annoying. At the outpost in the frozen land (and only at this screen), the only way to access the inventory is via the inventory shortcut (pressing I). The mousewheel method of accessing the inventory may still work, but I never used it so I can't say. The bug is a minor annoyance, and to be fair, it's the only bug I encountered throughout the game.
The Night of the Rabbit is exceptional. I recommend it to any fan of the adventure genre.

As someone with tons of hours on the Assetto Corsa clock, I sometimes long for a racing simulation that has the features that separate a circuit racing sim from a mere driving sim. Here is where Stock Car Extreme comes in. The game simulates racing weekends with practice and qualyfying, full flag rules, night racing, standing or rolling starts, tyre and brake temperature, tyre wear, damage, preconfigured pit strategies, championships and decent AI or alternatively the ability to host servers and race online. In other words, it is a feature complete racing sim with the exception of weather simulation. Disclaimer: I have not played the new Steam version of this game that much since it came out only two days ago, but I have driven lots of races on the last version that was distributed directly through the developer. So my basis for this review will be the experiences I had in these last months plus the 2 hours wheel time on the Steam version.
In terms of content, it has about a dozen different cars that cover a wide variety of types of vehicle and all behave very differently on track. From karts, Formula 3 racecars, a Camaro streetcar, Minis, the name giving V8 stock cars to F1-alike cars from various decades (list is non-exhaustive) the variety is greater than the number of cars available suggests. The over twenty featured tracks are all made to a very high standard in terms of detail and, according to people who live near them, represent their real counterparts very accurately even though the developer did not employ laser scanning in the modeling process. Most of these tracks are located in Brazil and they include the full tracklist for the 2014 Brazil V8 stock car championship, but a few others are present too, like the Austrian GP track or the now demolished former Johannesburg GP course. Since the game is moddable, there are literally dozens of user-made add-on tracks to download though and almost every major circuit can be found on the net (Head to
or nogripracing if you want to have a starting point).
The physics in this game are very predictable and they are conveyed with intuitive Force Feedback. They are not forgiving, but every spin feels deserved and I can always tell what went wrong easily. Physics feel is difficult to describe with words, so I will make a comparison here. Stock Car Extreme combines the firm, defined edge of control I feel in  rFactor 2 with the progressive loss and gain of grip found in Assetto Corsa. The Force Feedback plays an important role in that, because it strikes a  balance between representing the steering feel in a real car and giving the player all the information a real driver would feel through the chassis of the car rather than the steering. You really should play this with a good Force Feedback wheel and pretty much every wheel out there is compatible with the game. Assists like ABS, TC or braking and steering assists are available as well.
The AI is decent (i.e. miles ahead of Assetto Corsa or the console games), but not perfect. They are generally able to provide entertaining racing provided the difficulty slider is in the right place (default is 95%, beginners should start lower than that though while pros can go above 105%), but they are often too timid when behind and hesitant to overtaket. On the bright side they crash you out very seldomly. Since most racing sims have terrible AI, this probably still the best AI to be found in a racing sim today (Update: Raceroom has decent AI now, probably on par with this one). The online experience is great once you join a dedicated community with a server, but the public lobby is often empty (that might change with the Steam release though). The netcode behaviour is very good if all players have a decent connection. No warping and smooth movement of the cars. Things will start getting dodgy and warping will occur when pings are over 300, but even then there seems to be some safety net in the collision detection that makes the hit detection very generous when high pings are involved.
On the graphics side of things this is clearly a DX9 game, but high quality models and textures along with HDR make the picture pleasing for the eye, miles ahead of last gen console graphics but not quite up there with newer titles like Assetto Corsa or Project Cars. If you want to get a good idea of how the graphics look I would recommend watching some videos on Youtube , or example:
because racing sims in particular often look differently in motion. The graphics are good enough to make me immersed in the racing and on the flip side the system requirements are moderate even for 60+ fps gaming. One area that often gets overlooked in games is the sounds and Stock Car Extreme gets the job done in this department very nicely. Engine sounds, especially in the V8 stock cars sound amazing in the cockpit and the open cockpit cars have wind sounds as well. Believable sounds for tyre squeal, bottoming out or running over kerbs make the package complete here. Only the exteriour sounds are a bit dull, but the interiour ones makes up for that.
If you are looking for a Forza/GT style game on PC, you might want to look at Assetto Corsa instead because of the better graphics and bigger car list even though it lacks some features. Stock Car Extreme is a racing simulation that has all the essential features needed to represent real racing. With the exception of rain, it can simulate everything happening on the track on a real race weekend on top of the actual driving itself. Top notch physics along with some of the best AI in the market (because most competitors have terrible AI) and everything needed to simulate a full racing weekend or even a full championship make this an ideal title for offline racing. It is also a good choice for racing with a community online because of the reliable netcode and the ability for race admins to take race control actions like kicking, moving grid positions etc. Stock Car Extreme is the most well rounded sim racing package on the market today.

Simply the best racing sim I have ever played. I have been addicted to it ever since it was released a few years ago.
Every one of the various cars is a pleasure to drive. The closed cockpit of the V8 Stock cars is superb. Turn off all assists and the speed of the Formula V12 dares you to even blink, the Formula Extremes demand good throttle control in & out of turns, and in the words of James Hunt, you can go fast in the Formula Retro if you've got big balls.
I've enjoyed race sims since Indy 500 by Papyrus in the '80's, but the greatest for me was Geoff Crammond's F1GP - it had all the rules, scoring, tyre strategies, and excellent AI. I waited for something that would finally match it, but each time a new game was released, there was always something letting it down.
Until now.
Stock Car extreme is based on the GMotor engine, i.e the same as rFactor, Race07, GTR and others, but it is without doubt a racing sim in it's own right.
The Reiza devs have got inside the original code and amended it here and there (and they are still working on this so further updates & enhancements are possible), and in my opinion, the car handling, track grip characteristics, sounds and Force Feedback are the best I have found in any race sim.
Yes, I know there are games with more 'state of the art' graphics, but that does not detract from the detail that has gone into each track and car in this sim, and the way Reiza have kept udpating the game and adding to the cars & tracks at no extra cost is an example to all software developers.
There's a wide selection of cars, from Brazilian touring, to Mini, to Formula cars of all eras, to karting. All of them have their own unique character, and they really convey the excitement and exhilaration of racing at high speed. When you're on the limit, trying to shave another hundredth off your lap time, if you should drop a wheel onto the grass and lose control, you might sometimes find yourself taking your hands off the wheel and bracing for the impact.
The game is also very moddable, so you can paint the cars, edit the drivers and teams, create your own custom championships, and use third party cars and tracks, and there are many of them available on the web.
All of this means I can build the championship of my choice, for the best offline racing currently available.
It does have it's weaknesses, the main one being the lack of awareness of blue flags by the AI, and to be fair, this is yet to be implemented efficiently in any other sim. This problem only becomes evident if you are into longer races, such as full distance F1 races, but with some clever tweaking of the driver talent files, power and braking spread of the cars, and the aggression levels, it is possible to have the leaders lapping the backmarkers without much delay, and achieve great offline AI behaviour.
Others will cite rF2 and Assetto Corsa as being more advanced, especially graphically, but for me they are still way short of being the complete package, and they just do not offer the true driving feel that I get from this sim.
Stock Car extreme is the sim that finally stands up to the Geoff Crammond series.

The premise alone can be summed up quickly enough to make people laugh and want to try the game, which is a pretty great achievement in itself. And the game actually follows up with a solid experience. It's genuinely fun to blow people up, poison them, run them over, frame them when the cops show up, and stuff their bodies into sewer grates. Once you're used to it, the game itself is fun to play.
But that's the thing, you have to be used to it. After the tutorial, the game immediately throws you into a party of sixty people and lets you loose. There's no "learning curve" quite as much as there is being thrown in wholesale, where you need to figure out all the mechanics yourself. It's jarring, and it might shed players once they hit it. The level is, admittedly, easier than the others. But it's only easy once you know how to manipulate it, it's not _intuitively_ easy.
The story is thin. It tries to cover up its lack of substance by putting cheesy 80's-esque cop narration, but that doesn't entirely work either. The cutscenes between levels are a good idea (they reward you for winning by showing you how you get to the next party, or use the next character), but they're just not well executed.
But if you can ignore that, and are willing to stick with it until you've learned how the game works, it's fun and rewarding for a couple hours.

Well 'Game Stock Car' or 'Stock Car Extreme' as it is now called is a very versatile racing sim, the stock experience of this sim alone is worth the price if you would ask me.

- The Engine is quite old and it shows, while it definitely doesn't look terrible while driving, compared to say Assetto Corsa this is a non contest. It runs wonderfully on all sorts of systems though and supports pretty much every resolution you throw at it, it's just not as graphically impressive as other "newer" titles in the genre, just throwing this in for those who care much about that.
- It's a proper racing sim. Xbox 360 controllers are fairly useless, a wheel preferably with Force Feedback is an absolute recommendation. Especially since this sim has one of the best Force Feedback implementations in the genre. If you can get it dialled right, which leads me to the next point.
- A lot of options are in .ini files, for example if your Force Feedback is clipping (meaning the force is going over the wheels threshold and you basically get a really clunky feedback spike instead of a nicely rounded one) you need to go searching for the 'real feel plug in' and add smoothing factors* etc. or if you get motion sick like me from this horrible "camera shake at high speeds to simulate wind" nonsense, you have to go dig into the files**(location below) and disable it.
But that's about it, once you have it set up to your liking it is an absolute blast. One of the most immersive most complete racing sims out there and with its open modding capabilities you can even add even more content to the game. There are some really good mods out there, Racedepartment for example has a list of over 200 pieces available for free download. Definitely a recommendation from my side.
*RealFeelPlugin location '/steamlibrary/steamapps/common/Stock Car Extreme' -> RealFeelPlugin.ini
Search for this command line "DefaultSmoothingLevel=" and test out what level of smoothing suits your configuration best.
**disable headshake at high speeds go to: '/steamlibrary/steamapps/common/Stock Car Extreme/UserData/YourProfileName' -> open the "YourProfileName".PLR with notepad and search for "Cockpit Vibration" set all four command lines to "0" and you are good to go.
While you are in the User PLR you can also enable the virtual mirror while in cockpit by searching for:
"Virtual Rearview In Cockpit" and setting it to 1, as well as searching for "Rearview" and setting it to either "1,2 or 3" to determine what type of virtual mirror you would like to have displayed.
Anyway that's it from me i hope this "review" helped you to determine whether you like to buy it, have fun! :)

Vector Thrust is an incredibly well made game even though it is still incomplete. Nevertheless, the fundamentals are already there, namely the dogfighting mechanics that we all love in arcade simulators like Ace Combat and HAWX.
The game features tons of jets, from the ubiquitous oh-so-advanced F-22 (and its variants) to the more odd-looking prototypes such as the Hopeless Diamond (try to guess its shape ;) ).
Currently the campaign mode is a little bit basic as there are 2 short campaigns as of now, but there are other modes as well. A Challenge Mode (featuring various combat scenarios) is available to unlock aircraft for modes outside the campaigns, namely a Quick Battle mode that picks random scenarios one after another and a Skirmish mode that allows you to choose specific parameters, such as time of day, number of AI, unique modifiers and win conditions for the game.
Manoeuvring each type of plane feels tight much like Shattered Skies/Distant Thunder, and there is a toggle to turn off the angle of attack limiter that causes an increase in manoeuverability (and allows you to perform aerobatic stunts) at a cost of siphoning your plane's HP with every super sharp turn you make.
There is a healthy variety in the weapons, as the stats of the guns and 'normal' missiles can differ from one plane to another. For example, some planes might have a gun with a rapid rate of fire, but can overheat if fired for too long. Other planes with slower firing guns (which don't overheat) meant that there is always a chance that your shots will miss especially when tracking a plane doing a sharp turn. And then there's SP weapons...
The music is as good as those in other big budget titles, but the voice acting is a little hit and miss especially when the spoken lines do not match the in-game subtitles. Voices also sound quite funny at times, and the lines are somewhat informal to be spoken by military pilots especially in the non-campaign modes.
The AI can be described as brilliant at times, especially when they do various manoeuvres to throw you off their tail and when they manage to trick your missiles into hitting the ground by flying low. At their worst they are best described as suicidally insane, crashing into the ground whenever they feel like it although the prevalence of deaths by suicide in AI pilots is kinda low.
Although the game features cel-shaded graphics, each plane is lovingly detailed with numerous panel lines and the landscape looks alright when viewed from faraway. The water looks off, but the splashes it makes when a stray ordnance hits it look good.
Unfortunately, game-crashing bugs may be present as expected in an alpha, but the probability of these events are very small that you can still enjoy this game from time to time.
Much recommended. Get it.

Following up the highly popular Rome, Medieval II is, perhaps not surprisingly, very similar to its immediate predecessor. Anyone who has played Rome can look at Medieval II and see essentially the same gameplay with a few added bits. Thankfully those added bits improve the core game enough that Medieval II stands on its own, managing to escape Rome's shadow... a bit.
There are some silly issues that are often found in TW games: The AI is bad. Bad in the "I am suicidal with my generals" sort of way. At least they can actually fight battles competently enough, since this series has always (until Fall of the Samurai, perhaps) been at its best with swords, bows, and catapults. You do get the beginnings of the "pike and shot" era in this game, but really the focus is on the lovely middle ages.
As for the good bits, the Grand Campaign is, well, grand. A big map that can be made even bigger with mods, plenty of events that sometimes herald the arrival of new factions (ze Mongols!), and lots of fun with religion and crusades and burning  heretics. You have to unlock the rest of the factions by playing one of the starter nations (England, France, Spain, etc), but once you do there is plenty of replay value to be found here.
And, of course, there are mods. Plenty for Medieval II, though the real gems require its Kingdoms expansion.
So, if you want to lead big armies in the middle ages and charge around Europe setting stuff on fire, this game is plenty good for that. It's similarity to Rome might lead some players to get bored a little faster, but they can just get mods and play something fresh. Also get the Kingdoms expansion so you can delve into some of the best mods ever made.

It's finally here! Tomoyo After ~It's a Wonderful Life~ is finally on Steam! The tagline for this visual novel has been on my Steam profile description for as long as I can remember and while this VN is short, it has a powerful impact which I think is much more powerful than CLANNAD. Even so, CLANNAD and Tomoyo After still works on the same premise: the importance of family.
Tomoyo After ~It's a Wonderful Life~ is the spin-off to the highly acclaimed visual novel CLANNAD which picks up where Tomoyo route ended in CLANNAD. Developed by Key back in 2005, this VN was originally released as 18+ eroge thus why the voice actor for Tomoyo is different and the art direction is slightly different than how it was in CLANNAD. This time around Key didn't use Sekai Project to publish their game, instead they publish it under VisualArts brand while the translation is handled by another company using Doki's translation as a base (probably). Nevertheless, thx based Doki.
Tomoyo After picks up few months after Tomoyo's route ended in CLANNAD. Tomoya now works in a local workshop fixing home appliance while Tomoyo is now in her Senior Year. After the problem between Tomoya and Tomoyo in CLANNAD, the couple promise to be more forward with each other so they can overcome all the problem in life no matter how hard it is. One day, Takafumi, Tomoyo's younger brother, brought a young girl named Tomo which turns out to be the sibling's illegal stepsister. Takafumi, not wanting the Sakagami family to be torn apart again, decided to make Tomo live with Tomoya. Tomo is living happily with Tomoyo and Tomoya, despite that she still wants to be with her mother, thus began the journey to find Tomo's mother and the reason why she abandons Tomo to the Sakagami family.
Without giving too much spoilers, Tomoyo After follows on its tagline
by taking us on a journey of how Tomoyo overcoming her weakness with the help of Tomoya while Takafumi have to face the consequences of what he had done in CLANNAD and the burden that his choice has put upon him. Tomoya himself also wants to prove that he is no longer the person that he was back in his high school days and show the world that the love between him and Tomoyo are
and cannot be broken by anything for their power of love will overcome all troubles.
The art for Tomoyo After was directed mainly by Fumio and not by Hinoue, thus why Tomoyo looks similar but visibly different from how she was in CLANNAD. While Hinoue might not be the main art director like how she was in CLANNAD, she still helps with the character design. Everything else was handled in-house by Key with another notable thing to note is that Kashida Leo, a new scenario writer for Key, helped Maeda Jun in making the scenario for Tomoyo After.
The VN will take about 15-20 hours to finish depending on your reading speed. The VN alone is worth the current pricetag that it carry. But it doesn't stop there! As if the epic closure for Tomoyo story is not enough, they put an icing on the cake with Dungeon & Takafumi! A tactical role-playing game centered around the game that Takafumi is currently developing along with his overseas friend. It is time consuming and quite fun once you get the hang of it plus it has its own story centered around Takafumi and Kanako, Takafumi's girlfriend. On that note, I kinda dislike the fact that the Steam version lets you to play D&T even when starting Tomoyo After for the first time instead of unlocking it through the choice that you made while conversing with Takafumi in the VN.
Since this VN has many revision and re-release, I actually managed to read this VN multiple times across multiple version across multiple console. I will list all the edition here + the platform I read them on while also adding a comparison of what each version have and don't have.
Closing my review, I strongly suggest that you read CLANNAD before picking up Tomoyo After or at least have watched Tomoyo-hen otherwise you will be lost as to what is going on in the story. This visual novel is definitely a must have if you're love Tomoyo like I am or if you want to delve further into the CLANNAD universe.

What is there left to say about The Binding of Isaac? tBoI is a punishing, fast-paced, top-down platformer with simple stat-based character development through the use of items. I'm frankly surprised by how much replay value and content there is in a flash based game. Easily worth ~$5, especially with the Wrath of the Lamb DLC (comes with the 'tBoI Collection') roughly x1.5 the number of rooms, item, vendors, and endings.
The story is chocked full of what I can only describe as 'vague darkness'. Consistently twisted and subjected to depraved bloody nightmares, our poor protagonist Isaac becomes radically mutatilateded (mutated and mutilated) in every playthrough. Whether through dirty needles, poop, random pills, or a few blood pacts with the devil. You know, good wholesome american fun.
Graphically speaking, the game is timelessly styled, even if overly gorey. I look forward to the Binding of Isaac: Rebirth (the sequel released last week), but regardless find it hard to see the newgrounds reminiscient feel becoming dated. Just as I still enjoy multiplayer with Alien Hominide from time to time, a dungeon run with Isaac is, imo, a timeless joy. A timeless, perverse joy.

You do play 'blind' as in most rogue-likes. That is, you don't know the effects of anything - items, rooms, etc - it's on the player to figure those things out. Realistically you're either going to die repeatedly and rage quit, or do what I did
: look up the Wiki and go to town exploring the dungeon. It especially becomes fun after you unlock the D6, but I'll let each gamer figure out why on their own.
I run a fairly impressive rig, nothing that's worth bragging about these days, but enough to handle Crysis 3 at 40+ frames on medium settings, in a laptop. So, the slow downs in tBoI can be seen as either 'poor programming' (highly doubtful) or limitations of the flash player and flashscript. I ended up running tBoI on the lowest graphics setting and experienced very little slow down, even during several game-breaking item combinations. Ultimately it wasn't a huge problem for me, but it does exist.
The only other Issue I had with BoI on Steam was the screenshots. You cannot take screenshots using the steam overlay in tBoI, so you'll need to do it manually. Here's a typed guide:
- Play full-screen (the 'F' key in-game), move your cursor out of the way, and press the print screen or 'prt sc' key when you want to capture a screenshot.
- Pause the game, press 'F' again, open MS Paint, and paste (ctrl-v). There should be a copy of your screen at the moment you hit print screen. If not, you may have to hit fn+'prt sc' (this is especially true on laptops). Resume your game fullscreen and continue to do this with a new MS paint window whenever you want to capture a screenshot.
- When you finish your game, close out of Isaac and exit steam. Open a browser and navigate to your steam folder and goto "\steam\userdata\<yourUserId>\760\remote\" and see if there is a folder '113200' - that's Isaac's appID. If there isn't a folder there, create a new one and entitle it '113200'.
- Open the folder and create another folder within it called 'screenshots'. Open that folder and create another folder called 'thumbnails'.
- Now, maximize the MS paint with your first screen shot and go to File > Save As  and navigate to your newly created 'screenshots' folder. Entitle the photo with the date you are uploading the photo and its number like so '11-14-2014_00001' and save it as a JPG file.
- Then, before closing the MS paint window, click on the 'resize' button. Make sure that 'maintain aspect ratio' is checked and change the image to 200 pixels wide. Go to File > Save As and navigate to the 'thumbnails' folder and save it as a JPG.
- Close that MS paint and repeat until you've saved all your screenshots, making sure to make each image you save one number higher; '11-14-2014_00002'... '11-14-2014_00014'... etc.
- Finally re-open steam and goto Username > Content. Select 'upload screenshots'. You should see tBoI in the drop down menu now, complete with all your new screenshots.

I know I just purchased this game, but I played the unofficial English translation about 3 years ago, so I already know how amazing this VN is.
Tomoyo After is a branching plot line from Tomoyo's Route in the original Clannad Visual Novel. It's more or a less a "What if" scenario if Tomoya had formed a relationship with her instead of Nagisa. So yes, it is highly recommended you play her route from Clannad first before playing this game. It will really help you to understand the characters background, and other characters that were mention in her route in Clannad and make an appearance in Tomoyo After.
Now I must say, Tomoyo is a more independent charismatic character compared to Nagisa. Now I like both characters, but Tomoyo is far more enjoyable. Tomoya and Tomoyo have some really good exchanges in dialogue that really make the relationship feel "real". The supporting cast is interesting as well, with plenty of time given to them for their subplots to have satisfying conclusions, while also adding to the main plot of the story.
Also, my favourite part of the game is the soundtrack. My favourite song being the main title theme song called "Hope", and its played a few times throughout of the entire game. If your heart strings get pulled when you think of Dango Daikazoku from Clannad, then just prepare that they will be ripped entirely when you finish the game and listen to Hope. Honestly, this is strongly based on my opinion but I think Tomoyo After has very amazing ending that really will pulse out a large array of emotions towards you. It is in many ways, bitter sweet.
So yes! If you are a VN fan, and certainly a Clannad fan, pick this game up for sure. It will not disappoint, it is truly amazing, and 100% my favourite VN to date. Support Key, and hopefully we will see Little Busters next.

The game, at least early on, is completely about running into the trees and finding food. If you don't do this, and dedicate all your time to this, you will soon die of starvation. And don't think for a second that it'll be a slow death; you'll die in under fifteen seconds after your hunger bar depletes. To top it off, it's nearly impossible to hunt in early game, yet you need to hunt to get the skills to get things you need from animals to craft the very weapons you'd be using to hunt.
The average hunting experience is getting your friend to jog at the animal with you and throw 'throwing stones' at it so it is stunned, one of you hitting it with a pick or club while the other spams throwing stones. Don't ask me how to do it in singleplayer. The other way is tediously placing rabbit traps, if you somehow have the time (food) to actually do that. You'll have ten pieces of rabbit meat one day, and think you're good for a bit.
No.
It'll slide right down to zero again, before you even think of resetting the traps. The amount of time you need to reset the traps in the correct places would barely make the ends meet. Heres the kicker:
Yup. Your constant race for mushrooms, berries, and the occasional bit of rabbit meat will never stop, because if you don't play on the casual setting, if you die once, all your progress resets. Including all that time wasted on getting EXP so you can get crafting items from the rabbits.
The big issue, if you haven't noticed, is the food. I understand the need to have food in a survival game, but it's too much here, it's making it impossible to explore. The farthest me and my friend explored was some sort ranger station or something, but we died of hunger on the way back. To top it off, it makes it a time crunch for being able to gather resources to actually make the buildings. You know, the buildings that you lose when you ultimately die of starvation.
3/10 would rather starve than play again.

About 2 weeks ago, I bought the original Deus Ex and Deus Ex: Human Revolution: Director's Cut.  Really, I was buying Human Revolution, since that was the game I was really interested in.  I bought Deus Ex on a side thought, as it was $1.39 and all the old gamers kept saying "It's a masterpiece!"  Besides, I wasn't sure that Human Revolution would run on my potato PC.
2 weeks later, I finished the game, and for a couple minutes just stared at my computer screen saying "Wow".  I know realize that Deus Ex is indeed a masterpiece...although now that term seems inadequate.
Set in 2052, Deus Ex follows the story of JC Denton, nano-augmented agent for UNATCO, the United Nations Anti-Terrorist Coalition.  Basically, the world's gone to heck in a handbasket.  A horribly lethal virus, the Gray Death, has spread throughout the world.  UNATCO controls the distribution of the virus, but, as it is in short supply, UNATCO makes sure that the vaccine gets to the rich and powerful, the ones deemed "vital to society".  The lower classes have no options, and millions of them die on the streets.  As a result of the lower classes's poor treatment, multiple terrorist groups have sprung up, including the NSF in America and Silhouette in France.  As a member of the ANTI-TERRORIST COALITION, your first missions as JC are to fight the NSF in search of a stolen shipment of Gray Death vaccine, (known as Ambrosia).  Immediately, the games environment perfectly fits the bill.  The entire game is at night, or soon before morning, adding to the dark environment of the world.  On the streets of New York City, it seems that the only people are either terrorists, police, or bums.  The entire city feels oppressed and dangerous.  But the game doesn't stop there.  As events progress and truths are revealed, JC travels across the entire world, visiting such places as Hong Kong, Paris, and the famous Area 51.  There are certain open-world areas, although largely without the side-quests that were found in the prequel.  However, this is where Deus Ex's greatest strength is: freedom.
The open areas of Deus Ex are very large, much larger than anything we saw in Human Revolution.  Even the linear levels  were so open that I, in multiple cases, had to keep a rule to make sure I covered anything.  The same is true for the gameplay.  Within a level, there are multiple places to enter a place, achieve an objective.  Unlike games of its time like Half-Life, screwing something up in Deus Ex does not mean it's time to reload from the last save.  Even though it is sometimes simpler to do it the intended way, Ion Storm made a way to do it another way.  I'm sure that another player did something completely different then me based on their playstyle, weapons, resources, skills, and augs.
The game does have some flaws.  The graphics are incredibly dated.  Upon first installing the game, the game had poor lighting, making it nearly impossible to see in some areas.  In addition, some of the augs are pretty useless, being useful once or twice but never being worth purchasing again.  Other than that though, I can't find a significant flaw with the game.
This game is completely worth the price.  There is no reason not to get it.  9.5/10.

Like Hotline, except not really (spree-killing and parts of the aesthetic aside).
For one, Party Hard is very slow-paced. Your character walks at a speed slightly faster than civilian NPC's, can run, but runs out of breath half-way through a reasonably-sized room, and the levels are big enough to notice the slowness of it all. One could argue that it encourages a methodical approach, but in reality, once you find a quiet corner, all you do is press E when someone comes.
The other difference is that violence is not as visceral: most bodies stay intact, regardless of the cause of death, and they don't bleed that much.
Every level contains environmental traps, which allow you to kill about 50-60% of the population, and then it's back to stabbing walkers in a corner. The traps are nice to use, it's a pity there's so little of them on the map. Also, they are randomly generated within the level at every other retry (so, for example, a bike and a horse will swap places, or a music column won't load, etc.), so there is no streamlining a run to perfection over and over, you have to come up with the plan on the go. Considering the aforementioned slow pace and the scarcity of traps overall, this is a drawback for the game.
There is a story. It's presented between the missions and it has some "Eh" levels of voice acting, but there's nothing mind-blowing or worth mentioning about it. It's just there.
The tutorialising was done poorly (2 tips you've already understood which are given every now and then), the difficulty curve is all over the place, some menus are questionable, and the music is
even at the lowest setting.
All in all, fun while it lasts, but nothing to write home about.

The Good:
* The game is fun; I got right into it and had a blast.
* I found the difficult to be just right.  Not too difficult, but not too challenging.  Perhaps on par with Hotline Miami in terms of difficulty versus statisfaction.
* Lots of pop culture references subtly woven into the characters and animations.
* Dynamic gameplay.  Every playthough is different, and the special events add a fun suprise.
* The art direction is spot on.  It's consistent, entertaining, and the vibrant style adds a nice contrast to the voilent, dark events occuring in the game.
The Bad:
* When the cops catch you, the game doesn't end until they've carried you away, which can take awhile depending on the level.  It's a slap in the face to have to wait.
* Spelling and grammar mistakes abound.
* Items are rare and not that interesting.  All I ever got was stun, smoke, clothes, and poison.  None of them are really exciting or fun.  I think there was a big potential here to add another dimension to the game, but they didn't quite hit the mark.
* Failing is expensive in this game.  Others have mentioned this, and yeah, it sucks to put 20 minutes into a level only to get caught for something stupid.  But I found being extra patient meant this was rare for me, often deserved when it did happen, and overall the failures made beating the level all that more satisfying.
* The levels often devolve into a waiting game.  You have to wait until the heavens align for the perfect kill moment.  I feel like better items and environmental hazards would have helped the levels progress more evenly without all the waiting.  That said, waiting around wasn't particularly boring so I didn't mind this aspect that much.

Flight simulators are something I haven't been able to get into for many years, not since the earlier days of console flight combat when there were fun and less complicated arcade action experiences that focused more on intense combat than technical realism. Vector Thrust is the only of its kind in a long while to grab my attention and keep me plowing through the campaign obsessively the same way I did all those years ago, marathoning rental copies of Ace Combat for hours through late summer nights off from school.
In production for over two long years of dedicated development, Vector Thrust has already found a loyal fanbase of people such as myself who have been yearning for a lost aerial combat experience that is easy enough to hop into for all skill levels while still challenging enough to encourage thorough practice and countless heated retries in arcade spirit. Vector Thrust is a one of a kind aerial combat title that excels where the bigger companies have failed recently in delivering open dogfighting action that manages to keep me wanting to play through objectives over and over due to being just plain entertaining without the filler of modern games.
The game presents an♥♥♥♥♥kicking soundtrack as well as a slick cell-shaded style that while not exactly realistic gives a polished and stylish appearance to the explosive imagery of combat. Though it may not be a popular choice, it stands out and gave me a certain nostalgia for the cell-shaded visuals in Robotech: Battlecry and similar arcade-y air combat titles of the PS2 era.
The two campaign are a work in progress but already feature sixteen action packed missions between them that showcase everything from intercepting bombers to bombing carriers out in the ocean. These cover the core types of objectives you'll be carrying out as the game is fleshed out during its Early Access period and the campaign is crafted into a complete story with a narrative.
The variety and accessibility of the missions keeps the modest length campaign engaging from beginning to end, ground assaults feel a little rough with not a lot of risk of being shot down as you descend to bomb them but air-to-air dogfights are exhilarating and incredibly well done. Air-to-air combat is intense and fast paced and the A.I. is cunning and deceptive in how it maneuvers out of your view and attempts to keep you in sight at all times.
Before embarking on any given mission you're given a selection of true to life aircraft and their respective weapons to consider when taking on specific tasks. The selection is already great ranging from heavy and slow A-10 bombers to quick and deadly F-15 fighters and each excel in their own unique way, requiring you to put some thought into what you bring with you into combat. The environments you take flight in are gorgeous setting that paint the perfect backdrop for an all-out war, ranging from the dusty sand dunes of deserts to the sunny islands of the tropics.
The challenge mode appears to be the real bread and butter of the game being where most of the hundreds of aircraft are unlocked in the expansive tree of increasingly powerful choices. Each plane unlocked is a new mission earned, leading to even more unlocks for a massive amount of content that is genuinely exciting to blast through. The challenges are quick craft-specific tests of reflex and skill that present you with a seemingly simple task but must be conquered in expert speed.
These challenges are generally straight forward enough to finish, but the real difficulty comes in learning how complete each one in quick enough time to earn yourself a decent enough grade to move on and earn your next fighter and its respective mission. Each of the challenges include both a local and online score board enticing the player to revisit each of the diabolical scenarios to test your ability and see how you fare against the rest of the world.
Vector Thrust has come a long way since its already electrifying early alpha and is already the perfect arcade combat sim for people who just want to jump into some action and shoot their opposition out of the sky. With the promise of a fleshed out narrative that dramatically pulls you into the action in classic Ace Combat fashion, a more fleshed out multiplayer experience, and heaps more content to an already huge roster of available airplanes and modes this is the number one air combat fix to keep an eye on right now.
Whether you're a thrill-seeking arcade action fan looking for that quick dogfight or a hardcore sim veteran with a love for realism looking for something different Vector Thrust is absolutely the most accessible fun you'll have in a game in the genre which says a lot given the indie status, small budget, and even smaller team and it can only get better on its way out of Early Access.

Vector Thrust is an action arcade combat flight sim.  It has nice cel shaded jets, and not so nice ground textures.
Quite competent AI with two levels of difficulty (grunt and ace) and 25 degrees of competence per difficulty (1 being the easiest to handle and 25 being the hardest). So, almost anyone can find an opponent that's fun to dogfight with.
Controls are pretty solid and work just fine with keyboard, gamepad or joystick/hotas. Although, gamepad and joystick do require some rebinding.
Campaign is pretty good, since most of the time you're gonna be doing the fun part - dogfighting. When it's time for "destroy ground targets" missions, you might get a bit bored.
Additional customisation with purchasable jets and weapons adds some variety to the game and it seems that developers plan to add a lot more stuff there.
So, to wrap it up - very solid, pretty fun action arcade combat flight sim. (unless you do ground missions)

Tried to go back to it, really did.
So, I'll admit, I come from The Witcher 3.  This makes reviewing this game nearly impossible however, I'm going to give it a thumbs up based on how great I THINK it was at the time it was released because obviously we did not have Witcher 3 yet. With that said, the graphics still hold up well today when they are maxed out. The music and sound is still fantastic.
My biggest gripes that make this impossible to play after 3 are with the controls, combat, and linear feeling of the game. There are plenty of areas you wish you can go that you cannot. Plenty areas are "walled" off by nature or objects. Additionally, you feel like you are almost stuck on one path even at times where there are multiple directions present.
Controls... let me say, Witcher 3 even had some tough controls at the time of release. They went back and patched it adding an easier to move feel to Geralt that you can toggle on. Obviously Witcher 2 is absent of this and the controls are ROUGH. There are plenty of times where I feel like he isn't going where I tell him, and then in combat, forget it. The dodges feel wonky and not all that smooth. The camera can go crazy and sometimes you get lost with your view. I honestly felt like I was struggling more with the controls than having a good time just exploring for the most part.
With that said, I got a few hours in an gave up on it. Honestly, it had decent acting for it's time, and everything about it seemed solid, but obviously a few steps behind what they accomplished in the Witcher 3. So for now, I would not recommend it to those going back to Witcher 2 from 3. HOWEVER if you haven't played Witcher 3 yet, and have TONS of time to spare, go for it. Experience Witcher 2 and consider it a SMALL taste of what you are about to experience when you step up to 3.

I used to want to wait until games released to review them; but with games staying in EA longer and longer, and going on sale during, friends keep on asking me if a game is worth it. So here we are.
The Wild Eight is a co-op survival game where you play one of eight characters (each having a different strength), who have survived a plane crash in a snow-filled forest. You can play in single player perfectly adequately, or play with a group to survive and explore together. It focuses on exploration and survival (food, water, temperature and monsters), with a small amount of building (just a couple of set items) and crafting. Whilst the world and the items are quite limited at the moment, it really excels in atmosphere and some of the indoor locations are fantastic. Creepy, interesting and surprising in some ways - I'm not putting any spoilers here though! There is a quest system, but the game can be played fairly openly, you're not obligated to follow the order directed at all.
I was one of the 1200 folks to back this game on Kickstarter and I was pretty sad it didn't make any of the stretch goals, and barely got through at all. Nothing I've kickstarted has released on time, and this game is no exception, with a kickstarter release date of Dec 2016 (EA keys were sent in Feb 2017). I was a little disappointed back in February, but the recent bunker update was fantastic. It has made some decent progress since that date, and to me, the existing game is now worth the money - with the promise of much more to come so I'm happy to recommend it.
It's a game that needs more - more items, more locations, more monsters - but I'm pleased with the core of this game, happy I supported it on Kickstarter and happy to recommend it.

Everytime I was overwhelmed and impressed with immerse story that takes you all around the world, all these well written characters, movie-like screenplay and captivating sound environment.

A solid RPG shoot and loot! It serves as an interesting counterpoint to BL2, in a lot of ways. BL2 felt bloated and in length, featuring a great number of zones that while aesthetically were very interesting and all unique were ground together into a fine bland mush by the unending grind of its dull plot, monotonous plot.  (That is, till a certain point into the story when things become urgent. That's the part of the game I always enjoy the most.)
This game seems to be a polar opposite in that it feels much much shorter, you could probably run through its main plot in 24 hours if you were determined enough. It also feels like a much faster game, the tutorial is streamlined and most missions once you get going are more engaging and open new areas quicker. On the downside, Almost all the zones are extremely empty and samey, with the exception of a few late game areas.
Difficulty wise it is also pretty backwards form BL2. In BL2, the game starts out at a reasonable difficulty, but the curve exponentially increases as you progress the plot, when you start the second playthrough you are almost certain to be destroyed very quickly, unless you got super lucky with rare drops. The pre-sequel feels the other way around, with a much more challenging early game due to lack of guns that quickly eases up as you move on. Deadlift was probably the most difficult boss for me, simply because I was still using my lv.1 tutorial guns at the time.
The humor falls a LITTLE flatter, it didn't bother me much. Characters are a little more serious and story focused, which I enjoyed. I really enjoyed the accents, but I can understand why that wouldn't be for everyone.
All in all, while I would recommend this game on its own merits, your not getting nearly as much value out of it as you would get from BL2. I got it on sale for 15$, but I would be willing to shell about probably about 20-25$ for it, based off its length. Definately one to keep your eye on, but I wouldn't buy it at full price.

I've played all the borderlands games, this is easily the weakest one.  I would recommend it for one playthrough if you can buy it for super cheap or plan on playing with friends. This review is from a SOLO experience with two playthroughs.  I sampled several of the characters, but only really played extensively as the Jack doppleganger.  Here is my pros/cons list:
Pros:
- Low-G Butt-slamming
- Lasers (if you like that sort of weapon, I'm not a fan though)
- Ice weapons are fun
- I like the Grinder, but it becomes really annoying when you just start feeding in 3 good purple items only to get 1 in return of the same quality over and over (they should have made moonstones guarantee a better item, legendary, or luneshine weapon for purple)
Cons
- Boring side quests, very few are worth the time or reward
- The game's humor was really weak compared to BL1 and BL2.  Enough with all the Clap-trap jokes already... we get it, he's annoying and no-one likes him.  Stop beating a dead horse with a sledgehammer.
- The landscapes on this game have aweful layouts.  Also, they left out fast-travel stations in some areas, which makes no sense (examples... Veins of Helios, Regolith Range, Stantons Liver, etc.).  Be prepared to unnecessarily RUN a lot.
- I played through twice... and found the item rewards in-game were awful from actual quests/enemies/boxes. Almost all loot boxes give you crap (green, white, blue if you are lucky), which makes finding them not enjoyable. Maybe I'm just unlucky I dunno.  Maybe they did this to give more incentive to the moonstone-pay-loot-crates.  I dunno.
- I found the bosses incredibly easy, even on TVHM.  Maybe it was just my char build but I beat the first raid boss solo on my first try using Jack's doppleganger.  I beat the end boss on TVHM in about 2 minutes
- The DLC / season pass is likely not very worth it.  The Claptrap campaign add-on was somewhat interesting but I didn't care for the unpredictable Glitch weapons.
The best thing you can do for finding good loot is use SHIFT codes and then grind the purples you get from the gold chest to try for legendary weapons.  This worked pretty well for me.

I am the dominant power in the galaxy - The Children of Avarr. Though ostensibly a spiritual and diplomatic people, we are no strangers to war. When diplomacy has failed, I have been forced to use the stick, and thanks to my excellent aptitude for science we are more technoligically advanced than our peers. Our Federation contains the two other (lesser) major powers and together we have defeated 2 pre-cursor Fallen Empires who sought to exterminate us. Everything is going well. We have stared defeat in the eyes three times - two aggressive pre-cursor empires and one star eating leviathan. I should be coasting to victory...
Except...
The defeated pre-cursor empires, with their dangerous Jump Drive technology have ripped a hole in the fabric of space-time. Through that hole, The Unbidden have emerged. Inter-dimensional hunters, who seek only death. They opened the rift on the far side of the galaxy, well away from me. Before I can rally my fleets to close the portal, 10 huge fleets, the likes of which I had never seen have flooded into the area. They have swallowed two small empires already. They now chip away at my two major allies. I score victories, and have stolen their technology...but alone...I am not enough. Now, after everything I have been through - I think I am going to lose.
TL;DR - Rose to power and controlled much of the galaxy, rest of the galaxy were my friends and allies. Final enemy ripped a hole in space-time. Endless hordes of hungry extra-dimensional beings will now undo everything I have achieved. 10/10 would play again.
If you read the story above, that is but a taste of the true storytelling potential in Stellaris. It's a fantastic sci-fi experience. If you're a fan of other Paradox titles, you will find a lot to relish here. Though it has its own twists. Hearts Of Iron, Crusader Kings and Europa Universalis deal with real history. In Stellaris, you'll be creating your own, charting new areas of space and guiding a species of your own creation. It's also a much more "accessible" game than other Paradox titles, and does a pretty good job of teaching you its mechanics as you play.
If you're also a fan of Civilization, Endless Legend, Endless Space, Master of Orion etc. you will find a lot to love here.
Give Stellaris a try if you enjoy creating your own story/head-canon, you love sci-fi, and you want a strategy game that will last you a good while. So far I've put 50+ hours in, and have no plans to stop!

I'm a big sci-fi fan and I've been stung on a few 4x space rts titles in the past, so I was really excited when I saw Paradox launch one.  Big Paradox fan since Mount & Blade.
On the upside, the game looks good and runs well.  When I combat opponents, I can feel the push and pull between me and the game as it tries to find weaknesses in my strategies.  The race customization options, both at the start and during the course of play, are fun.  Overall, the title is promising.
On the downside, I've played through seven different games over 200 hours of gameplay and all but the last came to a statemate.  I develop my empire's military strength and manage diplomatic relations, and each time my npc allies waffle right before my npc enemies zerg.  In this last campaign, I managed to fly under the radar of all the other pc races, built up my empire strength and technology until I'm just about to peek out into the universe...  then the game suddenly decides that my empire is due for a revolt that instantly spawns invading troups on every one of almost a dozen worlds and a fleet three times everything I've got.  It was like the game saw I was doing well and spontaneously created an unwinable game event.
Between the fun I had when I was doing well and the disappointment I felt for seemingly impossible odds, my Stellaris experience feels like a wash.  I wish I spent those 200 hours playing a game that was more fun.

I'll start off with the negative: The game is very much incomplete right now. There's placeholder text in areas and some of the challenges don't work properly. In addition, the CCIP / bombsight does not work at all, and GBU's often won't land where they're supposed to, There's also major problems with volume on certain sounds (lock tone is a big one), and the sound effects in general are fairly dull at the moment.
With that out of the way, Vector Thrust is already incredibly fun to play, and the AOA limiter feature is great, even if it's not supposed to be available on all aircraft. Textures are currently very muddy (think PS2-style), but the aircraft are gorgeously rendered in that cel shaded style. The music is pretty generic but also not bad; I'd put it about on the same level as Ace Combat X2's music production value. In the game, there are currently a number of very interesting variations and experimental versions of each of the aircraft available, and while it's obviously not finished yet, the progression in unlocking these feels natural.
With the extensive modding support already being taken advantage of on ModDB, I can't wait to see what can be added to the game. Campaigns in particular are something that offers a limitless amount of user-generated content within the game's engine while remaining fairly accessible.
If you're a fan of Ace Combat or similar games, definitely give Vector Thrust a go. Now. If not, wait til it's not quite as rough and then give it a go. It's a ton of fun either way.

These games are really good.  The X series is a slow burn of space exploration, dogfighting, trading, and slowly clawing your way up from an insignificant speck in a vast and uncaring universe.  It's about having an impact on the world around you, forging your own path.  You could think of it like a single-player EVE Online, but without arbitrary time-based barriers to fun, and without the hassle of MMO bullcrap mitigating your own skill as a player.  X3: Terran Conflict was easily the best entry in the series, and Albion Prelude expands upon it with some much-needed features and fixes.
There's new ships and ship types, new sectors, some old sectors have had ownership rearrangements, and there's now an ongoing war between Terrans and the rest of the universe that you can partake in, as well as a functioning stock market.  Though, there's only one main storyline now, and playing as Terran locks you out of it.  And the loading times feel longer to me than they did in Terran Conflict.
But all of this pales in comparison to the single greatest fix in the series: battles that take place when you're not in the sector are now more accurately simulated, so that their results are more like what would've happened if you were there watching it.  Due to weird AI quirks and calculations made in previous iterations of X3, if your stuff was getting attacked, and you weren't there to watch the battle happen, your♥♥♥♥♥♥would just get wiped out 90% of the time.  Now, you actually have a chance.  This alone makes it worth grabbing AP if you play TC.
Anyway, go in expecting to put hundreds of hours into a single save file, and you'll have a blast.

The only reason I'd not recommend this game, is that Steam doesn't give a "lukewarm" option.
This game advertises itself as a super-customizable TPS, but the customization is still somewhat limmited in comparison with some other games advertising the same thing. The weapon options are unlocked in a manner that doesn't allow for the reasonably quick development of any particular play style, and the character unlocks (clothing, hair-dos, etc.) are only purchasable through real world monetary transactions. If you don't like "double currency" systems or "free-mium" games (games that are free, but rely on DLC and near-required in game purchaseable content to make sales), then this game probably isn't for you.
On top of all else, it's just kinda boring. There's not very many maps, and the available game modes are somewhat creative, but they're too easy and repetitive. It feels like the same match every time.
However, if you take it for what it is, it's totally worth the price :D. The graphics are good (I particularly like the weapon design), and I haven't encountered any performance issues (and I even have a really bad PC for gaming).

Think to Die is in Early Access at best and needs a lot more work before it can be considered finished. For a physics-based puzzle platformer, the physics are just too glitchy to make any puzzle work reliably. Puzzle difficulty is all over the place with very easy puzzles following extremely hard ones. The same can be said about the visuals. Whether or not I recommend this game is something of a complex question. I think that it depends on the type of gamer and the type of game you are looking for. Let me get this out of the way right now: X3 Terran Conflict and X3 Albion Prelude are NOT simple games. They do not provide a comprehensive tutorial and fail to explain a large amount of the basic strategies that a player should know in order to enjoy the game. You'll have to go to the forums for that, and you will find a mixed bag of documentation. Some of it is really good, and very helpful, but some of it is just not. If you are a casual gamer looking for something fun to pick up and play, this is not a game for you. In that same vein, this game is also really, really slow. If you're the kind of person who would like to simply just blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up and have a lot of fun action, you're also going to be sorely disappointed. X3:TC and X3:AP both suffer from the same issue: They want to include a lot of different features. This means that although combat works, and is fun, and there are a lot of good weapons, missiles and ship platforms available, it is sparse, and also tends to be annoying with the AI's tendency to crash player-owned ships into one another.
I do give this game a recommendation, however, as the other aspects of the game more than make up for the issues I have listed. Yes, the game is complex and difficult to understand, but that complexity brings in a high degree of control over player-owned assets, such as commanding ships as to how low their shields should be before they jump away from a fight, or setting the likely-hood of a ship launching any missiles that have been installed on-board. Weapons can be swapped out, and most of them are side-grades and depend on the role you are attempting to fill. The universe really does feel varied with several distinct different races to gain reputation with and buy their faction-specific ships. The plot is a bit thin and the voice acting is laughably bad, but personally it doesn't upset me too much when a sandbox game doesn't have a strong plot. Games such as Minecraft and Terraria have even less of a plot than this game.
It did take me an hour or two to figure out good strategies for fighting and trading, and quite a few trips to the forums, but eventually the game opens up and becomes actually enjoyable, and it allows you to be nearly whatever you want. Unfortunately, although the game allows for a "custom start" option, short of downloading X3 Editor 2 and manually editing the game's files to add a new game start, there is no way to have a truly customized start, which is disappointing.
In the most basic sense: Yes, this game is fun, if you are willing to put the time in to understand it. It is solidly made, most things make sense in it and although it has flaws, they are easy to ignore.

TL;DR at the end.
Disgaea 1 was a fantastic game, truly unique and original, with an okay storyline, great humor and fantastic, if grind-heavy, SRPG gameplay. Disgaea 2, in my opinion, is everything great about D1, only even better. D2 streamlines the gameplay, adds to the character roster, and has an upbeat, halloween/carnival-esque atmosphere.
Where D2 truly shines, however, is in the story and characters. In D1, while I loved Laharl, Etna, Flonne and the gang, the story was moving and poignant only up until the Red Moon Arc... then I felt the writers stopped trying. D1 took the silliness too far, and in the later third the story descended into flat jokes, monotony and bad characters (The entire Gordon and Earth arcs are garbage, and the final act is meh). The game was a parody of sorts, but it was rarely laugh out loud funny, so when the plot lapsed and the humor continued, it all collapsed. D2 however, places the humor where it belongs; peppered throughout, but not the main point (with the exception of Axel Mode, but I barely consider that part of the game). With plenty of humor and funny moments, the main story is compelling and the characters are moving and well written, and that puts this game in the upper echelon of RPGs in my book.
TL;DR: Recommended for its great use of humor and characters, superior story to the first game, and polished gameplay. Worth it even at full price.

I love strategy games, from the first time I played Shogun Total War 15 years ago, to my late discovery of EUIV a few scant months before Stellaris came out, and the plethora of classics in between...so you can see I have extensive experience with the genre.
Stellaris is a fantastic addition to that long line of titles, allowing you to build a formidable galactic empire that would make Palpatine blush, or nurture a federation that would make Jean-luc proud.
The race creation system is a gem, providing a lovely selection of anthropomorphised mammals, molluscs, fungi or avians - to name a few - before tweaking and toying with their minds to find the personality of your society. Would you like to create a race of enlightened, pacifistic fox scientists? Or would you prefer to stalk the galaxy with a bloodthirsty, militiristic xenomorph hive?
With that being said - there are issues with the game. At 6 months old, it has recieved 3 large patches that have made headway in fixing some of these, but the job is far from complete. Altough you could argue it will never be perfect - every developer knows, for every bug you kill, 5 more will take its place.
But is it worth £35? Absolutely. Get it, get hooked, and enjoy the vast amount of hours you will likely fritter away with your interplanetary commune of hippy space mushrooms.
