A solid RPG shoot and loot! It serves as an interesting counterpoint to BL2, in a lot of ways. BL2 felt bloated and in length, featuring a great number of zones that while aesthetically were very interesting and all unique were ground together into a fine bland mush by the unending grind of its dull plot, monotonous plot.  (That is, till a certain point into the story when things become urgent. That's the part of the game I always enjoy the most.)
This game seems to be a polar opposite in that it feels much much shorter, you could probably run through its main plot in 24 hours if you were determined enough. It also feels like a much faster game, the tutorial is streamlined and most missions once you get going are more engaging and open new areas quicker. On the downside, Almost all the zones are extremely empty and samey, with the exception of a few late game areas.
Difficulty wise it is also pretty backwards form BL2. In BL2, the game starts out at a reasonable difficulty, but the curve exponentially increases as you progress the plot, when you start the second playthrough you are almost certain to be destroyed very quickly, unless you got super lucky with rare drops. The pre-sequel feels the other way around, with a much more challenging early game due to lack of guns that quickly eases up as you move on. Deadlift was probably the most difficult boss for me, simply because I was still using my lv.1 tutorial guns at the time.
The humor falls a LITTLE flatter, it didn't bother me much. Characters are a little more serious and story focused, which I enjoyed. I really enjoyed the accents, but I can understand why that wouldn't be for everyone.
All in all, while I would recommend this game on its own merits, your not getting nearly as much value out of it as you would get from BL2. I got it on sale for 15$, but I would be willing to shell about probably about 20-25$ for it, based off its length. Definately one to keep your eye on, but I wouldn't buy it at full price.

The Night of the Rabbit is a splendid point-and-click adventure. The storytelling, aesthetics, and puzzle-centric gameplay are all somewhere between solid and outstanding. In all, it's like playing through a really good children's book, complete with lovable characters, sinister villains, and some surprisingly complex moral lessons.
Right off the bat, when you start playing this game, you will notice one of the game's biggest strengths--the lovely visuals. The Night of the Rabbit is simply beautiful. And even though each screen features a tremendous amount of detail, the game's various areas never seem cluttered. Important points of interest, such as items to pick up and tools to manipulate, are subtly and effectively foregrounded so that most (but not all) will draw your notice quickly as you explore new places.
The gorgeous environments go a long way toward shaping this game's effective atmosphere, as does its stellar music. Just listen to the title music at some point--it's lovely, evocative, and downright moving. Regardless of where you are in the game, you will be tempted to slow down and simply look and listen. The orchestrations usually focus on one or two instruments (such as fiddle, flute, or xylophone), and the music definitely carries a live-recorded vibe.
But while the game's visuals and atmosphere might be impressive, the game's single greatest strength is in its splendid cast of characters. It's hard to describe, but each and every character truly belongs in this game. Many of the characters can come off as a little one-dimensional at first, but as the game goes on, those same characters receive much greater depth and complexity in most cases (such as Steinberg the dwarf, the Little Man in the Green Hat, and the ornery hare patriarch). The game's cast of rounded, interesting characters even extends to its main villains and heroes. Jerry Hazelnut is not a simple character a la Link from the old Legend of Zelda games. And neither is his mentor, the Marquis de Hoto (and title rabbit)--or his eventual enemies.
The game also features excellent voice acting, which helps deepen the portrayal of the broad and varied cast of characters. Although there are a few oddly read lines here and there, and the subtitle text sometimes differs slightly from the spoken dialogue, the voice acting in this game is really well done overall. The voices for the different characters are as unique and interesting as they are, and the voices blend well into the fabric of the game's world and sense of storytelling. I can't imagine playing this game without listening to the characters' voices.
No point-and-click adventure can succeed without a top-shelf story, and The Night of the Rabbit definitely delivers the goods in this area. The story is rich and interesting, although the overarching plot can get a little confusing at times. This is one of those games that constantly promises that "all will be explained in time," and while most of the game's action doesn't depend on the purposefully obscure plotlines for meaning, it can still seem a little overbearing to go through so much of the game without understanding what is happening on a meta level. You don't even get a clear sense of who the bad guys are or might be until about halfway through the game.
In addition, the game is a little heavy on the front and back ends. There are too many layers of framing around the game in the beginning, and while the game does a nice job of integrating its tutorial so that it doesn't seem completely like a pointless exercise, you will wish the game would just step aside and let you play at first. The game's ending, too, features a lot of text and a lot of story exposition--mostly because the makers of the game save so much of the villains' backstory and motivation for the final sequences.
Nevertheless, The Night of the Rabbit's story somehow manages to live up to its lofty promises. By the end of the game, you really do feel as though you understand all the vagueries the game plagued you with earlier. The roles of the mysterious characters, the identity and purpose of the villains, and your role in bringing a peaceful resolution all come clearly into light at the game's conclusion. That said, I'd say the story's greatest strength is that it doesn't rap up every loose end or explain away every detail. Some characters who are in need at the game's outset are still in need at the game's end. Your actions don't solve every single problem in the game's world--they just show how so many problems can be dealt with through the power of community, friendship, and selflessness.
As a point-and-click adventure, this game requires a methodical approach. If you look everywhere and pay close attention to the game's visual details and textual clues, you can probably progress pretty smoothly. Most of the game's puzzles are highly intuitive, if you can remember which items you have and what the game's context clues suggested those items might be used for. The few times I checked a walkthrough for help, it always turned out that I was on the right track, and it was just the method I was messing up. That is a slight problem though--sometimes you can't easily figure out how to complete puzzles even though you know you're holding the right materials. A few puzzles are a little finicky or require an unintuitive arrangement of steps to complete.
Furthermore, the game's richest gameplay segments come at the beginning and middle. As the game goes on, and you finish exploring the core areas of the world, the game becomes much more linear. Once you reach the point where the game is introducing one new area at a time, you are likely done with the game's most interesting puzzles. Still, the end game's new areas and characters are just as fascinating as those from earlier in the game--and sometimes even more so.
The gameplay also struggles with some pacing issues. Jerry just kind of meanders from place to place regardless of plot context, and there are awkwardly long pauses between many lines of dialogue. The farther you get into the game, the more rough-around-the-edges the animations and loaded events (like subtitles/dialogue) get. But overall, if you can adapt to the game's slow-ish pace, your experience will be that much richer for it.
So yeah, The Night of the Rabbit is essentially an interactive storybook--a good story told by a masterful storyteller. It's lovely, it's deep, and it carries a surprisingly mature message: avoid humanity's darker instincts for selfishness and greed, learn to live peacefully with your friends and neighbors, and nothing is impossible.

Might be one of the best games I've ever played. Literally everything about the game itself is pretty good at WORST.
The game throws you into an incredibly rich and thought provoking world but still never lets you feel out of your depth if it's your first game in the series as it was mine. Prior story knowledge enhances the experience but is not requred, the right way to do a sequel of this kind. The themes this game deals with in its story are some that are not usually approached in such detail by video games of this scale.  I would assume that's because examining the rights of artificial life, humanity's predisposition for self destruction and trying to fathom why things are, can get really, really depressing.  And this game does get very depressing, but I would chalk that up as a gigantic positive that a game engaged me on that emotional level. The best thing though is that Nier: Automata doesn't just ask the hard existential questions, if you play through the whole of the 5 main endings it offers some pretty compelling food for thought in terms of possible answers too.
The game also presents dilemmas to you in ways that you may not expect.  Basic "choices" you make when playing any game, such as simply attacking an enemy, are given significantly more weight when you have the proper context applied. Each of the main characters in the story and several of the supporting ones also undergo a sometimes short but distinct arc which is a breath of fresh air coming off of some more recent RPGs where the main character basically learns that you have to be responsible, the supporting cast never change and that's it *cough*FFXV*cough*.  It took just the right moves to get me invested in just about every important character in the game.
The soundtrack is sublime. Start to finish the music is a powerful, subtle joy to hear. Some great soundtracks just steal the show so all you think about after is the music; personally I thought it just felt like every single song was more a great accompaniment to whatever moment it was layed gently on top of.
The combat wasn't as complex as I'd have liked.  I would have much preferred a little more depth to combo/defensive systems such as in Bayonetta, but it was still incredibly fun, responsive and visceral.  Even the shmup sections were a lot of fun.  Almost all of them struck the correct balance between challenge and frustration, and on top of that they never outstayed their welcome.
I don't think people give the level design enough credit either.  I personally found the open world in this game maybe one of the best in recent years.  It is subject to changes, sometimes minor, sometimes major, it has a large variety of settings with different enemies, music and a lot of the time playstyles and towards the end of the game I was still finding new areas I hadn't been in before and little tucked away secrets. The "collectibles" are also very rewarding.  Hacking open a chest is almost never a waste of time.  You can get anything from a report detailing important and well written lore or a new weapon to test out.
Aside from a few weird technical issues where the game would randomly lose focus on my PC to nothing at all on my 2nd monitor, the mouse not being locked to the screen in game and it popping itself back into windowed mode every time I Alt+Tabbed the port was pretty solid in terms of framerate etc.  The graphical fidelity is the one area where I wasn't simply blown away.  I mean the game aesthetically looks amazing, but in terms of texture quality and graphical effects it's not very impressive at all. On several occasions usually when a character is silhouetted against a bright light, they turn into an 8-bit version of themselves and transform into blocks around the edges.
That's easily overlooked in favour of the numerous other plus points though. A must play for anybody who enjoys Platinum combat, likes actually thinking while playing a game or if you just want to experience some of Yoko Taro's own brand of insanity!

I am the dominant power in the galaxy - The Children of Avarr. Though ostensibly a spiritual and diplomatic people, we are no strangers to war. When diplomacy has failed, I have been forced to use the stick, and thanks to my excellent aptitude for science we are more technoligically advanced than our peers. Our Federation contains the two other (lesser) major powers and together we have defeated 2 pre-cursor Fallen Empires who sought to exterminate us. Everything is going well. We have stared defeat in the eyes three times - two aggressive pre-cursor empires and one star eating leviathan. I should be coasting to victory...
Except...
The defeated pre-cursor empires, with their dangerous Jump Drive technology have ripped a hole in the fabric of space-time. Through that hole, The Unbidden have emerged. Inter-dimensional hunters, who seek only death. They opened the rift on the far side of the galaxy, well away from me. Before I can rally my fleets to close the portal, 10 huge fleets, the likes of which I had never seen have flooded into the area. They have swallowed two small empires already. They now chip away at my two major allies. I score victories, and have stolen their technology...but alone...I am not enough. Now, after everything I have been through - I think I am going to lose.
TL;DR - Rose to power and controlled much of the galaxy, rest of the galaxy were my friends and allies. Final enemy ripped a hole in space-time. Endless hordes of hungry extra-dimensional beings will now undo everything I have achieved. 10/10 would play again.
If you read the story above, that is but a taste of the true storytelling potential in Stellaris. It's a fantastic sci-fi experience. If you're a fan of other Paradox titles, you will find a lot to relish here. Though it has its own twists. Hearts Of Iron, Crusader Kings and Europa Universalis deal with real history. In Stellaris, you'll be creating your own, charting new areas of space and guiding a species of your own creation. It's also a much more "accessible" game than other Paradox titles, and does a pretty good job of teaching you its mechanics as you play.
If you're also a fan of Civilization, Endless Legend, Endless Space, Master of Orion etc. you will find a lot to love here.
Give Stellaris a try if you enjoy creating your own story/head-canon, you love sci-fi, and you want a strategy game that will last you a good while. So far I've put 50+ hours in, and have no plans to stop!

Taking cues from LucasArts' reign as top dog of the point-and-click adventure genre, Daedalic Entertainment seems to get better and better at creating worlds and stories that stand tall on their own, despite being inspired by classic tales we all know, and most of us love. If I were to describe Night of the Rabbit as X meets Y, I would say it's half Alice in Wonderland, half Wind in the Willows, which basically makes it a children-oriented fairy tale with furries and outlandish characters demonstrating thinly veiled moral points. Join Jeremiah Hazelnut in a quest to become a magician while also learning the importance of staying level-headed against adversity. Most of the game takes place in and around Mousewood, a pitoresque society of assorted small animals, and while at times the story turns a bit campy and preachy, it is, for the most part, an enchanting journey for children of all ages. In terms of quality and production value, the hand-drawn style fits the setting perfectly, the voice acting and music are more than adequate and the rich content (achievements, collectibles, side stories and a Go Fish-type card game) adds a layer of pixel-hunting to the otherwise simple puzzles. Although I detect a certain oscillation in the writing and animation quality (at times, tNotR feels more like an homage to LucasArts than a spiritual successor), I would definitely recommend this to anyone with a weak spot for fairy tales and puzzle solving, perhaps doubly so as an introduction game to the genre.
BUY IT if you:
-Are a child, either literally or at heart, and would rather curl up with an A.A. Milne book in front of a fireplace than join a gang and wack pigs in South Central.
-Enjoy lightweight adventure games and intuitive inventory puzzles.
-Are a fan of Daedalic Entertainment and the highly derivative but otherwise funny and enjoyable Deponia series.
DO NOT BUY IT if you:
-Want mature content in your entertainment or expect any kind of deep or complicated plotline to keep your juices flowing.
-Are a hardcore point-and-click adventure fan and are sick of all those "combine tuft of hair with stick to obtain brush and then use on an obvious brush-lacking trigger prop" newbie puzzles.
-Find the ten or so hours of raw gameplay unsatisfactory for whatever price it is at the time of purchase.

At time of writing this game is in EARLY ACCESS.
The campaign missions are there, but there is no story yet. The challenge mode is not yet finished with many challenges needing to be fixed / implemented properly. There's a minor bug where the lead indicator disappears occasionally, and the targeting system badly needs a revamp.
HOWEVER.
This game has earned my full support at this time. I am rather strict about my standards for flight games. Everything, every single one gets put up against Freespace 2, because that was my first. If you look through my reviews, I blasted Strike Suit Zero, because it is utter garbage.
This game is for lack of a better descriptor an "Ace Combat clone". That's a damn good thing. The only AC to come to PC has been that godawful Assault Horizon. This game is similar to Ace combat in basic arcade format gameplay, and it has all the basic features like radar, lots of missiles, etc. We've not had something like that to go to on PC, and now we do. It's not as hardcore as FS2 or Arma or Flaming Cliffs, but it's a good game for what it is.
The core gameplay is very solid. The cannon is actually useful, missiles behave like missiles and require proper use instead of spam, AOA limit release makes for more interesting dogfights. The primary mode people play right now is Skirmish mode, which has these incredible mutators. It's got 00 Gundam's Trans-am in "overdrive", it's got basic mutators like guns only, it's got an Itano Circus mutator, it's even got an "Eggplane" mode that SDs all the planes. It's like big head mode for a flight game, and big head mode has always cracked me up.
The game also advertises mod support. People have already produced new aircraft, and skins for existing aircraft, of course including idolm@s skins because I don't know how that caught on but I guess it's tradition now.
This game is still early access, and it's rather bare bones at the moment, but it's a damn good showing so far and if it's complete state lives up to the dev's promises, it'll be a great game, better than Ace Combat's recent showings for sure.

TL;DR at the end.
Disgaea 1 was a fantastic game, truly unique and original, with an okay storyline, great humor and fantastic, if grind-heavy, SRPG gameplay. Disgaea 2, in my opinion, is everything great about D1, only even better. D2 streamlines the gameplay, adds to the character roster, and has an upbeat, halloween/carnival-esque atmosphere.
Where D2 truly shines, however, is in the story and characters. In D1, while I loved Laharl, Etna, Flonne and the gang, the story was moving and poignant only up until the Red Moon Arc... then I felt the writers stopped trying. D1 took the silliness too far, and in the later third the story descended into flat jokes, monotony and bad characters (The entire Gordon and Earth arcs are garbage, and the final act is meh). The game was a parody of sorts, but it was rarely laugh out loud funny, so when the plot lapsed and the humor continued, it all collapsed. D2 however, places the humor where it belongs; peppered throughout, but not the main point (with the exception of Axel Mode, but I barely consider that part of the game). With plenty of humor and funny moments, the main story is compelling and the characters are moving and well written, and that puts this game in the upper echelon of RPGs in my book.
TL;DR: Recommended for its great use of humor and characters, superior story to the first game, and polished gameplay. Worth it even at full price.

There's a lot to love in the X universe, and I've dabbled with it since the first installment. The narrative is deep, has tons to discover and is stunning for a game of its age. Really, the game is bursting with promise - things to do, histories to uncover. Old hands will tell you it has a steep learning curve and this is true, but the curve is not around learning how to be good at the game, the curve is about learning how to *work around* the game.
First of all, for the starting player the game works hard to stop you from succeeding. Missions, traditionally the reserve of the new player in 4X games seeking to earn a few quid here and there, are almost universally impossible for a new player to complete. The game offers loads to you, but they are either too time limited to be possible in any beginner's ship, require more cargo storage than you can offer, or put you up against enemies leagues ahead in technology. The game makes no effort to help you figure out which missions are even possible for you and your capabilities. The old hands know this and only take combat missions with their super combat craft, but there is no possible way to know this for a new player.
So maybe you check out trading - a tedious but reliable way to make a living in 4X. Again the game stands in your way. For some bizarre reason, frequently you will find that the suppliers of goods have almost double the price that the customers will ever pay. The in-game economy is serving those demands through their own AI ships, etc, but there is very little room for the new player to make a slight profit without a lot of trial and error. Sometimes the prices jump without warning, leaving you stranded with a hold full of goods that you have no idea where you can sell. The vast variety of goods adds richness but it takes a lot of work to figure out where to sell.
You resort to online guides and figure out that the best way to make money is the stock exchange. This is absolutely true but in practice involves staring at a random number generator until it flips your way. The (corporate) stock exchange gives the illusion of realism but in practice is just nonsense.
After 17 hours of variously failing impossible missions, selling Argnu Beef at a loss, failing to find anywhere to sell Space Weed and finally making millions by staring at a number changing from 100 to 95, I realised the game is a false economy - the fun bits require just too much *actual work* to be of any value.
That said, you might enjoy it, and this relatively old game is certainly good value (I definitely got a few pence per hour out of it) but you have to be ready to spend most of a day of your life fighting the game, to try and get a glimpse of the heart.

Got into the game, started it up, but no matter what I tried to choose it would NOT let me use my added graphics card on the laptop. It made me choose my integrated card. Your choice, depends on if you have a good graphics card that's a bit older it may work fine. But a new one may not even pick up and it will use your integrated card and run like crap.
Story was good though, and the multiple choices to do things still made the game fun for the age it is... it's worth it, especially on sale.  Some really bad voice acting at times though. It seemed as if some characters(JC's brother) had used a cheap mic and recording software to get the voice.

Cons:
Risky if you have a newer computer GPU, it likely won't use it.

Magicka is one of my favorite games, and one of the few that does a good job making you feel like a wizard.
The Good:
The crown jewel of Magicka's design is its spell creation system.  It was not the first video game to allow you to design spells by selecting the path, area of effect, effects, and intensities.  The Elder Scrolls: Arena had that in 1994, and there may be earlier examples I don't know about.  It may be the first to allow you to create spells on the fly.  It is also noteworthy for having no limits based on a mana pool or cooldowns.  Instead, the main balancing forces are enemy resistances and the destructive power of your own spells.  It's very easy to make a mistake and kill yourself or your allies.
Magicka is also well known and loved for its voice acting.  Everyone speaks a mix of broken Swedish and jibberish.  Vlad is an over the top Romanian vampire in denial.  Death and Fafnir also sound great.  I would love to know what sort of processing they performed on their voices.
Magicka has one of the best soundtracks I've ever heard.  It's bombastic, complex, and memorable.  Unfortunately it may be hard to appreciate with it often being drowned out by the sounds of the chaos around you.
The Bad:
Magicka is very buggy, even by modern PC gaming standards.  Crashes and hangs are common.  Weapons and staves, which may be unique, frequently clip through the map and disappear into the void forever.  Players lose connection in online games often.  The DLC is even worse.

Difficulty does not scale based on the number of players.  The main game isn't that difficult to get through solo, but some of the DLC is very hard without a full party.  I found the final fights in

Flying technomages in a psuedo WW1 setting.
Animation.  Excellent and interesting character designes, fantasic action and battle sequences with a nicely polished and detailed world, barring a few very minor hiccups when CGI is used that are barely noticable.
Sound.  Adequate effects that bring the action to life, mostly forgettable musical score but I love that title theme!
Characters and plot.  Given the nature of the subject matter, an alternate reality version of WW1 ,it is handled realistically but tastefully, or at least as realistic as flying , spell flinging mages can be, with subtle but not glaring or in your face references  to certain organizations present at the time. There are also some religious themes , but they are used to further the plot and character development rather than being rammed down your throat one way or the other.
It's all fairly believable and appropriately thematic ( as insane as it is) and just unique enough to stand apart from being a dedicated 'war' series.  Every single main and supporting character here stands out. Each one is likable or memorable in some way but almost all dwell in a foggy grey area where you can find yourself booing the heroes and cheering for the villians at a moments notice.
The main protagonist/antagonist (depending on your view) is a delightfull little psychopath who happens to be far too clever for her own good.  There's good focus on interpersonal relationships and motivations between characters across a whole theatre of warfare and even minor supporting characters have distinct personalities.
My only gripe with the entire series is an almost throwaway , wasted potential recap episode half way through to pad out the series length.
Apart from that I would reccomend this in a hearbeat to anyone not put off by the WW1 style setting. Excellent viewing.

Might be one of the best games I've ever played. Literally everything about the game itself is pretty good at WORST.
The game throws you into an incredibly rich and thought provoking world but still never lets you feel out of your depth if it's your first game in the series as it was mine. Prior story knowledge enhances the experience but is not requred, the right way to do a sequel of this kind. The themes this game deals with in its story are some that are not usually approached in such detail by video games of this scale.  I would assume that's because examining the rights of artificial life, humanity's predisposition for self destruction and trying to fathom why things are, can get really, really depressing.  And this game does get very depressing, but I would chalk that up as a gigantic positive that a game engaged me on that emotional level. The best thing though is that Nier: Automata doesn't just ask the hard existential questions, if you play through the whole of the 5 main endings it offers some pretty compelling food for thought in terms of possible answers too.
The game also presents dilemmas to you in ways that you may not expect.  Basic "choices" you make when playing any game, such as simply attacking an enemy, are given significantly more weight when you have the proper context applied. Each of the main characters in the story and several of the supporting ones also undergo a sometimes short but distinct arc which is a breath of fresh air coming off of some more recent RPGs where the main character basically learns that you have to be responsible, the supporting cast never change and that's it *cough*FFXV*cough*.  It took just the right moves to get me invested in just about every important character in the game.
The soundtrack is sublime. Start to finish the music is a powerful, subtle joy to hear. Some great soundtracks just steal the show so all you think about after is the music; personally I thought it just felt like every single song was more a great accompaniment to whatever moment it was layed gently on top of.
The combat wasn't as complex as I'd have liked.  I would have much preferred a little more depth to combo/defensive systems such as in Bayonetta, but it was still incredibly fun, responsive and visceral.  Even the shmup sections were a lot of fun.  Almost all of them struck the correct balance between challenge and frustration, and on top of that they never outstayed their welcome.
I don't think people give the level design enough credit either.  I personally found the open world in this game maybe one of the best in recent years.  It is subject to changes, sometimes minor, sometimes major, it has a large variety of settings with different enemies, music and a lot of the time playstyles and towards the end of the game I was still finding new areas I hadn't been in before and little tucked away secrets. The "collectibles" are also very rewarding.  Hacking open a chest is almost never a waste of time.  You can get anything from a report detailing important and well written lore or a new weapon to test out.
Aside from a few weird technical issues where the game would randomly lose focus on my PC to nothing at all on my 2nd monitor, the mouse not being locked to the screen in game and it popping itself back into windowed mode every time I Alt+Tabbed the port was pretty solid in terms of framerate etc.  The graphical fidelity is the one area where I wasn't simply blown away.  I mean the game aesthetically looks amazing, but in terms of texture quality and graphical effects it's not very impressive at all. On several occasions usually when a character is silhouetted against a bright light, they turn into an 8-bit version of themselves and transform into blocks around the edges.
That's easily overlooked in favour of the numerous other plus points though. A must play for anybody who enjoys Platinum combat, likes actually thinking while playing a game or if you just want to experience some of Yoko Taro's own brand of insanity!

Quick summary: A strange, adult VN that is somehow more than the sum of its parts
(No spoilers review)
So here we have Crystal City, a quirky, apparently russian VN that first showed up on Nutaku, with all the erotic content that implies; barely censored on Steam, even without a patch.
6/10
First thing you'll notice about this VN is that the menus look worse than your average RPG Maker game; really, it's that bad. Backgrounds are rather simplistic as well, though diverse enough it's not much of a problem. Character sprites and CGs are quite easy on the eyes, on the other hand, and maintain a consistent style throughout, so the overall impression is still pretty good.
6/10
There's no voice acting whatsoever, as could be expected from a small indie VN, but the music is unobtrusive, sets the mood accordingly and never grows tiresome; in fact, I liked it enough to buy it. Then again, it was less than 50 cents.
7/10
So... Nutaku, adult-oriented, indie VN; I can already hear the warning bells in your head. But fortunately such fears are unfounded: though sexuality does play an important role in the narrative, the main focus is on the sci-fi setting and does so quite well, with a tale that's gripping thoughout and non-stereotypical characters carrying some very humane flaws. Even the sex is well justified, always serving some purpose within the story besides mere fanservice.
Unfortunately, one aspect that does follow the usual stereotype is the game's translation, which is very rough; it's not too problematic, but there's some weird phrases here and there. And for a less stereotypical flaw, the plot also pauses in the middle for an adventure-like minigame far too weird even for this novel's standards; fortunately it can be skipped, affecting nothing at all.
2/10
It's a kinetic novel, with no choices whatsoever, and it took me around 2.5 hours total to finish; not exactly a long read. But its pacing is quite good, and the ending is satisfying while simultaneously keeping enough plot threads hanging for a sequel, so I do see myself re-reading the novel at least one more time.
What can I say? simple graphics, no voice acting, rough translation and short length; it doesn't sound like the most enticing VN out there. Yet I loved it; the story's uniqueness, its excellent pacing, lovely CGs and well-rounded characters won me over. Fully recomended, and eagerly awaiting a sequel.

I love strategy games, from the first time I played Shogun Total War 15 years ago, to my late discovery of EUIV a few scant months before Stellaris came out, and the plethora of classics in between...so you can see I have extensive experience with the genre.
Stellaris is a fantastic addition to that long line of titles, allowing you to build a formidable galactic empire that would make Palpatine blush, or nurture a federation that would make Jean-luc proud.
The race creation system is a gem, providing a lovely selection of anthropomorphised mammals, molluscs, fungi or avians - to name a few - before tweaking and toying with their minds to find the personality of your society. Would you like to create a race of enlightened, pacifistic fox scientists? Or would you prefer to stalk the galaxy with a bloodthirsty, militiristic xenomorph hive?
With that being said - there are issues with the game. At 6 months old, it has recieved 3 large patches that have made headway in fixing some of these, but the job is far from complete. Altough you could argue it will never be perfect - every developer knows, for every bug you kill, 5 more will take its place.
But is it worth £35? Absolutely. Get it, get hooked, and enjoy the vast amount of hours you will likely fritter away with your interplanetary commune of hippy space mushrooms.

First of all I state that I bought this game because I liked it when Gronkh played this on Twitch.
This game is about a person who doesn't get sleep and so goes to different parties to kill dozens of people. You can kill them with your knife and with traps. Since there are always different traps and different people each time you start a level, the levels are never the same. So if you play the one and the same level the difficulty varies depending on the items you get, the number of bouncers in the level (who will bust you if you are not careful) and the number and sort of traps you get.
Stabbing people is pretty straight forward, of course you have to be sure that no one sees you or your knife is faster than their legs.
There are many sorts of traps, like poisoning the food, making a horse kick people to death, burning ppl in a stove, etc. If you kill ppl with a trap it will be considered as accident and not murderer even if you push them off a roof (Oh my, that wasn't on purpose). Only exception is poisoning if a poisoned person dies near you, you will be considered the murderer, though this can happen to other NPCs as well. Ppl standing near dead ppl are always considered murderer, even if they didn't do anything (like in real life).
In the levels you can different item. Their use vary. You can have spare clothes so you can change your appearance if you were seen red handed, so the police won't recognize you. With a smoke grenade you can kill people within the smoke without being seen. There is a katana to chop humans in little pieces.
And there are events. like a sharknado when sharks are raining on the party and start to eat the party people. Sometimes there are dancing bears going wild and looking for tasty young teens. You can make phone calls and different things happen, like fast food delivery so the party guests come out of the VIP section, Bikers appear and beat the crap out of everyone, etc.
The time a level takes depends on the way you are playing. If you don't want to be seen and hide every corpse you produce, it can take quite some time to beat a level, like 30 minutes, depending if the party guest are going in a lone corner or stay on the dance floor. If you use traps and kill 2-3 people in a row it takes about half the time. Normal gameplay is somewhere in between.
Oh, and in the game while carrying dead people is a no go, carrying drunk people is considered pretty normal (maybe the developer thinks for some people this is the only way to to literally pick someone up), so you can drag them to a dark and lonely place to introduce your knife to them. ^__^
If you are looking for a nice little game in which you can kill people in various and sometimes funny ways and like to play for short times, I can really recommend this game!

Summary: A good, item based point-and-click adventure game aimed at a younger audience. Nice story, setting and good voice-acting. Pacing problems, low puzzle variety, relatively tame humor and wasted opportunities prevents the game from being great. Still very much recommended, especially at a sale.
Full review: You play as Jeremiah Hazelnut, a young boy dreaming of becoming a wizard. When contacted by the mysterious Marque de Hotto, you jump at the chance to travel to mysterious places and learn magic. The story is overall good with a nice setting and some interesting characters. It seems to be aimed at a younger audience than me, however, with relatively toothless humor and tame villains. There are some darker parts to the game, but nothing worse than seen similar modern fairy tales for kids. The environmental message is nice, but perhaps a bit ham-fistedly told.
One problem is the pacing, which is a bit off. This game loves to hear itself talk to the point of overshadowing the gameplay. The endless exposition by the Marque at the early stages of the game bored my girlfriend to tears and I had to continue on my own. This continues to some degree throughout the game with dialogue being repeated a lot and taking just a little too long to skip when you are trying to see if a character has something new to say. An especially atrocious example of time-wasting is the fast-travel system which takes so much time to use it is generally more efficient just to double-click yourself scene by scene until you get where you want to go.
The puzzles are entirely item-based so if you’re looking for more puzzle-variety you’re not going to find it here. Even the spells you learn are essentially items and do not work together in any interesting ways. An example of wasted potential. As they are, the puzzles are mostly logical, but suffer from the same problems as other item based puzzle games. Additionally there are loads of red herrings in the game, with objects having no function, no function until much later in the game or having multiple interactive areas (for example tree and hole in the tree). This can lead to some frustration, especially if you’ve tried the item on the hole in the tree, but were given no indication that you were supposed to use it on the tree instead. There is usually no guidance or humor offered by the protagonist from using the wrong items either which is a shame.
To give some variety there are a fair bit of collectables, as well as a mini-card game and some additional audio books to listen to. Personally I found both the card-game and audio books rather dull, but it’s nice that they are there.
I mostly enjoyed my time with The Night of the Rabbit, but I could not shake the feeling there was a great deal of wasted potential. Perhaps it was because I’m not the age group it is aimed for, but the setting is so nice and some of the characters so interesting… it just seems like they could have done something more with it. It’s all very… tame. However, it is still a good game even if it is not great. So I do recommend it, but personally I would not buy it at full price (20 Euro atm).

Think To Die is a puzzle game in which your main goal is to kill your characters in order to progress. The concept, by itself, sounds cool, and the mechanics encountered through the game are quite interesting. However, the game feels poor in execution, at least in my opinion. As an example, some of the mechanics aren't well explained, leading to a lot of confusion in certain puzzles.
The art style is nice, but it can get in the way of some puzzles, obscuring the view or looking like certain parts aren't interactable. This game also has a fair amount of bugs, which can get annoying, as they force you to constantly restart a level until you get the appropriate result. However, it can work on your favour as well, as some glitches might kill your character in an easier way than what the puzzle required. The physics are also a bit wonky, which can get annoying in certain puzzles.
Well, I don't feel like saying much about this game. It was an easy 100%, and, as I said, it has an interesting idea behind, but it doesn't feel good enough to recommend it. I still wish I had a neutral option for reviews, but a thumbs down will have to work.

Even 4 years old this game is amazing.  It has phenomenal breadth, combat both fighter and capital ship level, trading at an individual level and (with the free bonus content) across the universe with trained merchants doing your bidding and complex factory and entire physical space factory complexes that feed the economy. There is a stock market that is a reflection of product and resource availability.  As others have suggested the learning curve can be intimidating.  Starting with just a handful of credits and a humble ship you can find the universe a very unforgiving place with massive ships and brutal pirates who won't think twice about crushing you.  This does make the achievement of your first  million something you really feel proud when you remember how you were scrapping for 500-1500 credit profit on your earliest of trading runs.  The graphics have held up well, good use of shadows, nice textures and the different races ships have their own specific sense of style.  There is no mistaking the organic influences of the Boron ships or the utilitarian blocky Split constructs.  Asside from the challenge of learning the game (not necessarily a criticism) there are a few minor gameplay issues that can annoy (autopilot AI will sometimes freakout and plow you into an asteroid or station) and the layout of complexes of factories can sometimes yield a nearly undockable (by AI controlled ships) end result.  Some careful planning and spending some time on youtube watching videos on how to avoid this helps a lot.  I bought this game on launch and keep coming back to it over the years. This is the game you're looking for if you have that jet fighter itch and don't have a PS2 to play Ace Combat 4. The controls feel nice and fleshed out for each plane to give each a pretty distinct feel. Some similarities are bound to occur since it has an arcadey feel, but overall you can feel what each jet can do the best with about 3 minutes of flying them. There's also some more complex controls that I haven't really used/figured out yet but they're all pretty simplified to access(using a 360 controller to play).
There are multiple game modes of which i've only played 2 so far. Quick missions is essentially a randomized assortment of DM/TDM matches as well as solo dog fights. Haven't had any ground attack missions so far since I like to fly fighters, but they might be in there. Campaign has a very similar start as AC4 did, although the story isn't exatly great so far compared to AC4. All I've gathered is that I'm a mercenary airman fighting in a war and that I need to win, who needs much more than that? Only small complaint I have on the campaign is that the mission objectives aren't exactly specified on your mini map/radar. You'll get a something like a "TGT" when it gets in sight, but nothing on the map really. A different color on the mini map could help, but I enjoy flying the jets enough to where i really don't mind.
Even though i haven't played it for a long time, it has that feel of a game that is on the verge of reaching the top and I'd highly reccommend it to anybody wanting a good jet fighter game even if it's still early access. I'll probably give an update as I get further into the campaign and game itself on the feel of the all the different jets and overall mission quality. As of now, I'd give it a nice 8.5/10 for a fresh game. Opinion may change as I get further.

Best 4X Space Sim bar none! Excellent in almost every way. You can really lose quite a lot of hours playing X3 and the Albion Prelude is a great continuation of both the plot as well as what I would consider the main open-ended game. Albion Prelude features just about every fix or tweak you could ask for and as a result is extremely polished.
Do keep in mind how this game rewards spending time. It's not grindy in an MMO style, but one can easily imagine how 'trading from bottom to top, earning millions' will simply take time. People who want an easier start should definitely start with the Humble Merchant setting and perhaps try their hand as the stock exchange market to get their first millions. Then after that you can essentially do whatever you like. The game allows for multiple save games, so there's definitely room for experimentation. Some things, like setting up an automatic trade route do often require specific space ship software systems, same goes for managing space stations you can buy and run. There's a slight learning curve to expect there, certain sectors in the game are easier / more difficult to get profitable stations going.
Exploring the X universe in X3: Albion Prelude is awesome. If I actually had more time to play, I'd probably easily spend hundreds of hours in this game. The open-ended nature and the freedom of choice is great.
(Also, do not buy X: Rebirth. So far X3: Albion Prelude is superior in every single way imaginable, except for perhaps the graphical fidelty. X3: Albion Prelude still is a great looking game though.)

Call of Duty®: Black Ops
Viktor Reznov's eight steps to escape the prison of Vorkuta:
"Every journey begins with a single step. This is Step One!" -- Reznov
Step 1: Secure the Keys - Overpower the guard and get the keys.
Step 2: Ascend from Darkness - Use the elevator to get to ground level.
Step 3: Rain Fire - Use the slingshot to destroy the three guard towers.
Step 4: Unleash the Horde - Use the prison broadcast system to rally the prisoners.
Step 5: Skewer the Winged Beast - Take down the helicopter with the KS-23 harpoon.
Step 6: Wield the Fist of Iron - Acquire a mini-gun from the vault with the help of Reznov.
Step 7: Raise Hell - Storm the prison guards and fight your way down the road.
Step 8: Freedom - Use the motorcycles in the garage to escape the prison.
Do these steps sound familiar? Yes...it's the same steps used in Call of Duty®: Black Ops II Zombies - Origins
Sounds exciting? Well, it might give you enough reason to buy this game (as well as Call of Duty®: Black Ops II). The campaign story line is epic and the plot won’t let you down. The characters are strong, well-crafted and dramatic moments give the story some intrigue and a tone of uncertainty allowing your missions to cover a vast diverseness of gameplay and geographics. Up until now I believe this game's campaign story is one of the best in the series.
Call of Duty®: Black Ops offers an online Multiplayer mode where you can earn experience points while leveling up, unlocking custom class slots, weapons, perks, killstreak bonuses, emblems, reticles and more...
And for those who want some more bang for buck, Black Ops offers a popular four-player cooperative Zombie mode. You'll fight to stay alive against endless waves of undead lusus naturae. It's a bold and bizarre endeavor, but with characters and personalities to entertain you through some bloodcurdling situations.
Nevertheless, the game at its core is terrific and in my opinion Call of Duty®: Black Ops (and its successor) has stood the test of time. So then, ffs, DO IT.

Stellaris is a middle of the road, unremarkable title. It isn't a great 4X game. It isn't a great grand strategy game. It's okay.
The principle flaws stem from a corporate culture that results in them making assumptions about what the game should have which doesn't play well to the systems in the game. The biggest headaches in Stellaris are related to ships and combat. The game, effectively, has a tactical simulation without any effective tactical AI. You will lose ships because they can't prioritise ships, so they will spin in circles under fire. Battles will be drawn out as your ships fly at a target, only to disengage before entering firing range and looping in this behaviour. Paradox has added a tactical simulation, but expects combat to play out the same as were it were one of their titles where forces engage if they occupy the same province. Ship design is opaque and the best strategy seems to be just to throw on as many high-ranged direct fire weapons as you can. Because with the bad tactical ai, range is a damage multiplier.
The game is bland. It has its moments and its faults, but in the end, the game is just unremarkable. Though Stellaris was a commercial success, it is, in terms of being a game a flop. It is the summer blockbuster you can't quite remember if you saw a week later and forget it exists a few months later. Eventually someone will say something about Stellaris and you will respond "Oh yeah. That." In terms of quality, it should be grouped with such titles as Sengoku, March of the Eagles and EU: Rome.

A very fun game which can be about as challenging as you want it to be.
The strategy on the world map is very important, and logistics are by far the deepest part of it. Not hard to get into, mind you, but it takes some time to master. The battle tactics are much more difficult to become skilled at, but the game gives you incentives to do so, and it feels rewarding and exhillarating when you do. And if over-arching strategy is more your thing, and you find the battles themselves either not to your liking or too difficult, you can always just auto-resolve, and this game has an auto-resolve that actually favors the player rather than the AI like in most games.
Excellent replayability, as there is a wide variance in unit type and viable playstyles between factions, not to mention you begin in different situations, with different neighbors, regions, and money.
If I had to mention a few cons, the diplomacy is broken. If you favor expansion, expect all of your neighbors to very quickly declare war on you, and they will very rarely make peace for anything. And even if they do, it won't last. Allies do not function properly (at all, really), and the Pope imposes debilitating penalties to your nation by demanding you not fight any other Catholic nation, even if those nations are the aggressors against you. The pathfinding for units is very bad, the enemy's battle AI, while efficient and skilled at what it is meant to do, is not overly intelligent, and understanding how to get infantry to attack properly is a nightmare.
Overall, though, it is a very good game that was quite lovingly made, with attention to detail and good voice-acting and music, even if there isn't that MUCH of those. Bugs are few, and it really makes you feel like a medieval administrator/warlord. Good stuff.

It isn't that easy to review games like these.
Visual novels have usually a great problem of balance between quality, replayability and concrete cost. And this one costs definitely too much, even if I bought it with some kind of heavy sale - it comes out at 6€ on Steam.
And it's very expensive for such a short game, even if it's nice.
The visual novel itself is a bit short but enjoyable, graphics are nice and the plot overall is good, even if you can't control almost anything.
There's a 15-levels mini-game that you can play at the beginning, granting you an achievement, and a point and click adventure in the middle of the game which isn't required to get to an ending (even if it gives you another achievement of course).
Apart from this, there's only the visual novel itself and if the plot suits your tastes as I said it's good, but really it isn't worth that price.
I hate the subgenres words (this is a "kinetic novel" according to those who know much many things more than me, which means basically that you can't make choices, but I still think you must review differently every single game - point and click scenarios for instance are not that common in visual novels) and so yeah, we have a rather short visual novel focused on sex, humour, utopia - that Crystal City you see in the title - and some nice ideas in the second part of the game where you'll get to know all the girls and their personalities.. and the robots.. and so on. The language mistakes (from Russian to English) aren't that heavy and bothering, but it could have been translated way better.
But anyways the price is insanely high for the content that the novel offers. So go for it only if you have a big discount coupon; in that case it's ok to spend a hour reading Crystal City. At a full price, or even over 1€, definitely not.

Stellaris is one of my favorite games of all time, and some of the reasons I enjoy it might not be the same for others. This is a recommendation, sincerely, but as truly fantastic and engrossing as this game is, it may well not be for everyone, for a couple reasons.
Stellaris is difficult to define even when compared to other games of it's kind. It bears the most in common with other grand strategy games, but is quite the departure, and at least marginally more acessible to the newcomer.
It is, essentially, a simulation of species, from the first steps outside of their solar system, to whatever future you make for them. Be it conquering and enslaving or seeking to form a federation for the ages, your options (and customizations) are vast.
Gameplay early on can be dreadfully slow, sending out your little science ship and learning more about your surroundings, but ultimately the second you colonize your second world, build your second ship, meet a neighbor, it starts to ramp up and doesn't stop. By the midgame you've got potentially dozens of planets, ships, surveying, each planet needing to be micromanaged into what buildings it has, all while desinging vessels to counter your neighbors.. it's a treat. It's a real time game, but much like FTL, the ability to pause is used frequently to stay sane.
It is, again, not saying this lightly, my favorite game of all time, and I shall be playing it indeed for the REST of all time.

Just last night I finished the game and I am looking forward to a sequel. Before my review I would like to note that this was my third point and click adventure game (all from Daedlic) so I am not particularly experienced on this field.
Story:
In my opinion the strongest point of the game. As the description says we follow the adventure of a young boy whose dream is to become a magician. On a summer vacation anything is possible! It sounds like and starts out as a light-hearted fairytale with talking woodland animals. (It reminds me a bit to The Whispered World.) However, even the starting cinematic hints that there are more to it. The story picks up slowly as Jerry, on his training to be a Treewalker, first just do all kind of chores for the locals, which took about half of my game time. But the subtle referances that things weren't as they looked kept me going. There are a couple of threats looming over Mousewood, the home of the woodland critters, some more immediate and more apparent, some not. The initial innocent tale about talking critters expands into a complex one with harsher elements. I find the plot intriguing and creative. It has more than one layer and gives a couple of twists in the second half of the game. We get answers to some of the mysteries, but at the same time more questions arises. There remain some loose ends hanging, that makes me hope there will be a sequel.
Gameplay:
There is only one click option, and the game decides whether you look, talk to, pick up, etc your target. Jerry's adventures centers around a place called Mousewood and its close surrounding. He needs to visit same places over and over again, but some other, smaller areas open up briefly too. The game lacks a bit on exploration-wise in my opinion. There are riddles, hidden objects and lots of item combinations. Unfortunately I found myself often opening a guide because my logic works differently than Daedlic’s. During his training, Jerry learns some useful spells. With the help of them some previously inaccessable places open up or he can interact with objects in new ways, which sometimes help solving puzzles or give extra flavour to the game. After a while day and night cycles are introduced too which, again, alters how and where we can interact with objects and people. There are collectible items too, built in, simple card game (the pictures on the card you collect too) and audio books as bonuses. I think these are good, refreshing ideas which brings the game above average. Unfortunately the puzzles I don’t find particularly interesting unlike the ones in The Whispered World.
Characters, voice acting and dialogues:
Jerry’s behavior is belivable and suitable to a 12 year old child: how he impresses himself when he manages something, his goodwill and slightly naive attitude to the wold, playful and adventurous. I find him a likable main hero. He meets lots of different creatures (funny ones, charming ones, witty ones, etc) and they have all well thought-out personalities. The voices are fine and matches the characters. There are a decent amount of dialogue options, and fortunately we can replay most of them or at least get a summary afterward.
Music:
The game isnot short on them. I really like the menu music and some of the in game ones, but there were a few which slightly annoyed me hearing it over and over again.
Graphic:
Charming cartoonish characters and spectacular, detailed backgrounds. I can only say good about it.
Overally I think The Night of the Rabbit is worth its cost. Because of its setting it is perfect for younger audiance, but it can suit well for older players just as well due to the deeper thoughts arising later during the plot. I don’t think it is the best game when it comes to puzzles but it definitely has some nice features, and because of the story I might even replay the game to see it evolve again, now with a better understanding of what is what and who is who in real.

Created by Daedalic Entertainment, this is the actually the first click and adventure game I have played from them and it appears that this game doesn't receive quite a lot of attention as the other more popular series (Deponia, Edna & Harvery, etc.) but The Night Of The Rabbit stands nicely  and here are my thoughts on it:
(Edited 19th November 2014)
1.) Graphics (9/10)
Ah, this section is where the game truly shines. The background environment is really beatiful with a mystical charm to it and almost every parts of the game are interesting to view. No doubt that they have heavily emphasize on the artwork that compels you to explore further into the world of anthromorphic inhabited world of Mousewood.
As for the characters, they are drawn in 2D graphics which works well for the beautiful background and simple to look at them. Quite a large amount of characters in here and most are based on animals.
Despite all that, they are some minor problems I have seen in this game, in a sense with the dialogues that appear on screen does not match with the voice acting. However, it isn't really bad enough to ruin the experience.
2.) GamePlay (7/10)
As for this part, it is a simply, straight to the point clicking around until you make progress story wise game. It is a nice of them to include in a short tutorial on the controls and it was done in a fun way. As you continue on, you are required to solve many puzzles along the way, which requires you to combine items and using them. There are also  some puzzles which requires to be done in a certain order that would only work. No doubt that some puzzles can be challenging and you have to think hard in order to solve it.
Unfortuntely, some puzzles can become cumbersome, back tracking involved routine and rather vague, despite the fact that you can refer to your journal which sadly offered only minimal help. There were a few several times when I got stuck completely  and had no choice but to end up relying on a guide by other players, which I have to admit this is a bit disappointing and it may cause some players to shy away. All in all, the puzzle part could have use more thought and polishing to it by the creators but still the job is done well enough for an indie game.
3.) Sound / Voice Acting / Music (8.5/10)
Oh boy this is another part where the game shines too, whereby most of all the characters (Except for a few particular residents of Mousewood) had their own voice acting that fits their personalities and appearance very well. From the main character to the most minor characters, it is nice to talk to them and listen to their various quirky and serious dialogues altogether.
The music is really good too, even the main menu for a simple click adventure game can sound really mysterious when paused. Every parts of the game had their own distinct music and in my opinion it fits well on every mood.
However, the most annoying part of the game is that during the process of solving a puzzle and if you made a mistake, you are forced to listen many of the same lines over and over again but thankfully this can be easily mitigated by simply skipping with clicks of the mouse.
4.) Story (7/10)
The main part of the game, hmm to be honest I have mixed feelings about it. You play as a young boy by the name Jeremiah Hazelnut or simply called Jerry, a very tenacious and curious boy who would one day strive to become a famous magician. He is currently on a summer holiday which will end in two days and so Jerry decides to spend his two remanining days looking for adventures in an innocent child perspective right nearby the comfort of his home that lies at the edge of the town in a forest. As time passes, a strange mysterious letter appeared inside his mailbox and in it contains an magical incantation and an invitation for him to come over into the world of Mousewood.
Jerry then gladly follows the instructions on the paper and with that it summons a very strange yet interesting character which happens to be an anthromorphic white rabbit namely Marquis De Hoto. The marquis turns out to be a magician and also a TreeWalker, who is capable of traversing through various portals found at certain places only and their main job is to help its inhabitants,  protect and restore the balance of many worlds. Being a naive minded yet excited typical of a boy, Jerry agrees to be his apprentice in order to become a great magician and from there the story continues.
The first part of the game starts off pretty slow but as the game moves on we start to dwelve deeper into the mysteries of Mouseworld and other worlds that Jerry will visit in his quest, which picks up the story. But sadly, towards the last part of the game feels kind of rushed, sloppy and the ending, in my opinion was a bit lacking in its punch and left a few things unanswered. I'm not sure if this was intended by the creators to open for a sequel which I hope it may bring a closure to it.
There is also the bonus content if you purchase the premium version of the game, it brings some stories which sets in the same universe of Mouseworld that you can see and unlocks along the way in your game play which brings a bit more content of the game
Conclusion (8/10)
In short, The Night Of The Rabbit excels in its Graphics and Audio department but slightly spoiled by certain tough puzzles and the lack of proper conclusion to the story as well as the quality dropping towards the end. Still, it makes for a good experience and I am certainly looking forward to seeing  a sequel being made for this game.

I would love to see a brief five minute tutorial where all the rules, effects of items, and NPCs to watch out for are explicitly laid out because with a tutorial the game would be less trial and error.  You never know what an item/NPC/trap/whatever is going to do until you try it and more than once I've tried it and been busted then and there.  There are some newspapers lying around that you can read for tips but they don't go into the finer points of the game. Overall 8/10 worth playing at least once.

Understanding that this game is still a very early release, it's got a long way to go, but it's already come very far.
Yes, there's some problems, but they're being ironed out as new content is going to be added, but whether or not the content in game is ripe enough to be adequately played at the moment is a question that comes down to a personal matter:
If you're here for the ground attack part of arcade flight games, things aren't too great for you right now. Not a lot targets to shoot at, objects to fly between, ground attack munitions are now more or less properly implemented, but there's little obligation to be low, and typical of Ace Combat, little drive to fly an attacker rather than a fighter.
However, if you're here for dogfighting action, most planes work roughly as they're intended, even those that aren't fully ready yet. Between the multiplayer mode, skirmish, and the mission editor, an intelligent player who came for the dogfighting will get their fill.
In the mean time, it's one of the best arcade flight experiences I've had in a long time, coupled with one of the more user-friendly editors (I'm looking at you, ArmA ), so even if it's nowhere near done right now, it's still quite a lot of game to sink your teeth into.
Oh. Not having fun? Set up a Skirmish with the mutators Itano Circus and Overdrive enabled. I dare you to not have fun then.

In Party Hard you play as someone who is really tired of the neighbors having loud parties.
Instead of calling the cops, you decide it’s a better idea to pay these parties a visit and kill everyone by using your knife!
Party Hard is a tactical strategy game created by Pinoki Games during a Game Jam and the team is backed up by TinyBuild. The game feels like an 80's game experience with the synthesizer music, flashing neon colors and pixel-art although the game is a true 90's horror slasher game.
Party hard follows a series of killings at parties throughought the United States of America, dialogued by a detective called Mr John West who will do the narrative about these Party-hard-killings.
The game has 12 levels to beat and some of them are quite hard to break, just like the old NES games back in the day.
Your main goal within Party Hard is to not get caught while you pick off victims one by one.
The only things you can use to your advantage are for instance traps within the environment, special guests by dialing a phone number and weapons/items found inside briefcases or  poison provided by dark merchants with creepy jackets.
Your opponents are the Cops, FBI, SWAT-team, bouncers, party people (who can notice your mass murders) and Mario the plumber/carpenter who locks off areas by blocking windows of trapdoors so you can't easily flee from the police forces.
I really can recommend Party Hard to anyone who is looking for a challenge to beat, to get creative on a bloodbath, pixel-art, synt-wave music, references to classic retro movies, games etc., dancing bears or simply if you like to Party Crash!
If the game is on sale then you really should pick up this title and give it a dance!

Party Hard is a strategy, stealth game and the main goal is to kill party goers, but will you want to try it out ?
Party Hard has a really simple story. You play as a man who get's annoyed by his partying neighbors at 3 AM so you get up and wipe out the entire house. But now the quench for blood begins and you set out to kill all party goers across the US.
Gameplay is simple but it get's complicated really fast. You can do three things. You can set up traps that will killd anyone around them, you can use the knife to stab people and you can pick people up and carry them around and hide the bodies or you can pick up sleeping people and carry them and stab them. But if you slip up, the victims can call the police which will patrol around the map trying to find the killer. You can evade police but it's harder each time they arrive at the crime scene.
Graphics are simple pixel art and they look awesome. Every little detail is just awesome. From the sharknado in the Miami level to the Mad Max vehicles in the Party Bus level. All of it is just amazing.
Soundtrack is just awesome. It's awesome and I would buy it by itself, it's great. Now there's not much sound effects apart from people screaming and explosions.
The game get's incredibly difficult. The Miami level is one of the hardest things I had to do period. Overall expect a challenge when playing this game, cause it's not easy.
Level Design is pretty simple. You see the map from a over head view and you see everything from there on out. But some levels are in open areas where there's no where to hide making it a pain to play through.
The game took me 4 hours to finish every level and the Miami level took me an hour all by itself. The game has a randomized levels. But this boils down to small details like certain traps not being there and more victims in the level. You do get one more character which you can use to play through the other levels.
If this review was written five hours earlier, I would have said it's pretty buggy, but after I closed down the game I found the patch that fixed a lot of problems. The game ran smoothly from start to finish apart from a minor bug where AI would glitch into walls.
Party Hard is a really fun game and without a doubt I highly suggest to try it out. It's addictive gameplay will make you want more murder and chaos and the incredibly fun gameplay will make you come back. I give Party Hard a 8.5/10

X3AP is an amazing space themed sandbox. There's so much to do that it can be quite overwhelming. But is strangely addictive and can easily drain your life away with its immensely entertaining game play.
Now the vast majority of this review is going to be about what I really didn’t like about the game; however, over all I still love this game and find it extremely entertaining.
First and foremost are the missions for the main plots. If I didn’t spend the time to research what they were and what I needed to do to qualify for them I would have probably never known they existed at all or how to unlock them. While this is an open ended sandbox game I felt that it was too hard to unlock the main plot missions and several of them such as the missions that require you to capture ships are next to impossible without consulting Google to see how others managed to complete them.

Another gripe I have with missions is that they can be very buggy which is a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥if you haven’t saved recently. You may end up having to revert to a previous save game file (assuming you used multiple files to save for each play through which I HIGHLY recommend for this very reason) I had several of the main story line missions just halt their progress. As an example, one mission I was supposed to be escorting a convoy and the entire convoy got killed because my capital ship was too slow to keep up with them. But rather than failing me and allowing me to redo the mission it just kept telling me to escort the dead convoy that was there and continually spawned fighters to attack me. I wasn’t even able to abort the mission in the hopes of restarting it and ended up going back to a previous save file and losing hours of work.
On to the different types of starts, I believe they are falsely labeled as to their difficultly. Some of the starts that Egosoft has labeled as average or normal such as the "Anonymous  Argon" are next to impossible to do, You can’t really take most of the missions because you have no weapons, no life support, no money , and virtually no way to get forward momentum in the game at all. While others that such as the "Bankrupt assassin" start are labeled hard and it’s possible to have a hundred million in your bank within a few hours with this start. The point being that to the novice player who's just trying to jump into the game with little to no understanding of how it works it’s extremely easy to become discouraged and quit simply because you wanted to play the "Easy" or "Normal" start and you ended up with a start that causes even advanced players to say "Yeah ♥♥♥♥ this♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; after 30 minutes.
Next is traveling. I'm a Avionics Technician and a helicopter pilot out here in the real world. I have worked in aviation for over 6 years and statistically speaking a real auto pilot fails around one time in a billion and even then most of the time it isn’t life threatening. Yet somehow the auto pilot in the game manages to kill me at least once an hour. Because of this little flaw traveling is extremely tedious and time consuming until you manage to get a jumpdrive and even then buying new ships is a pain. I'll use the Terrans as an example, the ships are sold in one sector, and the equipment such as jumpdrives are sold 10 sectors away where 5 of the sectors are full of capital ships trying to kill you so getting through there in a new ship without equipment can be challenging to say the very least.
My last big complaint is that this game is extremely complex which is a good thing, and at the same time a bad thing. Its good because it gives the player tons of options for fleet controls and commands but like all complex tasks it takes quite a bit of time to complete them. So when you get the game rolling and have a few hundred stations and ships it can get a bit time consuming micromanaging everything and in combat situations controlling fleets and issuing orders can be insanely hard especially since you can’t make custom macros (or at least I couldn't find out how using the vast resources available on Google) to do many of the ship specific actions like launching your marines for a boarding party. Something that needs to be extremely precise, requires you to go through 5 command and selection menus before they will get off your damn ship. All while you're in the middle of a battle. Where ideally all you would have to do is press a button or hells in real life just say the words "Get out."
Now despite all of the short comings have listed here and several others that I didn’t I believe X3AP is a truly beautiful game and it offers a type of play style and control that I haven’t seen in any other space game franchise. It has an immersive and rich universe that’s easy to get lost in and some of the most enjoyable space combat I have experienced in a game.
I give this game a 7 out of 10 it could easily have been a 9 out of 10 with some polishing by the game studio. It's a very fun game and I highly recommend it if you are looking for a space themed game. You should just have to expect to spend about 10 hours learning to master the controls.
