You know, of the forty or so steam games I've reviewed, this is the second "not recommended" game I've played, the other being Outlast. I'm surprised, as I thought something like this would be right up my alley.
Claire has you playing as, you guessed it, a young woman named Claire. Claire is visiting her mother in the hospital one night when things start getting really whacky. She must explore the hospital and some other areas and uncover the truth of what is going on.
The game uses an attractive 2D art style and is side scrolling, much like the far superior Lone Survivor. Using a limited inventory, you must solve puzzles and avoid monsters. The inventory is almost an exact copy of the one from Amnesia: The dark Descent, right down to the health and sanity icons. The inventory sound is almost exactly like the one made in Silent Hill 2. Between that and the obvious influence of Lone Survivor, this should have been a winner.
Unfortunately, a lot of what makes these games good is the execution of the atmosphere and story. Amnesia had a pretty compelling narrative, Silent Hill 2 has one of the best video game stories ever, and Lone Survivor was intriguing in its own way. This game, however, feels like a very standard and generic narrative, with obvious reflections of Claire's internal struggles and really simple writing. It doesn't have that spark that superior horror titles have, the depth that comes from the interaction with environments and unique enemies.
Speaking of that, another borrowed element from Amnesia is the fact that you can't fight enemies. Instead, you must run and hide. However, this presents some problems. Much like Lone Survivor, it's incredibly easy to get lost since you're playing in a 3D map using a 2D plane. I'm not exaggerating when I say that I was looking at my map once every five or ten seconds. This is exacerbated by the sameness of the hallways. The thing is that enemies don't pause when you open your map, so when you're being chased through multiple rooms, lost and confused, it's pretty irritating. This might be remedied if the enemeis were scary in any way, but they're plain black spider things with white faces. Not very scary. And I'm not saying that good monster design is a necessity, but it certainly doesn't hurt to have something that's creepy to look at.
The sanity system also annoys more than anything. There are enemies introduced about halfway through the game that don't directly attack you and instead drain your sanity, which will drain your health if it falls too low. There are several segments later on that require you to go through multiple rooms in a row with these enemies and the screen gets darker and darker the more insane you go. Stopping to heal is a bad idea since your sanity will only fall lower and lower. Again, it's more annoying than intense.
There are also some side quests to go on in the form of side characters, but, to be honest, these felt like nothing more than filler. Each one is solved easily within a matter of minutes, except for maybe one near the end of the game, but even that is fine. One of them has you meet a character weirdly reminiscient of Eddy Dombrowski from Silent Hill 2 (although in this game the person is far less interesting). You go through a few rooms just next door, grab an item he wants, bring it back, and bam, done. I didn't feel that these characters really added anything either. They didn't give me more insight or understanding of the story, but maybe that's because the story is so simplistic and basic to begin with.
One last thing is the sound. It's totally serviceable, but neither the effects or soundtrack stand out in any way. To me, at least.
So while the game is very pretty to look at, it honestly feels like a pale imitator of far better games. I really wanted to enjoy this, as it seemed right up my alley, but alas, not every game will be a winner. It's not the worst thing in the world, but it's very mediocre, with a bland and cheap story, dull exploration (side note: this game gives you tons of abtteries for your flashlight that aren't really needed as the default lighter, which uses no resources, is more than sufficient to see with), and random and out of place side quests. If you can get it on sale and have a few hours to kill, there are worse ways to spend your time, but I'd check out other horror games first. Games like Silent Hill 2, Amnesia: The Dark Descent, Lone Survivor, and Cry of Fear (latter of which is free on Steam and it's awesome!!!!)  before spending money on this title.

The Witcher 2 is a massive improvement from the Witcher 1, and after playing it, I'm excited to play the third installment. I would recommend the game to players that look for:
1. A story with moral ambiguity. This made choices thought-provoking. You couldn't rely solely on what you think is the 'good' thing to do, but you also needed to be informed and think about what consequences you could end up with. I think the game did a good job on immersion as well as giving the player freedom to choose how to play Geralt.
2. Complex characters. The characters in the game all have their own motivations, and they all seem to have an ugly side to them. There are no cookie-cutter characters, and I liked how the game made me suspicious of everyone.
3. Combat that requires preparation. Do you have enough information about how to fight the enemy? Have you brewed potions? Crafted better gear/weapons? You also have a lot more freedom in how you want to fight compared to the Witcher 1. You can rely on magic, daggers, bombs, traps or even specialize in blade oils and alchemy. Enemies can guard and can get bonus damage if they attack from behind.
My only minor complaints are that I wish it were longer and I had some problems with a few random crashes near the end of the game (possibly due to too many save files). Lastly, I might be called a prude or w/e for this but, I didn't like the few unavoidable fan-servicey scences that I felt were a bit immersion breaking.
. I don't have a problem with nudity when there's feeling or a point to it, but those were just awkward. That being said, huge improvement from the awkward 'romances' from the Witcher 1!

A dark, gritty story set in a medieval, renaissance-esque fantasy world, filled with choices that have (sometimes) far reaching consequences. There are a lot of crude language and mature situations, all being part of that particular world in which no one is completely black or white, starting with the hero, but sometimes the plot tries too hard to tie everything and everyone together... Still the story is interesting, there is a lot of room to choose how to play the hero, whether as an amoral monster killer in a violent world or as a lost, kind soul in search of his past, and while the events that unfold will sweep the hero  in their wake, the sense of having an impact in the world and the grand scheme of things is real, and that is the strength of this game.
The gameplay and combat is ok-ish, the maps are small with lots of backtracking to the same locations, the inventory is a pain to use and navigate and the crafting completely unintuitive (the character doesn't learn recipes, he has to keep them in his backpack and show them a  crafter NPC who will craft it for him for a fee). Thank god for the internet and the many help guides out there!
On the plus side, the graphics in their time were putting many machines to their knees and are still good, with a lush world, beautiful use of lighting, day and night cycles, dynamic weather that astounded me when I saw NPCs running for cover when the rain started pouring. The music helps set the mood with great ambient tracks, be it for battle or spending the night at an inn.
The story in this game is unbelievably beautiful, thank you Yoko Taro for making this masterpiece.

The second Witcher game has a significant graphical upgrade over the first, and retains the satisfying monster slaying and storyline that made the first one great.
I played on hard difficulty, which was quite hard at first, but got a little easier once I got used to the combat and got some better armour. I died a lot, mostly because I was too eager to hit stuff, when it actually requires more thought than the first game where that worked well the whole way through.
I loaded my save from the first game, which meant I started off with some of the items I had then, although they were pretty much indistinguishable from the most basic swords in the starting area, which was strange given that they were supposed to be powerful weapons. Makes sense from a gameplay perspective.
The story feels even better this time, although I'm not sure exactly why. Perhaps the whole assassination thing grabbed me nicely. I think there are more choices to make this time round, which influence things a good deal. I played through Iorveth's part, but I think after you leave Flotsam it's possible to go one of two branches, which is interesting. The dialogue system is sort of improved from the first game, but because of the floaty mouse I had through the whole game it was not as pleasant as it could have been. A lot of the dialogue choices are strange - you make a choice based on a small bit of text, and what Geralt ends up saying is often quite different to what you'd expect. As with the first game, it's great to have all the dialogue in the game voiced, and the voice actors do a good job. I played with the Polish voice-over.
Shorter than the first game if you only do one of the two chapter 2 paths.
Combat is different; you have only a fast and strong attack, and there is no timing element, as far as I could tell. Just mash the button and you will hit stuff. It's more difficult this time because enemies block and do more damage (at least on hard mode), so I think it was better. Enemies were scarier, especially larger monsters.
You start off with all signs, and they are different from the first game until you upgrade them. Igni and aard are ranged attacks, and you can improve the distance by skills or mutagens. I still don't really understand what sign intensity or sign damage means; it wasn't explained in an obvious way.
The skill system this time is sort of improved. You have trees through which you can choose different paths to get certain skills. There are dependencies so you can't just select a skill, which forces you to pick a certain route if you want something specific, which isn't great. There is an adrenaline system which adds a special attack, which you can use after building adrenaline, which builds very slowly. Each of the skill trees has a different ability.I think it's OK, and I made use of it reasonably often. Some of the skills can be ignored (arrow redirection, dagger throwing), and many of them don't make a noticeable difference, apart from the magic ones, which have a few nice things, like linking yrden, and various quen improvements. Problem is, the level cap is 35, so you only get 34 points to spend, on a total of more than 60 skills, some of which have multiple levels. Oh, and you can't see what the second level of a skill is unless you have the first.
I didn't like the potions this time round. Unless you choose to go a decent way into the potion skill tree, a lot of the potions have negative effects which far outweigh the benefits. Stuff like 40% damage reduction, -50% vitality and the like. I ended up using maybe 4 types of potions the entire game; cat, rook, swallow and wolf. I'm not sure how much of a difference they even made. The potion drinking animation is a little annoying to have to sit through each time. Potions also only last 10 minutes instead of the much longer time they lasted in the first game which means you have to drink them a lot if you make use of them. Blade oils are the same, lasting only 5 minutes, without sword or skill upgrades.
Mutagens were introduced, which allow you to mutate abilities, but only those which are quite far down the tree, and only for quite minor bonuses.
I did make use of bombs, but again not particularly useful.  Same goes for traps. I used several in the tutorial because I was told to, but in the actual game used precisely zero apart from when I had to use them for a harpy quest. I ignored daggers too, for the most part. Aiming and so on was fine, but it wasn't really worth it when you can just hit stuff with a sword.
The crafting system is pretty pointless. You can gather diagrams to make things like armour and traps and potions. Potion diagrams and diagrams for swords and armour could in theory be useful, but in practice I almost always  had better armour than I could craft, and the number of different types of equipable items you could make were very limited. I ended up having hundreds of crafting items but only crafting things a handful of times; a sword right at the end of the game, and a few ingredients for sword upgrades. Diagrams are generally quite expensive too. Sword and armour upgrades exist but I didn't really use many of them as I didn't think I'd be able to replace them once the armour was upgraded. The benefits are relatively minor. You can probably increase armour by 6 and vitality by 45 if you use the best armour upgrades on a 3-slot armour piece.
You don't get that much money, unlike in the first game where I had over 10k orens by the end. You can probably sell most of the ingredients you get for cash if you need it (which you probably won't). There are some times in the game where you might be able to find something useful to buy, like a sword or armour upgrade, but these are often prohibitively expensive (1.5k orens for armour quite early on in the game), or useless, because you'll probably get an upgrade quite soon anyway. Things are extremely expensive to buy and are bought extremely cheaply by people you sell them to. If you buy a diagram that sells for 500 orens, you might be able to get ~25 orens for it.
The dice game, through which you could make quite a lot in the first game is now less good. There is nothing indicating what you and your opponent have rolled, which means you have to look at the dice to see, which I suppose is more realistic, but I just found it annoying. Having to roll them yourself was  sort of a nice addition, but the way they fall somehow feels far too bouncy and weird. Also, I think all the games I played had a maximum winnings of 25 orens. Hardly a high stakes game, and not a good way to make money. The other mini-game, arm wrestling, was a reasonably interesting, although quite difficult sometimes.
Somehow, the inventory was improved and made worse at the same time. You can now carry weapons and so on as in most RPGs, which was good because I could now pick everything up. There is now a  weight system which means you can only carry so much, and if you're carrying too much you move slowly. You can sort by weight and value, and  how recently an item was picked up. But, generally the inventory is somehow bad. You can filter by categories, but the way items are displayed is quite bad. Often you can't see all of the details of an item, which will be in a little scrolling window at the bottom of the screen. Maybe screen size changes this, but it's really quite annoying.
Books and the journal are a little different this time. Each quest, character and location is written about from the perspective of Dandelion writing about it, which I liked. The text updates whenever something new happens in the quest or you learn  new information about something. This time the monster description books aren't really necessary, unlike in the first where you needed them to gather ingredients. I preferred the way it was done in the first game, because the books meant something. Also, it's impossible to know if you've read a book or not (as far as I could tell)

Ok, so, for starters, I just figured I should put out a message that the game
episodic, which is something I didn't know when I purchased it but it was cheap so it's all good.
This game, of the limited selection of point and clicks i've played, is definitely the one that not only made the most sense (not really any of that inverted adventure game logic here) but it's also the most ♥♥♥♥ed in the head, and in a good way. The world Mango Protocol have made for the game is one that at first glance at is at least a reasonable facsimile of normal life, but you'll soon find it's full of perverts and general weirdos, just going about their lives. You play as one of these weirdos, Nika, a seven year old girl who is on a mission to build a death robot and purge everything that isn't awesome. Isn't that awesome?
The game plays nicely enough, but it was obviously made with touch screens in mind (which isn't a bad thing, btw, quite the opposite) and after a patch the graphics options are enough to satisfy. The games controls are easy to learn and easier to use, and to be frank there's not much I can fault about the game. People say the ending is bad, but you've gotta factor in the episodic nature of the game, and to be honest it left me hyped for Mango Protocol's future games, Agatha Knife and Colossus Down, which are further continuations/extended bits of the MechaNika story (at least I think they are, not too sure). The art is nicely done, with a kinda doodle-y aesthetic which does well to hide the ♥♥♥♥ed up parts, and make them all the more ♥♥♥♥ed up. Soundtrack's good too.
But yeah, I'd definitely pick this one up (well i did but y'know) and be on the lookout for any of Mango Protocols future games, if they're up to this one's standard.

Back when this game first came out, I obtained a *cough* demo version, to test it out and see if I wanted to actually buy it.
My initial thoughts were that the game really just wasnt as good as the other borderlands. On top of that, I really didnt like Handsome Jack from Borderlands 2.
Then the borderlands pack hit the Humble bundle store.
I bought it and played the first one again and it was a nostalgic trip of bliss. I enjoyed it so much that I just went ahead and bought all of the games (Pre-sequel was higher up on the bundle)
Boy were my first impressions wrong. I freaking love this game. Handsome Jack is an amazing character in this game, and seeing him turn into the Handsome Jack from BL2 is an incredible story.
The Guns are even more unique than before, Cold elemental damage is probably one of my favorite things. But I've always taken the elemental class trees. In BL1, all the gun companies just altered their stats a little. In this game, every gun compnay varries greatly between each other. A Jakobs Sniper rifle vs a Vladov Sniper are two completely different things. One is basically a fully automatic Lead raining fury ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ LMG and the other is a 50 cal. head exploiding sniper.
While at first I thought all the characters were boring and I didnt really want to play as any of them, I bought the Baroness and she is INCREDIBLY fun to play. Her dialogue is less so fun.
After beating the game I tried out Claptrap, absolutley hilarious dialogue, his action skill has tons of different effects that varry depending on the situation you're in. I dont think I've seen all of his possible action skill effects yet. For instance, if everyone is dying and you use his action skill, he gets a medic gun, or if you kill someone with a melee attack and use it, he beceoms a psycho with a giant saw axe thing. You know the ones. I feel like on the surface the characters seem shallow and boring but if you actually play them all, they'll end out being more fun than you'd think.
One thing I didnt like was that some of the NPC's that I loved so much werent in the game. Dr.Zed is one of my favorites. But since you're not on pandora, it makes sense that they wouldnt be there. Still though, their replacements are enjoyable. I still wish I could hear zed say "Who needs a real doctor when you have my machines and their... Scary needles"

The mid-game especially feels lacking in anything to keep me interested. This all sounds negative, but the game does have potential. The early game- exploring, colonizing and meeting the first alien civilizations other than your own- is exciting and fun. Late game seems to have interesting events as well, but I haven't personally seen any. This game has potential. Maybe after a year or so of patches and DLC (unfortunetly Paradox games usually have a mountain of DLC but they also usually make them game better) this can be a great game. Right now though there simpily is not enough in the game to keep you hooked and playing like games such as CK2 or EUIV.

I started as a Militarist/Materialist/Collectivist Squid people of the Valroran Science Directorate.
My two allies were the UN (Filthy humans) and the Akkadian people (Some Fungaloids).
We started at the top left corner of the galaxy, we're an organized group so this was going to be a federation victory anyway. To our immediate south was a fallen empire, Fanatic Xenophobes... great. Between our 3 allied factions were a faction of horrible Insectoid people called the Vir, they were an upstart empire that had huge chunks of territory, they were an IMMEDIATE THREAT, they were Fanatic Xenophobes, Militarist, and on top of all that, they were also strong and rapid breeders. The Humans started off as the weakest of the 3 allied empires, with the Valrorans and Akkadians as the two dominant powers.
Our first task was to cause chaos to our neighboring empires, invade them and liberate the new worlds under our names so they adopt our ethos and love us, it was a huge success thanks to the Akkadian Empire's massive ground armies. The entire top left of the galaxy was soon a cookie crumb of small civilizations that hated each other except for their saviors. Our next task was to destabilize the Vir roaches. It was a lengthy campaign which costed tens of thousands of lives, it took almost 60 years to break up the Vir roach empire into little vassals, even after their downfall the Vir roaches were almost impossible to deal with, being fanatic xenophobes the Vir people were almost impossible to intergrate properly into the Valroran empire without rebellious factions popping up.
My empire had conquered and enslaved several primitive planets at first (Middle ages, space age civs) and adding stellar empire races into my list of slaves was starting to feel like a burden, so I immediately opted to first regulate slavery for better working conditions, then ban slavery all together.
. Not only were these ungrateful lesser races not happy with being emancipated, they also started forming more rebel factions faster than ever. After 10 years since I passed the law to ban slavery, I immediately reinstated it (Xenos only of course). The next 20-30 years my allies were helping me fight off rebel wars happening in my territory.
Suddenly, the fallen empire to our south awakens, we almost break our economies just to field a fleet large enough to fight the greatest threat in the galaxy so far. The Valroran fleet warps in first taking the brunt of the hit, then the Akkadians and finally the Human fleet. The battle was tense, the Valroran fleet was wiped out in the first battle against the 50k fleet power Fallen Empire. We thought we had won, we suffered extremely heavy casualties, suddenly the Fallen Empire's second fleet warps in, 60k fleet power. During the battle, the Akkadian fleet suffered extremely heavy losses, losing the entire fleet in the process, but somehow the Human fleet pulled off the impossible and destroyed the remaining Fallen empire fleet with less than half its fleet power. Now the Human Empire became the strongest force in the galaxy, with the strongest lead in technology and economy, as well as fielding the most powerful ships. The Valroran owned the most planets, the Humans had the strongest tech and economy, the Akkadians had the largest and most professional ground army in the galaxy.
Skipping ahead, the Fallen empire to the south was completely eradicated with technology we stole from them and a much larger overall fleet size. Not even the scourge threat were a match for our combined fleets.
During peacetime, my Human ally asks me if I could purge a planet for them from the annexed fallen empire systems. (The Human empire had a strict no slavery no purging policy). They send me control over the planet temporarily, I start purging the inhabitants of the planet and pass control back to the Humans. The Valroran Empire now deals in slavery and purging services for a nominal fee, the biggest customer is the Human Democratic Utopia.
Our game isn't done yet, but
: My empire has now devolved into an empire that deals in black market services such as installing slave processing plants, purging races and exporting slaves.

I really want to love this game. The visuals are stellar; it gives a very winnie the pooh-esque vibe that fills me with nostalgia. The characters are adorable and the writing in terms of dialogue is fantastic. This is just not an enjoyable GAME. Mind you, I've played Walking Dead, all of the Monkey Island games, three Ace Attorney  games, All three seasons of the new Sam and Max games, I even played a few Myst titles and Milo. This game has very little understanding of common logic. You grind every piece of furniture and tools in where you wish for it to go. No characters are helpful in terms of advice, some even lie to you about how you are expected to solve certain challenges. What frustrates me is what clues ARE given are just vague enough to drive you crazy. Puzzles like "draw on a rock" in the middle of several areas FULL of rocks can be quite maddening. Or perhaps you have all you need to solve a puzzle with a certain character, but the game refuses to recognize your solution until a certain amount of other events have come to pass elsewhere. Some Point-and-Clicks are quite guilty of this, but never has such a problem stopped me dead in my tracks so utterly. When I played past games and came to a solution, I felt satisfied, happy even. Here, I am frustrated at how much time is lost due to a require psychic understanding of the programmer's problem solving. I will give the game credit: the story is stellar. A very Whovian quality to the intention. I would reccommend watching it. or playing through it with a guide. But this is a very frustrating adventure game. If there was a more straightforward way to offer hints, or if the level design wasn't built to offer misleading soutions, I'd reccommend it. in it's current form: I only say watch it for its story.

A disappointing collection of features, really. Sectors are still ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, like they were at launch; whole sectors starve because the AI just doesn't create food-buildings, and it builds infrastructure extremely slowly even with a population present to work the buildings. The start of the game has always been extremely slow as well. It really takes a LOT of time to finally get going.
Other species types more or less just make them like or hate you more, it does not affect what they actually do what-so-ever. You'd think intelligent species would be great at research, or strong ones would focus on armies and mineral boosts, but no and no. The only thing traits seem to do is change your starting relation you have with them. Otherwise, I have experienced all empires to be just as aggressive as any other. Even Pacifist empires does not seem to affect this. The only empires that seem to behave differently are the genocidal maniacs that will be hostile to everything and everyone.
The Ship Designer could be much better, but it's fair enough. You have several module slots you fill with weapons, shields, and reactors, and a separate section where you put in engines, scanners, engines, warp drives and such. With this ship designer you can create fleets that can hard-counter enemy fleets, but the enemy can do the same, so you gotta have a balance. The Ship Designer is one of the better aspects of the game, and is a bit of fun to tinker with.
However, the most fun I have is throwing massive fleets at other fleets. Seeing potentially 400 ships engage in combat is quite a sight. But even that experience is underwhelming, since you have literally zero control of your fleets once they engage. Yes. Z-E-R-O involvement, if you exclude that one button that retreats your fleet into a nearby system. There is no targeting priority for ships, although it seem like the size of weapons have a bias for "equally" sized ships; so medium weapons target medium ships and so on. There is no other fleet formation other than the default formation, which is absolutely crazy they have not implemented yet after so long. The game really wants my important ships to stay all the way in the front so they all die first, while the cannon fodder derp around not doing much until it's too late. If your fleet engange two or more enemies that are a distance from eachother, the fleet will split into randomly sized chunks and fly towards their target. I've seen 10 or so smaller frigates slam their dead hulls agains several battleships. You cannot select any singular ships in combat and focus down the most important enemies. You cannot micro damaged units behind your fleets so they don't die. There is just no control, and it's really sad to watch.
For a 4X game it's very meh, with colorful combat. If you really like space based 4X games you may enjoy it. If you are on the fence, don't buy it.

‘The Wild Eight’ is the best Survival game I have played in a while. This game is incredible and I love it very much so far. Basically it is a normal survival game without any zombies, but the most terrifying creature in the world. Wolves. Now I know what you are thinking, ‘Slither, Wolves aren’t that scary in survival games’. Woah. Trust me, they are the main concern, especially when you can't get a ranged weapon (bow) for a while.
Audio - Nice sound effects. Brings a horror aspect to the game, especially when you can hear wolves howling in the distance. I like the sound of the wind and snow, feels very realistic when you have the sound on, playing on your headphones. I think the sound is one of the biggest things that made me love this game.
Gameplay - You have 4 ways (very similar) you can play this game. You can either: Play your own adventure (Solo), Play your own adventure with friends, Play the side-missions to progress the story with friends or Play the side-missions to progress the story (solo). Either of these does not change the main objective of the game. You may even decide to play your own way and once get bored, adventure through the side-missions. Now, In this game there are building options (not many), Skills menu and a crafting menu. To access the Skills and crafting options, there are 2 buildings you must build. The Workshop (Crafting) and a Tent (Skills). While progressing through the game (either way), you obtain skill points depending on your last action. For example, walking across a big area will obtain mobility skill points which you can then spend them on your movement speed and other skills. You can also upgrade the tent and unlock new options in the skills menu. While progressing through the game (either way), You will obviously need weapons, tools, armor and bandages. You can obtain some of them by either raiding an abandoned building or crafting them. To do this, you need to build a workshop and place it. Learn this, the more times you upgrade your workshop, the more things you can craft (i.e Bone knife, Bone Tools and leather armor.)
Story - There is not much to say about the story without spoiling it. I am just going to say what happens at the intro and the rest is for you to discover.
Graphics / Visuals - The visuals are really nice and smooth. To me, they are geometrical and up to date with the latest sandbox games (like Totally Accurate Battle Simulator and Hello Neighbor.)

Party Hard is essentially trying to be a stealth game. Every stage consists of one pixelated screen featuring a giant boat, biker party, disco setting and the like. Your mission is to murder everyone involved without being caught. Activating traps usually can be done while being in the vicinity of NPCs, however the act of murdering should be done without being seen, as all NPCs will call the police, which will arrest you, without you being able to actually do much about it, unless you are close to a window to jump through without the cop being able to follow you. As soon as you have been detected, the NPC in question runs faster than you are able to move around the screen and thus a restart is more often than not warranted.
The premise of murdering partying neighbours is undoubtable funny, however the gameplay for me is too slow paced and not offering enough variation. The peak in the level’s difficulty is right when you started, since, as soon as you cleared a certain part of a level, you can freely murder everyone daring to walk into that area. Most confusing for me was that when the police was called due to your murderous actions, they merely stuff the bodies into bags and are on their marry way again. Future discovery of these body bags does not lead to any response. Thus you can easily murder everyone and just walk away without caring about future discovery, as long as you are not nearby while the body is seen. This leads to a quite boring mid to endgame, when about a third to half of the partying pixelated pornstars have been dealt with. With about half the screen cleared or at least a certain area of the map cleared, you just wait and slowly drag the targets one by one into that part and kill them. This is tedious, repetitive and quite frankly boring. But it still took me about seven to eight minutes after having essentially won the level, to achieve victory without facing any challenge whatsoever. I would love to see more interesting kill mechanics or possibilities of mass murder. Also, the movement speed of the player is sooo slow, even with the running shoe item, you feel sluggish. Overall, for my taste it takes too long to clear the level, with the stage getting actually easier and easier as you progress.
The big thing would be to implement some kind of a panic mechanic, which would lead to the rest of the people fleeing from the party, ending the level prematurely after a certain amount of discovered bodies for example. In contrast, if the player would manage to secretly hide the bodies and avoid too much discovery, he would be able to kill more party guests and thus earning much more points, which incentivises more stealthy play.
All in all, I currently cannot recommend Party Hard, as I feel it is too slow paced, bares much challenge and does not offer any interesting stealth possibilities. The Twitch integration is nice, however does not enough to spice up the game for the general crowd.

So far, very fun. I like survival/ crafting games but typically find them hard to keep my attention. After a while, once you build your base and get stocked up on food, I always end up feeling as if ive beaten the game so to speak. However, this game has a very unique feel to it. To hear my full thoughts on Claire, listen to my review on
Claire is a sidescrolling survival horror game with 16-bit-esque graphics. The horror is of the psychological variety, with you questioning what is real throughout the game. The game controls like a typical sidescroller but gameplay is firmly rooted in classic survival horror games. You have to explore, find items, solve puzzles, and avoid being killed by enemies, all while uncovering the story of the game. Along the way there are also a number of other characters to meet who present side quests and choices for you to make. Your choices, including whether or not to complete these missions, determines what kind of ending you get, of which there are many.
Overall, we found the game very enjoyable in a twisted way. The game relies on building a constant sense of tension, rather than jump scares, in order to frighten players. You have no way to defend against enemies, items you need to survive are scarce, and you can only save in certain rooms which are spread out across large areas. While all of this makes the game very intense to play, it can also potentially lead to frustration since dying means a significant loss of progress.
What's more frustrating though is trying to navigate sprawling 3D environments while moving in a 2D plane. Every time you enter a new room it's not clear if you are moving north, south, east, or west. Luckily, there is a map to help with this, but it's terribly inconsistent and lacking in detail. As a result, a lot of the game is spent feeling lost, which may be a good or bad thing for a survival horror game, depending on how you look at it.
If you can get past these frustrations, Claire is a great survival horror game that I think fans of the genre will really enjoy.

Title: Party Hard
Genre: Action, Indie, Strategy
Developer: Pinokl Games
Publisher: tinyBuild
Release Date: 25 Aug, 2015
Game key was supplied by the publisher.
--------------------------------------
Party Hard is a top down, 2D,  mass murder simulator in which you play as a someone who gets a little cheesed off at his neighbours for having an extremely loud party at 3am. He decides to take matters into his own hands and goes on a murderous rampage. As you do.
As much as I hate to say it, that is pretty much it with the story. However, you do get a quick cutscene between each mission which shows the story of detective John West as he tries to catch the ‘Party Hard Killer’. Although these cutscenes are extremely badly voice acted, and even though the speaking characters are changing, it sounds like the same voice actor desperately trying to put on a different voice but failing miserably. If you are looking for a game with a detailed progressive story, this is not the game for you. Although most people buying this will see from the get-go that this game is not designed for it’s story.
The gameplay is as you would expect, fun but shallow and without any real challenge. Your character will walk around the party wielding a knife, slowly bumping each person off until no more remain.  If you murder someone, the police will pay a visit and put the body in a boby bag, leave it on the middle of the dancefloor and then bugger off somewhere else without even investigating what happened. This will continue happening as you stab as many people as you see fit until the dance floor is strewn with body bags and the rest of the party attendants still dancing their night away like nothing has even happened- occasionally going off to the buffet table because the sign off a mass murder has given them a craving for pineapple and cheese sticks.
The fun element will come from the traps that you can use throughout the map. There are a great amount of traps and each time you replay the mission, the traps may have changed or may be in a different location. These traps range from exploding speakers, to poisoning the food and even driving a car over a hoard of people (you do not control the car) However, these traps still fall under the same problem as the stabbings – the car could have driven over 10 people at once and they are now currently mush on the pavement- but nobody else will care (they won’t even call the emergency services) because THE PARTY MUST GO ON!  Trying to get the perfect ‘massacre’ is where the fun begins and ends, trying to get best kills without getting caught is really the only thing this game has to offer, which is a real shame.
If you do managed to be silly enough to get spotted and you cannot wipe them out before they get to the phone to call the police, then the police will come. Only one officer though. You now must escape. How do you do that you ask? Drive away? Kill the police office? Don’t be silly, just play the ol’ switcheroo by climbing in and out of a window (or other trap door locations) Just as the police officer gets near you, climb out of a window, and then as they try going back round the front door to get to the other side, climb back in. Once you have used an escape route to escape from a dimwitted officer, Mario will come and board it up and you cannot use it anymore (seriously, he looks like Mario).  Be careful though, the police are not the only ones who will arrive- other units such as the SWAT team and FBI can also make an appearance, which makes the game a tad bit harder.
You are able to hide bodies in certain locations. This will help stop anybody from seeing the dead partygoers and in turn, the police will not be called. The thing that irks me is that you can stuff as many bodies as you want into a dumpster. Want to cram 50 people in there? Sure, go ahead! Games such as Hitman have done this better by only allowing a maximum amount of bodies to be hidden in one location. The game would have provided gamers with a bit of a rush to make the body disposal areas in places that maybe get a bit more lively. Having a dumpster outside that only about 1 person walks to at a time makes no challenge. However, putting a disposal area in say a bedroom cupboard, where you have to quickly dispose of it before any moment someone can come walking in. (although this would not work because you can see the entire map and where everyone is at anytime, maybe they needed to add in a line of sight feature)
One of the redeeming features were the songs they used in the game, I am a bit disappointed that there was such a small amount of music variety used. What is currently there is amazing, it gets stuck in your head instantly and is very enjoyable to listen to- but a larger library of music would have been preferred.
Another redeeming feature is the graphics. This art style has been done many times in the past, so don’t expect anything to ‘wow’ you, but it really does work for this game. Everything looks simplistic and you can easily see the entire map. Saying that, there are some problems with height of things, sometimes I get caught because I think a window is a lot lower than I thought- so I couldn’t just walk under it holding a dead body over my shoulder.
All in all, I just couldn’t recommend the game, it just doesn’t do enough right for me to really enjoy playing it. If the AI reactions to murders was maybe a bit more realistic then I would have enjoyed this a lot more. There just isn’t much difficulty in a game where you can leave dead bodies around and nobody will care, the police won’t even investigate the brutal murder(s) that just happened. It seems that most missions can be done by standing by an area where bodies can be hidden and slowly killing 1 by 1 until you get to a lower number, then going and killing off anybody that’s sleeping and then activating any traps to kill more.
If you don’t mind a game that has no challenge- you just want to run around killing people in different ways and try to beat your previous times/scores- then you should take a look at buying this (you can always refund it if it’s not for you) Personally, it wasn’t for me.

A fantastic game that defies generas; one moment you are playing a bullet hell, the next a twin stick shooter, then an open world RPG and then a Dark souls style action RPG.  Further Playthroughs unlock more of the story and context as well as some different mechanics that were not in the original play through.  Minute to minute, hour to hour, you perception of the characters and story is always changing.  What is the right choice and who is making the most moral decisions?  This is a question that you will continually ask yourself as you go to unlock all 26 endings of Nier: Automata.
In the past, I’ve had many problems with Open world games.  I find that very often, a company works to build an open world and ultimately populates it with quests that are of no consequence to the player.  They also focus too much on the overall size of the world and not the content of that world.  Its as though these worlds are just offline MMORPGs. After the witcher 3 was able to take all of the side quests and give them meaning and depth, I started to hold all future open world titles to that standard.  Nier: Automata does have some busy work style quests but they are not mandatory nor do they detract from the world.  Nier feels less like the Witcher 3 and more like a dark souls style world that happens to have many more NPCs and story elements.  The world in Nier is much smaller then many of the other popular open world titles but there is a ton of content to be played through here.
As mentioned above, you will end up playing the game through multiple times if you wish to fully enjoy the game and story.  There is much more than meets the eye with Nier Automata.  With each play through more and more of the story unlocks and it feels less like you are playing the same game over again and more like you are just playing a continuation of the story. (I can’t really say more with out adding spoilers).
You don’t need to be familiar with the past titles in the Drakengard and Nier series to play this game.  Though there are some call backs to the first Nier title, the story stands on its own (you can get all of the story from Nier through Youtube and other sources though be wary of spoilers.).   There were moments in this game where I literally cracked a smile at how clever and interesting the story was.
PlatiumGames really does some amazing things in this game as well.  There are some really interesting things to be said about the use of camera angles to change the game play and even the game genera.  The action based combat system is also extremely strong and does not get repetitive even after 20-30 hours of playing the game due to the amount of variety in the mechanics.  PlatiumGames really shows that not only can they make some great and difficult spectacle fighter games, but they can also make quality side scrollers, twin stick shooters, Bullet Hell shooters, action RPGs, spectacle fighters (of course), open world titles, platformers, FPS games and even Visual novels. Moment to moment there are pieces of mechanically stunning beauty in Nier Automata that you wont get from many other titles (if any).
Even if you don’t like games from the east (the anime aesthetic) nor the general story line; the social commentary and meta narrative about games in general is certainly worth the price of admission. Nier is a mechanically strong game with a deep narrative as well as many cool and interesting twists and turns along the way.
If you do have concerns about the bugs and software problems that people have mentioned in the other reviews, there are plenty of community made fixes that are floating about in the forums that help patch up these problems.  I'm sure the developers will also eventually add in their own fixes and iron out any of the left over bugs.  Also, make sure to keep a controller on hand; while most of the game can easily be played with a mouse and keyboard, some of the mechanics can be easier with a controller (though some are easier with a mouse).
Overall, Nier Automata came out of nowhere for me.  I got it because of the rave reviews I saw, the fact that it was made by platinum and it's interesting aesthetic.  That initial draw did not lead me astray and frankly I put Nier up as one of the most innovative titles that has been created in a very long time.  For me, Nier Automata is an easy game of the year and a contender for game of the decade.

This game.  This game starts off by confusing the hell out of you if you don't know what to expect.  Which is always fun.
I was going to write a long review, but I won't.  Suffice to say, it IS worth buying, it IS awesome, and it IS unique.  You will be confused, but happily, and you will rage, but click Continue anyway.
I actually have no idea when the game will end.  26 endings, and some endings are not endings but beginnings.
Cons?  Yes, one or two.  I WISH androids learned how to parry, rather than just dodge.  I WISH combat felt a little bit more visceral, as it's not always evident you actually hit anything.  I WISH the tutorial type beginning was a little more detailed (pod-throwing isn't even mentioned).
But hell who cares.  The gameworld is ridiculously superb, the ... let's say, cast, is just awesome.  The music.. my god the music.  It's just impossibly atmospheric, and you absolutely don't care if you hear it over and over.  And then you'll get to a certain point in the game.. and hear it all over again - and you still won't care.
Get the unofficial mod.  Set it to your maximum screen and window resolution, to avoid the clunky port upscaling (which I hope SE are going to fix).  Buy vitality pack.  A LOT.  Seriously.  Resist the urge to play on Easy mode, really, don't do it.  When you feel you just HAVE to, refrain from using the autoplay chips.  You'll enjoy the game a lot more if you feel like YOU defeated each boss.
And trust me.. these ARE bosses.  No spoilers.  Just throw away everything you know about other boss fights, as they're pretty useless here.
Try to play the game without using a game guide.  When (not if) you get lost, stuck or confused, just backtrack and try again.  If you STILL can't quite figure out what's next, find a spoiler-free guide.  You do NOT want story spoilers here, trust me.
Imagination, slightly out-the-box gameplay, stunning storylines.  THIS is what gaming should be about.
I know, after the 100 hours or so it's going to take to finally finish this, I'm going to have a 2B sized gap in my soul.
Next to a Velvet Crowe one.

MechaNika is a game about a bright little girl named Nika who hates her school and most of society. It is a lighthearted point and click adventure of her actions to create a device to reshape the world.
First off, this is definitely NOT a kid’s game. Although the game looks very child friendly and downright cartoonish, there are many situations, characters, and dialogs that are way out there. As mentioned, the graphics are nothing spectacular and can be considered a little lazy at times. Still I think the design fits the story better than high resolution graphics would.
The music in this game is good. There are a couple of really good scores in some of the locations. However, they are all quite short and repeat quickly. Especially if you are going back and forth between different locations a lot.
The controls are pretty standard. You mouse over something and you have options based on the item. You click on Nika and you can access your inventory, setting, or help.
The game is quite short. The first time through it will take a few hours just to figure out how some of the puzzles work and the order of running around. After that, you will be able to complete the game in under an hour. Considering the price of this game and the extra elements, it is definitely worth the price.
The worst things I can really say about the game are. First the start of the game tutorial. Unless I missed something, it is completely un-skippable and is very slow. Once you get out of the classroom, the game speeds up. The second is the main menu and settings.
There are no advanced settings for this game. There are a couple of simple items like changing the resolution, sound, and type of mouse pointer. For me resolution was the hardest thing to work with. I have my PC connected to a 4K TV and it did not want to work with any resolution I clicked through. In the end, I had to manually set my resolution via editing the preferences file. Once I did that, I had no more issues with video.
Ultimately this is a great demented point and click adventure. Hopefully there will be a sequel!

Very Fickle Recording software.
Considering all the options I tried that were available. This one was the best. There's obviously plenty out there that are better. But your choices in recording software range in price. You either pay out enough money that what you have is a statement. Or you settle for the free option that limits you. PlayClaw 5 is the middle ground.
This program does it job and it does it well. When it wants to. It's really a matter of what you're trying to record. What's great about this is that you don't have to do much in convuluted setups to get a recording going. And I like that. The GUI is rather simple and doesn't require you to ask people online for hours on end for an answer to a problem.  Startup PlayClaw 5, Boot up your game, and it's ready to record. Just press a simple Hotkey to start recording and go.
It isn't a space hog either. A lot of people will bring up that it sucks that you have to have Steam open, along with this and your game open all at once. But at least this program isn't a total space hog. I can have things open in the background like Google Chrome, Skype, Discord, whatever, and not have issues. Does suck when PlayClaw 5 picks up the beeps from messenger programs though.
Issues
That's for games that PlayClaw 5 agrees with however. It agrees with most games...(Keyword: most).  Other games is where PlayClaw 5 starts to act like a diva. Depending on the game, the program will either crash, record nothing at all, stop itself from recording, or continue recording despite that you hit the hotkey to stop it. Other times I record a different screen, I'll see one of my overlays appear in the recording as a messed up pixel (Usually the FPS counter). Worst case is when I get slideshow recordings, That's where it'll record maybe a few frames then freeze, then maybe, MAYBE move to another frame. It really doesn't like dealing with certain games or programs.
Give a few examples.
Bluestacks Emulator - You'll record nothing but a screen that says Bluestacks.
Alphadia Genesis - I have the FPS counter mess up. Then got where the video froze and gave me slideshow gameplay.
Dragon: A Game about a Dragon - Random Black Screens
League of Legends - Play Claw recorded the startup screen. But not the gameplay
Those are just a few examples. Some can be worked around. You can change the recording setting to not hunt for the window that has the game but just record the Desktop or Everything. Others I can't work around it and have to pray that a rerecording will fix the problem. Or just find a different recording software altogether. Not fun.
Another issue that pops up and that's if you're recording a high end game for a very long time. You get no warning about your Hard Drive being full. Once it reaches it's peak that's it. PlayClaw5 will forcibly stop then. But you won't get any warnings except from maybe your PC itself that you're out of hard drive space.
Customer Service
Customer Service is nice but not always helpful. They at least respond to your problems. I blame the program itself however. Cause when I ask for help from them they always tell me to send the crash dump file.  A lot of problems however aren't recorded by the crash dump file. So it leaves me in an SOL situation. Thankfully I haven't had any future problems in the recent few months but it's still a haunting memory that this could happen again.
Steaming
I only tried this out maybe once or twice. I don't really like it. I mean it's better than some alternatives out there that make you pay for a monthly service or just leave you hanging out to dry to solve problems. But PlayClaw 5 for streaming is meh. When I first tried it. It was trying to stream content to my viewers at 10,000kbs and I didn't know it. That's very problematic. So I had to cut that down.  I haven't really tried it again. Never found a reason to. I don't like livestreaming in the first place.
Overall
PlayClaw 5 for the price I got it for. Which was like 30 bucks due to a sale. Is worth it. It does it job right when it wants to. Doesn't interfere with my gameplaying too much. And that's generally what I like. Something can do its job and do it right. Even though it does get angry with me and fight me at times. It at least does better than many other screen recording software I tried out.

Stellaris is a great, if unfinished, 4X space game.
The core gameplay is fulfilling, and you can see where the devs are going with it. In that sense it's very fun to watch the game evolve while learning how to master it.
What they have now is a strategy game where you create the space faring stories of your own species. I found creating my own xenos with different government types very satisfying. It makes you feel invested in the stories that unfold.
Leviathans pushes everything in the right direction, mostly adding more of those story events that can define entire eras of your empire, like uniting your forces to kill a star eating monster.
You might find some of the mechanics lacking as of now, but you can still sink hundreds of hours into Stellaris, and it's only getting better.

While with a few hours of tweaking you can get decent recordings, but if you have a recent pc with any newish nvidia GTX with shadowplay [NVENC] or any cpu thats i5 sandy bridge or later [Intel Quicksync] You can capture using hardware with nearly lossless video quality using shadowplay or OBS, which makes this program a tough sell.
For starters, this software requires online activation EVERY LAUNCH, EVERY TIME. Your internet goes out and you want to record something to give you something to do? too bad.
The best method for recording video using this program for me is mjpeg or motion jpeg. Works well even on lower end gaming rigs but it comes with a caveat if you use adobe premiere or adobe premiere elements (i use elements 13). You will need to buy a codec called Morgan M-Jpeg Codec 64 bit in my case.
The support was decent, my mac pro pc was having problems because of its xenon processors and they made a special beta just for me! Now on my nice i5 1050ti gtx gaming rig there is almost no need. Using OBS I can capture 1080p 60fps using quicksync (onboard graphics processor IN the cpu) If your using a graphics card that onboard isnt used so it can be used to encode video making the cpu and graphics card not take any hit.
Shadowplay with nvidia cards is also a very tiny hit since these cards come with hardware built specifically for this. This can also be accessed in OBS called Nvidia NVENC came out with the geforce 600 series in 2012.
So the question you have to ask is do you have a sandy bridge intel quicksync (or amd equivalent if there is one)  or do you have an nvidia graphics card with shadowplay (or an amd equivalent)?
If you dont have either, Such as an older AMD chip with an older AMD graphics card and OBS isnt working for you.. this "could" be an option. But the online DRM makes it impossible to recommend. Online DRM should never exist and I will never recommend a program using it.
At 40$, its too much, I got the program for 25$ or so and still feel its too much. I say use MSI afterburner or OBS which are both free. Online DRM plus so many better alternatives makes this hard to recommend.
At the time of this writing I cannot remember if you can record to a file that has both mic and game audio seperate but I think recording to .ts like obs and using ffmpeg to split out the audio and encode it is the only option.

Purchase Stellaris.
Spend over 600 hours of your wretched life playing it.
Play around with mods to enhance your experience.
Finally find a few mods that helps with the convoluted war system that mires an otherwise exceptional gameing experience.
Install mods like Exterminatus and finally have the ABSOLUTE WARS you always wanted.
Create an extremely cute race of butterfly aliens that are just the sweetest things in the galaxy.
Unleash this blood-thirsty, genocidal, alien-purging tide of death on the rest of the beings of this pitiable universe.
Finally♥♥♥♥♥♥off the largest Empire in the Galaxy by purging DOZENS of smaller Empires and/or turning them into your tributary slave-nations.
Declare exterminatus on the delusional, democracy-loving aliens. The war will not end until they win or every world they control is wiped out.
Send your armada, outnumbered 3-1, led by your most senior but aging butterfly admiral to stop the alien horde.
Hope for the best but expect little.
Be amazed as this aging butterfly erases the largest Empire in the Galaxy clean off the map through 4 massive battles and dozens of planetary bombing routines, utilizing the tender embrace of flesh-melting chem-torpedoes and the loving touch of nuclear fire.
Observe in amazement that in the decade the war lasted no less than 4 tiny empires have emerged from pre-spaceflight xenos-worlds and now block your way home.
Laught as your legendary admiral erase their cultures and turn them into dust or tributaries in a few months and finally return home in triumph.
Regret that it's not possible to actually reward this admiral for her billions of aliens purged and the fact her species die around 135 years old, she lasted beyond 155.
Look for another mod that let you reward characters... while you realise you will spend another 600 hours on this addicting grand-strategy game and it's many exceptional mods.
TL;DR: Stellaris is extremely fun and entertaining, if oyu enjoy this genre of games and can immerse yourself in them However, it will consume all your time if you are not careful and mindful of the time you spend.
While it has flaws, most of those boil down to unresolved bugs, some clunky systems (like the aformentioned war system that, due to balancing concerns, is rather counter-intuitive) and virtually all of this can be handled with mods, of practically any flavor you desire. I woudl advice players to play a game or two in the vanilla game first, then look over mods for whatever aspect of the game you desire to change, as there is little point in modding a game you don't inherently enjoy playing.
Mods are spices, not replacements, after all.

This game is so well balanced that winning is all but impossible. Conquest is carried out one system at a time, in fleet battles. When you fight in a fleet battle, you're allies have a handicap because you showed up. Instead of your elite squad tipping the scales and sweeping through your enemies, your allies are turned to cannon fodder while you desperately try to wittle down the enemy to a managable size before you and your squad are the last ones on the map. Even this would be tolerable if the game would let you defend a system that way, BUT NO if your allies all die, the system is lost, YOU DON'T COUNT! And suppose you do manage to defend a system? Say hello a second enemy fleet before you can even reload your missle bays.
So the solution is to stay on the offensive, right? WRONG, your allies are too busy to reinforce you when you assult a system. Oh, sometimes they show up, but don't count on it. If you've reduced an enemy to only a couple systems, THEY GET A BONUS! And yes, they will manage to push you back time and time again.
This game is so balanced that the player is reduced to an ineffectual cog, at the mercy of the RNG. As powerful as you are, your enemy will be just as powerful. As much as you help your allies, the two front wars will screw you over every time. You don't have the information or the tools to turn the tide, and while you may get your money's worth of enjoyment, a fun beginning will lead to a frustrated end.

Deus Ex is a fantastic classic game. It is very reminiscent of System Shock 2, but not as good in my opinion. To start with a brief overview, it's got good, enjoyable mechanics. The cutscene driven story does a good job of portraying J.C. as a character which is cool since he's not just a blank Mary Sue. There are few decisions to be made, but I actually found myself making them along with J.C., since he's such a stand-up guy. It wasn't like in some games (Last of Us, Bioshock Infinite, others) where the main character says "And now we'll do X" and my response is "noooo you suck, stop it." I guess if you're a cool person too, you'll enjoy J.C.'s decisions.
Moving on, my unintentional test of how well I enjoyed this game was that I made it about half way through when my hard drive crashed. I hadn't backed up my save files (rookie mistake. go back up your save files before you finish this review). I then started completely over and didn't think "oh ♥♥♥♥ this♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;, but rather understood it as an opportunity to play a different game. There are many ways to tackle a given obstacle. For example, a door is locked. You can:
1. pick the lock
2. break the door down (crowbar, explosives, shoot it with a sniper rifle with a high enough sniping skill level)
3. crawl around it through vents
4. find the unlocked door on the other side of the room and not use any resources but time
5. hack a nearby computer to unlock it
6. find the key for it nearby or on the other side of the level
Each level unfolds very organically, and there is significant value to the strategic lessons you learn as you play this game. I got better at conservation of supplies by spending my time searching more effectively for progression means.
There are also a good number of options for the default mode of progression - bypassing enemies. You can kill them, blow them up, knock them all out, incapacitate them with pepper spray and run away, or just stealth past them. There's also no point at which you're forced to do any of these except the boss encounters, which are easily solved by re-loading once you know there's a bossfight up ahead and then chucking some explosives to where you know they're going to be. I didn't actually have any real 1:1 encounters because I was a cheap ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and exploded them as soon as I got in the room.
Unfortunately, it's not all good. This game is very unforgiving. Poorly constructed kind of unforgiving. It seems constrained by contemporary practices. When you die, the camera circles your body until the menu loads. Every new area, a message states that the game is saved, but I definitely never saw any of those saves. Also enemies will arbitrarily notice you; sniping someone from 100 yards with a tranquilizer dart will let everyone around him know exactly where you are.I eventually had to bind the numpad + key next to my right mouse hand to the quick save function so that I could sporadically mash that and avoid losing an hour's progress. After 40 hours of play, my save file has less than 20 hours because I had to reload so often.
There are also frustrating aspects regarding combat. I had resolved to kill nobody. I was using my stun gun and tranquilizer darts to progress. I don't want to ruin this approach for anyone, but it's just about impossible to actually do that. Also, sometimes I'd successfully knock everyone out without any casualties, and the gunnery sergeant would give me♥♥♥♥♥♥for killing people. Then there are the enemies late in the game that have just a stupid amount of health. It almost seems like they wanted to force people to diversify, somewhat like "well I know you wanted to be a peace officer and not kill people, but sometimes life just sucks". Almost.
10/10 would thunderbolt/burn/crush/explode/revive/gun-down/drown friends again.

Combat:

Logistics:

Red Sectors:
NEVER EVER EVER tell your ships (unless its the one you're flying) to enter a red sector... the game will spawn ships for the sole purpose of killing it, I've tested this on countless occasions and its 100% spawn rate, and its always a ship ether able to 1 shot it, or a fleet of ships able to kill it in less then 5 seconds...
*Ways you can get through red space with other ships:
YOU MUST escort them!!!
Going from gray sector to red you'll enter first then have them follow you.
When you get to the next gate, have them fly through first but be ready to enter the gate within 10 seconds of them entering or it'll spawn a enemy patroll / capital ship on the other side.
When exiting red space (red to gray) ensure the other ship exits first, then you can follow.

Your NPC ships have the mentality of a civilian ship and will just idol as they get murdered... keep this in mind and always fight enemies 3v1 in your odds, be ready to lose ships by the fleets as if the enemy ship is larger it will kill everything with 1 missile... Argon in red sectors (or past them any other aliens whom they dont build faction with)
Pirates whom are easy to deal with as most of the time they'll ignore you or you can find and kill their base as they dont randomly spawn like Argon do.

*Variety in Ships/Stations
The spaceships you can use, destroy, board, capture or disable are plently. Different classes (Scout, Fighter, Heavy Fighter, Destroyer, Carrier, Transport, Cruiser, Capital Ship, Boarding Ship, Missile Boat, Lasertower and many more)
Each Race owns different stations with different properties which require different materials, goods and also provide different resources or weaponry parts etc.
* Quests, Tasks, Missions
Besides the main story, there is a VERY large range of things to do in the game.. Buy the asteroid data or sector maps, build stations for others, follow ships to their secret meetings, escort or raid ships etc. You will find many things to keep yourself busy if desired.
* Immersive Design and Fluentness
It may sound weird, but you know there are some games that you want to play awhile but ending up playing hours of it and not even know how the time passed... Yeah, its that because there is always a great transition between the things you did, can do and will do in the game that you wont find a proper time to say : Ok Im done with it for today
* Harsh environment
You can deny if you want but we all know that is always better to succeed a hard task than a simple one... Sometimes, your mistakes or miscalculations in industry will cost you severely. Good thing is, there is always a way to bounce off the bottom rise again, it pushes you to think while playing too.
* Quality Soundtracks
That is actually my opinion, but usually every sector you fly to will put you in the mood of that zone... Except combat, combat music is a bit.. meh... But again, that is just my opinion
* Mod Support
Does this Need explanation? Very large texture or gameplay mods to improve gaming experience... DUH!..
NEGATIVE
* Insufficient Tutorial
Well the game does have a tutorial system, but just enough to say "yes it does have it" it only teaches you the basics and the most fun parts (advanced systems, complex installations, running economy, ship design and weaponry etc.) are either learned from the internet or experience... It was both in my case. So be patient if you really want to taste the game's true potential and trust me, its not Quantum Physics, you can get the hang of it in no time.
* Needs more User-Friendly Prompts, Commands and Interface
What I mean is, this game is very deep and large in scale and detail that even though game offers very advanced and complex ways to fulfil your tasks or goals you still need various interactive ways to make things more accurate or better. It falls victim to its own depth in gameplay.  (There are plenty of mods to improve this, you can still be satisfied with the current system if you aren't a fan of mods and prefer vanilla experience, so no worries)
* Minor AI problems
As I said, they are minor... Sometimes (Rarely) a huge transport ship you hired from Paranid Empire can not fly to the jump gate because of small asteroids or similiar objects and detours indefinitely. This has very simple solutions with no fix or mod requirement (like flying out of sector and waiting for it to come) and similar little problems like these. In case it is needed, mods to fix these issues can be found throughout the web.
* Needs More
Yes, yes I know I said this game has plenty to offer but you would understand if you played. They make the game so large that you will start asking for more even though it has serious amount of features in it already... Frankly, they released a patch (which is in expansion pack size) with a whole bunch of new things and 2 major storylines and more sectors with races and such... The developers provide, respect.
OVERALL
I would give this a clear 8.5 / 10
Mainly because it gave such an experience that I bothered to write a review about it!... Oh yeah, its my first review. Hurray.
Also, I have played EVE Online for 4 years so if you already know that game, you will be familiar with the concept of this game. I also recommend X3 Terran Conflict & Albion Prelude to those who own the latest X title (X Rebirth) because you will witness completely different experience nevertheless!

They updated it, after all these years they still improve their masterpiece, not only did they release 3 major patches all in the size of DLCs that add tons of new content, they updated it even when it did not have almost any issues at all, just to improve its stability, gameplay and mod-support. Moreover, they updated the entire X series, not just this game, X3, they even updated X4 as well on the very same date, and they updated that one with immense content again... I have no words to describe my loyalty, gratitude, appreciation and respect for the devs.
