Not quite sure how to recommend this game. Overall i feel it's a mediocre game. It feels kinda flat to me. Once i got the best ship/gear that i could and still found myself overmatched and ineffectual at overall game progression (conquering the sector) the game lost its allure.
I'll try to review the game by going down the bullet list of key features from the store page.
>Squad RPG progression via skills & perks, upgrades & modules.
Yes, to a VERY basic extent. your squad has 10 levels, 2 options per level. If there are gear upgrades, they've not been implemented yet, or are somehow so hidden that i've not found them in my hours of playing.
>Deep trade system with dynamic supply & demand, affected by events, piracy & conflict.
I dont know that i'd characterize the trading system as "deep" however its not bad. General supply and demand is spelled out for planets.  "random events" consist of something happening on a planet. Diseases require medicine, civil unrest requires worker placation, starvation requires food, etc. That's how you can get exp as a merchant, by fulfilling needs of planets. However, its drastically slower and more difficult to xp up as a merchant than it is as a fighter. I found it particularly frustrating that you only get xp for "completing" the task. "We're sorry captain, you only hauled us 90 units of food and we needed 95, we will reward you with nothing and give all the recognition to the guy who hauls that last 5 units in." It's the same way for kills in combat, but at least there you can see the enemy ship's health bar and try to manage accordingly. There are no numbers for planetary demands, so its 100% black box. I did feel that trading in a certain area would lose profitability over time, so that was a nice mechanic.
>Fluid real-time combat with tactical pause & a wide variety of weapons.
Combat is fluid, pause is necessary/nice. There are a variety of weapons, but i dont really feel that they distinguish themselves greatly from one another. Most function very similarly to each other IMO, while a few are novel, but i cant see how they can be utilized effectively (plasma cannon is very energy efficient, but travels so slow that unless you're ONLY hunting capital ships, its never gonna hit, and that hamstrings its potential so much that i never touched one.) Missiles are missiles. The bigger ones cost way more than the tiny ones. Maybe i'm a cheapskate, but i always used the starting ones (cheapest) and spammed them when appropriate (almost dead stuff to get the kill) and docked frequently to reload. There wasn't very much differentiation between missiles, they just all kinda did the same thing. There's one to shut down a ships engines, but to what effect? Moving out of range to snipe him? The shut down isnt long enough for that tactic to be meaningful. Retreat option? Not really, the only time i had to retreat was when there was a SWARM of♥♥♥♥♥♥after me, so one or two missiles stopping one or two ships was gonna be pointless.
>Resource gathering to upgrade to higher tier modules and looting of combat kills.
In addition to universal currency (credits) there are two resources (ores) that must be spent on higher tier equipment. They are available from various sources, mining, conquest and mining worlds. Availability used to be poor, but has been changed and is much improved. I find the concept annoying as♥♥♥♥♥♥ I can sell excess ore to SOMEONE for money, why the hell cant i buy ore from that same SOMEONE if i have excess credits? It's just dumb.
>Factions will conquer & defend systems with fleet movements. Your actions, big or small, have a major effect on the tide of conquest!
Factions do conquer and defend systems. The AI seems to have a good ebb and flow where the 3 major factions seem to keep each other in check. If one gets a few extra systems, the other two seem to leave each other alone and gang up on the one who appears to be "winning".  According to the forums, factions down to 1 planet go into overdrive, spitting out a nigh-endless stream of ships. Stupid.
As for my actions having major effect on the tide of war? I have not felt that way in the slightest. Even with a pretty dominant ship and crew, i do not dominate system battles between two factions. Not saying i should, but it would be a very concrete way of seeing my effect on the "tide of conquest". I suppose the mechanism is that my hours of pirate purging in my chosen faction's space has allowed their economy to flow much better, leading to faster ship production and therefore larger fleets that can conquer systems better. However, i get ZERO feedback that this is taking place, so the reward for my actions is very nebulous, and can easily feel nonexistant.
>Random events offer opportunities and also ensure no two game plays out the same.
The random ship events feel very much tacked on and dont have any large meaningful effect on gameplay. There's only one significant beneficial one i've found, and many that are utterly worthless, ie a delivery mission deep into enemy territory for paltry reward.
>Random encounters offer interesting side-quests or tough choices with major consequences.
I guess they somehow felt the need to differentiate this from the previous bullet. Its the same thing i guess? I never felt any major consequences from these encounters.
>Many classes of ships offer different tactical possibilities, including Carriers!
There is some meaningful differentiation among ships. Turrets, missiles or drones. Some ships favor one over the other. I'm a turret man myself, i passionately hate running out of ammo when you've almost downed that big enemy for a fat reward, so i haven't played some of the other possibilities. However, i'll admit that when i bought the bigass capital ship that came with 3 large drone bays, they were a pretty sweet addition.
>Clever enemies that fly their vessels to abuse their strengths. Fast & agile ships will flank and out-speed your big guns, large ships will broadside tank with their strong directional shields.
They make it sound fancier than it is. Small ships fly around somewhat wildly, making targeting difficult, while larger ships.....dont. The only strength that clever AI's will "abuse" is their ability to go OFF THE EDGE OF THE ♥♥♥♥ING MAP, or hide behind the minimap or squad portraits where you cant click. They will SIT there and shoot back at you. Its not a HUGE deal, but its beyond infuriating sometimes and I dont understand how the dev thought that it was acceptable to have the game operate in that fashion. It could be easily rectified by having enemy ships hit the edge of the map the same way a player ship does.
>Take part in epic fleet battles with Capital Ships duking it out among support ships and hordes of combat drones!
In order to buy a capital ship, i had to play on roguelike, so death was a deal. Now, a huge battle like that is a great opportunity to have a bunch of enemy ships spontaneously decide to WASTE you in very short fashion, so while these epic fights sound great on paper, when you're actually in the middle of one its utter chaos. Additionally, its a nightmare to manually shoot in the melee, since the computer gets very pissy with friendly fire.
>Tweak-able Squad AI, never be caught flying with stupid, ever.
Squad AI seems decent. I've never seen a squadmate randomly take off after a whole damn fleet by himself and get blown to♥♥♥♥♥♥ so thats a plus.
>Challenging, but fair Rogue-like-esque gameplay.
99% true. "Bounty hunters" have ships that have inflated stats.

The factions will backstab each other, and ones with fewer systems will build ships faster (which makes lots of sense, right?) to preserve the status quo. Not much fun once you start figuring that out.

X3:AP is the answer to the question: "Can I rule the Universe?". And as it turns out, the Universe is huge, and often doesn't like being someone's plaything. Whether you rule through sheer economic control, or by your mind bogglingly vast array of ships, or even rule at all, it's entirely up to you.
You start off as a speck of dust fighting against Solar winds. You trade Ore, Energy Cells, Space Weed, anything to increase your bank balance. Soon enough, you're able to buy a second ship, leaving your rusty old trader to do the menial task of trying to make you more money while you, in your M5 class Recon ship the size of a VW Bug, start scouting the worlds around you. You discover Pirates, anomolies, sprawling asteroid fields, dead planets, industrial sectors, weapons smugglers, slavers. The rest of the Universe ignorant to your very existance, carrying on with their lives. You decide to buy an M3 class Fighter, something with a little more bite than a Recon ship. You hunt Pirates, thieves, and a sentient AI race long since relegated to this portion of the Universe. You buy an M6 class Corvette, your first 'big ship'. You swat Pirate fighers away with ease, go toe to toe with anything smaller than you without a scratch. You join the war effort, but never picking a side, you're only involved to make more money. Now you control a fleet of ships from the helm of your M7 class Frigate, patroling portions of the Universe for your chosen 'side'. Your vast number of stations churning out much needed goods and weapons for your all consuming fleet, generating you money on the side to replace your losses. You now straddle the world around you from the helm of your M2 class Destroyer. Impervious to anything smaller than you, you're a beacon of sheer militaristic domination. Entire fleets surround you as you patrol your own corner of the Universe, safe and content to reap the profits of greedy nations, consuming weapons and ammo in their campaigns against each other. You relax, with a bank balance to rival most nation's, safe in the knowledge that there will always be more war, and more profit to make somewhere.
X3:AP will make you feel stupid, but then very powerful. Once you get over the initially very daunting interface, it all becomes second nature. Tapping off T>C>2>1 to tell your targeted ship to engage enemies, or T>C>3>3 to get your trading vessle to trade. It is difficult to learn, but the menus are consistent throughout the entire game, so once you've learnt it, it becomes childplay, your fingers almost dancing over the keyboard while issuing commands to ships on the other side of the Universe to you.
Then once you get the hang of the UI, the entire game opens up to you. You can be a trader, a pirate, a smuggler, a salvager, work for militaries involved in a bitter, almost endless war. You can choose to shape the Universe through your actions, or to ignore the Storyline completely and carve out your own trading empire. Maybe you want to be the largest Ore producer in the Universe, muscle out the competition, start your own Ore cartel? Or maybe be the Tony Stark of the X-Universe, be the largest weapons manufacturer ever known? Sell guns to both sides, then sell more. You can hunt pirates, or maybe join them as an ally, or maybe a neutral party, selling them drugs and slaves as they need it while avoiding the wrath of Military police?
The issue new players have with X3 is the sheer scale of it. Most players would be put off of a game where you are given a ship, 100,000 credits, a rough direction to head, and told to go play in the sandbox. You have to make your own fun, almost. My recommendation is to just use your imagination. Set a lofty goal and strive to reach it, it'll give you purpose in a world that will happily carry on without even knowing you're there.

Title: Party Hard
Genre: Action, Indie, Strategy
Developer: Pinokl Games
Publisher: tinyBuild
Release Date: 25 Aug, 2015
Game key was supplied by the publisher.
--------------------------------------
Party Hard is a top down, 2D,  mass murder simulator in which you play as a someone who gets a little cheesed off at his neighbours for having an extremely loud party at 3am. He decides to take matters into his own hands and goes on a murderous rampage. As you do.
As much as I hate to say it, that is pretty much it with the story. However, you do get a quick cutscene between each mission which shows the story of detective John West as he tries to catch the ‘Party Hard Killer’. Although these cutscenes are extremely badly voice acted, and even though the speaking characters are changing, it sounds like the same voice actor desperately trying to put on a different voice but failing miserably. If you are looking for a game with a detailed progressive story, this is not the game for you. Although most people buying this will see from the get-go that this game is not designed for it’s story.
The gameplay is as you would expect, fun but shallow and without any real challenge. Your character will walk around the party wielding a knife, slowly bumping each person off until no more remain.  If you murder someone, the police will pay a visit and put the body in a boby bag, leave it on the middle of the dancefloor and then bugger off somewhere else without even investigating what happened. This will continue happening as you stab as many people as you see fit until the dance floor is strewn with body bags and the rest of the party attendants still dancing their night away like nothing has even happened- occasionally going off to the buffet table because the sign off a mass murder has given them a craving for pineapple and cheese sticks.
The fun element will come from the traps that you can use throughout the map. There are a great amount of traps and each time you replay the mission, the traps may have changed or may be in a different location. These traps range from exploding speakers, to poisoning the food and even driving a car over a hoard of people (you do not control the car) However, these traps still fall under the same problem as the stabbings – the car could have driven over 10 people at once and they are now currently mush on the pavement- but nobody else will care (they won’t even call the emergency services) because THE PARTY MUST GO ON!  Trying to get the perfect ‘massacre’ is where the fun begins and ends, trying to get best kills without getting caught is really the only thing this game has to offer, which is a real shame.
If you do managed to be silly enough to get spotted and you cannot wipe them out before they get to the phone to call the police, then the police will come. Only one officer though. You now must escape. How do you do that you ask? Drive away? Kill the police office? Don’t be silly, just play the ol’ switcheroo by climbing in and out of a window (or other trap door locations) Just as the police officer gets near you, climb out of a window, and then as they try going back round the front door to get to the other side, climb back in. Once you have used an escape route to escape from a dimwitted officer, Mario will come and board it up and you cannot use it anymore (seriously, he looks like Mario).  Be careful though, the police are not the only ones who will arrive- other units such as the SWAT team and FBI can also make an appearance, which makes the game a tad bit harder.
You are able to hide bodies in certain locations. This will help stop anybody from seeing the dead partygoers and in turn, the police will not be called. The thing that irks me is that you can stuff as many bodies as you want into a dumpster. Want to cram 50 people in there? Sure, go ahead! Games such as Hitman have done this better by only allowing a maximum amount of bodies to be hidden in one location. The game would have provided gamers with a bit of a rush to make the body disposal areas in places that maybe get a bit more lively. Having a dumpster outside that only about 1 person walks to at a time makes no challenge. However, putting a disposal area in say a bedroom cupboard, where you have to quickly dispose of it before any moment someone can come walking in. (although this would not work because you can see the entire map and where everyone is at anytime, maybe they needed to add in a line of sight feature)
One of the redeeming features were the songs they used in the game, I am a bit disappointed that there was such a small amount of music variety used. What is currently there is amazing, it gets stuck in your head instantly and is very enjoyable to listen to- but a larger library of music would have been preferred.
Another redeeming feature is the graphics. This art style has been done many times in the past, so don’t expect anything to ‘wow’ you, but it really does work for this game. Everything looks simplistic and you can easily see the entire map. Saying that, there are some problems with height of things, sometimes I get caught because I think a window is a lot lower than I thought- so I couldn’t just walk under it holding a dead body over my shoulder.
All in all, I just couldn’t recommend the game, it just doesn’t do enough right for me to really enjoy playing it. If the AI reactions to murders was maybe a bit more realistic then I would have enjoyed this a lot more. There just isn’t much difficulty in a game where you can leave dead bodies around and nobody will care, the police won’t even investigate the brutal murder(s) that just happened. It seems that most missions can be done by standing by an area where bodies can be hidden and slowly killing 1 by 1 until you get to a lower number, then going and killing off anybody that’s sleeping and then activating any traps to kill more.
If you don’t mind a game that has no challenge- you just want to run around killing people in different ways and try to beat your previous times/scores- then you should take a look at buying this (you can always refund it if it’s not for you) Personally, it wasn’t for me.

This game was a gift to me & I must say - so far i'm not dissapointed.
This game feels like a pixelated version of Silent Hill 3.
From the blonde main character, to going through creepy corridors in a seemingly other wordly demon dimension.
It has similar sound effects too, as well as the mandatory "save" areas that are marked by a floating symbol.  Even the map style, functions & markings are similar to Silent Hill, which is handy as the map automatically updates with the areas you've been to, marks areas that are locked/blocked & things of interest.
The game play is fairly simple, you play as Claire & must navigate your way through endless dark rooms & corridors.  You have a lighter & flash light to aid you {although it seems best to save the flash light power if possible as it runs on batteries that you need to collect}
It's easy to lose your way within the game as a lot of the rooms  look similar & there are MANY rooms.  So it's handy you have a map to refer to.
I've not played tons of the game yet but instantly you're aware of what you need to do & the controls are fairly straight forward.  So far the story line appears to be unfolding about Claire being in hospital, visiting her mum.  Swiftly everything gets dark/dirty & instantly scary.  Armed with your light & a little help from a random dog you must find your way through the corridor maze & try to avoid creepy dark shadow people.
Even from playing very little, I get the feeling it's going to be long, have a decent storyline about Claires traumatising past & you'll probably be able to predict how the game will end about half way through the game.
Great atmosphere & a splendid little horror that will make you jump.

Simply fun! Party Hard puts you in the shoes of effectively a 90's Slasher movie, where you are the serial killer.
You travel the country going party to party, silencing the fun, and ending all heavy parties you can. In between each level is a rather interesting little narration/interview where a police detective is being interviewed about the case and what they tried to do to catch you.
It makes the rather long loading screens bearable , as this takes place during each level.
The soundtrack is also great, although I would have liked if more tracks were played during each level. For me it takes an average of 30 minutes per Party; and during that time difference music would be fantastic.
As mentioned the average level takes me around 30 minutes, this is because you have to be rather patient during your kills.
You can't just go nuts and slash madly, you have take your time; wait for someone to be isolated and then deal with them. Accidents are key though, and the more the better. Sabotage items, and have people fall for that. That way you don't have the attention drawn to you.
Even with as many precautions as possible though, make sure you are Never spotted near a body. Even if it was an accident, if no one saw the accident, and they then see you they will instantly connect you to the death and call the police.
If the police is called on you though, you can escape them. First you can try and find a change of clothes, that'll make them lose you right away. The other method is to use trap doors to move between areas. Eventually the police officer will get tired and just leave.
Once this happens though; Mario shows up and proceeds the lock and block off these escape routes.
Occasionally you also need to deal with Bouncers; which will beat you down until you die. Avoid them, until you get the chance to take them down which can be a challenge.
All in all Party Hard is a heck of a lot of fun. I've played 6 levels so far and I'm still really enjoying it.
I would happily recommend it to anyone.

This game exceeded expectations for me! I have played this with a few friends and hours just slip by as you combat the harsh weather, defeat difficult AI, conquer your surroundings, all whilst discovering the story engraved into the Alaskan wilds.
Firstly, the story is incredible, if you have the patience to do the grinding to get the levels. The game is so much more rewarding with a few friends to play with, as the element of difficulty remains, yet objectives are easier to reach. A lot of negative reviews highlight the 'lack of content' in this game, yet I have to staunchly disagree. There is a plot, and it's very interesting. I have only ever reached the 'end of part one' after 4 hours playing with friends, so there's defintely way more to this game than meets the eye.
Obviously some down sides to this game are that there are glitches. At the time of writing this game is in early access, yet I've seen a few patches and a few updates to the game, so the devs are clearly still working on the game. Even so, some of the glitches are 'game breaking'. I died when I was flung into the air having defeated a wolf after 3 hours of playing. Needless to say I had zero motivation to continue that game and reclaim my stuff after grinding for so long. However, I know I'll pick up the game again within 24 hours and have another crack.
Overall, I'd say this game, once the bugs are ironed out, will warrant a 10/10 rating. At the moment it's 9/10, with huge potential. It's defining a new path for survival games, smashing 'bars' set by games like Don't Starve Together. Can't wait to sink my teeth into this game some more, and I'm hoping the developers add lots more to the game to make it action packed!

Party Hard plays as a stealth game with action elements, as you attempt to murder everything in sight without getting caught. The levels in their first few playthroughs work, but eventually they will only really be replayable for those who like score attacks and perfecting runs. It gets the subtle humor of a horror movie down with little things, and overall, it's the kind of game that some gameplay footage shows exactly what kind of game it is: and that's a good thing. Whether or not it's for you is whether you like the strategy stealth genre, and if you have patience.

Easily the best game I've played in a long time. Please buy this game and play it.
Nier Automata is a fantastic game on its own and as a sequel to Nier which is a game I hold close to my heart. While it doesn't have the most in depth gameplay you'd find in other Platinum titles, they really brought out a solid and good feeling gameplay to compliment Yoko Taro's great direction in plot and settings. It's a game that tells its story as much from its presentation and mechanics as it does from its cutscenes and there wasn't a single point that the plot didn't grip me in some way.
As with any good game it's still going to have its flaws but I don't feel they hold it back but it's worth mentioning that the grind is a bit silly near the end if you want to get 100% and the flow of combat can eventually be stale once you find your optimal setup.
To finish the compliment sandwich and not end on a note of complaint I'll say the side quests are (with few exceptions) just as interesting and gripping as the main plot and add a lot of value even if a lot are just fight and fetch quests much like the original Nier.
Bottom line is this game expands on everything Nier needed to and still keeps the wonderful plot full of twists and turns that will make you feel uncomfortable or even upset and is absolutely worth your time to play to completion. Please don't spoil the game for your friends either!

Fun game. Was gifted by a friend so that we could play early access multiplayer. I will say that its alot funner to play with other people and easier of course. Playing solo should be fine though. Dying and server resets would just suck alot more.
You basically wake up post-plane crash and told to surivive. It has a story line so its not just about straight up surivival. Story is interesting and feels a bit like LOST but in the snow.
Keep in mind my observations are as of the date posted and I've only played multiplayer. Check the dev logs and more recent reviews to see if they are still applicable.
PROS:
- Graphics look great. The models for the actual characters could use work but the environment looks amazing.
- Gameplay and UI is really easy to learn and get into.
- Story line gives you something to do other than surivive. They plan to have multiple story lines which would keep the game interesting.
- Dying sucks pretty badly (your levels and gear reset), but its not an unrecoverable position if you've planned for it because anything you've made like fires and chests still exist with their contents. (Not sure if this is the case in single player) Plus you can find where you died and pick up your old inventory, you just might not have enough inv slots to carry it all since that requires leveling up your character. There is no level restriction to use stuff, just to make it.
CONS:
- Biggest and obvious drawkback is that the game is still a bit buggy. Animals glitch out sometimes, dropped items glitch, etc. One time wolves only appeared for one of my friends while 2 of us couldnt see them. Stuff like that.
- My friends were working on a MP server for quite awhile before I joined them and I guess because of an update or something, we had to rehost the server and start over. Be prepared for that if you purchase early access.
- If you play MP, you wont be able to see your friends on the map (need to talk to them and use grid coordinates to meet up) or see their map progress (if they explore something and you dont, you would never see it on your map)
- Aggro can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ If you're running from a boar and and it runs into another animal it will trigger aggro on you even though you're just running. A single boar or wolf chasing you can turn into a huge problem really quickly.
- Once you beat the story lines, I'm not sure this game will have alot of replayability. In this case, its simplicity becomes a negative. You're not in any pressing danger to do anything really. The closest thing to that are winter storms and they don't really become an issue once you've leveled up. Scarcity of hunting and especially stone is a thing and that might be the only reason you have to move on from an established camp.
CONCLUSION:
Its a great game and has a ton of potential. Early access has only been out a month and has alot of room to grow. Would def recommend if you are into these type of games. Would keep an eye out for updates and the dev log though since it is early access and the game as it is right now can def use work. If the improvements stop, would probably not recommend buying it as it would probably just end up a 40-50 hour game.

As cute as the game looks and starts out, don't be fooled into thinking that this is a game suitable for kids! There are several dark and/or mature subjects that are dealt with in the game. Also, graphic images (yes, even cartoon nudity can be 'raunchy'). I understood the creator's intention of being hilarious and shocking in a game that looks like you'd least suspect it, but playing this when there are people are not around is generally not a good idea. Unless of course you don't mind explaining yourself and the filfth that is on your screen all the time.
The game objective is fairly simple: find items to make the ultimate killing machine! The how is simple as well: get them by talking to people and/or doing this for them. It gets a bit repetative, to be honest. As long as you keep this in mind: your objective is never to open up locked area! You could finish this game very fast. There is ONE place however where all gamers appear to get stuck. Everyone knows what I'm talking about - when you've acquired a certain outfit. Gentle hint: find places to hide in WITHOUT entering a house or building. Good luck with that.
Another major disappointment is the climax that the game reaches. Nika's tension is building when you receive more items over time. You actually find yourself getting excited with her. So what is to expect when she finally manages her objective? Well, nothing much... Whether that is nothing much because Nika's plan is grander in her own mind than put to practise or because the game is just a short little indie plot, I'll leave you to discover that for yourself.
I wouldn't recommend the game. Its settings are a bit too much over-the-topness mixed together. There are so many places that are locked, that you imagine there is a lot (more) to discover, but no...closed is closed (off). Nika is much too gifted to be 6/7 or whatever, but whatever. I started as a Militarist/Materialist/Collectivist Squid people of the Valroran Science Directorate.
My two allies were the UN (Filthy humans) and the Akkadian people (Some Fungaloids).
We started at the top left corner of the galaxy, we're an organized group so this was going to be a federation victory anyway. To our immediate south was a fallen empire, Fanatic Xenophobes... great. Between our 3 allied factions were a faction of horrible Insectoid people called the Vir, they were an upstart empire that had huge chunks of territory, they were an IMMEDIATE THREAT, they were Fanatic Xenophobes, Militarist, and on top of all that, they were also strong and rapid breeders. The Humans started off as the weakest of the 3 allied empires, with the Valrorans and Akkadians as the two dominant powers.
Our first task was to cause chaos to our neighboring empires, invade them and liberate the new worlds under our names so they adopt our ethos and love us, it was a huge success thanks to the Akkadian Empire's massive ground armies. The entire top left of the galaxy was soon a cookie crumb of small civilizations that hated each other except for their saviors. Our next task was to destabilize the Vir roaches. It was a lengthy campaign which costed tens of thousands of lives, it took almost 60 years to break up the Vir roach empire into little vassals, even after their downfall the Vir roaches were almost impossible to deal with, being fanatic xenophobes the Vir people were almost impossible to intergrate properly into the Valroran empire without rebellious factions popping up.
My empire had conquered and enslaved several primitive planets at first (Middle ages, space age civs) and adding stellar empire races into my list of slaves was starting to feel like a burden, so I immediately opted to first regulate slavery for better working conditions, then ban slavery all together.
. Not only were these ungrateful lesser races not happy with being emancipated, they also started forming more rebel factions faster than ever. After 10 years since I passed the law to ban slavery, I immediately reinstated it (Xenos only of course). The next 20-30 years my allies were helping me fight off rebel wars happening in my territory.
Suddenly, the fallen empire to our south awakens, we almost break our economies just to field a fleet large enough to fight the greatest threat in the galaxy so far. The Valroran fleet warps in first taking the brunt of the hit, then the Akkadians and finally the Human fleet. The battle was tense, the Valroran fleet was wiped out in the first battle against the 50k fleet power Fallen Empire. We thought we had won, we suffered extremely heavy casualties, suddenly the Fallen Empire's second fleet warps in, 60k fleet power. During the battle, the Akkadian fleet suffered extremely heavy losses, losing the entire fleet in the process, but somehow the Human fleet pulled off the impossible and destroyed the remaining Fallen empire fleet with less than half its fleet power. Now the Human Empire became the strongest force in the galaxy, with the strongest lead in technology and economy, as well as fielding the most powerful ships. The Valroran owned the most planets, the Humans had the strongest tech and economy, the Akkadians had the largest and most professional ground army in the galaxy.
Skipping ahead, the Fallen empire to the south was completely eradicated with technology we stole from them and a much larger overall fleet size. Not even the scourge threat were a match for our combined fleets.
During peacetime, my Human ally asks me if I could purge a planet for them from the annexed fallen empire systems. (The Human empire had a strict no slavery no purging policy). They send me control over the planet temporarily, I start purging the inhabitants of the planet and pass control back to the Humans. The Valroran Empire now deals in slavery and purging services for a nominal fee, the biggest customer is the Human Democratic Utopia.
Our game isn't done yet, but
: My empire has now devolved into an empire that deals in black market services such as installing slave processing plants, purging races and exporting slaves.

A disappointing collection of features, really. Sectors are still ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, like they were at launch; whole sectors starve because the AI just doesn't create food-buildings, and it builds infrastructure extremely slowly even with a population present to work the buildings. The start of the game has always been extremely slow as well. It really takes a LOT of time to finally get going.
Other species types more or less just make them like or hate you more, it does not affect what they actually do what-so-ever. You'd think intelligent species would be great at research, or strong ones would focus on armies and mineral boosts, but no and no. The only thing traits seem to do is change your starting relation you have with them. Otherwise, I have experienced all empires to be just as aggressive as any other. Even Pacifist empires does not seem to affect this. The only empires that seem to behave differently are the genocidal maniacs that will be hostile to everything and everyone.
The Ship Designer could be much better, but it's fair enough. You have several module slots you fill with weapons, shields, and reactors, and a separate section where you put in engines, scanners, engines, warp drives and such. With this ship designer you can create fleets that can hard-counter enemy fleets, but the enemy can do the same, so you gotta have a balance. The Ship Designer is one of the better aspects of the game, and is a bit of fun to tinker with.
However, the most fun I have is throwing massive fleets at other fleets. Seeing potentially 400 ships engage in combat is quite a sight. But even that experience is underwhelming, since you have literally zero control of your fleets once they engage. Yes. Z-E-R-O involvement, if you exclude that one button that retreats your fleet into a nearby system. There is no targeting priority for ships, although it seem like the size of weapons have a bias for "equally" sized ships; so medium weapons target medium ships and so on. There is no other fleet formation other than the default formation, which is absolutely crazy they have not implemented yet after so long. The game really wants my important ships to stay all the way in the front so they all die first, while the cannon fodder derp around not doing much until it's too late. If your fleet engange two or more enemies that are a distance from eachother, the fleet will split into randomly sized chunks and fly towards their target. I've seen 10 or so smaller frigates slam their dead hulls agains several battleships. You cannot select any singular ships in combat and focus down the most important enemies. You cannot micro damaged units behind your fleets so they don't die. There is just no control, and it's really sad to watch.
For a 4X game it's very meh, with colorful combat. If you really like space based 4X games you may enjoy it. If you are on the fence, don't buy it.

Genre wise, Stellaris seems to be somewhere between 4x (with closest game being most likely Galactic Civilizations series) and grand strategy (like Europa Universalis 4), but... It is really hard to evaluate this game just based on genre.
While playing, I often think that - instead of trying to copy various elements from other games - designers just wanted to create space game based on their dreams - and this is very visible in a gameplay.
Stellaris is very unique even when comparing it to already very innovative Paradox grand strategy games - while in most of Paradox games combat is the main focus and everything else are just means of making the conquer easier/harder, Stellaris is highly focused on exploration and economy/society management. From one side, this is just perfect - game is unlike anything else, it is simply fun. On the other hand, it is basically impossible to create randomized interesting exploration encounters, so they start to repeat even on a second gameplay and you know almost all of them after few more gameplays. Game is still fun, but loses big part of its "magic" because of that. I am fairly sure that incoming DLC will fix this issue, at least for next few dozens of hours.
From technical side, graphics are good - not perfect, not bad, just fitting the game well. Ship design and combat could receive more touch, but - as combat is very small part of the game - this is not that important, and combats make up for that with huge scale of end-game battles. Music on the other hand... Just a masterplace. Seriously, even if you didn't bought or don't want to buy this game, try to find a sample music from this game and listen to it. You won't be disappointed.
To end this review, I also have to add that developers got away with lots of gameplay elements that would cause scandal/activists outrage if the game was set in more present-day or past settings - just imagine a WW2 game where you can purge the whole nations (or enslave them), genocide your own population or kill people who do not see the world in the same way as you do. This game is playing with things like that all the time. (and this is a good thing, at least in my opinion)

With the Deponia series up to a trilogy, Daedalic Entertainment brings you another one of their line-up of games that attempts to try and restore the nostalgia of the early point-and-click games from the 90's. That game is "The Night of the Rabbit", alternatively called "The Rabbit's Apprentice".
Although the title is not a major problem of the entire game (considering how most of the game is focused on a young 12-year-old boy named "Jerry Hazelnut"), it's harmless enough.
In my opinion, this game feels ENCHANTING to play through. From the moment you start playing it from the moment it concludes. It's exactly how I feel a magical adventure needs to be driven. Obviously, I haven't played the Deponia series yet, so I wouldn't be familiar with the gaming elements that Daedalic Entertainment incoporates in their line-up of game titles.
The story has a couple of pacing issues here because of the puzzles but even that dosen't deter that the puzzles are creative and thought-provoking (not to a brain-aching degree). The puzzles in this game were logical and that makes it much more prouder. But when the story picks up, it's usually around 6 hours into the game. Turning from a light-hearted beginning to a dark twisting turn towards the end. The story is deep, complex and revolves around the dark side of Mousewood. Many people might find this to be a derivative story, as Harry Potter had this kind of plot also but while I find it not the best story a game has to offer, it's enough to make a game to support it.
The HD-graphics provided in the game are lush, clear, vibrant and sometimes colourful and really blends in with the tone of the story. Throughout most of the game, I took most of the magical setting of Mousewood and wanted Daedalic to expand more on the mythology of Mousewood as my interest is high.
The music is absolutely WONDERFUL and it matches the music quality of Rayman Origins as my favourite video game soundtracks of my past gaming experience. Throughout the soundtrack, it follows one leitmotif and is heard in a couple of variations throughout each track and if you recognize that leitmotif, you'll know the whole game. Tilo Alpermann has done a great job of captivating the story of the game and transpired it into music.
The characters are also well done, too. Each character I interact with has their moment on the screen. There is no comic reliefs, no over-the-top characters and DEFINETLY NO LOVE INTERESTS. The characters here are subtle and help add more to the story, development to the main characters and more to the history and setting of Mousewood.
However... the voicework is a bit off. Most of the time, the acting ranges from "not even trying" to "I'm REALLY trying" and yet comes off as a first read of the script, with Jerry becoming the weakest.
The sound mixing is inconsistent. For example, I had my music volume to 50 and my voice volume to 100 and yet I STILL cannot hear a word they were saying half the time. But a subtitles overlay option available resolves the issue.
The dialogue was OK, but sometimes, the dialogue in the game can be a bit repetitive, as if they were trying to help pad the length of a point-and-click game. Repeated lines like a laugh, a "Bah!", or even "mumbles", "whispers", croaks" & "snores" really makes me want to skip that portion of the dialogue. Sometimes, the characters in the game tend to slow down the speed of their dialogue to an absolute snail's pace.
There were also a couple of bugs and glitches I spotted during the 3rd act of the game and that almost ruined the game's experience for me as it lags, stutters and just stops, and I had my computer down to the lowest settings.
Oh, and the "Quartets" mini-game is the worst mini-game I have EVER played. The reason being is that the card game is like "Go Fish" and the opponent ALWAYS KNOWS WHAT CARD YOU HAVE!
If you are a huge point-and-click fan, BUY THIS GAME. If you like being challenged with thought-provoking puzzles, BUY THIS GAME. It's one of those point-and-click games that wants to be explored and will be with you forever.

'Deus Ex' is easily amongst the top five RPG games I've ever played. Ancient PC and backwards-compatibility *cough* is a match made in heaven. I'm a bit late to the party but glad I ended this absolute classic.
Coming to the game, the environments were expansive, open, involved a lot of running around and backtracking. This was in contrast to Human Revolution which proved to be fairly linear in comparison. Voice-overs were monotonous and emotionless. But I didn't mind it too much as it suits the entire grim cyberpunk-themed setting of the game. HR was no different in this regard either.
Mission structures were very well done. Lots of alternative routes to complete objectives. Many games have a broken system but Deus Ex was flexible enough to cater to both playing styles. I liked how you could go full stealth, all guns blazing or settle with a mixture of the two.
Exploration rewarded bonus points which were redeemable in the form of skill upgrades. It was virtually impossible to fully upgrade all skills early in the game so my protagonist never felt over-powered at any point. My main gripe was with the augmentations. Apart from a few augs, I never really found any utility for the others and I tried a variety of playing styles.
The story was excellent! It was rich but not too convoluted or branched-out as is the norm in RPGs these days. The plot was focused and almost all side missions had relevance to the main storyline. And the story characters were largely interesting, in a peculiar sort of way.
Some observations about its prequel, Human Revolution. I like how it stuck to its roots and also fixed many of the original's shortcomings. Hacking, for instance, was a much improved feature and augs were better utilized.
In terms of similarities, playing style was appointed at the very start. You get to choose between a knife (if you like hand-to-hand combat) or a crossbow (if long-range is your preferred method). Some unforeseen choices determine the fate of your friends and allies. Boss fights were, again, laughably easy. And not to forget, multiple endings right at the final juncture.
I loved this game. Had the option to apply mods to improve the textures and lighting but I chose to play it in its original glory. Even after more than a decade, this game not only holds but has also aged very well.

An excellent puzzle platformer with Paper Mario aesthetics mixed in with dark, morbid humor.
I wasn't expecting much going into this, but I ended up having a ton of fun playing it.
The maps are decently sized, and it's filled to the brim with a vast assortment of fun, quirky npcs you can interact with.
The gameplay revolves around you aiding said npcs by finding items they need in order to progress.
One of the main selling points of the game is that the whole world is made of paper and stickers. You can peel parts of the map to reveal hidden objects or characters, and you can even slap one sticker onto another to get through a puzzle. There's also the ability to read minds which always leads to some silly dialogue.
Overall, I loved this and found this to be a pretty enjoyable and memorable experience.

Medieval II: Total War is probably my personal favorite entry in the Total War franchise. This is partially due to my love of the time period, partially due to my previous obsession with the original Medieval: Total War (if they added that to Steam, I'd snap it up in a heartbeat), but largely because it managed to find the perfect balance between complexity and simplicity when it comes to campaign options - a balance which later entries in the series have tried to reproduce but often fall to one side or the other in attempting.
Like all Total War games, Medieval II features a turn-based strategy map where the player manages their armies and cities, and a real-time tactical battlefield where they play out combat against opponents' armies. Medieval II covers the medieval period of Europe (and includes northern Africa and portions of the Middle East), allowing your faction to attempt to conquer the entirety of the western world of the time.
It's fantastic and an enormous timesink. The graphics hold up surprisingly well for a game that was almost released a decade ago, in large part because the spectacle is so based on the massive numbers in the armies instead of incredible detail on the individual units.
Medieval II is a wonderful game, and I heartily recommend it to any strategy fans.

It’s not bad. Just disappointing.
You’re a dude who has an alien stuck in his brain and now he has telekinesis and mind reading and a bad guy is after the alien. The story is pretty simple and overall, it progresses at a good pace. Each level has a mini story and an overall mission. Each character you interact with is a piece of this overall mission and you do the standard adventure game logic of “get item, place item, reward”.
However, the characters are kind of boring. Each one only has one trait and they usually disappear after one area so they don’t feel interesting. Each one spurts 1 or 2 lines and except for one joke referencing the godfather, I didn’t laugh at all. I didn’t know much about these characters and I didn’t want to.
It’s an adventure game. Talk to people, collect items, repeat. In this case, you collect stickers which you can apply to other characters and objects. However, the gameplay isn’t super deep. With one exception, each sticker is used exactly once and it’s not challenging at all. Just make an entire trip through the level talking to everyone on the way and they will literally tell you what sticker they need most of the time.
There are also platforming sections but the only challenge is the fact that dudes chase you through the section if they see you. In the later levels, it gets pretty tedious because you basically have to stand in a particular location, place a sticker on a dude, and run for it. It’s trial and error rather than anything fun.
The art style of paper in a 3D environment is just fantastic and it really is super creative visually. Not a fan of the characters personally but I can see that a lot of love went into the visuals. The voice acting is varied and there are a lot of characters but see above for boring characters. Ran great and never crashed.

I'm all for games taking inspiration from other works, as long as they use that to build on their own concepts. Silent Hill is, of course, a brilliant horror game to take inspiration from, representing such a deep well of gameplay and oddities to choose from. Claire chooses not only to take inspiration from Silent Hill but also Lone Survivor, another indie game inspired by, you guessed it, Silent Hill. So what does that leave us with?
The game opens with Claire fighting off nightmares while dozing in her mom's hospital room. When she steps out for coffee, everything goes all shitworldy and she ends up running from actual nightmares, reliving several traumatic moments in her life, and trying a million busted doors. The side-scrolling gameplay is strongly reminiscent of Silent Hill games, with a huge, sprawling map of rooms you can only get into about half of. You usually have a goal you're trying to reach, but unlike Silent Hill the purpose in reaching it is never very clear. Nor is how you get there, because a great big building is really hard to navigate in 2D. It's a similar problem to Lone Survivor except way worse, because each of the three areas you scramble through is like SH3 mall-sized.
Unlike the games that inspired it, however, Claire has no combat. Instead, you are expected to flee from the strange ink-blot looking monsters that roam the endless halls. Ironically this actually takes a lot of the tension out of the game, because you have a generous amount of sprint and can run directly through and past your foes. As long as you are paying the tiniest bit of attention, you can easily avoid ever being caught. This renders most of your inventory items moot, since most are for healing your health or your sanity, a system cribbed from Amnesia but without any clear purpose. And if there are no weapons or ammo or any pressing need for healing items, there's no real reason to explore, is there?
I keep seeing this trend in indie games where they take heavy inspiration from a popular game but only get halfway to the same level of design. Much like Our Darker Purpose was to Binding of Isaac, Claire has all the parts of a Silent Hill game (or Lone Survivor successor) without actually making them work together. The enemies inspire no terror, the items are pointless, and the maps are confusing and sprawling without giving any reason to explore them. A disjointed story is laid over all of this about an angsty teen being an angsty teen because maybe bad things happened in her life? Whatever it is, it takes far too long to get to the point.
I honestly started out pretty okay with this game because it was simple and the art is really good, but after 90 minutes I could no longer push myself to finish it. The story was going nowhere, the level design was just hallway after hallway with more and more monsters, and then I found a really cool room that killed me without warning. Literally without warning, it just suddenly popped up the pause menu, except I couldn't unpause because I was dead. Well, I can take a hint, Claire.

I've read parts of the books and I believe that the neutral path is closer to Geralt's thoughs in the books, so I expected a neutral path explored here, but it's no big deal. The "bad" thing is that is mandatory to chose a side and I don't feel that way is the way of the Witcher. Overall the game is shorter than the first one, it has few things to do and they don't delay the story so much so expect it to be very straight foward.
The gameplay was the improvement I noticed the most. The skill tree they made for the game allow you to chose between 3 paths that will shape the gameplay. I liked that. Now you have a better focus on your equipment and on the alchemy system, unlike the first Witcher where you could beat the game without changing too much your equipment or using alchemy at all. The exploration and the map are smaller, it gives you the famous "false open-world". In fact you are confined to the city of the act you are and its surroundings, that aside the pontual sidequests and the beautiful views, has nothing more to offer. Also the swords styles are now simplified. You retain the silver / steel sword mechanic, but the group / strong / fast style is gone, and that's brilliant. Now you start with normal style, neither strong neither fast, and you improve it in the skill tree. The group attack stype is an upgrade on the tree, so you don't have to switch the style in the mid of the battlefield anymore. Thanks CD Projekt Red for that, the game feels much more natural now.
Talking about the sidequests, the sidequests were a nice surprise. So far, no sidequest was equal, you have the idea that every sidequest is unique. Yes you have a coupleof sidequests that involve trolls and destroying monster nests, but even those ones require diferent methods to beat. You have somewhat 10 sidequests per chapter which boosts the game for more or less a dozen hours.
The music is fantastic and reminiscent of the first game. Let me just say that the field music in the first Witcher was way better,but you won't be disappointed. It's still very good and suitable to the game. Graphically it's needless to say that is better, showing that they put a good use to the money they made with the first game. Fantastic views and villages, the NPCs no longer look all the same and there are many more people wandering in the villages. The locations are well made and not bland anymore by a long shot.
Now the flaws... Bugs. It's full of them. The game is bad optimized, even though this is the enhanced version. The game simply exited to the desktop a couple of times, it's very annoying when that happens because you lose all the progress. People appear / disappear from nowhere and chests don't give everything they have, some items just stay stuck there and it isn't a way for you to claim them. The minigame of the iron arm had some bugs too, sometimes it doesn't allow you to win, even though you reach the end of the metter, not to talk about the dice game where sometimes the dices fell out of the table and didn't appear anymore on the table, making you lose instantly. Even though, it has less bugs than the Witcher 1. None of them is a major fault but the one that makes the game close.
Summarising, it's a very good game with a very nice story, good gameplay, good characters, good ambience and music. It's not perfect but I can count with the fingers in my hand the games that are perfect. It's completely worth the 4€ I spent for it in 2014. It's like the best game you can buy for that price and is often in the steam sales. If you like RPGs it's a must and mandatory before playing Witcher 3. Not for hack and slash fans, this is a full fledged RPG and is played like one, keep that in mind when you buy it.

Of course, if you liked the weapons from Borderlands 2 (my biggest complaint about the game), then you'll probably also find a few types of guns you'll like here.
One minor point about the game is the lack of really memorable characters. No catchy "CATCH A RIIIIDE"'s to be found here. However, Jack is absolutely perfect. His arch fits the world so well and I can't help but actually feel for the dude.
The new mechanics are nice as well. The added item slot, the oxygen mask, adds some very nice gameplay and mechanics to further specialize a character or build. The oxygen requirement in certain areas dictated play in a few areas, but none of it seemed negative. The new stomp attack is done well and really helps close range combat which I always felt was a major negative in this series.
All in all, the game was fantastic. A solid 8/10.

You wake up in a airplane crash and find yourself lost in an cold area. Get ready to survive!
　 The Wild Eight forces you to run after resources for your survival. In the game you can walk, run (with skill), open doors, read notes left by people who didn't have same luck, face wild animals and even other players. The controls are simple and structured.
　 The game also has an intuitive crafting and skill evolution system. At first you will have a tent and a workshop, these items are unique, you can pack them and load them to another base. They cannot be created again and in case you die, you will receive new ones. They have upgrades, which allow you to craft better tools / weapons and get more advanced skills.
　 In The Wild Eight, you will face wild animals, and heave to deal with other players, the multiplayer mode has pvp and chat integrated, you can fight or create alliances. System is awesome, no lags and the loadings are fast. The game also has the singleplayer mode to adapt you to the game in the third person. The camera has a great zoom, you have a map and a list of quests to complete.
The graphic engine reminds me of "The Flame in the Flood", almost on realism but with a cartoonized touch. The scenery is cold, beautiful and the places where you can explore are rich in details. The soundtrack is instrumental and original, always passing a feeling of solitude and isolation, calm and sometimes melancholic songs.
Amazing. I'm kind suspected to say, for loving survival games, but The Wild Eight has exceeded all my expectations. Game can be beautiful without requiring too much of your computer, the multiplayer system works perfectly, without lags. The game isn't easy but not impossible. HypeTrain has managed to structure everything in the right measure to have an incredible game. Low price for a high quality game. Worth it!

MechaNika feels very fresh. It's cute, twisted, lighthearted and funny. I struggle to remember the last time an adventure game was this cool. The mischievous Nika with her grand but misguided ambitions reminds me of being a kid again, while the adult references and quirky humour make it entertaining.

The Game was fun, and boast alot of potential. Graphic and setting were simple and nice in maintaining the feel of loneliness and chilled fear of what is lurking in the dark.The diverse roles really opening the game to different experiences per play.
The Issue though is it is more for co-op than it is for single player. With the current gameplay logic and rules you consistently haved to worry about food, warmth, and life. Food, continuously going down and even faster during  when gathering, to add it is scarce unless you get some hunting equipment up and most of them I question their functions. You haved to maintain you warmth no matter what, when you start you can huddle by the wreackage of the plane, but progressing it act as a limiter to how far you can travel which isn't bad, but when also having to keep an eye on food and supplies it can pose a challenge or halt on progression. Then Life The main stat which matters above all, can easily go down with lack of food, freezing, suffering an injury, or illness. To avoid most illnesses you haved to cook food or have medicine handy. to avoid freezing must find ways to maintain warmth which can pose difficult when you haved to figure out a way to balance it with getting food , gathering needed supplies and not getting killed by something. It can become over complex repetitive job which kills the fun.
I am not saying these are bad, suriviving out in the cold is never an easy deal and it is what fuels the game. From what I see though is that they game was intened more towards multiplayer as their are different roles like the fighter, gatherer, builder and healer. This would divide the work load and allow for easier self progression along with building team progression. So unless you really want a challenging single player surivival experience or have a couple friend thatll consistently play by all means this is worth a shot , as some issues do clear up far later in the game as you increase you skills.
For me though I won't reconmend only because there are other games that have fully developed that deliver a more reasonably polished experience both in multi-player and single-play, even for a better price. That do not use a four direction camera which honestly killed it for me as you really do have a limited view especially when trying to kill a wittle rabbit or surivive a wolf. Finally that arent early access games as I am usually cautious when purchasing, as games like these as amazing and full of potential they are often get set to finished way to early or stay in early access hell, despite the heavy feed back one may commit .

The swordplay has weight and the combat becomes very instinctual and fluid once you get the hang of it. And if you're playing the game on 'hard' it is HARD AS ♥♥♥♥, which is awesome. Only about five hours in and the story is already building tension and mystery. Also, the soundtrack for this game is breathtaking. It reminds me of the original Ghost in the Shell film OST, which is what I think they were going for considering the many similarities between the two. So far, it's one of the best RPG's I've played since The Witcher 3, and the best game released within the past year, and I've only played so little of it. I had to come and leave a review because of this euphoric feeling I have from playing this game. It's truly a work of art.

Claire awakens from a happy dream about happy friendship bears to find herself at home in bed with shadows lurking over her. The shadows close in and you're given a choice to call for your parents, hide or get out of bed. The room is covered in pink, but marred in shadow. The only light sources come from a clock that reads 3:33 and an open window that lets in some moonlight. When the girl hops out of bed to scurry out of the room in a 2D side-scrolling fashion, she's yanked back toward the shadows that lurk over her bed.
After that she's allowed to scour her darkened how looking for the brother and parents. Windows illuminate dark hallways that have shadowy birds flying through them. The screen begins to flicker, shake and glitch as each room gets darker than the next. Static on the television, the only lights pop as Claire walks by and shadowy soccer balls roll by her feet. Minutes tick by, but the next clock still reads 3:33 as well. The moon must be shrouded as no more light shines through the window's open curtains.
When Claire reaches her parents room, everyone is gone, the bed is floating and her mom tells her that everything's going to be okay. That's when Claire wakes up curled in a ball on a chair inside the St. Barbara hospital pediatrics ward. There's a photo of a happy couple in the background with a different photo of a beach over it. The room is lit by a light overhead and red candle that flickers. The curtains are half open and its pitch black outside.
Claire is a young blonde girl with barrettes in her hair wearing a hoody and jeans. Claire knows that she needs to stop sleeping there, because that place is getting to here. From that point Claire wanders the hospital floor. The place is pristine and nothing out of the ordinary other than she's the only person there. There are still hints that a black fog or haze watches her from just beyond the light's reach.
She can run, jump and open doors to get from one area to the next. We can assume that since she's in a hospital that's the reason why she can't run fast or run a long distance without running out of breath. There are plenty of maxcell batteries and cola for her to collect marked as shinny objects here and there to catch her gaze.
Several doors are locked or blocked. She can even hear the television on inside and the doors that are unlocked Claire wants to leave the inhabitants in peace. Its routine for Claire, she says its always been quiet at night. Hallway after hallway, they begin to get darker and unfriendly. After searching through a dozen hallways its safe to say that Claire is alone.
There is then a sign of life, her phone rings,s he answers, but the person on the other end hangs up. She finds plenty of things to interact with, plaques, couches to curl upon and rooms that let her save any progress. Upon reaching a coffee room, Claire says that there are still a few hours before school starts and she needs to get back home. Then she says she misses sleeping in her own bed. So it seems that Claire has a conflict. Stuck in a hospital overnight that she needs to go home from. Waking up in a chair rather than a bed. She's in street clothes instead of a hospital gown.
It is just an ordinary, mundane hospital. The water tastes like dirt, there is a rickety elevator that almost breaks with her in it. The elevator opens on the wrong floor. She feels that she must have pushed the wrong button. Soon the rooms become uninviting. Rust seeps out from vents. The bright lights get dim. There's a scratching sound and before she realizes, she's staring at a hospital bed with a red candle on it and a shadowy mist hovering over it.
The mist slowly consumes the entire room before  Claire herself is on a table with red candles around her on the floor, shadowy figures walking around and a giant, fleshless, meaty creature hovering above her. Does it have a face? Is that a face? No is that also a face? Are those four giant teeth or four giant nails? What are those dozen shadow people around her? Claire is stuck, something is holding her down.
It all comes to an end though as a barking German Shepard makes the shadow men dissipate. She knows this German Shepard, its her dog Anubis or Ani as Claire likes to say. With her faithful dog here, the bond is broken and she's free to move while the fleshless muscle creature stays clung to the ceiling.
Claire realizes her phone is busted, the hospital is dark with only dim lights or red candles here and there, so she's forced to use her lighter to guide the way. This lighter never runs out of fuel and she soon finds a flashlight to light the way, but it requires Maxcell batteries.
The hospital has changed completely and its in disarray. Furniture strewn about, doors have giant chains and locks around them. Some hallways are blocked off with rubble. Claire has to push things aside to get into doors. Something happened in this hospital.
With her faithful dog here with her, she needs to meet the challenge to survive going room to room in a labyrinthine complex. Going through air ducts, elevators, doors and so on. She checks each closet, bathroom stall, locker and trash bag looking for items to stay alive. Lucky for her she has a map that shows where she'll be headed, what doors are locked and which ones need keys. Claire can pick a door's lock with a hairpin and enough time to do it. With each cooridoor containing plenty of doors, Claire can find herself lost with each new hallway without checking her map.
Anubis growls, Claire wonders what it is, but she soon learns to recognize that when Ani growls, there's a presence with them. A shadowy figure with a white outline of a face that will charge the two of them and chase them from room to room. If she hides beyond a door, the creature will smash the glass and begin to course through the door turning it black until the being springs into the room with them. Their only resolve then is to hide in a laundry basket or closet. The creatures make static screeches to crawl up Claire's spine.
Every time a shadow creature touches her it drains Claire's health and the only way she restores it is by chugging various types of cola or coffee. She also has a sanity factor and the more she sees, the crazier she can become. Depleting health or sanity mean most certain death for her.
Claire's only real power is to face her fears and bait these shadow creatures through room after room until she finds a closet to hide in so the creature can walk by. This hospital is a hostile place with scarce resources. There is a limited bounty of batteries and cola so when she's out, that's it.
As isolating, atmospheric and terrifying as the hospital can be, there's someone else in St. Barbara. There's another patient here that Claire will inevitably find. You get choices for Claire at key moments, but I feel they are of little consequence.
The danger comes from more than these creatures and giant shadow reapers, there are a few hazards here and there, such as her own mind working against her. Claire has dark hallucinations of when she picked a dog from the pound. Her mind twists the memory into something horrifying. The dogs int heir kennels are only a pair of glowing eyes. You can begin to wonder what is her reality. Who she is and why she's stuck in this hospital.
I think the bottom line here is that the game is a tense experience that gets lost in hallways.

Purchase Stellaris.
Spend over 600 hours of your wretched life playing it.
Play around with mods to enhance your experience.
Finally find a few mods that helps with the convoluted war system that mires an otherwise exceptional gameing experience.
Install mods like Exterminatus and finally have the ABSOLUTE WARS you always wanted.
Create an extremely cute race of butterfly aliens that are just the sweetest things in the galaxy.
Unleash this blood-thirsty, genocidal, alien-purging tide of death on the rest of the beings of this pitiable universe.
Finally♥♥♥♥♥♥off the largest Empire in the Galaxy by purging DOZENS of smaller Empires and/or turning them into your tributary slave-nations.
Declare exterminatus on the delusional, democracy-loving aliens. The war will not end until they win or every world they control is wiped out.
Send your armada, outnumbered 3-1, led by your most senior but aging butterfly admiral to stop the alien horde.
Hope for the best but expect little.
Be amazed as this aging butterfly erases the largest Empire in the Galaxy clean off the map through 4 massive battles and dozens of planetary bombing routines, utilizing the tender embrace of flesh-melting chem-torpedoes and the loving touch of nuclear fire.
Observe in amazement that in the decade the war lasted no less than 4 tiny empires have emerged from pre-spaceflight xenos-worlds and now block your way home.
Laught as your legendary admiral erase their cultures and turn them into dust or tributaries in a few months and finally return home in triumph.
Regret that it's not possible to actually reward this admiral for her billions of aliens purged and the fact her species die around 135 years old, she lasted beyond 155.
Look for another mod that let you reward characters... while you realise you will spend another 600 hours on this addicting grand-strategy game and it's many exceptional mods.
TL;DR: Stellaris is extremely fun and entertaining, if oyu enjoy this genre of games and can immerse yourself in them However, it will consume all your time if you are not careful and mindful of the time you spend.
While it has flaws, most of those boil down to unresolved bugs, some clunky systems (like the aformentioned war system that, due to balancing concerns, is rather counter-intuitive) and virtually all of this can be handled with mods, of practically any flavor you desire. I woudl advice players to play a game or two in the vanilla game first, then look over mods for whatever aspect of the game you desire to change, as there is little point in modding a game you don't inherently enjoy playing.
Mods are spices, not replacements, after all.

This game is an insult to any sim-game, particularly those from the late 80's-90's Maxis era of sims,
First, its not actually a capitalist simulator. Capitalism is a complex system of self-interest that has many players. As the "capitalist", your role is as someone who "earns" money and then reinvests it according to that self-interest. But there is no reflection of this in the game.You don't have to manage how many workers that a business has, what wage they are paid, the various taxes you must pay, the various input costs of the units that you are selling etc.  All you do is click on a type of business you want to buy and as you click one input unit, the price increases per unit. The money then earns itself. Microeconomics fail.
Second, you don't actually have to "compete" with any other capitalists. This means that you employ monopolist tactics. For example, a key mechanic is buying a business. However, cost of each unit of "business" increases with every purchase. Eventually you will be faced with a decision where the price of buying another business outweighs the actual payoff where you reach the limit of "marginal revenue vs marginal product". The game tries to accommodate for this limitation by roughly doubling the speed you earn money, which would in theory work, but the game prices for each business are "balanced" in such a way that it still isn't economically sensible to actually invest in a premium number of units, because your other developed businesses earn more than the relative investment you are making. Macroeconomic fail.
Third, there are a lot of mechanics that could be implemented that would actually make this game fun. Lobbying for/against a government change that helps/hurts your business, dealing with pollution as a consequence of a vast production, dealing with labour problems if your workers go on strike (do you increase wages or outsource the jobs to scabs?), expanding your market to international territories which brings new advantage as well as costs (ie exchange rate? labour/capital costs?), raising money for new ventures/businesses. Do you go to a bank for a loan? Or do you issue equity? When competing with other capitalists, do you actually stay competing? Or do you risk collusion for safe money at the expense of being found out by the regulator?
Finally, the thing that makes "sim" games fun is the learning experience in that you get to understand complex dynamics that occur in managing quite complex systems and understanding the feeling of accomplishment that stems from building something big from something small. All this "sim" involves is a unit-input clickfest that doesn't teach you anything and doesn't reward risk....the thing that capitalism and good games do.
I'm not even going to address the "Angel" mechanics or the "buying gold" (ie spend real money for valueless in-game money) mechanics, as I am too disillusioned with this stupid game.
