TL;DR Fun, fast paced (combat) space sim, deep trading system that is super simple to understand (and exploit), and lots of variation in weapons, ships, skills and factions so no 2 runs have to be the same.
This game is NOT what I expected, and I'm very pleased it delivered so magnificently on every thing it does.  Halfgeek or Huy did a spectacular job with this game.  I love the fact that even though it's a 2D game, it factors in the 3D of space by adding the evasion stat!  The factions are drastically different, and each of their ships not only have their own variations between factions but also within! (You like fast, nimble ships? Starborn ships are basically the equivalent of the ship grade below, but can take less dmg.  Wanna be super beefy? Omni ships have no shields but regen hull HP AND get better dmg resistances just for being Omni!)  There's 3 selections of "profession" in the beginning, and while I've only really experienced the hunter in depth, the pirate seems feasible too.  You can play this however you like.
The weapons have a nice balance, the ships are well done, and the overall balance of the game is fantastic.  You may run into trouble with one faction or another due to your weapon types, but with a little research, a little money, and some experimentation, there's nothing this game throws at you that you can't take.  The faction standing system is well thought out, and adds a great kind of currency that makes you really work for it.
Overall, this game is good.  Not great, but enjoyable, replayable, and madly entertaining for how, for lack of a better word, repetative the gameplay is (which I normally abhor, but the whole fight, loot, sell, and fight some more works).  It's a little lacking in the RPG aspect.  The skills of the pilot you play and the team you recruit are well done, but there's not a lot of "story" to the game, so if you're looking for that, this game isn't it.  Not to say there isn't some good story-telling going on here, the NPC quests are well done, if a bit short.
The devs, who are responsive and play this game probably as much as any of us will (Halfgeek responded to my review the day I put it up!) are currently working in new content despite the game being "finished" (first major addition after I picked this title up were a whole new class of ship for one of the factions that drastically change the way you fight!).  So all in all, this game is superb.  The asking price is a PITTANCE for what they could be charging and still receiving.  Don't let the looks or the low price tag fool you, this game has moxy, guts, spunk and a few cans of whoop♥♥♥♥♥waiting to be opened!
First Glance:
I want to start off by saying I bought this for the relatively low price and expected to get something that would hold my interest for brief periods at a time.  To my very pleasant surprise this game is great.  There's not a lot of hand holding or tutorial, it plays like an 80s/90s game where you have to read the "instructions" (and this made a massive difference in my success after taking the time to read it).  I don't have a lot of hours in this, and I'm not very far either, but it is wildly fun, despite the fact that the encounters (at least thus far) don't have a lot of variation to them.  The selection of ships, weapons, types of weapons, modules skills and so on is downright impressive, varied and a lot of freaking fun.  The only complaint I have is the ore currency is a little confusing.  If you try and mine it, it's unclear if you've obtained any before docking at a port, which sucks because it costs you 250 (which, yes, is a pittance once you're going and on a roll).  I'd also like a little more detail in the planet descriptions when you scroll over in the map to help with understanding purchasing ships/loadouts (like the fact that a "capital" planet will have the best ships for that faction, but the best weapons will be at say a research facility or factory planet or so on).   The one serious complaint I actually have is the fact that the random encounter that is supposed to send you to go get your first squad member is well, not a have to do thing.  I thought the guy was setting me up for a trap and declined to go!  But otherwise, this game is a lot of fun for anyone who likes space sims with squad set ups.  Anyone who's played the Star Wolves games should enjoy this, but maybe not quite as much as those games.

Stick It To The Man is a hilarious adventure game first, but it also contains elements of platforming and stealth, and it's what I imagine what would look like if Beetlejuice-era Tim Burton made a stage play.  You play as Ray, a regular man with a regular life who by accident is suddenly merged with an alien entity named Ted, who confers him telepathy and telekinesis via a giant purple hand that sticks out of his head.  On the run from a shady organization with evil plans, Ray must find a way to return to normal while also stopping the organization, all the while using his newfound powers to help people around him.
I've been interested in this game since its release, but I've put off its purchase for a long time.  I instantly regretted that once I started playing.  This game is easily worth its full price.  Following the storyline and getting every achievement will net you between 4 to 5 hours of playtime, which is the perfect spot for the price while still mantaining the novelty of the gameplay.
It's a really easy game (though, like in all adventure games, you're bound to get stuck for a bit at least once), it's more about the experience than the challenge.  Outlandish characters, fourth-wall breaking, and overall funny dialogue are the meat of the game.  Gameplay-wise, the majority consists of using your abilities to solve puzzles, by both reading minds and make use of stickers to change around the environment.  There's also some light platforming and a few stealth sections, but they're there just to add some variety and they're mostly a means to an end.  They're not by any means bad, they're just the least interesting part of the experience.
What else can I say?  Buy this game now, you won't regret it.
Still better than its successors, even it doesn't have a multiplayer campaign.

Claire is a 2d psychological horror game very reminiscent of  Silent HIll. You play as Claire as she navigates multiple locals to complete missions and progress the overall story. You have no weapons, only a lighter/flightlight, your wits and your pet dog (Who will only warn you of nearby enemies, but I suppose that is more than my cat would do) to navigate through the nightmarish halls to out run and out smart the lurking monsters.
Speaking of enemies, some will attack you physially while some will attack you psychologically, causing you to become scared. If Claire stays scared for to long she will begain to take physical damage, so in essence you have two health pools to manage.
Like any survival game, you can explore and scavenge for health items, notes and batteries for your flashlight, not to mention some pretty interesting puzzles to find and solve. If you explore the right locations you will occassionally come across other survivors who can offer you side missions to do while exploring. These are not mandontory and can be skipped all together.
There is replayability value in the game as there are multiple endings you can unlock based on what you do in game. Completing the story with a decent amount of exploration you can expect to finish up in 4 to 5 hours.
If you enjoy survival horror I highly recommend this game. I also recommend the coffee, again.

Borderlands: TPS is a uninspired, uninteresting, boring, repetative, and tedious romp through a boring, uninspired world. The game does manage to be funny, for the first half hour. I bought this during a sale about a year ago so my cousin and I could play online together. It just wasen't fun. I did manage to beat it eventually, mainly out of curiosity, to see if there was some redeeming quality I missed that was saved for the late game. There wasen't one.
After getting deleted, I decided to try again, this time in The Handsome Jack Collection on my PS4, to see if it could suck me in all over again like Borderlands 2 did. Nope, within a half hour I was reminded of why I hated this abomination. The skill trees are all centered around anarchy-like skills, do this ... thing and get temporary bonuses. The Aussie humor is terrible and the psychos no longer shout funny stuff (if you can even understand them). The maps are convoluted and irritating with backtracking, confusing pathways, and insta-death pits. Oxygen is a pain in the a**. Claptrap is useless, which is a funny story in itself. The game "warns" you if you heard of Claptraps crazy action skill and asks if you still want to play as him. This should be taken as a warning. He is rendered useless by his totally unreliable action skill. I would also say his skill tree is crap but they all are. It takes a long time to get access to the extra inventory slots. It felt like I was running around for half the game with 2 weapons. I could go on with more faults about the game but you get my point.
I'll sum it up with this; if you are thinking of getting this to scrath your Borderlands "itch", don't. Just go back and play Borderlands and Borderlands 2 again with all the DLC, which there is plenty of. If I had to score it I would give it a 4 out of 10. Why? The entire first drawn out paragraph says most of it, but on the plus side, it seemed to be relatively bug/glitch absent and it had great production values. After the first half hour, it's all downhill. Pass on this.

Let me just say that Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel does muster up a lot of the good old things in Borderlands 2 but it also lacks a lot in depth.
The Pre-Sequel is set on Pandora's moon Elpis and is taken place between the first and second Borderlands.  While having to venture out as the villains or "anti-heroes" in this game.  We actually get to see the events of what happened prior to Borderlands 2 (the rise of jack, dah's involvement both on Pandora and Elpis, etc).
There isn't much there besides that most of the game does remain the same as Borderlands 2 there aren't any major changes aside from low gravity and O2 kits for oxygen.  The low gravity in this game takes some time getting used to and it's frustrating to go up against enemies that simply jump up and fly away (problematic for second winds and snipers).
Menus remain exactly the same as it did in Borderlands 2 and of course the graphics still look good. But the major problems here are the consistent bugs throughout the game.  There's way too much clipping with you and your enemies.  Sometimes it's easy to get stuck against the wall and find it hard to escape without exiting to the main menu.
Lunar rovers and stingrays replaced the original vehicle give it a cool feel to have but also make for some really wonky controls.  In addition to this game we have laser weapons that are neat but overall aren't the biggest game changes. They do however start off with a good amount you can carry. I don't think they will replace most of the weapons archetypes that we've been accustomed to.
As for the story, well it's quite a bit short but personally it's satisfying I enjoyed playing Borderlands on a different perspective.  Apart from the main characters (who remain great throughout the game) most of the B and C list characters throughout the game were very bland and boring.  The humor is very dry and characters tend to be very one-dimensional/lackluster.  And for the most part have reused a lot of aspects of previous Borderlands (Marcus' vending machine using exact catch phrases from previous Borderlands).
Skill trees are quite reptitious and it's new that sets it apart from previous perks for leveling.
While it's a fun game, it isn't worth it's overall price tag.  Consider buying the Pre-Sequel on sale as you wouldn't get much from being a short game.  If you wouldn't like playing in low-gravity (good portion of this game is) I suggest skipping this game.
The Pre-Sequel isn't bad but it falls short of it's predecessor.
If there's any redeeming quality it's because it's on a different setting and facing Jack or "John" differently this time. Overall, it's still a pretty good game.

Wow, I honestly don't even know where to start with this review. I have not been blown away by a game on this level in such a long time and I feel somewhere in my heart I won't find another game to match this feeling at all. I had high expectations for NieR:Autotmata but it surpassed it in every single way. The story was told beautifully and was very complex and deep. The music for the game was absolutely stunning and easily one of the best OST I have heard in a game. I don't believe there was a single piece of music from this game that I didn't like. I'm going to try and keep this review fair with my pros and cons with it, as well as avoid any major spoilers as much as possible.
I can't delve too far into the story without spoiling anything but I can give a little insight on it. NieR:Automata is a sequel from the Original NieR game, but it's not connected where you have to play the original NieR to understand this game. From what I've read as I did not play the original NieR, this game takes place thousands of years after the original. There are a few tidbits that will make reference to the original and a few characters from the original do make a return but nothing that will hamper you from playing the game. The story starts off about a war between androids and machines  who were created by aliens. Humanity had to escape to the moon in order to survive and sent androids to rid the machines and aliens so life on earth can resume once again. As you progress through the game, you will see how deep it really begins to hit, how little things that seemed insignificant at first actually play a deeper role in the meaning of the story. Taro Yoko did a fantastic job at a story that really toys with the "what does it mean to be human" aspect and that made the story that much stronger and hold a bigger connection with it.

The graphics for this game were absolutely beautiful. From the crisp feel of the grassland, to how clear the water looks, excellent lens flair from the sun and overall textures of your surroundings. I will admit (which I will touch more in the cons) there are some areas that look lackluster graphic wise, however the overall world of NieR has beautiful graphics that really set the mood for what is happening at that moment.
This soundtrack was phenomenal. As I said before, I can't think of a single piece of music from this game that I didn't like. I am honestly one of the people who hate vocals in game music, except for maybe credits or a cutscene, but then I played this game and the vocals with the music blew me away. I really love the idea they did with the music where it will change based on the mood of the game, whether it's a scripted event or just completing a quest. A quest or scripted event will change based on the mood of that moment. It's fantastic and it makes the game have a stronger connection as during those moments you see how music can quickly change your overall mood within the game and what's going to happen next.
Very interesting with how this game has played out. It's a hack and slash game, but also carries aspects of Bullet Hell, Open World exploration and of course an RPG/JRPG. A few of my friends have compared aspects with the game having a feel of Dark Souls and Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance which I won't argue their points with that.
One thing I really liked is the Network System that was added in. Basically if you choose to connect to that, any player who has died in a certain spot in the world, you will find their body which you can choose to retrieve and in turn will give you a certain amount of Gold and a temporary boost to 3 stats. You can also choose to revive them and have them as a temporary ally to help you fight until they either die or blow up from being alive for too long or you leaving them behind by dashing faster than they can hope to keep up with you.
Onto the cons which I know can either break a deal for people but I want to be fair with this review.
- The game had a bumpy launch, I won't even try to deny that. It was bumpy as it there were some users who couldn't play the game on a 960m, 960, 970, RX 480 and even the Pascal GPUs. People were mentioning either really low FPS, white screens or flat out crashes. This had me worried as I was planning to play the game on 4k, while most of these people were on 1080p and having these issues. Thankfully this was not an issue for me and 4k ran without any issues. Some people in the community have made their own little fixes for now that can help you play the game or get the desired FPS if you're playing on a lower-end system. The devs are working on their own patches on this game to get everything up and running for everyone.
- Cut scenes are capped to 30 FPS. Capped FPS is a word that will turn a lot of people off and I don't blame you. The cut scenes would look absolutely stellar if they were uncapped, even with the cap I love how the graphics look for cut scenes. I can only wait until they're uncapped. Some users have mentioned the audio isn't fully correct in the cut scenes and that FPS can also tank; I have not had any of those happen to me but I want to mention it just as a small heads up.
- Apparently the game was locked at 900 resolution for users, even if you had a monitor with a much higher resolution. This wasn't the case for me, but others have to use 3rd party programs such as Borderless Window in order to have the max resolution of their monitor.
- Earlier I mentioned there were some parts of the game that had poor graphic spots. Most of the time I noticed this by windows where the sun was showing in, where the glare from the sun would look a little blurry and/or pixelated. The
is the best example I can think of with this issue. Other than that, I've only really seen it a few times when near water and at a weird camera angle.
- This personally isn't a con for me, but I know it will be a con to others. This game can be tedious at the start. You will be doing a lot of back tracking until you progress far enough into the story where you can freely transport between places you have discovered. Quests will have you running back and forth. Item collection will require you to grind enemies to further increase your level and give you items to survive at the later levels. If you're someone who enjoys this stuff, it won't be a con at all for you, but I know some people prefer to play games as quickly as possible without having to grind or backtrack a lot.
- Fantastic story that has a deep meaning behind it and really sucks you into the world of NieR. A very serious, touching and at times has it's funny moments.
- Music that keeps the mood and setting of the game which further delivers the experience to you and makes the moment feel more alive that it would be without the music.
- Beautiful graphics that really shine no matter where you're at in the world, giving you a whole new outlook on what is around you at those times and scenery you won't forget.
- Gameplay was a perfect mix of adventure, attacking and of course story telling. Enemies scale with your level and the world around you changes as time goes on.

NieR was the perfect game for me. Honestly it messed me up after finishing what routes I've finished already because I feel in my heart I won't find a game to match this story. I have never felt connected to a story at all, especially on an emotional level, but NieR honestly went above and beyond my exceptions with everything that came with it. It has easily become one of, if not my favourite game. It's a game I will always cherish to own and be a part of. The story, gameplay, music. 10/10.
I honestly cannot recommend a game more than Nier;Automata and I hope Taro Yoko gets the recognition he deserves from this masterpiece!

Before I get into this review, let me just say that I really like this game. No, seriously, I do. Rather, I really really want to like it.
This is a 2D psychological horror at it's finest. At least that's the impression I got when I loaded up the game. It takes indirect inspirations from games like Lone Survivor, whilst at the same time taking direct inspiration (and even sound samples) from games like Silent Hill. The story is presented in a way that makes me really want to keep on playing. And makes me hope that I actually can keep on playing.
Which brings me to why I am not recommending this game, and I will leave it that way until I can determine if this download simply is bugged (wouldn't be the first time) or if the game just really is generally this buggy. Yes, there are a lot of nitpicks that I have with this game, such as the wonky controls, the strange way the flashlight works (it's not like it doesn't make sense, but it just feels and looks awkward), and the general map set up (It's 2D, and if you expect to know where you are, you're going to need to use this map) are problems that hamper the overall game's feel.
But these are ignorable, just because the story seems very interesting. No, the main problem with this game is the bugs. Holy cheese and crackers Batman, this game is incredibly easy to break. At least that's the way it feels. The first time I tried playing through this game, I ended up getting stuck, and wandering around the same areas over and over again trying to find what I needed to progress. Oddly enough, it was a door that wouldn't open for me. When I tried a second time, it was actually a puzzle that would not respond to anything that I did a little later into the game. Between that, various sound glitches, and other weird occurances, I just  found myself not wanting to play this game.
The only reason I even decided to try again the second time was because it was brought up by another player in a Top 10 Horror Games of 2014 list. So with that said, I cannot say for sure that this game truly is not worth recomending. I personally cannot recommend it, but if one can't, and nine others can, I say it might be worth giving it a shot if it's on sale. I will edit this review and change the reccomendation to an immediate "Yes" once I've discovered that it was just a defective download. Because while this game is far from perfect even without the game breaking bugs, it's still an experiance that looks like it's worth checking out.

I got the Hidden Gems bundle because I was interested in this game. I've always liked point n click adventure games, as I played a lot of them, such as the Reincarnation series, back in the day on websites like NewGrounds. If you're looking for a long game like Deponia, this isn't it. This is more akin to those previously-mentioned games on NewGrounds and Kongregate.
MechaNika is about a young girl who has a pretty rough life. Your quest is to find parts to destroy everything she hates, basically. If you get stuck, you can get wasted and she'll give you a hint. There's a lot of fun little quirks in the game that you can interact with, that may or may not actually impact the story. You can complete most of it in any order you please.
I got it for $2.99 and I feel it was worth my money. If you want a more complete story, you might wait until MangoProtocol makes more in this series, but they have said the rest won't be point n click. But if you're looking for another fun little (dark) point n click game, this might fit your bill.

For a game with dated graphics, Deus Ex is hella fun. This was my first experience with a stealth-action game, and the thrill of my guard-evading caper, on the rare times when it worked, was AweSum. The new Human Revolution has a more Blade Runner cyberpunk feel to it, but level design and combat in Deus Ex is just better (no quick-time events), and the crazy "all conspiracy theories are true" story of Deus Ex creates a great dystopian atmosphere.
Sometimes the stealthing fails, and you have to shoot-hack your way out of a shady corporate-triad office. Thankfully, unlike Dishonored, this game does not base your ending on the number of people you did/didn't kill. Don't judge me, game! I have real life to do that already.
The story is a bit hard to follow, and the obsession with passwords hidden in obscure places to link up with non-sequitur computers halfway across a mazelike map is definitely from an era where gamers had weird ideas about what "fun" was. But it's a solid stealthy (or shooty) game (though I have not played Thief), and worth replaying and doubling back, to see if you could have handled that shooting-at-the-police-station thing a bit differently.

So I want to start off by saying that this game is an epic game and though it does have some shortcomings it makes up for them in its strengths and in the dedicated development team behind it.
Let’s start off with the positives
1.	A massive multiplayer map selection with huge amounts of maps from 2-8 players.
2.	A diverse group of factions to play from giving much diversity and uniqueness to every game.
3.	A fun community with an extremely caring development team that is friendly and responds in good amounts of time.
4.	Makes me feel that old might and magic.
5.	The diplomacy system in multiplayer mode.
6.	Hero units with unique abilities adding more depth to the game.
7.	A fun and pun- filled campaign that actually has a lot of surprise twists and turns designed around all playable factions.
8.	A game set up that allows for a turn based strategy game to be finished in 1 sitting with up to 8 players and not be rushed
9.	A seasonal system in the game that once again adds more depth to strategy.
10.	An in game card system that adds to the depth of strategy that also connects to what heroes you have giving all players different options to keep you on your toes and the cards are also linked to the seasons. This also adds more thought into when one would play a card.
11.	A rather interesting ranked points system (I love taking the points of others muhahahaha)
There are many more positives of the game but I feel as if these are the key ones for me that make me love this game as I have been searching for a long time for a game with the might and magic feel while at the same time being something new.
Now for the negatives. Though small in comparison to the positives there are some negatives that are in the game; though keep in mind some of these are being worked on by the developers already.
1.	Occasional disconnects from the server. Now this wouldn’t be so bad if it were not for the AI that takes over for a turn but we will get to that. (in regard to this one there is a system set up to reconnect to a game you have dc from)
2.	The AI unfortunately, in this game makes for a poor opponent as they don’t understand how to use the cards.
3.	As a streamer much of my community has expressed a desire to play the 2 unplayable factions in the game (side note – not sure if there is plans for more DLC in the future to remedy this or not)
4.	A rather odd set up for joining ranked games
5.	Lastly the most unfortunate thing the population the game has is not large enough (I know the developers are working on raising popularity)
It is after considering all of these factors and more as well as playing Legends of Callasia for 143 hours that I recommend this game 110% to all strategy and fantasy lovers try out the demo and if you’re having a rough time finding someone to play add me and I’ll try to set you up LoC is an epic game and I hope you join the fun!

Update:
In many spacesims, your actions have no consequence. Like kill endlessly respawning ships, moving goods around mean nothing because there's nothing behind it.
Star Nomad 2 is one of the few spacesims where your actions make a difference in the gameworld, like trading with a faction makes them prosperous or destroying Pirate raids lead to more merchant activity and helping the faction grow stronger and they conquer others.
I'm a smuggler, dropping drugs on unsuspecting colonies, getting them all addicted & unproductive! It's funny seeing an entire faction crumble due to me hauling drugs to their worlds.
There's very little hand-holding going on, which can be good and bad, depending on whether you want to think and make your own story or progress on goals. It would be bad if you want the game to give you objectives or goals and you follow it.
The Star Map in the game is excellent, simple but it provides all the info you need to decide where to go to further your Pilot's career. It provides info on which goods the worlds export and import, it tells you if there's a major trade shortage, like rioters demanding fresh Playthings (yes, think naughty robots!) or some kind of alien outbreak and the people want weapons.
If you're a Hunter, the Star Map also shows all the bounty opportunities.
One major thing you should know, the game has a "Killing Blow" system for bounties. If you don't get the last kill shot, you get no rewards whatsoever. There's no "hey, I helped you kill that Pirate, gimme something!"...  it took a few bounties before I got used to it. Justy time your strikes, focus on weakened targets.
Oh, if you meet some stranger who wants a love letter delivered to Ionus, go do it!

Star Nomad 2, a game I've been looking for. growing up Galaga was my favorite arcade game to play. Since then space games have always held a special place in my heart. Recently I had an itch to find a game to put my time into over my winter break, as my college gives us a full month. I tried a free game called Endless Sky, it's free to play. I recommend that game as well. Then I found Star Nomad 2. Everything Endless Sky was trying to accomplish in it's game Star Nomad 2 had already done and then some. The only thing the two games share in common is the level of customization. The depth that SN2 takes the aspects of it's game is very impressive. Halfgeek, the developer of SN2, is an amazing designer. Not only is the game already great, but the content just keeps coming. Even if you find some aspects of the game you don't enjoy Halfgeek is consistently patrolling the community forums replying to suggestions and helping new players learn the ropes.
Gameplay in SN2 is as complicated as you make it. You can let the CPU fire your turrets for you, or you can fire them yourself (firing the turrets yourself saves energy that you can use for a speed boost). You can fly lone wolf, or slowly compile a squad of unique characters that have their own stories to tell. You can be a corvette loaded to the teeth with missles and run circles around larger ships, or play a larger ship and laugh as your drones tear apart everything in the sector. The gameplay is only limited by the amount of time you have to put in, as this game does involve some grind for reputation with certain factions to aquire their ships. Traveling in the game can be a chore, as larger ships must move slower. There isn't much of a fast travel system to you end up spending some time trying to boost thought empty systems. This is slightly rememdied by the random encounter system or roaming pirate/pirate hunters. The difficulty in this game is also quite customizable as you it has a rouge-like setting for those that like "it hurts so good" gameplay. OR if you're like me and Dark Souls is how you get that fix and other games tend to be more casual, then you can pick hard or easy mode.
The story in SN2 is relatively shallow overall. The premise is there and laid out. There's just enough story to let players make a moral decision on who to support and why three factions are constantly at each other's throats. I personally prefer this over a convoluted story for a game like this. I'd rather there be more content gameplay wise for this game as there is only one developer that I am aware of. With only one person to write the story, the issue of them "ruining" it by implementing an idea that sounds good them them but ends up resonating poorly with the community is a very possible situation. The story as it stands now is more than adequate. As mentioned before there's just enough for the players to understand what is happening, why it's happening, and what should they do.
The full price of this game is very justified at this time. The amount of content and updates the game has recieved since I've purchased the game is on level with triple A titles DLC's. I wouldn't be suprised if the creator decides to bump up the price after a few more months of consistent content drops. Star nomad gets a 8/10, 10 being a game that's never existed.

Hidden gems, that's why I love the gaming industry so much. From the day I have discovered Gothic, I was looking for the next game that will take me by suprise and keep me playing for hours.
I have always enjoyed sort of table top/board game/risk like games. We have had some in the past like 2-3 risk games, Slay by Sean O'Connor or Desktop Dungeons. I was wondering what will be the next one to capture my attention and here it is: Legends of Callasia.
This game is an excellent example that there is still room for improvement within an existing genre. It has it's own unique style and what it aims to achieve it does superbly so.
I have recently finished Rise of Tomb Raider and have been frustrated by the game's artificially inflated systems that were design to create an impression there is variation and different options. Instead RoTR has created a boring environment where I was just getting frustrated that devs have introduced 2-3 things that are basically the same and are not only pointless but also annoying, like the arrow head climbing.
In Legends of Callasia every card, every unit or building serves a specific function and has it's use. I also enjoy the visuals, they are crips, bright colours allowing you to quickly read the situation on the map. Little touches like clouds or dragons flying over the map show the attention to detail. I also greatly enjoy the short briefings before each campaign mission which give you useful info on where from to expect an attack.
Games even has room for some plot twists. That along side with custom objective in the campaign really creates nice challage. Another thing worth mentioning is the replayability value and it is pretty great in this game. I have played one map multiple time and each time I ended up executing different strategies.
Game always you to skip battles if you do not wish to watch them.
The only two things I would list as negatives (not ruining the experience but fixing of those would make the game near perfect):
- if there was some well design system to actually play battles manually that would add another layer of depth, but this would have to be well designed really or otherwise it would spoil a great game
- I wish there was a way to complete skip watching the time between turns and make it go faster, but I know that many turn based games suffer from it (total war series for example).
TL:DR version:
Great game, offering good level of chalange, engaging, with both single and multiplayer, worth it's full price.

Before playing Nier Automata I was simply unaware that a video game is capable of evoking such strong emotions in the player. Mr. Taro's masterpiece is a game that will  remain in your memory until the day you die. I don't want to talk about the specifics because literally anything I say could be considered a spoiler. I'll just say this: If you happen to harbor deep love for gaming as a medium, not playing Nier Automata would be a crime. If you want games to evolve beyond silly shooters for teenagers, this is it. It's a game that will not only make you appreciate video games. It will also make you appreciate fellow human beings and the constant everyday struggle most of us find ourselves in

Claire is a 2d horror exploration game where you play as a girl
learning about the mysteries of her life and her memories.  The atmosphere
of the game is very well done.  The story is not handed to you;  you have
to explore and understand what is going on.  The spooky theme of 'danger
around every corner' is unsettling, but not necessarily in your face with
violence and monsters.
The level design, as with many 2D games is mazelike;  the reusage of
similar hallways and doorways causes you to have to backtrack a lot.  It can
add to a feeling of being lost and contribute to the atmosphere, but for me it
was too much of getting lost and try over and over again to get to the next
destination.
There is a lot of fetch quests in this game.  Personally I feel like the
game didn't respect my time, as most of it was spent retracing steps and going
on continual missions that just prolonged the gameplay.
The atmosphere is terrific, the story is not what is expected, but
enjoyable, and it has a mazelike feel that I found not to be to my taste, but
if that is something you enjoy, this could be a game for you.

MechaNika is a funny point & click, where you play a seven year old girl that plans to destroy the world.
It's a very simple game to play, but the gameplay isn't the attraction. It's the funny dialogue, and characters.
Nika tends to be smarter than everyone around her, so when interacting with other people, you get the option to mess with them, or question them, and it gets pretty humorous.
There's a girl who wears an eyepatch and calls herself pirate girl, and a kid in the playground that makes a living from being a dealer. As in, weapons dealer. Yes, the game has some funny darker stuff like this too.
The game's art style looks really cute, and isn't ruined by any HUD. You access your inventory and menus by clicking on the character, so the game looks pretty clean. If you get stuck, you can drink fro her flask, containing a special concoction. She'll give a vague enough hint for the game to still be fun incase you're really stumped. It's a nice option to have.
The music is really great as well. It adds to the atmosphere in different places.
Overall, it's a fun, and very cheap game. So if you're a fan of point & clicks or this type of humor, check it out!

A good 2D survival horror game, obviously inspired by the aesthetics of silent hill, and perhaps some plot elements from those games as well.
There are a few cool puzzles, and side quests one can do that add to the replay value of the game, as well as three different difficulties, and a plethora of different endings.
The game is fairly easy, so one can probably get through it without too much difficulty on "hard" ("nightmare" may prove more of a challenge though).
The severeal endings are contingent on how many side quest one chooses to do, which is nice because it gives one incentive to explore the world a bit more.
The game can be completed in two hours if one were to rush though it. However for the kind of person who enjoys to explore and discover everything a game has to offer, I can see maybe 10 hours of playtime for this title.
One feature I would've liked to have seen in the game is an option to play it without taking any damage, so I could go through it and enjoy the pixel enviorments at my own leisure, but that is of course a minor thing that doesn't detract from the experience at all.
If the game does have a major flaw it would be that the dialouge, and story could have used some work, while I understand everything that was going on, the story could have fleshed out the characters a bit more.
There is no combat in the game, and while this is an interesting mechanic, I felt it could have been handled better than it was, for example there were not enough spots to hide.
The flashlight did not do much and wasn't required to beat the game, this felt like a missed opportunity gameplay wise, as I feel flashlight use could have been made more useful. To be specific maybe the flashlight could make you immune to being scared while it's in use, or perhaps it could temporarily scare off monsters?
The biggest issue I have with the game is there are parts of it that seem impossible to complete unless you have a whole bunch of health items stacked up, and this is becuase of your "sanity meter". If one has low "sanity" they start taking damage, the worst part is aside from items, there isn't really a way for one to restore thier "sanity", or at least none I could figure out.
Laslty it would be nice to have an option view all of the endings/notes one has unlocked.
This game currently would garner a 3.5/5 from me, if the game fixed all of the above I would have rated it higher.
Still it's a neat little indie title, worth one's money, and especially worth one's cash if bought on sale!

The new Human Revolution has a more Blade Runner cyberpunk feel to it, but level design and combat in Deus Ex is just better (no quick-time events), and the crazy "all conspiracy theories are true" story of Deus Ex creates a great dystopian atmosphere.
Sometimes the stealthing fails, and you have to shoot-hack your way out of a shady corporate-triad office. Thankfully, unlike Dishonored, this game does not base your ending on the number of people you did/didn't kill. Don't judge me, game! I have real life to do that already.
The story is a bit hard to follow, and the obsession with passwords hidden in obscure places to link up with non-sequitur computers halfway across a mazelike map is definitely from an era where gamers had weird ideas about what "fun" was. But it's a solid stealthy (or shooty) game (though I have not played Thief), and worth replaying and doubling back, to see if you could have handled that shooting-at-the-police-station thing a bit differently.

Medieval II: Total War is a strategy game from Creative Assembly and published by SEGA. It is a sequel to the previous games, Rome: Total War. This time the game is set on medieval era.
Medieval II: Total War retain many elements of gameplay from Rome: Total War with many enhancement such as the improved religion system and world events like the Christian Crusade or the Islamic Jihad. As a Christian Kingdom you can answer the call of The Pope the conquer the land considered infedel by them. Settlement are now divided into 2 type, a castle and a city. Settlement can be converted between.
Graphics of Medieval II: Total War are improved in many ways from the previous game. Each soldier has a varying number of elements to him, such as arms, legs, body armour, shield heraldry, and so forth. Each element has a varying number of styles. Arrow and fire arrow effects feels more alive. Blood effects has also been introduced, but without gore effects.
Medieval II: Total War is a great sequel of Total War series. Medieval era especially the Crusade era is one of many interesting setting in Total War. With improved graphics, the performance of the game still great, the game runs very optimized. I recommend this.

There are many aspects you will find familiar from titles like Space Rangers 2, Gratuitous Space Battles, and SPAZ, but it brings its own unique take on space and combat to classify it as a game of its own. I’ll break down this review into two categories to fit the meta.
Ship control doesn't feel like you are skating on ice, and you have the option to have your weapons auto target, or manual fire for reduced energy consumption. You can find NPCs on various planets to join you, and the AI and control options are simple and effective. Getting credit for kills means getting the last hit, which gives a sense of accomplishment for good timing.
The game is designed to be simple, so it isn’t overwhelming to get started, but there is enough depth in character development, knowledge of enemies, and ship design to keep it from getting stale.
There are three sizes of ships, with a fair many hull choices to suit different play styles including faction specific ships. Weapon selection is medium, but each weapon type has its own damage, range, rate of fire, shot speed, etc to differentiate it from the other types. There are slots for engine, shield, armor, and other mods on ships that further develop how well it performs. Ship progression happens fairly fast but leaves plenty of room for late game speccing.
Trade is as simple as buy and sell based on prices in different sectors, and delivering goods that are scarce to regions in need. How well a faction is doing is directly related to trade and piracy, so you can affect your allies and enemies by making the right deals.
in patching bugs, fixing game data, and updating with new and improved content. This is a great thing because while this game is good as is, it will be AMAZING with more work.
Of the three character starts, being a pirate isn’t really a viable option. Pirates aren’t a true faction currently and I can’t see how they fit into the game from a progress standpoint. They are mostly just there to mess with factions and block trade/military.
Combat is what it’s all about. Being a trader and mining are great things to do, but ultimately lead to a life of killing.
through quests that begin on planets. The only quests I have encountered are through or related to the NPCs you can get in your squad. I would love to see a robust level of chat dialogue, quests, and other happenings that would add immersion to this universe. Cut scenes, NPCs, unique bosses, and challenges outside of the typical skirmishes. No planet should be a boring port with little more than a few generic commodities to trade for. Give me enemies and allies that I can love or hate. At the moment picking a faction is just a choice and I don’t feel the struggle between them.
Like the pirate faction, the Zerker faction needs developed. They don’t own any space, and while I love how they behave in combat, they are just a bit too mysterious and lack any influence on the map.
Star Systems are all the same layout. I would love to see varied sized systems, with multiple planets and varied locations for planets on the map.
That’s my $0.02 on this title. Come for the combat, stay for the continual development.

Do you like space sims? If yes, get this. Simple as that. It doesn't even matter whether you like trading or fighting, building great empires or simpyl breaking other's toys. It doesn't, because X3AP has it all.
This is the most authentic experience any space sim can offer. How often do you read marketing trash like "bring the universe down or see it rising under your leadership" and other piles of ...? It is all true in X3AP. Via trade or construction, performed by you personally or by your owned ships, you can see empires rise and working. With ships you either fly or via countless choices in fleet management you can experience epic battles of hundreds of fighters and dozens capital ships clashing for control of systems. Good thing X3AP has very vell optimised engine because once you get this sort of fleet fighting you will never want anything else.
And the last great thing? Modding community. Scripts addind basicaly anything you ever wanted into the game, complete overhauls and mods that give you anothoer hundreds of hours spend in this epic universe.
This game is a jewell, a thing anyone who things highly of space sims should play. No matter what you liked on space games you will like it even more after this.
This game has one downside though. Some call it a bit complicated. I see that as a misunderstanding of the concept of the game. Just as you can't compare CaC and Europa Universalis you can't compare X3AP and any other space sim that is scaled down and simplified to smashing buttons and marrying the space princess after five hours of arcade shooting. This game is great and complex and gives you great tools to achive things. But if you are looking for an arcade shooter or arcade builder, look elsewhere. This game is by no means simplified and it gives you all the control you could have ever wanted. It gives you the power to do great things, and if that scares you ore you don't feel like doing that, look elsewhere. But for the rest of us, this is a must-have.

Stick it to The Man! is a thoroughly enjoyable adventure game with a bold identity. The mind reading, platforming, adventure, stealth and paper tearing mechanics take chances and fit great together. A minus point is that some of the puzzles verge on moon logic and some items don't work when they feel they should. For instance, near the beginning of the game there are two puzzles that revolve around teeth going on at the same time, so which solution fit where was a bit confusing. These issues are common in many excellent adventure games though (Grim Fandango for example) and in this case don't distract from the many, many great things this game has to offer.  I'm the kind of person who exhausts every dialogue tree in an adventure game so I really enjoyed reading minds and learning about the misfits who inhabit this crazy paper world. Great stuff, I'm happy I grabbed it on Chrono.gg when it was on sale!

This is my favorite space sim game.  It has many strengths and many weaknesses.  I will start off with the weaknesses of the game to get them out of the way so I can focus on the fun parts of the game.
This is a single player game.  There is no multiplayer, so if you were hoping to play this with others, this isn’t the game for you.  To many, this is actually a good thing.
The graphics isn’t really up to par for 2013, but I don’t find them too objectionable.  There isn’t many similarly capable space sims on the market *yet*, so beggars can’t be choosers.
There is a somewhat steep learning curve since there is so many aspects to the game, and the built in tutorial doesn’t really do enough explaining and is even fairly easy to skip over by accident.  To get the most from this game you probably will need to spend a lot of time researching how the game works by a combination of reading Egosoft forum postings, watching youtube videos (which there are some great ones), reading other guides online, and general trial and error accompanied with a lot of saving and loading.
Probably the thing I hate most about this game is collision.  The autopilot is somewhat bad and will sometimes guide your ship into other ships or gates in space which will seriously damage or explode your ship.  If you have a fleet of ships in system with you it only gets worse.  I can’t believe they left it as is.  Basically every time you go through a gate, there is a chance the autopilot is going to collide with the gate and blow you up.  It gets worse the bigger the ship you’re in.
Missions:
The main storyline missions are fun and rewarding.  As rewards you are given things like  spaceships, space stations, and an entire private sectors.  These missions are somewhat easy, especially as compared to older incarnations of X3.  For example, you will have a much easier time completing the hub plot as compared to X3: Terran Conflict.  They have stripped out much of monotonous aspects of the storyline missions.  You still have to work for them so you are not left feeling like you didn’t earn them.
The random side missions that you find everywhere are a mixed bag.  Some of them are impossible or nearly impossible to complete, with strange caveats, or strict time limits.  If you play for a long time you kind of learn which ones to skip and which ones are worth doing.  I feel like they could improve this so you don’t waste as much time.
Trading:
In this version, they added a Stock Market, which can be exploited to give you a quick infusions of starting money.  That’s all I ever used it for, as a network of trading ships seems to be more reliable and earn quicker.
The trading system is one of the best things about this game.  There are lots of goods for sale and lots of buyers, so there is plenty of opportunities to make money.
You can manually trade goods yourself and or set up huge fleets of automated traders so you can get a lot of passive income while you focus on other tasks.  This takes a bit to fully get working as you have to download a bonus addon pack and spend some time learning how to configure your ships to use them.  But once you have this going, you can have 50+ ships automatically finding the best trade runs and doing it on your behalf and sending you the profits.  All you have to do is replace them when they eventually get blown up.
Building:
You can build vast networks of your personally owned stations generating weapons and goods for use, or for selling.  Creating player owned stations is probably my favorite aspects of the game.  These can quickly give you a lot of money which you can further reinvest to expanding your holdings.
Once you acquire the “Player Headquarters” from a storyline mission, you can reverse engineer other ships to acquire the blueprints so you can build your own.  You can also scrap other ships here which breaks them down into resources to build other ships from.  The one downside to the Player Headquarters is that it’s slow.
Combat:
With multiple sizes and classifications of ships, weapons, and shields, combat can be extremely fun.  You have everything from your quick interceptor/scout types that move fast with low hitpoints and weak weapons, all the way up to nearly immobile capital ships with massive weaponry and that can act as carriers which allow you to transport and field a large number of smaller ships.
You can cause pilots to bail out of their ship, which you can then claim as your own,  and also board their ship and take it over from within.  The boarding is very fun once you have capable enough marines and have the tactics down.
Mods:
There is a fairly easy to get into scripting interface with a largish modding community, and lot of existing mods you can download which can improve many aspects of the game, such as the above mentioned collision problem.

The Wild Eight
On Saturday, February 18, 2017, my friend and I read the initial reviews and were skeptical of The Wild Eight. At this time it had only been released for several days. While I was more sold on the idea, my friend was hesitant because of some prior early access titles that were a huge letdown. The reviews implied that there were bugs, sketchy multiplayer servers, and some “boring” gameplay. After winning a bet with my friend, he decided to buy the game. We spawned into a server together and the game ran very well. We were almost immediately immersed, taking on our roles as airplane crashed survivors. After building a riddled tent and a shelter to make some tools, we began a small journey around the snowy woods. We spotted a rabbit. We chased it, throwing rocks at it and yelling. The rabbit got away. It was at this moment our stomachs began growling and our feet were turning purple. We died before making it back to camp. So we started over.
After figuring out the basics, we set up a large and upgraded campsite, got a stockpile of food, and made ourselves some high tier clothes and weapons. This process took around a couple hours. Our new goal was to complete a series of quests and to discover what was on the map. I have to say, the map size and variability on The Wild Eight is very impressive. It immediately brought me back to my days on Terraria. We would get back from an hour long adventure and see that we only discovered about 5% of the total map size.
Pros:
Huge map with lots of variables and procedurally generated content.
An actual storyline and main / side quests to be completed.
Besides forest, areas exist such as caves, old facilities, and abandoned towns.
Challenging gameplay, where hunger drains rapidly and the cold always lingers.
Smooth graphics, 60 fps, and a great top-down engine.
A soundtrack that is relaxing during the good times, and terrifying in the bad.
A variety of NPC animals both to hunt, and to hunt you. Boss battles as well.
Cons (most cons are only there because of early access bugs):
Animations sometimes are glitchy. Your axe will swing a foot away from your arm, ECT.
The animals will sometimes be out of sync with you and other players. My friend was killed by an animal that he couldn’t see and I could. He would swing at an animal when it appears 10 feet away.
There is also building bugs between players. I sometimes can’t see structures that my friend builds.
All in all, the gameplay is very challenging. If you die, your character’s leveling / building progress restarts and you have to loot your body for the gear you had. I would highly recommend to not play by yourself. On Saturday my friend and I got the game. We played for 13 hours straight. We still have lots more to do and discover. Bugs exist in this early state, but nothing game breaking. No crashes or failed saves or anything. If you enjoy survival games like Rust, a cooperative experience, and an adventure such as Terraria, then The Wild Eight, a 20 dollar price tag, is fully worth it and I highly recommend.
UPDATE: We played in stretches for a couple more days and are now taking a break. We finished most main missions and discovered most of the map. Admittedly, we both rage quit after losing max gear / levels lol. We are awaiting further updates. In my opinion, my 16 hours of gametime were fully worth my 20 dollar purchase.

Unplayable on Mouse and Keyboard
Now, let me preface this by saying. Yes, I am aware that this, along with most spectacle fighters, are primarily supposed to be played on controller. Yes, I know Japanese games' checkered histories with PC port. I have successfully managed to play Dark Souls on keyboard and mouse, so I have a pretty good tolerance for this sort of thing.
I'm also not going to get into the obvious graphical issues (clear upscaling, 4:3 resolution(the FAR fix didn't work for me), etc)
I get a pretty bad feeling from the very beginning when the settings menu doesn't include any keybinding(Instead it's in a "Controls" section that you find with each save). In addition, menus are designed so that as long as you have your mouse hovering in the screen and not out of it, when you try to scroll using the mouse wheel, it is stuck to whatever you're hovering over.
Then I get into the game itself. Ho boy. The default controls are a mess; very odd buttons all around, but nothing keybinding can't fix. For some reason the PC version has no evade button while the controller does? I don't even...
In the twinstick shooter sections, it seems like the mouse has to act exactly like an analogue stick. So when you try to move in one direction, it tries to override you to point in that direction, unless you keep on moving the mouse to the other direction. No aiming reticule or anything to show where your cursor is, either.
Camera control in third person is just abysmal as well. It's struggling just to move the camera, and there's no lock function like in Dark Souls. And again, no evade button - instead you doubletap keys.
So I'm pretty damn frustrated, and I go to try and fix this a little in keybinding. And there's the final straw - you can't rebind your mouse controls. Only keyboard.
Frankly, this is ridiculous. I expected some clumsy controls, maybe lack of mouse support in menus, but this is just unplayable on keyboard and mouse. I'll give the game a week or two to see if they come out with a patch(or a mod fix), and if not, I'm refunding the game, which is a shame, because I was very excited for this title.

So i got this gift from a friend for Xmas and after playing it a little bit, i have not much desire to go on, sorry to say.
So we have this game about a girl who, after a short introduction of her childhood that had a traumatic event, is waking up next to her comatose mother and wants to get a coffee.
Then all of a sudden the hospital turns to hell and she has to find her way back to her mother.
That is pretty much the main story so far as i understood.
Graphics:
The graphics are nicely done with their 2D pixels and a lot of details to see. I enjoy it, so that is no issue.
Sound:
Creepy music, scary sound effects, the game has them all and i like it, good one here.
Gameplay:
2D sidescroller, you walk, you run, you push objects, go through doors and pick up stuff, nothing overly special, but it works. In between you meet enemies that you cannot attack and weird characters you do a task for (mostly finding an item somewhere).
That is basically all i saw so far.
Navigation doesn't work well, you need to check your ingame map constantly or else you get lost quicker than you can say "What?".
Add the fact that all the corridors look alike and you don't even have any distinctive feature to let you know where you are, which makes running around and looking for something specific tedious and boring.
Controls:
Claire can jump, run, pick up stuff and use objects, but it would've been nice to have the option to remap the controls. Using an XBox controller, i was unable to remap the buttons and had to use the (little intuitive) default setting to work with it.
Even after so many tries with the map, i cannot get a feel for the menu navigation.
Otherwise the controls are responsive and your control over the character is good.
Story:
I didn't make it far into the game, so i cannot say much about it, but at this point i am more confused than anything else, nothing makes sense and so many questions pop up, i don't know which one to ask first.
I suspect a "It was all a nightmare" kind of ending for this, even if i am wrong, i doN't have that much hope for the story.
Conclusion:
The game looks good, sounds good and makes a good first impression and then drops as quickly as a hot potato in your hands.
The boring explorations of seemingly endless and repetetive corridors, the lack of action (you basically just run through or away from enemies) and very few exciting parts make this game not worthwhile to me so far.
Check out a let's play of it somewhere before you decide if you want it or not.

You often read statements (be they from game developers, reviewers, or whomever) about a new product being a "love letter" to a particular genre or sub-genre of game...and usually these games tend to be somewhat "retro" in stylings, therefore perhaps begging the more cynical to label the claim as something of an "apology".  Something along the lines of: "Only one or two people made this game, ♥♥♥♥ you, we're not Valve or Gearbox and therein had a budget of precisely ♥♥♥♥-ALL, so you're gonna have to put up with the fact that this doesn't look or play anything like Bioshock Infinite."  But herein, of course, can lay the beauty of the whole endeavour...that perhaps not ALL of us want to play games like Bioshock Infinite; certainly not ALL the time.  Nice to have a little variety in our life experiences, right?  Which is precisely where "indie games" come in, for those of us adventurous enough to take a chance on them.  And Claire, I'm pleased to say, is by and largely one of the good ones.

Getting back to my opening sentence, this is a game which could be readily described as a "love letter to old-school survival horror".  Well...sort of.  Firstly, there's the name of the lead character, who happens to wear a red jacket-y thing...a bit like a certain "Claire Redfield" character beloved to fans of the Resident Evil series.  Greater overall similarity, however, lies with the almost equally famous and long-running Silent Hill series, at least story-, tone- and location-wise (hospital, school, apartment); and then there's the slightly lesser-known but still quite significant Clock Tower series, which to the best of my knowledge kicked off the whole "stealth horror" notion of hiding in closets rather than actually FIGHTING beasties...a tradition which this game merrily follows in.

Oddly enough, though - and perhaps just a little less admirably, I'm sad to say - the game to which this arguably owes the greatest debt is a very, very RECENT one, itself a "love letter" to survival horror realised in crude-but-oddly-effective 2D, pixelated form.  Lone Survivor was the name of that game, and I'm kind of suspecting that THIS game may not have existed without it.  That was ALSO a shameless Silent Hill love-in, but y'know, as a huge Silent Hill fan myself, I'm really not gonna complain too bitterly about about EITHER game's existence.  I will, however, opine that Lone Survivor was at least marginally more successful than this one, and now I'll attempt to explain why...

The biggest problems with this game are, quite simply, the mapping and saving systems, neither of which I recall being so problematic in Lone Survivor.  This game faces much the same challenges mapping-wise as the earlier game - that is to say, both being two-dimensional games with confusingly three-dimensional maps - but it's a little poor how few significant locations (including, sometimes, the save points themselves) are clearly marked on the map once you've discovered them.  Expect to get lost...a lot.  The other problem herein is the monsters/evil ghosties you encounter...as they have a tendency to move about as they see fit, knocking down doors and what-have-you.  So not only are you lost, looking for the location of a save point or a puzzle which you are finally able to solve, but there may very well be monsters in the way which weren't there before!  So you try to avoid them (by awkwardly "jumping" over them!), maybe take some damage, maybe waste some health items, only to find you've gone the WRONG ♥♥♥♥ING WAY!  A bit unnecessarily frustrating at times, in other words.
Look, I honestly don't have many complaints beyond that - well, okay, there is the fact that the "action" bits don't particularly work and get way too frequent towards the end - but I'm certainly grateful that people are inspired to make games like this, and eagerly look forward to whatever the developers get up to in the future.  Suffice it to say, if you loved Lone Survivor, you're gonna like this one too, and the same probably goes for the (at least more open-minded) Silent Hill fan-addicts out there.  Just think of this as the more "stealth"-oriented of the two super-pixelated Silent Hill "homages" recently unleashed upon the market, and decide if that sounds like your "thang".  If it does, you're unlikely to be disappointed.
Verdict: 8.5/10.

Ok, so, Borederlands: The Pre-Sequel.
I thoroughly enjoyed exploring the moon of Elpis, with a brand new story connecting some of the mysteries from the original Borderlands games. Also, watching the (non-DLC) playable characters become how we know them in Borderlands 2 is pretty awesome. The addition of laser and cryo weapons is pretty nifty, and I'm hoping that they include these into Borderlands 3, if, and when Gearbox make it. I say this because there are still a lot of questions unanswered, and new questions introduced with this game. Overall I enjoyed the game, characters and the Grinder is pretty awesome as well.
HOWEVER. There are a few things that I wasn't really pleased about. Firstly, I found it quite amusing at first, when I realised that all the new characters had Australian accents. Unfortunately, the amusement just seemed to drain, and I ended up finding it rather annoying by the end of the game (I'm sorry Australian people :C ). I felt like it was an idea thrown in to make the game funnier, but it quickly wore off. Also, my main problem with this game. The DLC. After playing Borderlands 2 quite a lot, I loved the playing the DLC campaigns, full of new missions, and the inclusion of 2 new characters, as well as all the fun Headhunter challenges (Grandma Torgue can bugger off though). Anyway, I expected the DLC in this game to be just as good, or, even better, and purchased the season pass with the game near enough as soon as it came out. Now that all the DLC for the season pass has been released, I am, quite frankly, disappointed. Whereas Borderlands 2 introduced 4 huge new campaigns, The Pre-Sequel gave a single DLC campaign and 2 new characters. Also, there was some Holodome crap that no-one really gave a damn about. Yes, The Claptrap DLC was fun, but I feel like I could've done more with the money used to purchase the season pass.
Overall, the game is good, and the Claptrap DLC is definitely worth playing, but I wouldn't say that the DLC is worth the price on Steam. At least wait until the sales have started up again.

text:
Deus Ex is a classic of gaming, often considered the greatest PC game of all time. While I would give Thief II that honor, it's not hard to see why this game tops so many "best of" lists, and it's one of my personal favorites. This game may also be one of the best examples of why you shouldn't judge a book by it's cover, as it looks like absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥ with freaky-looking human models, blocky levels, barf-inducing textures, and subpar voice acting. However, if you can get past all that, you'll quickly find that this game is something special.
Deus Ex appears to be an FPS on the surface, but it's really an FPS-RPG. Throughout the game you acquire skill points that you can use to upgrade your skill with certain weapon types (pistol, rifle, heavy, etc.) You can use any weapon you find and have room for, but to be even remotely competent with them, you'll have to upgrade the respective skill, which increases damage and accuracy, and occasionally adds some other benefits. There are also other skills you can upgrade, such as Computer, which allows you to hack ATMs for money and security terminals to deactivate cameras and reprogram turrets, and Lockpicking, which decreases the amount of disposable lockpicks you need to open a door. The great thing about Deus Ex is that there is no one correct way to play the game. Every skill in the game, with the exception of Swimming and arguably Environmental Training, is useful, and there is a way to beat any mission with any skillset. You could use Multitools to bypass a security keypad to open a door, or you could hack a security terminal and open it from there, or you could lockpick your way into a drawer with a datacube containing the code, or you could just blow the door open with an explosive. There is always more than one way to solve a problem, something that is very, very rare in even the best games out there.
The amount of depth this game has amazes me. Once I was in a high-rise apartment, and I decided to break the window and jump out, merely for the entertainment of seeing how far up I actually was. I instead landed on a balcony, lockpicking my way into a room with binoculars and a computer terminal containing interesting details about the lore of the game. My jaw was literally agape. I could not believe that such an obscure location would actually have something noteworthy in it. No matter how many times you play Deus Ex, you will always find something new, be it a new way to complete a mission or just a fun easter egg, and this makes the replay value extremely high. The game is massive, and I believe this to be in part due to the extremely low-budget graphics. Since so little time and money was spent on the look of the game, the mechanics could be polished to a mirror shine and the world expanded in a meaningful way, with things to find in every nook and cranny.
I would also be remiss not to mention the game's fantastic story. It's a wonder the game managed to be so compelling despite the awful voice acting, and it speaks to the quality of the writing that this was achieved. The characters you encounter are lovable, and the overarching plot is both extremely complex and full of twists and turns, which is why, in the interest of avoiding spoilers and laziness, I won't be providing a plot summary. You'll just have to find out for yourself.
Lastly, there is the music, which is phenomenal. Alexander Brandon's compositions are varied, memorable, and always fit the location and the themes of the story (edit: I derped, there are two other composers as well, named Michiel van den Bos and Daniel Gardopee). On top of that, the music isn't just nice to listen to: they also serve a gameplay purpose. During the missions, the music that plays will normally be very ambient and fade into the background, but when enemies are alerted of your prescense (this game has optional stealth), the music will become more intense, not only to change the mood from that of quiet sneaking to fast-paced gunplay, but also to let you know the enemies are on to you even if you're too far away to see or hear them. The rest of the sound design is solid, with satisfying gun noises that make shooting satisfying if you have to get into a fight. The only sound that isn't good is the sound of assault rifle bullets hitting a wall, which is utterly dreadful. It sounds more like rain hitting the ground than bullets colliding with solid steel, and it takes you out of the intensity of combat.
Overall, Deus Ex's presentation has some problems, but the overall package is one of the deepest, most complex and most fun games ever made, and it also has the advantage of being utterly unique. No other game is quite like Deus Ex and few are as well-designed and compelling.
Score: 10/10
P.S. If you're a newbie and you want to play this game for the first time, I highly reccomend downloading this mod for the game:
It makes several balance changes to the game, ranging from small changes like buffing some of the melee weapon's damage, to massive overhauls, like replacing the useless Swimming skill with the very useful Atheltics skill, which increases speed and jump height on land as well as in water. There are also some new additions, like the ability to do a Thief-style wall mount if you upgrade your Athletics skill to Advanced, the ability to pickpocket keys from guards, and white phosphorus grenades. Additionally, the game runs smoother, saves take less time, the game autosaves when maps change, and overall it's a straight upgrade from the unmodded version. Initially I was hoping to give the game a positive review, given that I believe its made by one person and for better or worse it shows. However its the little painfully stupid things that kept poking and then eventually cracking me. It amazes me how little it takes to make what would otherwise be a decent game to instead be a nightmare.
Not 30 seconds after leaving the starting world I died. Large amount of brown and red ships descended upon me and made me go boom in seconds. Later I learned that your initial foes, the pirates and the zerkers, both wield massive fleets that wreck everything in their path. Manage to kill a few of them? You then better not die, because as soon as you do the enemy counts reset, so you can essentially battle forever in the same system. Thankfully death costs nothing, but sadly if you want to actually kill anything you have to spend vast amounts of money on missiles. Your turrets might as well be pea shooters. So you are left with the choice of either not fighting and flying around the masses hoping to not get noticed and pick up some scraps, do some mind numbing trading, or go asteroid mining which involves pressing a button every few seconds.
Ill keep at it as I have nothing better to do at the moment, but for newcommers I recommend staying away for now unless youre willing to suffer for some possible enjoyment later. Oh and the zerkers shooting through your shields? Yeah, thats a "negative review" feature right there.
