I'd love to be able to recommend this game, but unfortunately, I can't.  It has a lot of good things going for it.  It is pretty looking, for one.  The emergent story-telling via events is a nice change from the usual bland 4X routine.  There is a lot of data, but it is well-organized, and I never felt overwhelmed.  I think it gives a good first impression.
Unfortunately, it suffers from some serious flaws.  It is a slow game.  Very slow.  Expect to be playing it on Fastest speed for a lot of it, just to get to something to do.  There doesn't seem to be as much meat to it as I'd like.  The combat doesn't seem quite right, and though they show combat ratings, due to the variances of weapon types and defenses, those are very inconsistently accurate.  It's not unusual to either be annihilated by or dominate similarly scored enemies.  That makes battles "fun".  The deepest flaw, for me, is the War Goals and War Score, which is something ported from their grand strategy titles.  This is essentially a major constraint on a player's ability to wage war:  you are required to pre-declare the goal of your aggression, build points by doing certain things, and then "spend" those points at the end of the war to actually accomplish anything.  This translates to taking over a dozen planets, but only being able to "afford" to keep 1 when the war ends.  It is as odd a system as it sounds, and it does not work in a 4X environment, in my opinion.  The only up side is that your enemies play by the same rules, so players are less likely to be knocked out of the game in a single war.  There are other more minor flaws and annoyances besides those, and an oddity with achievements only unlocking on Ironman mode, which seems needlessly anti-player.
Overall, it is not a bad game, but an ambitious, slow one with some critical flaws.  It keeps a bit too much of its grand strategy pedigree, and suffers for it.

Deus Ex is an old game, but still among the best cRPGs you can find. It offers a wide variety of options and choices, which are supported by a complex and conspiracy-heavy storyline keeping up your interest. Just don’t forget to get the community-created patches to make the engine compatible with modern video cards.
The internet likes lists, especially if they want to collect the best of all times in a specific category. If you find one about the best cRPGs, you’ll more than likely see Deus Ex near the top of that lists, and for good reason.
The gameplay is all about freedom. Freedom in play style: you can take out your enemies in lethal and non-lethal ways (you can finish the whole game with only taking one life), or you can sneak past them using cover, or create a diversion (throw an object, hack security, or even blow something up). You can rely on your wits, your items or your special augmentations, which– like magic in fantasy games– let you do supernatural feats as long as your energy levels remain.
There is also a freedom in the story. Almost all goal can be reached in at least three different ways; all of the maps include several hidden spots and secret routes that lead you to shortcuts, additional rewards or sometimes even new secondary goals. And to make the list complete, you can choose among different endings for the story, which is something that even some of the best RPGs out there couldn't tell about themselves.
The game was made on arguably the best engine of its time, Unreal, which really shines in night scenes. (Pardon me the oxymoron.) This not only creates a very fitting atmosphere, but it's also integrated into the game: there are plenty of dark corners to hide – and that’s another reason why Deus Ex is often compared to another successful FPS/sneak hybrid, the Thief series.
The plot itself is an amalgam of all modern conspiracy theories ranging from the little grey people of Area 51 to the Illuminati and government-controlled epidemics. Still, it’s a very complex story with a lots of questions regarding human nature and sociology. And if we add in the excellent and memorable soundtrack, it's easy to understand why this game is still ranked so high even to this day.

The developer has some mealy-mouthed bulls­­h­it excuse for placing this in the "Free to Play" category, rather than the "Demo" category where it belongs. It basically boils down to "we want to sell this game on iTunes/Play Store and only want people to have to purchase it once".
Which, of course, is absolute nonsense. The devs could very easily generate a Steam Key from within the iPhone/Android version (Valve hands those out to developers like candy, little to no questions asked), and could just as easily generate a "registration key" for the mobile versions within the Steam game.
What they really want is to get a lot of downloads, get a captive audience (i.e., people actually opening the game and experiencing it), and then hope that people impulsively buy the full version once they realize this is just a demo.
I might be inclined to be slightly more charitable if the devs mentioned the full price - $19.99 - anywhere in either the Store Description, the "About the Game", or the forums thread where they try to rationalize their categorization of this game. But nah - they want you to get as close to buying the game as possible before finding out the price, which is a really scummy way of selling a game.

Okay, this game has potential but I absolutely cannot recommend it. Brief synopsis:
Pros:
1. The graphics are beautiful
2. The gameplay is fun and enjoyable
3. Lots to explore and see and do
4. Enjoyable crafting and farming mechanics
Cons:
1. When you die you lose everything (to include the buildings you built, all your upgrades, your levels and your experience). You start back at zero on every level. The materials you farmed do not re-spawn so you farm everything, use it to build/upgrade buildings and then die and lose the building essentially deleting entire forests every time you die.
2. The game is incredibly difficult and you WILL die... a lot. Meaning you will spend hours and hours of your time farming and leveling up to try and have a better chance at survival, only to die 3 hours in and completely erase everything you've done over the last 3 hours.
The game (in its current state) is a complete and total time sink. If this were a "hardcore" option that would make more sense, but this game is by no means for the casual gamer. It's incredibly difficult and extremely frustrating. Be a badass gamer or find another game.
EDIT:
The developers have added an easier mode which basically addresses the biggest issue with the game. I have changed my review to a recommend because of it. To the skeptics, dying in the game is not always due to mistakes, sometimes things out of your control get you killed and then you still lose everything.

This is a pretty fun game.  It's a 2-D puzzle platformer, which I'm usually not too fond of, but in this case, I didn't mind it.  The main draw of this game is its sense of humor.  The $15 price tag is a bit high, but then again I say that about 90% of the games I play.
The game plays fairly nice.  There's a bit of platforming, but it really isn't that challenging.  Some of the sections with enemies can be a bit tricky, but after a few attempts you can develop a strategy to get around them.  There are also puzzles which revolve around reading people's minds and moving stickers to manipulate the world around you.  The puzzles are really easy, as long as you're careful when exploring the levels.
The story's pretty good.  You're a guy named Ray, who got hit on the head after returning from work.  When you wake up, you realize that you have a hand sticking out of your head.  This hand can be used to grab stickers, pins, and read other people's minds, all of which are used to solve puzzles.  The story is unique, the dialogue is quite funny, and the voice acting is pretty nice.
If I had to make one complaint, it’s that the game is rather short.  It only lasted about 5 hours for me, and I even got all of the achievements.  What the game has is fine, but a little more wouldn’t hurt.
Overall, I would suggest picking this game up.  It will make you laugh, plus the achievements aren't too bad to 100%.  I just wish it was a little bit longer.

What is this game like?
This game reminds me of Dont starve. Where you dont have time to just sit and fart around. Time is essential. The long Dark is another similar game. If you like Dont Starve/The Long Dark, then you will like this game. If you hate time essential games then you will not like this game. You either love it or you hate it kind of game. Some people are giving it a bad review because they are dying from starvation or freezing. I dont think the game needs to be tweaked in that regards.
What are you doing in game?
Its free roam. There is a goal, but you can go where you want. You are constantly looking at your hunger and cold stats. And these are the most killers. You will often die numerous times just to figure out what you need to do to survive and then thrive. The map is randomized to an exctent.
Is it worth $20?
I was jumping back and forth the first couple hours on whether to refund this game or not. After i hit the 2 hour mark, i decided to just keep playing it since i own it now. And i am glad I did. I would not of realized this real gem if i refunded in the first 2 hours. Most likely in the first 2 hours, you are just going to be figuring out the AI and how to survive....not much else. And there is much more to this game. I consider a game worth it if i spend $1 an hour on it. So if you can imagine yourself playing 20+ hours ($20 = 20 hours), then it is worth it.
How are the devs?
They take input from the steam forums for future features. The make patches. So far they seem very well linked with their users. They have promised more features and bugfixes. Yes there are bugs present, but it is in development. These are to be expected. There are currently obviosuly missing features, but they are promised by the devs to be in future updates. So far i trust these devs. I see other reviewers who base their review on bugs/missing features/etc. But the game is evolving day to day at this point. Bugs will be fixed so why give it a bad review because of that? The devs respond to bug threads saying that they know about it and are fixing it, or whether you informed them of a fresh bug, etc. Based on the devs in discussion this is chapter 1 of 3. So they are planning much more.
My Opinion:
When i was playing Dont Starve and got sick of it, I wanted a game like it, but not itself. This is what i was looking for. This is a game you have to die to learn how to survive. Sometimes I just have to put the game away for a day or so after death. But I keep coming back for more.
NOTE: I am a loner, and prefer to play games in single player. So these are reflections based on single player.
UPDATE:
So far i am about 12 hours on this game. I have figured out how to stay alive...but i feel like i have not explored much at all. I feel like i am just starting the game.
UPDATE2:
After 40+ hours in game....In the beginning your mode is survival, but after you beef up your stats your mode switches to exploring. The game has the same quests, but because of the random generation, it makes replayability available. Once you are able to beat the game and go 100% everywhere the game starts to get a little boring afterwords. One of the nice things is things are random. So a single wolf attack might be a pack of wolves attack in the next game. Once you know how to run through the levels quickly you start to get bored having to restart.
Multiplayer:
I started on single player, but i noticed over time that multiplayer seems to be more fun, can get you more game time, and makes it easier. For example if you do it co-op another player can drop off leather to you after you die, to help up you level up quickly. They can give you iron tools, food, etc. As after you are leveled up they are not as dire as when you first start. So it can make it easier to play with other people. If you join a server, you can save and exit and use that save file later by yourself. Most people prefer co-op, but some people do a PvP server....and the fire pits give away your position...but yet is required. So there are a couple of different game play types. For co-op...2-4 people are a good number if you all agree to do quests together. Its more fun than each person doing a quest on their own. 8 people you miss out on quests...its just too many people.

While I will recommend this game for anyone who enjoys space flight sims, 4x games, or strategy games, I do so with the caveat that it is not for the faint of heart.

From what I've seen and played, the game is quite fun and somewhat original. Each gun has its own unique feel and playstyle, and each weapon type has its own advantages and downfalls (except Pulse. Fraggin' blue-balls are a little TOO good at everything), and every match -no- every battle within a match can play out differently than anticipated if you're careful about what weapons to use and how to use them. Though "Billions of combinations" is a bit of a hyperbole (Sure, you can have 20 variants of the same gun, but they all handle the same and deal nearly the same damage) there is a decent bit of customization with a decent sense of progression (unlocking certain items allows you to unlock more of the same style), and I take great pride in naming my custom weapons if they perform well.
Unlike most Free-2-Play games, which are actually "Pay-2-Win", this one is quite subtle about it. By paying up, you're only gaining cosmetic items, or a slight bonus in cash-gain or exp-gain through boosts, and not directly benefitting from it (I.E: If you still go 1/10, you're not going to be rolling in dough.); I, however, find it a little rediculous some of the "locked" options they have (more than three loadouts, more than six guns, etc.) that you can conveniently pay to no longer be a pain in your creative (and sadistic) gaming experience. A free player can technically have just as much freedom as a paid player, however with some difficulty and MUCH more grinding by comparison.
The gameplay itself isn't bad at all, with smooth animation and responsive controls for PvP, and the bots are well programmed if that's more your thing - being tougher than human opponents on occasion. Though I've yet to see a regular deathmatch mode, that's not necessarily a bad thing - the games' different maps and modes are unique enough to be replayable and enjoyable, with many different approaches to victory on each.
All-in-all, I enjoy the game. I probably will for a good long while, as there aren't many arena-style shooters out there that are worth flying a pig off a mountain for. However, much like Planetside 2, it suffers from a "Be dedicated or be broke" currency style that will be eating 5-10 matches out of your day - every day - if you want to keep upgrading your weapons. I recommend you give the game a try, even if this isn't normally your gig.

One of the finest RTS games I have played and probably my only real favourite in the Total War series.
Within this game you start off as one of the monarchies of the medieval era, England, France, Spain etc, inhabiting the West with the Turks, Egyptians, the Moors etc controlling most of the Eastern regions.  And I use control loosely, for this game is about constant strife, border control and damning your so called allies to your own religious hierarchies.
The gameplay itself is split into two halves.  One half is the typical RTS strategic combat, where two armies with varied units, face each other on the battlefield to determine a victor!  In this part of the game, there is a Rock Paper Scissors style of strategy, with Spears besting Knights, Knights besting Archers and Archers besting Spears, though as your own technology expands and your coffers grow larger, more diverse units will be available to you.
The AI can be a little stupid at times, often forgetting your commands or taking an insanely longer route than it needs to travel to reach it's destination.  So some micromanagement is needed there.
The second part of the gameplay is entirely Turn-Based.
You begin with a selection of territories relevant to your faction's Monarchy, you also have your own Royal Family who each have their own needs and quirks which affect your overall strategy.  And in this phase of the game you'll be charged with building your resources, exploring the world, and interacting with your neighbours.
Honestly I find this part of the game to actually be rather interesting, it's always fun to approach your neighbours with peace offerings and treaties, only to plan treachery for when the time is right.  And there are numerous and inventive ways you can attempt to accomplish this through, in a very Game of Thrones style of diplomacy if you're familiar with the subject matter.
I found this to be the better of the Total War series.  Others will have their preferences to Rome, Shogun or maybe even the Napoleonic Wars, but if you have any doubts of either, just do your research.  I hope my review will help contribute to that.

Short Review:
A very well good game, one of the best of its time, who perfectly merges stealth, story, and action into a unique package. And "almost" all of the aspects are done greatly, especially the story which is amazing. In addition the game is very long and will most likely take you over 40-50 hours to complete, with a lot of exploration, and a lot of ways to complete the game.
Avoid it if you prefer new stealth games.
Long Review:
I never played this game back when it was released, and I heard great things about this game: when I started, I was rather frustrated but the more I played, the more I started to enjoy it and it's no wonder if I'm going to say "It's one of my favourite games...but not of all time".
I want to be fair on one thing: the game is good, and I TRUELY recommend playing it. Trust me, it's a good game, a fantasticly made one...but it didn't age well and you'll see what I mean from the very start.
Let's skip the graphics, since they never make a game: what fails in this game, is the stealth mechanics and the "so called" rpg elements.
The stealth in this game is extremely clunky: if you EVER run near an enemy they will hear you. "Obvious", but even when you're far, they can still hear you. "Little less obvious", but then SOMETIMES when I crough nearby an enemy, he suddenly "hears" me and discovers me. "Wtf?"
In a lot of occasions the game makes up stuff like that: I try to sneak around, yet they see me. Also, it's SO HARD to take out enemies while sneaking, since if they scream (which happens often) your position might be revealed: instead, you want to stun them, however the stun doesn't always work properly and will attack you. The only good way I found to get past the enemies, is to stun their waist...it takes one shot, they go down without screaming, and you can hide them as you like. This is such a huge problem because it forces you to avoid all the enemies, but sometimes you MUST take out enemies and there's no way to do that without a stunner. I tried killing, but they always scream once, and if they do that you're in high trouble.
In addition, a lot of times they seem to be able to see me in the dark, despite them not having a torch,...and one time they managed to see me from the other part of the map! I'm not kidding, I heard the music, I saw gunshots...and there was a soldier shooting me from another building, which wasn't even in sight!
The stealth is very flawed and not aged well...is it bad? No, but it will take you some determination to endure the "clunkyness".
The second problem is the rpg mechanis...which aren't exactly rpg-like: basically, the more you do certain things, mostly exploring the areas, the more skill points you obtain: this part is well done because the game wants you to explore and grab as much points as you can, but at the same time is rather...lacking.
Infact there's no real growth or anything and if anything, you'll want to focus on few things, like lockpicking and hacking and unless you're wanting to go "rambo style", you really need nothing else.
Infact, if you play stealthily, you just want to ugprade those two skills and forget the rest, or maybe upgrade something else but in most cases you'll focus on lockpicking and hacking because they can take you almost anywhere! Infact, if you don't train your skills with guns you can't aim at all, as it takes a lot of time to aim properly. It's a good way to test if you're curious, but it really hinders you a lot if you don't go stealth.
So the game isn't really as open as you think, by the end, since you -really- want to be stealthy and being stealthy makes you able to do most of the things much easily.
In addition the game lets you choose some augmentations, like invisiblity and higher jumps, but here's another flaw: you can choose, but the best choices are just one and if you don't take those, you're severely hindered.
For instance, one upgrade gave you faster speed and jump, while the other gave you muffled running...easy to say, that the higher jump really was useful in many occasions.
Another one gave you invisiblity for organic enemies (humans), while the other was for bots...I let you take your pick.
And another one gave you more resistance and the other gave you underwater breathing: this is actually occasional, but considering that you won't be fighting much, you'll be happy with aqualung instead, since you can swim a lot too.
Although I do admit, the game gives a lot of freedom on many other things: you're free to complete the missions as you desire (you can kill the persons or not, and the result will change some things on the futurue). It may be flawed, but it's still a very good story to follow and the challenge of the "clunkyness" kinda gives you a satisfactory rush whenever you pass to the next part of the game. So yeah, even if aged, I definitely loved this game, and still remains one of my favourite.
Absolutely worth a try, and keep playing it until you get the hang of it. You won't be disappointed.

DEUS EX is a Role Playing Game with First Person Shooter elements in it, made in the year 2000 by Ion Storm and published by Warren Spector, releaced for the PC, using the Unreal 1 engine.
This is the greatest game ever made of all time (PC)
No I'm not kidding, lying, or even just saying that to signify it's importance or how great it is:
This really IS the greatest videogame ever made for the PC.
It has won over 200 GameOfTheYear awards, and many areas of videogame ideas and influence of even compleatly different generas can be traced back to Deus Ex.
The concept for Deus Ex came from Ion Storm (Austin) being split into three groups:
Group 1 was dedicated to creating the best PC exclusive FirstPersonShooter ever
Group 2 consisted of people with a lot of experiance in RolePlayingGames, and
Group 3 mostly included people from Looking glass studios, whose recent success in Thief: the dark project, wanted to see a future version of their FPS Stealth game.
And by combining the ideas and thoughts of all 3 groups, Ion Storm (Austin) created the greatest PC game of all time. And when you play it, you won't find it hard to believe.
The plot is set in a dystopian world during the year 2052, and follows the rookie United Nations Anti-Terrorist Coalition (UNATCO) agent JC Denton (hint: YOU), as he sets out to combat terroist forces (the NSF), which have become increasingly prevalent in a world slipping ever further into chaos, through a highly contaigus viris called the Grey death, only curable by the vaxine Ambrosia. As the plot unfolds, Denton becomes entangled in a deep and ancient conspiracy, encountering various organizations (to say whom would spoil too much), conspiracies, lies and twists, that carry on throughout the whole game, as he travels through various environments and cities, from NewYork, to Rome, to Hong Kong, and manny more.
The RolePayingGame parts include Upgrading skills and Augmentations to increase JC's effectivness in the field, and choosing diologe between characters, which not only effects the way characters treat you, but also the effects of the multiple endings, and the multiple roots and pathways PRIOR to said multiple endings.
But the real inovation in Deus Ex lies within the open-endedness in the levels: It's not a sandbox game, but its levels have manny pathways to the objectives and manny ways to approch them. You can go in all guns blazing, which gun is up to you, or choose different weapons, Lethal or Non-lethal, and try to stealth through it, and because JC has an inventory system, this is possable, although that certain weapons take up a bigger space in the inventory slot, and the re-aranging of the items has created the name "Inventory-Tetris".
Remember when I said Non-lethal? Yes it is possable. You can stun, or knock out enemies to make them unconsious, meaning you didn't kill them, or hack a security turret to kill them, meaning YOU didn't kill them. Also, you can skip past the Boss fights entirely, not killing them or knocking them out.
Heck, it won a guiness world record for being able to compleate the game and only have to kill 2 PEOPLE.
It's that kind of deph you will find here.
Obviously, it's not just stealth, and a few areas require you to shoot through them, and the FPS elements are pretty good:
There's no iron-sights since they hadn't been invented at the time, although you can upgrade some weapons to have a scope on them, although if you aren't trained in these areas, your aim and crosshair will fumble and spread all over the place. There's no regenerating-health (F that cow-waste) or Heath-bar per say. Damage is taken through to the different parts of your body. Too manny arm shots & you're gonna struggle with aiming. Too manny leg shots, and you're gonna have trouble with movment. Health is replenished by using Med-kits on the different body parts, eating food found in certain places (i.e a drinking fountain or resteraunt), or using Androids found in a few places in various environments
And the MUSIC: holy heck the MUSIC. Just look up the Unatco theme on YouTube, and you'll see how AMAZING the music is.
It was composed by Alexander Brandon, who also did the Unreal tournament music, and a few others I haven't listed.
OK...
Now I've praised Deus Ex long enough, time to get into the problems.
It's not perfect. When I say best PC game of all time, I mean that all the things good about it outweigh the bad parts so much, that it makes it the best Pc game of all time: it's THAT good.
The first problem is for the modern era: it has aged like absolute COW-WASTE. The visuals are very dated, & it wasn't ground-breaking for it's time either, and that can put off a lot of first-timers.
The second problem is with the design choices:
Certain skills & augmentations are downright USELESS.
Ask any Deus Ex veteran about the "Swimming" skill, and they'll instantly get what you mean. The skill is never needed to progress ANYWHERE in the game. This is the same-ish issue with "Environment training", because being able to use radioactive suits, dull effects of poisons, and things of that nature isn't that helpful.
The skill for "Melee weapons" is also debatable in usefullness, because half-way through the game you are given a powerful sword that can kill most enemies in 1-2 hits.
Stealth can be a bit glitchy with certain weapons downright wierd.
The Crossbow with tranquilliser rounds for instance:
The effects on the poison depend on where it hits the body. If it hits the head, it takes 1-4 seconds to pass out. Anywhere else and it takes 5-12 seconds, during which time the enemy can run around, warn other people, set off alarms, & be a downright pain.
Also, the final problem, and this is directed at YOU if you plan on getting this, is that it has a VERY small accessabuillty factor.
It can be hard to get into, if first-timers don't know most of the flaws.
They read all of the reviews saying how awesome it is, and load up the game, expecting a good old time; YOU DON'T KNOW WHAT YOU'RE GETTING INTO. They'll see the character creation screen, put a few points into lethal weapons, and gun handling, expecting to shoot their way through the first mission, only to find themselves out of ammo, and not killing anything.
People who expect to play through the game, and listen to all the audio diologes, collect every weapon, hack all the security cameras, and upgrade everything on the first playthrough; It will JUST NOT HAPPEN the first playthrough.
You may get into the universe, and master everything in the game, but this WILL NOT happen during your first playthrough.
But at the end of the day, Deus Ex still stands the tests of time, and deserves ALL of those GOTY awards it got.
You know the saying with Deus Ex? Every time you mention it, someone re-installls it? Yeah, there's a reason for that.
So the 2 big questions are:
Is it Really the best game ever made of all time on PC? and
Should you play it?
To answer both those questions simply: YES*
And I said Yes with the asterix ( * ) as a disclaimer for first timers.
Because there are problems with it that you should watch out for, but get over them, and there really hasn't been a better game then this.
Deus Ex also had 2 sequels: Invisible war, and Human Revolution (the latter better well known), and while fans will argue till their mouths are sore over which is better, out of the 3, Deus Ex is the best of them.
I  EXTREMALY HIGHLY recommend this game to pretty much anyone into this.

Stick It To The Man’s unabashed insanity is its saving grace.
Though it took trudging through a serviceable yet tedious adventure game adjoined to an awkward platformer, developer Zoink’s oddball game about a dude who suddenly finds he can read people’s minds is so consistently amusing and clever that I found I rarely cared that I was only playing for the writing.
In a lot of ways Stick It To The Man is really refreshing. Few games venture into the realm of comedy, but Zoink jumps in head first with no reservations. Every line and character is progressively more absurd than the last, with each joke zipping by so fast you might miss it if you aren’t paying attention but making it easy to enjoy the ride due to having little time to actually dissect what’s going on.
stick it to the man pic 1If you were to break it down I doubt Stick It To The Man would elicit much more than a chuckle, but it’s how fully embedded it is in its ridiculous plot and satirical commentary that makes it all work. Every time I started the game it would take a moment to adjust to its outrageous style of humor, but a few minutes later I’d be sticking stickers all over things they don’t belong on and having an immensely good time watching the chaos unfold. Stick It To The Man is like a roller coaster that only goes up, with the stakes and quality of gags getting more and more insane the longer the game goes on even as you’re waiting for it to all come falling apart.
That’s not to imply Stick It To The Man is a particularly long game, clocking in around 3-4 hours, but it’s so densely packed that I think that’s all I could realistically take. It often felt like I’d been playing longer than I actually had simply do to how much stuff was always happening and continuing to happen even while I was trying to comprehend the scene before. It’s frankly a little exhausting to play, but in a way that makes you glad for its brevity because it ends right when you want it to.
There’s undeniably a lot of Stick It To The Man that’s little more than functional boredom, whether it’s the dull and obtuse puzzle designs or the few aggravating times you come across an enemy and have to manage the clumsy platforming controls to avoid them. There are only a few instances of this sprinkled throughout the game yet each always longer and worse than the last time you came across one. These scenes might work on a technical level, but there’s never any need for them to have been included.
But then everything circles around again to how delightfully written Stick It To The Man is even at its worst moments, and how that was more than enough to counteract its mechanical deficiencies for me. It’s as stupid as it is clever and delivered with enough style to make even the most cringeworthy joke work. Even though I can’t say I had a lot of fun playing Stick It To The Man, I was more than happy to spend some time reading the minds of its terrible, oh so entertaining hooligans.

Excubitor is a little bit different in the tower defense and shoot em up genres, Excubitor is a mixed bag of gameplay. The game has its moments of fun, where you get a new weapon to play with and you try something completely new. But it's also weighed down by some repetition, and a lack of oompf in terms of gameplay: nothing really strongly stands out in the genres in terms of mechanics in the end.
Different levels present different challenge which keeps you engaged and the choice of setting a turrent or a generator keeps you thinking.  When the level design goes off the beaten path, it can be pretty fun, as you're dashing around, trying to juggle things before your big ship gets destroyed. It does have an addictive quality to it at times.
A good collection of weapons. Upgrades do make a reasonable difference, so you have to manage that too. Do like the strafing adding a bit of skill into the mix.
Controls seem a little bit different at first, and it does take some getting used to. There's some nice details in the visuals. While they can clash at times, each art asset seems reasonable for what they are using here.
Sometimes, it feels like the choices of turrets really doesn't matter. This has to do with the fact that you really can make up for any weaknesses of your turrets in the end.
Difficulty on normal seems a little low. If you're a veteran of either genre, play on hard.

Excubitor is a game that says it merges tower defense with with top down shooter, or even bullet hell. Is it successful mix? Not very.
In Excubitor, most levels look like that: somewhere on small or medium sized map is placed Antares, your mothership. Your task is to defend it from drones - which take forms of various ships, mechs and other land units - using Hammerhead - your fighter and turrets.
Turrets can be placed on few specific places on map. Sadly, they are mostly useless. What is wrong with them? First, there is no information about damage they deal, their range, firerate etc. Secondly, they are simply weak. While during early missions they can kill and heavily damage weaker enemies on their own, with later missions and higher difficulties, with more and stronger enemies, they become more and more useless. Theoretically they can be upgraded, but there is problem with resource used for that - electricity. You gain set amount of it before each mission, and can gain some more by building generators. Building one takes some voidshards - other source used for buying and upgrading weapons - and one of points for building turrets. Those generators don't give much energy, and cannot be upgraded further. So either you will have bunch of useless turrets, or few strong ones heavy cannon turrets at one point, and all others unprotected. On higher difficulties and some missions you will probably skip all damaging turrets together and will just built cryo and emp turrets, which will slow down enemies and disable their weapons, so you will have more time to shot them down with fighter.
Fighter has quite large selection of weapons, which is nice. The weapons also feel and work different, which is additional plus. Sadly, just like for turrets, there are no stats for weapons. Each weapon can be upgraded three times, but is hard to say whether that "damage +14.88%" upgrade is worth it or not without any stats. What is also bad is the fact you can take only two weapons.  This completely removes point of having varied arsenal with different weapons having different roles and strengths - add to that lack of stats and in the end, you will probably just be flying around with newest weapon or the one that feels most comfortable to you. Also there are no maps in this game in which you are fighting against one type of enemies like in many tower defense games - so there is no planning like "lost of small enemies - I will take shotgun and flamethrower" or "few heavy enemies - I will take railgun and rocket launcher".  Later on you will also get weapon that is much better than any other so all of this becomes meaningless. Anyway, it definitely should be changed - from what I have seen, in beta versions there was inventory of sorts, and I think it wasn't bad idea. Either you should have access to all weapons after buying them, but with limited ammo, or you should have ability to rearm at Antares during mission.
You can also upgrade your fighter speed, shield, armour and weapons system. Of course you can probably guess that there again are no stats, so you don't know how much your speed or shield is boosted. Personally I wasn't feeling difference before and after upgrades. Only noteworthy things from them are berserk and repulsor skills. Honestly I would preferred if Antares could be upgraded instead of (or in addition to) Hammerhead. It would greatly benefited from stronger shields or having ability to recharge them.
During missions, it's best to stay near one of the roads and to kill enemies as soon as possible. Theoretically you can also explore the map, but with each level there is less reason to do it. There are some destructible structures, and powerups and voidshards containers that can be captured. Problem with them is that value of voidshards they give doesn't scales with levels. So early they give quite big amount, but later, when upgrades cost tens of thousands, single 20 voidshards form destructibles is laughable and not worth flying to second end of map. On one level there is capturable additional generator, on another there is laser drill that continuously gives you voidshards. Sadly both appear only once in entire game. Why? Things like that actually make exploration fun and worthwhile.
There also additional and secret objectives, but they don't change much expect giving additional voidshards, even though game tips say that doing them gives additional skill points.
Enemy variety is rather mediocre. Enemies are varied, but number of their types is not that big. I felt few times jealous of their weapons - why I don't have shockwave that harms everything near? Why I don't have tractor beam that stops enemies?
Graphic is quite nice, game is mostly stable, I had one or two random crashes, also on one level I could fly off the edge of map.
Still the game is not worth 14,99€ - you can get better tower defense games or top down shooters for that price or cheaper, and compared to them this games doesn't really have replayability. Only thing there is is new game + which is redoing the same levels on much higher difficulty. It's also very unfun, relying on usage of skills and slowing turrets, in which single enemy can destroy Antares on his own with few attacks. Still maybe it could be worth to pick on high discount on sale if you want to try.
Also the game heavily suggests addon or sequel - if it will happen, the game should be heavily remaked, or perhaps turned into just shooter or just tower defense game.

Bullet hell and tower defense combine to form something both better and worse than either alone.  As a standalone TD or shoot em up, this game wouldn't feel quite up to par - but the end result of hybridization plus plenty of upgrade-progression is surprisingly enjoyable.
When two individually tasty items are combined, one of three things usually happens:






Given the above method of simplifying the universe, Excubitor is firmly in category C.  The Tower Defense and Shoot-Em-Up parts of the game both seem to be lacking some of their usual appeal when considered individually, but still work strangely well together.
The tower defense gameplay initially seems rather unimpressive, as your towers never feel like they're really doing what they should (which is stopping enemy waves in their tracks).   The fixed points for building usually aren't strategically sound, the towers seem extremely weak, and even building towers can be a challenge when using a controller - (you have to target each tower build spot, with no close-enough lock on mechanism to aid you).   However, this should all be taken with a grain of salt:  the main point of tower-building in this game seems to be simply softening up foes juuust enough to take them down on your own.
The shoot-em-up section is also rather flimsy when considered on its own merits.  As long as you continually strafe/circle opponents, your ship is never in much danger from the enemies (they're mostly just trying to destroy your larger base at the center of the map), and even dying only costs you a few seconds to respawn with no real penalty.  You simply need to seek out clusters of enemies and destroy them before they have a chance to damage your central base too much.
The exception to this lackadaisical shmup-action is the epic boss battles, which throw swarms of enemies at you and your base from all directions, while you try to not-die and protect your base at the same time, even as you discover the trick / weak-point of the boss which will allow you to win.  These boss battles are spectacular and extremely challenging on even the 'normal' difficulty, and will be much more satisfying to those who love bullet-hell games.
Now this is where it gets interesting.  As previously mentioned, the towers in Excubitor aren't very strong, but they are still extremely necessary to successfully complete a mission - you can't guard the multitude of enemy paths all on your own.  Choosing the correct combination of towers thus becomes very important, as you want them to do at least a little damage to help thin the ranks, while also slowing/stunning ships as they approach so that your base doesn't take too much damage before you can swoop in.
Of course, even building these towers isn't easy, because time spent flying to the build spots is time taken away from defending your base - and for some reason, the enemies don't feel like being good sports and giving you free time to build up your defenses to stomp them.  Further complications arise with bonus objectives on the map to destroy and environmental hazards you can activate to take out a chunk of enemies and give you some necessary breathing room.  And it all becomes doubly tricky when your home base feels like repositioning 'for reasons' and makes your old towers semi-useless.  All of this makes managing your time betwixt shooting and building a rather entertaining challenge.
:
I do feel the need to point out a couple of negatives to the game that don't directly relate to the gameplay, but may influence your decision to purchase the game.
Currently, the audio is terrible.  Not merely mediocre, but full-out
awful.  The devs mentioned they're looking into it in the forums, so hopefully this will be fixed sooner or later - but for now you might as well put the game on mute.
Another negative is the controls - the frantic shoot-em-up-gameplay calls for a controller, but said controller makes building towers and selecting menu items like upgrades needlessly complicated.  The game could use a little more controller love, as well as a soft-lock when clicking on tower building areas.
:
This big ol' pineapple pizza of a game will probably be loved by some and hated by others.  By combining TD and SHMUP game styles, Excubitor compromises some of the strengths of each of its roots - but it still makes for a surprisingly tasty hybrid concoction in the end.  Despite the weaknesses in the game, it's a heck of a lot of fun and an innovative combination of genres.  If you think you might like an unusual actiony-defense game with some challenging boss battles and quite a bit of upgradeable progression, then you should give Excubitor a shot!

Overall the best and most feature rich, while still being user friend recording software out there.
If you can't get/don't like ShadowPlay™'s performance, this is definitely for you.  This has very little impact on pretty much everything, granted you have a quad core or better.  I personally use it to record everything I do, especially battlefield.  In BF4 I'm regularly getting 45-80 FPS on the ultra preset(4xAA) @ 1080p, and while running playclaw I only dip down to 40, still going up to 75+ in some places.  That's very minor performance impact for something that's actively compressing files for you.
As for size, its active compression is also very effective.  A 2 hour 30 minute video recording in 720p 95% quality (better than fraps, fraps is 90%) was only 45GB.  That's very impressive.
Playclaw also features a pre-record feature, which is probably my favorite feature.  It actively records into your RAM, and keeps recording (up to) the last 10 minutes of your game, making sure you never miss the recording of that amazing 1,300 meter headshot.  This pre-record feature has saved my bacon on a LOT of amazing clips I wanted to capture for one reason or  another.  It also has very little performance impact (granted you have the RAM available.)
Lastly, a very often overlooked feature in a recording software, is it's write protection.  Playclaw runs a separate process for all it's video writes, saving your clip even if playclaw, or more often your game crashes.  This means you get every last second recorded and you don't get corrupted video or write faults on your hard drive.  A few other programs *cough* dxstroy *cough* don't have this.  It's truly one of the most overlooked features in recording software.
Sidenote: Playclaw 5 supports Intel™ Quicksync™, which makes the recording process almost entirely ineffective towards your performance.  I don't have any experience with this being an AMD user, but I've heard good things.  Supposedly you should be looking at a 1% performance hit instead of around 5% to 15% without it, thus making it a better option than ShadowPlay anyways.
Edit note: Playclaw now supports the same Nvidia compression engine as ShadowPlay.  This means you get the same performance as ShadowPlay, but with playclaws interface and overlays.  A benefit to some.

DEUS EX is a Role Playing Game with First Person Shooter elements in it, made in the year 2000 by Ion Storm and published by Warren Spector, releaced for the PC, using the Unreal 1 engine.
This is the greatest game ever made of all time (PC)
No I'm not kidding, lying, or even just saying that to signify it's importance or how great it is:
This really IS the greatest videogame ever made for the PC.
It has won over 200 GameOfTheYear awards, and many areas of videogame ideas and influence of even compleatly different generas can be traced back to Deus Ex.
The concept for Deus Ex came from Ion Storm (Austin) being split into three groups:
Group 1 was dedicated to creating the best PC exclusive FirstPersonShooter ever
Group 2 consisted of people with a lot of experiance in RolePlayingGames, and
Group 3 mostly included people from Looking glass studios, whose recent success in Thief: the dark project, wanted to see a future version of their FPS Stealth game.
And by combining the ideas and thoughts of all 3 groups, Ion Storm (Austin) created the greatest PC game of all time. And when you play it, you won't find it hard to believe.
The plot is set in a dystopian world during the year 2052, and follows the rookie United Nations Anti-Terrorist Coalition (UNATCO) agent JC Denton (hint: YOU), as he sets out to combat terroist forces (the NSF), which have become increasingly prevalent in a world slipping ever further into chaos, through a highly contaigus viris called the Grey death, only curable by the vaxine Ambrosia. As the plot unfolds, Denton becomes entangled in a deep and ancient conspiracy, encountering various organizations (to say whom would spoil too much), conspiracies, lies and twists, that carry on throughout the whole game, as he travels through various environments and cities, from NewYork, to Rome, to Hong Kong, and manny more.
The RolePayingGame parts include Upgrading skills and Augmentations to increase JC's effectivness in the field, and choosing diologe between characters, which not only effects the way characters treat you, but also the effects of the multiple endings, and the multiple roots and pathways PRIOR to said multiple endings.
But the real inovation in Deus Ex lies within the open-endedness in the levels: It's not a sandbox game, but its levels have manny pathways to the objectives and manny ways to approch them. You can go in all guns blazing, which gun is up to you, or choose different weapons, Lethal or Non-lethal, and try to stealth through it, and because JC has an inventory system, this is possable, although that certain weapons take up a bigger space in the inventory slot, and the re-aranging of the items has created the name "Inventory-Tetris".
Remember when I said Non-lethal? Yes it is possable. You can stun, or knock out enemies to make them unconsious, meaning you didn't kill them, or hack a security turret to kill them, meaning YOU didn't kill them. Also, you can skip past the Boss fights entirely, not killing them or knocking them out.
Heck, it won a guiness world record for being able to compleate the game and only have to kill 2 PEOPLE.
It's that kind of deph you will find here.
Obviously, it's not just stealth, and a few areas require you to shoot through them, and the FPS elements are pretty good:
There's no iron-sights since they hadn't been invented at the time, although you can upgrade some weapons to have a scope on them, although if you aren't trained in these areas, your aim and crosshair will fumble and spread all over the place. There's no regenerating-health (F that cow-waste) or Heath-bar per say. Damage is taken through to the different parts of your body. Too manny arm shots & you're gonna struggle with aiming. Too manny leg shots, and you're gonna have trouble with movment. Health is replenished by using Med-kits on the different body parts, eating food found in certain places (i.e a drinking fountain or resteraunt), or using Androids found in a few places in various environments
And the MUSIC: holy heck the MUSIC. Just look up the Unatco theme on YouTube, and you'll see how AMAZING the music is.
It was composed by Alexander Brandon, who also did the Unreal tournament music, and a few others I haven't listed.
OK...
Now I've praised Deus Ex long enough, time to get into the problems.
It's not perfect. When I say best PC game of all time, I mean that all the things good about it outweigh the bad parts so much, that it makes it the best Pc game of all time: it's THAT good.
The first problem is for the modern era: it has aged like absolute COW-WASTE. The visuals are very dated, & it wasn't ground-breaking for it's time either, and that can put off a lot of first-timers.
The second problem is with the design choices:
Certain skills & augmentations are downright USELESS.
Ask any Deus Ex veteran about the "Swimming" skill, and they'll instantly get what you mean. The skill is never needed to progress ANYWHERE in the game. This is the same-ish issue with "Environment training", because being able to use radioactive suits, dull effects of poisons, and things of that nature isn't that helpful.
The skill for "Melee weapons" is also debatable in usefullness, because half-way through the game you are given a powerful sword that can kill most enemies in 1-2 hits.
Stealth can be a bit glitchy with certain weapons downright wierd.
The Crossbow with tranquilliser rounds for instance:
The effects on the poison depend on where it hits the body. If it hits the head, it takes 1-4 seconds to pass out. Anywhere else and it takes 5-12 seconds, during which time the enemy can run around, warn other people, set off alarms, & be a downright pain.
Also, the final problem, and this is directed at YOU if you plan on getting this, is that it has a VERY small accessabuillty factor.
It can be hard to get into, if first-timers don't know most of the flaws.
They read all of the reviews saying how awesome it is, and load up the game, expecting a good old time; YOU DON'T KNOW WHAT YOU'RE GETTING INTO. They'll see the character creation screen, put a few points into lethal weapons, and gun handling, expecting to shoot their way through the first mission, only to find themselves out of ammo, and not killing anything.
People who expect to play through the game, and listen to all the audio diologes, collect every weapon, hack all the security cameras, and upgrade everything on the first playthrough; It will JUST NOT HAPPEN the first playthrough.
You may get into the universe, and master everything in the game, but this WILL NOT happen during your first playthrough.
But at the end of the day, Deus Ex still stands the tests of time, and deserves ALL of those GOTY awards it got.
You know the saying with Deus Ex? Every time you mention it, someone re-installls it? Yeah, there's a reason for that.
So the 2 big questions are:
Is it Really the best game ever made of all time on PC? and
Should you play it?
To answer both those questions simply: YES*
And I said Yes with the asterix ( * ) as a disclaimer for first timers.
Because there are problems with it that you should watch out for, but get over them, and there really hasn't been a better game then this.
Deus Ex also had 2 sequels: Invisible war, and Human Revolution (the latter better well known), and while fans will argue till their mouths are sore over which is better, out of the 3, Deus Ex is the best of them.
I  EXTREMALY HIGHLY recommend this game to pretty much anyone into this.

This is going to be a review for 3 different potential buyers:
1. The buyer, who has not played this game before and has the equipment and money to play most modern-ish games
This game has its good moments, but it really has nothing unique that you wouldn't find anywhere else. If you're still interested in this bad-comedy-action type racing game, may I suggest later titles from this franchise.
2. The nostalgia buyer
You might be pretty tempted to buy this old 'gem', especially since its price gets pretty darn low on sales. Before you add this to your cart, let me just mention some of the issues I encountered:
*I don't remember the non-Steam version having frequent framerate issues. This does. Most notably on the edges of the map, but they happen pretty much all over the place. And I don't mean drops by just a couple of frames. I'm talking about motion sickness level nosedives.
*Speaking of frame rates, I averaged about 38-40 fps, with 1920x1080 resolution and all other graphics settings on the lowest possible setting. I don't know if that's a sign that this port is badly optimized or that my computer is sh*ttier than I had previously thought. For reference, I can play project cars on medium settings with the same resolution and almost never go below 60fps. Not really an issue other than I'm a bit spoilt.
*You still have to grind through the bland story missions to gain access to the good cars
*In my case, it didn't really provide the entertainment I thought it was going to deliver. After 10 hours you've completely depleted the game and it has nothing more to offer you.
That doesn't mean I didn't have fun, but the framerate issues were the things that killed it for me.
Ultimately, it's your choice..
3. The buyer, who has not played this before, but can't really run or afford any better quality alternatives
I think the story and voice acting are irrelevant to this type of game. Sure they are bad, but I think it was intentional. It would be worse, if they tried to make it serious and ultimately failed at that. And it's not even that annoying. Besides, you should be able to skip most dialogue. Anyway, you are realistically buying this for the action stuff, and as far as that is concerned, it is very solid. Some cars are even a joy to drive. Great for creating low budget action sequences, if that's a thing you're interested in. And when it costs under a euro, it's a steal. Would recommend.
Thus ends the review

I own this and Fraps and I have to say that each has their flaws, but for the most part I prefer PlayClaw 5. It's a lot more customizable generally, and that's what I appreciate about it. It lets you set what quality you want to record, it lets you put overlays, with the ability to enable or disable them showing up in your video, the amount of overlays are insane, ranging from computer info like usage and temperature all the way to just having time or your icon as a watermark. Fraps is a great program for beginners who want a program that for sure will work with the highest quality video and the most minimalistic UI, but PlayClaw 5 is great for those who know wha they're doing, or even those who want to do LP's. I'm not really a fan of many of them, but it does let you do a webcam overlay.
My only real gripe with PlayClaw 5 really is that it doesn't always work properly. For instance, it doesn't hook onto Zandronum (A Doom source port engine), and while it does hook, for some reason it doesn't show the HUD of The Typing/House of the Dead: Overkill. I haven't tried it with any emulators, but I have a feeling that it wouldn't work for that either. My recommendation is to get this when it's on sale and get Fraps, that way you'll know for sure you'll be able to record, and you'll have a, in my opinion, superior option when it does work, which is most of the time.
Edit: Another gripe is that you have to open it when there's nothing else open that it could potentially record, so don't have Skype or Firefox or any games open because it'll crash that program while crashing itself. I also noticed that when I recorded Doom 3 that all in-game screens were just black, so I don't know what's up with that, but it didn't do that with Fraps.

This has been the first game in a long time that I find very difficult to put down, there is always a lot to do and it's all fun. The game goes for a philosophical theme that a lot of people like to condescendingly put down to make themselves sound smart. The philosophy is implemented in such a way that it's more show and less tell, it's not shoved down your throat but it's there for you to think about or ignore at your own leisure. It adds depth without being pretentious or preachy and I'd say they got it perfect in that regard. Most importantly to me is that it never gets so deep into existential philosophy or so convoluted that it stops being grounded or making sense.
The story itself is often serious and intense but it also doesn't take itself too seriously. It cracks jokes when it's appropriate and provokes emotion when it's appropriate. It doesn't break the 4th wall so much as it tries to blur the lines. Game elements like UI, death, and saving are implemented in a way to prioritize immersion over mechanics while still giving the functionality and player choice necessary.
The RPG elements can use up a lot of time for people who enjoy loot grinding and min-maxing but are not so essential that someone couldn't play through without ever stopping to grind and still get the job done. Player progression can be divided into 3 parts, weapon upgrades, software enhancements, and exp levels. Aside from being able to equip software to boost exp gain, there isn't anything to the levels, no skill trees or points to distribute. The weapons feature an upgrade system with 4 levels per weapon and requires a combination of currency and materials to enhance. Simply doing occasional side quests and a little bit of looting during the story will be enough to max out a couple weapons well before you need them, but maxing all the weapons is an endeavor. Harkening back to the first Drakengard game, all weapons have a story that gets revealed with each weapon level. Lastly, the software in the form of chips is where players can tweak their builds to suite their playstyle and manage their HUD. Throughout the game the player will receive enough chips to keep their character functional, but optimizing a build, while unnecessary, will involve a lot of looting and is very rewarding. The game seems to be balanced around inefficient chips that are doled out during the story so people who go out of their way to min-max will likely find themselves overleveled and overpowered.
There are difficulty settings to tweak the experience. I haven't played on easy but there are a plethora of optional chips a player can use to make the game play itself almost, so players who aren't very skilled can still enjoy the game. The higher difficulties receive a lot of mixed reviews for being way too hard or too easy, and I haven't seen any complaints about the normal setting. The one thing I can assure you is that you have options. While the game does not feature permadeath, it does have a death system similar to Dark Souls that can potentially be more punishing. If you don't recover your body before dieing a second time you lose your chips, which can be crippling. The game does not use auto save for immersion purposes so this can be gotten around in the rare case of a bug or for players who would rather wimp out and reload than lose a lot of time investment in chip building. I personally don't blame them as that would cause a lot of quitting if there wasn't a workaround, especially in the case of a crash or bug.
The combat is what you can expect from a platinum game, fast paced, emphasizes timing and dodging, and mixes melee and ranged attacks. It's the meat of the game and the most fleshed out part, it's fast and fun and keeps the game going. It's probably the biggest reason I struggle to put the game down.

For once, this is a Yoko Taro game I actually wanted to replay to get different endings. It's a really great sequel to the original NieR, but even if you haven't played that, this game still holds up well on its own.
Music is great, setting and story are interesting. I honestly can't think of anything "bad" to say; not everything is perfect of course, for example the combat, while fast and fluid, is a bit shallow and spammy, and upgrading your weapons and using damage-boosting chips/items makes you stupidly OP. Some of the side quests are generic "go here, then here" or "kill x enemies in this location" or even the dreaded escort mission (where you can friendly-fire your client). But most of the side quests helped flesh out the world and characters a bit more. Also each run of the game is relatively short, but there is cool new stuff leading to each different ending. The characters have potential to be more fleshed-out but that doesn't really happen until at least the second playthrough, so until then they're sort of "ehh". The environments were pretty but somewhat lacked detail, there's not really much going on in them. But all this is basically nit-picking, I just wanted to present a more balanced view. One thing I did like was that, although most of the enemies you fight are machines, they have lots of variations and different abilities to make it a bit more interesting.
tl;dr it's not "OMG EPIC AMAZING" but it's highly enjoyable, both for Taro fans and newcomers, and has lots of replayability and new stuff constantly being unveiled.

I recommend this game, with a single caveat. If you don't like rogue-lite games, you won't like this one. As far as the genre goes, I find this game to be more forgiving than, say, Spelunky, but the difficulty is still bitingly hard. Its a top down shooter where you can shoot in four directions as you try to fight off your homicidal mother with the power of your tears. You get various useable items, consumables, passive upgrades, weapon (tear) modifiers-- none of which are fully explained in-game. One must play (or use the wiki or various YTers) to determine the effectiveness of various items and item combinations. Its a game of skill, with many luck based elements. Even the best players will still lose from time to time. The art design can be drab at times, as it is often just brown on gray, but that slides into the background as you get lost in min/maxing your character to get the strongest run possible.

Stick it to The Man! tries to be an offbeat and funny sidescrolling platformer, and it mostly succeeds.
You start the game by getting hit on the head and developing a superpower which lets you read other people's minds and conjure/manipulate objects in the world (which are called stickers). With the help of these stickers you solve all the "puzzles" in the game. I put puzzles in quotations because they're not real puzzles, there is basically no thinking involved, you just try sticking every sticker where it is possible and you solve it, that's all there is to it.
Similarly, there is no difficulty involved with the platforming in the game. And sadly the same goes for avoiding the enemies. They move in predictable patterns and it's easy to lose them even if you get spotted, that means that you're just going thorugh the motions most of the time.
Despite all that the story, dialogue and art style are here to save the game. It's hard to do humour in video games and Stick it to The Man! manages just that quite often. I am not talking about laugh out loud moments, but I was most certainly entertained throughout the game, even if there is a bit too much of listening to oneliners when you're reading people's minds. Finally, the art style alone is worth checking out, it gives the illusion of everything being made from paper or carboard and it achieves a very nice effect which doesn't get old until  the end.
I couldn't recommend the game based on the gameplay alone, however the style of the game is absolutely worth checking out.

An open world space simulation sandbox with some persistent elements.  If you can overcome the nearly vertical learning curve that has plagued the X series you will find a rough gem of a game within.  Be a mercenary pilot, a merchant or even a pirate and anything else in between.  The introduction of war within the X universe isn't fully fleshed out although it will add a nice distraction when you need something more than the sandboxy experience.  You can pilot anything from a small fighter to a heavy carrier and command a sizable fleet with an admittedly awkward control system.  Mods aplenty here with most X3:TC mods being compatible: I recommend MARS, the updated Universe Trader and of course the bonus pack from Egosoft's website.  Be forewarned, the game is unforgiving and you will spend a significant amount of time reading/watching videos on how to accomplish most things within, but if you have the patience it is a unique experience.

TL;DR: Yes, play this and the first one before you play Witcher 3 - it's worth it.
Jumping straight into this right after finishing the first Witcher game was quite an experience. Gone is the clunky navigation and combat, dated graphics, pen-and-paper book UI, and cheezy character design - replaced with intuitive and modern controls, surprisingly gorgeous graphics, a simple but effective UI, and detailed fantasy characters. Being able to control Geralt so smoothly was a serious breath of fresh air. Aside from the open world aspect, Witcher 2 has a lot more in common with 3 than it does with 1 - and that's a good thing as far as I'm concerned. Absolutely everything just flows better.
I'd heard complaints that the combat in this game was hard or unintuitive, but I'm not sure what those folks are talking about. Personally, I found it much easier to deal with than the click-timing system from the first game - and certainly less challenging than something like Dark Souls. (That said, blocking and dodging alone might not save you as relilably as in those titles.) Combat in the Witcher 2 is one of many enormous improvements over the first, because most importantly - it's fun. Geralt leaps from one enemy to the next, fluidly slicing his enemies to bloody mush, and the character progression is tangible. It's a blast.
Did I mention the graphics? They may not be the freshest thing in 2017 when I played this - but after the first game, I feel like I moved from Gumby to Lord of the Rings in terms of visual presentation. Art style and animation have taken a huge step forward. The voice acting is better, too.
So - gushing aside, this game picks up right where the first leaves off - with Geralt at the side of King Foltest after an attempt on his life. Another king has just been slain (depicted in the opening FMV), and the wheels of fate are turning. Like the previous game, there are choices that affect the events and outcome of the game - perhpas moreso. There are 16 possible endings! It was possible to tip-toe the line of neutrality in the first game (though I fell off that tightrope myself) - but not this time. Each choice has tangible consequences for how the game plays out, and for the ultimate political ramifications.
The game isn't perfect - I found myself digging through the wiki quite a lot - though that may have been my own impatience and curiosity at work. Out of the 50 or so hours I played the game, I think I experienced 3 or 4 unexpected crashes to desktop. Still, I enjoyed this game immensely, and the few difficulty spikes I experienced were actually just puzzles in disguise (unlike that one certain fight from the first game I won't mention again).
The story is intriguing, the characters are interesting, the choices are meaningful, the combat is great - the game is fun! I highly recommend it.
Witcher 1 and 2 are completely worth playing through before getting into the 3rd - you get all kinds of character background, and some great experiences to boot. Play them - you won't regret  it.

I've never been a big D.C. (or Marvel for that matter) fan, and I've played fewer fighting games than almost any other genre. In other words, I'm not the target audience for this game. Yet I really enjoyed every moment of 'Injustice: Gods Among Us'.
I don't know what die-hard fighting fans will make of it; maybe it's too accessible for some of them, but as a relatively casual player I can't think of much to criticise. I *do* wish that Batman's playstyle was a little smoother -- playing him seems a little trickier than the rest of the characters.
The story is surprisingly good -  the fighting fits within the narrative rather than the other way around, and this is probably why it was such a success. The sequence of events feels natural, and not just an excuse to line up the next opponent. Many of the story fights actually add to the plot in some sense, and so the player is always left with an impression of progress which runs much deeper than just beating the current level.
I bought this game in the sales but would in retrospect happily pay full price -- the amount of content is *very* impressive. There are enough unique challenges to not only acquaint you with all the characters, moves and settings, but to also fill dozens if not hundreds of hours. (The fact that I haven't logged many more hours on this is largely due to the fact that I'm not very good with fighting games and just *know* that I won't get very far with the additional content.) This game, in brief, is definitely worth your money and time.

Excubitor is the debut game from Tesseract Interactive and is published by Kasedo Games. For those of you who may not know, Kasedo Games is the digital first division of Kalypso Media who are famous for among other things their fantastic Tropico franchise. Among their other titles are Imperium Romanum Gold Edition, Skydrift, Crookz – The Big Heist and many more. Therefore, before I even had an opportunity to sit down and play the game I had reason to be quietly confident that I would be presented with a potentially great new indie title.
After playing for a sufficient number of hours to experience the game and to be in a position to review prior to release I have to admit that I was not disappointed. Fans of the tower defense and bullet hell genres will rejoice when they get their opportunity to play Excubitor.  It manages to marry the combination of the two genres perfectly together to create an exciting title that is bursting at the seams with action but providing a significant chunk of strategy as well.
It’s very rare for me to put a significant number of hours into a game before it is released to the public. I’m not a huge fan of betas or early release games (not Early Access games that are purchasable by the general public). However, Steam credits me as having spent over 140 hours in the game as of writing. While there were periods where I was idle within the game I’ve definitely spent over a hundred hours in the game (and reset achievements twice so as to show the game off to friends as new). That speaks volumes to the amount of enjoyment that I have already received from Excubitor.

Hello everybody, Shaun Meyers from Universal Gaming Reviews here to bring you a short summary from our review for Excubitor by Tesseract Interactive and Kasedo Games.
If you'd like to read our full review for the game, you can find it here:
Excubitor is a very unique combination of a bullet hell game and a tower defense game and at first glance you might be like me and think, "That can't possibly work well together" but the suprirising part is, it does.
The game puts you in control of a small fighter ship known as the Hammerhead. Using your ship to fly around the map you'll be abe to fight off incoming waves of enemy ships using deployable turrets. During missions you'll also need to protect a ship called Antares. If this ship is destroyed it's game over.
The game features 17 weapons in total and each of them has 3 upgrades for you to purchase in the armory. There are also a wide range of turrets available for you to construct as well. There are also points on the map that you'll be able to interact with that will often aid you in the game as well. These include factories that will mine resources, fans that will destroy any incoming enemies and many others to discover.
The game's control felt very fluid and the game was equally action packed. The game is also quite beautiful to look at as well.
I imagine the game won't be for everyone but it's definitely a fun (and challenging) game that will no doubt please fans of bullet hell games and tower defense games.

A little bit different in the tower defense and shoot em up genres, Excubitor is a mixed bag of gameplay. On one hand, you've got a game that does try a little bit of something different, and when it really opens up the level design with some new and interesting concepts and challenges, it really can bring the fun factor. The game has its moments of fun, where you get a new weapon to play with and you try something completely new. But it's also weighed down by some repetition, and a lack of oompf in terms of gameplay: nothing really strongly stands out in the genres in terms of mechanics in the end. And the game left with a little bit of motion sickness at times.
It's one of those games that will not make purists of the genre happy: there's little quirks here and there will all of its mechanics, and that's going to annoying some people, where the action of the shmup comes face to face with the slow strategy of tower defense. If you're a gamer that likes a game going off the beaten a path a bit, but still being in familiar territory, then this is worth a look. Otherwise, it's one of those titles that I'd wait for a sale on.

Borderlands: The Pre Sequel is definitely a fun experience. Overall, the game is well made and I really can't stress how entertaining it is. But, is it worth the price tag? The blunt answer is no. Luckily I did not pay full price and got it bundled with the season pass for $20. $20-30 is the most this game should've asked for. While it has quality content there isn't much. The story itself takes maybe 15 hours at most. The world is much smaller, the story is shorter, less sidemissions and fewer interesting personalties than in Borderlands 2. The vertical leveling was also quite annoying and made finding your way around or find missions or mission objectives a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
The story is pretty solid, with some entertaining bit sprinkled in and a few returning faces. The huge problem I had with the story was I didn't have any sense of urgency. In BL2 you feel this urge to defeat that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Handsome Jack who is threatening Pandora. In BLPS you can't really get that connection to any of the "villains". Zarpedon is the closest you get to that and she really isn't an intrecate part of the story. You might hear her shout something to her soldiers like "Blow this up!" or "Stop him!" but that's where it ends. Some of the plot is really confusing too. Why are we following Athena's point of view when you're not playing Athena? Even in multiplayer it will show Athena in cutscenes and not the entire group.
The characters were okay. Janey Springs was well done, so was The Meriff, of course Crazy Earl and that little kid I can't really remember. I've heard a lot of people complain about Janey and they're usually sad sap loonies. There weren't an awful lot of characters and none of them really have anything terribly intresting about them unlike the ones from BL2 we all loved. The player characters were excently done though, and interact with Jack and other NPCs differently and actually talk. I thought the different abilities were pretty nice, escpecially the DLC ones. Enemies on the other hand weren't done so well. The scavs and lunitics really aren't as good as their raider and pyscho counterparts. They never really say anything intresting or have much variation other than charcter models.
Other than that, the UI is basically the same, there's moonstones (which is basically eridium), laser weapons which are pretty cool, Australian accents everywhere, butt slamming, cyro weapons and Mad Moxxi.
Don't buy on full price, wait for a sale and you won't regret it.
