Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is the follow up to Borderlands 2 and fallows on the rise of Handsome Jack. But will you want to play it ?
Borderlands TPS takes place after the events of Borderlands and before the events of Borderlands 2 and follows on four new vault hunters. Athena, Wilhelm, Nisha and Claptrap get a message from a hyperion worker who happens to be Handsome Jack. After the Dahl soldiers take over the space station they try to destroy the moon of Elpis and it's up to you to stop them.
Gameplay is identical to Borderlands 2. The only new thing is the new Oxygen system. You have a bar which starts to drain when you are outside the oxygen field for too long. Then you start to suffocate. You can also use the double jump to get on higher platforms. You can avoid the oxygen system by picking Claptrap as your character. The new abilities are awesome and all of them are very fun to use.
Graphics are stunning as ever. They look awesome and all the colors are very nice to look at. The textures are kind of mediocre and some of the character models look very bad. Overall the game looks great apart from minor flaws.
Audio is pretty bad. The game's audio for me stopped during firefights and I couldn't hear anything the characters would say to me and sometimes the Echo Com screen didn't transfer the dialogue and I couldn't hear anything which wasn't a problem in Borderlands 2. The soundtrack is alright, there are some great songs but a lot of them are kind of mediocre.
The game is pretty easy for the most part until the final chapter where there is a massive difficulty spike and the final boss solo is incredibly hard. The boss fights are very team oriented meaning the game expected you to play with people from the start.
Level Design in some parts is abysmal it took me massive amounts of understanding where my objective was and where the side quest start. This by far the worst level design in a borderlands game.
The game took me 22 hours to complete every quest and to get to level 27. The game like other Borderlands games has tons of replay value with different vault hunter modes and trying out other characters and of course not to mention the DLC which I will have to check out one day.
The game is pretty stable from the most part. There where some parts where the game wouldn't open a certain door to progress through a quest but a quick reload always fixed the problem.
Overall this game is not as good as the other titles in the series and without a doubt not worth it at the full price. I am a massive Borderlands fan and Pre Ordered this game once I saw it and I can safely say it wasn't a bad game but it's not as good as the other Borderlands games. For other people only buy this on a sale. It has a lot of horrible side quests but this is an overall good game and I highly suggest you to check it out on a sale. I give Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel a 7/10

I was really hoping to be impressed by this game. I think an hour is ample time to give this game a chance. I have a tendency to find the best horror games in the little played and little understood games but this one was a huge miss. The main problem is that there is no direction or hint of how to play or succeed in this game. You have to build trust with other characters but the whole thing is guess work and I didn't even know what works and what doesn't. The lack of a save feature makes this even more frustrating as I have no break or comparison to tell if what I'm doing is right.
The next major problem comes with the nightmares. I know the story mode skips them but I don't see why it makes sense to have to break a game to make it playable. It seems to contradict common sense. The nightmares are confusing and add little to the game. Without them it's more of a visual novel but to be honest I think this game would be more enjoyable if it was. The nightmares a literally a waste of time and cost you all your collected items.
Which brings me to the items. Collecting random things and giving them to random people is how you progress in this game. As stated before you do not get any hint of who likes what so it's basically a guessing game that'll take several days. The days seem to be too short to get anything done especially in nightmare mode as you lose all your items upon waking up.
tl;dr: This is a boring game with wonky controls. It is a guessing game with little reward (I didn't really gain anything playing for an hour). The story is uninspired or at least to minimal as my time playing didn't give me any drive to want to know more. Basically it's just a boring game with little reward. I got it for less than a dollar and am still wondering if it was worth that.

#0, the author uploaded other versions of this game for free to various websites.  Google the name, you can apparently play version 1.01 there.  So....
#1, there is no way to save.  The game has checkpoints at the end of every chapter, but it will take you multiple in-game days worth of guess and check in order to get past the first one.  The game is rare enough that there was no guide until I wrote one.
#2, The primary gameplay mechanic is to search out plot items that are scattered across the map, whose locations and purposes you are generally not given, and try to figure out who to give them to.  If you try to use them on someone who doesn't want them, they still disappear out of your inventory.  Also your inventory clears every night* (in Nightmare mode : there is now a story mode that fixes that, and also skips issue #3).
#3, Nightmares.  Each day is timed, and after an amount of time that I'm guessing is in the 10-15 minute range, the day is over and you are teleported into bed.  You then proceed to the Dark World where monsters run around draining your sanity meter.  You are stuck in the dark world until you find and touch the three portals that spawn at semi-randomized locations on the map.  You can find clues to their location during the day using the smelling salts, but you have no map and no way to find them at night aside from blundering around.  If your sanity drains all the way, you die, and must restart the game from your last checkpoint.  You can skip the intro cutscene if you press the right buttons, I think the spacebar is what does it.
When you hit the third portal, you can return to the waking world...with no inventory items, so you have to go around and try to collect things again, if you even can.
The dialogue is interesting, I'm curious where it's going, I want to like the characters and get to the bottom of all this, but I'm not sure if I have the stamina to try to speedrun around this place over and over and over and over under a timelimit.  Without the day system, I think I'd enjoy it a lot more -- but, again, steam seems to have given me version 1.01 and not the 1.02 update that ought to solve that problem.
I don't know.  I'd advise going to play the free version to see if you want this.  The soundscape is hilarious though, and I enoy the tinny ragtime music and heavily-accented voiceover.  Don't play it unless you really enjoy delving into the stories of B-grade games, but I kinda do.
[Edited to add] : The game is using the Unity engine, but a graphics resource pack from RPGmaker.  The More You Know . . .

Getting the game: I bought the game on sale for $30, Totally worth $40! I immediatly bought all the DLC. This game is worth every penny.
Where I'm at: I have around 40 hours in the game so far. First thing I did was spend 6 hours making 6 different races that fit my ideal story line. I then started a TINY game to learn the basic of the begining and what I really needed to focus on (try to focus on more influence).  Then I started a medium game trying a race I created but was uncomfortable with, early into the game the newest DLC was released (Leviathans Story Pack) and I quickly started over. I'm now part way into my next attempt at a full round. I've met my 5 other races, unintentionally, none of them are my allies creating quite the unintended story. I created a federation with two of my local allies and we have started to pick apart the solo races.
My Suggestions: Spend tons of time making a race you think you'll enjoy, then  take the time to test it out on a TINY map. Learn the basics, then go for the big stuff!
Who should play this game: Anyone who likes space, 4x games, this is the better version of Galciv III, and by far better than any CIV game since CIV III. (CIV:BE was garbage)
Suggestions to Devs: Just on playing a medium sized map, I had several recurrences of meeting the same gas like race that needed assistance, more options and encounters would be nice. and as always more race options.
Thoughts on playability: I've played/started 3 rounds so far, encountering entirely different races (other than the ones I designed) each time. There is thousands of combinations giving you a new game every time. This game is amazing.
Dear Devs: QUALITY. I love that my introduction, and choices are all based on my decisions made when creating my race. Don't start a new game, just expand this one! THANK YOU!

Fun little game that reminds me of something Double Fine/Tim Schafer would make.  It's a platforming puzzler where you pick up stickers in the area or from reading the minds of the colorful cast and placing them to progress. This isn't a very difficult or long game, but the humorful dialogue is really where the game shines.
Pros
-humorous
-interesting art style
-plenty of game and movie references
Cons
-the jump controls can be wonky sometimes. It's sort of like the older Castlevanias where you're locked in to your jump distance. Largely, this isn't a problem outside of a few horizontal jumping segments.
-I had a few times where a sticker couldn't be pulled or placed. If you have it go off screen and come back, it tends to fix itself.
Notes
-Press M to bring up the map
-You can skip cutscenes by holding Backspace. This is useful if you're going back through the chapters to read the minds you've missed
-I've got 5.3 hours logged for total completion (with about half an hour or so of idle time). This can either be a pro or con, depending on your budget and free time. All in all, the game feels very complete and tells a whole narrative, while still having an opening for a sequel.

It's years late but finally a review for Magicka has arrived!  Wow, what a great game.  Let's just start off with that and get into it!
The gameplay in this game is truly where it shines above tons of games that are like it.  It's all about the Magick system.  The combining of different elements together to make super powered spells is amazing, and trying to figure out which spells work against which enemies the most effectively makes the game extremely unique and spellbinding (see what I did there???....I'll stahp...).  A lot of games implement something similar to this but not quite to this effect and definitely not this successfully.  Casting spells is fun.  A LOT of fun.  Obliterating an enemy with a single giant rock never ever gets old.  While pumping arcane fire and electricity into a giant troll until he pops is something everbody has to experience.
But it's not just the fun and hilarity of casting spells (and it is hilarious at times), it's the simplicity at which all of this is done.  The casting system might feel complicated at first because we as gamers are so used to simplistic controls or default schemes, but it really is very intuitive.  And once the player gets the hang of it, the Magick just flows from the fingers.  And as if finding different combinations isn't fun enough, there's also a multitude of ways to cast these spells.  Shoot them directly at your enemies by clicking, create an AoE inferno by shift + clicking, give yourself rock armor by casting on yourself, or even imbue your sword with magic and cut into your foes with a giant icy blade that is sure to decapitate even the largest of foes.  Whatever way you decide to use the Magick, you're sure to have a great time.
The graphics in this game are nothing to scoff at either.  While they're not top of the line graphics like those in AAA titles, one must remember this is an indie game.  And for an indie game, the graphics fit the style of this game perfectly.  The hilarious effects, the mesmerizing spells, and the little robed wizards running around annihilating everything, just adds up to an incredible experience for the eyes.  My particular favorite level graphically?  Definitely the underworld.  There's not a lot to look at in there, but it's the absence of everything and.....well....the boss at the end that actually make that level slightly creepy.  Let's just say that the bosses in this game do NOT share the same sense of humor that the rest of the game carries.
Being completely honest here, while the game starts out with a silly plotline that seems like it will hold throughout the entirety of it, the game gets pretty dark and serious.  There's still comedy aplenty though.  Was very surprised with how creepy and powerful some of the bosses came across though.  Basically the game starts with happiness and silliness, and ends with a classic save the world or all will perish scenario.  But it is all pulled off very well.  Great story.
The sound in this game is pretty spot on as well.  The language spoken throughout the game is definitely not english or anything remotely similar, but you still might be able to translate a little by the end of the game.  And while the language is a garbled, hilarious mess, when it's translated by some of the more powerful creatures of Midgard, it comes out as terrifying.  Spell sound effects really give that extra oomph that we're all looking for when casting things like arcane rock (or any spell) as well.
With adventure mode, versus mode, challenge mode, and online play available, this game has an extremely long lasting lifespan.  As mentioned before, the spellcasting just doesn't get old.  Add in 10 tons of dlc and this game could take months to get tired of.
TL:DR  Buy this game, get past the tutorial, summon Rock five times, charge it up, shoot it at any enemy.  Enjoy.

I was recommended this game by a friend who told me that if i like Resident Evil 4 then i would probably like this game since its fan base tends to refer to it as Resident Evil 4: Boat Edition. After playing the game all the way through in about 2 sittings or so I managed to get to around 7 hours of gameplay and, honestly, had no desire to give it a second playthrough, and after thinking about it for a while, I personally did not like the game.
TL;DR: I can understand how some people would like the game, but I personally do not recommed this game. The cons that this game has outweigh the pros a lot imo, and there are so many better games on both Steam and GOG, that i would just recommend finding and playing one of those (REmake, System Shock 2, CB Undying, RE4, Outlast, ...). 6/10.
The Good
--The atmosphere is great. The entire time spent on the boat is actually really good and i really did enjoy a lot of the things that it had to offer, such as the constant moving if you are on the outside of the boat, strong waves can and will hurt you or even kill you, and the whole feeling of you being literally suck in the middle of nowhere.
--The combat i feel is solid even if it does have some techincal issues on the controls side, but it does very much feel like the RE4 combat.
The Bad
--Obviously i feel as if the game is too short. I have around 7-8 hours on record but some of that does come from me being idle and having to reload a previous save due to techincal issues (not the games fault). I would say that you can beat this game in 1 sitting and in about 5 hours or so with no problem, which for a survival horror game is pretty short imo.
--The controls do have their share of problems but nothing too serious as some people might of had. I played this with a controller so maybe that had something to do with it because i think this game was made more for the PS2 than the PC so if you want to play it i HIGHLY recommend a controller.
--A serious pet peeve of mine when it comes to survival horror is when a game tries to make a game "harder" by introducing random variables (or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t as i like to call it) or by removing things that at this point in time should be a standard. For example, you do not have a map in this game, and while i do praise the boat for its originality, some of the rooms do feel the same and the areas after following the boat are far too similar and you can get lost very easily. Also, and this really annoyed me, it violated the sanctity of the safe room with no warning. Granted it only happens once, but after playing many survival horror games the safe room is the one place you can fall back to. Even games like Silent Hill The Room that do turn the safe room into a dangerous place to be in, it does it over time as if it is warning you that the place you feel safe in will sooner than later become hostile. Finally, there are moments where the only time that an enemy is approtching or around a corner, is by trial and error. Sometimes you have to die to know what is behind a wall you cant see behind from your angle and if i dont forgive better games like Resident Evil 3 for doing this, i wont forgive this game for it.
--The enemies I feel are bullet sponges, and can be too easy or too hard. Too easy in the way that they stay still and take the punishment, either by your positioning or by the game having issues, and too hard in the way that they charge you and they can take about 2 clips of ammo before falling. Also the final boss is a total pushover, super easy and the ending leaves you with that "that was it?" feeling.
Overall i would give this game a 6/10. There are so many better games out there that the only way i would really recommend this game is if it were on sale for pretty cheap. Im glad that some can find joy in a game i didnt, and maybe i am alone on this opinion, but this game is not worth the "cult classic" hype people give it.

I really do wish to recommend this game but the issue I'm having is whom I would recommend this game to. It is by no means a bad game! I actually do like it. But it suffers from one MASSIVE flaw...
The Pre-Sequel is NOT anywhere as good as Borderlands 2.
The two factors that made Blands 2 so awesome were it's entertaining story and it's characters which were (for the most part) entertaining to play. The Pre-Sequel does not deliver in both these areas. The story is only okay, and the playable characters are fairly under-whelming, even compared to the original Borderlands game. So I was tempted to recommend maybe playing this game BEFORE Blands 2, but even that leaves a sour taste in my mouth. The fact is, Blands 2 is cheaper. You can purchase it with it's major expansions for less than this game and it has TONS more content, all much more enjoyable.
So who would I recommend this game to? The only players who come to mind would be the Borderlands fans (like me) but those gamers should have already played (and been disappointed by) this game. So who else is there? Maybe, just maybe, the very casual gamer who is taking thier sweet time getting to this game, but even them I'd recommend playing all the expansions for Borderlands 2 first, and then probably just starting yet another character in that game (or the original Borderlands) instead.
And just FYI, I do own two copies of this game now. I originally purchased on console to play co-op with my son, and now have it on PC because it's the gaming system I prefer. And I will play even more of this game, but I just can't in good conscience recommend anyone else to do the same.
So in conclussion, my feeling is if you haven't purchased this game already, then there's really no need to at this point. Either play Borderlands 2 (and it's expansions!) or just wait for Borderlands 3 instead.

I have mixed feelings on this one. tl;dr I ended up buying Fraps to get my game captures.
About me: I make a lot of fragshow/machinima movies and have about 10 years experience. This program didn't work out so well for that purpose. I also did some research on YouTube for reviews prior to my purchase, but unfortunately my mileage varied quite a bit.
I found I had to alt tab a few times to get the overlays to appear - like it wouldn't select the open game for a while. Then, even when turning all overlays off in the settings, they still appeared in my recordings.. and yes, i had turned the overlay off from the active game prior to recording!
Another problem I had was that I had to close and reopen the program a lot, and relaunch my games so PlayClaw would show up, which caused steam to go "hold the phone! we're closing or opening something" all the time [black Steam box in middle of screen.] I'd also get "failed to launch app" as PlayClaw or its "hook" which displays/hooks into games would get frozen in the background. I'd have to restart my games, steam and eventually my PC to try to get things going.
Can't blame the dev for that though, as it appears to be how Steam handles licensing. However, I can blame the dev for this: I emailed explaining my issue, and asked for a license for the non-steam version (which is feature-same, does not have new features) and was refused saying to try the new beta.
I don't want to try new betas. I want to have working software delivered through Steam if thats how I purchase it. But if one of my core issues is that I'm having problems LAUNCHING the app, I should be given a key for the non steam version as I had requested.
I can see this argument.. if you buy a game on steam, and it has issues, would you get given a normal CD key for the game AS WELL? well, no. But this is a piece of software designed to run alongside games, and maybe Steam isn't built for that.
The program also always prompts for admin rights (Win 8.1 x64) which, if you're reopening it multiple times, becomes quite the annoyance. Also each time I quit the program it would display a variable error.
Then comes the quality. I found recording the same footage in Fraps vs in PlayClaw resulted in about a 60% smaller file in PlayClaw. Maybe this is good for some people, but it wasn't good for me as I wanted to retain as much quality as possible using this type of recording method.. meaning the reds got junked up a bit due to compression.
I guess I'll close in saying that PlayClaw seems to have some cool features which I'll try to use eventually since I paid for it but it has some problems - which all software does. What wasn't cool for me was the developer refusing to let me use a non-steam version of the program I had bought a license for.
If we buy on Steam, we shouldn't have to manually install things. In my opinion If we opt to do that, we should be granted the privilege.

This game is merely a port from the consoles. It shows very noticibly, especially when I had to modify some CFG files just to enable the developer console. Get this game while it's half off, and be sure to get the expansions only if you plan on playing the zombie maps that come with them.
There is a pet peeve with the way you find a multiplayer game (this doesn't apply to zombies). With multiplayer, when you want to find a game, you can either search for a ranked server to join, or you can manuelly find a server via the server browser. This game is at a half-life or so, but it's no problem to find a game on Nuketown! If you want to play the map Crisis or Hanoi, however, you better find a server that has a full map rotation, and it's hard even to find a popular map that's on DLC! This is al kind of bad, but this server browser, much like Garry's Mod and CS: S, has servers mainly, if not all, hosted by a clan or person. I know this one set of servers that has a Player vs Player zombies mode on Multiplayer! It's really fun. It's basically Halo Infection but with CoD physics and stuff. With all servers, though, there isn't a vote map thing like in Black Ops for consoles. There isn't even a map change timer to change your classes on it! You'll have to go to Custom Games to change your loadout for Online (and in custom games, you cannot have every gun like in Black Ops 2 or 3 custom games. What you have for your loadout in custom games is also what you have in multiplayer, but Combat Training has a separate class loadout and stuff.) Since most, again if not all, servers are run by a group of people or person, you will rarely find a cheater or hacker that stays more than 30 seconds because Admins can just kick them. If you fire a semiautomatic weapon too fast too many times, you'll have to wait a whole half second before being able to shoot again, and you won't be able to fire as fast as you'd like to. This sucks for me because I have a naturally fast trigger finger.
Zombies? It's the exact same as Console; you search for a lobby and the game finds others that are searching at the same time then it groups you with each other. There is nothing special, and you can't play mods in zombies on the scale that you can on WaW. There are mods, don't get me wrong, but it's mainly just a change to the guns and game modes. Here is an excerpt from
: "It's official, BO1 and BO3 will be receiving mod tools capable of creating custom zombie maps! BO1 is a 3rd party project, while the BO3 tools are official product. / Posted by TheSleepingObama on May 23rd, 2016." Maybe BO1 will have modded maps when you buy it, but right not there are none. (current date: October 16, 2016) There is a leaderboard, but there isn't a ranking system like in Black Ops 2.
What about differences between Console and PC? PC DOES have much better and crisper graphics! Even on 360, the text on certain things are blurry, but on PC, everything is legible. There isn't a surprise there, but maybe someone thought that the graphic fidelity on the consoles is what Treyarch maxed the graphics out at. The marketplace for screen capture tools is starting to get quite crowded, but PlayClaw stands out as it strikes a great balance between ease of use and quality.  The main competitors are Bandicam, Fraps, and Dxtory.  PlayClaw beats Fraps as it is much less resources intensive, and produces higher quality ouput than Bandicam in most cases.  Using PlayClaw usually results in nothing more than a 1 to 5 frame rate decrease and very few dropped frames during recording.  Dxtory, coupled with the Lagarith codec produces slightly better results, and is even less resource intensive, but takes a bit more effort to set it up; in contrast the PlayClaw UI is very easy to navigate.
The main features are: Record in-game footage. Record the desktop. Buffer a period of footage (from 5 to 600seconds). Take screenshots. Configure input from multiple audio sources including mic. You can also stream to Twitch, YouTube and Customer Server (not tested yet)
Recording desktop / in-game and activating recording to capture the buffered footage never show any interuption or performance hit.  I have tried streaming to a 10,000prm HDD, and also 5400.  As with all capture tools the faster the hard drive the better, but footage was still OK on the slower drive.  Being able to define the number of CPU threads the software utilises really helps performance.  Other essential options are the ability to define frame rate for capture and set the resolution (although I would recommend recording native and then scaling during editing).
One thing I really like is the ability have PlayClaw write audio tracks in seperate files.  This makes it a lot more convenient if editing audio as each each source (in-game or mic) gets it's own file. So no bother with extracting audio from the video file, or having all audio streams mixed.
Taking screenshots produces a nice overlay effect - it really lets you know a shot has been taken without being intrusive. Other overlays can be configured to show frame rate, recording duration, buffer, a clock and many other features. One of the most useful overlapys shows how large your recording is.
The main area where PlayClaw could improve is around the MJPEG codec.  It appears they use their own custom codec and many have found it can be a pain finding editing software to support it. (Protip - If you have problems opening the files in your editor, try installing the free version of Bandicam - this will install / update the codecs - it certainly worked for Sony Movie Studio 12 and 13).  It spoils what is otherwise a very easy to use application.  It would be nice if they supported advanced options that allowed the user to install their own codecs.  Edit:  The developer has kindly clarified the MJPEG issue. But out of all the capture software I have tested over the years, PlayClaw is the only one that caused problems like this. So I am not changing my comment, as many people have found my 'pro tip' useful.
Overall PlayClaw is a great piece of software.  I am using it exclusively to capture footage.  It does a great job.

Visual motifs are often used as symbolism and I think that may go unappreciated between the panty shots and the robots pantomiming a reproductive act that they barely understand. It's important to know that the real meat of this game doesn't get served until after the credits roll for the first time. A second playthrough has you playing as another character with an entirely different opening sequence. New enemies are introduced, old enemies are found in greater numbers, and tougher enemies will spawn in places they hadn't before. I saw this game at PAX and honestly thought it wouldn't interest me that much, but it has absolutely blown me away. Building on a familiar platform that games like RISK and Heroes of Might and Magic have introduced, Legends of Callasia brings new innovations to the genre. The introduction of simultaneous turns to a game like this is a stroke of brilliance, and in addition to shortening the time of a match considerably, it also adds a wealth of depth to strategic and tactical play that simply cannot be found anywhere else.
The PvE content is solid, having roughly 40 hours of prestructured missions, as well as vs AI play, but where this game really shines is the multiplayer. While the base game play is easy to learn, it is incredibly difficult to master, and you need to legitimately outplay and out think the opponent in order to secure a win.
In addition the dev team behind the game is very accessible, both through their Discord channel, as well as their regular twitch streams. They are eager to listen to feedback, and have taken suggestions from players and incorporated them into the game on several occasions. They really love their product and want their players to love it too - and it is great to see a dev team that cares that much about both their product and their players.
Overall I have to give Legends of Callasia a solid 10/10.

By far my favorite 4X game I've ever played. There are so many random occurrences and unforseeable possibilities with each game (not to mention multiplayer) that it's completely impossible to play anywhere near the same game twice. What I found really fun when I first started playing is seeing all the other empires form around me and peeking over at them to see what they were doing right. Kind of like cheating on a test. That meant that after I inevitably went bankrupt while waking the sleeping bear by attacking someone's vassal, I could then use everything I'd learnt and build on it from the start.
Even during my second playthrough when I'd had a really strong grasp on how things worked and the tactics involved in keeping up with your peers, I still found myself at the mercy of my neighbors and their impressions of me. Suddenly the empire east of me wouldn't hear me out at all and started encroaching on my borders en masse. It made me have to rethink my entire strategy and declare war on the smaller friendly empire to the west. This allowed me to expand further in that direction and buy myself time while I caught up in naval superiority to my easterly rivals (although I felt dirty for crushing those poor colonies).
Naturally, the whole cold war between myself and the other was rendered a moot point when I researched Jump Warp Drives that accidentally tore a portal open in the fabric of spacetime and unleashed a bunch of ethereal beings onto the galaxy. Proceeded to completely eat up my neighbor and my empires both. BUT IT WAS ENJOYABLE.
Onto game #3, using my previous two empires as templates for some of the AI so I can face myself in a way haha. During each game you pick different traits for your species and different policies for your empire so you wind up playing differently anyway, no matter how well you know the game. First time around I was a military dictatorship, second time around an individualist democracy and now I'm going for a materialistic logician oligarchy of sorts, all of which play entirely differently and massively dictate how the game molds to you.
Long winded, anecdotal "review", sorry about that, but hopefully the genuine satisfaction I get from this game comes through. As of writing this I'm at 29 hrs played and I got it less than 2 days ago :3

Greetings!  Welcome to my review of The Binding Of Isaac.  After playing this gem to completion over eleven months I felt it was time I give Isaac his due, a proper review.  The Binding Of Isaac is a roguelike game with some RPG elements thrown in for flavor.  I will briefly cover the different elements of the game without spoiling the fun of discovery for those so inclined.

The first thing that caught my attention while playing TBOI was the art style, so we'll discuss "the look" first.  TBOI is and looks like a flash game.  Gamers who enjoyed the flash offerings of Newgrounds in the early 2000s are going to wax nostalgic the first time they start TBOI up.  The graphics are sharp and bright, and feel very polished for the style of game TBOI is.  My sole complaint with the graphics is a flaw found in many flash based games, occasional frame rate drops.  It's never prevented my continued rise to TBOI glory, but the frame chugging happened on a few occasions on more that one computer.   Does the game suffer in the playability department because of frame rate drops? No it does not, but I do consider it a factor in how the game looks while playing it.

The Binding of Isaac really shines in the audio department.  From the introduction to the credits, the music and sound effects are excellent.  The soundtrack really nails the morose theme perfectly and some of the end game sound effects get stuck in my head for days at a time.  From an auditory perspective, TBOI is gaming perfection.

So TBOI looks good, and sounds even better...but what's it like to play?  "Playability" is where TBOI draws it's line in the sand.  It is a very difficult game to master, and those interested in seeing all TBOI has to offer have hundreds or even thousands of deaths to look forward to.  All levels in TBOI are randomly generated each time you play.  Death is permanent and progress through the levels can't be saved.  In other words, each time you play you either complete the game or you die, that's it.  This mechanic would be frustrating in a game that doesn't offer some other form of progression, and TBOI clearly understands that.  There are a TON of unlockable items and several unlockable characters with different strengths and weaknesses.  Anything picked up during a TBOI run is added to "your collection" and can potentially show up again in another run.  Item combos are satisfyingly powerful and allow you to occasionally turn the tables on a very difficult game.

TBOI has a plot that some people will enjoy, others will not.  It deals with mature themes and is meant to be played by adults.  There is alot of Christian imagery run through a twisted filter on display in TBOI and is definitely not for the easily offended.

In conclusion, for the brave TBOI offers a gaming experience unlike any other.  The replayability is endless.  The often discussed difficulty makes completing the game truly feel like an accomplishment.  With a full remake right around the corner, (and a discount for original owners until release day) there's never been a better time to check out The Binding Of Isaac.

Magicka is like an arpg but with a really unique combat system. To cast spells you must combine elements by pressing the qwer and asdf keys in correct orders. Once your elements are lined up you press mouse button to cast. There are tons of different spell combos and effects. You can mix simple ones like water and cold and get icy shards for example. Or earth and fire for fireballs. But you can also go more advanced and mix stuff like arcane, water, fire to get steam, then add lightning and now you have a steamy electrocuting beam of death. Endless possibilities and all good in different ways depending on your playstyle and enemy.
Beyond that there's also other spell effects that maybe don't damage like a spell for hasting yourself or going invisible. Cool stuff. You can also fight with your sword and a huge assortment of other weapons.
The story is cool and the setting is funny. I loved the graphics. The pace and difficulty of the game is just right too.

The weather, water and atmospheric effects are very well rendered and smooth. The shadows are clever - many times I turned to fire on a bundle of ropes or a gas cylinder that looked like an attacking beastie. The sound is also cleverly designed - door hinges sound suspiciously like the howling of some of the creatures, things go bump in the night due to the ship rolling, caged beasts bang on doors, walls, etc. The creatures themselves are well rendered - if they get up and close, you can see every deformation, every bulbous growth, etc. Altogether, this makes for an immersing environment, and - at the beginning, at least - quite a tense one.
While the art is excellent, the level design is mediocre at best. It was ambitious to have a large chunk of a game like this on a relatively small ship, but as it turns out, it may have been a bit TOO ambitious. While the art and environment are excellent and immersive, there are many points one re-encounters, crosses over, and at many points, objectives are simply names of places you haven't been yet, so you rather stumble around aimlessly hoping to hit what you're looking for instead of making clear progress or heading through a relatively fixed course. As with many other TPSs, the camera angle is fixed in most enclosed spaces, which makes it absolutely useless for exploring a room, moving through the room, or spotting/fighting enemies. This leads you to spend most of your time in the pseudo-FPS, "over-the-shoulder" aiming mode, so that you can actually see where you're going.
Save points are pre-set. You can encounter some pretty stupid obstacles pretty far along beyond a save point and find yourself repeating 10-15 minutes of gameplay, sometimes more than once. That alone can be infuriating.

You run through the snow all day poorly trying to kill animals and whatever whilst blindly searching for any sort of buildings (whic are very few and far between) you can go into whilst being certainly killed by wolves (which the game fails to inform you about in the tutorial and they helpfully have a wolf spawn right by the first objective so you have NO way of killing it other than respawning and running back to it and just zerging it down over and over).
There is also no way to warm yourself inside most buildings as you cannot place a fire down inside, which when you duck inside the building to take cover from a wolf that half glitches through the wall and you have no way of killing and don't want to run back again and again means you are screwed because you die ridiculously quickly from cold and lack of food.
As of today, I have refunded the game, however I hope that they will progress it to the point where I will feel okay to buy it. However, as is the story with most developers that "decide [they] want to get the community involved and let you support [them]" which basically, in usually in most cases means: they want your money, but can't be bothered to finish the game (which again, I would like to re-iterate I HOPE HOPE HOPE is NOT the case).
Another thing that makes me sceptical is the early access bio.
Firstly, "This does not mean that the game is unplayable or lacks features, it’s actually vice-versa... we have all the core mechanics and features already in the game" So it's essentially a finished game? But you put it in early access?
Secondly, "Even though we have all the core mechanics and features already in the game, we feel that it can be so much more, but it can become that only with your help.
Your participation in Early Access will be crucial to the game’s future, because we will listen to your feedback and improve the game over the time, especially if it fits our vision of the game." So basically, they have everything they wanted to do in the first place, but they want us to tell them our ideas and will most likely only implement them if it fits their idea of the game? SO WHY DO YOU NEED US TO HELP IF YOU WANT /YOUR/ VISION OF THE GAME?
I am also unsure as to whether they put any effort into testing this game at all, as anyone who has played the game will very quickly realise you get stuck into a vicious cycle of: respawn, run to last death (whilst starving/freezing), chop wood for new structures (since when you die your old base gets wiped (I know, fantastic idea right?)), get mauled to death by a wolf that you can't see until it's killing you, repeat.
The last thing I did before I refunded that ultimately made be refund was I spawned at morning so it wouldn't get cold too quickly and then I just ran in a straight line to the West. Before I starved to death I found not a SINGLE building. No, not a single one. And yes, I would expect from a game like this to be able to find some sort of actual content and not just more f***ing trees to chop like maybe perhaps even like a little shop with even just some food in or SOMETHING rather than just easily pre-generated terrain.
According to others too (although I had not the chance) multiplayer is incredibly terrible and buggy (huh, could have sworn somewhere I read that all the core mechanics and features were already in place somewhere... Oh, right in their EARLY ACCESS BIO).
If I see at a later date that this game has /actually/ improved then I will re-purchase it and update my review.

When will mad scientists ever learn?
Messing about with the creation of new life will, at best, lead to an angry mob bearing pitchforks and flaming torches paying your laboratory a surprise visit or at worst, end up with you being dragged screaming like a girl halfway up a wall before having your head bloodily ripped from your shoulders by one of your mutated experiments which memorably happens in Cold Fear.
It has been described as "Resident Evil on a boat", which is a bit unfair as later on action does move onto an oil rig although to carry the mad scientist analogy still further, it has no qualms about looting the undead corpse of its more famous relation and cutting off as many good bits as it can carry to graft onto itself later.
The game gets off to an encouraging start with a short FMV movie showing a crack squad of SAS types being slaughtered by a large number of unknown assailants before switching to you, who happen to be in the area, thus making yourself the best of what is left.  You and your colleague board an apparently deserted Russian whaling vessel and here the game begins - and what a start it is.  One of the games strengths is the wonderful use of weather and water effects, your first enemy being the huge waves that constantly pound the sides of the ship which itself is madly rocking back and forth, making the tilting deck a dangerous place to be, even before you factor in things like missing guard rails, swinging hooks and burning crates.  You obviously can't stay outside so you must venture into the dark dank depths of the ship to uncover its mysteries.
And here to begin with the game shows impressive restraint in not revealing all its cards at once.  The first 15 minutes or so are extremely tense as you stumble across the aftermath of a massacre and the game doles out its shocks slowly - a shifting corpse here, a sudden attack by a surviving mercenary there, that by the time you discover your friends eviscerated body in a toilet, the attack by your first zombie is almost an anti-climax.  As you work your way through the floating death-trap, when you are not cursing the third person camera angle which is unresponsive even by the standards of a game of this genre, you will find a lot else to impress you.
The actual combat is very well thought out, which when coupled with the ability to move and shoot at the same time gives combat a much needed precision, especially when ammo is running short and the cabin that you are in is rocking as the ship moves.  And unlike Resident Evil, it does not force you to wait for the more powerful guns to give you access to the Holy Grail of survival horror, the perfect head shot.  Even the first weapon you come across can, when teamed with a laser sight and a steady hand, burst a zombies cranium like an over-ripe watermelon.  And indeed such behaviour is encouraged as ammo can be tight, forcing you to pick your shots carefully and use the terrain to your advantage.  You will need all the help that you can get as things can get pretty dark in places, giving you a real sense of the ship slowly failing as lights start flickering out causing previously visited areas to become a lot more dangerous and you hear the distant groaning of overstressed metal.
By the time that you have rescued the scientist's feisty daughter, encountered a possessed undead killer whale in the hold and smashed into the oil rig where the experiments began you will have been sucked into the storyline and be eager for more.  Sadly this excitement will slowly ooze away like fluids from a semi-devoured body.
For a start the rig is a lot bigger than the ship - and a lot more awkward to navigate around as one corridor can look very much like another and the occasionally vague instructions that you are given can lead you running aimlessly from one area to another  trying to find out which doors have now been opened, or on one occasion a vent in the corner of one room being unblocked.  A map would have been a huge help.
And the storyline remains generically X-Files stuff - Russian scientists, parasitical life forms, unethical experiments and unfortunately this is something that you only ever discover through conveniently discovered notes and memos.  I am not sure if characters were removed during development but in sharp contrast to the large and varied supporting casts of games like Resident Evil or Silent Hill you merely get one scientist who lasts approximately 3 minutes, one mercenary captain, whom you only meet to kill and the end boss whose existence you can only deduce before he makes his appearance.  Surely it would have been better to have him pop up at various points in the game during different stages of mutation to taunt and hinder you?  Even the standard enemies remain much the same, with only 3 or so new variants being introduced.
So the second half of the game ends up being more about exploration and monster killing than anything else which is disappointing  to anyone who enjoyed the first half and were expecting it to step up a notch, although the atmosphere is as strong as ever - you really feel as if you are in a slowly decaying structure in the middle of the hostile ocean and the weather effects, especially when you are edging your way across an exposed catwalk struggling against a force 9 gale and near horizontal rain, remain as excellent as ever.
So in summary it is very much a game of two halves.  A better than expected first half and a slightly disappointing second half.  It is atmospheric, but a shorter ride than you might imagine and cannot really be considered a serious threat to survival horror's "Big Two" - Resident Evil and Silent Hill.  It does however have some decent ideas and manages to keep the pacing up throughout.  The potential for greatness was there but perhaps a bit more time in the lab was needed!
Recommended to fans of survival horror or B-Movie connoisseurs, all of whom will find something in this game to love.

Deus Ex is probably best described as a first-person RPG. Set in the near future, you take the role of JC Denton, a nanomachine-enhanced agent working for UNATCO (United Nations Anti-Terrorism Coalition), and set out to foil terrorists and terrorism plots.  I'm not going to spoil the story, but I think in general it's compelling.
The gameplay is sublime in that it offers you a variety of ways to approach your objectives, coupled with some of the best level design I've seen in any game.
One way of breaking down the game is that you'll receive mission objectives: find this, kill this person, get into this building and so on, but you usually have multiple approaches as to how you tackle them.
Deus Ex has you find and use the weapons and tools you find in the environment. In that respect it is familiar ground if you're used to old-school Doom/Quake/Duke Nukem-style first-person shooters. However, unlike those, that primarily focus on the shooting (of course), in Deus Ex it's generally an equally viable option to use stealth and incapacitation to acheive your goals  Or, you can be sneaky in an alternative way and take the cyber warfare route- hack computers to open doors for you if you don't want to look around for the door code, or if you don't have a lockpick to use on it.
Your inventory has limited space (think of your items as shapes on a grid that you have to try and slot together as best you can), and the skill points system means that you'll place different emphases on different items. Some will be more useful to some players than others.
The skills system is the most prominent RPG element. As you explore places and complete goals, you will earn skill points that can be invested into different skills in order to level them up. Do you want to upgrade your skill with rifles, so it's easier to kill them with a sniper or assault rifle, for instance? Maybe you could use the points to upgrade your hacking abilities instead. Maybe you can use them so that you can heal more health with medkits? Your choice, and in general, neither option is 'wrong'. There's a nice tradeoff between "Do I drop my rebreather so I can pick up the knife?", for instance, and "I've found an underwater passage- I wish I didn't drop my rebreather", if that makes sense.
The level design is great, and complements the wide variety of options. For instance, you'll usually find a door code written down somewhere if you aren't able to hack it open. You can usually disable alarms that would attract enemies... Or you can shoot your way through them if you're feeling confident. There's a wide variety of options to access areas in most instances- it is pleasingly complex.
Regarding shooting... it's a double-edged sword. Deus Ex has combat in it. It's certainly permissible to upgrade the different weapon types and kill enemies that way, but it's.... I'm trying to think of how to put it.... It's not that it's not a shooter, or you can't play it like a shooter, but it really is not like Doom, for instance, where it's not an option to avoid your enemies, really.
The way the weapons work is that you keep your aim on the enemy for a few seconds in order to make the shot accurate. You can find in-game weapon mods that increase clip size, accuracy, add scopes and silencers for instance, but in general it means that if the game becomes a firefight with you and a bunch of terrorists, you will be likely to miss a lot if you keep moving around. This is in contrast to the likes of Doom, that relied on you moving out the way of enemy fire, and never penalised your accuracy for it. Here it's slower, and dare I say, a bit clumsier, because, well, it's just not a straight-up shooter. It doesn't seem to be designed like an FPS, put simply.
Basically, if Deus Ex were only a FPS, it would not compare that well to the classic PC shooters- Doom/Quake/Duke Nukem etc.
As it stands though, it's a fantastic game, with intricate level design that allows multiple angles of attack, as well as multiple tools and skills that allow you to choose your approach, and by extension, how you choose to play the game, without seeming like you're forced onto one track, the mentallity of "I put points in lockpicking, so I have to keep picking my way through doors each time.". Nope- perfecly feasible to look around for a code if you feel like it.
It's a fantastic example of level and gameplay design, Deus Ex. Thoroughly recommend.

I really do wish to recommend this game but the issue I'm having is whom I would recommend this game to. It is by no means a bad game! I actually do like it. But it suffers from one MASSIVE flaw...
The Pre-Sequel is NOT anywhere as good as Borderlands 2.
The two factors that made Blands 2 so awesome were it's entertaining story and it's characters which were (for the most part) entertaining to play. The Pre-Sequel does not deliver in both these areas. The story is only okay, and the playable characters are fairly under-whelming, even compared to the original Borderlands game. So I was tempted to recommend maybe playing this game BEFORE Blands 2, but even that leaves a sour taste in my mouth. The fact is, Blands 2 is cheaper. You can purchase it with it's major expansions for less than this game and it has TONS more content, all much more enjoyable.
So who would I recommend this game to? The only players who come to mind would be the Borderlands fans (like me) but those gamers should have already played (and been disappointed by) this game. So who else is there? Maybe, just maybe, the very casual gamer who is taking thier sweet time getting to this game, but even them I'd recommend playing all the expansions for Borderlands 2 first, and then probably just starting yet another character in that game (or the original Borderlands) instead.
And just FYI, I do own two copies of this game now. I originally purchased on console to play co-op with my son, and now have it on PC because it's the gaming system I prefer. And I will play even more of this game, but I just can't in good conscience recommend anyone else to do the same.
So in conclussion, my feeling is if you haven't purchased this game already, then there's really no need to at this point. Either play Borderlands 2 (and it's expansions!) or just wait for Borderlands 3 instead.

Nier Automata is a good game whose merits stand above the sum of it's very flawed parts. I am of the impression this could have been amazing, but as it is, I'm somewhat disappointed. There's plenty to talk about with a game like this, and a lot of subjectivity involved, so feel free to take this with a grain of salt, but I'll try to weigh out the most objective points.
Pros:
+ One of the best soundtracks I've heard in a game for a very long time now. It's quite unique and implemented with innovation in the game.
+ Great voice actors in the Japanese dub. The English dub ironically winds up sounding far more like an anime.
+ A positively charming roster of robotic foes. A big part of why I bought this game was my previous experience with Platinum's Vanquish, whose collection of Russian Space Robots (tm) had dozens of behaviors, alternate combat styles, and were very emotive even in the heat of battle. This was well founded, as the machines here are the real stars of the show. They're adorable, formidable, and have prominent personalities.
+ You're never going to have sore eyes playing in the shoes of 2B. In an age where gorgeous heroines are going the way of the Dodo, she brings it back with an unexpected vengeance. If Judge Dredd was a robot maid with a 12 foot long sword, it'd be 2B.
+ A couple levels in particular are very memorable, most notably the Amusement Park and Forest Kingdom, bringing in some flavor and worldbuilding that rounds out the story.
+ The combat itself is fluid and frenetic, as one might expect from Platinum. I'm not sure if it is enough however, and that will take us to the cons...
CONS:
-PC Port is pretty dodgy. I wrote an initial review all about this but here's the jist of it: Get a controller, use one if you already have it. Between unclear key bindings, a strange control layout, and aiming/movement being restricted to the 8 directions you can get from the WSAD keys, the native PC controls are incredibly uncomfortable and will ruin a lot of otherwise flowing sequences between sidescrolling, isometric and third person combat. You don't need the controller, but I heavily reccomend against using the keyboard and mouse.
- Graphical quality isn't consistent. Some character models like our protagonists, supporting characters and the robotic foes all look great, but the environment and it's textures range from the good to the straight up hideous. Take one look at the metal crate next to the transporter in the resistance camp and tell me otherwise. I say this as someone who played at maxed out settings.
- The writing is... divisive, to say the least. I have a sneaking suspicion that a lot of the people who praise Nier's story aren't particularly well read in actual science fiction, as most of the topics explored in Nier were already covered in classics like I Robot and 2001.
The story is scatterbrained- it can't seem to pick a focus and stick with it. The game is happy to touch down on a lot of compelling topics and themes: what constitutes our consciousness, what it means to be alive, finding one's purpose, the nature of man, AI, etc etc. It sounds very compelling when you list it off like that, but the harsh reality is Nier Automata can't bring itself to much more than scratch the surface of each topic. The result is a perpetual sense of being lead on: a new topic, a point of contention is introduced, our characters start to follow the thread, and just as it starts to get interesting, something new happens that completely shifts the focus of the plot.
Moreso, characters have erratic arcs that come out of nowhere, or simply feel unearned. There are two positive exceptions in the form of 9S and his Pods: a character I initially wrote off as just being an annoying sidekick but eventually becomes the emotional crux of Nier's many half-baked philosophical gauntlets. He does a lot to add some weight to the events, and is proof that even at it's worst, the game still has merits.
Don't get me started on the endings. We'll get to that in a bit.
- RPG number bloating. Nier Automata is a curious intersection of action and RPG, and I absolutely assure you the best parts of the gameplay stem from Platinum Game's efforts in the action department. The RPG aspects however bog it down in the worst ways possible, with an arbitrary need to drag leveling into the mix. The result is a difficulty curve closer to a Bethesda RPG, where a higher difficulty simply means the same old enemies just have higher damage output and obnoxiously big healthbars. Suddenly your fast and frenetic Platinum Games action becomes turgid and monotonous, where you wind up having to grind so it doesn't take you a minute of solid button mashing to kill the most basic grunts in the game. This game would have greatly benefited from being a pure action title, because the core gameplay is centered on it.
And that leads me to the biggest problem with Nier Automata:
The game itself is simply too small for Taro's narrative ambitions. If you have ever played a Platinum Games title before, you'll know they're generally pretty quick. Vanquish and Revengeance could both easily be beaten in about 6 hours of dedicated effort. Nier Automata on the other hand, takes about 30 hours to wring out it's winding, scatterbrained story. So if you want to see the full story, you're looking at replaying the game at least 3 times, and by the time you get to Route C (third playthrough) most everything that was fun and compelling the first time around has simply become stale and familiar. The combat's depths have been thoroughly plumbed, the enemies have become predictable even with the addition of some new behaviors, and any sense of exploration has been replaced with a perptual sense of backtracking.
Even the bosses seem to run out of creativity by the end, and you'll basically have to fight the same stupid giant Robot Eyeball Spider so many different times if you're like me you'll have developed an irrational hatred of it.
Essentially, Yoko Taro wanted to tell a large story through a small, if not well polished game, and it just didn't work for me.  It's repetitious and the story, while ambitious, is too quick to spread itself thin and wide.
And yet for all my seeming pessimism, I do think this is a good game. I think it belongs in a special pantheon of titles that manage to be memorable in spite of their glaring flaws; games like Dead Rising, Condemned, FEAR, etc. Nier Automata is very flawed, but there is absolutely nothing else quite like it out there, and for all it's flaws, there is a charm to it. If you like Platinum Games, if you like Yoko Taro's creative works, or if you even just like robots, there's a lot of heart to this game worth getting into. I don't think it succeeds at it's goals, but it definitely gets an A for effort.
I think that says something about a title if you can sink 30 hours into it, not be satisfied and still feel like you came away with something you'll be able to talk about years down the line.
So I would reccomend it- just not at full price. Wait for it to go on sale later down the line, and use the money you saved to get yourself a controller and adapter.

Simply put, this game is nothing short of a masterpiece. Between the rich story with well thought out characters, the beautiful world design and incredible soundtrack, NieR: Automata is an amazing experience from start to finish.
The story is done in a way that can only truely be realized as a video game, but it's impossible to elaborate without spoiling significant parts of it. The main story is roughly 30 hours in length, however the side quests are all very much worth completing for the depth it adds to the world.
Combat wise, the system is simple yet satisfying, and the plug-in chip system (almost similar to badge system from Paper Mario) give you plenty of ways to customise your skills. There's a huge variety of weapons from small swords, large swords, spears and combat bracers (punching gloves), each of which you can upgrade both to enhance the weapon as well as tell the story of the weapon's origin.
As for the negatives, while the world's concept is fantastic, the execution can be rather shoddy. This is very clear in the starting city as many buildings are very hollow and featureless yet are abundant with invisible walls. The quality of the world design veries heavily from current gen back to earily ps3-era graphics. The performance doesn't quite stack up either as it's quite a bit more resource heavy than the visuals would lead you to believe. I would reccomend downloading the fan patch (simple one-button install) on the steam community forums before you starting.
Overall, the positives more than make up for the negatives and is an overall joy to play. Despite the low amount of advertising, I hope this work of art gets the recognition it deserves. I can't reccomend it enough.

Stick it to the Man! is an adventure game, using 2D puzzle-platforming as the vehicle for its clumsy humor. You'll solve puzzles by reading people's minds, and manipulating them into thinking about a certain item that you can use somewhere else on the chapter. It's certainly not a hard game, with it nicely structured levels, always subtly guiding your way, never proving frustrating.
It's been said to be "Psychonauts" spiritual successor. While I have not played Psychonauts, I've played other Double Fine games, and the influence is clear! While the game mechanics don't seem to take the spotlight, they're very well conceived, and fit very well with the game's theme and aesthetics. It was one of the more enjoyable games I've recently played!
This is probably the highlight in this game. Everything from the visuals, to the music and the voice acting is awesome!
It's a very colorful game, done in 2.5D. This is achieved by making every sprite like a cardboard cutout. The levels are then set in layers. While the game is mostly 2D, you can sometimes walk back and forth, discovering some charming details that would otherwise be blurred.
The character design is also great. While everyone looks silly, their designs clearly shows their personality, coupled with the problems you'll solve and the voice acting... It's good.
The
is mostly jazz (it reminded me of the bebop soundtrack in Grim Fandango, maybe a bit silly at times) with a bit of sci-fi synth thrown in, at times. I really liked it, and it's certainly something that not only fit the game, but it's also something I'll listen to after I'm finished with the it! (You can get it here:
with a PayWhatYouWant model)
The
Also fit well with the cartoony style. Never felt out of place, so that's good.
The
was also great! Reinforcing the characters and the overall feel of the game, and was mostly well done! There were a few characters that felt a bit inconsistent, but nothing too major. Also, you can rewind and fastforward their speech, making the voices even sillier, with a higher tone, if you're in a hurry. It's these details that make this game so enjoyable, honestly!
The game's
is great as well! It's not anything deep, as you can imagine (although it does hint at some major issues, in a very lighthearted way), but it's certainly funny, if you're into this kind of humor.
The game's divided by chapters, each with its theme, set of characters and puzzles. You can always go back to previous chapters through the menu, so you don't need to worry about missing an objective and being blocked from going back. This is something I very much appreciate! I hate being blocked for apparently no reason.
Most of the chapters also have some achievements. Most of them are just a guide to silly characters that were more well hidden. It's a good use of them, to be honest! There are a couple of them that were more skill-based, if you're into that. But the Stick it to the Man! is a very laid-back game, and it never really tests your skills or patience.
Each level has lots of checkpoints, and you'll never lose any progress. The worst that can happen is you being sent a few meters back, but you never lose items or conversations.
Each level is about 20-40 minutes long. It felt just the right length for me. I played each chapter in one sitting, sometimes 2, and it never felt too short or to drag on. Also, since the levels can be fairly long, walking back would be a pain. As such, they've implemented a sort of fast travel system. Once you reach a certain point, a pipe open up, and you can go back instantly (and go forward once again).
It's a very comfortable game to play, as weird as it sounds. It's never frustrating, you're unlikely to walk around back and forth pointlessly, it's not punishing... just a nice, funny experience, overall.
Basically, you're hit on the head, and an alien just happens to
get into your brain. When that happens, a giant floppy pink hand grows out of your head, which only you can see. Nah, of course you're not crazy! It's
.
Anyway. This giant hand gives you the ability of reading people's minds, and materialize their thoughts. As freeing as it sounds, it's a very "linear" game. They'll only think of things you need, of course.
When you encounter a character, you'll learn about their problems, and then have to find the solution, somewhere. The game's is very similar to a point n' click. However, while the solution aren't too obvious, at first (since they're very non-sensical -- in a good way!), you can easily find everything by walking around and getting more items. If you have more than one, you'll store them, and can switch between them with the mouse-wheel.
If you stay put, your character will also say something about the item, leading you in a general direction. There are also very subtle environmental hints, so I doubt you'll get stuck.
So yeah. You'll walk around the level, speaking to the characters and reading their thoughts, often leading to some very peculiar situations, as you solve their problem in funny ways.
Again, it's not a game you'd play for the mechanics, but they're still very well put together! They fit with the theme, and even amplify it, never proving a nuisance, unlike other games in a similar style. It's very well designed!
It's pretty hard for me to get more to talk about. The game is very good, but it doesn't seem to do anything that jumps out at you. Everything just seems to fit together brilliantly, to me.
Usually, games like this opt for the point n' click genre, rather than 2D platforming. As a result, their movement system is also very clunky and slow, going around the screens, taking seconds of waiting at a time. Stick it to the Man! avoids that entirely, by giving you total control at all times!
It makes the game incredibly better, in my eyes. It's not that I have anything against Pn'C games, but I usually find myself frustrated when I have to walk back and forth very slowly, simply to try a random combination of items.
This game, however, makes movement faster, and every scene seems to have
little detail that makes the walking around even more enjoyable.
There are games that benefit from being punishing and challenging. This is not one of them, and the developers recognized it very well. It's not that there isn't
challenge. There certainly is (mostly by being chased around the guards -- which people didn't enjoy very much!), but even if you "fail", you don't lose progress, and the more challenging sections are short, just keeping things varied.
Last point I want to make. You rarely have to backtrack to solve a puzzle, at least to the point of annoyance. You'll usually gather items as you go, and use them either very near the place, or further ahead. On the times you do have to go back, the solution are clear, and there's usually an easy game to get back. Again, the point of the game is to present you with a silly story and character interactions, and it does that very well!
I don't have anything else to say, honestly. I really,
enjoyed the whole way through. It's on the short side, but it's certainly worth it. If you like Double Fine's games (the Stacking and Grim Fandango particularly coming to mind -- And Psychonauts for most people), give this one a go! I'm sure you won't be disappointed.
Even if you don't... if the description sounds appealing, I still recommend it. It's just a very good game!

By far my favorite 4X game I've ever played. There are so many random occurrences and unforseeable possibilities with each game (not to mention multiplayer) that it's completely impossible to play anywhere near the same game twice. What I found really fun when I first started playing is seeing all the other empires form around me and peeking over at them to see what they were doing right. Kind of like cheating on a test. That meant that after I inevitably went bankrupt while waking the sleeping bear by attacking someone's vassal, I could then use everything I'd learnt and build on it from the start.
Even during my second playthrough when I'd had a really strong grasp on how things worked and the tactics involved in keeping up with your peers, I still found myself at the mercy of my neighbors and their impressions of me. Suddenly the empire east of me wouldn't hear me out at all and started encroaching on my borders en masse. It made me have to rethink my entire strategy and declare war on the smaller friendly empire to the west. This allowed me to expand further in that direction and buy myself time while I caught up in naval superiority to my easterly rivals (although I felt dirty for crushing those poor colonies).
Naturally, the whole cold war between myself and the other was rendered a moot point when I researched Jump Warp Drives that accidentally tore a portal open in the fabric of spacetime and unleashed a bunch of ethereal beings onto the galaxy. Proceeded to completely eat up my neighbor and my empires both. BUT IT WAS ENJOYABLE.
Onto game #3, using my previous two empires as templates for some of the AI so I can face myself in a way haha. During each game you pick different traits for your species and different policies for your empire so you wind up playing differently anyway, no matter how well you know the game. First time around I was a military dictatorship, second time around an individualist democracy and now I'm going for a materialistic logician oligarchy of sorts, all of which play entirely differently and massively dictate how the game molds to you.
Long winded, anecdotal "review", sorry about that, but hopefully the genuine satisfaction I get from this game comes through. As of writing this I'm at 29 hrs played and I got it less than 2 days ago :3

So, first of all, this seems like an incredibly fun game, I also really like that the race you're given to try is morally ambiguous. Seems like it has good mechanics, a fun singleplayer campaign, AND I actually saw another player online the other day! With all that said, I really found the F2P model to be underwhelming. Massive props to the devs for not using microtransactions, but it would be much better, in my opinion, to let the player try each faction. As it is, you get 2/8 of ONE faction to try. The other factions have 6 and 4 single player missions, but we don't even get a taste of them. My advice would be to either make one of each faction's missions free, or to write a separate "tutorial" mission for each faction, which would be included in the free game. That way, I would be sure that I like more than 1/3 of the game before spending $16-22 for the full game. I don't think this would decrease the number of people buying the full game, as people would become even more intrigued by the new stories.
In conclusion, I absolutely loved the small bit of it that I was able to play, and I am considering buying the full version just based on that bit. However, if I could even have a small taste of what the other factions were like, and they weren't a complete disaster, I would buy the full version of this game as fast as I physically could. Great game, really exceptional story writing, just wish the F2P model could be a bit better.

Stellaris manages to capture the feeling of standing on a hill outside the city lights at night, staring up into the sky and wondering what's out there. I did not expect this from a realtime strategy game.
Basically, Stellaris is a lightweight mix of Europa Universalis and Crusader Kings in space with a heady note of Galactiv Civilizations. It's the most accessible of all Paradox strategy games, but this isn't a bad thing by far. There's still plenty of options how to create and run your stellar empire, democracy or military junta. Empires have genuine personalities mapped to them, and you never know what's waiting out there for you.

Greetings!  Welcome to my review of The Binding Of Isaac.  After playing this gem to completion over eleven months I felt it was time I give Isaac his due, a proper review.  The Binding Of Isaac is a roguelike game with some RPG elements thrown in for flavor.  I will briefly cover the different elements of the game without spoiling the fun of discovery for those so inclined.

The first thing that caught my attention while playing TBOI was the art style, so we'll discuss "the look" first.  TBOI is and looks like a flash game.  Gamers who enjoyed the flash offerings of Newgrounds in the early 2000s are going to wax nostalgic the first time they start TBOI up.  The graphics are sharp and bright, and feel very polished for the style of game TBOI is.  My sole complaint with the graphics is a flaw found in many flash based games, occasional frame rate drops.  It's never prevented my continued rise to TBOI glory, but the frame chugging happened on a few occasions on more that one computer.   Does the game suffer in the playability department because of frame rate drops? No it does not, but I do consider it a factor in how the game looks while playing it.

The Binding of Isaac really shines in the audio department.  From the introduction to the credits, the music and sound effects are excellent.  The soundtrack really nails the morose theme perfectly and some of the end game sound effects get stuck in my head for days at a time.  From an auditory perspective, TBOI is gaming perfection.

So TBOI looks good, and sounds even better...but what's it like to play?  "Playability" is where TBOI draws it's line in the sand.  It is a very difficult game to master, and those interested in seeing all TBOI has to offer have hundreds or even thousands of deaths to look forward to.  All levels in TBOI are randomly generated each time you play.  Death is permanent and progress through the levels can't be saved.  In other words, each time you play you either complete the game or you die, that's it.  This mechanic would be frustrating in a game that doesn't offer some other form of progression, and TBOI clearly understands that.  There are a TON of unlockable items and several unlockable characters with different strengths and weaknesses.  Anything picked up during a TBOI run is added to "your collection" and can potentially show up again in another run.  Item combos are satisfyingly powerful and allow you to occasionally turn the tables on a very difficult game.

TBOI has a plot that some people will enjoy, others will not.  It deals with mature themes and is meant to be played by adults.  There is alot of Christian imagery run through a twisted filter on display in TBOI and is definitely not for the easily offended.

In conclusion, for the brave TBOI offers a gaming experience unlike any other.  The replayability is endless.  The often discussed difficulty makes completing the game truly feel like an accomplishment.  With a full remake right around the corner, (and a discount for original owners until release day) there's never been a better time to check out The Binding Of Isaac.
