Honestly I am here because I usually played the android version.  And even if somehow I prefer the android version over this PC version, there was no story mode in the phone version, so I bought this (on sale) just to watch the story...
The story was entertaining, although there are too many scenes that were specifically tailored to be a 1-on-1 combat, and some of them are too "forced", such as when Batman fighting his twin in Batcave just because they simply had different idea, or when Flash escaped the regime but confronted by the others, who "conveniently" came one by one...
The game is mostly okay, especially if you're already a DC fans. Character choice start from Batman or Superman we all know and love, to the slightly less famous such as Killer Frost or Zatanna. You better have a controller though, since playing with keyboard can turn a good religous person into a hell-spawn swear-machine... I'm lucky to still keep my old logitech f310 from 3 years ago...
The moves aren't that hard to perform compared to Mortal Kombat, mostly just a sequence of 2 or 3 directional buttons, followed by an attack button (example : down, forward, punch). The one thing I love from this game is the supermoves, which brings you to a cutscenes. You can watch Superman uppercuts his opponent through the atmosphere, or Raven summoning his daddy Trigon to unleash the ultimate punishment...
That being said, after you finish the main story mode, there is nothing more, unless you like to duel your brother or friends. The reason somehow I prefer the phone version over the PC version, is that the phone version rewards your play time more. Upgradable powers, gears, levels, and new characters are often introduced in the "far less balanced" phone version, while the PC version is just "choose a character and bash your opponent skull" kind of game. It's getting boring once you finished the main quest and have watched all the characters supermoves...
(FYI I've spent much much more for in-game currency in the android version compared to what I spent to buy this discounted PC version...)

To summarize an already brief summary, I wholeheartedly recommend it.

So I've never played Deus EX: GOTY Edition before the last couple weeks. And I'm really close to calling it the most laughably overrated game of all time. The stealth mechanics are bad. The way you can access a menu, come out of it, and the game automatically brings you out of crouching is bad. The way you can fall off ladders because your camera isn't squared exactly right is bad. The way every single enemy in the game carries a useless knife that takes up space in your inventory is bad.
Through two chapters best weapons in the game by far are the stun gun and the police baton because the game is set up to basically force you to use those two if you don't want to play it like DOOM and have people swarming you. Which you are actually much better off doing, for the most part. I mean I got the hostages out of the subway by finally saying ♥♥♥♥ it to stealth (after a couple dozen failed stealth rescue attempts), just rocket launching the guys guarding the entrance, and shooting the hell out of everyone else. Hostages saved, I get a lecture about my violent ways. But this is how♥♥♥♥♥♥gets done in America, son. The world ain't all sunshine and rainbows.
The parts where you can wander around and not fight are cool. I liked the cloak and dagger♥♥♥♥♥♥where you're digging for info in a bar, and sneaking into your brother's hotel room to access his secret James Bond computer hidden in the wall. But man the combat in this game is turrible if you actually try and stealth it. Why is this so highly rated, as in "often pimped as best PC game ever made"? Because it has a very basic skill tree?

By far my favorite 4X game I've ever played. There are so many random occurrences and unforseeable possibilities with each game (not to mention multiplayer) that it's completely impossible to play anywhere near the same game twice. What I found really fun when I first started playing is seeing all the other empires form around me and peeking over at them to see what they were doing right. Kind of like cheating on a test. That meant that after I inevitably went bankrupt while waking the sleeping bear by attacking someone's vassal, I could then use everything I'd learnt and build on it from the start.
Even during my second playthrough when I'd had a really strong grasp on how things worked and the tactics involved in keeping up with your peers, I still found myself at the mercy of my neighbors and their impressions of me. Suddenly the empire east of me wouldn't hear me out at all and started encroaching on my borders en masse. It made me have to rethink my entire strategy and declare war on the smaller friendly empire to the west. This allowed me to expand further in that direction and buy myself time while I caught up in naval superiority to my easterly rivals (although I felt dirty for crushing those poor colonies).
Naturally, the whole cold war between myself and the other was rendered a moot point when I researched Jump Warp Drives that accidentally tore a portal open in the fabric of spacetime and unleashed a bunch of ethereal beings onto the galaxy. Proceeded to completely eat up my neighbor and my empires both. BUT IT WAS ENJOYABLE.
Onto game #3, using my previous two empires as templates for some of the AI so I can face myself in a way haha. During each game you pick different traits for your species and different policies for your empire so you wind up playing differently anyway, no matter how well you know the game. First time around I was a military dictatorship, second time around an individualist democracy and now I'm going for a materialistic logician oligarchy of sorts, all of which play entirely differently and massively dictate how the game molds to you.
Long winded, anecdotal "review", sorry about that, but hopefully the genuine satisfaction I get from this game comes through. As of writing this I'm at 29 hrs played and I got it less than 2 days ago :3

Stellaris manages to capture the feeling of standing on a hill outside the city lights at night, staring up into the sky and wondering what's out there. I did not expect this from a realtime strategy game.
Basically, Stellaris is a lightweight mix of Europa Universalis and Crusader Kings in space with a heady note of Galactiv Civilizations. It's the most accessible of all Paradox strategy games, but this isn't a bad thing by far. There's still plenty of options how to create and run your stellar empire, democracy or military junta. Empires have genuine personalities mapped to them, and you never know what's waiting out there for you.
The most recent DLC is hilarious, at least if you - like me - consider a poor lonely Scientist vessel in the depths of space being ripped apart by madness when encountering a planetsized tentacled horror to be funny.
Stellaris is wonderful escapism and manages to spellbind you if you let it.

This fills a nice little niche that not many games do.  Let's say you like strategy games, obviously, youre looking at this game right?  But maybe you don't have time to play Civ 5 or Endless Legend.  Or you don't want to make the time investment for those games right now.   What options do you have if you want to play a world conquering grand strategy game.  Not many.
In steps Legends of Callasia.  This game is akin to super Risk(the boardgame).  It's a dudes on a map game with some extra stuff thrown in to make more interesting.  That extra stuff includes heroes, you can't move armies around without them, ala Heroes of Might and Magic.  You also have cards that can boost your kingdom, think strategy cards, or can help in battle, think tactics cards.  These add enough flair to make it better than risk.  Throw in a bunch of different maps and multiplayer  and you've got a game you can get some mileage out of.
I did a quick video series shopwcasing the campaign, that you can check out if you want to see the game in action.

Better... much better.
While playing the first Witcher game was an exercise in pushing through bad gameplay in order to see the rest of a decent storyline, its sequel fixes most of the gameplay problems and has an even better storyline to go with it. Combat is the most obvious source of improvement, now actually being worthy of being called such as opposed to being something out of a crappy old MMO. That alone made the game better, since side quests were alright to do and didn't bore me. Not really a fan of the minigames though, but thankfully that, along with (most) QTE's are optional. The less a game forces me to do stuff I don't like, the better. :3
But what really made this game for me was its storyline, with interesting quests, characters, and some seriously uncomfortable choices to make. If there is one thing this game succeeds at, it is creating decision points where I'm forced to make choices that feel like something is lost in exchange for what is gained. Helping this along are the characters, who are (mostly) a morally grey bunch in a crappy world where horrible things can happen to anyone. A world that seems like it only got much worse at the end as we head to the third game in this series. Witcher 2 remained consistently interesting throughout the course of the game.
If I have one complaint, it is that storyline interfered with gameplay at a few moments. Battles I won with ease were followed by cutscenes where Geralt was having a rough time of it, or even was losing. Also why didn't they let me kill that jackass ambassador when nothing was there to stop me from doing so? I know they want to make decisions more difficult to make by not giving me everything I want, but those handful of moments were among the few things I didn't like in this game. Games with more freedom to act remain my preference.
And... I think i'll just leave it at that. I could keep mentioning stuff, or getting more specific about other story events that stood out, but that would spoil things a bit. I'll just say that this was a pretty good game and that I look forward to seeing what the third game is about. I hear that one is even better. :o

Cold Fear is a 2005 action-horror developed by Darkworks, a studio mostly notable for spending half a decade developing I Am Alive, then dying before the game was even released. Funny that a game called "I Am Alive" killed the studio.
This game, however, is a fantastic game and you should play it.
Blending fixed-camera angles and third-person shooting in not the most seamless manner (but still one that's way more fun to play than it has any right to be) and trudging around the whaler in Cold Fear is legitimately fun. Despite the fixed camera angles, it forgoes tank controls in favour of almost spritely 1:1 control.
On one hand, this means that navigating the environment is fast - almost breakneck with your very generous sprint meter - it's responsive, and makes dodging/tactical movement viable. On the other hand, it does mean that Cold Fear is balanced towards the easier side, in the same sense that the Titanic was balanced towards the bottom of the sea.
Except on Extreme, where enemies one hit kill you. Don't play on Extreme.
It's short, but contains enough variety and pacing that this isn't by any means a bad thing - especially with its bargain bin price. You could get more out of it by replaying it on Extreme, but don't. Don't do that. You don't even get anything for it. 5 hours long, and another hour or so if you ignore my advice and get destroyed by the first enemies in the game.
They will just shoot and insta-kill you, and there isn't THAT much mechanical depth.
For the shooting from your end, there's a decent selection of weapons, all your bases covered. Nothing exciting, but only one is wholesale useless (flamethrower, of course, as if that weapon hasn't been burned enough) so what more could you ask for.
Shooting your way through the ship, there's some fantastic environments to go through - all rainslick with some contextually impressive tech. It does get repetitive - most environments are some amalgamation of rust, metal, rain, and Russian, but the core art design is there and shines through.
Following these environments, we've got a surprisingly experimental OST, all full of baby's cries and bike bells, and some SFX that gives the weapons a nice punch. Not Vlambeer's level of gun-wizardry, but enough to make them nice to use.
The story is subpar. Like how a brick to the face is a subpar meal.
Characters are completely forgettable - so much so, that I'm surprised they didn't go with the bald marine version of Tom Hansen they show off in the concept art. Dialogue is "modern action" tastelessness, plot threads are dropped - including a couple of major ones - the lore is one-note, and the climaxes are as marred by a distinct lack of boss battles as they are by missed opportunities.
Bad writing doesn't stop Cold Fear from being what it is - a mechanically impressive action-horror game that delivers non-stop action instead of trying to be something it's not. All with some pretty visuals and a bargain-bin price.
Horror may be a saturated genre these days, but Cold Fear is timeless. It's well worth your time.

Deus Ex is one of those games that you just keep going back to.  That said, like most older games, most people who go back to it are those who grew up with it.
The graphics are very blocky and occasionally have horrible transparancy.  The voice-overs aren't really that great.  Shadowing is horrid.  The AI is occasionally as dumb as a brick.  Those are the things I would be saying, had this game not been made 14 years ago.  Everything with this game was absolutely cutting edge when it was released, and it started a cult following that exists even today.  It's still one of the best Single-Player FPS games I've ever played.  So much so that I got it on Steam because my CD wore out from pulling it off the shelf every few years.
So how do I rate this game?  I honestly can't.  I'm one of those cult followers who have fond childhood memories of this game being the best thing EVER...  That said, It is an outdated game both in graphics and gameplay, but that doesn't stop it from being a top 10 single-player FPS game.  It's got the tech feel of Shadowrun, mixed with the cloak and dagger of Hitman, and then they tossed in a little Wolfenstein politics.  What's not to love about it?
If you can see past the 14 year old technology (Graphics/Sound/Etc) then you are absolutely going to LOVE this game.  If you're someone who cringes if the goatee on a character looks "painted on" then avoid it.  However, if anyone asks I'll always recommend it.

This game reminds me of a good Roger Corman film, where despite of the kindergarden dialogue and having more cliches than Commando and Rambo combined, you manage to have lots of fun with it.
Just as Dead Space, this game screams "RE-inspired,clone,fanfiction whatever" all over it, mixing the RE 4 over-the-shoulder mechanics with the fixed angle of older RE titles (definitely better than RE 6 and scarier than RE 5).
So, I recommend this game because of:
+ Enjoyable survival horror.
+ Interesting story.
+ Good lore.
+ Engaging atmosphere.
+ Excellent use of environmental hazards (at least in the first half of the game).
+ Good use of combat mechanics.
What you might not like/My nitpicking:
- Unresponsive mouse. Whenever this glitch shows it can definitely be a pain in the a$$ because enemies will bvtt♥♥♥♥ you while you move your mouse 2 miles just to move the cursor 2 pixels. Fortunately, you might not experience this.
- Short story.
- Terrible dialogue.
- Cutscenes feel rushed.
- A wide variety of enemies that by today standards you might find way generic. Certain types of enemies are underused.
- Too many weapons. From the six weapons I can remember I found myself using less than a half of them throughout the game.
SPECIAL ADVISE:
* While I did not have any of these, several users have raised concern over a couple of issues that they experienced with the game.These being a launch error and a graphics mold glitch that makes the game look like you're playing Sin City: Mutant Undead Boat Edition. As I said, I didnt experience these issues as well as many other owners and you can find the solution for these in the community boards.
So, while certainly there are lots of nitpicking, you can find a very enjoyable game in this criminally overlooked little gem. If you're a fan of survival horror, cheesiness, B movies, Syfy Channel or good ol' RE games, this is definitely a must buy. Did I mention that it's better than RE 6?

Honestly, I didn't expect to enjoy this game - but I did!
I don't have much time to play epic strategy games, so the 1 to 2 hr play sessions works for me. Mechanics are simple, but it offers a lot of strategic choices. I've tried the beta during the Greenlight campaign where there are several maps and heroes to choose from, so each game is different. Can't wait to have those unlock in this version. But I'm glad they finally added campaigns! I usually play against AI, and I get addicted playing over and over again until I win. Multiplayer has been challenging, but that's just me not being as good as the other players. I love the character art, as well as the clouds and dragons that move around in the maps (when they're not blocking something important). Initially the game struck me as stylistically reminiscent of Psychonauts, but the more I played the more I kept getting reminded of Rocko's Modern Life, so I guess if you take those two, mash 'em together, and then put them in the context of a 2.5D point'n'click (move'n'stick?) adventure, this is what you get.
The gameplay is relatively simple; you grab read people's thoughts, grab stickers, and then stick those stickers in the proper spots to solve the various puzzles, all while avoiding getting caught by the various thugs sprinkled as obstacles throughout the game. There are some platforming challenges involved, but calling them "challenges" is really stretching the definition of the word. The whole thing definitely leans on the casual side of the gaming fence, but what it lacks in challenge it more than makes up for with a great soundtrack, stylized and attractive visuals, and writing/voice acting that at the least got me to smirk for most of my playthrough if not made me laugh out loud a few times.
A short but thoroughly enjoyable experience and a game I'd highly recommend giving a shot.

There is a lot of detail in this game and it has a high learning curve, but that makes it all the more fun. The in-game help and narration is essential to getting off to a good start.
Totally recommend this game!

I've played Shogun TW, Medieval TW, Medieval 2 TW, Empire TW and Shogun 2 TW and this game by far is the best of them all. It's one of the best strategy games I've ever played. I'm speaking from a strictly SP POV though. The game is pretty old now but it still looks quite nice with the settings turned up.
I've never been able to figure out diplomacy in this game so I always just end up making a lot of enemies and crushing them by brute force. I'm not sure if that's my play style or a flaw in the game's diplomacy system though.
The AI is decently intelligent both on the campaign map and on the battlefield.
I absolutely hate and despise naval battles in all TW games after this one. It's one of the main reasons I haven't been able to enjoy any newer TW titles. Naval battles in Medieval 2 are simple. You build a fleet and all battles are auto resolved. Easy, fast and out of the way so you can concentrate on the really fun stuff - land battles and expansion. I don't know if I'm alone in thinking that naval battles are trash and have ruined the newer TW games, but you definitely don't have to worry about that in this game.
There are a lot of factions you can play and they all have small differences but you can generalize all of them into 4 super factions that share a lot of similar traits and units: western Europe, eastern Europe, north Africa and middle east. Playing through the campaign as different factions is fun and rewarding.
The bottom line is this game is pretty amazing and you should definitely give it a try.

I love RPGs and I really love those with a great story. The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings stands tall in lore and the complex web it weaves with politics and intriguing characters, that keeps you oblivious until the very end of the game as to what the plot is actually about. The game is not about slicing your way through enemies and slaying monsters. If someone has enjoyed The Witcher 2 solely for it's gameplay and coming away with the feeling of being a hero, has then missed the core vital part of the game making you realise- how unimportant and small you are in the grand scheme of politics in this sequel to the first game, The Witcher. The lore got me so intrigued that I decided to start reading the witcher books. I am half-way through the first book, The Last Wish and now I realise the books are even better than the game. I am enlightened with a completely new perspective now on the witcher world and have come to understand that the witcher is not merely a game. The world of witcher is much bigger and the whole package is pure art. The story in this game is exceptional and for those who pay attention to lore, its quite a treat.

Quests are good, though one or two are known for bugs. Always a good idea to keep saves around and not delete them. The combat is good in my opinion but I've heard some say its not good or that its hard. My only gripe with the game is the input lag when drawing your sword or when you click your mouse for interactions for eg: opening a door or a chest. It's not there at other times though, which is a relief. Choices matter and the game offers great replayability as early on you are to choose one of the two paths, with each offering different middle games and consequences. And After you're done completing the game making the right choices (or atleast you feel you've made the right ones), make sure you put your saves into Documents>Witcher2>gamesaves from your steam save directory- Steam\userdata\[userid]\20920\remote to carry your choices over to The Witcher 3.

The graphics are a bit dated. That's about the only con I found with this game. It wasn't bad enough to be immersion breaking for me, but I appreciate that most people have a threshold somewhere between current and old where you stop being able to take the game seriously because the people look like funny square mannequins...
I think one of the things I found really refreshing was that it didn't hand hold you. Many games now you'll have a nice interactive map which shows where you are, where you're going and perhaps marks out important stuff around you and an arrow on your HUD pointing the way on. Deus Ex will give you a grainy aerial shot of the area with a handful of labels indicating  which buildings are which... if you're lucky.
There is a a fair amount of reading available. As an augmented human being you naturally log *everything* so you can always check back and reread any notes you read or conversations you had when you need to. There are multiple ways to fulfil your objectives - you can go in guns blazing, pick enemies off with traps or from a distance, turn security systems against their users, or lurk in the shadows knocking people out or even avoiding (most) conflict altogether.
There are two ways to "level up" your character. One is with the addition of biomods that offer you the ability to permanently  develop one of two skills for each body part (for example legs - you can run/jump/fall faster and higher or you can quieten your movement until nobody ever hears your footfalls) and these are gained by finding canisters scattered throughout the game. The other is skills which allow you to hone your techniques in everything from weapon usage to hacking to swimming. Skill points are awarded for completing quests and also (to a lesser degree) for things like exploring giving you more than just the usual "quest for stuff" reason to run around poking in nooks and crannies. Inventory space is limited, but not to an annoying degree meaning you will have to make choices about what to lug around with you.
The story is of course the main reason to play though as it evolves around you based on the choices you make. Although it has to be said in the endgame, (I think) regardless of what path you've chosen up until that point you are offered three different objectives which lead to the three different endings.
If it wasn't for the fact I'm trying to play through the series at the moment I would probably just stop here and replay this one over and over and find a zillion more little hidden places I never noticed before and different ways to play out the storyline. It also feels (and sounds at times) a lot like System Shock 2 so if you enjoyed that then this is a good game to go on with.

Nier Automata is a good game whose merits stand above the sum of it's very flawed parts. I am of the impression this could have been amazing, but as it is, I'm somewhat disappointed. There's plenty to talk about with a game like this, and a lot of subjectivity involved, so feel free to take this with a grain of salt, but I'll try to weigh out the most objective points.
Pros:
+ One of the best soundtracks I've heard in a game for a very long time now. It's quite unique and implemented with innovation in the game.
+ Great voice actors in the Japanese dub. The English dub ironically winds up sounding far more like an anime.
+ A positively charming roster of robotic foes. A big part of why I bought this game was my previous experience with Platinum's Vanquish, whose collection of Russian Space Robots (tm) had dozens of behaviors, alternate combat styles, and were very emotive even in the heat of battle. This was well founded, as the machines here are the real stars of the show. They're adorable, formidable, and have prominent personalities.
+ You're never going to have sore eyes playing in the shoes of 2B. In an age where gorgeous heroines are going the way of the Dodo, she brings it back with an unexpected vengeance. If Judge Dredd was a robot maid with a 12 foot long sword, it'd be 2B.
+ A couple levels in particular are very memorable, most notably the Amusement Park and Forest Kingdom, bringing in some flavor and worldbuilding that rounds out the story.
+ The combat itself is fluid and frenetic, as one might expect from Platinum. I'm not sure if it is enough however, and that will take us to the cons...
CONS:
-PC Port is pretty dodgy. I wrote an initial review all about this but here's the jist of it: Get a controller, use one if you already have it. Between unclear key bindings, a strange control layout, and aiming/movement being restricted to the 8 directions you can get from the WSAD keys, the native PC controls are incredibly uncomfortable and will ruin a lot of otherwise flowing sequences between sidescrolling, isometric and third person combat. You don't need the controller, but I heavily reccomend against using the keyboard and mouse.
- Graphical quality isn't consistent. Some character models like our protagonists, supporting characters and the robotic foes all look great, but the environment and it's textures range from the good to the straight up hideous. Take one look at the metal crate next to the transporter in the resistance camp and tell me otherwise. I say this as someone who played at maxed out settings.
- The writing is... divisive, to say the least. I have a sneaking suspicion that a lot of the people who praise Nier's story aren't particularly well read in actual science fiction, as most of the topics explored in Nier were already covered in classics like I Robot and 2001.
The story is scatterbrained- it can't seem to pick a focus and stick with it. The game is happy to touch down on a lot of compelling topics and themes: what constitutes our consciousness, what it means to be alive, finding one's purpose, the nature of man, AI, etc etc. It sounds very compelling when you list it off like that, but the harsh reality is Nier Automata can't bring itself to much more than scratch the surface of each topic. The result is a perpetual sense of being lead on: a new topic, a point of contention is introduced, our characters start to follow the thread, and just as it starts to get interesting, something new happens that completely shifts the focus of the plot.
Moreso, characters have erratic arcs that come out of nowhere, or simply feel unearned. There are two positive exceptions in the form of 9S and his Pods: a character I initially wrote off as just being an annoying sidekick but eventually becomes the emotional crux of Nier's many half-baked philosophical gauntlets. He does a lot to add some weight to the events, and is proof that even at it's worst, the game still has merits.
Don't get me started on the endings. We'll get to that in a bit.
- RPG number bloating. Nier Automata is a curious intersection of action and RPG, and I absolutely assure you the best parts of the gameplay stem from Platinum Game's efforts in the action department. The RPG aspects however bog it down in the worst ways possible, with an arbitrary need to drag leveling into the mix. The result is a difficulty curve closer to a Bethesda RPG, where a higher difficulty simply means the same old enemies just have higher damage output and obnoxiously big healthbars. Suddenly your fast and frenetic Platinum Games action becomes turgid and monotonous, where you wind up having to grind so it doesn't take you a minute of solid button mashing to kill the most basic grunts in the game. This game would have greatly benefited from being a pure action title, because the core gameplay is centered on it.
And that leads me to the biggest problem with Nier Automata:
The game itself is simply too small for Taro's narrative ambitions. If you have ever played a Platinum Games title before, you'll know they're generally pretty quick. Vanquish and Revengeance could both easily be beaten in about 6 hours of dedicated effort. Nier Automata on the other hand, takes about 30 hours to wring out it's winding, scatterbrained story. So if you want to see the full story, you're looking at replaying the game at least 3 times, and by the time you get to Route C (third playthrough) most everything that was fun and compelling the first time around has simply become stale and familiar. The combat's depths have been thoroughly plumbed, the enemies have become predictable even with the addition of some new behaviors, and any sense of exploration has been replaced with a perptual sense of backtracking.
Even the bosses seem to run out of creativity by the end, and you'll basically have to fight the same stupid giant Robot Eyeball Spider so many different times if you're like me you'll have developed an irrational hatred of it.
Essentially, Yoko Taro wanted to tell a large story through a small, if not well polished game, and it just didn't work for me.  It's repetitious and the story, while ambitious, is too quick to spread itself thin and wide.
And yet for all my seeming pessimism, I do think this is a good game. I think it belongs in a special pantheon of titles that manage to be memorable in spite of their glaring flaws; games like Dead Rising, Condemned, FEAR, etc. Nier Automata is very flawed, but there is absolutely nothing else quite like it out there, and for all it's flaws, there is a charm to it. If you like Platinum Games, if you like Yoko Taro's creative works, or if you even just like robots, there's a lot of heart to this game worth getting into. I don't think it succeeds at it's goals, but it definitely gets an A for effort.
I think that says something about a title if you can sink 30 hours into it, not be satisfied and still feel like you came away with something you'll be able to talk about years down the line.

Simply put, this game is nothing short of a masterpiece. Between the rich story with well thought out characters, the beautiful world design and incredible soundtrack, NieR: Automata is an amazing experience from start to finish.
The story is done in a way that can only truely be realized as a video game, but it's impossible to elaborate without spoiling significant parts of it. The main story is roughly 30 hours in length, however the side quests are all very much worth completing for the depth it adds to the world.
Combat wise, the system is simple yet satisfying, and the plug-in chip system (almost similar to badge system from Paper Mario) give you plenty of ways to customise your skills. There's a huge variety of weapons from small swords, large swords, spears and combat bracers (punching gloves), each of which you can upgrade both to enhance the weapon as well as tell the story of the weapon's origin.
As for the negatives, while the world's concept is fantastic, the execution can be rather shoddy. This is very clear in the starting city as many buildings are very hollow and featureless yet are abundant with invisible walls. The quality of the world design veries heavily from current gen back to earily ps3-era graphics. The performance doesn't quite stack up either as it's quite a bit more resource heavy than the visuals would lead you to believe. I would reccomend downloading the fan patch (simple one-button install) on the steam community forums before you starting.
Overall, the positives more than make up for the negatives and is an overall joy to play. Despite the low amount of advertising, I hope this work of art gets the recognition it deserves. I can't reccomend it enough.

The mark of a good idle game is one you can play while playing other games, more of a thing you build and check in on with a minimum of actual active time investment rather than having to do a lot of active play.  It's the difference between AdVenture Capitalist and Clicker Heroes (both of which show their strength by laying off the addiction urge---you might think about them when you're at work or out on a date or playing Skyrim, but they don't take over your life) and games like Cookie Clicker and Ice Cream Stand, which don't really work right as idle games and therefore end up as annoying Skinner Box time sinks.
This is idle gaming done right.  And it's free, with the option to reward the dev financially in exchange for ultimately meaningless stuff that isn't pay-to-win (although what you're "winning" in that scenario is an open question since this isn't a multiplayer game.)

There's just a few things that I liked about this game, but a lot of things that I really wish were better;
Pro's;
The storyline has an interesting concept, the protagonist being a member of the coast guard sent to a ship which had been sending out a distress signal for some time.
There were some decent scares, but not enough to have me at the edge of my seat cringing and scared to move on like some games do.
For it's age the game still retains some playability and nice features, but not enough to be
features, though some were unique.
Con's;
For a horror game, I was shocked to see that not many scares were implemented and many areas were predictable with the ones there were. In an honest opinion, it could've been very much better if there were more.
Some areas of the game were a bit buggy, but not game-breaking.
Unique features that would seem like a good implementation throughout the game were not fully utilized as they could have been.
After a bit into the game, the storyline becomes bland and slightly hard to keep my interest, it seemed as if the game had been rushed after the opening chapters and the developers lost interest.
That's about all I can say about the game for now, if you still want to take a shot at it, feel free to, remember. Everybody's playthrough is different with games like these, especially older ones!

Heinlein Review
I've played Heinlein for about 30 hours since it was released. Overall Heinlein is a modest improvement to the UI and combat and a slight improvement to colonization, diplomacy, and endgame content.
Good things about Stellaris:
1. It's a space 4x title with fantastic art, sound, and music.
2. It tries to integrate a lot of interesting ideas (pausable real-time strategy, more complex diplomacy, etc.) that are in other Paradox titles.
3. I've only played one other space 4x that has attempted a galaxy of this scale and complexity.
Unfortunately, the game still suffers from many problems that it had at release:
1. The early game is fun and engaging (lots of anomalies and events), the mid game is okay, and the end game is a tedious and painful chore. During the end game I've literally hit the fastest speed and alt tabbed to a web browser to wait 15 minutes for a tech to finish researching or for something significant to happen.
2. Every playthrough *feels* pretty much the same. Although there are a wide variety of race traits, none of them feel significant enough to encourage different playstyles. Contrast this to a game like Master of Orion (the 1993 original) where each race's playstyles are radically different.
3. Most of the tech tree is boring. Weapons are usually a slightly better version of the previous weapon (Laser 1, Laser 2, Laser 3). Tile blockers are pointless filler techs.
4. Combat isn't tactical. Ship configuration is somewhat irrelevent since 99% of the time it comes down to who has the bigger doom stack of ships.
5. The AI is sometimes bugged/irrational. In my last game I was at war with an awakened fallen empire and it would not attack me for 20 years even though it had vastly superior forces. Then when I finally destroyed their homeworld defenses, it suicidally sent 15 different troop transport fleets (with no weapons) at my massive fleet of warships.
6. Game performance slows to a grind on galaxy size medium or larger towards the mid or end game. Same with combat with a large number of ships. I have a brand new top of the line Macbook Pro with a dedicated video card and 16GB of RAM.
7. Endgame management bloat is mitigated by sectors but the survey ship/construction ship/mining station cycle still feels like spreadsheet management.
8. No spying, intel, or substantial trade
I keep on thinking that this game will finally be great with the next update. It is improving, but it is still only fun for the first few hours of each game. Maybe it will be better in another 2 years.  Maybe I should wait for Stellaris 2. For now I'm putting it back on the shelf.

I would like to begin by saying this is one of the best survival horror games I've ever played!  It's tone and atmosphere were pitch perfect.  From the beginning there was a deep sense of forbodding on the abandoned whaler.  Then the Rogue Russian soldiers appear and the shooting begins, the creepy events happen off and one.  Then the big reveal of the zombies/mutants.  I also like that they are not called zombies in the game, they are simply called Mutants; they're not using the zed-word!  But the lack of calling them zombies helps to keep it from becoming a joke, especially ten years after the game was first released.  The story isn't bad, in fact if you read all the in game notes its done fairly well, but the ending is extremely abrupt and doesn't give the characters the closure I think they deserve.  Parts of the game were difficult, particularly the final boss battle, but a little attention to detail and focus on what the monsters are doing and where their weaknesses are helps make the battles pretty straight forward.  I honestly consider this game much better than many present-day Tripple-A survival horror games; such as some of the recent Resident Evil, and Silent Hill games.  On a personal note: I like it much better than the recent trend of survival horror games where you just run and hide. rather than fight back against the monsters.  It has plenty of terror, creepiness and jump-scares, but enough guns, ammo, and environmental weapons to encourage gamers to rise to the challenge.  And despite plenty off gun battles it never loses its horror atmosphere.  And how can I not recomend a game that includes killing both zombies and Soviets?  This game is an unnoticed gem from the time when survival horror was still on the rise, and I encourage anyone who enjoys horror games to give it a try.

You build a fleet and all battles are auto resolved. Easy, fast and out of the way so you can concentrate on the really fun stuff - land battles and expansion. I don't know if I'm alone in thinking that naval battles are trash and have ruined the newer TW games, but you definitely don't have to worry about that in this game.
There are a lot of factions you can play and they all have small differences but you can generalize all of them into 4 super factions that share a lot of similar traits and units: western Europe, eastern Europe, north Africa and middle east. The bottom line is this game is pretty amazing and you should definitely give it a try.

Every now and then I’ll encounter a game that completely flies under my radar due to the amount of triple-A titles that demand my attention. I was introduced to Stick it to the Man after a friend showed me his copy on PS4, and after watching a few minutes of gameplay I knew right away that this was an adventure that I needed to track down.
In most aspects, Stick it to the Man is heavily influenced by Double Fine studios, and the art, humor, and platforming style invokes Psychonauts heavily throughout. There are actually a few easter eggs sprinkled in the game that reference Double Fine (such as a stuffed doll of Double Fine’s double-headed logo), but it doesn’t feel as if this title is stealing too much from the larger company. I very much enjoyed the concept of the game, living in a sort-of shadow box world with cardboard cutouts and interactive stickers, and the level design is varied and unique. Game difficulty isn’t an issue, although I did encounter odd bugs once or twice which prevented me from making forward progress (namely, sticker mounting points would not immediately appear next to important characters or locations). Also, when several interaction points are clustered near each other, your controls can get squirrelly as the game attempts to snap to context-sensitive areas (and this happens quite frequently).
The story is nonsensical and lighthearted, which I found to be a refreshing change of pace with so many games recently sticking to dark and brooding or sardonic main characters. Ray, the protagonist, is very sweet and helpful to everyone he interacts with, including Ted, the goofy and forgetful alien taking residence in his brain. This isn’t an award-winning story, but it’s wholly entertaining for about five or six hours, though a second playthrough isn’t really needed, save for achievement cleanup.
Stick it to the Man is short and sweet, and I’m very happy that I picked up this platformer when I had the chance. Recommended for most – it’s often listed at a cheap price digitally and is worth a single playthrough.

Stick it to the Man is being hailed as a "spiritual successor to Psychonauts", a title that I have a few problems with. Sure, it deals with similar subject material and has a similar design aesthetic, but that's like saying "EVE Online is a spiritual successor to Galaga". The games are barely similar, the matching artstyle is the closest you're going to get.
SITTM plays more like a graphic novel with limited adventure game puzzle solving mechanics. You'll get that nice rewarding feeling from putting the right item into the right slot, but the majority of your time will be spent patiently listening to every mind-reading audio file, regardless of whether or not the puzzle is already solved. You will feel a compulsive need to read EVERY mind you come across, even if it's unnecessary, and you probably should because there's an achievement for it. Ultimately, while having the game come to a stop every 30 seconds so you can read a new mind does indeed break good, natural gameplay flow into splintery pieces, I immediately forgive it. The game is never boring, and no amount of dialogue could stop be from being impressed by the beautiful design.

A very nice puzzle-platformer/adventure game hybrid with quite an enjoyable story and sense of humor.
It's basically 2D psychonauts in terms of writing, let's be honest. Both in the humor and the fact that the focus of the story is around brains. That's not a problem. I like psychonauts. It doesn't really rip off any elements or steal any jokes from the game, either, so it ends up working really well. Ray does sound quite a lot like Rasputin though. Which is fine.
The main gameplay is jumping around platforms, grabbing stuff with your magic spaghetti hand, solving puzzles, and avoiding enemies. There's not a whole lot of depth to it and the game ends up being rather short, but it doesn't ever feel repetitive either. The stealth segments are probably the weakest, since most of the time there's no reason to not just brute-force your way through them. The puzzles aren't too difficult as usually you're told exactly what you need and where, which is good since they'd be very adventure game-y puzzles otherwise. The weirdness of the scenarios actually adds to the variety and it's amusing to see just what the game decides to do next. The game also looks great and sounds great, the paper aesthetic is played with quite nicely and the music is pretty fitting for the tone and style. The only real downside is the length; while it makes for a pretty complete package, the $15 price tag may not be enough to justify the experience for everyone. Still, I'd definitely call this a great game.
At a low cost, the game is worth it for the story, though it is really short. Must-buy for DC fans.

In the opinion of many professional (and unprofessional) video game reviewers and commentators, Deus Ex is hailed as one of the singular greatest arguement for the greatest game of all time. The in-depth story is as long as it is captivating, taking the player on a global journey from New York City, to Shanghai, to Paris and California and a rather surprising ending location. The story is unparralled in it's depth and creativity, despite broaching a genre which has been entrenched in many fictional works. The gameplay is superb, and serves as a model for close to every FPS/RPG succeading it. Ultimately, the excellence of this work is somewhat inhibited due to the aged graphics which it holds, the faces being a notable point of contention. But this minimially detracts from the experiance, and the atmosphere is unparalled despite this. However, Deus Ex belonged to a generation of games helmed by Warren Spector and other early PC innovators. This collection of programmers and coders worked on some of the most renowned games of all time, System Shock 2 (1999), Thief (1998), and other celebrated classics. They run in tandem with a more focused RPG genre, led by the Fallout games, Elder Scrolls games and other Dungeons and Dragons isometric games largely held as the culmination of masterpieces for the PC. In a sense, Deus Ex is sort of the harbinger of a new age for PC games, one which sort of loses a touch which System Shock 2, Thief and Deus Ex had, and this is inherent within the sequel, which abandons many of the tropes which made Deus Ex a masterpiece. Morrowind serves a similar function albeit for the RPG side, with Oblivion and Skyrim notably streamlining many RPG aspects within that particular game. That is not to say the sequels for Deus Ex are bad. On the contrary, Invisible War is good - but strange. Human Revolution however is noteworthy and worth a playthrough, if only for the grandiose set-up it leaves for this game. Overall this series is one of the innovators within gaming, and thus should be worth consideration.

Some words of warning: this game looks and feels its age.  Graphics are really poor by modern standards and even at the time I hated the feel of the modified Unreal v1 Engine that this game uses, so those who put a high premium on look and feel should stay away.
If, however, you can tolerate these shortcomings, you should know that everything that made Deus Ex one of the best games of all time is still intact.  This game pioneered open-ended gameplay and still does it better than most modern imitators: the level design and character creation system enable players of every persuasion to meaningfully approach the game with their own style.  For example: some bosses can be insta-killed through dialogue if thorough players found, via hacking, the necessary code words.  You can even kill everyone that the game's plot absolutely cannot do without, and characters will react accordingly.  The plot is rich and the world is immersive, with secrets that cannot be discovered by players of one build or other, creating a sense of credibility - like Dark Souls (my other favourite game ever), Deux Ex doesn't willingly give up all its treasures, but demands to be explored.
In summary, this game started a genre, and it's still the paradigm of the action/RPG because it does so many important things so much better than its modern imitators.  If you're a fan of immersive, reactive action/RPGs, you NEED to play Deus Ex.

Deus Ex: Game of the Year Edition is a masterpiece. If you didn't play it yet - you definetly should.
An exceptional mix of FPS / RPG / Stealth / Adventure. Took me 62 hours to get the whole 3 endings and still didn't get enough of it.
You get to play as UNATCO (United Nations Anti-Terrorist Coalition) agent J.C. Denton. Not a simple agent, but an augmented bionic man. Find out betrayal, carefully choose who your friends and enemies are and, finally, decide the fate of the world.
The game gives you freedom in everything. You don't get a Game Over except you get killed, throw yourself from a building, drink booze or do drugs till you overdose, or smoke cigarettes till you get cancer. Overwise it doesn't care what path you choose as long as you can survive the consequences. And there are choices to be made every instance. Use lockpicks to open a door or find a key for it, look for computer login info or use your computer skills to hack it, find acces codes for door keypads or use multitools to disable them, jump on your enemies and slaughter them the way you like it, or look for alternative ways, tunnels, air ventilation systems, etc, and avoid unnecessary kills. It's very rewarding also. A lot of augumentations to choose from, a big variety of weapons, ammo, tools, enemies, locations, etc, which will increasingly keep you interested in going through this cyberpunk conspiracy story.
Proclaim yourself God, be part of The Illuminati, or plunge the world into another Dark Age. The choice is yours.

I enjoy strategy games.  I approach "Conquer the Universe" type of strategy games in a specific way.  Even though Stellaris is designed to frustrate me in every aspect of how I want to play the game, it's worth playing.  (My intent was to recommend this game, but after writing the below I just can't)
LEADERSHIP system:  Leaders run things more efficiently, so they are good.  You are only allowed a very limited number of leaders, which is bad.  To illustrate:
Early game, I like to send out lots of science ships to get as much tech, early, as possible.  For a science ship in Stellaris to be able to do anything, it needs a leader as ship captain.  Military fleets can engage in massive battles without a leader, but for a science ship to survey a star system, it needs one.
Middle game, there are battles and to survey the debris from those battles, you need science ships.  However, by now you have exceeded the six planet limit and have sectors.  Sectors need Govenors, fleets should have Admirals, all three research fields need Scientists, and science ships need Captains.  All of those take from your available number of leadership positions.
This one function of the game is designed to keep you small.
INFLUENCE:  After 24 straight hours in game I have no idea how this works, but it is maddening.  Outposts project physical influence (even more than colonies - don't ask me why), pushing your borders across the void.  Many planets may not be habitable (yet), but a couple systems over has opportunity.  Solution?  Outposts!
The problem is that the most viable tool available to expand influence is also a drain on a resource called Influence.  Energy Credits, Minerals, and Influence.  Ouposts cost influence points to build; the further from your borders, the more points required (makes sense).  However, each outpost costs an influence point, monthly, to maintain.  Since populated planets provide less physical influence than outposts, it becomes near impossible to maintain borders.
edit:  While I originally labeled the Leadership mechanic as a hinderance to growth, Influence far outstrips Leadership when it comes to expansion.  While it definitely is designed to limit growth/expansion, after starting a new game I realized it's meant to artificially lengthen the game at least as much as it's designed to hinder growth.
HABITABLE PLANETS:  While I understand not every planet is habitable, as your technology level increases some borderline planets become acceptable.  What I'm going to describe probably happened because I have open migration policies with multiple alien governments:  Middle game, looking over the map, I notice several icons denoting habitable planets.  Cursoring over them, 70%, 85%, etc ratings are seen.  Build colony ships and send them forth.  Not one of them is able to establish a colony.  Why?  Because that % rating seen when cursored over breaks down into 70% for Race A, 30% Human, 90% Race B, and so on when looking at them from the solor system view.  Admittedly, many alien races are now citizens in my government, but without any ability to build a colony ship for a specific, non-original, race I now have dozens of "habitable" planets sticking their tongue out at me, going, "Nya nya, you can't colonize me! Ha! Ha!"
edit:  Did start a new game and the same unusable "habitable" planet issue happened after conquering another empire's planet.  It's an absolutely disgustingly horrible game mechanic.
AI:  What AI?   Seriously!  My introduction to AI was, as a child,  a computerized chess game that would cheat when losing.  The higher the difficulty level, the more grossly obvious the cheat.  Strategy games usually give economic bonuses to compensate for bad AI.  Stellaris also gives technology bonuses.  This game suffers horribly because it doesn't understand the "Goldilocks Principle."  AI governments are either incompetent and pathetic excuses for ever crawling out of the slimy gene pool, or given such extreme bonuses that they are able to field multiple massive fleets, which a single one would bankrupt you within a couple months (ie: a couple minutes real time), if you were capable of building it.
This is a  game.  I want a real rivalry, a real challenge; not a choice between conquering the undefendable pathetics, or being stomped on by a race with a God like technological advantage.
I could go on for hours and describe things I don't like about this game.  That said, there are things Stellaris does (or tries to do) that I like.  Having been a beta tester, in the past, my gut instinct is this game simply wasn't tested thoroughly by people who weren't involved in its creation.  There's too many "easy" to fix items that should have been taken care of before release, but would have been ignored by people "too close" to its creation.
I purchased for 25% off and would recommend it if at least 50% off.  With DLC being released this weekend, I think updates to the core gameplay are done.  Unfortunate, as there is lots of potential in this game.

Although my playtime says I've only played it for a little over an hour, I've completed the game and had I played it through Steam, I'd probably have most of the achievements. Not that that last part matters all that much, but it gives you an idea of how interesting even the side content of this game can be.
That being said, even disregarding what my playtime says, the game is pretty short in length (probably around 6-8 hours, I'd say, less if you don't read everything's mind) and while some of the enemy evasion sections feel a little on the strict side in terms of getting them just right to get past the guards, the rest of the game is very enjoyable. Especially so if you're not sure what to make of the game and pick it up on a sale. Many of the puzzles are amusing and creative in their own right, often pulling themselves together through the pleasantly bizarre mechanic that the game hinges on, peeling the thoughts from other characters and inexplicably making them real, or peeling parts/items from other characters or the environment for use elsewhere.
There are some moments where you may find yourself wondering where to use some of the gathered items, the stickers as they call them (hence the game's name), but generally it becomes a rather straightforward affair of picking up what you can and figuring out what remains available to interact with to progress. If you're looking for a laidback puzzle platformer that takes more design cues from old adventure games than games like Braid, and an interesting art style, an enjoyable soundtrack, and a somewhat amusing sense of humor, you can't go too wrong with this game.
What it may lack in length and challenge, it more than makes up for in its variety of amusing scenarios.

The Wild Eight is a low-poly survival/crafting game. Your plane has crashed in Alaska and it's up to you and anyone else who is alive (up to 8 players, obviously) to gather supplies and survive the harsh environment.

+Graphics. This is obviously personal preference, but the graphic styling of this title is a low-poly/high-res mashup that works all too well, creating a very unique feel.

+Audio! The soundtrack to this game is rather enjoyable. I sat in the title screen for a minute waiting for a buddy to setup a server and was surprised that the track playing was actually creating a sense of anxiety...perhaps foreshadowing.

+Cannibalism! Do I really need to explain? I may or may not have eaten my brother...
+Explore your map and push the limits of staying away from camp. Everytime you think you have enough food and inventory slots unlocked, the wind and wolves will remind you otherwise.

+Collect cooperatively. Set up a battle plan and assign roles to your group instantly. A buddy and I survived 26 days (a 3 hour play session) by having him hunt/build traps while I ran around and gathered the necessary supplies to craft said traps.
+Crafting is splendid, even in Early Access. It comes across as a little shallow at first (if you have played any other titles in the survival genre), but that's something I'm willing to accept considering the current game state. If you finally start to get ahead and have a nice little stock pile of supplies and food, start putting out storage chests at camp. Lumber and ore are the big players currently, collecting these in combination with unlocking different crafting recipes in your workshop allows the upgrading of your tools and structures: (axe and pickaxe--->Bone Axe/Bone pickaxe, etc.).

+You'll have to hunt. Right now hunting is basically crafting stun rocks and hurling these stones of stun at unsuspecting wildlife and then sprinting up and beating them OR you can set up a flurry of traps and 'herd' the animals into them. It currently takes about 3 traps to knock a full health animal down into chow.
+Skill Points/Skill Tree is realistic. You can level up your mobility(speed/sprint), your backpack's inventory capacity, the drop rate from animals/resources,etc. The way I see this is the longer you have survived, your character 'hardens' up. Can carry more, run faster for longer, etc.
+There are actually quests! So surviving was hard enough, right? Now you have the opportunity to follow side quests and explore abandoned facilities, settlements and labs. This adds a level of depth to the game which isn't 'needed' but is definitely appreciated.
+It's hard. That's right, I said it. You will get frustrated, you will panic, you will die. Accept this and try your best. Try not to freeze to death as you venture out.(hint: build a campfire right behind the resources you are harvesting and then you can work, relatively safe and relatively warm). If you die, that's it. You lose all that hard work you put into leveling up.
-Multiplayer servers (as stated in other reviews) were maxed out and this caused connectivity issues. The devs however have actively replied on the forums and stated that they are aware of such and are putting more servers online.
One of the few early access titles that I would actually encourage players to buy. Even in it's early access state, this game is worth every penny($19.99). I can't wait to watch The Wild Eight continue to grow/update and 'survive' the sh*tstorm of disappointing Early Access survival titles that plague the Steam Marketplace at the moment. Do yourself a favor (especially if you like hard games) and get this gem asap.
Thanks to 2 or 3 patches: (these are some of the updates that I've personally appreciated and noticed in game)
You can now load a saved game without breaking UI.
You can also select a region when joining or creating a server.
Animals and buildings have all experienced multiple upgrades (buildings now provide immunity from blizzards and additional 50% cold defense and animals that have less than 25% HP are inflicted with a -30% speed debuff.)
Weapons have had their bleed/stun chances altered(increased).
EASY MODE IS AVAILABLE...that's right. If you thought the game was too hard originally, this option now exists. The effects of cold and hunger are reduced and you don't lose skills and structure levels upon dying.
Campfire's have HP (something so simple being so game changing).
Of course there are more bugs that have been fixed, items updated, etc. Make sure to check out the patch notes frequently. This game is moving fast. The devs are A+ in my opinion!

Much shorter than the original, or, rather, it feels shorter if you only play one path of the branching story. The Witcher 2, being a very risky episode between much more ambitious entries, feels a little bit aimless (or is it pointless?). My ending was the anti-climax I was looking for, though, despite all the revelations that were provided in a long, heavy stream of expositive verbal diarhea. Story-telling was not the forte of CD Projekt's writers in the bigger, more elaborated plot of Assassin of Kings, although the smaller, more personal stories are told well through exploration and the player's own curiosity. Perhaps they were building up the setting where a major conflict occurs behind a witcher's more "mundane" odd jobs.
I'd say I found the first Witcher game more entertaining, believe it or not. Its predecessor was an eyesore and an obsolete RPG (even at its time), but it was more varied in my opinion. The Witcher 2 is prettier and offers an overwhelming range of choices, but it focuses in a conflict that is beyond our control and interest (seriously, is there any good reason why Geralt chooses to fight in Foltest's army instead of just living a not-so-peaceful life with, say, Shani?). Granted that could be the purpose of the narrative, to make Geralt/the player feel impotent and minuscule in front of these bigger-than-life events he can't avoid. Or perhaps Geralt's journey to regain his memory was too boring for a AAA game and the developers had to spice it up with the international conflict from Andrzej Sapkowski's books.
If you're interested in fast-paced RPGs and you plan to play The Wild Hunt, Assassin of Kings is an essencial prelude and a must-have. Just don't expect to get the best results out of your choices, 'cos the world is very complicated. This power fantasy is mercilessly humbling.

Binding of Isaac might disgust. It might amaze. It might baffle or hook you. But one thing it is not is forgettable.

I may be late to the review party, but I finally got around to finishing this game. I've owned it for probably over a year. But, as this is on Steam, there are bound to be more gamers giving it a go. So, here is my review on
When I first picked it up, I really wanted to like it.
Now, don't get me wrong, I do not hate it; I just don't like it...much.
I will dive right in with the Pros-v-Cons.
Despite a little too much bloom effect on some of the models, and the occasional clipping, the overall graphic quality of the game was enjoyable.
There is a catch (see Cons). I use an XBox 360 controller for all racers, and the control is fairly good in this with the occasional understeer issues aside. For me, keyboards just don't make good racers. The on/off switch controls just won't cut it in my opinion. Kudos to those who can pull it off with good results.
The translation from German to English is laughable at times. And the English voice acting is, in a word, atrocious. I would love to hear feedback from German speaking gamers on whether or not the original actors/script were any better.
Great rockin' soundtrack and the ability to add your own tracks made for an enjoyable time.
I loved how the car fell apart and stopped performing accordingly.
Here's the control catch. My first issue was the camera. Too often, I found myself going around a winding road corner and smacking right into another car that I could not see from the camera scheme offered. Or worse yet, a sneaky little outcropping in the wall, strategically placed to catch you unaware and throw you off your line. Both things that you could see in the first person camera if not for the lack of left/right control. The 3rd person high camera was what I would typically gravitate toward, but you still could not see what was coming around the corner. I realize some driving line planning is in order here, but being able to use the right joystick for camera control left and right would have been ideal. Nobody drives with there head and eyes glued straight forward.  Unless, of course they are staring at a cell phone (Don't even get me started on that).
At times, finding missions was harder than it should have been. I've read, in several online posts, that you had to be in a particular car, in a particular place, for HQ to contact you. However, in many missions, I would start off in said particular vehicle only to have to drive back and switch to another vehicle to continue the mission. It shouldn't be that difficult.
I actually enjoyed playing this game once I figured out the no mission issue.  I always read reviews to know what I'm getting into before purchasing a game.  Occasionally, I will steer clear of one because of them.  However, ultimately, enjoyment really depends on each individual gamer.
Would I pay sticker price for this game?   Well, THAT is what I read reviews for.
As much as I love to support the creators as much as possible, I am on a limited budget so the games I pay full price for need to be really worth it.  So, the answer to the question, is no.
That being said, I will most likely be trying "
" soon. And I hope the other 2 installments will be released in the U.S. as well.  Why?  Because most people tend to get better as they learn more and develop their craft.  I hope the same rings true for Synetic.  Everyone has to start somewhere.  Give "
" a try. It's no Need for Speed, or other big budget racer, but it can be entertaining.

Oh man, I really don't want to do this, but sadly I must give Black Ops a negative review.  Mind you I like this game.  As a game it's top notch and worth playing.  However I'm quite annoyed at the actual PC version of this game.
The problems stem from the fact that there's NO niceties and at least one VERY big flaw.   First the opening interface is HORRIBLE on PC.  You literally MUST have a keyboard for the game to work.  Even a mouse won't allow you to use the menu efficently.  So trying to play this game with just a controller  is a horrible experience.  In addition even though controllers work in game, they don't work well.   You can get all the functionality you expect in game, but on the pause menu the controller only works with the pause button.   You can't select anything with out a mouse or keyboard.
Even when the controller works in game, it doesn't work out of game, so the main menu still doesn't work, and will require a keyboard and a mouse if you are ever use big picture mode.
That isn't a big problem, however the interface all over feels like a interface from 2005, even in a 2010 game this is outdated, but again I could live with this.
However there's two major issues I have.  First the game does try to cloud save something but does a horrible job of it (nothing is stored in the cloud) but the worse problem is if you somehow run out of memory as you play the game (not impossible) the game will actually delete your save data.   I ended up losing my entire progress because of this when nearing the end of the game, a second time.
I mean seriously? I had a save game that was quite far, and then there was a dialog telling me the game was out of memory, and when I quit to fix the problem, my save game was wiped.
Black Ops was one of the best Call of Duty games in years, but I'd recommend a console copy if you want to play it now for the single player.  The PC version is ok, but definitely showing it's age.   Of course if you want mouse and keyboard you'll have to play on the PC, but that'd be the only reason I'd recommend playing this game,
It's not a bad game, but damn it, the game should be far better than these problems.

Truly incredible 4X series. Very high learning curve, takes a lot of time and patience to learn and understand, and single-player only. Don't let that dissuade you if you love in-depth, highly advanced, and fully engrossing gameplay. Being able to advance from a simple pilot with a single ship to a massive empire involved in full-scale wars with entire space-faring civilizations makes this series one for the record books on awesome.

If you added a map to this game, it would be very good. Not brilliant, perhaps...certainly not "perfect"...but very good. As it is, you require an almost-photographic memory to work out where you're supposed to go next, even though you've probably been there a few times before.
Could this have anything to do with the fact that the first half of the game takes place on a cargo ship, and the second half on an oil rig, so, y'know, a lot of the scenery looks pretty much the same? Forgive me for not remembering where the "upper corridor next to the secondary science lab" is, 'cause I've seen a FEW of those of late, I swear to ♥♥♥♥ing God!
Yessiree, a map would have be nice. Or some of those more new-fangled, Bioshock-y arrows pointing you in precisely the direction you need to go, failing that. But a map? Even better. Heck, the very first Resident Evil had one of those, and this game certainly doesn't go out of it's way to NOT rip off virtually every other aspect of that classic game, so...again, a map? Too much to ask?! Apparently so.
There's a few other problems, too. Granted, ones which are SLIGHTLY more forgivable, given the era this is from. The save points are kinda crap (it chooses them for you, sometimes miles apart from each other), some of the third-person aiming with the laser sight on your guns is kind of abominable (gotta love them stairwells), and the plot is as bizarre as bat guano.
Having said all this, it's a defiantly "old-school" survival horror game, and anyone who enjoyed Resident Evil 1 through 4 is sure to find it a virtual must-play, if for no reason other than the fact that games like this are pretty hard to find. And how many times CAN you play those first four Resident Evils before you tire of them completely (the answer in my case being MANY times, but there's still a limit, even for hopeless addicts like myself).
Sincerely, there's a lot to love about this game - the atmospheric rain/wind/rocking boat effects are particularly impressive - and, regrettably, a few things to detest. But I got past them. And so will you, if you're the kind of person I just described.

I agree with most of what people have written, both positive and negative, but I'll try to underline those things that most stood out to me in contrast to Borderlands 2.
The pre-sequel's greatest strengths are also it's greatest weaknesses. The more nuanced story adds drama and a few shades or moral grey, but it also sucks a lot of joy out of the experience. The casual violence that the series is known for becomes less fun (at least it did for me), when you realize that you are slaughtering people who are selflessly trying to do what they think is right, or in some cases, are completely innocent of any wrongdoing. Also, you may see certain beloved characters from Borderlands 2 in a new, less favorable light.
The low gravity platforming adds variety to the formula, but it also causes frustrations when you are knocked off ledges or slide off a surface you thought you could jump on. Furthermore, enemies are generally more maneuverable than you, with faster, longer leaps or the ability to fly around indefinitely. Jetpack soldiers are a nightmare for snipers and others with slow firing weapons, since they like to fly around in circles over your head while shooting at you. Enemies can also use the stomp maneuver as many times as they like, since they don't have to worry about spending oxygen on it. Some of them will just do this continuously until you manage to get away or kill them.
Gameplay is largely the same as Borderlands 2. The introduction of freezing weapons adds some interest, but doesn't really change combat significently. Similarly, lasers are basically just another gun with one major difference. Some lasers have "continuous fire" damage bonuses, which can lead to insane damage, especially if they also have a rapid fire rate. Once Moxxi gave me a gun like that, I used it for the rest of the game. As others have noted, this game is significently shorter than Borderlands 2, although still substantial.
The entire section on the moon (Elpis) feels lower quality in every way, including voice acting, humor, dialogue, and plot. It isn't until you're about to go to the space station that things start getting interesting. On a second playthrough, I found it much more enjoyable to just rush through the first section as fast as possible.
If you liked Borderlands 2, I recommend buying this game on sale. I paid about $25 for it and thought it well worth the value. If you haven't played Borderlands 2, you should do that first. It's the superior game in every way.

Stick it to the man is a game that bases itself in absurdity in quite a pleasant manner. This, combined with the world aesthetic can lead to some pretty extraordinary and hilarious situations. And when I say hilarious, I mean times I genuinely laughed at the clever dialogue and puzzles before me. I even went through and tried to find all the funny dialogue I could, which is quite the achievement.
The aesthetic for the game is a world made of paper, string to hold things in place, and stickers. With your giant purple hand, you can remove and place stickers in different situations to solve puzzles. For example, if you place a horse head next to a singer, she'll think she's being attacked by the mob, and scream, at which point you can take her screaming mouth and use it somewhere else. It's very creative, fresh, and compelling.
The story and characters were very likable, especially Ray. He wasn't a perfect person, but he made a perfect protagonist. Paired with lovely voice acting, it was truly something special.
If I had one problem with it, I would say that there were too many chase areas in the levels. While you could create a checkpoint after clearing it once, there were too few ways to solve them for the number of times it was iterated, and often was unreliable at times when trying to grab thoughts and hitting pins instead, resulting in a quick death.
All in all, this game was a nice experience. It didn't take too long to beat, around 5 hours, but the time I did spend with it was incredible. An excellent story wrapped up in a competent game with an amazing presentation.

Currently the game sacrifices gameplay potential for roleplay potential. Next update they'll change it so that the game will sacrifice roleplay potential for gameplay potential. Is that a good thing though?
Stellaris is different from previous grand strategy games IN SPACE due to this roleplay potential I said earlier. Whilist other games in this genre try to create its own universe and narrative, Stellaris instead creates a sandbox where you fill in that narrative yourself. Want to roleplay the Imperium of Man? Go ahead. Want to roleplay as the Galactic Republic? Go ahead, and it just goes on and on again. You can essentially roleplay as anything from all of Sci-fi (that includes interstellar space empires of course). This is because Stellaris is very abstract, it does try to put in a bit of lore to it via some of the events, but its usually lackluster and uninteresting.
Though there is a lot of variety (eg. 3 FTL types, 3 Starting weapon choices, A dozen or so species traits) this variety has no impact on gameplay, or the META would overshadow your roleplay gameplay style. There is a lot of criticism on Stellaris's gameplay which I need not to explain here. If you want a good game experience for the sake of playing a game, and you have no imagination or no knowledge of any sci-fi universe you won't have a good time with current Stellaris. If you want a game just relax and roleplay with, this'll be a gam-er-product for you. Paradox games in general (specifically the grand strategy ones) manage to find a good middle-ground between these two aspects, immersion/roleplay capability and gameplay. Recently, Stellaris and HOI4 are having trouble doing that.
So what's the point? Wait till the next update if you want a good game (I am honesting bored with stellaris due to me not having imagination and the gameplay not being as rewarding as it should be-OR MAYBE I HAVE DRAINED ALL THE CONTENT STELLARIS HAS TO OFFER WITH THAT 1000 HOUR COUNT). Or play now if you want a taste of how space 4Xs play like. I'll recommend this as being positive appears to be more neutral than being negative, I'll rereview this once 2.0 comes out (lol not stellaris sequel nub, its the new update version number).
