Injustice 2 has already been out for several months and is leagues better than this game.  Unfortunately, WB's track record with PC ports has not been great and they have made the decision - for the time being - not to bring it to Steam.  It stands to reason that anyone looking at this game now is likely either unable to get Injustice 2 or simply doesn't want to pay the huge bucks it currently costs.  So is this release worth it?
Honestly, if you can grab a console version, get that instead.  This release is a port, and it's not an exceptionally clean one, but it's still playable.  The biggest issue is framerate - even with a pretty decent PC, you should be able to run a game as old as this one smooth as butter.  Considering that I can play MKXL, a newer and more intense game (ported by the same guys, too) without any issues, it's weird that the optimization for Injustice is just terrible.  A second, nitpicky kind of issue is that if you are not playing with default layout (maybe you use a stick, maybe you just don't like their ideas, whatever), some of the minigames in the story mode are busted because it tells you to hit A, but it hasn't adjusted for your rebinds.
As for the game itself, it's a simplified fighter and a different beast than MK.  For Injustice, NRS took a streamlined approach (even moreso in the sequel) to ensure fast pick-up play.  While you won't be doing ridiculous juggle combos off the bat, anyone can pick up a controller or stick and be competitive with pals at or about the same level of play.  There's three attack buttons measured in strength, so no bindings to limbs (e.g. kick, punch... it's all in the mind... sorry), one to activate individual powers which vary from awesome to turdtastic, and one dedicated for EX-like attacks (here called meter-burn).  Like MK, inputs are simple and don't require diagonals so playing with a d-pad is absolutely fine.  Replacing MK's X-Ray attacks are these set-piece ultra attacks that do a decent amount of damage and have the same spectacle of a fatality, albeit without the blood and gore.  Speaking of, there are no fatalities in this one and it's safe to play with a younger crowd.
All that being said, you'll be looking at mostly single-player, off-line stuff for this one as the community has long-since moved on, which is to be expected.  But don't fret, there's plenty to work with and a lot of content to go through so you can easily waste away several hours and get your money's worth.  Moreover, local fights are always an option and always a blast if you have the ability to call pals over (sorry if you're foreveralone.jpg).  The story mode takes a lot from MK9 in that the cinematics usually are a lot longer than the fights themselves - however, as the first game out the door after MK9's release, NRS learned a lot of lessons and one of them was this - gimmick fights♥♥♥♥♥♥off players, so you won't find any here.  There's no ridiculous Goro-like boss or 2-on-1s awaiting you in story mode; it's simply cutscene -> fight -> cutscene until you're done.  It won't blow your mind, but it's what you'd expect from a typical comic book yarn, and it's much better than watching BvS.
Still, the appeal is to see all of your favorite and not-so-favorite DC characters get together and beat each other up, and if you know your stuff, this game is a real treat.  Probably one of the first non-Lego games to give DC a good treatment.  However, if your DC knowledge is weak (like mine), you'll find quite a few guys and gals in here that will have you going "Wha?  Whodis?"  Thankfully, an archive is available to give you quick summaries on every character in the game, including the bundled-in DLC characters, so it'll save you some time on wikis if you care (FYI, a lot of DC wikis suck).
One last thing - the skins in this game are awesome.  I did not expect to see all the different skins for the main cast (DLC characters have no alts).  While they are ultimately cosmetic, they are tributes to some of the more popular yarns to come out of DC in the last few decades and they pay homage to lore.  For example, you can deck out Supes as Red Son,  make John Stewart the Green Lantern, play as the Black Flash, etc.  Couple this with unlocking artwork and stuff from years past and there's a treasure chest full of DC goodies available to unlock.

If you love the time period and liked Rome Total War then this game is for you.  I was not that happy with the game until I learned how to effectively charge knights. In Rome Total War you simply double clicked on what you wanted dead. In Medieval ll  you have to keep your formation in line before attacking. This is accomplished be judging the ground between you and the enemy unit you want to decimate.  When you are at a run with your knights and they are formed up in line hit the attack order (Double click).  Hitting them head on is a must (unless they are pike men then hit them from the back) spearmen don't stand a chance when a formed charge hits them. The diplomacy in  this game is involved and steeped in history. The different agents can help you do things like cement alliances with marriage or steal money from other nations with merchants.  The pope has impact on your decisions when you are a catholic nation. The crusades are very fun and a good mini quest which will help you groom princes to become better kings. The family tree adds a personnel touch which makes you actually care about your generals. The availability of mods also makes this a great game for instance if you get tired of the same old game then you can download something like Stainless steel mod which overhauls the entire game.

Man oh man I have mixed feelings on Witcher 2. The fact that I had issues with crashing with the whole game quite a lot, even with my specs listed in my profile is rough. From what I know, it's from a savegame bug where if you have too many, it makes the game crash more and more. Which, because of it, near the end, I had to delete all the older saves of mine and I only kept the newest ones. I'm a frequent saver if I can. Can't help it.
I loved the story though. It was a wonderful one and perhaps someday I'll play through it once more, seeing the 'other side'. (I won't go into many spoilers, it's worth seeing on your own.) Narrative wise, it was really tight. Gameplay wise, if I compare it to Witcher 1, CD Projekt Red certainly didn't fail to improve the nagging inventory system from the first game, and the combat (once I learned it well) was fun to play through. The big minus is the tutorial is really incomplete. You have to either look it up or learn as you go along.
I'd wished it was more of an open world, but I know Witcher 3 solves that problem as well. The 3 Hub worlds though, are pretty open and explorable. I wasn't really a fan of most of the sidequests, unless I wanted to try to craft something. They got rather tiring. The minigames I liked except for the dice game. I STILL couldn't figure that out. (Never looked at a walkthrough for it. I figured if I couldn't learn it from the game, it wasn't worth my time.) The few puzzle solving sidequests especially was not my thing. But that's more of a personal beef I had. I'm sure a lot of players enjoy that sort of thing, even how to spend XP for Geralt effectively.
The ending though, since it was obviously intended to sequelize the whole thing with Witcher 3 was rather lacking. I enjoyed it, but when your last boss is easier than the boss beforehand, it created a kind of disconnect for me. It fits within the narrative though. As a small warning, there IS a cuscene after the credits. I'd suggest however, skipping it and just looking it up on YouTube. The credits are so long it's not worth it.
All in all I'd say it's very much worth playing even full price. I'm seriously hoping that Witcher 3 does the same thing, when I finally wind up playing it. (2 years late!)

After completing The Witcher, my expectations were very high. I loved the first game, and I couldn't wait to see the continuation of Geralt's story. The second game was such a far cry from the first one, that I actually had to step away from it for a few weeks to readjust myself to the incredible changes of look and gameplay. When I came back to it, I got caught up in a very beautiful and complicated story.
The game is beautiful. It could be described as one giant screenshot. I played the game on Medium specs, and wondered how it could possibly get any better. But than again, I''m pretty new to this type of quality in gaming. Up until 5 months ago, I was still playing on a Playstation 2, so there you go... So yes, it is very pretty, sounds pretty, awesome characters, you need to do all the side quests because they all are necessary blah blah blah. We know all that already. Let's get nitpicky or this will be just another review saying that this is the second part of a trilogy leading to the greatest game of all time forever...
Now, the story is very very very political. In comparison to the first game, it felt more like a historical drama that just happens to take place in a sort of fantasy Eastern European setting. You may have to constantly check your journal to refresh yourself on all the characters and who is in what faction and the kingdom's leaders so you choose the side you want to join, and possibly end up backstabbing anyways because the world of The Witcher is.....so.....complicated. At the end of the game, Geralt says,"I'm tired of choosing the lesser evil." I was right there with him. This game is not about right or wrong. It is all about ethics. This game really does right the game mechanic or not having a clear cut right/wrong answer. There are only consequences.
The world is beautiful but finding your way around it is horribly confusing. The world map is very hard to read as far as knowing where exactly you want to go. It is very small. Also, it does not help with the circular mini map that is on screen. I never had a problem navigating in The Witcher. As much as I enjoyed exploring the world, I wish navigating it had been less complicated.
The combat system is very different from the first game. It took a lot of getting used to for me since I loved the combat in the first game. I had to play the game on Easy to get a handle on it. I do intend to go back and replay it again on Normal. The idea that Geralt has to drink potions before battle is annoying and understandable at the same time. Boss battles are easy to prep for, while other times you want to drink a potion in the heat of battle that you didn't see coming but you can't because you are in the heat of battle!
This game was very enjoyable. It takes huge leaps forward in terms of how it looks, while the combat system may be a turn off to those who enjoyed the first game. As much as I enjoyed it, I would say to those that play the The Witcher FIRST, take a few days/weeks off of the series to clear your fingers and eyes mindset.

I found Crash Time II to be a rather enjoyable car chase/racing game that allows you to speed through a European city and wreck havoc, while no one seems to mind.  The trick to really enjoying this game, however, is that you have to get past the frustrating first mission.  You know how most games give you easy tasks at the beginning of the game, and just about the time you think you got the hang of it, the difficulty ramps up until you begin to feel like a failure?  Crash Time II does just the opposite.
The first mission requires you to perform a rather tricky maneuver, followed by extensive car chase in which you need to disable the car you are pursuing by ramming it over and over until it's an immobile pile of metal.  This is more difficult than it sounds, especially when you are new to the game.  In fact, it took me over three hours to complete the level.  After that, however, the game became much easier, with the next several missions being timed tasks, races, or chases that only require pinning your target instead of destroying them.  Yes, the game has several other frustrating missions that require multiple attempts, but by this time your skill is better and they don’t take as long or seem as daunting.
I played this game both with a controller and with a keyboard and mouse.  Personally, I have no preference and found both methods adequate.
Helpful Tips to make the game more fun and reduce frustration:
1.  Play in easy mode.  The chase missions are hard enough -- a simple wrong turn can allow an enemy to escape in an instant.

2.  Read the manual.  At least scan it. I spent a lot of time driving around doing nothing early in the game until I read the manual and figured out why missions weren't triggering.

3.  When you are required to completely disable another vehicle, avoid pinning it for too long.  Back off and let it get going before ramming it again.  What the game neglects to tell you is that all the criminals have graduated from Hogwarts and, when pinned, will suddenly disappear and reappear elsewhere, sometimes far enough away that they can escape before you even have time to turn your vehicle around.

Finally, the voice acting is brilliant!  No, I didn’t say it was good, well written or well acted.  Just brilliant.

I agree with most of what people have written, both positive and negative, but I'll try to underline those things that most stood out to me in contrast to Borderlands 2.
The pre-sequel's greatest strengths are also it's greatest weaknesses. The more nuanced story adds drama and a few shades or moral grey, but it also sucks a lot of joy out of the experience. The casual violence that the series is known for becomes less fun (at least it did for me), when you realize that you are slaughtering people who are selflessly trying to do what they think is right, or in some cases, are completely innocent of any wrongdoing. Also, you may see certain beloved characters from Borderlands 2 in a new, less favorable light.
The low gravity platforming adds variety to the formula, but it also causes frustrations when you are knocked off ledges or slide off a surface you thought you could jump on. Furthermore, enemies are generally more maneuverable than you, with faster, longer leaps or the ability to fly around indefinitely. Jetpack soldiers are a nightmare for snipers and others with slow firing weapons, since they like to fly around in circles over your head while shooting at you. Enemies can also use the stomp maneuver as many times as they like, since they don't have to worry about spending oxygen on it. Some of them will just do this continuously until you manage to get away or kill them.
Gameplay is largely the same as Borderlands 2. The introduction of freezing weapons adds some interest, but doesn't really change combat significently. Similarly, lasers are basically just another gun with one major difference. Some lasers have "continuous fire" damage bonuses, which can lead to insane damage, especially if they also have a rapid fire rate. Once Moxxi gave me a gun like that, I used it for the rest of the game. As others have noted, this game is significently shorter than Borderlands 2, although still substantial.
The entire section on the moon (Elpis) feels lower quality in every way, including voice acting, humor, dialogue, and plot. It isn't until you're about to go to the space station that things start getting interesting. On a second playthrough, I found it much more enjoyable to just rush through the first section as fast as possible.
If you liked Borderlands 2, I recommend buying this game on sale. I paid about $25 for it and thought it well worth the value. If you haven't played Borderlands 2, you should do that first. It's the superior game in every way.

Atmospherically, Cold Fear is an enjoyable (and sometimes quite scary) action game. While Cold Fear does not exactly establish itself as a high-quality survival horror game, the involved story and occasional interesting gameplay element make Cold Fear worth playing, and there are
.
In
, you play as
, a US Coast Guard officer who has been sent to investigate a mysterious Russian frigate on a windy and stormy night in the middle of the ocean. You find out early on that the boat is occupied not merely by hostile Russian soldiers, of which there are plenty, but also by alien creatures that feed on the humans and provide a severe threat from both inside and outside their host bodies. Your investigation leads you to a few friendly faces and many threatening ones as you uncover the mystery of the ship and its lethal cargo.
The perspective is third person, with the ability to go into a first-person aiming mode through which you can freely guide your view. Although the fixed camera gives a wider glimpse of the scene, it's not easy to keep fluid control when going back and forth between cameras, which is a problem as you try to maneuver around the boat and take out the enemies you encounter along the way. Additional controls let you crouch, run, and scroll quickly through weapons, which is slightly more intuitive in the PS2 version, thanks to the extra trigger buttons. However, since the weapon scroll is placed on the white/black buttons on the Xbox controller, the difference is not that severe. The PC version works well with the keys, though I doubt it will have any coltroller control, (unsupported at least.) Running brings up an onscreen meter that, when depleted, prohibits you from running anymore. This helps to make certain puzzles more challenging, and you will find yourself monitoring the meter frequently, but it does not detract from or add to the gameplay in any significant way.
Because Cold Fear takes place in ocean-locked environments (and it looks very cool), the control scheme is affected by the movement of the waves. This is mostly noticeable when you are outside, and at times it looks like you're walking almost completely sideways, due to the volatile movement of the deck beneath you. This adversely impacts the controls, but the trade-off is a unique and interesting component of the gameplay. As you fight against the tossing of the boat, timing yourself to cross decks only when the waves are low, you encounter some of the most compelling aspects of Cold Fear. Unfortunately, the outside environments are not tapped to their fullest, and you'll spend the majority of the game, past the first hour, in generic indoor locations, though you do need to go outside once in a while.
Your objective in Cold Fear is to discover the story behind the vessel's apparent destruction and the emergence of the nonhuman creatures upon it. Despite being a highly derivative story about a genetic experiment gone wrong, the relationship between characters is interesting, and the story is neat and simple. Most of the plot exploration is conveyed through notes that are littered about the environment and through dialogues with characters (for the short duration that the people on the boat other than Hansen manage to stay alive). The notes are well implemented, and they drive the story and reveal critical information about weapons, environmental objects, and enemies.
Although you start off with merely a handgun, there are a number of different weapons to be found in the middle of the ocean, including a submachine gun, an AK-47, a speargun, a flamethrower, and a grenade launcher. The weapons are almost all equally effective, except for differences in power. The speargun is the only weapon that is not used explicitly for dealing damage, and when fired, it releases a gas that draws enemies near it. This is a great tactic to use in conjunction with one of the more explosive weapons such as the shotgun or grenade launcher. Otherwise, the objective of the game is to make headshots on all humanoid enemies, which can be exceedingly difficult as the enemies draw nearer to you. Fortunately, most of the weapons have either a laser sight or flashlight, which aids your precision. The point of the headshot is to conserve ammunition, although enemies will not die unless they are decapitated. This means that if you shoot an enemy anywhere other than in the head, and merely knock it down to the ground, you have a certain amount of time to run over and step on the head before the enemy gets back up and attacks you again.
Many of the
are possessed by
, which are spidery beings that alternate between crawling on the floor and the ceiling before attempting to take possession of a human being by reaching out a long tendril into a human's mouth and then climbing inside. Outside of a host body, these exocels are fairly easy to destroy--usually one bullet sends them rolling up into a ball, and a second one takes them out--but given their flexibility and their penchant for appearing out of nowhere, including bodies you've just killed, they provide a formidable threat if not dealt with quickly. More advanced abominations of genetics appear later on, but with the more difficult enemies, it's sometimes easier to merely avoid confrontation and run along to the next room. If you choose to run, you'll find these creatures often jumping on your back. When this happens, you're given a button sequence to throw the enemy and try to achieve a critical hit. If you successfully land a critical hit, enemies are killed much more quickly than if you had gone about it the normal way. Because of this, it's sometimes tactically important to let Hansen be jumped by enemies, as long as you can throw them quickly.
Other game tactics include using pieces of the environment to do the work for you. You can shoot explosive barrels, fire extinguishers, and different-colored valves to create an environmental trap for oncoming enemies. From time to time, you'll encounter a fight between two of the enemy species, and you can let them fight among themselves before you intervene. Environmental effects, such as laser beams and swinging obstacles, can often be used to pick off the less bright enemies, and the rocking of the boat will send a zombie or you overboard, if you're standing on the wrong side of a slippery surface.
That's all good, but a significant drawback to the gameplay is the lack of an in-game map. Hansen declares early on that he is able to remember some Russian, so he can translate the signs on and around the doors if you look at them with enough reverence--but because of the similarity of the areas and the sheer number of open paths at any given moment, you'll spend a great deal of time backtracking and trying to recall exactly which path to take. There are clues here and there, such as new enemies and changes to the environment, but for the most part you're left to wander the boat and figure it out on your own. And wander you will, though there is lots to explore.
The atmosphere's major saving grace is the music and sound effects. The music is dramatic and very flexible, changing with the mood as necessary. Although a couple of the tracks get repetitive and even slightly grating, for the most part the music does nothing but help the game. Likewise, the sound effects are appropriate to the environment, including the harsh creaking of the metal boat and the constant splashing of the waves upon the deck.

This is not too surprising when you consider that the studio that made it, Darkworks', previous horror game before this was Alone in the Dark: New Nightmare, another Resident Evil-clone game. In fact, the studio seems to have this big thing for horror, as they have released six games in the last 15 years, and half of them are horror titles (the newest one they released was I Am Alive).
Cold Fear plays like possibly the truest form of new Resident Evil meets old Resident Evil I have seen. The game switches up between a Resident Evil 4-style camera (when you're aiming, during certain gameplay segments), and fixed camera angles (ala' old-school Resident Evil). Assuming you aren't horrible with fixed-camera angle controls, the transitions were done pretty well and weren't nearly as disorienting as I thought they might be. They were handled and placed well in my opinion. A few good subtle scares, mixed with shoot-shoot, bang-bang, but with some limited ammo edge (though not extensively). And while it isn't the prettiest game around (even back for when it came out in 2005) it is not a bad-looking game, and had a few special effects throughout I thought were pretty ace.
The audio was also pretty nice. The voice acting was surprisingly okay to good, the music fit the mood perfectly with a few rather unnerving tracks, and the sounds in the environment did a lot to help build up the couple of locations that appear in the game.
I also have to mention now that I love ocean settings, and though Resident Evil Revelations most recently took place on a ship in the RE universe, this game handled its ocean setting much better I feel. They included things like furniture sliding around based on the turn of the ship (yes, the ship occasionally will churn itself back and forth), waves that sweep up onto the ship decks you have to watch out for or else they might sweep you away, actually pretty good rain effects, Some slight sea-fairing mist in a few places... The setting felt a lot more believable and more oceanic, which is good in my eyes.
Probably the single most surprising elements for me was how interested I got into the story. Not so much the character drama (which there's a bit of, and not many of the characters are that-well fleshed out) but the story told in the files in the game. While it wasn't mind-boggling and there wasn't any twists to be found, I found the background story and papers about the monsters and people who were here immensely interesting, probably the most interested I'd been in a horror games files in a long while. There was one file towards the end of the game that was a bit stupidly long, but they were mostly well-lengthed as well. Unfortunately the game has one of the most disappointing endings I've experienced in a while as well.
The combat in the game felt a bit like a poor-man's Resident Evil. It was serviceable and fun, but not anywhere near RE or Dead Space levels, though I must give credit that a lot of the monsters were rather original for this type of game. What is unfortunate is that some of them were almost hilariously cheap. The lesser 'cheap' enemy of the two I refer too is actually one of the main enemies in the game, which is this parasite thing that kind of looks like a starfish with extendable limbs. Ala' RE4, these things sometimes pop out of enemies when you kill them (they make a distinctive chirping sound). What is cheap about them is how ♥♥♥♥ing tiny they are, and how stupidly long their reach is. They can crawl on walls and ceilings, and can be hard to spot, but from several meters away (like, the length of five grown men from head to toe) they can extend their limbs to attach onto you and start rapidly draining your health away. They won't let go until you either get out of their range, or kill them, and they can drain health fast. And they almost never appear alone, they usually have a pack of themselves around.
The second annoyance, and the biggest gripe for me in the game, is an enemy takes on the form of a dog-like thing. He appears in the second half of the game, and HE IS CHEAP. This enemy can crawl on ceilings, usually appears in really dark locations (where you can only see its eyes), can crawl into vents and appear elsewhere (this was before Dead Space, so wasn't inspired by that), and is the fastest enemy in the game. This would all be fine, EXCEPT when the enemy gets two meters close to you it will ALWAYS, ALWAYS trigger a one-hit kill move. There is a chance to avoid it with a REALLY quick QTE, but it's hard, and this enemy does this so ♥♥♥♥ing much, and it doesn't even make sense as the attack takes about 2-3 seconds to do, which would be enough time to get away from the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but the moment he triggers it you're locked into an animation with him and can't move. You don't face many in the game, but god dang it, they killed me more than anything.
And it wouldn't be as bad, but the saving system in this game only happens at story intervals. Sometimes you'll go long segments of gameplay without a saving point, sometimes you'll get a save point almost immediately after the last one. Typically appear around cutscenes, but think something more Resident Evil 1 or 4-ish would of worked better here, especially as you do some backtracking in this game (like the older Resident Evils).
But outside of my complaints above, I actually really enjoyed the game. Some of the enemies were really interesting (and most pretty fair), some of the scenarios and scares were actually pretty well-done. It was a pretty good length, and while a few rough edges, I would say the game was a pretty decent knock-off, worth it for those who like this sort of style of horror game. It has an action-survival focus, but it was scarier than any recent Resident Evil game I can recall. And like a lot of good horror games from yesteryear, and though I couldn't say it's a 'great' game, I think it's a good game that is worth it for anyone who is interested in this type of thing. It's well-priced for what it provides, and I honestly do think it's a shame this game never got a follow-up.
But it also reminded me of how I actually miss the days of games like these being circulated. Horror games have never stopped circulating with clones (just look at all those Slender, Amnesia, and Dear Esther clones out there), but game's like this, maybe not amazing or groundbreaking, but competent and entertaining B-tier games that have a bit of heart in their soulless ripping-off methods and some twists to everything to make it their own... A reminder why the middle-tier game almost being non-existent these days is so disappointing. Even with the horror genre on the up-rise again, it doesn't seem like these type of games will be continuing anytime soon.
But modern sentimental feelings aside, I think this type of game might be more appreciated now as it was really one of the last of its kind before developers decided that the horror genre was dead and that middle-tier games are a dying breed. I'm even impressed to say that Resident Evil Revelations, which I thought was a pretty good game, is at ends with me on Cold Fear, as I feel Revelations does some things better, while Cold Fear does other things that tops it at times.
Tl;Dr: I played a boat with zombies on it. Starfish are ♥♥♥♥♥es, and I am sentimental about B-tier and horror games like this. Spare the time to give the game a good checking out if this type of thing is up your alley, though some frustrations do await.

Point and click has been a genre that has struggled the last ten years, With the market peaking in the 90’s with games like, Monkey Island, and ever since then the genre has struggled to find a foothold with the rise of counsels. Point and Click was hard to do on a counsel because you will, point and click.  There have been attempts to revive the genre, but not much has happened with it except for re- releases and re-makes. Until now,
Stick it to the man is a game that advertises as an action platformer, but its really a point and click game in disguise, it also a game very much about comedy.  Here Let me give you a basic plot description, The Main Character Has Psychic powers, can read peoples minds to help solve their problems, its has a unique artstyle and sense of humor. There is also platforming and puzzle solving.
Now if you know anything about good games your mind should instantly think of Psychonauts, and if you don’t know Psychonauts, 1st you should, and second go watch the Zero punctuation review on it or something, but if you’re to even do that then ill explain, Psychonauts, is an action platformer, puzzle solver, with unique art style and sense of humor, The main character also can read minds.
So now that i’ve gotten that comparison out of the way, I’ll talk more about this game, The art style of the game is a mixture between the weirdness of psychonauts, and the Cardboard of tearaway. The game also has a depth to it, you can move up and down the foreground, and background like in little big planet, but  the game never uses this to its advantage, i can only remember using it one time and that was when i discover i could even do it.
The Music in the game is repetitive unfortunately, every time you run into an enemy it plays the same music until you’ve successfully escaped, its always the same no variation of bad guy music.
The Gameplay of the game is centered around one central gimmick, your mind arm, Your mind arm is somthing you get in the very beginning of the game, and its what makes this game. It is your  cursor, its what you use to interact with the world, It's what lets you read minds to solve problems, it helps you platform acting like a grappling hook. Its what manages your inventory, and tears off stickers.
Sticker by the way are exactly what they sound like they are parts of the world that have been highlighted that you can rip off and stick to other things using your mind arm. You can get stickers by finding highlighted things in the world, or by reading someone's mind see what they are thinking of the literally ripping the thought out of their mind as a sticker. Stickers are the items used to solve the puzzles the game presents you with and you can have more than one at a time, this is where the inventory comes in. The inventory is just the d-pad left and right on the controller, it keeps it simple and easy.
The Control of the mind arm is… not so great. It you use the right analog stick to aim the arm, then it has an auto lock on to objects, the auto lock works but its also a problem. When there is more than one character next to another (which happens a lot by the way) it becomes hard to lock on to who you want to read  the mind of sometimes only allowing certain angles. The platforming is also floaty, it just doesn't feel super responsive, some of that may be attributed to the artstyle, but at some points especially when around enemies, you just don't feel like you have the amount of control you should.
Floaty Controls aside, its the story and style that makes a point and click game, and boy does it have it in spades. This game is funny, thats hard to find in games now a days, you either have absurd humor, like goat simulator, or good character dialog like in borderlands. This game does both surprisingly well.
Ill give you an example of one of the puzzles, in one portion of the game you are tasked with escaping an insane asylum on and island. You meet tons of crazy characters each with different personalities and goals, You meet a captain who says he’s slain a great whale, you eventually find this whale decomposing, you also meet a taxidermist in the asylum, you bring her to the what and she sows it up, you then meet a man who is hyperventilating into a bag, you take this mans you take this man to the whale and he blows into the bowl hole filling it with air, you now have a raft made out of a dead whale that you use to escape the island.
If dead whale raft isn't funny to you, then something's wrong with you, or your an animal rights activist who doesn't like video games. The entire game is filled with over the top moments like that.
This does bring up some points negative though, almost all point and clicks suffer from this, and that is convoluted puzzles, you know when you just don't know what to do so you have to try everything with everything else, yah that moment. Fortunately it doesn't happen that often but when it happens it really slow the games pace down.
The game also has a lot of backtracking, like most point and clicks . Most of the game takes place on large maps that you have to fully explore to solve the puzzles, and get to the next area, but the backtracking isn't that bad and there are some parts in the game that will let you do a quick travel to certain areas.
Although this game definitely suffers from all the problems that have always plagued Point and clicks, it works well and is definitely the benchmark for a counsel point and click game, so if soul successor to Psychonauts sounds good to you, dont hesitate to buy.

Currently the game sacrifices gameplay potential for roleplay potential. Next update they'll change it so that the game will sacrifice roleplay potential for gameplay potential. Is that a good thing though?
Stellaris is different from previous grand strategy games IN SPACE due to this roleplay potential I said earlier. Whilist other games in this genre try to create its own universe and narrative, Stellaris instead creates a sandbox where you fill in that narrative yourself. Want to roleplay the Imperium of Man? Go ahead. Want to roleplay as the Galactic Republic? Go ahead, and it just goes on and on again. You can essentially roleplay as anything from all of Sci-fi (that includes interstellar space empires of course). This is because Stellaris is very abstract, it does try to put in a bit of lore to it via some of the events, but its usually lackluster and uninteresting.
Though there is a lot of variety (eg. 3 FTL types, 3 Starting weapon choices, A dozen or so species traits) this variety has no impact on gameplay, or the META would overshadow your roleplay gameplay style. There is a lot of criticism on Stellaris's gameplay which I need not to explain here. If you want a good game experience for the sake of playing a game, and you have no imagination or no knowledge of any sci-fi universe you won't have a good time with current Stellaris. If you want a game just relax and roleplay with, this'll be a gam-er-product for you. Paradox games in general (specifically the grand strategy ones) manage to find a good middle-ground between these two aspects, immersion/roleplay capability and gameplay. Recently, Stellaris and HOI4 are having trouble doing that.
So what's the point? Wait till the next update if you want a good game (I am honesting bored with stellaris due to me not having imagination and the gameplay not being as rewarding as it should be-OR MAYBE I HAVE DRAINED ALL THE CONTENT STELLARIS HAS TO OFFER WITH THAT 1000 HOUR COUNT). Or play now if you want a taste of how space 4Xs play like. I'll recommend this as being positive appears to be more neutral than being negative, I'll rereview this once 2.0 comes out (lol not stellaris sequel nub, its the new update version number).

One day I saw this game on a ridiculous offer: 4-pack at 0,99€... Then I said why the hell not??!?!
Orion: Prelude is a classic FPS set inside arenas with waves of... Dinosaurs! There are wide valleys/arenas to play in and you mainly need to protect your power generator (base) from the mighty dinosaurs! Occasionally you must conquer outer bases (by simply standing there for a few seconds) and from time to time one or more Big Dinosaurs will be spawned like the Triceratops, T-Rex or the usually quiet (and herbivorous...) Brontosaurus and stegosaurus as kind of boss enemies.
Between every wave you can purchase inside your base new abilities and weapons (with ingame credits, this isn't a pay-to-win, absolutely), tools, automated turrets and so on. Parked near outer bases you will find different kind of vehicles you can use to drive over dinosaurs or shoot at them (this depends whether it has a machinegun already or not).
There are more game modes including the classic ones as deathmatch and capture the flag.
This game is strongly recommended for Co-op gaming or online gaming but if you don't want to you can still play on your own sidekicked by bots. It won't be the same but better than nothing. Actually I'm playing on my own because my friends refuse to play with it as they say it simply sucks. And they're not totally mistaken actually. I like the game but it's not... well, let's say "polished".
The first thing is the Engine. Orion Uses The Omnipresent Unreal Engine But I guess it has been abused or badly optimized because in my laptop it runs as if it was the Cryengine 12, I had to set almost everything off and Mid-Low details to get a decent framerate... And I agree, my laptop is not a Top-Gaming gear, but it's an i5 with 8Gb RAM and Geforce 840M. It can run better games with way better details. Even the cursor in the main menu is kind of stuttering.
Apart from the technical issues the worlds are quite nice and pleasant to see. The real problem is the confusing aspect when The dinosaurs kick in. I understand it has to be difficult, and dinosaurs must camouflage themselves but it really looks kind of confusing.
But still I personally like the game. Sure, this isn't a masterpiece, but the ideas are good, the game himself is fun for me and I really love the epic musics, which is somehow unexpected. I like the gameplay, the classes, the jetpack and cloacking device, the Dino mode... Because you can play as a dinosaur and go around eating human players as well! XD
I personally see some potential in this team.

After completing The Witcher, my expectations were very high. I loved the first game, and I couldn't wait to see the continuation of Geralt's story. The second game was such a far cry from the first one, that I actually had to step away from it for a few weeks to readjust myself to the incredible changes of look and gameplay. When I came back to it, I got caught up in a very beautiful and complicated story.
The game is beautiful. It could be described as one giant screenshot. I played the game on Medium specs, and wondered how it could possibly get any better. But than again, I''m pretty new to this type of quality in gaming. Up until 5 months ago, I was still playing on a Playstation 2, so there you go... So yes, it is very pretty, sounds pretty, awesome characters, you need to do all the side quests because they all are necessary blah blah blah. We know all that already. Let's get nitpicky or this will be just another review saying that this is the second part of a trilogy leading to the greatest game of all time forever...
Now, the story is very very very political. In comparison to the first game, it felt more like a historical drama that just happens to take place in a sort of fantasy Eastern European setting. You may have to constantly check your journal to refresh yourself on all the characters and who is in what faction and the kingdom's leaders so you choose the side you want to join, and possibly end up backstabbing anyways because the world of The Witcher is.....so.....complicated. At the end of the game, Geralt says,"I'm tired of choosing the lesser evil." I was right there with him. This game is not about right or wrong. It is all about ethics. This game really does right the game mechanic or not having a clear cut right/wrong answer. There are only consequences.
The world is beautiful but finding your way around it is horribly confusing. The world map is very hard to read as far as knowing where exactly you want to go. It is very small. Also, it does not help with the circular mini map that is on screen. I never had a problem navigating in The Witcher. As much as I enjoyed exploring the world, I wish navigating it had been less complicated.
The combat system is very different from the first game. It took a lot of getting used to for me since I loved the combat in the first game. I had to play the game on Easy to get a handle on it. I do intend to go back and replay it again on Normal. The idea that Geralt has to drink potions before battle is annoying and understandable at the same time. Boss battles are easy to prep for, while other times you want to drink a potion in the heat of battle that you didn't see coming but you can't because you are in the heat of battle!
This game was very enjoyable. It takes huge leaps forward in terms of how it looks, while the combat system may be a turn off to those who enjoyed the first game. As much as I enjoyed it, I would say to those that play the The Witcher FIRST, take a few days/weeks off of the series to clear your fingers and eyes mindset.

TL;DR: Simply not worth the money. This is roughtly equivalent to what would be a DLC campaign in BL or BL2. I got it on sale for approx $21 with the season pass and I still feel like I may have over paid.
I am a huge Borderlands fan. I have a bunch of collectibles, Marcus bobble head, Butt Stallion Diamond Edition statue on the way, posters, the works, and I CANNOT IN GOOD CONSCIENCE RECOMMEND THIS GAME.
It is not a bad game, but it is super mediocre and it does not feel like Borderlands. There are a lot of good single moments, but these are ALL in SIDE quests (such as explaining the origin of Jack's invisibility and how Nakayama got a scan of Jack's brain).
CONS:
- Very few decent guns. There are basically threee good unique guns, and you get them after you are levelled up beyond them.
- VERY annoying characters. Especially Pickle and Springs. I have Australian friends, I prefer the Australian audio track of Mad Max, I am totally capable of understanding Australian linguo and accent. I have no idea what Pickle is saying half the time and Springs is an insulting caricature.
- SHORT. Of all three games, this campaign in the shortest, and that's saying sometihng considering the next CON.
- You  are locked in to dialogue. In the previoous games, you could continue down the road while everyone talked about the quest. In Pre-Sequel, you are stuck and cannot continue for as much as 10 minutes while characters talk to each other about crap that doesn't even matter. You do not get a waypoint and often you are trapped in a room with nothing while this goes on. In the words of Tiny Tina (who only appears via narration) in the second playthrough of the game, "Uggh, so much boring talky talk, get back to the shooting."
PROS:
- It fills in the story of what happened to a few things that didn't make an appearance in BL2. A few things.
- The Claptastic Voyage DLC. This is really the only reason to get the game and is what the main game should have been.
And that's pretty much it. There are only a couple fun quests.
They really should fix keyboard and mouse gameplay.

You're going to have an emotional attachment to any character with more than 10 minutes of screen time, and you're going to genuinely care about them and their struggles. I would recommend playing the original NieR and Drakengard 1 & 3 before or after this for a more complete picture of the lore, but NieR: Automata works absolutely fantastically on its own with no prior knowledge of the series.

If that didn't convince you let me say some pros and cons.
Pros:
+ Lasers! we get to use lasers and some of them are really op.
+ Lunar jumps adds a new and cool feature to the game.
+ Glitched weapons on Claptastic Voyage dlc are so funny.
+ The new vault hunters are totally different from previous borderlands games, used Athena, Jack's double and claptrap (the fragtrap) so far and they all got a great playstyle and are much different to each other.
+ Hell, you can play as Claptrap!!1010!
+ The dlc "Claptastic Voyage" is by far the best dlc from all borderlands games (along with Tiny Tina's assault on dragon's keep imo), i couldn't stop laughing while playing it and the antagonist is just plain awesome.
+ The 2nd run (TVHM) to the campaign is somehow different because it adds new "joke lines" to the game you couldn't expect.
Cons:
- The main story is quite short, larger than Borderlands but shorter than Borderlands 2.
- No pearlescent weapons anymore... Maybe on future dlcs? Who knows...
- Many legendaries are only obtainable by using the "grinder" (a machine you sacrifice items to make new ones) or on vendors (that pretty much will be 1 in a thousand chance).
- Due to those many legendaries being obtainable only from grinder, playing it the legit way (that means not duping/editing like most people do) makes it sometimes too hard to get the legendary you need since you get a random legendary from the kind of weapon you sacrificed (smg, shotgun, etc etc) not a fixed one.
- Forget "chest runs", they're no longer worth farming; I've played above 130 hours atm and just got 1 legendary out of chests so far, probably on 95% of them you'll only get white/blues and the other 4.99% maybe a blue or purple, 0.01% legendaries.
- Only 1 "invencible" raid boss yet and it's actually quite easy to solo (even on UVHM) once you get some decent equipment. Actually the final boss from dlc Claptastic Voyage is much harder than that Invencible.
Totally recommended after all, maybe wait to get it on a sale, 9/10.

endgame crisis always tends to show up just a moments after i loose my most powerful fleets fighting ancient empires. Ironman mode is kind annoying but you can disable it.
gameplay wise, research is wisely done. you don't get a regular tree like always do, you have 3 categories, and have a random 3 technologies (of course, no endgame technologies on start, you need to progress) to choose from.
You can regain technology from destroyed enemy ships, but not magically have 100% working tech from a derelict, but it gives X% of progression in that technology. That helps a lot if normally the technology isn't available for your empire.
next up, you have economy, is fair and simple, however, in the lategame, it seems that you need to focus on energy worlds more than ever, to upkeep your big empire.
military wise, you have different weapons and defence modules, that allow you to meet different enemies with different loadouts. Although, long range weapons are somehow more effective than anything else.
now, we go to politics. you have many political systems to choose from, each having own rules regarding policies your empire allows and bans. you can adjust them manually later on too. Your populace dislikes orbital bombardment that can hurt people? You may ban this! of course this limits your fleet operations, but hey, people ARE happier.
also, politics empire wide are also very developed. forget warmongering through the galaxy 100% of the time. now you need to plan your wars and chip off your enemies little by little, or whole, if you are strong enough. you can also liberate their planets to assimilate them later, to reduce happiness penalties. Many deals and trades to be done as well.
next up, we have species. There is really so many you can't cover them all. you can set them as you like, with special traits, and characteristics, you want them to be fanatical xenophobes? no problem. want them to love all that alien? go ahead. want to make your populace that cannot function properly without slaves? go ahead.
3 warp drive methods, you can play with one enabled, or all 3. but i dont like it when people use different technologies for warp, its harder to catch their fleets.
Now, you need to explore your galaxy, meet special events, find space creatures hostile and neutral alike, scan your planets.
Its much more to this game i've forgot to mention for sure, but its a very nicely done game. I recommend. My hours add up :)

The year is 2387, and the galactic community is on the verge of extinction.
The Prethoryn Scourge came to the Milky Way galaxy in 2368, in isolated pockets which were quickly dealt with by the Outer Rim empires. But everything would change, the main force arrived only 3 months after.
At the beginning, the galaxy united together to fight off the Scourge, but setback after setback, the Scourge pushed deep into the galaxy within the next four years, assimilating all forms of biomass they could find and eradicating any resistance that stood in their way. At first, it was the smaller, weaker empires that went first, the cannon fodder while the major galactic powers consolidated their forces and entrenched their worlds and secured their borders.
But then, the Scourge targeted the two Fallen Empires in the galaxy. The galactic community all sighed in relief, the Scourge would surely be annihilated in mere moments against the powers of the Fallen Empires. But within the next couple of weeks, the Fallen Empires fell silent, with infected ships pouring out from their borders. The Scourge had assimilated the Fallen Empires, and now nothing could stop them. The galaxy was stunned.
The panic set in all across the galaxy, a once unified galaxy, now fractured as Empires began fending for themselves.
As the Scourge advanced, some some species thought they would kill themselves rather than become a twisted horror of the Scourge. Entire Empires were wiped from existence as they nuked themselves into oblivion, committing mass suicide with casualties reaching into the billions.
Over the course of the next 20 years, many Empires would stage a brave final stand at their homeworlds, fighting until the bitter end before being snuffed out like a flame from existence.
During the 2380s, the United Nations of Earth were one of the last remaining empires still militarily capable of fighting the Scourge, but by 2386, the UNE had lost a majority of their colonies to the Scourge, billions dead or transformed into nightmarish horrors.
In 2387, humanity staged their final stand in the Sol System, having lost contact with most of their allies, they accepted the fact they were now alone. The first engagments of the Battle of Sol were small. Small scout fleets entered the system and were quickly destroyed by the remnants of the United Nations Earth Defence Fleet (UNEDF). The first major Scourge fleets were dealt by layers of defence platforms and fortresses built across the entire system, with most of the outer Sol system mined, it was an absolute death trap and would've been considered suicide to assault, but the Scourge had no fear. Within months, the Scourge had broken through the the layers of defensive placements and now directly besieged the worlds of Earth and Mars. The UNEDF was mostly ruin, reduced to a few corvettes, destroyers and cruisers.
The fighting on the surface of Earth and Mars was terrifying. Entire armies annihilated by hordes of the Scourge's abominations. The capital city of Earth, Geneva was lost within hours of the planetary invasion, now reduced to nuclear ash.
The date is November 11th, 2387, Humanity's grand fleet and army continue to fight desperately in their home system, heroically defending their homeworld against the endless onslaught of the Prethoryn Scourge, hoping for an impossible miracle, or die trying.
This, is the galaxy's last stand.

In a spectacular world made entirely of paper, Stick It to the Man provides an opportunity for reliving your childhood dream of slapping stickers on everything. Well, perhaps not everything.
The game opens with Ray, the player character, whose job is testing hard-hats. The symbolism behind Ray’s career is soon apparent when an accident occurs that leaves him with severe head trauma. The moral? Wear a hard-hat on construction sites, literally. While not offering a great deal of difficulty with its platform-style mechanics, Stick It presents gamers with something refreshingly unique in a video game – a comedic look at the tragic effect of a decadent society on the mental health of its members. Ray’s ability to read minds and the obstacles that follow as the result of the accident become a constant, subconscious reminder to always keep your head, i.e. mental health, protected.
When Ray wakes up, he a notices that there is a neon-pink arm sticking out of his head. This chimerical arm is your best friend. The arm gives Ray the ability to read minds and navigate the game space. It also serves to help Ray rip stickers (in traditional puzzle solvers these would be the “items” in your inventory) out of the game world as well as NPC minds, and stick them in different places to solve puzzles. Ray, however, finds the protuberance alarming and sets off to find a way to get rid of it. As no one else can see it but himself, Ray’s first plan is to head to a psychiatrist who, we soon see, needs more help than he does.
The game is divided into ten chapters in which Ray is faced with several obstacles to moving on to the next stage. Ray gets around these hindrances by helping other characters with their troubles – and a colourful cast of oddballs it is who require Ray’s help. From a suicidal taxi driver who wants a new set of teeth to a woman with an abandonment complex who prefers her pets taxidermied, Stick It leaves no allusions to obsessive compulsions or mental ailments untouched. The game does not stop there. The social stigma that accompanies those with mental disorders is also represented by a cast of mental institution staff and law enforcement officials who are constantly chasing Ray and locking up those who are deemed unfit.
Stick It does not suggest slapping stickers on, what are serious problems in real life, as a solution. That would be all too easy. What Stick It does do, is create a turbulent backdrop of a modern city with the imaginative use of art and colour in order to present, and make you think about, a tragic social problem. More importantly, it does so in a game that is packaged with distinct style, charming characters, comedic dialogue and a genuine, if naïve, notion that love will conquer all.
I say play it.

Like the concept, graphics, and music.
I feel like this game needs a fair bit of fine tuning though.
First and worst is that you cannot change the controls. If you like WASD you'll be fine, if you don't (like say you're a lefty or you prefer something else) you're boned. This game is also in dire need of hotkeys as manipulating the inventory with "mouse click on icon, then press use key" is extremely clunky. To me the controls are yuge minus. Being able to set your keybinds is a must.
Save games are broken due to hotfixing. You will lose hours of progress which is a termendous fail.
Multiplayer isn't working properly either, which is a bummer for a title billed as a co-op survival.
The inventory is way too limited for a crafting focused game. Yes you can expand it but it takes a long time and it can be lost.
For a game with an extreme penalty for dying, it also throws some very fast "boom dead" first encounters at you which is highly frustrating. Death penalty is harsh but in a counter-intuitive way. You lose all your skills and building upgrades, but can (potentially) keep all your items. This seems opposite of how it should work and it takes long time to get back what was lost.
The day/night cycle is a pain as well. The days go by fast and you sit twiddling your thumbs with nothing to do while your character sleeps all night. You just cannot do very much before it's time for bed and another 2 minute wait.
Can't recommend right now, needs work.

When I first played this game, the first thing that came to mind was, "Ho-ho-holy s**t!!" Yeah, it's that awesome.... The weapon crafting is literally what sells most people....that or the insane amount of gore, profanity, nudity and craziness. The video previews do actually kinda exaggerate the gameplay, only slightly though.
There are only 4 weapon types: Pulse, Launcher, Beam, and Rifle. Sounds like a few, but wait until you customize your gun. You can literally change every part of your gun from the type of ammo, barrel, sights, and stock. Projectiles and their movements can also be customized. The best part is that you don't have to buy weapon parts with real money, everything is entirely unlockable. The ONE downside is that character customization requires real money purchases. Word to the wise: it is really expensive, don't do it unless you are ready to drop some real cash. The good thing though is that you can get these customizations for free but by randomly picking a Daily Prize which happens every so often after a match. The game modes follow after Call of Duty (I know, I'm starting to compare this to COD.....Blasphemy!). The modes are as follows; Blitz (Domination, pretty much), Extraction, Death Snatchers/Snag (Collecting dog tags after a kill), Jackhammer (Capture the Flag, but the flag is a weapon and every kill boosts the value of the flag), and Annihilation (a ranked match against players). Each mode requires that you and your teammates work together and win. Going commando in this game makes you look like a d****e and will get you killed.
So if you like COD, Team Fortress 2 and Borderlands, then try this game 'cause it takes all of these, puts it in a blender.........and MY GAWD is it beautiful!!

Gmod is one of the few games that players have full freedom.
In sandbox mode, one of two base game modes, the player's given the freedom to run around a map with no real objectives,
instead, they're given the ability to build whatever they feel like with a selection of props and ragdolls, mostly imported from HL2.
If you run out of ideas or just get bored, the steam workshop is filled to the brim with user made content, from new game modes (DarkRP being my personal favorite) to weapon packs, to new maps and prop packs.
In Trouble in Terrorist Town, the only base game mode other than sandbox, players are assigned three teams, detective, innocents, and traitors. Everyone knows what their own team is and who the detectives are, but only the traitors know who each other are. There's two objectives to the game:
Innocents and the detective are tasked with finding, and killing the traitors,
and the traitors are tasked with killing off all of the innocents, and detectives without being killed.
The most popular gamemode to date, DarkRP, offers players the chance to go about their lives as a citizen living in some city. The best thing is though, almost every server is different from the other, with different characters you can play as, different weapons, different game mechanics and maps.
And thats just the three most popular.

of game modes to choose from.

Having played countless hours of Borderlands 1 & 2 on both console and PC, I could not wait to play this edition of Borderlands once it was announced. Having played the game a full 13 hours, I found myself to have completed the game. While I know this game is designed for multiple playthroughs, the Campaign felt far too short for my taste. Additionalyl, the campaign contained none of the awesome boss fights found in previous editions of this series. To be honest, the campaign was neither intriguing nor as funny as previous Borderlands games. It is also important to note that at least 3 of the 13 hours it took my crew and I to complete the game were spent dealing with the many glitches that one encounters while playing this game. For one, the saving system, and checkpoints are abysmal. Also, they somehow managed to make the driving even worse than it was in previous games. Finally, the "moon" enviroment that seemed so amazing before the game came out was nonexistant within this game. All locations seemed to be reskins of previous games, and to make it even worse, reskins of those reskins. The gravity was nowhere near as fun as advertised, as i'd say around 50% of the game is played without the benefits provided by the lack of gravity on the moon. I really wanted to like this game, but quite frankly, I found myself having a very difficult time doing so. Although did indeed manage to pick the game up with the season pass for around $25 bucks during the summer sale, I find myself wishing that I could get a refund. If only I had known that the game would remain largely the same as the first hour, I would have certainly taken advantage of the new steam refunding policy.  Sadly, given the quality of this game, I doubt I will ever be as excited to play a new borderlands again. Deus Ex, which many of you probably know due to the infamous "Bomb" scene, is a true revolutionary by the literal definition. It's a game people seem to respect more than enjoy, but I disagree. It's probably jsut me, but I don't see its age at all, and I still consider to have the best replay value I've ever experienced with a game. Why is that?
One simple word, choice.
Deus Ex isn't a perfect game. Hell, it has more flaws than I can list, but it does what no other game I've played outside of anything Eidos has made, it gives true free choice, no illusions, no cop-outs, no story routes that converge, true freedom. It counters the world of the game. Deus Ex takes place in a dystopic United States, whose government has seized control of the planet. Paranoia plagues this world after terrorists attacked New York and destroyed the Twin Towers and the Statue of Liberty (This game was made in 2000, what a coincidence) and an anti-terrorist organization named UNATCO polices the world against the terrorist organization, the NSF. You are JC Denton, a cyborg recruit for UNATCO. A plague called the Black Death sweeps the globe, killing off the Proletariat, its cure in the hands of a select few in power. Suspicions are raised, questions are asked, paranoia grows. Is the government sacrificing freedom for safety? Where has this plague come from? What is the true intention of UNATCO?
And that's about all I can say without spoiling. The game has enough twists and turns to make even M. Night Shaymalan blush. The game is everything you'd expect from a dystopic sci-fi fiction combined. Everything is thrown into the melting pot of conspiracy: the MIB, Illuminati, the Templars, evil corporations, Area 51, hushed up alien landings, gene-splicing experiments, the debate of man VS cyborg, and self aware AI are all crucial to the plot. The result leaves you as paranoid and confused as any other person living in this time, and the morality of good VS evil become decisively grey.
There is unbound choice and freedom in Deus Ex. Being an RPG that just so happens to be in first person, the game doesn't have a black and white good or evil morality system. Instead, the storyline judges you from the sidelines in secret. The choices you make don't really matter (Some are a tad more advantageous) and none prevent you from unlocking a new skill or getting a new ending. There are an infinite ways to solve a scenario. Facing a boss? You can run away! You can knock them out if you wish (it is entirely possible to beat the game without killing anyone if you try hard enough). Need to break into a building? You can kill everyone and walk in, you can crawl through nearby sewers, you can hack the security to turn on the guards or disable it altogether, the list goes on.
Deus Ex is also something most modern games struggle to be, it's balanced. Throughout the game you can score new Augmentations, cyborg superpowers. Each Aug is a choice between two different play styles. Do you want the Aug that makes your footsteps silent or do you want the one that makes you run faster and jump higher (Go with the 2nd actually, it is so much more beneficial for creative players)? Being an old RPG shooter, EVERYTHING requires skill points, but unlike System Shock 2 (A very similar game) the game doesn't punish you for investing in other skills (Though if you stupid and just fully max Poison Resistance and Swimming then you're ♥♥♥♥ed) because each scenario can be solved in so many ways and each way rewards a different playstyle.
The choices in Deus Ex are some of the hardest I've ever had to make in any game. No, no choice gives you a different gun or anything and they don't affect the game, but there's deep rooted philosophical questions and ideals tied to every choice. The title is derived from "Deus Ex Machina", "God of the Machine", which means that no matter how hopeless a scenario is, something good will come out of it. That being said, I can not think of a more ironic title for a game as this one. Nothing good comes out of Deus Ex, and each dilemma typically involves judging the fate of mass groups or even few individuals between two evils. Do I allow this terminally ill man suspended in stasis to live with the hope that he can one day recover or do I put him out of his misery? It doesn't affect the game at all, but it's still one of the most haunting decisions I've ever made in a vidya.
And that's the genius of Deus Ex, it's a game that sticks. It's story is so massive and so deeply rooted in real life conspiracy and philosophy that it's impossible to decipher in one go. Deus Ex tells a story most films struggle to, it is a sprawling epic that hits hard and never misses. Each little choice feeds into our larger and ever growing fears of our privacy being seized, secret oligarchies, tyranny, anarchy, and forces us ourselves to ask the most important question, "s there any better alternative in a world as ♥♥♥♥ed as ours?"
The struggle of JC is one I will never forget, and the game itself created the core of modern gaming to say the last. 14 years later and games, and even the creators of the game itself, are still struggling to surpass Deus Ex. It still has the best and most established writing I've encountered in a video game while also allowing for free choice and having the storyline mold around the player. The game's penultimate moment is choosing between three possible endings, and it's still the single hardest decision I've ever encountered in gaming. Each one is dark and depressing but a necessary evil in some eyes and all 3 tie in different philosophical views on humanity and the state of the United States, which become more relevant with each passing day.
It is a given that the difficulty curve is beyond ridiculous and it takes a heavy investment to know how to create your own style, but it's well worth it. There's an old saying on ♥♥♥♥♥ and is in fact written in the Rules of the Internet, "Every time you mention Deus Ex someone will re-instlal it". But I find this gross, as I can never imagine uninstalling it in the first place. It has been and will probably always be my favourite video game, and what I consider to be among the very top greatest games ever made. I don't rate games but if I had to it'd probably be 9/10, the difficulty curve is Satanic on a first playthrough and the voice acting (Specifically in Hong Kong) at times is hammy at best. But that adds to the charm to me, but I know it isn't universal.
Also, the soundtrack is beyond Godly,

The Binding of Isaac looks and feels like a flash game; something you could play for free online. It looks like someone had an idea, said "hey, wouldn't this be cool?" and made it.
But if you can get past that, The Binding of Isaac is surprisingly thorough. It's a Roguelike - you die, you start again. You gather items and powerups in order to ramp up your character and clear the dungeon. And boy are there a lot of items; it wasn't until at the very least my fifth playthrough that I started to see repeats at all, and according to the wiki, there are dozens of things left to discover.
That being said, there's no way to see what some of these items actually do before using them. The tarot cards which are usually one-time effects have consistent effects through all playthroughs, but there's so many of them it's hard to remember. There's multitudes of passive collectables you could potentially find which end up helping you create a 'build', and you never know what you'll get (or what they even do, if they require an activation).
Despite finding multitudes of what I thought were "broken OP" items, the difficulty in this game is fairly high, and despite at least twenty attempts, I've only managed to beat the game once. And like any Roguelike game, exploration, while rewarding, is extremely dangerous! Unlike a game such as FTL where you are encouraged to finish every encounter you can in order to build up enough power, Isaac's hard limit on healing items forces players to rethink trying to explore the entire dungeon, and for once, NOT exploring can sometimes be the tactical choice.
The game produces mountains of tough little choices. Do you permanently lower your health for a good item? Which active ability is best to keep, since you can only have one? Do you go through the spiked door where you will take guaranteed damage for a shot at loot? Do you use your key on the chest in front of you, or is there a shop down the road that can help you unload cash?
Unfortunately, these decisions are sometimes uninformed. Again, without a way to see what an item does before picking it up, experimentation is required. This can be painful when you are asked to pay a health container or two before even figuring out what it does, or you activate something that teleports you, or some other unexpected event.
If you can handle the sort of gross nature of the environment, this is a Roguelike which'll keep you busy for a few hours.

The year is 2387, and the galactic community is on the verge of extinction.
The Prethoryn Scourge came to the Milky Way galaxy in 2368, in isolated pockets which were quickly dealt with by the Outer Rim empires. But everything would change, the main force arrived only 3 months after.
At the beginning, the galaxy united together to fight off the Scourge, but setback after setback, the Scourge pushed deep into the galaxy within the next four years, assimilating all forms of biomass they could find and eradicating any resistance that stood in their way. At first, it was the smaller, weaker empires that went first, the cannon fodder while the major galactic powers consolidated their forces and entrenched their worlds and secured their borders.
But then, the Scourge targeted the two Fallen Empires in the galaxy. The galactic community all sighed in relief, the Scourge would surely be annihilated in mere moments against the powers of the Fallen Empires. But within the next couple of weeks, the Fallen Empires fell silent, with infected ships pouring out from their borders. The Scourge had assimilated the Fallen Empires, and now nothing could stop them. The galaxy was stunned.
The panic set in all across the galaxy, a once unified galaxy, now fractured as Empires began fending for themselves.
As the Scourge advanced, some some species thought they would kill themselves rather than become a twisted horror of the Scourge. Entire Empires were wiped from existence as they nuked themselves into oblivion, committing mass suicide with casualties reaching into the billions.
Over the course of the next 20 years, many Empires would stage a brave final stand at their homeworlds, fighting until the bitter end before being snuffed out like a flame from existence.
During the 2380s, the United Nations of Earth were one of the last remaining empires still militarily capable of fighting the Scourge, but by 2386, the UNE had lost a majority of their colonies to the Scourge, billions dead or transformed into nightmarish horrors.
In 2387, humanity staged their final stand in the Sol System, having lost contact with most of their allies, they accepted the fact they were now alone. The first engagments of the Battle of Sol were small. Small scout fleets entered the system and were quickly destroyed by the remnants of the United Nations Earth Defence Fleet (UNEDF). The first major Scourge fleets were dealt by layers of defence platforms and fortresses built across the entire system, with most of the outer Sol system mined, it was an absolute death trap and would've been considered suicide to assault, but the Scourge had no fear. Within months, the Scourge had broken through the the layers of defensive placements and now directly besieged the worlds of Earth and Mars. The UNEDF was mostly ruin, reduced to a few corvettes, destroyers and cruisers.
The fighting on the surface of Earth and Mars was terrifying. Entire armies annihilated by hordes of the Scourge's abominations. The capital city of Earth, Geneva was lost within hours of the planetary invasion, now reduced to nuclear ash.
The date is November 11th, 2387, Humanity's grand fleet and army continue to fight desperately in their home system, heroically defending their homeworld against the endless onslaught of the Prethoryn Scourge, hoping for an impossible miracle, or die trying.
This, is the galaxy's last stand.

My personal favorite in the Total War series. Medieval 2 gains a lot by being set in a time and place that is more or less easily recognizable to westerners.
Assuming you start the game as the default English or French, you'll be mostly battling accross Europe with late game forays into northern Africa, western Russia, and the Middle East. Your units will, for the most part, also be familiar and easily understood. Even a casual student of medieval European history will understand why charging a spear wall with calvary is a bad idea, or why you don't use tight formations to advance into arrow or catapult fire. The game's medieval atmosphere is further boosted by a provocative musical score, accurate sound effects, and nation-themed voice dialogue.
Gamplay in Medieval II, like any Total War game, is dividied between the strategic global campaign map and tactical maps where battles are played out.
The strategic gameplay is solid, and players will be required to juggle tax income, religion, unrest, noble desires, and public health with the logistical demands of supporting your armies between battles. While the game lacks the research tech tree introduced in Empire, technology pacing is present through city building. As you build and upgrade your stables, archery ranges, and barracks you'll gain access to new troop types while smithies, jousting fields, and swordsmen guilds will enhance the equipment and quality of troops.
Tactical gameplay is fantastic with players having strong control over formations, positioning, and abilities. Complexity is added in with morale and stamina mechanics, both of which are easily understood and implemented in a way that makes sense.
The few faults that do exist in the tactical gameplay only emerge when directly comparing the game to more recent Total Wars, like Shogun 2 or Rome 2. Combat and unit cohesion in Medieval 2 can feel more rigid and unresponsive than its successors, but never enough to seriously impede gameplay.

Stellaris will be a good game someday. But as it is, most of the fun comes from modders adding content to what is on its own really just the framework for a much better game waiting to be created. I imagine as the years pass and Paradox, being as DLC happy as they are, release more and more updates and expansions we will eventually see Stellaris blossom into a solid 4X game to rival even the best on the market. But for now it's a glorified sandbox for modders to play in. It reminds me a lot of Paradox's Crusader Kings 2 in this regard, which was also a game that was merely okay upon launch and didn't really come into it's own until many expansions later.
So if you don't mind browsing the workshop to bring out the games potential, certainly pick it up. And then put it away and check back in a few years when Paradox has totally overhauled it via expansion packs and DLC.

Stick it to the Man! is a really humorous game. It's kind of a puzzle-platformer combined with a point-and-click adventure game. I myself am no big fan of P&Cs in general, but still I liked the game.

I found the puzzles to be fair in difficulty. I actually played this 9 months back, so can't recall exactly but I think I managed to complete it without consulting any guides. Or may just once time. Thing is, I am not a P&C gamer so if you are used to playing stuff like that, this shouldn't be a problem.
Length wise, I'd say the game should be around 5 - 7 hours long, depending on how fast you solve the puzzles of course.
I'd say Stick it to the Man! is a one-of-a-kind game. Surely, if you either love humour, or puzzle-platformers or P&Cs (better still if you love two or more of them!), you need to get this game!
