In just a little over 3 years, this decade of gaming will be coming to a close.  Eventually, when we're all just a bunch of nostalgiac old folks looking back at this era, what are we going to remember most?  In a discouraging period of unfinished games and broken promises, which productions will truly stand above the rest, leaving their mark on videogame history?  I've been a gamer as long as I can remember.  I've been waiting for that "perfect game", the one that grabs you by the shoulders and doesn't let go until you've experienced every little ounce of detail the developers so masterfully placed within its frame.  Today, I'm ecstatic to announce that my wait is over.  All the years of sifting through garbage have finally paid off.  ORION: Prelude is the game that I'm taking with me to my deathbed.  Even at surface level, ORION: Prelude is a beautifully crafted masterpiece.  Never before have we encountered such extensive level design that truly leaves the player breathless.  The first time I stomped into the world of ORION: Prelude as the bold, massive Spinosaurus, I was nearly brought to tears.  ORION: Prelude does not care that this decade still has a few years left.  It's fully prepared to present itself in all its prehistoric glory as the best game in recent history.  The intricately crafted but comfortable controls, gorgeous level design, and gripping story leave me yearning for nothing more.  It's all I've ever wanted in a game.

Well, it's a game.
It's F2P, but a lot of the customization options are locked off by money.
There are also direct upgrades you can get, but money users can get them faster with the ingame currency of Blutes. EXP also contributes to that.
Let's go on to the weapon customization itself, which is the big fat load of the game.
There are 5 types of weapons, the boring usual slug kinetic, healing rounds (oh boy i want to be a MEDIC!), buff juice (i want to buff everyone!), tesla which makes anyone who gets affected by it go angst and fire. Fire makes your weapon suck at damage, but it will really annoy the guy on the receiving end. Sniper rifles are underpowered unless you are a quickscoping champion. Then they become decent. But again, the Beam type is for any range, and can snipe them way better. When I'm sniping, I want to deal damage. Not have everyone shoot me at once, which does more damage than one shot from my gun.
I can sum up the rifles in one word. Useless. The "Pulse" type is way better, and it shoots these silly looking stickybombs.
So there are basically a few rifle combos:
Fire Big MG: You just set everyone on fire. Why not use the Beam type, which has way more ammo and isn't a slow reloader. Plus, it actually can shoot at long range.
Sniper Headshots: Use the Beam type again, it's way better as a sniper. You want it to properly pay off, right? The only reason for this is to show off your TF2-like "Ambassador" that only deals 101 damage on a headshot.
Tesla Shotgun: Use rockets. There is no self damage, and it's way easier to aim. Plus, you can make it home in on your enemies.
Bolt-Action Shotgun: Completely worthless. It's a half-arsed rocket that deals 20 more damage if you can aim your every shot. Did I mention that shotguns are useless farther than 3 meters? That's right. They deal no damage past 3 meters.
You can also test your weapons, but you can only test past what you have unlocked, and what you've bought. So if I want to test out how a bolt-action compact narrow shotgun works, I have to buy the Shell Loading attachment, the Scatter attachment, the Aluminum attachment and the wide scatter attachment. But it doesn't matter, because shotguns are inferior to rockets. You can even put attachments on the rocket to give it higher damage, like full auto in a 1/1 clip for some reason.
And when I'm sniping, the optics are Rakurs sights, and you need to pay a lot to get the full 5x scope. The iron sights are worthless too, because you don't get to see the straight center of your screen, just four far away red lines. The Bio-scanner is a straight upgrade to it. Unless you have a color blind problem with green light, you will get to see all enemies and friendlies' health, like thermal vision.
There is also character customization. It reminds me of Battlefield Heroes, because in both games, 99% of the character customization costs money. Since nobody even bothers about the character anyway, you wind up with a game where the world looks exactly the same, as if everyone is a sibling of another. The avatars cost cash too, and nobody will really care anyway.
The problem is, there are only a couple viable weapons, because of the gamemodes. In this, there are four gamemodes, which all have rubbish names. I just want to know what I'm playing. Imagine if I was using the Wii, and a prankster decided to move the boxes all to different areas, and put half in the SD card. That is exactly how these modes feel like.
Death Snatch - aka Kill Confirmed for you BO2 players. Sniping isn't viable here, but it never was.
Extractor - You collect these blutonium things. I don't even know how you get points in this mode, while you assist the collector. Maybe I wouldn't get so confused if it actually told me what the modes are.
Jackhammer - aka Capture the Flag. Except the flag is a one shot kill hammer, which you would think would be balanced because it is only melee, but the range on it is insane. Luckily, the fire rate is low.
Capture Points - It's not named capture points, but the names are so confusing I would have forgotten it anyway.
**It's named Blitz.
Let's talk about the maps and matchmaking system. Well, to put it simply, it's a pain in my butt.
The matchmaking only lets you play two modes. Versus humans or versus bots. There is nothing more after that. The friends system is confusing, because it doesn't take steam friends. You have to ask your friends for their username. You can't join a server from the Join Game button in the friends tab. Although it takes around 1 to 5 minutes to join a match, depending on your luck. And my luck is terrible. I think I speak for everyone when I say this, everyone picks a singular map. That's because there is one map that has you making jumps all over the place, causing you to fall to your death multiple times. Most of the time, people pick based on the mode. The maps are also very counter-intuitive. In that map where you fall to your death, there is a capture point that needs you to make a jump. Countless times I have had my team falling to their death trying to contest the point. It's not helping that the actual room is dark and depressing, so you can't actually see the platform.
Okay, so let's go to actual gameplay. Wait a minute. Why are the spawn points so bad? As it turns out, when the round begins, everyone spawns in the same place. Am I playing a game, or am I in a boxing ring? Then, we have those people healing you. The problem is, the healing bullets look like poison darts, and new players naturally run away from them, and usually running off a cliff because of the level design. Did I mention gravity is screwed up too? You jump pretty high, but then gravity makes you fall exponentially fast. Another reason to screw up your jumps. Also, you throw grenades which are instakills. Luckily, the range on them is pretty small, and 1 out of 6 people know that there are grenades, which makes them a rarity, unlike Contract Wars, where grenades instakill people on all maps even if you see it coming. You can also replace the grenades with stuff like disguises and turrets. Too bad the disguises cost so much to unlock, yet alone buy, and the turrets are super easy to shoot down.
When you win or lose the round, there is a lot of nudity that is not automatically turned off, like watching a character's buttocks or his phallus. No wonder this game is called "Loadout". The phallus is blurred, but that doesn't help.

I totally love the Borderlands series, having invested over 600+ hours and counting in Borderlands 2. I love the artwork, humor, dialogue, quirky characters, and the GUNS. Borderlands 2 was one of the best games I've ever played and will always hold a special place in my heart.
However, this review is not on Borderlands 2, but on Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel. Yes, it has incurred a ton of criticism for not being as large as Borderlands 2, falling short in places, and it retaining most of the gameplay features and mechanics from Borderlands 2. However, this was to be expected. Gearbox Software had repeatedly stated that Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel would not be as large as Borderlands 2 and would be built off of it, being more of an "extended" expansion pack. In addition, the development cycle for the Pre-Sequel was only 2 years, and it would certainly be tough to craft an entirely new game that would wow fans and blow them off their seats at E3.
Despite that, Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel has some flaws that cannot be denied. (Let's go look at the cons first)
1) The unbelievable price tag.
Although this game is certainly good and it would be a great thing to support the devs, I feel like forking out $60 USD is definitely not worth the content. Even worse, if you wanted to grab the Season Pass with all the DLC, the price would be even higher. For a game that doesn't contain that much material and substance as Borderlands 2, I find that unacceptable. I bought the Pre-Sequel + The Season Pass bundle for around $25 and I find that a much better buy that is worth the money. $60 for a main game that lasts you barely 20+ hours (including completion of side missions and the main campaign) is not worth the buckaroos in my opinion.
2) The endgame.
Borderlands 2 had a great endgame with far more replayability than the Pre-Sequel's endgame. In Borderlands 2, even after you've completed the side missions, you still had tons of stuff to do, bosses to farm, and loot to acquire. In the Pre-Sequel, I felt strangely lost and aimless after completing the main campaign and main side missions. There was not much left to do and I wasn't as motivated to go for multiple playthroughs.
With the cons out of the way, let's go into what makes this game stand out from Borderlands 2.
1) Player-characters.
Let's face it. The Pre-Sequel has the best player-characters in the franchise. I had tons of fun experimenting with WIlhelm, Athena, and Nisha, and I've yet to play as the other 3 characters, which is something I look forward to doing. The difference between each character is noticeable and the playstyle you adopt varies with the character you choose. You can't play Wilhelm the way you play Nisha and vice versa. In addition, I love how some of the dialogue differs with the player-character you pick. It's a small touch, but I feel that it adds to the characterization and personality of each player-character, which was something missing from Borderlands 2. In Borderlands 2, I felt like a silent participant of events. Your character doesn't talk much and doesn't give any verbal responses to questions or happenings in the story; but in the Pre-Sequel, you get to see how each individual player-character responds in the same situation. One of the few reasons I went for multiple playthroughs was to experiment with the different playable characters and hear their unique dialogue.
2) Story.
Although the story isn't the most intriguing and engaging one I've experienced as of yet, I felt that while it is shorter than Borderlands 2, it is better in certain aspects. While the story of Borderlands 2 was easy to craft since the Borderlands lore had plenty of area to explore and improvise on, linking the events of Borderlands 2 with another event is something different. I enjoyed seeing how the game portrayed a somewhat heroic and actually likable Jack slowly transforming into the villain he would eventually become in Borderlands 2. This game gives some background information to Borderlands 2 and once you've played this game, you can play Borderlands 2 from a new perspective and view Handsome Jack a little differently.
3) Added features.
I personally loved the addition of lasers, the cyro element, and low-g environments since they added new depth to the game. Lasers are diverse and they are extremely fun to tinker with. The glitch weapons from the Claptastic DLC are also awesome and I would recommend getting that DLC or the Season Pass if you want the whole lot of DLCs and playable characters.
In conclusion, this reskinned Borderlands 2 has its flaws and upsides, and it does balance them out quite evenly. I wouldn't recommend buying this game at its current price of $60, but buy it during the summer or year-end sale and you'll get something worth your money. If the price is low enough, go ahead and the get the Season Pass too. Just as long as you're a fan of the Borderlands series and are not expected something similar to the scale of Borderlands 2, you won't regret obtaining this game.

In my opinion one of the greatest RTS games after Empire: Total War and Warcraft, Medieval II puts you back in Medieval Europe as you fight for dominance over Europe and the Middle East. Use the heavily armoured cavalry of the Holy Roman Empire to trample your foes beneath the dirt. Use England's yeomen to mow down enemies from afar. Go cannon-fodder with the Aztecs (let's face it, you need to be an expert to be able to pull off a victory with them). Backstab your friends. In short, muck around with history and try not to die.

A solid hybrid between the magic of Crusader Kings and the magic of Master of Orion
Stellaris is not Crusader Kings 2 in space. Nor is it a normal 4X game. Like a classic 4x game, you start off with one planet and a small fleet and gradually expand and build up to become an enormous galaxy-spanning empire (assuming you can crush or convert the others who are trying to do the same). But on top of that, Paradox adds some really clever elements that make that journey feel less like a really complex board game and more like you're watching the scope of galactic history unfold. In the time I've played, I've had dozens of little emergent stories play out, from small things like the science officer who became an addict and died investigating a derelict solar sailer to the time I accidentally let all my neighbors form a federation to hold off my expansion, and how I pushed through and conquered them regardless. There's enough depth and reactivity that deciding how to expand or what technologies to research or how to divide your empire into sectors feels like a roleplaying decision as much as a mechanical one. To be sure, the fact that those decisions are divorced from the familial relationships and arcane rules of medieval succession seems to prevent the game from being quite as good as a strategic role-playing story generator as Crusader Kings II. Again, this is not Crusader Kings II in space. But it does have more than enough Paradox magic to make it the most interesting and replayable 4X game I've ever seen.

This game was one of the best adventure games I've ever played. The jokes were close by, each of them funny and punchy. The music was fun - most of it wasn't memorable at all, yet it fit perfectly, but the title song was magic. The art was unique, original, fun, and throughout the game world are little background and foreground jokes that add a bit of spice to an already fantastic looking game. Characters were lively, silly, voiced EXCELLENTLY, their inner thoughts giving way to some very good jokes - it's little homages to gaming were tasty icing to naturally good comedy - that actually handle scat humour with real wit. You learned to love our little protagonist and his head... thing. While the puzzles were strange, they made sense, and the wonderful thing about this game that they were solved simply by curiously peeking into peoples thoughts everywhere you went, and you wouldn't play this game if you didn't want to do that. And, like many other people, the game is actually fun for the brief sections where you run from the guards. Those parts get harder with a proper curve, and are fun, and briefly exhilirating. It was a nice way to counter balance the slow puzzling. And the length? It had a story to tell, and it told it quickly. This kind of game was more like a movie than anything else, and the running gag can only last so long. So, by not making looong pointless areas, they condensed everything to a perfectly proportioned pie of funny and pictures and visual stimuli, with a quick, fun story. I wouldn't want it longer, because everything they did felt good. I didn't feel like I wanted more - was satisfied, and laughing. And that, with good voice acting, art style, jokes, pacing, gameplay, game mechanincs, characters, music, and identity, is really, all you can ask for, isn't it? And this game had all of that in SPADES. LARGE SPADES. SHOVELS, EVEN.

Let me elaborate and strap in, this will be a long one:

(maybe theres a setting for that? i dunno) Interrupting these anims to perform other action is a no go, or it takes too long.
Using an item sometimes take multiple imputs for reasons unknown.
Lack of in game options or key bindings.
Inventory/trade menu got ♥♥♥♥ed hard, It is a scroll down list with multiple filters now, the windows are small which makes it hard to do some management and it takes a long time to do so since you have to scroll up and down to see all the stuff you drag around. Potions now require meditation through separate menu and last shorter time. So if you don't know the game (which you probably don't if you play it for a first time... duuuuh) you can't prepare effectively or they run out mid combat making them pretty much useless. This is a huge dissapointment for me since it was a crucial W1 mechanic.

Character bonuses. This is a particullary ♥♥♥♥ed up part. To get them you have to play the game in certain way and you have to know where they are or when the event happens. I totally love the Borderlands series, having invested over 600+ hours and counting in Borderlands 2. I love the artwork, humor, dialogue, quirky characters, and the GUNS. Borderlands 2 was one of the best games I've ever played and will always hold a special place in my heart.
However, this review is not on Borderlands 2, but on Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel. Yes, it has incurred a ton of criticism for not being as large as Borderlands 2, falling short in places, and it retaining most of the gameplay features and mechanics from Borderlands 2. However, this was to be expected. Gearbox Software had repeatedly stated that Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel would not be as large as Borderlands 2 and would be built off of it, being more of an "extended" expansion pack. In addition, the development cycle for the Pre-Sequel was only 2 years, and it would certainly be tough to craft an entirely new game that would wow fans and blow them off their seats at E3.
Despite that, Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel has some flaws that cannot be denied. (Let's go look at the cons first)
1) The unbelievable price tag.
Although this game is certainly good and it would be a great thing to support the devs, I feel like forking out $60 USD is definitely not worth the content. Even worse, if you wanted to grab the Season Pass with all the DLC, the price would be even higher. For a game that doesn't contain that much material and substance as Borderlands 2, I find that unacceptable. I bought the Pre-Sequel + The Season Pass bundle for around $25 and I find that a much better buy that is worth the money. $60 for a main game that lasts you barely 20+ hours (including completion of side missions and the main campaign) is not worth the buckaroos in my opinion.
2) The endgame.
Borderlands 2 had a great endgame with far more replayability than the Pre-Sequel's endgame. In Borderlands 2, even after you've completed the side missions, you still had tons of stuff to do, bosses to farm, and loot to acquire. In the Pre-Sequel, I felt strangely lost and aimless after completing the main campaign and main side missions. There was not much left to do and I wasn't as motivated to go for multiple playthroughs.
With the cons out of the way, let's go into what makes this game stand out from Borderlands 2.
1) Player-characters.
Let's face it. The Pre-Sequel has the best player-characters in the franchise. I had tons of fun experimenting with WIlhelm, Athena, and Nisha, and I've yet to play as the other 3 characters, which is something I look forward to doing. The difference between each character is noticeable and the playstyle you adopt varies with the character you choose. You can't play Wilhelm the way you play Nisha and vice versa. In addition, I love how some of the dialogue differs with the player-character you pick. It's a small touch, but I feel that it adds to the characterization and personality of each player-character, which was something missing from Borderlands 2. In Borderlands 2, I felt like a silent participant of events. Your character doesn't talk much and doesn't give any verbal responses to questions or happenings in the story; but in the Pre-Sequel, you get to see how each individual player-character responds in the same situation. One of the few reasons I went for multiple playthroughs was to experiment with the different playable characters and hear their unique dialogue.
2) Story.
Although the story isn't the most intriguing and engaging one I've experienced as of yet, I felt that while it is shorter than Borderlands 2, it is better in certain aspects. While the story of Borderlands 2 was easy to craft since the Borderlands lore had plenty of area to explore and improvise on, linking the events of Borderlands 2 with another event is something different. I enjoyed seeing how the game portrayed a somewhat heroic and actually likable Jack slowly transforming into the villain he would eventually become in Borderlands 2. This game gives some background information to Borderlands 2 and once you've played this game, you can play Borderlands 2 from a new perspective and view Handsome Jack a little differently.
3) Added features.
I personally loved the addition of lasers, the cyro element, and low-g environments since they added new depth to the game. Lasers are diverse and they are extremely fun to tinker with. The glitch weapons from the Claptastic DLC are also awesome and I would recommend getting that DLC or the Season Pass if you want the whole lot of DLCs and playable characters.
In conclusion, this reskinned Borderlands 2 has its flaws and upsides, and it does balance them out quite evenly. I wouldn't recommend buying this game at its current price of $60, but buy it during the summer or year-end sale and you'll get something worth your money. If the price is low enough, go ahead and the get the Season Pass too. Just as long as you're a fan of the Borderlands series and are not expected something similar to the scale of Borderlands 2, you won't regret obtaining this game.

As a fan of PDX's previous grand strategies I was slightly disappointed that Stellaris leaned more to 4X than GS, but I had then realised something. They fixed all the problems I had with 4X games. 4X games tended to become too much micro and tedious in the late game because of the amount of endless turns due to your empire/fleet sizes that you knew 100% you'd win every battle with.
It's why I absolutely hate turn-based 4X games now because they always boil down to this. Stellaris takes aspects of GS with combat, it's more about building counters and overall battle strategy than micro managing each decision of a ship, this is not a RTS, and doing that in 4X never made sense to me like in Masters of Orion. It would be impossible to do that in Stellaris because the scale of wars and battles you fight are enormous compared to typical 4X. Not just that, but they made it challenging, every 4X around the end of mid-game you've basically become impossible to stop, where as in Stellaris there are many events that can occur that completely upsets the galactic balance, it keeps a campaign fresh and unpredictable.
The amount of mechanics at play in Stellaris is more rich and deep than any other space 4X, none compare to its depth, and the innovated research/tech system is a welcome changing since in other 4X games you just railroad obvious tech trees and tech/research is very stale in those games - not the case in Stellaris, tech/research is not always the same each game, plus your science ships can find new tech too, it gives that element of sci-fi from Star Trek. I have never seen a 4X game that has the diplomacy depth than Stellaris does, all other 4X games are simply "declare war", "surrender", "give me money". Stellaris fortunately added more depth, but still not the amount you'd expect from a PDX grand strategy like Stellaris.
If you are a 4X fan you'd like Stellaris, if you are a grand strategy fan it's not 100% that, but they're working to make it more of a grand strategy by improving diplomancy to a standard it is in their other games. The developer continuously support and improve their games for years and Stellaris has a bright future.

One of the few games I finished since it's really not that long. :P This one I would put somewhere between item finding games and RPGs. Similar to Zanzarah but also a bit more. Combat is turn based and simple, trying to find weaknesses of enemies and exploiting them. Although on medium difficulty this would often mean you'll have healing potion just sitting in your inventory, on high difficulty it does matter a lot since you have finite number of potions and no vendors. Character progression is nicely done, you can see your character grow and become stronger with every new augment. But also there are too many reskins of the same armour. Tattoos are also not that inventive, mostly modern tribal shapes that don't really fit into the theme. There are often two routes of dealing with some situations, rather simple but ok system since it gives you some way of controlling game progression and changing character interactions. That said, character interactions... They have visible discussion effect, but mostly no visible outcome. They will like you or dislike you and that's about it. And I would put that 'con' under the game's storyline that... (spoiler) sigh... continues. Or to be precise, game is a finished product and I haven't found any bugs or glitches, but it looks like developers had in mind a bit more for for it, but for some reason it was cut short. There are hints of romance system, and characters do express feelings towards a player, but again there's no visible outcome (I don't count text cloud with 'I love you – I love you too' that shows once and doesn't have any impact on the game as a visible outcome). Also the ending is anticlimactic and left me with: "Wait?! Is that it?!". Art during loadings showed a bit detailed vision of the game someone had in mind and a bit more NSFWish, Brian Froud-ish adult and fantastic imagery. And that would be ok, since there aren't that many games like that around. Even the story setup showed a bit larger scope of things than it delivered but the storyline is not bad. It's refreshing and I did found myself immersed in it. Item/character finding quests can be a bit tedious but they were not that complicated and there is a sense of a reward after finishing chapters. Do I recommend it? Yes I do.

Didn't expect much and ended up being pleasantly surprised, there's quite a few good ideas in this game that might make you wish it had been succesful enough to warrant a sequel.
The gimmick of being able to fly in particular is quite pleasant, you know how in rpgs you often have fetch quests or quests where you gotta talk to x or y person? In this game those take just a few seconds simply because you can fly at breakneck speeds from one end of the map to the other, and there's usuallly an elemeny of verticality too so isn't just from one side to the other, but from bottom to top too. Considering how the default in rpg is slowly running around a vast area, faery certainly makes that common and repetitive quest type more fun then usual. It's also nice to enter a new word and familiarize yourself with layout quite fast by just having a little fly over.
The rpg/fighting system is simplistic but having your character's physique change depending on what evolution you pick is a nice touch, along with equipment and gear also having visible changes on your pc. For its length the rpg mechanics and levelups are fun enough.
The inventory system was interesting enough in that other then having 2 tiers of gear, most items are sidegrades rather then upgrades. So a t1 armor will have the same stats as another but one might boost your fire damage, another empower your physical strikes, that kinda thing.
Game is a bit on the short side (finished it in just under 8 hours it seems) but i enjoyed my time with the game and didn't regret my purchase one bit. The real downer is knowing the game did poorly so devs won't be doing any sequels but well, that's life i guess :/
What matters is this game is enjoyable enough on its own, and besides, you don't see people telling others not to play half life 1/2 because 3 will never come out.

In my journey to beat the whole franchise in order, I’m finally ready to jump onto The Witcher 3. But before let me bring some light to this title:
If you managed to finish the 1st one, you’re clearly ready for this. TW2 is smoother, faster and more beautiful. You’ll notice how fighting finally makes sense, and the signs are totally useful (not like in the previous one, where one could simple spam the stun sign for one shooting almost every enemy) and it feels amazing.
+There’s also plenty of choices to take everywhere, much more than in TW1. This feature helps building a custom story which will force you to think about politics, justice and equality. A different perspective is always welcome.
+What’s a Geralt of Rivia’s game without dice poker and fist and fighting?? Yeah boi this title brings this surprisingly addicting games, plus a new one: arm wrestling. When you get bored of main quests just go around and earn some coins rekting scrubs.
+Hunts are here! All kind of monster contracts await your arrival to destroy with everything. Unleash your silver sword and get ready for some mass murdering.
-But remember, this isn’t a sandbox. Every quest you skip will disappear once you complete the main goal of a zone. There’s no turning back, a thing that only The Witcher 3 achieved to add. This adds an extra pressure for completing side quests, and I personally didn’t like it.
-I said combat gets smoother, and it does. However, most of the enemies get pushed when Geralt attacks, so in the vast majority of 1v1 fights you can rush the opponent spamming the fast attack.
HUGE SPOILER V

-The map is basically useless. Maybe you’ll locate a blacksmith and a merchant, but don’t expect to use it as a location tool. It’s terribly designed, but don’t worry: when the moment arrives you may understand. The inventory also is quite chaotic, and it’s hard to get used to it.
-Playing with a controller has some minor issues like not being able to pick which object to gather when looting, so there’s high probability of being overloaded.
Overall, is a title that I enjoyed, but having The Witcher 3 on my mind was hard to focus on it. It did a great improvement compared with the previous game of the franchise, but still has some holes. If you’re a perfectionist there’s a ton of things you can do around, and I’m pretty sure this title suits you. On the other hand, you can also rush only for the story: there’s no way of not enjoying The Witcher 2. So pull yourself together and let’s do this!

Stick it to The Man! is... strange. It's a puzzle platformer that's more of a point-and-click, but neither of those facets of the game aren't super successful.
The main mechanics of Stick it to the Man! are reading people's minds to gather information and manipulating the world by peeling off stickers and placing them on other things to solve problems, all while avoiding government agents out to get you.
The mind reading part is tedious. The voice acting is great, but some characters speak very slowly and by the time you finish reading the subtitiles, the character is only halfway through his or her speech. Dialogue cannot be skipped in pieces or scrolled through, only sped up or skipped entirely.
The puzzles themselves aren't anything special. One of the recurring "puzzles" (if you may call it that) is escaping the agents trying to get you. I didn't enjoy any of these segments. I'm assuming the game expects you to cleverly sneak around the enemies, placing stickers on them to make them fall asleep or distract them. However, this is usually impossible to do as you can't see all the agents on the screen at once and you have only a few seconds before they notice you and start chasing you around. It's much easier to just run to the other side than trying to spend time sticking stickers on people and getting caught.
Stick it to the Man's strongest element is its art style. The character design is amazing as every character looks unique with a different personality. Everything has a cardboard or paper-y texture, but it's different than, say, Paper Mario. It's almost as if the game would be stronger as a cartoon instead of a video game, or maybe if the focus was more on a point-and-click style than a platformer.
Overall, I don't think I can recommend this game as a game, but, if you like art and design, it might be worth it to at least try it.

The first thing I have noticed with this game is it hard. Don't expect a rich in resources game where nothing is a challenge. You are constantly having to gather wood and stone just to be able to sleep. Hunger is also a big challenge and you have to quickly get enough to survive and stay alive.
You will die over and over again, lose your skills points and loose upgrades you have done to any player craftable structures.
There are dangers out in the world that you will have to keep an eye on. Don't go blindly exploring unless you can defend yourself.
Playing with friends brings its own challenges, suddenly you have more mouths to feed so you are constantly having to gather and hunt.
This makes a refreshing change to some survival games that pose no real survival challenges except to watch out for other players.
There is a quest system in the game, but apart from the basic tutorial and a couple of the missions following that I haven't done much of this.
The devs seem to be active in the forums replying to questions and taking suggestions on new content or changes to existing content.
If you are looking for a survival game that is challenging then this is the one for you.

Had to completely delete my initial review, as I've now had a chance to delve deeper into Albion Prelude. The first and most important thing that needs be said: this game NEEDS mods. I recommend XRM at the very least.
This game has an epic scale to it. There are hundreds of ships available, ranging from tiny scouts to immense capital ships. Unfortunately, this game famously suffers from one of the most convoluted interfaces in modern gaming. Mastering Albion Prelude is as much about learning how to navigate through the menus as it is actually playing the game.
This is not a game for casual players. Even after sinking in over 100 hours, I still haven't experienced a fraction of what this game has to offer. It is a formidable title, with a multitude of choice available. One of the biggest problems I've had every time I started a new character in Albion Prelude was deciding what to do after the loading screens had finished.
Well worth a play if you have the time, but bear in mind that the game suffers from a complex interface and little guidance as to where to go or what to do.

Magicka got campaign mode : 12 chapters in which you find items and magicks(special kind of spells) . The story is straightforward - world is in danger and you can save it. NPCs treat you as a fodder and make fun of you until you prove how strong you are with your spells. Also game itself make fun of silent protagonists in general. Devs put a lot of different references in the game so you can go and try to hunt them all .
Combat feels a bit like ARPG , prepare your weapon, point at the enemy and kill it .. but without the enemy droping any valuable loot. And your weapon is mainly your spells... or a melee weapon you pick from a corpse.. or a machine gun.

Spells is pretty much the only reason you would play this game.
You have 2 kinds of spells.
Main one is the combination of 5 elements of your choice and then the secondary is magicks found while playing in which you have to pick set elements to make a different kind of skill that isnt part of the basics.
But lets start with the first one.
You have 10 elements : Water,Fire,Lighting,Earth,Cold,Shield,Arcane,Life,Ice(combination of water + Cold) , Steam ( Fire + Water). You need to have in mind that some elements are opposite to others and they cant coexist in your spell.
Another thing to have in mind: each element got its own form so you have to pick carefuly how to create your spell.
And last but not least you have 2 ways to cast the spell, either on yourself or somewhere on the screen.
Magicks on the other hand got a set elements and form . Some of them affect only specific ... targets like sprint,revive,teleport while others affect the whole screen like Blizzard or Meteor Shower. Now some of the spells are kinda complicated to learn them fast so you might better off writing down somewhere the combination of key presses so you can cast them faster.
Another thing worth noticing is that you can be affected by different elements like you can get wet and when you are wet you cant use lighting and if you try to do so you gonna take dmg. You can be wet, "iced" or set on fire and in order to remove those you need to cast the opposite element on yourself so... have fun !
While Solo play is fun, co-op is even better ... because of the moments "Sorry, I didnt mean to blast you THAT far ."
During co-op there is friendly fire... or more like of insta dead in some cases. While in co-op you can cross beams (ghostbusters anybody?) for stronger effect.. unless you are using opposite elements which lead to someone dying.
Teamwork is a must if you want to deal with enemies faster than usual.
The game over a bunch of boss fights which usually requires you to think about what is the opposite element of the boss itself though often several elements will hurting him, there is one that do more damage than the rest. Also have in mind that part of bosses got 1shot skills so .. be careful !!!
Its quite enjoyable game for what is worth and co-op is one of the funniest I played so far. Though solo play is good I suggest you to go for co-op only.

The good: simple basic gameplay.  Easy to figure out what is your goals are, and what you need to do to accomplish them.

The bad: upgrading your ship is clunky.  You can only upgrade once, and the others you should sell, but you are not told that.... opps. I expect I will get about 12-15 hours total in before I get tired of the game - but for the price I paid that is an excelent deal - and I hope the dev finds it worth wild as well.

Cashtronauts is a game where you get rich and unlock risks, which then give boosts to your income depending on how hard they are. You can collect money by selling ores and Teeth dropped by Raptors, which are enemy ships who are on the hunt for you once you go outside your city barrier. You have limited fuel and ammunition, which can be refilled/restocked, so is your health, however it's not replenishable, so fight wisely! You can carry only so much items at a time, whether it to be teeth or ore, so you have to make many trips from outer space back to your settlement to be as efficient as possible ,you're going to need lucky and hopefully you won't bump into any cops or Raptors trying to kill you. Speaking of cops and murder, don't carry red ores! You will be murdered, it is illegal to carry around. This is a sandbox game, where the only objective is to get as much money as you can in a run, which unlocks more risks once certain money milestones are achieved to get even more money. Some risks give invisibility cloaks to unseen Raptors, other introduce new gameplay mechanics, such as civilian transport ships (murderable, carry lots of money, will get you into police trouble) and generally the more riks the more fun the game is.
It's a sandbox playing area which at early game is a bit difficult to navigate due to not having any minimap of any sort, but easy to pick up the general game. The speed rapidly builds up as you unlock the harder risks, such as sometimes while on low fuel you accidentally shoot a passerby insetad of an enemy. This builds up adrenalin and tense times that will be remembered. This technique leads to many addictions being made along with an actual relationship to the ship you're playing as. It's simple to understand. You get items to sell, you sell them, get rich, restock, repeat. Over, and over, and over. It's fun, knowing your ship can blow up at any time when your about to beat an all time high score.

The game regularly reminded me of the demo disks back when PlayStations were the rockin’ new thing, and I half expected the game to fade to black after a couple of quests and tell me it would be ‘Out this Summer’ in goofy Comic Sans.
Initially, you select from one of three premade characters with predetermined stats, and character-specific talent trees.
There is another female character available by purchasing a DLC pack, but why this hasn’t simply been patched into the base game is beyond me.
The campaign plot is incredibly bland with your typical ‘washed up on a desert island and must escape’ theme. Expect a linear set of quests with little to no interesting objectives in between, a shallow sense of freedom, and an overall repetitive experience.
All quests are fetch-to-receive with objectives and go-to points clearly located on the map, making the entire game for too simplistic to be considered survival at all. There is a visible % completion marker on the menu, and I couldn’t believe how quickly I was progressing through the main campaign whilst seemingly achieving nothing.
You can, of course, skip side quests, but there is so little else to do except mindlessly grind zombies on islands that are far too small, so I would recommend doing them if you do decide to play. I warn you now that they are borderline ridiculous, and if you’re looking for a more serious game you should avoid this completely. Monkeys and talking parrots destroyed whatever little immersion had been built for me and reduced it to zero.
Many dialogue boxes don’t match up with the voice acting. This is more irritating than game breaking but feels as if the voice actors were working on a different script. I could understand if it were worded differently for the purpose of a journal, but it isn’t, and as subtitles, it just looks unprofessional.
[A major annoyance for me is a continuity error with ‘Emily’s quest’ and a sound file. Maybe I’m being picky, but I noticed it, and it bothered me, so I’m mentioning it.]
‘Kovacs Rules’ are scattered around the island providing you with tips as and when they occur in the campaign. The video cutscenes for these tutorials are unskippable and fairly irritating when you find a duplicate. This would have worked a lot better with a large tutorial island and a separate campaign map.
Zombie game Veterans will most likely be disappointed by this amount of hand holding.
The difficulty also varies as you progress and feels uneven. I don’t consider this game-breaking but it is very disjointed with the overall tutorial feel. The combination of the two does not work well.
Certain survival mechanics such as fishing and hunting are largely useless, as edible plants and roots respawn frequently, and water stores are easily located on the map with icons. There is little to no danger of starvation or dehydration, making these trackable needs unnecessary. Rest areas and fire pits for cooking are also marked, dulling the experience further.
Inventory management is awful and very unintuitive. There are far too many steps required to simply move an item around in your backpack. Designated areas for food, weapons and craft mats would have been more sensible.
There are many craftable weapons which is a shame considering all end up feeling rather similar, not to mention certain weapons obliterate enemies with one or two hits. This allows you to cheese all the content and leaves all other weapons largely redundant. I’m looking at you, bladearang.
You are able to dismantle certain craftables, however, so you don’t lose or waste materials if you craft the wrong thing or need the parts for a better item. This I
liked. It’s been more than once that I’ve wasted rare mats and realised I already had three of what I just crafted, in several games.
Graphics are probably the biggest positive; visually the game is very nicely presented, with a decent amount of detail, however, there are no in-game resolution or graphic sliders, and this must be done in a config menu before launch.
As for design, I actually really like the character model movement. There is a little bit of weight with each step you take - an overall sense of a backpack stuffed with items, aching limbs and exhaustion as you trek through swamps, scrub grass and jungle - it’s almost tactile.
On the flip side, enemy design is basic and mostly uninteresting, which is a shame. Just your standard bunch of corpses with different models and occasional movement speed tweaks, with a few behemoths thrown in here and there for good measure.
The day and night cycle is pretty cool, and things do get very tense with the nightfall soundtrack that always put me on edge. It does become rather grating at times, but it certainly lets you know things 'could get ugly' at any moment.
It feels as though development was hastily packed together, and never fully completed but still packaged as a ‘finished game.’ This becomes more apparent when you consider that various standard game content (difficulty and challenge modes) are available as DLC. I did not purchase these and so can’t comment on how well made they are, BUT, all -should- be part of the base game and not individually charged for, especially considering the store price.
More and more commonly now developers appear to choose the drip feed route, and slowly milk players with very small amounts of basic content rather than releasing a complete game, which I don’t agree with. Just do the right thing, patch the game, earn the respect of people you’re creating for (who have paid for your product!) and be a little more passionate
.

Prelude is a FPS where you primarily defend your base against waves of dinosaur enemies. It's not well-explained where you are or why dinosaurs are attacking your base especially the herbivorous ones, like Stegosaurus and Triceratops, but that perhaps misses the point: shooting dinosaurs. This aspect feels pretty solid; big dinosaurs are hard to deal with and can easily kill you, little ones surround you and can take you down in a short period of time. I'll tackle major aspects of the game below instead of a list of pros and cons. If you're looking for deep gameplay, look elsewhere. If you're looking for a little bit of fun, especially with friends, this is well worth your one dollar but perhaps not much more.
Looks solid most of the time, but things get wonky when dinosaurs die, and when playing in 3rd person. Switching weapons results in a very low-quality model for the first second or so. Dino models are solid, character models less so, bot costumes -> horrific. Environment looks good all around, weather effects look great, but hinder visibility in ways that are counterproductive to a FPS.
I've only ever played the standard co-op wave survival game type (with bots and/or friends), but there are other game modes. Each of three classes has a specific ability and set of weapons, which are adequately differentiated. Difficulty scales nicely over the ten waves, and rewards for defeating dinosaurs allows you to purchase weapons, turrets, and/or item upgrades. This all feels pretty good, but the weapons could be slotted into 4/5 categories which feel almost exactly the same. Vehicles (which seem mostly ripped from Halo's assets) are an interesting addition and are fun to use, but somewhat difficult to steer. Dinosaurs' models match their power level neatly, and you'd better be packing top-tier weapons when more than two at a time are nearby. Killing an enemy while downed allows a self-revive in addition to teammates' ability to revive you.
One of my biggest issues with this game is the AI. The dinosaurs will not know what to do if you are outside of their attack range and will waggle back and forth below seemingly forever. Cloaking immediately breaks aggro of ANY dinosaur and seems to prevent re-acquiring you as a target for a few seconds. Teammate AI is even worse. They rarely revive you, fail to efficiently capture points, routinely fail to headshot dinosaurs sitting in front of their face, and have garish joke outfits like sandwich hats and wizard cloaks. Playing with bots is really only worth it for two reasons: they aggro dinosaurs and can for some reason accurately take down dinosaurs flying at/near the game ceiling.
All in All ORION: Prelude is a really good Dinosaur-Action Game!

When I first started looking at this game, I was expecting a point-and-click adventure game, and I am not a massive fan of those. However I was taken by surprise. This is not a point and click adventure game - it's a platformer and a damn good one at that!
There are some really tricky platforming challenges throughout the 9 chapters. You will be swinging and jumping from platform to platform to out run the bad guys. The actual puzzles in the game are more trial and error, there were moments where I was absolutely stuck and couldn't work out what to do next,  and had to result to just spam clicking each object in hope something happened.
Control wise, very simple. I used the Xbox controller and had absolutely no problems at all. I can imagine it would be a little more difficult with keyboard and mouse, but name me a platformer that isn't like that.
The story is actually quite enthralling as well.  I didn't really think that such a simple looking game would have such a fulfilling story.  I couldn't wait to find out how the game ended. There are plenty of little "side stories" which all come with some sort of value to the puzzles as a whole.
The games definite strong point is the humor in the writing. I was laughing throughout the whole playthrough and if you like a good laugh while playing a video game, you will not be disappointed here.

This is an interesting concept for a game. Basically a man named Ray get's hit on the head and brain slug possesses his mind, giving him the ability to read other peoples thoughts and rip them out to convenience himself. The game plays like a fast paced point and click game where you wander through the levels reading minds and taking their thoughts and using the objects taken to get others help you get through each chapter. The humor goes from dark to self aware, but always keeps this upbeat additude that makes  anything dark hilarious. Like a chef who wants to flavor his stew, and requires the tears of a broken heart for flavor, and then pulls a severed human arm out to taste test the stew. You also have to contend with a mysterious organization that wants the brain slug back and the become an obstacle in Ray way and slowly becoming the big threat in the game.
As far as replayablity goes, it's pretty much non-existant save for getting any achivements you haven't gotten. The games charm comes from interacting all the characters and their quirks and once you beat the game, and complete the puzzles  these points become pointless and you can pretty much beat the game in a third of the time in a second playthrough. because of this, the 14.99 price tag seems steep, so i would recommend getting it when it goes on sale. But, either way
it's an enjoyable experience the first go through, and you could always get someone else to playthrough the game and watch.

A joyful, lighthearted experience that will be most appealing to those who are into "frustrating" games such as I am Bread or Surgeon Simulator.
The game does have some subjective issues, the most prominent ones being its length and how it handles difficulty. The game can be completed in roughtly 2-3 hrs. The length may be a bit underwhelming for some although it kept the game from dragging on as i felt it concluded in a somewhat timely manner. Theres collectibles and leaderboard times (including the dev times) to try and go for if you're the competitive or completionist type which will add another few hours to the game. There is also 2 "shorts" that are seperate form the main story that add a bit more time to having a fresh experience. While the length is problematic there is a workshop with fan made levels that will help give you more to do after the main game is completed.
The game's difficulty curve is almost non-existant. you'll go from handling managable tasks to being thrown to something much more complex, with neither of the 2 coming in a specific order. The final sequence in the game amps up the difficulty quite a bit and almost feels like a difficulty spike. With this in mind i'd advise against using a track pad by any means neccessary if using a laptop. Try to get a hold of a mouse or a controller, or prepare to struggle.
This game has a story but its very minimal and only serves to drive the gameplay and scene changes. It follows the life of the main protaginist trying to fit in a world he's fond of being a part of while struggling to keep suspicion at bay. It has almost a Pixar-esque feel and while I admittedly got attached the main character and his family, they do very little to add character to everyone other than octodad, and even he doesnt get much development throughout the game. The lighthearted humor will either be hit or miss depending on who you are but its quite similar to the physical slapstick humor you'll find within the gameplay. I found myself having a quick chuckle along some of the toung-n-cheek dialouge and the absurdity of having Octodad fling his body across a dinner table with no one suspecting a thing.
The game overall is simple and doesnt try to be anything more than it is, which I respect. I reccomend getting this game DURING A SALE. The length makes the price tag a bit too much to ask for, but for what it does provide in its short number of hours is a pleasent experience that you can use to get away from all the serious titles flooding our libraries and enjoy the antics of an 8-armed father trying to avoid destroying public property wherever he goes. No one suspects a thing.

Blowing up monsters, beating numerous side quests, leveling up like crazy, having really awkward conversations with a shaman dude, Iesabel has it all. If only it weren’t a mobile game.
Now, I have nothing against mobile games, or mobile ports, but Iesabel suffers from the common downfalls of an Android and iOS port. While the graphics of the game aren’t terrible, and manage to actually retain their quality throughout the game (which is better than about 75% of games these days), I found myself constantly stuck on walls and bugging through trees. The UI seemed a little too rushed in my opinion, and while it didn’t really clutter my screen, it just didn’t look nice.
What really hurt was the targeting system. Just clicking on an enemy doesn’t always mean your character will attack it, and using abilities require you to be facing in the right direction. It wasn’t unplayable by any means, but it wasn’t fun either.
Okay okay, enough trash talk, lets get to the redeeming qualities.
The game’s got a story. It’s not particularly well written, but the plot is pretty good. There are twists and turns and characters that I actually like. There’s plenty of dialogue and a semblance of world creation. It’s not Diablo III, but I promised myself I wouldn’t compare this game to it.
There are plenty of side quests to do. Unlike other games I won’t mention, side quests are actually needed to go through the game. While this can be annoying at times, I personally enjoyed doing them, as I felt like I was actually a part of the world.

This game materialized in my library one day. I never purchased it, it was just there. I installed it out of boredom and expected the game to be no better than those "X SIMULATOR" games you see here on Steam. I was pleasantly mistaken, because this game, despite being made on an almost non-existent budget, is surprisingly solid. What the game lacks in originality, presentation, and innovation, it makes up for with solid controls, and really great vehicle physics. There's a fair amount of attention to detail here, too. Your car, and every other car in the game as well, can be absolutely smashed into an ugly mess, with way more convincing looking damage than what GTA IV and V have to offer. You can park in front of a train, let it smash your car's front grille in, go flying, land, and not be able to control your car at all because your front wheels are now several feet away racing eachother down the autobahn without you. The gameplay is pretty generic and repetitive, but still solid. You'll get bored eventually, but until then you'll have fun chasing criminals, smashing into everything, and racing. Traffic will move the ♥♥♥♥ out of your way when you turn on your sirens, and when you finally catch up to the bad guys and P.I.T. them into a wall, you'll have to hold them still there for a few seconds in order to "arrest" them. There's things to collect and vehicles to unlock, including an excavator and a massive armored personnel carrier with six wheels, which absolutely smashes everything out of its way including buses and large trucks, even in oncoming traffic. All of the cars are unlicensed rip-offs of real world vehicles, which I'm glad the developers managed to do. It's not a BMW, it's a Semir! They're different! We swear!
All in all, it's a solid game. It's not the best game in the world, but it's definitely not bad either. It's just decent. A 5/10, or I guess 7.5/10 if you go by IGN's rating system. If you like racing and police chase games, and don't mind games with low budgets, pick this one up on sale.

Your basic income is to collect minerals by shooting rocks to pieces, but as the game expands more riskful options become available and the game often puts you in situations where you'll want to chose between safely hauling your cargo back to base or risking it all for a much bigger reward. Overall the concept is basic, but it's well executed. The controls are fluid, though right stick aiming feels a bit inexact – but that could be my controller getting old. Cash accumulation over multiple plays to unlock the Risks that unlock gameplay features with new challenges and bonuses lends the game a rougelike-like-like-like generation/legacy element.

Medieval II Total War is a good game, a fun game. But when put beside it's predecessors, it's also a very small game. I am not talking about size here, or even the scope of the game but more it's advancement over the previous installment. It's that same question you always have to ask yourself every time a franchise you enjoy comes out with a new installment.
Should I get the new one or just replay the old one? In the case of Medieval II the answer is, you might as well go play another campaign in Rome.
While Medieval by itself is a great game that promises hours of entertainment it doesn't really do anything that you couldn't already do in Rome. Most of the new features are minor in nature or simply cosmetic the lack of advancement is instantly noticeable when you realize that Medieval even managed to bring over a few bugs from Rome that were never quite fixed.
For the newcomers to the series, Medieval II Total War is a mix between a real time strategy game and a turn based grand strategy game. The turn based aspect focuses mainly on empire management, improving your cities, raising and moving armies and conducting diplomacy with other factions. This area has traditionally been the weak spot of Total War games and Medieval makes no changes there. The system is clunky and bugged, the AI is completely worthless and the diplomacy might as well not have been included. Anything the grand strategy aspect of Total War tries to do has already been done a thousand times better in pretty much every other grand strategy game.
But then again, you don't buy a Total War game for the cerebral strategy. You buy it for the guts and glory of the the real time battles where armies clash and legion perish all for the hope of victory and while the satisfaction you get from a successful maneuver is still present so is the complete lack of any sort of intelligence on the part of your opponents. As with all other Total War games, the AI is incapable of doing anything beyond the classic attack move with no concern for formation, flanking or skirmishing leading to almost every battle being a cakewalk unless you are terribly outnumbered.
Graphically the series still impress although the uniformity with your units is beginning to show, the sounds work well enough that you are never taken out of the action and the soundtrack is acceptable most of the time.
All in all Medieval II is a good and fun game that you can spend hundreds of hours in easily. Should you buy it still comes down to that same question however. If you have never played a Total War game I would always recommend you get the newest in the series. Medieval II is still an advancement over Rome, albeit a very minor one. If you already own Rome however then there is little new for you here and you would probably be better off saving your money for further down the line when another installment in the series comes along with a more profound leap in mechanics and technology.

I purchased this game expecting a simple turn-based rpg and I was satisfied.
One of the better points of the game was the upgrade system. When you level up, you can choose different skills to pick from, such as healing, fire attacks, physical etc.... This allows you to work around the skills of your allies and keeps you from losing effectiveness when choosing your favorite characters.
The levels themselves are rather small, think "Mario Galaxy", on a bit larger scale. Fortunately the game uses a flying system that allows you to speed around the map quickly and easily, making traveling rather trivial. I really enjoyed this aspect of the game because it allows you to explore the map freely and uncover secret nooks and other such things.
Two of the negative aspects I can think of is the lack of voice acting and the shortness of the game. This game utilizes a text based system, much like any other game, but the lack of voices kinda keeps you from being immersed into the world. I often found myself just clicking through the dialogue because I really didn't get much out of reading what was there. Honestly it was a rather weird mix of story to begin with. You are part of the faery world helping the king solve issues around the kingdom, which includes a "ghost pirate ship" for some reason.
My major complaint would be the shortness of the game. It just suddenly ends. I though it was going to load a new world or start off the second half of the story, but no, the game is just over. For the $3 I paid, I felt like I got my moneys worth. I played the game while listening to podcasts (no voice acting) and had fun with it. Would be interested in seeing the sequel to this game.

Dinos, explosives and robot suits. What's not to love!
[The good]:
- Pretty much everything is balanced. The guns, the creatures, the vehicles. Nothing is overpowered to the point of being gamebreaking.
- Map detail is really pretty. A bit like Rust on low-graphics or Firefall. And the texture models for the dinos are quite realistic.
- Literally just about every weapon and vehicle you could imagine. Sniper rifles, flamethrowers, rocket launchers, smgs of all sizes, heavy MG's, bows, melee weapons, mech suits, tanks, ATV's, assault aircraft. If you can imagine it, this game has it.
- Everything is nicely porportioned. Distances between objectives and timings between waves of dinos are quite fair but not tedious.
- The weather. Probably my favorite thing about the game. Realistic rain is almost impossible to find. The drops actually fog up your visor and add a small but amazing touch.
[The not-so-good]
- Animations. Though the artworks is pretty and all, its not uncommon to see both dino and human models with their limbs contorted at unnatural angles.
- Clipping. Suffice to say, its possible to get stuck inside a dino or a rock.
- Optimization/latency. Random ping spikes ^300+ from a ~80 avg. Random fps drops to <20 previously running at ~50 avg. If you die while inside a creature, after respawning your weapons will sometimes not fire.
- Map design. Looks aren't everything. In terms of playability the 4 maps I played on had fairly dull gameplay. Mostly flat/hill terrain. Little to no high ground for snipers. Too narrow of an area for vehicles to do work, yet too wide for explosives to be effective.
- Hitreg. Even perfectly placed shots will not do damage and shots that really shouldn't hit, do.
- Economy. While the weapons themselves are balanced, the prices really arent. On medium servers, there are ~13 waves of dinos. Assuming you kill 50% of the wave, you're going to spend more than half of the game grinding up to buying some semi-decent weapon other than a starting pistol. (protip, always go for the c9 revolver if you cant afford a good rifle. its a 2 tap headshot and deadly accurate for a reasonable price)
- Drops/loot. Mainly the fact there is none. It'd be nice to have the occasional airdrop of ammo packs or something. Having to rebuy ammo every round is really tedious.
All in all, its a really fun game and worth the price. The devs could do a few things too improve it but as it stands it's totally worth the price.
Full disclosure, I did get the game for free.

I recently finished Witcher 2 and throughouly enjoyed it, but make no mistake here, Witcher 2 is a superb game where it excels, but it fails laughably where it doesn't. It's not as shining a game as people praise it to be.
Pros:
+Story story story. I can't heap enough praise on this for the world, the story here is fantastic. Incredibly engaging and well thought out. This game is worth the price by this merit alone, it's that good
+Sidequests are all incredibly thought out and fleshed out, even the ones that seem token at first glance. From delving into a monster-infested cave to validate the claim of a suspected spy, to confronting a wraith accusing a soldier of murdering her family, it really goes all in. Even a quest chain revolving around an arm wrestling minigame ends up memorable.
+The choices you make actually make a huge impact on the story, the progression, the ending, everything. Most of the important choices actually made me take a step back for a few minutes to think over what I really wanted to do. It truly feels like you're the commanding force in where the story goes, rather then being along for the ride.
Cons:
-This game collapses under the sheer weight of gameplay mechanics it can not fully support given the game's relatively short length. Alchemy, potion drinking before combat, potion toxicity, weight system, subweapons, status resistances, ability mutating, persuasion methods, and a full crafting system are just a few I can list off the top of my head. All of these systems end up either pointless, or downright clunky and obstuse.
-The game operates at an absolutely draconian 24:1 buy/sell ratio for shops. Each shopkeeper sells items for a massive *twenty-four times* its worth. The game's entire economy is completely unworkable, as there is no methods for actually producing the sheer quantities of currency the game expects of you. It's completely broken.
-No fast travel. While, to be fair, the hubs are small and dense, you will be end up doing an annoying amount of backtracking through the same areas regardless. It gets grating.
-The game has over 100 abilities you can sink levels into. The problem is that the max level you can hit is a palty 35. Even focusing all of your possible level ups into one of the skill trees in isolation results in you barely scraping getting each skill leveled up. You will never hit "max strength", not even close to it.
-Killing monsters gives no tangible exp- all your exp gains come from quest completion; often 2-3 levels at a time, even. Since making money is also a winless game as well, this means any nonessential fights are better off just being ignored entirely, especially considering how difficult it is to restore health.
-The game expects you to drink potions before combat, but the game had a hard time telling when you are and are not in combat, as well as letting you know when a good time to potion up would be. The game only lets you drink potions outside of combat as well, a completly unneccessary restriction.
-The ai for friendly npcs you need to follow is atrocious. It is very rare that the ai doesnt randomly stop or get stuck on nothing. It's often easier to just ignore the person you're following and run there yourself, its often that bad.
-There is no clear indication of taking damage. There is a full battle log hidden in the bottom right corner where you would never be able to read it in the heat of battle, but that textbox is the only indication you have of whats going on. Fighting a group of enemies is especially aggravating, as you will often get swiped by the enemies you aren't targeting, taking a large chunk of health without so much as an "ow".
-A very wierd restriction of being unable to change keybindings outside of the main menu. Why is that a thing? No clue.
tl;dr Must buy if you like exceptional plots, avoid if you care anything about game mechanics.

Warning: The game ends on a cliffhanger and unless it makes a lot on Steam, parts 2&3 are probably never coming.
3d computer animated graphics, a flying system that was a lot easier to master than I figured it would be. The game has a lot of features you rarely see in similar computer RPGs, but made sense once I read it was released on consoles originally. Lots of nods to the folklore/myths/fairy tales (and plays, and novels...) of multiple cultures.
Allows non-violent solutions to many problems - the combat is repetitive once you figure out what works on each enemy, but they at least tried to have their own unique battle system allowing strategy - it just makes me wish that they did get to make a sequel where they could build on what they learned from this game about how to do turn-based combat. I'm disappointed all the other games from this studio on Steam are action RPGs, if there were other turn-based games from them I would have picked them up.
It's charming, especially for someone who gets the references, and not a bad way to spend a few afternoons. I prefer games where it's clear the production team actually wanted to be making this game, things with heart instead of focus groups - instead of making something cookie-cutter, they made a flying mechanic so we were actually playing as a flying fairy instead of just doing the lazy 'hovering slightly off the ground' most games do with characters like that. Then there's all the sometimes-literal mythology gags. Sadly, unique games rarely get decent budgets, and this team chose to not skimp on the production values and cut corners (cut the entire flying feature) to free up the money to create more areas and models). Ending on a cliffhanger instead of cutting the Oberon plot and doing something to wrap it up feels more honest than frustrating: no, ending it there would not be a decent ending, and they could hope that by creating demand from a sequel they could get the money for Part II.
They could have made a good but incomplete game, or an incomplete but shoddy one, and I respect them not compromising their desire to make a genuinely good game. Get it on sale, sure, but unless not having a neat resolution genuinely bothers you, I'd recommend picking this up if you enjoy fairy tale/mythology nods and want something charming and unique.

As a fan of PDX's previous grand strategies I was slightly disappointed that Stellaris leaned more to 4X than GS, but I had then realised something. They fixed all the problems I had with 4X games. 4X games tended to become too much micro and tedious in the late game because of the amount of endless turns due to your empire/fleet sizes that you knew 100% you'd win every battle with.
It's why I absolutely hate turn-based 4X games now because they always boil down to this. Stellaris takes aspects of GS with combat, it's more about building counters and overall battle strategy than micro managing each decision of a ship, this is not a RTS, and doing that in 4X never made sense to me like in Masters of Orion. It would be impossible to do that in Stellaris because the scale of wars and battles you fight are enormous compared to typical 4X. Not just that, but they made it challenging, every 4X around the end of mid-game you've basically become impossible to stop, where as in Stellaris there are many events that can occur that completely upsets the galactic balance, it keeps a campaign fresh and unpredictable.
The amount of mechanics at play in Stellaris is more rich and deep than any other space 4X, none compare to its depth, and the innovated research/tech system is a welcome changing since in other 4X games you just railroad obvious tech trees and tech/research is very stale in those games - not the case in Stellaris, tech/research is not always the same each game, plus your science ships can find new tech too, it gives that element of sci-fi from Star Trek. I have never seen a 4X game that has the diplomacy depth than Stellaris does, all other 4X games are simply "declare war", "surrender", "give me money". Stellaris fortunately added more depth, but still not the amount you'd expect from a PDX grand strategy like Stellaris.
If you are a 4X fan you'd like Stellaris, if you are a grand strategy fan it's not 100% that, but they're working to make it more of a grand strategy by improving diplomancy to a standard it is in their other games. The developer continuously support and improve their games for years and Stellaris has a bright future.

TL:DR - great game, with a few minor flaws that may've only been a personal thing. Well worth playing if you like a decent story, good characters (mostly) and where choices matter. Absolutely excellent value for money if played further than just 'running to the end of the game on one path only'.
Likes: the story/writing, characters, the fact that different nations were generally voiced by regional accents (e.g the kaedweni were welsh, redanians were irish and the dwarves were scottish), the fact that none of the 'fetch/kill' quests felt like that - I found I wanted to do them, as opposed to being forced to do them, the multiple endings (16, i believe. I did 4), the way that people/events from the Witcher were mentioned/had a small effect in the Witcher 2, the variety of quests/scenarios, decent voice acting, the replayability, the value for money. A Must-Have at sale price!
Dislikes: the ui - I personally had no end of trouble with the ui, 99% of which involved the inventory and crafting system. I did get the hang of the crafting after a while, but even at the 3rd/4th playthrough I was still losing god knows how many pairs of boots because the default is on the RIGHT on open inventory and on the LEFT for near enough everything else! Upon trying to read the book I've just got, I was dropping boots or swords - and when you drop equipped stuff, it isn't on the floor to be picked up again! There were numerous little nitpicks like this for me with the ui. Also I felt more disconnected from all the info I gathered - on people, places, monsters etc., because it was (slightly buried) far less obtrusive in the menu system.
Neutral: combat - I liked it, but it did feel slightly unwieldy once every now and again. Especially when you were waiting for a counter signal to appear and it didn't, or you didn't have that particular sword equipped because of the dodgy ui! Also the levelling up of skills system - again, I liked it, but I just didn't feel quite so connected with it as I did with the first game.

A compulsive twin stick asteroid-mining rogue-like set in procedurally generated space with a brilliant "risk" system where at the start of the game, you can choose to enable any or all of 10 different scenarios to make the game more difficult in return for a higher percentage of profit.
One risk makes your armour weak so only one hit can be taken. Another adds gold to some asteroids but also adds competition in the form of big mining ships.
The game eases you in gently, the 10 risks are unlocked as you play, letting you add more challenge as you get more confident.
You have a starting area which includes an ammo and fuel shop, a shop to sell minerals to, a place for upgrading your ship parts and a police station which rewards cash-monies for any teeth you bring them as proof of a baddy bashed.
From here, you go out exploring space, blowing up asteroids to find juicy minerals to sell on for profit, searching for cash crates, ship upgrades to beef up your engines and weapons and bad lads who drop teeth and cash on death.
Blasting benign civilian ships into space dust and collecting their cash and hopefully ship upgrade parts will set off a GTA style wanted state where police will chase you around the starting area until it wears off.
The game keeps you on your toes, every time I've gotten cocky or I've started to relax a bit, I've been chinned.
The starting screen shows your own personal high score and the highest score from around the world for that day which spurs you on to have "just one more shot".
This is early access but feels like a complete and polished game already. There are no reasons not to jump into this right now.
60fps, plays great with both pad and keyboard and mouse.
Highly recommended.
The music is also worth a special mention, can't stop bopping in my chair while playing this :D
