Disclosure: I was given a code to receive this game for free from a third party in exchange for providing honest feedback.
Overall, I enjoyed this game for what it is. It is a simple simulation game, but not like many other simulation games. It is compared to GameDev Tycoon, but they are not alike. I found the game to be extremely easy. I have failed at GameDev Tycoon, but I cannot see anyone running out of money in Arcadecraft. Still, I did enjoy my playthrough of it, which took me over three hours to do.
Some of the issues I saw with the game (Yes, some of these are just me being very picky):
1. I do not see much replayability to the game as I would do the same things again. I even achieved five of the six milestones in the first playthrough and would have done the sixth if I had looked at them prior to turning down the first import console.
2. There are not enough employees. I found myself wishing for a second employee to repair broken machines. While some would argue that I may want to sell a machine instead of fixing it, so this should not be automated, this is not the case as the "sale" price of the machine increases by the repair cost when it gets repaired, so either way, I get the same amount of money if I sell it immediately.
3. The one employee that I do get (which I saw more value in than others have), did not empty all coinboxes. There were several that he never emptied (e.g. Mario, I mean Contractor Twins, all of the imports, and several others.) I placed these in various places and left them full, but he never emptied them. Instead, I would see him empty non-full machines. If he were a real employee, I would have had a conversation with him about priorities.
4. POWER OUTAGES! These were just annoying. As I see it, they serve two purposes. One, to make sure that I have not walked away from the game and left it running to just keep making money. Two, to punish me for having a successful arcade that is the largest possible and full of machines. First, games should never punish a player for success. Second, if the purpose is to keep me from walking away, then there are better ways to address this. (I did understand the first one, though, as it happened just when I had the maximum number of machines before needing to increase power. It does not, however, make sense when I am at the highest power level.)
5. There are only 28 or 29 days in February, not 30.
6. I was left wishing for more expansion opportunities. There is space in that room to allow 40 machines without moving to a new space.
7. The pillar in the middle of the room was annoying and blocked the view to part of the room at all times.
Other than these mostly minor issues, I very much enjoyed my playthrough of this game. I would recommend it, and unlike what others have said, I believe that it is worth the $9.99. After all, I pay more to go see a movie which lasts less time and is often less entertaining, so this is a decent price for the amount of entertainment that I have already received even if I never play it again, and I am not saying that I won't!

Either I'm a complete madman or I have some sort of addiction to this game.  Maybe both.
It's true what they say, the game is dead or sure as hell as close to dead as possible, but there's just something that keeps bringing me back from time to time.  No, I did not own the game during a more livelier time of development, the only one that I've ever received my time being here was the last one.  The one that fixed performance, which I was indeed thankful for.
For some reason, I can't help but recommend it.  I wouldn't say it's worth twenty dollars, unless you're easily entertained by something that's consistant of the same thing (shooting your opponent in the brain and his pawns in the brainless heads) or something that can be used to waste time in a humorous or even entertaining manner.
The game itself is simple, mostly comprised of building a base strong enough to protect your brain in a jar, much like a skull would, if a skull could endure bombs and such.  You bring in mindless clones, controlled manually or with basic AI, to defend your base.  This main concept is build upon with multiple gamemodes such as the campaign, in which you assault other bases and try to take over the planet for that sweet gold income.  The major flaw is that this game itself relies a lot on the community, as it'll easily get boring with just the same few factions you're given in the base game, often requiring you to grab mods.  If you don't like repetition, even though it can be amusing at times, or dev abandonment, this probably isn't the game for you.
I have not, however, tried out multiplayer seeing as I'm a loser with no friends in my close area.  If you want a game to hotseat and probably die laughing with a companion as the two of you crab bomb the hell out of eachother, maybe this is for you as well.
Just be sure not to add too many crabs, you might die from hyper-accelerated crab particles or other deadly crab-related radiation.

I got Cortex Command in a Humble Bundle Indie 3 that came with VVVVVV Cogs, And Yet It moves, Atomj Zombie Smasher, and Braid.
And I think I still want my money back.
Cortex Command has an interesting premise,  Physics based combat platforming.  It's just an utter shame the execution completely falls apart from begining to end.
From the main screen the game claims it's fully functional and yet it might have bugs or unbalanced gameplay.   And this game came out in 2012... Uh Oh.
I mean from there we know what we're getting into, unpolished, gameplay "Early Access" type game that never got completed, and... well that's pretty much what it is.  The Tutorial is horrible, difficult and throws a lot at the player before he's ready.  The controls are atrocious.  And while the Physics are nice, it doesn't save a weak game.
The tutorial though... if you set it for the lowest difficulty, and give yourself infinite resources, you still don't get a lot of teaching, but even beyond that, you still get attacked by a strong force.  The game doesn't really teach you how to beat them, but for me, I just teleport in strong enemies.  Oddly enough, half the time I call in resources, the rocket explodes... No reason, just... that's what happens.   Maybe there's an explanation, maybe it's just...  You know what, no, it's just bad gameplay.
And that's the thing, everything about this game comes down to either bad controls, bad gameplay, or unfair gameplay.   I didn't even want to play the campaign after the tutorial because the simple fact is I had no clue what I was doing.  I eventually won a tutorial by heavily abusing the amount of cash I had, and getting a huge force, and somehow getting that force to land, but this game really shouldn't be this much trouble.
In the end, I couldn't play continue playing this game.   Sadly I own this game, but trust me, don't spend money on this game, this is what Early Access was like in 2012.   Go... really play anything and you'll have a better time.  Personally I love Terraria, but that's just a 2d Minecraft game, but it's really fun.  Cortex Command... sigh.. I really do want my money back.

I really wanted to like this game. It looks great, but the gameplay just isn't right. When I started the game, I went through the first tutorial mission. With the camera positioned where I like the view of the car and beyond, the arrow that points which way to go is only a line. This same arrow also gets in the way a lot and I can't see where my objective turned. The UI should never obstruct the gameplay like this.
The vehicle controls felt clunky to me in the first tutorial, so I tried putting the open world to use and drive around to get a better feel for the controls before going any further. This lead to mission pop-ups stopping the game rather frequently in patrol mode. After turning it down several times, I ended up accepting the first mission it offered (forced onto) me, which is to escort a truck that already has 2 escort vehicles that quickly get done away with by a couple SUVs. Instead of taking out the SUVs, as would make sense, the objective is to get beside the truck, so your partner can jump to the truck to drive it... If this truck needed police escort, shouldn't it already have an experienced driver at the wheel? At any rate, I don't know how it works beyond this because whenever I got into position, traffic or barriers were in the way and I had to either crash or fall back.

In the end, it could be a fun game, if there weren't so many things wrong with it. The graphics are great, the basic mechanics are decent, but the actual gameplay, in-game UI, and poor mission parameters ruined it for me. If you want to try the game out, catch it in a bundle with more worthwhile games, or at a really good sale that costs you less than $1.

This game still gives me chills.
Following the story of Issac you escape into the basement and then proceed deeper finding nightmarish things as you go. Using your tears and any items you can geather as weapons you fight your way through these dungeons not sure of what you will have to overcome next. The Binding of Isaac features your classic Zelda dungeon system with map and all but you won't feel like your playing any dungeon crawler you've ever played before. This is because of the unique and fresh ideas Isaac brings to the table. Isaac first of all uses his tears to fight the enemies that emerge from every dark corner. That being said Isaac can find items along the way that can improve how he fights, like increasing his rate of firing tears or increasing their range they travel. You'll be needing these items as you progress down to harder and hard dungeons each ending with a boss battle. As you progress through these dungeons you won't be feeling deja vu anytime soon since the rooms are randomly generated and the creatures are unique and vast in selection making every playthrough feel different from the last. As if this wasn't enough to keep gamers replaying the Binding of Isaac even offers rewards for completing the game a set number of times and even making the game harder at around the 5th playthrough. Through each play through the player can also try to unlock different characters with different abilities allowing for a more strategic gameplay based on what you start with and what you can do.
In summary, the Binding of Isaac isn't fast paced nor will it be forcing you to make hard decisions. It's more like a kind of casual 3rd person shooter as you stroll through dungeons checking each room for treasures. It's certainly not a game that you will be boredom of anytime soon offering a lot of variety and replayability.

The numerous ways to play and the ability to create a species practically from scratch, create a background story for that race, and then play in a galaxy of varying sizes is a breath of fresh air to a percievably stale genre of game. Not only this but you have devs that genuinely care about the success of the game, consistently fixing the game, releasing interesting (yet maybe a little overpriced) DLCs, and an active forum presence. Not to mention the fact that there are hundreds of mods that also add different ways to play the game, or maybe adds buildings, ethics, species, etc. that the community wants, such as the Playable Robots mod or (one of my favorites) the Alpha mod. And with an upcoming update which is adding new FREE content to the game as well as many bug fixes, this game is after my little 4X loving heart. Truly a great game and in my opinion on par with the greats of the 4X genre. If any of this sounds good to you, I heartily recommend buying it for a near endless amount of customizability and just sheer fun.

TL:DR: The game is cut a bit short, but ABSOLUTELY worth the money anyway.
This is hands-down one of the best RPGs I have ever touched. The story can evolve very differently, the characters are well made and have very distinct personas and the art is gorgeus. The mechanics are very simple and easy to learn and the combat resembles the Final Fantasy series alot. Flying is done by looking in the direction you are going and pressing a button (as I used WASD it was W, but you can also use your mouse for this).
The character creation is simple, but gives a lot of possibilities for your characters look. The leveling system and skill gaining (called metamorphosis) also impacts on what your character looks like. As an example: Focusing on fire magic means that your character has dragonfly wings that grow and gain a pattern later on. Tattoos in the face, around your leg and arm signify certain skills as does differet wings, tails, horns, auras and trails. Absolutely loved this.
The story is also good, but is cut short as this is the first part of a non-finished trilogy which I am very sad about. This story had A LOT of potential and could have been amazing when finished. Considering the price it is still worth the money though since the game has a lot of re-playability due to the fact that your actions change the story as you go along and you can play around with skills as well.
The art of the game is also gorgeus. A lot thoughts has gone into the visual aspects and all of the areas are thought through from which faery creatures appear there to the general feel of the area through background music.
The references are on point. Laggy on a potato computer... =P 9/10 on my computer. 10/10 on a better one.

I haven't played this game for long at all but so far I don't like it although my feelings are somewhat mixed.
The best part of the game, and the reason I bought it, is that you play as a faery and can properly fly around. Unfortunately, despite this nice bit of control the game is let down by its combat which takes you away from the flying, go-anywhere feel, and puts you into a dull turn-based combat system.
All that having been said, the game does have its good points. The characters in the game look really original and are distinctly different from each other almost to the point of being caricatures. As you level up in the game you can unlock new spells and when choosing which one to obtain you affect the appearance of your character by changing parts of them; this system makes you much more invested in your character.
Overall I feel like this could have been a great game if only all of the lovely monsters and their animations had been an open part of the game rather than being put into a turn-based combat system that rips you from any immersion. I would also have appreciated a nicer UI and, as many other have mentioned, some voice acting.
I will eventually play through the game some more if only to see some of the things in the screenshots that look so imperssive and will change my review if it gets better.

I gave this game a fighting chance, but in my opinion it's really difficult to enjoy.
It's an adventure/platformer with a huge Little Big Planet feel. You play as a dude who has an alien in his brain, which gives him mind reading powers and, since the alien is basically a stretchy arm, the ability to jump between platforms and grab things like stickers.
There is a lot of dialog, which might not be unusual for an adventure game, but I feel like I'm never really playing the game. I was unexpectedly shuffled out of a level without being able to finish all of the tasks, because there was no indication to which tasks were the important ones. The game is full of strangers in the city that you have to help, as you run from some bad guys trying to catch you because of the alien attached to your brain.
To find out what each stranger needs, you have to read their minds with the sticky arm, which is a really cool, unique feature. But like I said, it slows down the game play so much and a lot of the tasks feel really pointless. The graphics are awesome as well, and I love the paper world feel. But the platforms are easy to jump between, or just frustrating when you've got identical bad guys chasing you so that rather than enjoy the new area you just discovered, you have to instead rush through it to get away.
I really want to love this game, but it's almost impossible. Also, the adventure puzzles are really easy to solve. Once you read everyone's minds, it's really easy to see that you just visit a bunch of places in order and grab the stickers from them and put them elsewhere.
And this one is really just my opinion, but the characters are so overly dramatic and cliche that I find it grating. I realize they're probably like this on purpose, but for a game with more adult themes it's weird how cartoonish and childish the cast is.
If you really want to experience this game, maybe wait for it to go on sale. Who knows? You might really like it. It's not a horrible game, but definitely not one I would recommend to buy at full price.

Only bought it for the story to be honest, as
is one of my favourite series. The game's campaign is divided into 12 chapters, each featuring a particular hero or villain through which you explore the story and beat the crap out of the Regime's forces. In this respect, the story is properly paced and kept me entertained throughout, although it's lighter on the details than the prequel comic series. It is a bit on the short side however, clocking in at around 4 to 5 hours with difficulty set to Very Easy. Like I said, here for the story. Character models are, for the most part, pretty great, with the exception of Wonder Woman and, to some extent, Superman.
At the end of the day though, this is a fighting game so the majority of the content (backgrounds, portraits, skins, etc.) is locked behind X amount of fights with this or that character. Personally, I wish it had been tied to the single player campaign itself, at least some of it. Also, I found the tutorial to be incredibly boring, to the point I decided to quit and just jump into the story. Hopefully,
integrates a more organic tutorial.
I'm not particularly keen on fighting games, so I didn't bother mastering all of the different combos for our heroes. Nevertheless, I did try to learn some of them but failed spectacularly, especially when it came to moves that combined the left stick and the buttons as I rarely made any of those work. What I did make work (sometimes) were the specials and they were really neat, if repetitive. Some variety for the sequel would be nice. I also appreciated that you could use your environment during the fight, even if it is fairly restricted. Still, I am left with the impression that the game has a pretty high learning curve for those not experienced with fighting games like yours truly, further vindicating my decision to set the difficulty to Very Easy. This would not have been a fun ride for me at a higher difficulty. I'm sure I could get better if I threw enough hours of my life at it, but there are simply too many other games I'd rather be playing.
If you're looking for a good brawler, I'd say it's probably not half bad, but I would strongly suggest you check out more specialized reviews. If, like me, you're here for the story, I'd say it's worth a purchase but only at a discount.

I tried to like this game. I tried really, really hard, but I just couldn't.
the skills are horribly thought out, or simply not thought out whatsoever. some skills are so weak compared to others that they lose all value, and crafting skills come at the expense of combat skills. levelling skills beyond their bare minimum also seems to lower the value of those skills, given that the mana cost for the skill increase is much lower than the benefit of levelling the skill. overall, the entire skill system seems as though it was simply thrown in at the last minute, or that it was half completed when the game was considered complete, and so they added a bunch of filler to make it at least seem like there is a worthwhile skill system in it.
gameplay is also horribly broken. if you're playing as the ranged class, it isn't as broken, but it is still broken. horribly broken. the game feels both unresponsive, and poorly designed in the gameplay aspect, especially targetting, in which the player always seems to target the 'closest' mob, regardless of which mob you are clicking on, unless 'manual targetting' or whatever is enabled. manual targetting doesn't completely fix the problem, but it does alleviate it a tiny bit, so that it is (very) slightly more playable.
the item system is also terrible. it, like the skills system, seems as though it was simply thrown in at the last minute, or half completed and thrown in anyway, with some filler included. at least this, however, comes with some explanation, if you find the pane which describe the benefits of the stats. this, much like everything else in the game comes with almost no hint of where to find it, or its' usefulness.
the levels are mediocre, with very basic enemies, and the poor player responsiveness, as well as the terrible targetting system makes the game so trying, that you end up resenting the time you spent trying to like the game.

NieR: Automata has got to be one of the most impressive games that I have played as of late.
First of all, the game looks fantastic. The open world just bleeds with the old world nostalgia of what once was. Sure, most of the buildings are empty, but it's supposed to be. Humanity has been gone for thousands and thousands of years, and what's left has been wrecked by an endless war between androids and machines.
The overgrown city gives you that Last of Us feel, the desert feels endless and the amusement park is creepy as ♥♥♥♥. Enough said.
The only downfalls in my opinion are the randomly low-res textures in some of the objects in the world. Since everything else looks amazing (including the character models) this is particularly jarring, even if they are few and far between.
Which leads me to my next point; not only do the characters look amazing (let's be honest, 2B's butt is pretty fantastic), but they are incredibly likeable. They also do something that a lot of newer games fail to do, and that is character growth. Throughout the game, you see the characters grow and change through their hardships, for better or for worse. And to me, that's something special. Not many games manage to incite emotion in my blackened heart.
And to the final-and biggest-point: replayability.
Upon finishing the first playthrough, I was disappointed. It was short, and not many things was explained to you. I thought, "Damn, I payed $60 for this?"
But then a message popped up, saying that each playthrough was different.
So I said OK, let's do this again.
And wow, it was like playing from a whole new perspective, and it shone a little bit more light in the world.
3rd playthrough, everything was ♥♥♥♥ing different and it just drops you in the middle of the♥♥♥♥♥♥that lead from beating the game the previous time.
You get the idea.
Combat is another gold star for this game. Fighting was fast paced and felt responsive, leaving you feeling like an absolute badass whenever you manage to dodge an attack that otherwise would have rekt you.
The different combat modes were a fun little extra too, switching from the normal 3rd person hack 'n' slash to a 2D side-scroller/platformer to aerial mech bullet hell segments.
It was all fun, although I had two minor complaints. Hacking segments felt like a chore to me, breaking up the action a little bit too much for my liking.
Another complaint is while combat was fun, it felt a bit too easy. This could be because I played on Normal mode, but whenever I played on Hard, everything was taking too long to die, and the fights started to feel like a drag. But this could just be due to my personal skill levels, so I won't put that against the game.
All in all, NieR: Automata was an amazing experience. It had an intruiging story with characters you actually cared about, nice little twists, and all backed by the solid action oriented gameplay experience. It was also surprisingly immersive. Whenever you took too much damage, your audio/visuals would start to get screwey to reflect your injuries, even un your menus. Even the loading screens were masked by an immesrive android boot-up sequence, winning them that extra little brownie point for me.
I would definitely recommend it for those who prefer a darker story, and for those who are fans of 3rd person hack 'n' slash games.
I give this game a solid 9/10. There were just a few things that prevented a perfect score for me, like the random low-res textures, the sometimes grating soundtrack in some areas (most of the soundtrack was amazing btw, just the Forest and Desert areas got on my nerves a little), and for me, the action-breaking hacking sequences.
But overall, those complaints are tiny when compared to what this game did right.
I hope this game sets a good example for future developers.

I'll be honest, my review is of the first few hours of the game and isn't totally fair. But give me a break, the negative reviewers seem to have severe mental deficiencies.
But let's get into some first thoughts, I always have some more technical issues I worked around towards the end:
I had been looking into NieR a lot when I heard this announced. I knew nothing of the series but I've loved Platinum games. They've survived notorious producers and made Metal Gear Rising Revengeance. Yeah go ahead buy that game too, it's awesome.
But NieR is an ambitious game that looks to combine hack n' slash and bullet hell with an over arching RPG style. I was shocked when the first few minutes played more like a touhou game than what I thought it was going to be. But then after that section it feels more like a hack n' slash. Then it's both. Hard to explain because most devs rather throw you in a sleeper RPG, (ahem Todd Howard.)
The game is simply beautiful, it crafted an amazing world with an unforgettable design. As someone who is an extremely (awful) amateur artist I fallen in love with it during it's development. I've also fallen in love with 2B, go ahead smite me.
This brings me to another point, don't worry so much about being talking about 2B's butt or Kotaku crying about an♥♥♥♥♥♥to scare you from this game. This is a typical response to a lot of Japanese games whose dev's have shocking and bigoted desire to have character look pleasing.
Oh yeah, already listened to the OST too. Beautiful stuff.
An I can't ignore technical issues, after all my computer is roughly potato quality now. I have a gaming comp thats a little outdated, I can talk about specs more if you message me but tl;dr it isn't very good. There are fixes to resolution issues, and it never hurts to investigate from your side too. Often times you won't realize it but you messed something up. I don't mean this in an insulting way either, it took me a pathetically long time to realize i could have fixed all my performance issues in a few minutes. But my craptop is still getting 60fps and potato settings still look better than most modern releases.
I've read complaining about a lack of autosave too and making the first mission frustrating... If you can't beat the first mission on at least easy you might have some bigger problems in life. Unfortunately, some games have a difficulty curve and you have to simply "git gud." But you will get better, effort pays off.
My main suggestions are troubleshoot wisely if you have a potato rig and have a controller. I made sure to use as little time as possible getting my game to run before the two hour mark. If your pc can't handle it on low settings and low resolution you might not be able to play it on your current set up. Next, the controller isn't essential because some people like keyboard. You can look up a dash button "fix" for keyboard but I'd advice getting a nice controller. After all, Japan develops for console, thus controller first, and their efforts aren't totally director towards the mouse. Personally, I don't see it being unreasonable for someone who plays video games on his pc to own a controller. Might just be my elitist opinion though.
In closing, this is just some opening thoughts from someone with performance issues who wants to help people in the same spot. Feel free to drop me a line if you need some help with the game performance-wise. I just wanted to share some thoughts because most steam reviews are generally garbage. The port is fine, and I've gotten the game running smoothly.

TL;DR Nier Automata is the best game I've played since The Witcher 3 and it's expansions.
Nier Automata tells a story about very bleak distant future where Earth became a battleground between human-like androids and machines controlled by aliens. Some time before events of the game humanity succumbed to alien invasion and relocated to the moon bases. Now elite android units are sent to the ruined surface to hopefully finally reclaim Earth. If this sounds outright bizarre and silly to you then I assure that there is more than meets the eye and story of Automata becomes much more complex and interesting as you go. It is sad, beautiful and very unpredictable.
Gameplay is another part of Automata that stands out. Developed by people behind Bayonetta and MGR:Revengeance, it is fast, fluid, very responsive and deceptively simple at first glance. Between fast and heavy attacks, weapon switching on the fly, quick dashes and acrobatic dodges you have a lot of options to approach any threat that may come your way. Androids don't use ranged weapons, instead they are aided by robotic drones, with variety of different defensive and offensive functions. You can further customize your character by using performance enhancing chips that allow various buffs and passive abilities. Some chip combinations are borderline overpowered but there are four difficulty options that can be adjusted at any time should you fancy being brutally murdered in one blow. If that wasn't enough, Automata also contains parts that blends several action genres together. It is not uncommon for camera to move from classic third-person action to 2D platformer to top-down twin-stick shooter with bullet-hell elements sometimes even in a single combat scenario.
Automata doesn't have classic New Game + mode. After concluding it (takes about 20-25 hours), you unlock effectively new chapters that flesh out this complex narrative even more. Including 5 main endings, there are 26 different ways to finish this story that vary depending on actions you take during your playthrough.
Any gripes I'd have with Automata would be nitpicks. You could argue about how worldmap is designed, about washed-out color palette, about lack of tutorials for certain mechanics, but I feel that it was all done on purpose. It is rare to play a game with ambitious storytelling, polished combat system, replayability, incredible soundtrack, chunky jRPG elements and open world gameplay that doesn't suck.
I hope to see another Platinum/Yoko Taro collaboration. Highly recommended.

-Is it fun?
*Yes. Yes, it's very fun. The combination of hero abilitys and maps makes this far more than an Overwatch clone, and I've played OW for a year now.
-Is it really different?
*At first I didn't think so, there was just too much similarity between the heros and their abilitys (And their catch phrases, holy hell haha) but after a number of games (Now nearing level 20, with three characters almost mastery 10, and several others mastery 4 or so.) I found out, the differences are what make game uniqe enough to be on it's own terms.
-It's free though?
*Yes it's free, but a number of characters are behind a paywall, you can pay about 20$ US, for all characters, a mount and a few chests to give you cards, cards unlock certain features for abilitys if you equip your character with them, allowing for a different style of gameplay.
-Would I recommend it?
*No. I can't in the least, until they fix three, very very big things, that have been bugging the living hell out of me.
1. The load times/queue system, is unbearable. Horribly unbearable. You can sit in the lobby for around 2 or more minutes waiting for a game, sometimes a LOT longer if it's competitive (I've heard about people waiting 20+ minutes) and the icing on this cake is, when the game goes to begin, ALL PLAYERS HAVE TO CLICK "JOIN" FOR THE GAME TO START.
If they do not, the player who didn't gets a 2 minute or so "Time out" from play matches. Everyone else? They have to wait ALL OVER AGAIN, for another set of people wanting to play. And this happens, ALL THE TIME. Multiple times, before you may get a game. I've had it happen around 5 or so times before I was able to play one match. Highly, highly annoying.
(A "fix" for this, might be to merge servers at certain times, be a bit looser on the games match making at times there are less people on, or just start the game even without players, and allow people to play a free for allish style battle until another player is found.)
2. Character hitboxes. Ohhhh boy. This one hurts me. Characters who are small, like the willo character, her hitbox, does not fit her tiny frame, and snipers and other shooters alike have NO problem hitting her, even when she's behind cover, by aiming above her. I wish I had some of the time's I've been killed due to them hitting the air two feet away from me.
On a side note, that may pretain to this, certain abilitys on characters that allow them to escape, again, like willos flutter, allow people to seemingly shoot the spot you were at, and still get the kill, even though they never hit you. It may be a bug, or it may be that they are hitting your gigantic hitbox as you swoosh away.
(A fix for this? Fix the hitboxes. Maybe the net code. I hear a lot of people say it's the pings fault. Due to my next complaint, it may be.)
3. The biggest one of ALL. And by far the most hair wrenching. The kicks from games. It doesn't matter or seemingly have any regard as to when it will happen.   You just wait five minutes to get into a match, and everyones got their characters, everyones picking what cosmetics to use, and 5, 4, 3 - KICK. Back to the lobby with you.
You just got that sweet play of the game, you are sure, sweeping their entire team with one big blast, and then BOOP - Kick.    Your entire team is down to the wire, you're the healer, you're restoring  health left and right, you need just one more small push, you go into heal the tank as he nears his limit and - KICK.
You get the point. I'm pretty sure it has nothing to do with my own internet. I pay for 100 MBPS, and live in a pretty suburban area, with no kicks on any other game, and rarely lag. The game just seems to punt everyone in that match out, like it never existed.
(Fix? No idea. Better servers? Better netcode? Better something)
With these three huge faults that just seem unfair and infuriating, I can't say I'd recommend the game to anyone just yet. It certainly is fun, and I'd love to play with friends, but I wouldn't put the constant kicks, hitbox kills and tremendous amount of time it takes to even get in a game, on their shoulders for my sake.
Also other notes:
-A lot of heros are behind a paywall.
-Costumes behind a paywall (Understandable)
- ALL costumes are behind a paywall (With a few having the option of using in-game currency to be bought, kind of understandable)
- MASTERY OUTFITS ARE LOCKED BEHIND A PAYWALL (Not understandable, AT ALL, why even require them to have a level limit, if I have to pay for them anyway?)
- Cards/Loadout (They change the way your character plays, that can make that healer and annoying heal denial/stunner, or turn that healer into a super tanky ultra healer, or anything inbetween, etc)
- The game has mounts (Mounts are given to you upon spawning in/after death as well. Some maps are very big, and require a way to get around quickly, thus mounts. Getting hit knocks you off a mount. A good stratagy is for a flanker to knock enemys off horses at their spawn, to give your team time to push)
- Mounts are locked behind a paywall. (Other than the default mount. Payed mounts have no special attributes other than look)
- Competitive mode (You need several characters at mastery 4 to get access)
- At player level 15 you get access to in-progress maps (You can give feed back/a short survey on the map after you have played)

The premise of this game is garbage.  I can see the appeal as a funny idea, but there isn't enough here to make that idea a worthwhile game.  You're an octopus pretending to be human and trying not to draw attention to yourself and make people notice your secret.  Somehow you get married and have 2 kids... I have no idea how that makes sense.  The physics alone boggles the mind!
The controls of this game remind me of I Am Bread, which is to say they aren't good.  You use 4 inputs to control Octodad's 4 exposed limbs, resulting in a rag-doll motion that never succeeds at doing what you want.
The game is interesting for about 30 minutes, after which point you realize that you're literally doing the same thing over and over again with the garbage controls.  Every task the game gives you involves walking to a specific location, navigating your limbs to grab one specific object, and then moving that object to a specific location.  The settings you do these tasks in are the only aspect of the game that ever changes, and that's nowhere close to enough creative input to make this game worth finishing.
Do yourself a favor and just watch a funny YouTuber play the game and keep you entertained.  The commentary will be vastly better than the frustration you will personally feel while flailing around in Octodad.

I guess as a player that gives me something to do and keep an eye on, but I would expect my highly paid staff to do their job and empty all machines. I played through the game completely twice and easily managed to get all achievements, also being a little OCD on second playthrough, getting both sets of triology games and keeping the starting 5 machines to the end to see if they would go super classic or anything, which they did not. I had to put serious thought into whether or not I would recommend this game. Just giving it a thumbs up or down doesn't seem fair. It's a very simple RPG and not the most fun game ever, but there are some things the studio got right.
To give you some basis of my review... I purchased the game while I was sick with a cold and looking for something cheap and fast I could play casually while I was stuck in bed.  I finished about half of the game, recovered from sickiness, then forgot I even had it on my computer until I was upgrading the system. I guess the fact I forgot Faery was there is a telling sign that this game isn't very exciting.
You start off in Legends of Avalon as a male or female fairy/elf, customised to your liking, and with the usual bout of gameplay amnesia. Apparently your character decided to become comatose for some amount of years because the lands of Avalon were getting too weird. Long story short, your job is to go around different aspects of the faery plane and figure out why the magic is supposedly all janky and the inhabitants are acting crazy/aloof/lazy. Let the fetch quests begin!
Here is what the game does right...
1. Flying around is superbly easy and actually fun. You will spend 100% of your time flying in this game. Controls are simple with mouse and keyboard or a controller. A good portion of my logged hours probably come from me just zooming around and testing the borders of each level's space. The scaling of your character and its environment is also nice. You really do feel small when you're flying around or talking to the bigger more humanoid characters.
2. Upgrading your character actually changes its physical appearance. This ranges from changes in armour to actual body modifications like horns, wings, tails, tattoos, etc... Each addition adds perks or changes your fighting style and/or element. It's really great seeing how your character changes through the game.
3. Traditional faery lore. You can see that there was some thought put into how the game world would be constructed and it definitely borrows from the older legends of fae.
4. How you respond to other characters changes the game dynamics. Not terribly, you won't be locked out of any quests or not be able to finish the main mission. The game is still very linear and definitely nothing at Mass Effect level moral decisions, but your actions do affect the style of your gameplay. For example, if you say something which conflicts with one of your followers, they'll begin to dislike you. If you're awesome to them, they'll give you gifts of armour or weapons. Fetch quests often give you the ability to choose between combative solutions and conversation based solutions. Sometimes you can get out of going through a horde of tedious turn-based battles if you opt to assemble a tool or talk to a certain character the right way.
5. Battles are turn-based, so you might like or hate that. However, you can avoid many battles simply by flying over them. Most of the time, unless it's a boss or necessity to get to a new area, you choose when you want to fight. Of course, if you ignore too many battles, your level will be too low to take on a boss. Most of the battles are pretty simple and require only a minimum amount of strategy. This might be good if you have no experience at this type of gameplay. There's no blood or gore (enemies either fade away or slump over when defeated), quite low on the violence level, so this might be good if you're looking for something more kid friendly.
Here is where the game has problems...
1. The level design is quite boring. The textures are good and everything is well modelled, blah blah blah... But it's all just rather dull looking. If it wasn't for the characters, you could pluck the bulk of the landscapes out of any other game. With the exception of maybe the scarab level, it's just not very "magical" feeling. Even though the levels appear huge because you're a small fairy, the levels are tiny and there are tons of invisible walls. I imagine it's akin to the feeling a mouse would have being locked in a living room. If you're looking for an open word type game, this is definitely not it! The game world starts feeling small very quickly.
2. Fetch quests! Not necessarily a bad thing. Everyone goes into an RPG game knowing that they're about to do fetch quests. But these quests just feel kinda empty most of the time. You can't interact with objects in the environment and there are practically no FMVs. Collecting a special item (and by collecting I mean flying over to it then seeing it disappear) and returning it to the correct NPC just makes your screen fade to black then open up to you in another dialog screen. It's very unfulfilling. At one point... !!!SPOILER!!! ... You're tasked with helping a baby dragon hatch, but you never see the process at all. The dragon just appears next to you as a follower.
3. On the note of NPC's, get ready to see a lot of the same models over and over again with just different clothing. Even their mannerisms are the same. Dialog is done through text only, there is no voice acting. If you're an old school gamer, you won't so much mind the lack of voices, There are plenty of games which do just fine without having that element of sound. But it is very awkward watching the characters mouth every word of the subtitles. Faery feels more like a game meant to have voice acting, but the studio might have run out of money to finish that part.
4. This is the first and last game of the series. You get the four small levels that come with Legends of Avalon and that's it. The story was left open because of the intention of this being a series of Xbox Live titles. Very anti-climatic. Faery was produced by a small studio and it didn't make them enough money to continue the series. You can tell that the team has talent because of the awesome looking concept art during loading screens and the attention to lore. It would be nice to see this game redone by a larger studio with more funds and time. Seems like lost potential for a game world which could have been much more immersive and interesting.
Would I recommend this game? Yes and no. If it's only £5/$5, then yes. It did entertain me briefly so I don't feel like I lost money. I got a stable, playable game for the same amount of money as a sandwich and chips. Do you need to go out of your way to play this game? No.  You won't be missing anything important.

This is the smashiest first person shooter. Those who know me personally will understand that this is probably the highest praise I can give. I just gave this game a try since it pretends to be an "open-world driving game", and that got me curious. Alas, after just over one hour of trying to come to grips with it, I have to admit I give up on it. It's not an awfully bad game, far from it. The graphics are more than decent, considering it's a game from 2009. On the highest settings (not that there are that many settings...), the cars look nice and the environment is more or less ok - bar the awful pop-ups in front of you of several objects. The driving model is fair, nothing special, but when played with a controller it feels fine. The music, as so often with this type of game, is all too repetitive for my taste so I switched it almost immediately off. There are some possibilities for adding your own music tracks to the game, so for those interested in this, the game offers something extra.
The bad thing about the game is the "gameplay" - actually, there hardly is any, at least I did not find much of it. There are several modes: a free patrol mode, in which I searched in vain for anything to-do other than driving through a generic-looking city with roadsigns that kept saying "Köln 2300m" all the time. You can do a normal city race, which is fine for just a quick try, but the "story mode" is what lets the game down. The various objectives are simply hilariously difficult - most of the time one has to damage an opponent to 100%, but whenever he gets further away than 200m, the mission has to be restarted. Since the AI miraculously can teleport itself down bridges or through walls, this got me first staring in disbelief and then lauging out loud. I guess this game can be fun to some, but to me it's a no-go: there are simply too many other good games out there, including large-scale racing games, to put any more time into this.
Overall score: 3.5/10

Meh:

I give this game 3/5 stars.
First the good: Do you ever dream of flying? I do sometimes, and this game has captured something of the feel of the weightlessness and mobility of that dream. I could play for at least a few hours enjoying the twisting and turning of being a leaf on the wind.
It also has a pirate ship sequence that can't help but make me feel like I'm Tinkerbell in a Peter Pan play. And that is simply fun.
I also think the music is soothing, just the kind of thing I want to listen to when I'm flying around.
The leveling system is unique. You gain various faery attributes as you level up, choosing between different sets of wings or tattoos that give you different abilities. It was entertaining.
Now to the middling qualities of the game:
In terms of RPG plotting, this is pretty much baby's first adventure. If you're looking for something to get younger children into gaming, this might do it. There's not anything really scarey, no one is permanently killed even when they're defeated in battle, and the game usually offers two solutions: one that is peaceful and one that is a straight up battle. It also provides a scenario in which there are no good options. You will either need to fight or lie to get what you want. So I give it some credit for a level of moral complexity.
It was not a difficult game. I think I used a light healing potion 5 times total. There's no way to adjust the difficulty.
It uses a combat system very similar to JRPGs.
The bad:
It was unvoiced.
It required a lot of wandering around talking to people asking if they had heard of any of the parts of the solution to the puzzles. If it were a walking game, I'd call it a walking simulator. Fortunately, the flying improves this situation.
It's short. Though I give them credit that the $9.99 price is fair for what you get, and if you wait for a Steam Sale you can usually get a bargain at under $3.00.
In the end, I'm glad I bought it. It was enjoyable, and I'll probably play it again some time because of the flying and the leveling system. But if you're looking for something serious or challenging, look elsewhere.

I will be editing this review as I play with my thoughts over time. I'm doing this mainly because at the time of writing, I can't wait to review this game.
This is already starting out better than the other games did, and I loved both of them immensely. A good part of that quick start is the Action Skill available at level 3, rather than the usual level 5, meaning you get into the real heart of the game a lot more quickly. I chose Athena, with my friends being Nisha and Claptrap. Athena's action skill, Kinetic Aspis, makes for a very interesting weapon. It is a shield that blocks and absorbs attacks, then is thrown at enemies to deal damage. It deals more damage based on how much it absorbs. My friends like their own action skills as well. vaulthunter.exe is perfect for someone who wants something different every time, and Showdown is a good skill to have if you don't want to be precise all the time. But I think all of our favorite parts about the action skills is their quick reset time. Athena's and Nisha's abilities have a base cooldown of only 16 seconds (!!!). Compare that to the 42-second cooldown that Axton (my main in BL2) starts with, which can only be lowered to 21 with the best possible class mods and investment in a specific skill. As a result, the game feels a lot more fast-paced and fun. (Wilhelm is the exception with his own 42-second cooldown, but none of us have played him, and his action skill could be fun to make up for it.)
One of the other fun features is lowered gravity (note: the lower gravity does not apply to vehicles, as myself and one friend figured out). It's a lot of fun to be able to enjoy "parkour" again. In the first game, exploration was heavily encouraged by free loot at the top of the tallest buildings and most inconspicuous locations. The second game had very little benefit to exploring beyond easter eggs. Don't get me wrong, I enjoyed finding the Minecraft section and experiencing the double rainbow with Claptrap, but loot lasts longer than laughs (there's no reason we can't have both, right?).
The dialogue is more interactive than ever before. The characters respond and interact differently based on who's present. At the very start of the game, Claptrap begs the players to get moving. At the drop pod, Jack flirts with Nisha. Once you hit the moon Janey flirts with Athena. The characters never interacted like this before, and it makes it seem much more like you're playing people rather than robots (except Claptrap, who IS a robot. Let's ignore that for now).
Currently, this game seems to be well worth the money.
Started a game as Wilhelm. I think I prefer him to Axton already. Wolf isn't exactly the most helpful, automatically killing the small enemies I need to revive myself during boss battles, but it's better than a stationary turret that can't follow the boss if he goes around a corner. Saint is proving to be useful. He recovers my health and draws enemy fire, so no ill effects there. Other than that, so far there isn't much else to say. Until I get the perk that lets me fire while running, I don't rally have much else to add.
Started another single-player game with Claptrap this time. I'm not certain how I feel about him yet. I'm level 9, which is normally the time rolls of the dice start to become more minor (until TVHM). The skilltree I went down (the least useless for single-player) makes RNG more important than ever. Random "subroutines" make specific weapon types more powerful and the rest less powerful, or increase shields/health and make ALL weapons less poweful. The subroutine chosen is random, and changes every 100 ticks. It's a great fit for Claptrap, since his Action Skill is also chosen by RNG (as well as certain criteria). My favorite part so far has been beating Deadlift in less than 5 seconds when I had The Funzerker skill active, the Vault Hunter Loyalty shotgun, and the Shotgun subroutine. He stood no chance that attempt. My last 2 attempts were not so lucky, with Blightbot senselessly flying through walls, doing next to no damage, followed by Miniontrap being accidentally thrown to the most useless and secluded corner (Thanks, jump pad). But that third time, he didn't stand a chance! Jokes aside, that is a perfect example of how you can expect the whole game to go as Claptrap. Random numbers can make you go from useless to overpowered in the span of 10 seconds. Ridiculously dependent on numbers. That said, it was a ton of fun and I want to do more.

So far, I have completed normal mode with two characters (Nisha and Claptrap) and played a little bit of TVHM.
As others have said, this feels like an extension of Borderlands 2 (but inferior to it). Combat, aesthetics, user interface remained largely the same. Naturally, it makes sense to focus on the differences between the two.
The main aspects of TPS that I thought were improvements were more interesting skill trees (more variation in progression of skills and between characters themselves) and likelier legendary drops (I have found quite a few legendaries just in vending machines throughout normal mode). Laser weapons were a fun addition. I also liked that the playable characters partake in dialogue with their own unique lines.
There were some things that became non-issues. I wasn't a big fan of the varying levels of gravity in different areas at first, but eventually got used to it. Similarly, I didn't like the oz mods at first, but ultimately, they didn't detract from the experience. If anything, they add another side to combat compared to relics, which merely provided stat boosts.
Then there were areas that definitely felt sub-par to BL2. The writing was not nearly as funny or entertaining (though I'm finding that TVHM dialogue is funnier, with Tiny Tina and Brick commentating over the story). Map design is really confusing for anyone on their first playthrough. In addition to excessively vast landscapes and multiple floors, there are often no clear paths or landable platforms. Consequently, you may have to guess where you need to make a leap of faith (usually to your death). Side missions were often tedious, with a lot of running around, and the tedium was usually compounded by the overly expansive map design. Most NPCs were not very interesting at all, and some were just downright annoying.
Overall, the reason TPS got such a negative response was because the fans were expecting a game on the level of BL2. On its own, it was a decent game. Its flaws don't discount it entirely, but the disappointment is understandable.
UPDATE: My original review of the game still stands, but since then, I have bought the Season Pass. I've now played through at least normal mode with almost all of the characters. With their variety of skills, the characters, including the DLC, are still fun to play. I especially enjoyed the Claptrap DLC campaign and consider it one of the best campaigns across the series. In fact, I enjoyed it more than the main campaign of TPS, as it featured a much more interesting setting, sensible maps, and improved dialogue. Overall, the main story of TPS offers some welcome improvements over BL2, kept many of the mechanics that made me a fan of the Borderlands series, but didn't really build its world and setting as well as its predecessor. Its one DLC campaign showed a glimmer of its former glory, so it makes me hopeful that the Gearbox will take into account the shortcomings of this game to deliver the best sequel they can.

*Yes. Yes, it's very fun. The combination of hero abilitys and maps makes this far more than an Overwatch clone, and I've played OW for a year now.
-Is it really different?
*At first I didn't think so, there was just too much similarity between the heros and their abilitys (And their catch phrases, holy hell haha) but after a number of games (Now nearing level 20, with three characters almost mastery 10, and several others mastery 4 or so.) I found out, the differences are what make game uniqe enough to be on it's own terms.
-It's free though?
*Yes it's free, but a number of characters are behind a paywall, you can pay about 20$ US, for all characters, a mount and a few chests to give you cards, cards unlock certain features for abilitys if you equip your character with them, allowing for a different style of gameplay.
-Would I recommend it?
*No. I can't in the least, until they fix three, very very big things, that have been bugging the living hell out of me.
1. The load times/queue system, is unbearable. Horribly unbearable. You can sit in the lobby for around 2 or more minutes waiting for a game, sometimes a LOT longer if it's competitive (I've heard about people waiting 20+ minutes) and the icing on this cake is, when the game goes to begin, ALL PLAYERS HAVE TO CLICK "JOIN" FOR THE GAME TO START.
If they do not, the player who didn't gets a 2 minute or so "Time out" from play matches. Everyone else? They have to wait ALL OVER AGAIN, for another set of people wanting to play. And this happens, ALL THE TIME. Multiple times, before you may get a game. I've had it happen around 5 or so times before I was able to play one match. Highly, highly annoying.
(A "fix" for this, might be to merge servers at certain times, be a bit looser on the games match making at times there are less people on, or just start the game even without players, and allow people to play a free for allish style battle until another player is found.)
2. Character hitboxes. Ohhhh boy. This one hurts me. Characters who are small, like the willo character, her hitbox, does not fit her tiny frame, and snipers and other shooters alike have NO problem hitting her, even when she's behind cover, by aiming above her. I wish I had some of the time's I've been killed due to them hitting the air two feet away from me.
On a side note, that may pretain to this, certain abilitys on characters that allow them to escape, again, like willos flutter, allow people to seemingly shoot the spot you were at, and still get the kill, even though they never hit you. It may be a bug, or it may be that they are hitting your gigantic hitbox as you swoosh away.
(A fix for this? Fix the hitboxes. Maybe the net code. I hear a lot of people say it's the pings fault. Due to my next complaint, it may be.)
3. The biggest one of ALL. And by far the most hair wrenching. The kicks from games. It doesn't matter or seemingly have any regard as to when it will happen.   You just wait five minutes to get into a match, and everyones got their characters, everyones picking what cosmetics to use, and 5, 4, 3 - KICK. Back to the lobby with you.
You just got that sweet play of the game, you are sure, sweeping their entire team with one big blast, and then BOOP - Kick.    Your entire team is down to the wire, you're the healer, you're restoring  health left and right, you need just one more small push, you go into heal the tank as he nears his limit and - KICK.
You get the point. I'm pretty sure it has nothing to do with my own internet. I pay for 100 MBPS, and live in a pretty suburban area, with no kicks on any other game, and rarely lag. The game just seems to punt everyone in that match out, like it never existed.
(Fix? No idea. Better servers? Better netcode? Better something)
With these three huge faults that just seem unfair and infuriating, I can't say I'd recommend the game to anyone just yet. It certainly is fun, and I'd love to play with friends, but I wouldn't put the constant kicks, hitbox kills and tremendous amount of time it takes to even get in a game, on their shoulders for my sake.
Also other notes:
-A lot of heros are behind a paywall.
-Costumes behind a paywall (Understandable)
- ALL costumes are behind a paywall (With a few having the option of using in-game currency to be bought, kind of understandable)
- MASTERY OUTFITS ARE LOCKED BEHIND A PAYWALL (Not understandable, AT ALL, why even require them to have a level limit, if I have to pay for them anyway?)
- Cards/Loadout (They change the way your character plays, that can make that healer and annoying heal denial/stunner, or turn that healer into a super tanky ultra healer, or anything inbetween, etc)
- The game has mounts (Mounts are given to you upon spawning in/after death as well. Some maps are very big, and require a way to get around quickly, thus mounts. Getting hit knocks you off a mount. A good stratagy is for a flanker to knock enemys off horses at their spawn, to give your team time to push)
- Mounts are locked behind a paywall. (Other than the default mount. Payed mounts have no special attributes other than look)
- Competitive mode (You need several characters at mastery 4 to get access)
- At player level 15 you get access to in-progress maps (You can give feed back/a short survey on the map after you have played)

This is the best of Call of Duty.  This is why:
- SETTING: it's not soldiers in WWII yet again, it's not elite special operatives twenty minutes from now again and it's not supersoldiers of the future; it's something a bit different.  Sort of soldier/spies (well, Black Ops, in fact...) in the '60s, in fact.  This allows two things to really stand out, and they are:
- STORY: A genuinely engaging and very memorable narrative that integrates real historical figures like Castro and Kennedy and some really good settings for action setpieces - Vietnam war, Hong Kong in a thunderstorm, Russian mountain bases and space-launching facilities and more.  The voice acting is very good, things take unpredictable turns and even if you do see things coming, this is entertainment in the same mould as '80s action cinema - it may not be art, but it's fun and extremely enjoyable.  I don't want to spoil it but it is the kind of story that would make excellent movies in their own right, and a fun thing to replay in the same way you might rewatch a cool action TV series.
- WEAPONS: instead of the same old WWII guns or modern day guns which we've seen in game after game, the setting allows for some unusual and really cool weapons, and the variety is excellent.  Many are admittedly wildly anachronistic, but the era in question has produced some of the most interesting guns in history like the ASP or the H&K G11 and many are available here, along with iconic guns of the era like the FAL or Uzi and early versions of things we've all used, like the pre-A1 version of the M16.  Crucially, pretty much every gun was fun to use and useful in one application or another.
- MULTIPLAYER: CoD is deservedly known for being the thing that made ranking up and unlocking stuff the core of the multiplayer experience, and that's in here - but incredibly, it's secondary.  The actual experience of playing the game was the main attraction.  If you want, you can prestige ten or fifteen times; I did it once for the extra player slot and left it at that, but I've played 320+ hours of the MP game; that should tell you something about the basic gameplay experience.  The weapon balance and map design for this had a great deal going for it (aside from one or two slightly overpowered guns and the horror that was 24/7 Nuketown servers) and the use of currency to buy unlocks along with the option to gamble it on matches or complete contracts to earn extra was the peak of CoD multiplayer.  The transformation of the create-a-class into essentially a weapon shop, allowing us to unlock whatever we wanted as long as we had the cash, made everything seem fairer and freer and more personalised.  If I wanted a silencer or a sight or a paint job, I earned the cash any way I liked with whatever weapon I liked and bought one.  Then there was the introduction of the emblem editor, a staple of Treyarch CoD and another wonderful way to add personality to the game.  After this, things became much more locked down again, for reasons I've never understood.  Oh, and there were actual dedicated servers, with maplists and rules and localised languages and everything.  None of this peer-to-peer silliness.  You could frequent a place and have a sense of community, and depend on moderators to kick idiots and cheaters.  Nowadays MP is like any game that's passed its prime - you'll struggle to find populated servers, and if you find one and you're new to the game, you'll be surrounded by people who've clocked up hundreds of hours and likely know every trick in the book.  However, it does have...
BOT MODE:  The 'Combat Dummies' aren't the most brilliantly programmed AI in the world, but on low skill settings they're a good way for more casual players to experience multiplayer maps and modes, and mess about with weapons.  If you want a game in which you can use well-crafted guns and feel like a massive badass, this is exactly what you need.  Hardcore mode (extra damage, no HUD) is recommended to level up.
TECHNICAL:  It was never the most gorgeous game ever made, including at release, but it looks perfectly OK, has a good period feel to its art and runs very smoothly even on old or low-spec machines at the time of release.  There's nothing to actually complain about; no-one but elitist fools are going to look at this and complain about how it looks or runs when they're actually playing unless they're determined to pick holes and don't understand it's no longer a new game.  It's also very stable.  The old engine means that programming it is well understood, and so moving is very natural and intuitive, and shooting is viscerally satisfying.
ZOMBIES:  I never got into this, frankly I don't get the popularity of it and the zombies are stupidly hard to kill (zombies are meant to be easy to kill...), but it seems massively popular and hey, it's a whole third game mode.
In all, it's still a great game and I'd say it's worth playing for the story alone.

Got it for cheap. Went into it expecting an unironically bad game, got an ironically good game instead. I didn't even know it was based off of a TV show.
Pros:
- You have almost absolute control over your vehicle and beyond. Everything from blinkers to nitro boosters to camera angles to slow motion. (I found even the keyboard controls to be acceptable, but I do recommend an Xbox 360 controller.) AI will sometimes respond to your vehicle's behavior. Damage can range from a smashed bumper to a popped tire to engine failure.
- Best handling cars I've ever controlled in a game. Each one has its own strengths and weaknesses, and there are quite a bit to drive. Even with the huge variety, I rarely find myself losing control of any vehicle. This contributes to the feeling of the game feeling like an actual challenge, instead of feeling like I've been forced to drive a gimped vehicle.
- Decent graphics. Some of it looks akward, such as the lack of civilians, and the building pop-in from the skyboxes. The chromatic aberration was a good call, and the texture detail is agreeable. I especially like the cows who explode into steak with a single touch.
Cons:
- Sometimes hard to figure out where to go and what to do. I've wasted a bit of time during and between missions searching on the internet for what I need to do to progress, as the game often does not explain it well enough. I didn't know how to start a mission or what button I needed to press to detonate a drone, before looking through outside sources. The minimap also fits into this category. It does not show all of the roads, and often suggests a longer path that wastes more time.
- Some of the missions suffer from strange design. It's hard to explain, there are so many different things, but I'll take an example: The Poisoned Beer mission. All you have to do it pull up next to the truck and hold that position for a few seconds to get it to stop. I mean, I get it, I've beaten it, I've done that mission several times. It doesn't matter if you beat him to the supermarket or are just a few seconds late, you fail if you don't do that. Does that really conform to logic? If a truck smashed my there-and-waiting police car out of the way to park behind the market, would I really say "Uh-oh, guess I didn't get there in time?"
- The voice actors for the main characters are terrible. It's localization at its worst. It's so bad that it makes the rest of the voice acting sound good.
Meh:
- The music might as well not exist. It's not terrible, but I don't think it adds anything either. It can be turned off if you want.
- Again, localization. Except for the voice acting, it's not horrific, but even changing the text language does not change the spoken language, so you're kind of screwed either way in that department. Also, there's a lot of German signage to notice during the game, some of which can be pretty amusing.
Overall, the game is pretty good, or at least, better than I would have been previously lead to believe.
Now, I must make my ausfahrt... I mean, exit.

Magicka is a fun top-down ARPG that focuses around magic. You can create your own spells by mixing the elements, use pre-built spells that can have some special effects, and play either a short (Took me 7 hours) story mode, a challenge mode with a decent amount of maps (More if you buy DLC), or PVP where you test your skills with magic against other players.
The story was comical but not very interesting. In team-based modes you have a friendly fire that really gets in the way due to the top-down perspective. The graphics are a bit outdated but nothing I personally minded. Every character speaks in a fake language like in the Sims, except the narrator between levels, which I found really annoying.
The gameplay is fun though, and that is a core element of ARPGs. This game is iconic in its originality but mediocre in most other ways from graphics, to sound effects, to the story, to the lifespan. I still had fun though and would confidently give this a 7/10. Not something you need on your shelf but it's always fun to have a comical coop game available.

I would like to give this game a good review because it can be a lot of fun.  Unfortunately there are far too many problems with this game for me to recommend a purchase.
The multiplayer is very strange.  There are often connection issues, and glitches during multiplayer.  I had to start at least half of the the levels over due to glithes.  This wouldn't be such a big problem if the game was balanced for singe player, but the game doesn't seem to scale in difficulty whether you are playing with one or four players.  I found some sections of the game almost unplayable because I couldn't connect with a friend in multiplayer and the enemies were so numerous the only way I could win was by cheesing the enemies and trying to glitch out their AI.
The second problem is that the game is horribly balanced.  I can go through a level and kill everything no problem and then get to a group of regular enemies that one shot me no matter what.  Then I'll get to the boss and kill him in like 2 hits.  It's very strange.  The levels don't seem to get harder other then just throwing more enemies at you.
The third problem I had is that the game runs very choppily even on high end machines.  The graphics are not very good, but my computer and all of my friends comptuers will run this game very very slowly at times.  Even if the framrate is quite high, it will take quite a while for the game to catch up to my input.
The game is quite interesting, and the spells work great and look cool.  I really liked some of the time I spent playing this game, but frustration with the glitches and performance and balancing issues made this game almost unplayable.  I will be looking at magicka 2 to see if these issues were addressed, because the idea is there, the technical side just needs to catch up.

So far, I have completed normal mode with two characters (Nisha and Claptrap) and played a little bit of TVHM.
As others have said, this feels like an extension of Borderlands 2 (but inferior to it). Combat, aesthetics, user interface remained largely the same. Naturally, it makes sense to focus on the differences between the two.
The main aspects of TPS that I thought were improvements were more interesting skill trees (more variation in progression of skills and between characters themselves) and likelier legendary drops (I have found quite a few legendaries just in vending machines throughout normal mode). Laser weapons were a fun addition. I also liked that the playable characters partake in dialogue with their own unique lines.
There were some things that became non-issues. I wasn't a big fan of the varying levels of gravity in different areas at first, but eventually got used to it. Similarly, I didn't like the oz mods at first, but ultimately, they didn't detract from the experience. If anything, they add another side to combat compared to relics, which merely provided stat boosts.
Then there were areas that definitely felt sub-par to BL2. The writing was not nearly as funny or entertaining (though I'm finding that TVHM dialogue is funnier, with Tiny Tina and Brick commentating over the story). Map design is really confusing for anyone on their first playthrough. In addition to excessively vast landscapes and multiple floors, there are often no clear paths or landable platforms. Consequently, you may have to guess where you need to make a leap of faith (usually to your death). Side missions were often tedious, with a lot of running around, and the tedium was usually compounded by the overly expansive map design. Most NPCs were not very interesting at all, and some were just downright annoying.
Overall, the reason TPS got such a negative response was because the fans were expecting a game on the level of BL2. On its own, it was a decent game. Its flaws don't discount it entirely, but the disappointment is understandable.
UPDATE: My original review of the game still stands, but since then, I have bought the Season Pass. I've now played through at least normal mode with almost all of the characters. With their variety of skills, the characters, including the DLC, are still fun to play. I especially enjoyed the Claptrap DLC campaign and consider it one of the best campaigns across the series. In fact, I enjoyed it more than the main campaign of TPS, as it featured a much more interesting setting, sensible maps, and improved dialogue. Overall, the main story of TPS offers some welcome improvements over BL2, kept many of the mechanics that made me a fan of the Borderlands series, but didn't really build its world and setting as well as its predecessor. Its one DLC campaign showed a glimmer of its former glory, so it makes me hopeful that the Gearbox will take into account the shortcomings of this game to deliver the best sequel they can.
