This hybrid of genres (RPG, First Person Shooter, Stealth and Adventure) is a gem. Despite the years, is a very complex game and introduced a series of mechanics which are still praised today.
PROS :
- Incredible story (What begins as the simplest thing in the world, ends up becoming a story full of conspiracies and betrayals to the point of not knowing who to trust, followed by a climax that few games can reach).
- The decisions you make along the adventure change the narrative of the ending.
- Completely open-character to all missions (From the first to the last, you have multiple ways to fulfill your primary and secondary objectives).
- Long campaign (If you dare to explore absolutely everything, you will ensure a minimum of 60 hours of gameplay).
- Multiple options for character customization (Integration of augmentations that allows you to perform specific actions and skills that can be enhanced at different levels).
- You can mold the character to fit your playing style (If you're a pacifist, you can create a stealthy character to avoid direct confrontation, or if you prefer to face the situation
John Rambo, you can create a real killing machine).
- Wide variety of weapons (From improvised weapons to non-lethal, knives, pistols, shotguns, rifles, bazookas, energy weapons, etc. Many of these, completely customizable in their performance).
- Various options to interact with the NPC's (Resolving a situation by the way of the dialogue, intimidation or force. Your choice affects the opinion of other characters and their behavior towards the protagonist).
- The exploration is encouraged (Many hidden areas that keep items, ammunition, experience points to spend, etc).
- Features Multiplayer option (Amazingly for a game of these characteristics, you have the option to play in LAN or Internet. At the time of writing this Review, there were about 15 active servers with people in them).
CONS :
- Relatively small inventory (Although this is not necessarily a bad thing, but merely strategic. You must decide very well which items to carry).
- Some bugs and graphical glitches (Textures that become invisible, walls that inexplicably you can go through in certain situations).
An unforgettable story set in a Cyberpunk atmosphere of the mid-21st century. The multiple customization options added to the various narratives that you have for your style of play, ensures that the Single Player mode will be played more than once.
Note : Played it on Windows XP - SP3

I just finished playing the game.  Here are my thoughts...
Should the game have been released?  Yes.  Should it cost money?  No.  Why?  Because the game is so full of bugs that I would honestly consider this a Beta and NOT a full release.  Until they are fixed this should be free.  Some of the bugs: the game minimizes to desktop regularly; the player will get stuck in terrain; some monsters glitch causing them to not able to be hit but are still able to do damage to you; the game does crash though rarely...etc...
Gameplay...  I understand that the developers' primary language isn't English.  I can accept this.  But I cannot accept a translation that leads to very juvenile, confusing and idiotic dialogues.  Most of the time I felt like the NPCs and even my character were 3 years old.  It was completely annoying and made the game's plotline difficult to follow.  Near the end of the game I just didn't care anymore and clicked my way through all the conversations.  Also, the lack of proper translation leads to Axes and Mauls being labelled as "2 handed swords" and etc...  Basically, most weapons are labelled as a "sword".
The fighting...  The game missed the mark on this.  One would think that you could click on the enemy and be able to kill them.  But this isn't always the case as lootable items laying on the ground will interfere with your targeting.  Sooner or later you will just click on the Sword button in the action toolbar to attack and stop clicking on enemies to attack.  I only played as the male fighter but I noticed that if I only used my sword attack I didn't receive much damage.  As soon as I tried any of the special skills I immediately recieved a large amount of damage.  This made it so that I completely stopped using or caring about any of the special skills as the use of them would severely damage or kill me.
Let me wrap this up...  The game in this current state is playable and at times very enjoyable.  But because of the many shortcomings I can not recommend paying for this game.  Until these things are fixed, I would advise you to NOT get this game.

Faery is a budget RPG with problems, no other way to put it.
Good points first: it has a very beautiful visual style and a fitting soundtrack, and the game scales pretty nicely across difficulty scales. On harder difficulties combat is nice and rewarding, and on easier difficulties the game becomes a breeze to get through.
The worlds are filled with unique characters and quests that are well thought out and fit in the world, and you encounter many different races on your journey.
Sadly, this game feels unpolished in many other aspects. All the dialogue is unvoiced and delivered through subtitles, and the music, while fitting, sounds like a repetitive rip-off of the Harry Potter movie soundtrack.
It also has very limited controller support: while you can control your character in the world with it, for menus and combat you're forced to use a mouse and keyboard combo. At least with my setup. The game is marked as both Partial and Full Controller support, which I guess means just that.
And sadly, as of right now (October 2014) the game is broken. The executable will not work, so you'll have to track down a patch from another site as well as copy the PhysX DLL to the game folder to get it to work at all.
As I'm writing this review, the game costs €2,50, and for that price, I think it's definitely worth it. I suspect it will give me easily 10 hours of playtime or more to get through, and I do want to continue. So it gets a thumbs up, with warnings.

Judging by the fact that you are reading this, you have most likely glanced at the game of which this review is about. And you may have noticed the fact the title is partnered with the ostentatious declaration of "game of the year edition". One of my biggest problems with this game is that it does not deserve such a title. A more appropriate accolade would probably have to simply be "Deus Ex: Game of century edition".
Yes, that's right, I found a game that's better than Half-life 2, deal with it 2012 me!
This is the part where one usually describes what the game is and a bit about the gameplay, but Deus ex has an exception. But, as a rule of thumb, most people classify it under the simple and undeserving title of "FPS", a name unworthy of such a masterpiece. This is due to the seamless blend of RPG elements, Stealth and, of course, First person gameplay of the shooting variety (and no, Fallout 3 is not a "better example" because Bethesda never quite grasped what the words "role-playing" mean, and give out skill points in as plentiful quantities as the loading time in their games due to the excessive consolization that plagues this industry like the Grey death). Of course, the game is much more complex than this, as you are not necessarily limited to sneaking around urban dystopia and secret laboratories. One can simply go in guns blazing (but this usually results in immediate death) or, in contrast, can complete the entire game without killing a SINGLE person whatsoever. The amount of choice and the way it reacts to your decisions is frightenly high.
But, nothing is perfect. The gunplay is fairly weak and the graphics and animations are fairly dodgy, due to it running of the already fairly dated unreal engine. The levels, whilst very expansive and well designed, are a bit boxy and bland, even within the context of a ruined 2052 cyberpunk setting.
Its true strength, however, lies within its story. Without spoiling too much it revolves around the player, a "nano-augmented" agent (don't worry, it is kind of explained in-game) called JC Denton, who works for UNATCO (United Nations Anti-Terrorist Coalition), a group formed by the united nations in response to increasing global tensions, including a terrorist strike on the statue of liberty (the game was made in 2000, so it was still perfectly fine to discuss terrorist attacks on New York). But as the player fights the various organizations, he starts to realise there is something very wrong with his overlords, and finds himself a player in a secret war for world dominance. The themes, factions and events in the game are likely from a conspiracy theorist's nutty dream, but simply keeping up to date wiht the state of the world simply provides foreshadowing for the dystopia presented in this game! Whilst most of the exposition and dialogue is extremely well written, its delivery and voice acting is not as refined, simply watch any play through of Hong Kong or Paris to get the idea. But, I suppose there is some charm to hearing Asian triads debate about philosophy in silly accents!
On the subject of sound, it is quite obvious that the music does an excellent job of making up for the questionable voice acting. When you first boot up a game and simply get chills from the title screen, you know you've got a gem in your hands! All the the levels have an apprpaite soundtrack that suits them, with seperate themes for ambient, combat, conversations and death. Ah Hong Kong, never again will I be able to go anywhere remotely Asian without feeling like stepping into Wan Chai market for the first time...
My final word is that you should absolutely buy this game. It is very cheap ($1.74 in a sale!) and there is simply no excuse for not playing this. There is a well-known phrase that "Every time you mention Deus Ex, someone will reinstall it", but this is complete bullocks because no one in their right mind would ever uninstall it; it is the best 700mb on their hard drive!
The point being, this is easily the best PC game, if not the best overall game, ever made. It is really quite sad how no game has ever been able to match it after 14 years in terms of complexity and competency.
What a shame...

I found the demo for this game back on the PS3 several years ago, downloaded it, engaged in it and got sad when the demo was done. So far I'm pretty much enjoying this game. There is no voice acting, which is a bit weird to me after having played through so many games that involve voice acting, but it's not terrible! I almost wonder if voices would ruin it, and it allows you to imagine how the characters would sound, without the disappointment of the characters actually not sounding like you imagined.
So far the story is engaging. It's kind of fast paced but at the same time slow, if that makes any sense. It definitely isn't slow to the point where you aren't engaging yourself, but also not too fast so you're missing things. The artwork, to me, is a bit weird and the outlines are jagged, but that just might be my computer.
As for the controls, I wish the mouse sensitivity was able to be set a bit higher. I'm one of those people that like it when the camera can turn fast without having to lift my mouse to move it three times just for it to rotate 90 degrees. The controls are still giving me h*** and I keep trying to use control to fly faster instead of shift. Overall it's pretty fun being able to fly as a fairy instead of having to walk or run everywhere. You can zip around fast! The combat system is turn-based, and fighting is an option to solve many quests, but it's not the only option! You actually have peaceful options to work around some quests. Which is nice if you're trying to play a more peaceful character. You also have the options to be nice/mean as well.
Overall I definitely think this game is fun, and definitely worth it at a low price (I got it 75% off, yay!). I've heard that it hasn't been finished and won't be finished, but I'm not sure if that's true or not. Either way, for what it's worth so far, it's an enjoyable and slightly different game than others I've recently played.

Ask yourself a simple question: "Can I come up with anything I should rather be doing?"

In the beginning you will not find Isaac very enjoyable. This is due to the fact that you will die a lot. A... LOT...
After you are done cursing the only deity you know, you will press "Replay". This will happen over and over for many moons. Suddenly you will look up from your computer and realize that it is very quiet. You start to wander around your home and runs into the family that lives there now. It is not your family and these people are wearing space helmets. You have to since the world is now so polluted that even China doesn't live here anymore. You start to wonder where your friends and loved ones are. You try to call their cell phones but realize that that is an impossibility due to the fact that no one uses cell phones anymore. You ask the strange family for help. The lady hugs you. She knows that they are all sure to be dead a long time ago. The family hasn't had any problems with you until now, so they let you stay. Over time, you come to love the family and them you. But somethings off with the mother and when finally confronted about it, she tries to kill you, but you escape to the lower parts of the house and thus your own version of The Binding of Isaac begins...
What I'm trying to say is: You will spend a lot of time playing this game.
After a while you will be able to recognize a lot of the monsters' patterns.
Throughout this process of trying again and then again you will gradually get better + you will unlock a sweet amount of items. This makes it easier to complete this piece o' shi-at time comsumer.
Have fun!

Cons:
1) The "Nightmarish Trip" achievement is certainly nightmarish.
2) Character Level up system takes A LONG TIME to finally unlock new abilities, then when it does you get 3 or 4 abilities all at once. I would like to see a more gradual progression, perhaps 1 unlock every 5000 kills.
Verdict:

With Injustice 2 on the horizon, I thought it was a good time to dust off the superpowered-brawler and see how it has held  up all these years. Short answer: it’s still ok.
Injustice is a fighting game starring the DC comic heroes and villains. This is your chance to have a brutal rematch between Superman and Doomsday. Or to go for an all-out melee between underdog Green Arrow and demigod Black Adam and make the latter bite the dust. The assumed premise is a bit awkward; Seeing Harley Quinn, a gymnast, go toe to toe with the likes of Superman and Zod, but Netherrealm has got you covered.
Like with Mortal Kombat 9, Netherrealm went the extra mile (for fighting game standards) and included a story line. It mostly serves as an excuse for the aforementioned match-ups, but it also straightens out a lot of other jinks that comic readers might have. The plot borrows from a pair of episodes of the Justice League animation. There is an alternate world where Superman used his absolute power to end crime entirely by simply murdering anyone who went against the grain. The alternate Batman is the inevitable apostate and summons a handful of heroes from the regular dimension to help him take out the tyrant from Krypton.
It’s not a long story, you don’t even get to play as everyone but it gets the job done by letting you try out the most popular character choices. From there you can complete hundreds of challenges to master the characters.
The fights play out much like MK9. The characters adopt the same rigid stances and the timing and speed at which you input commands is more important that frame-links. You work with a light, medium and heavy attack, as well as a character action that allows for more variation. Actions include extra projectiles, stance changes and sometimes entire move sets get swapped out. Mastering the system is key to conquering the toughest challenges and other players. Furthermore, the stage also features throwable objects and if you can pull it off, you can even smash your opponent into the next stage for added damage. There is a lot going on at a time and since Injustice has chip damage on all its moves, blocking is a less viable tactic than in Street Fighter. The overall feel is still very Mortal Kombat, but with more screen wide action as all the fast and flying heroes take their speed to the match as well.
Unfortunately, there are downsides as well. Unlike MK9, the game is more sparingly in its content. While super moves are cool and all, they don’t have it over an actual fatality. Furthermore, a lot of character designs are hit or miss. Superman works from certain angles, Catwoman just looks like a mess and Wonder Woman is just plain wrong. The colours also feel washed out and bland. Eventually, most characters just look like spandex mannequins with either a cape, or no cape.
Making up for the bleak looks are the stellar voices. Really, Neatherrealm got everyone from the cartoons and new series on the phone to voice their respective characters (except Mark Hamil. However, I’d pass too considering what the Joker looks like in this game). It adds a sense of legitimacy to the game that really sells the overall DC feel from before they decided to make bad movies.
In all, the looks haven’t aged so well, but the gameplay is still very nice. Easy to pick up, hard to master. However, whether you should invest time in getting good at this instalment at this point is up to you. Get it a discount for a great deal. Get it now if you want to throw punch Batman straight through the centre of the earth and back again.

BACKGROUND:
Octodad: Dadliest Catch is an interesting game developed by Young Horses. The most unique thing about this game is that you play as an octopus disguised as a normal man who somehow manages to raise a family and go about his day completely unnoticed. Despite the games colorful visuals and hilarious cutscenes, the game has some of the most difficult controls I have ever seen in a game.
FACTORS AFFECTING REVIEW:
-I played through the entire game with my brother.
-I have not played this game in months.
-We used Xbox 360 controllers to play.
REVIEW:
I genuinely enjoy games with some of the weirdest premises in all of video games. I greatly enjoyed playing Me and My Katamari on the PSP and I love the wacky, fast-paced rhythm game Elite Beat Agents. Naturally, I figured that I would enjoy a game where you have to be an octopus in the real world. When I first bought the game, my brother and I played it nonstop. We had fun whenever we played it and we laughed whenever one of us could not move our limbs properly in order to solve the puzzle. In the game, you have to maneuver four different limbs on Octodad in order to move around the world and solve puzzles. It does not seem so hard at first to move him around, but believe me, it gets super hard later on.
Even though my brother and I genuinely loved playing this game, I have to say that it may not have been much fun if I had just been by myself playing it. The game clearly has multiplayer in mind when it comes to its design and is more suited to be played with friends than by one's self. The game is completely possible to beat by yourself, but the charm and fun that you get by playing with a friend is worth more than just doing it on your own. The multiplayer experience really makes this game more fun than it actually is.
FINAL THOUGHTS:
All alone, Octodad: Dadliest Catch would probably not be much of a fun game; however, when played with a group of friends, the game will providde loads of laughs and a ton of fun. I highly recommend this game to those who are looking for a game to break out at parties and social gatherings where you can gather together and watch some people hopelessly stumble around a virtual world as an octopus. For that reason, I have to give this game two different scores- one for a single-player experience and one for the multiplayer experience.
SCORE:
Single-player: 4/10
Multiplayer: 7.9/10

This game was my first foray into Paradox's strategy games, and boy was I impressed. The sheer scope of features at your fingertips here is immense. Basically, you choose or create a "species" that starts the game after just having discovered FTL ("faster than light travel"), and take them on a journey from that point to wherever the universe takes you. This includes everything from exploring the vast corners of space, to colonizing new world, to dealing with space pirates and independence movements within your empire, to scavenging and documenting from other empires and alien species.
The sheer scale of the game is a little intimidating at first, but those who start will quickly discover that Paradox has included a highly helpful tutorial mode to teach you its new features. After a couple of early-game playthroughs, you will quickly become accustomed to the mechanics and will not be able to put the game down.
Each playthrough is unique--the maps, species, and events you encounter will be different each game, and the premade empires (which you may use if you don't wan to create their own), even have their own small quest chains.
In addition, the developers are very active with the fan community and are going to continue supporting the game long term. Tons of new content is getting released this month, with much more on the way afterward.
I only have a few criticisms:
(1) while the militray/construction space ships and systems are ver well designed, there are no systems for civilian ships. Although "trade" techinically exists in your empire, you will never see trade ships, civilian transports, or any other signs of everyday life in your empire, even in your largest galaxies. Supposedly, content to this effect will be introduced later
(2) no espionage system
(3) the diplomacy system is not very intuitive. It's very difficult to figure out exactly how to get a contact's trust up enough to the point where they will actually make fair trades with you. In my experience, I've had to bribe them until they've gotten to that point, which kind of defeats the purpose. Diplomacy is also getting a bit of an overhaul in the next patch though
Apart from that, I am very happy with the game, and couldn't recommend it more!

Before I get into the review a few things you should know: This game has no spoken dialogue. It's the first part of what was to be a trilogy, but those plans were scraped so although the stories in the game all resolve, the main plotline does not, it ends on a rather big cliffhanger. So if either of those facts bother you, then you should steer clear. However, if you're okay with that, then this game is worth a play-through if you can get it on sale, or full-priced if you really like the subject matter.
That said, Faery - Legends of Avalon is a pretty decent RPG set in a world rarely seen in video games, which makes an otherwise average game fairly interesting. It's also short, it took me just 7.5 hours to 100% everything... but because of that it doesn't overstay its' welcome. As you might have suspected, it's not a game with any real grinding either; just story missions and sidequests.
Despite the flaws I mentioned at the start, it's got a lot going for it: While the graphics aren't super cutting edge, there is a nice overall style that's very consistent and fits well with the theme. Most of the characters are pulled straight from legends and fairy tales, but Spiders have done a good job of putting thier own spin on these characters and blending them together well.
The gameplay is pretty standard classic rpg fare. There are four environements that you spend your time in, and they're all quite different from one another. The environments are well designed and fun to explore as you go about your business completeing quests and battling foes. It's got JRPG style turn-based combat. Unfortunately it's a bit simplistic; there is room for strategy, but the enemies are all weak enough that they never give enough of a challenge to force strategic thinking. As a result, fighting becomes a bit of a slog by the end of the game.
But thankfully there isn't much of it. In fact, for almost all quests that involve fighting they give you a frequently more interesting alternative route to take that doesn't involve violence. The dialogue is not amazing, but it's decent enough to keep you entertained, as are the stories and quests. Overall, it was seven and a half hours well spent. Now if only Spiders and Focus Home Interactive would get around to making parts 2 and 3.

Bamboo Moon has lots of cute little interactive things, and I'm sure Bamboo Ball is great, but Bamboo Heart is exactly the game I've been desperately wanting for years. I would've paid at least double this price for Bamboo Heart as a standalone game, and I can't wait to discover what else there is to find.
The combat is as deep as Nidhogg and as fast paced as Samurai Gunn, but I'm also reminded of Nuclear Throne by the very deliberate ability and equipment progression throughout the game, though with some added special moves that you gain as you progress and simplified survival elements. Sometimes action does ramp up to a point where it seems almost impossible to follow, but really this is a game that rewards careful play and deliberate use of your various abilities and techniques. It even has a neat little story and some awesome secrets, including one that ties in to the Bamboo Moon menu area.
Very happy with this purchase, planning to play it a lot more, and honestly I can't wait to see what else they make!

Cortex Command is a game where you have a Brain that is like a Commander, and you order units that are considored "Soldiers". You are also greeted by the Buy Menu. Not only that, it's a side-scrolling game where you have to defend your brain and sometimes kill the enemies brain but that's rarely the case. Now, to the part where the reason why I gave this a bad review. Cortex Command has been out for eight years. And it still hasn't changed drastically since then. All games should change in those years. Yet, the developers were extremely lazy and rarely update this game. The Developers also rely on the Modding community to fix and optimize their game. But what if they don't? I'd say, don't buy this game. The game is terrible. And guess what, this game is the only game out there that lets you buy units and deploy them from the skies, and control them manually too. I listed a pro's and con's list.
PROS
Lag Optimization: Recently, the Developers released a update where it improves the FPS. Now this is actually good for a game, as FPS matters. Before the update, the lag was horrendous and I couldn't even stand it.
Scenario Battle: Yes, the mode everyone knows and it is a truely loved feature by every Cortex Command player out there is the Scenario Battle. This mode is heavily modifable. As you can test out costume factions, units, weapons and more in this mode. This mode is infamous because you could easily add new modes in the Scenario Battle. Think of Void Wanderers for example, this mod was added into Scenario Battle to make it ten times more easier.
CONS
Campaign: The Campaign has a huge potential but the Developers didn't cared about it and didn't even touched it at all, which is why all Cortex Command players hate that mode. In this mode, you select your own faction and you need to rely on your own faction to build bases, defend and assault. What I don't like about the Campaign is that it has very limited scenarios to play it. And you would expect that the bases would be randomly or procedurally generated by the AI, well. Actually it's not. It is simple just a prefab of the enemy base.
Boringness: Games are ment to be fun. And this is actually not fun at all. The reason why is because matches can take an extreme long time to finish, some matches do. The reason for that is the dumb AI, the AI controls your units and the enemies units terribly. Forcing you to micro-manage your units in order to make sure they are actually breaching in the enemies bunker correctly. The AI diffculty does not change nothing at all as well.
AI: Yes, the AI is the worst. Out of all of the Cons, I hate this the most. The AI is just stupid. As I mentioned before, the AI has problems controlling your units and the enemies units. Not only that, they designate deliveries in the worst areas possible. For example, they literally order a Drop Ship on your built-bunker, drop units then get destroyed by your units then falls and the explosion bits hit your units and kill them instantly. Making the enemy unit safe. This is extremely unrealistic and unintelligant. Not only that, when breaching in your or the enemies bunker. They would dig to their brain instead, making the process slow when invading the enemies bunker. Instead of going in the best way, like entering a tunnel that is heading deep in the base, they would choose that. What's worst is that the enemy AI might notice and deliver units to the unit digging down. Inevitably killing them.
In conclusion, I DEFINETLY do not recommend this game to ANYONE, only to those who like bad AI and very inactive developers. I certiantly hope the Developers will see this Review. I will change my review to positive if they update the game more often, but I highly doubt that. Don't buy this game until the developers decided to fix this game.

A short game with poorly balanced combat, merchants and skill progression, all i can really say it's got going for it is the witcher's story and characters.
Monsters essentially do not play any significant part in gaining experience, almost all of your experience will be gained from completing quests and nothing else.
Further, monster loot and other crafting items are heavy, worth nothing to merchants and not particularly useful. Beyond collecting items for quests just to get xp, it's not really worth picking up anything that isn't a better sword or piece of armour.
Almost nothing is worth selling to merchants except in very large amounts - which will fill up your available space quickly.
The value ratio is apparently 24-1, meaning that merchants sell items at 24 times the price for which they will buy them.
The game appears poorly optimized and buggy, and i'm almost positive that it was a console port. The combat mechanics are especially terrible on keyboard and i found myself forced to use a gamepad, else having to reach all the way across my keyboard to use a sign quick key. Further, it seems that you cannot rebind your keys from within the game, nor change your graphics settings. This has to be done from the launcher, or by manually editing the files.
It also seems that almost all mods you could get for the game work by simply overwriting previously existing files - more stat tweaks and texture replacers than anything. As a result, most mods overwrite the same file meaning that they cannot be used together unless you use special modding tools which may or may not be available anymore to manually combine them. There are very few mods for the witcher 2, and one can only wonder why.
The game has numerous references to other franchises such as south park and lord of the rings. It does little more than break my immersion when i hear geralt talking about collecting one of the 20 legendary rings of power and throwing it into a volcano barefoot during a serious conversation.
It is not possible to even come close to fully unlocking each skill tree as you reach your maximum level long before then.
There are no invincibility frames when dodging, meaning you can be easily surrounded and stunlocked when a large group of enemies pop up and surround you, which happens many times. A good example of this would be the harpy queen's nest.
I went the magic route in my skill tree, and i have to say that the majority of spells are essentially useless, even with a completely non-upgraded sword skill tree and fully upgraded magic tree i found myself relying almost entirely on my sword.
Igni does essentially no damage compared to a sword, far from enough to kill but the weakest of enemies, and is only remotely useful against large numbers which are tightly grouped once fully upgraded, as it recieves an AOE effect with a very short range.
Quen is probably the most helpful in a lot of situations, but the fact that it stops vigor regeneration means that you cannot use other spells alongside it against more than a few enemies, but then other spells don't do much anyways.
Axii can be useful against groups of enemies in tight quarters, essentially where they must pass through a door single file - causing the brainwashed enemy to block the door and give you a moment to collect yourself. Otherwise, it wears off quickly even when fully upgraded and doesn't do much more than take some pressure off temporarily.
Yrden is only useful against perhaps one to three enemies - preventing them from circling you and stabbing you in the back while you take care of the others, or against single large and powerful enemies that you can't simply stunlock with your sword - which i found to be few and far between. Further, if you strike an enemy which has been stunned by yrden, they are no longer stunned and can immediately attack and chase you.
TL;DR
If you liked the original witcher or the witcher three and want to get the story inbetween then go for it, but i can't say i'll be likely to play this game again now that it's finally over.

Stellaris is a real-time 4X grand strategy single and multiplayer video game for the PC by Paradox Interactive. Released on the 9th of may 2016 Stellaris gameplay revolves around space exploration, managing an empire, diplomacy and warfare with other spacefaring civilizations.
You start by picking looks and traits for your species. Then you choose some governing ethics like xenophobes or xenophiles or maybe materialists maybe spiritualists it’s up to you but your choices can dramatically affect other empires opinions of you. Once you decide you can choose a government based on your governing ethics these can be a form of democracy with elections and rulers with mandates or dictatorships or monarchies. You can also pick ship and city designs, and your mode of faster than light travel.
The game starts on your home planet in the year 2200 just after the invention of faster than light travel, now the stars are finally within your grasp. You will soon find other empires and countries some may have the same feelings and values as you and be willing to form migration treaties and alliances, However not all empires are happy to co-exist in peace, or give in to your evil demands depending on how you play.
As a result you must research new technologies and design more advanced ships to stay ahead of your enemies in an interstellar arms race or to explore the unknown first.
As your empire expands some of your citizens may discover new ideas and philosophies and ethically diverge, some may want to abolish or legalize slavery or grant a star system its independence. How you keep your nation together is up to you but, as it says in the trailer, “there are always things to challenge even the most stable of empires”.

I would highly recommend this game to anyone who likes these things.

„Faery: Legend of Avalon“ is a singleplayer roleplaygame in a 3D fantasy world.
You can create your own character (face, hair, eyes, make up, lips and so on) and join a world full of fairies, trolls and other mystic creatures. The story is told like a beautiful fairy-tale and makes you curious how it continues. I don’t want to tell you too much about the story, because I don’t want to spoil the game adventure. But what I can tell you:
You play a „Faery“ and as such you fly through the game! Really a great feeling (especailly the fast fly with 'Shift'). You will visit different worlds, you have a main mission and you can do lots of small quests. The battles are turn based and with every win you will get experience points to raise your level. With a higher level you get skill points and you have to decide which ability you want to learn or to improve. Some skills also change the characters look (for example the „better avoiding“ skill looks like a cattail). In the different worlds you can also find treasure chests (for some of them you will have to fight) but it’s worth it because you can get health items and also equipment for your character (e. g. new armor with also different looks and elements).
Absorbing! 10/10
Lot‘s of options and alternation in this game which keep your attention. 10/10
The controls are easy to handle (okay the flying is not always that easy). 8/10
It’s not the best graphic but still enough to be comfortable in the fantasy world. 7/10
No special music. The sounds are okay but far away from stunning. 3/10
9,99 € - in my eyes a fair price for this game.

There are games that become instant classics. Faery: Legend of Avalon is not one of those. You might say it is the very definition of an underdog. Why? Well, do not expect all the features that made Skyrim great in here, because this isn't Skyrim. It wasn't meant to be. In fact, if there is a tried and true formula for fantasy genre games, this title is as far as it gets from it. And that's not really a bad thing - do we need another typical RPG?
Faery: Legend of Avalon is shockingly different. Not in turn-based combad (which feels more like a JRPG), nor in character development from a series of "perks". But the setting, the world, and, best of all, the "feel" of the game". A fairy tale set in a world that actually fits the bill. And the artwork is great, despite somewhat limited textures. Plus, the fact that there are non-violent solutions available, means you don't have to be a serial bad♥♥♥♥♥(not killer, since winning a combat here doesn't mean wet work).
Different "worlds", or whatever those are properly called, are very small. But there is so much to do, that, at some point, those begin to feel too large. And there are no "clearly cut villains" - each of these worlds is besieged by a host of problems, mostly due to neglegence or an unhappy turn of natural (including supernatural) events. Something that you have to put right.
As you go on about your quest, and your character evolves, you tend to "grow" things. Like a tail or horns. And if you build a character solely on ability choices, you might have quite a frankenstein's monster in the end. Not sure if that's a good thing or a bad one.
Sadly, there are a few software bugs there (had the game crash to desktop immediately after finishing character creation, so make sure to save often), and dialogs aren't consistent across genders (whether you are a "he" or a "she", in some cases they still refer to you as "he").  But that all doesn't matter in the end. This game still has the "one more turn" factor, and is guaranteed to make you go to sleep a few hours later than you planned. :)

The video game industry has fermented itself through decades as quite a vicious competitive space. And with such competition births ideas that take shape in the hands that did not conceptualized those ideas in the first place. Ideas that work from a design standpoint, that constitutes success due to sheer brilliance, yet, of course, comes with the unfortunate outcome of being mirrored, sometimes to the core, by those eagerly intending to emulate its success. It's those kinds of cycles that, with much dismissive outlook by the public eye, are common throughout the industry, because let's face it, if something sells, it works, and if something works, it's bound to get copied. But to their credit, sometimes the end result does prove to be a worthy contender to its original source material, and sometimes, god forbid, be even BETTER. Let's explore on a game that falls neatly into the criteria of the dreaded industry cycle; a game that garnered quite a dubious reception due to its striking resemblance to another game which shall not be named. Does the game deserve the overt negativity it has amassed due to its derivative design philosophy? I'll tell you outright that it definitely does NOT. What I'm here to elaborate on is how it holds up as a game, and if it's something that should be a consideration as an alternative to its more successful twin.
First of all, and this is what I believe to be the most fundamental point in the game's favour, and that is the fact that the game is Free2Play. This sets it apart from Ove... I mean, "that game", because such a full fledged title normally entails a premium price of admission. Now is this game as fully-fledged? No, in fact not even close. And the very reason for that is because it's still in beta form, or in normal terms, in its infancy. Which is why I was hesitant in writing this review in the first place. But considering the game has gained some traction in terms of garnering a respectable audience, not to mention the fact that Hi-Rez, the folks behind this, are slipping in micro-transactions as a central way to subsidize their endeavour, I figured the game is at a stage in its life where criticism are most welcome. So, what is the game about? Well, to summarize, it's essentially, in its most basic form of explanation, a team-based FPS. But we all know that's been done to death already, so what sets these kinds of games apart are their reliance on unique character attributes that dramatically alters the course of the battlefield, much like a MOBA. It's those attributes, colloquially known as "skills", are what adds a whole new dynamic to this newly established sub-genre. So each character are assigned different skills that suits variance in play styles. And in the case of Paladin(as of this writing), there are a colourful cast of 29 characters, which are ever expanding. Every single one of them are designed in a way that exudes charm and distinctiveness, which I definitely admire. Moving on to the game play, each one of those characters, known as "champions", are assigned 4 skills, each specializing in different combat scenarios, and their own unique weapon(s). To elaborate, one skill specializes in movement, the other in unleashing their secondary fire, one or two skills independent on the champion's given weapon, and finally an "ultimate". Ultimates are what turns the tides of battle, and are often the most valuable tool in your arsenal. Ultimates can only be used once they are fully charged up, with each champion having variance in their length, and once fully charged, can be used by the click of a button, and then immediately goes back to its initial charge point once used. Ultimates are a thing of beauty, and a welcome addition to games like these, because it adds a layer of tension to the game play; Should you use your ultimate now? Does the enemy have their ultimate ready to make a devastating comeback? It's those kinds of things that add layers to an already complex game design.
You start with a team of five, with a similar count on the enemy's. Understandably, you can't choose the same champion on the same team, but the same rules does not apply if the enemy picks the same champion as you do. The goal of the game, based on the most common game mode, is to capture the objective, usually situated at the center of the map. You capture by standing there until you've collected enough points to reach a certain limit when, once reached, will win you the capture point. Of course, you will get contested by the opposing team, which is evidently after the same goal. So you fight your way through their horde to clear the area and give way for you and your team to gain those points. This type of game play creates a battlefield of sort, where the main point of contend is at one focal point. But it's not over yet; Once captured, it will spawn a "payload", a cart basically(don't ask why), and you have to push it all the way to the point located near the enemy's base in the allotted time. You push by staying near it for as long as you can muster, and the enemy have the capacity to push the payload back should there be no bouts by you and your team. In the event that you failed the push, which will happen a lot, believe me, the first match ends and the enemy team will be rewarded one point for triumphantly defending their objective. But of course, you were awarded one point also due to your initial capture. So that's how the game works, you basically are at war to see who gets to a total of four points first, to which the game ends. Now of course, there are some intricacies to lend some depth to the game play, such as an interesting system known as "overtime", where, for example, if you run out of time in your strive to push the payload, but there's still at least one of your teammate at the payload's vicinity, you will be granted an overtime, where you will be given a chance to push, and promptly ends when there are none of you there. This is definitely a welcome addition to a game mode that's quite simple in nature.
In the champions department, there are 4 roles specified to each champion; Damage, Flank, Front Line and Support. Each suited to fit the team's composition. A damage is meant do as much "damage" to the enemy as possible, essentially making a dent on the their defense. Conversely, there are the front lines, who excel at taking objectives due to their resilience and difficulty to take down. This is complimented by the supports, who gives the team some much needed reprieve and soothe their wounds in battle by healing them. And then there are the flanks, whose primary play style is, as the name suggests, to eliminate the enemy from beyond their sights. This is thanks to their exceptional speed and movement capabilities. To give you a secret, a flanker's best friend is full map-awareness. Which brings me to the map design, and overall, I'd say it's serviceable. There are nine maps altogether, with their accompanied theme and design. However, each map have the same structure, that is to say, there's a middle point, and two paths branching away from each other, coming around in a circle. My main problem with this is, despite knowing its full intentions, each of those feels similar to each other and adds little variety to the game. The characters are well-designed and brightly coloured to match the motif of the game, which is highly charming. Although it could use some some work in the technical department, because even in absolute max settings, it still looks dated and doesn't quite match the calibre of games of this age.
Okay, so here's the main point of contention, the thing that makes it stand out from the crowd. The customization. You see, Paladins took a bold attempt to give the players some sense of progression, and this is through giving you incremental levels and currency which is used to buy, on top of cosmetic items for your champions, cards. Crash Time 2 is a very enjoyable game. It's not without bugs, but I think the experience is certainly fun enough to warrant fighting through those.
Visually, it's fantastic, and I had no framerate issues at all running with max graphics on my GTX760 (1680x1050 fullscreen). The cars have great damage models—you can literally knock the wheels off your car, and you will actually feel it. Knock off both your front wheels, and you can't steer anymore and must reset your car. I really liked that touch.
The missions are fun and varied. Even if you do similar things in some missions, they tweak the mechanics enough that you never feel like it's completely monotonous. Driving the RC cars (bomb detonators) is particularly fun.
The world is HUGE, and it's a lot of fun to explore. Granted, there aren't really "side missions", but it's fun to just drive around nonetheless. There were quite a few moments where I went off drops at max speed, and it gave me a real sense of adrenaline flying through the air (fortunately no one was around to mock me shouting, "Woah!!")
The story is interesting enough to keep you engaged, but it won't win any awards. The same is true for the voice acting. For a racing game, it's probably slightly above par.
A good selection of cars are available, and you can pick and choose the cars you use for some missions (though certain missions can only be performed with certain cars). They have completely different feels to them, but for the most part, you're going to want to stick with the faster vehicles for most missions.
I paid $0.99 for the game, and I would honestly have been happy paying $5 for it. I definitely recommend it.
The downsides to this game are the bugs, and here those are (with recommended workarounds if available):
- On "wreck the car" missions, if you flip the opponent's car over, the car disappears and respawns somewhere near you (the same thing that your car would do if it got stuck upside down). If the opponent's car happens to respawn behind you, that means it will likely turn around and drive the other way. I recommend doing your best to not flip over the cars or completely pin them where they can't move. Just keep hitting them with force or get them behind you then keep bumping them as they try to pass you.
- Sometimes, it's just plain hard to find a mission. You drive around for a while and nothing appears. In these cases, try switching cars (look for ones with mission indicators), and try switching starting locations. You shouldn't ever need to be driving around for more than a minute for the mission brief to play, so keep moving about until a mission appears. Annoying, but workable.
- The navigation arrow is absolutely useless sometimes. It will recommend jumps over bridges when your car isn't fast enough to make the jump. Fortunately, the mini-map has a much better direction indicator that adjusts for different routes and recommends shortcuts. I highly recommend using that primarily (even though you have to look off the screen a bit).

The gameplay is very simple to pick up and Heroes can be customised via card loadouts and additional weapons, skins etc are available, but at a cost.

Magicka is an action-adventure game set in a rich fantasy world based on Norse mythology. The player assumes the role of a wizard from a sacred order tasked with the ultimate goal of stopping an evil sorcerer who has thrown the world into turmoil, his evil creations besieging the forces of good.

Do I recommend this game? Yes.
Graphics: Good. The graphics are very smooth, pretty even despite the game's vile theme.
Story: Meh. The story is basically: Isaac's mother is trying to kill Isaac because she wants to prove her faith so Isaac hides in a trap door he finds in his room and 'disappears into the depths below' which happens to have monsters in it, this game is lucky that it doesn't need amazing story to still be a very good game. The story isn't horrible, just a little bit too basic and if you're only looking for pure story this game may not be for you.
Gameplay: Very good. The gameplay's main point is via the items you can pick up, such as Technology 2; Instead of tears you will fire a laser, and that's only one of the 100+.
Bosses: Meh. The bosses are very well designed artistically and may be hard to take out the first two or three times you fight them, but their attacks get very repetitive and easy to dodge. They're far too easy.
Overall Replayability: EXTREME. You will get hours and hours spent on this game, almost everyone who buys it will spend over 10 hours. I have 135  hours in it as of now (May change later though)
Friendliness To Older PCs: Bad. The game was created in Flash causing it to be hard to run on even the best of PCs, but it's worse on older PCs.
Overall rating: 9/10. It's missing points only because the lack of good bosses, friendliness to older PCs, story and maybe even... No, nothing else. I really really recommend it :) have fun!

Before Deus Ex, shooters were simple-minded games with only a backstory but no in-game storytelling.  Most shooters back then didn't even have cutscenes; you just loaded the game, shot at things until you got tired then saved your progress and exited.
Deus Ex was the first shooter to introduce rpg storytelling and character progression.  It was also the first one to open up the game world to give you multiple paths to an objective and multiple ways to do the objective itself.  It even has multiple endings.
You can thank Eidos for breaking open the shooter genre and extending it to the shooter rpg.  Since then most shooters now attempt what Deus Ex excelled at by having story in-game, and multiple ways to pursue objectives.  Even after all these years, though, they still don't quite do it right.
Splinter Cell: Blacklist, for example, advertises that you can go Ghost, Panther, or Assault; but you're still channeled through a very narrow playfield in comparison to Deus Ex, and actually have very few ways to accomplish the missions; I can never quite do it the way I want.
Deus Ex does have some limitations, mostly due to how old it is; but there is so much freedom and so many ways to go it gave me hours and hours of replay; which is great considering it's an extremely long game by todays standards.

When I look at Steam Store Page of some product, and see publishers, how they put those positive reviews into the description, sometimes I just wonder what was that certain magazine or website thinking. Yes, everything is subjective about this, even categorization or meaning of words, but god damn, calling How To Survive in 2013 a "GEM"? Hell no!
Game wants to be either Dead Island or The Walking Dead, or even both, but as I see for majority of players it doesn't work and neither for me. If they used quotes from TWD, at least they could be more picky about selection. It's not like market is filled with zombie games, it's more like market is filled with average and bellow zombie games, and I can't help myself, but I feel How to Survive is just another regular zombie genre product with zero to none originality. But hey, it's still better than Dead Island Epidemic :D
Story is near average, same with overal script, but I liked the variety of weapons and also crafting of recipes. Visually, the game is nice looking, soundwise I didn't like it that much. Animations of finishers will get repetetive soon and so the fights will. Game will lasts you easily over 10 hours. Add another 10 for DLCs.
From survival point of view, it's yes. How to Survive feels above-average difficult, and it really gets interesting at Iron Man or Kovac's difficulty. If you feel as an player with people in the game, for me I had to say no and most probably you'll feel same.
To sum it up, nice, fast, difficult zombie action with lot of things to do, lot of crafting and fighting which might get repetetive after few hours, enough types of zombies makes the game more fresh, but still it has some major flaws, not just story but the whole game in overall. If you can get it during sale for 3-4 euros/dollars then get it, otherwise full price is no-no. I'm going to leave blue thumbs up just for the sake of two options Steam offers so far.

EDIT: 1/11/16

Unlike certain games, How to Survive was one that I tried so badly to enjoy, but just had to give up. The gameplay idea itself is rather simple: You're stranded on an island, have to find way off island, guy goes crazy, and that's as far as I've managed to go. Say, does that beginning remind you of a game? *Cough* Dead Island *Cough cough*
Anyway, the actual gameplay.
“Offers a different experience for zombie game veterans” – Co-Optimus
Let me just state now, no, it's not. I am far from veteran when it comes to a zombie game, let alone any game. This game however, was like a stroll in the park, only that would've required more effort. You're practically handed everything you need or want and that's it. All items are easily obtainable, all supplies such as food and water are abundant. There was zero challenge.
“Has a lot more going for it than smashing brains and gory, red goo ... With a surprisingly deep crafting system” – GamesRadar
Nope, no it really doesn't. That's literally all you do in this game. Smash zombies heads in, watch blood and brains go everywhere. That's the best part out of the entire game; watching the blood erupt from the zombies like a fountain while you blast them to pieces with a shotgun or your ridiculously powerful triple bone-blade boomerang. Otherwise, the crafting is so simple that I gave up crafting anything altogether. All you do is click on the component or item you want, hit combine and choose what you want to combine it with. Then if it's a gun or weapon, you bash it with a hammer and a bunch of nails. How the f*** do you get a working handgun out of a bunch of rusty old pieces held together by what was most likely a bunch of duct tape? Hey, this is a video game though, so f*** logic.
The survival area of this game. Oh boy. There is no survival in this. You can't die of thirst or starvation or exhaustion, the only possible way to die is a zombie. Otherwise, just look onto your map and you can easily locate a well to obtain water, and if you've upgraded to it, where an animal is. There you go, instant food and water. But wait, what about sleep? No worries, just clear out the already built safehouse and sleep there, but just be sure your fatigue level is below 50% or it won't work. What about weaponary to defend yourself or hunt? No worries yet again, just look for the random blood splotches on the ground and you'll be able to indentify the location of an item. Then all you need to do is put a bunch of random components from random everyday objects and whip out your trusty duct tape (A.K.A Hardware Box), then voilà! You've got yourself a gun! Now just use those seemingly endless piles of junk named "Handmade gun ammo" and blow those zombies away in a hailstorm of bullets!
The storyline is rather mediocre and serves literally no purpose quite frankly. The whole game revolves around running back and forth over islands, eviscerating zombies with your weapons, retrieving an item and delivering it to the correct person or area. Then you're rewarded with dialogue and a slight step further into the story. My favourite, a game where I endlessly beat the s*** out of zombies while collecting items and taking them back only to have some poorly written dialogue with ridiculously over-acted speech.
The final problem is they went ahead and made achievements for the DLC. Yep, the DLC must be purchased if you're one of those people who like to aim for 100% completion. Not only is this total bulls*** but it's low. They charge you for additional content that should've just been part of the game, but instead they got greedy with it and made people pay for the extra gameplay and content that was most likely originally planned to be in the game but later scrapped and made as DLC. Not to mention that DLC makes up a fair few achievements, so good luck getting that 100% without the DLC or an external program such as S.A.M. Otherwise, it's yet another example of developers not satisfied with the tremendous amounts of income and become greedy, desiring more money for things that just shouldn't be DLC. You don't make extra gamemodes into DLC when it's something like a "Survival/Endless" mode.

Have you ever felt that video games were too interactive? That really, the core functionality of any game is the memorization of a lot of gameplay mechanics, and the rest just gets in the way? If so, you'll love Injustice. It's a cinematic masterpeice and almost, sort of a fighting game. Tired of having any effect whatsoever on what goes on onscreen? Then you'll jump for joy at the sheer number of pre-scripted sequences that each stage and combination of characters has to offer. Traditonal cutscenes more your style? Injustice has you covered, and then some, with more than ten gigabytes of FMV. And no expense was spared to make the cutscenes memorable and entertaining. The voice acting and production values are top-notch. After just a few hours, you'll be able to see exactly where the development budget went.
And if you happen to be one of those oddballs that enjoys a fighting game for the approximated fighting it offers, you'll be glad to know that there's some of that on offer in Injustice. It plays like a combination of the Ps2-era Mortal Kombat games and 16-bit Killer Instinct. Use an attack, wait politely for the game to realize what's going on, a little more polite waiting for the overlong animation to finish, and then zoom(!) - you're able to use another attack. Its pacing is sorta like playing Windows 95 solitaire on a computer that's just a little too old to run Windows 95. And if you're playing the game on a computer that has a GTX 970 and an i7 processor (as I was), or anything better, you'll have no doubt at all how deliberate the pacing of the fighting is.
Injustice is the product of a great deal of forethought, and succeeds at everything it tries to do. It's a wall-to-wall cinematic experience, made with top-notch voice talent and some of the best CGI animators this side of Pixar. Which is exactly what's wrong with it. It's a fully-realized DC film burdened by a vestigial game component. Not as burdened as the player is by the vestigial game component, of course, but burdened nonetheless.

Stellaris is a game that I really want to like but ultimately it comes up short. What we have here is an interesting game engine without much substance. All the game features are too generic. I don't find myself caring about any other factions. There's nothing that immerses me in the universe. I'm just playing around with generic templates with no real end game (there are late game "mega events" to try and mix things up but they are also rather bland).
Having played and loved EUIV I can sort of see how they might have ended making Stellaris like this. There are similarly generic mechanisms in EUIV but the trick is that the terrain (i.e. Earth) and the real world history behind each nation provides enough flavor and differentiates the otherwise generic cookie-cutter nations. In Stellaris, there's no terrain, just a big open space with stars scattered around, and the other races have nothing to make them stand out as memorable in any way.
At best this feels like a proof of concept for a game engine that could be used to make a compelling game. Whether they knew that and are relying on modders and/or DLC or if they just didn't realize the shortcomings is unclear to me.

Make no mistake, this game is still an early access product. In its current state, it is unfinished, poorly documented, and counterintuitive.
At first glance it seems like it stays true to the classix 4x formula of master of orion and others like it. Then it goes beyond handholding and straight into handcuffing the player. You are initially limited to direct control of 5 planets. Any more than that and you are required to assign them to an AI managed sector, in which you have precisely zero control over building or upgrading. While this is nice as an option for those who prefer a macromanagement approach to such games, forcing people to use it is inexcusable and a slap in the face to players who prefer to micro, or even those who want to step in during a crisis that would be easily solved with a few timely building upgrades. Adding insult to injury is that calling the sector management AI such things as "unoptimized" is being diplomatic at best. Options are a good thing. But force a player to use a tool, and it is no longer a tool but a constraint.
Then we get to stations. The most common station you will be building in this game is a mining station, armed with a single weapon that on paper upgrades as you research new tech in that weapons category. In practice, that only applies so far up the tech tree as the newer weapon types fall into different categories, so the automatic upgrade doesnt apply to the stations default weapons. This would be fine if you were allowed any kind of control over the design of your most commonly built installation, but you arent. By midgame you are stuck with systems full of outdated, vulnerable resource production stations that are the backbone of your economy and research, critical to your survival, and yet completely impossible to update to current tech! Paradox could learn a thing or two about proper unit design options from Malfador Machinations and thier Space Empires series.
So if the main focus of the game is on macro level strategy, wars must be really spectacular, right? Well, not so much. You cannot simply declare war on another race or empire, you must declare war goals, and good old fashioned extermination is not an available choice. In fact, depending on your peoples ethical traits, you may not even be able to destroy an empire at all, even one that has sworn itself to your extinction. Instead you may make them a vassal empire, which has all the management issues of a sector with the added bonus of being full of a people that likely despise you and can rebel against you at any moment. There is, as far as I can find, no way to alter or sidestep these ethical traits mid-game. so much for the hard choices and social and political evolution that make up a big part of what "space opera" means.
Graphically the game is pretty. I would not call it impressive, but the graphics do the job. Sure its cool to see a mass of ships in realtime slinging an amount of missiles at the enemy that would give a Robotech pilot pause, but that only goes so far and gets old fairly quick. Whats left is a game that is cumbersome to play, and seems to want to handicap and cut off the players options at every possible turn. Its playable, but only just, and doesnt really live up to the spirit of its predecessors. Longtime fans of the genre would be better served to look elsewhere.

The video game industry has fermented itself through decades as quite a vicious competitive space. And with such competition births ideas that take shape in the hands that did not conceptualized those ideas in the first place. Ideas that work from a design standpoint, that constitutes success due to sheer brilliance, yet, of course, comes with the unfortunate outcome of being mirrored, sometimes to the core, by those eagerly intending to emulate its success. It's those kinds of cycles that, with much dismissive outlook by the public eye, are common throughout the industry, because let's face it, if something sells, it works, and if something works, it's bound to get copied. But to their credit, sometimes the end result does prove to be a worthy contender to its original source material, and sometimes, god forbid, be even BETTER. Let's explore on a game that falls neatly into the criteria of the dreaded industry cycle; a game that garnered quite a dubious reception due to its striking resemblance to another game which shall not be named. Does the game deserve the overt negativity it has amassed due to its derivative design philosophy? I'll tell you outright that it definitely does NOT. What I'm here to elaborate on is how it holds up as a game, and if it's something that should be a consideration as an alternative to its more successful twin.
First of all, and this is what I believe to be the most fundamental point in the game's favour, and that is the fact that the game is Free2Play. This sets it apart from Ove... I mean, "that game", because such a full fledged title normally entails a premium price of admission. Now is this game as fully-fledged? No, in fact not even close. And the very reason for that is because it's still in beta form, or in normal terms, in its infancy. Which is why I was hesitant in writing this review in the first place. But considering the game has gained some traction in terms of garnering a respectable audience, not to mention the fact that Hi-Rez, the folks behind this, are slipping in micro-transactions as a central way to subsidize their endeavour, I figured the game is at a stage in its life where criticism are most welcome. So, what is the game about? Well, to summarize, it's essentially, in its most basic form of explanation, a team-based FPS. But we all know that's been done to death already, so what sets these kinds of games apart are their reliance on unique character attributes that dramatically alters the course of the battlefield, much like a MOBA. It's those attributes, colloquially known as "skills", are what adds a whole new dynamic to this newly established sub-genre. So each character are assigned different skills that suits variance in play styles. And in the case of Paladin(as of this writing), there are a colourful cast of 29 characters, which are ever expanding. Every single one of them are designed in a way that exudes charm and distinctiveness, which I definitely admire. Moving on to the game play, each one of those characters, known as "champions", are assigned 4 skills, each specializing in different combat scenarios, and their own unique weapon(s). To elaborate, one skill specializes in movement, the other in unleashing their secondary fire, one or two skills independent on the champion's given weapon, and finally an "ultimate". Ultimates are what turns the tides of battle, and are often the most valuable tool in your arsenal. Ultimates can only be used once they are fully charged up, with each champion having variance in their length, and once fully charged, can be used by the click of a button, and then immediately goes back to its initial charge point once used. Ultimates are a thing of beauty, and a welcome addition to games like these, because it adds a layer of tension to the game play; Should you use your ultimate now? Does the enemy have their ultimate ready to make a devastating comeback? It's those kinds of things that add layers to an already complex game design.
You start with a team of five, with a similar count on the enemy's. Understandably, you can't choose the same champion on the same team, but the same rules does not apply if the enemy picks the same champion as you do. The goal of the game, based on the most common game mode, is to capture the objective, usually situated at the center of the map. You capture by standing there until you've collected enough points to reach a certain limit when, once reached, will win you the capture point. Of course, you will get contested by the opposing team, which is evidently after the same goal. So you fight your way through their horde to clear the area and give way for you and your team to gain those points. This type of game play creates a battlefield of sort, where the main point of contend is at one focal point. But it's not over yet; Once captured, it will spawn a "payload", a cart basically(don't ask why), and you have to push it all the way to the point located near the enemy's base in the allotted time. You push by staying near it for as long as you can muster, and the enemy have the capacity to push the payload back should there be no bouts by you and your team. In the event that you failed the push, which will happen a lot, believe me, the first match ends and the enemy team will be rewarded one point for triumphantly defending their objective. But of course, you were awarded one point also due to your initial capture. So that's how the game works, you basically are at war to see who gets to a total of four points first, to which the game ends. Now of course, there are some intricacies to lend some depth to the game play, such as an interesting system known as "overtime", where, for example, if you run out of time in your strive to push the payload, but there's still at least one of your teammate at the payload's vicinity, you will be granted an overtime, where you will be given a chance to push, and promptly ends when there are none of you there. This is definitely a welcome addition to a game mode that's quite simple in nature.
In the champions department, there are 4 roles specified to each champion; Damage, Flank, Front Line and Support. Each suited to fit the team's composition. A damage is meant do as much "damage" to the enemy as possible, essentially making a dent on the their defense. Conversely, there are the front lines, who excel at taking objectives due to their resilience and difficulty to take down. This is complimented by the supports, who gives the team some much needed reprieve and soothe their wounds in battle by healing them. And then there are the flanks, whose primary play style is, as the name suggests, to eliminate the enemy from beyond their sights. This is thanks to their exceptional speed and movement capabilities. To give you a secret, a flanker's best friend is full map-awareness. Which brings me to the map design, and overall, I'd say it's serviceable. There are nine maps altogether, with their accompanied theme and design. However, each map have the same structure, that is to say, there's a middle point, and two paths branching away from each other, coming around in a circle. My main problem with this is, despite knowing its full intentions, each of those feels similar to each other and adds little variety to the game. The characters are well-designed and brightly coloured to match the motif of the game, which is highly charming. Although it could use some some work in the technical department, because even in absolute max settings, it still looks dated and doesn't quite match the calibre of games of this age.
Okay, so here's the main point of contention, the thing that makes it stand out from the crowd. The customization. You see, Paladins took a bold attempt to give the players some sense of progression, and this is through giving you incremental levels and currency which is used to buy, on top of cosmetic items for your champions, cards. Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing

at this point, i'd like to share a passage from "The World Could Be Anything" by Terence McKenna:
"A long time ago, 700 million years ago, more or less, the great Tree of Life made a primary division between the vertebrates, the creatures with backbones, and the invertebrates. Evolving along the invertebrate line and reaching the greatest brain size and complexity of nervous system on the invertebrate side of things, were the cephalopods. Now, you may have heard this fact and assumed that it had to do with camouflage against their surroundings so that they can avoid predators. This is not what it’s about at all. Octopi change color, and they can also change the shape of their skin from smooth to rugose and wrinkled, and then what’s called pileate, little points all over it. They can go through all of these color changes and texture changes. And, octopi have extremely well-evolved eyes. In fact, evolutionary biologists always compare the eyes of octopi to human eyes, as an example of what is called ‘parallel non-convergent evolution’ because clearly the two are not related. But, the problem with the small mouth noises form of communication is: I have a thought. I look in a dictionary that I have created out of my life experience, I map the thought onto the dictionary, I make the requisite small mouth noises, they cross physical space, they enter your ear, you look in your dictionary which is different from my dictionary, but, if we speak what we call ‘the same language’, it will be close enough, that you will, sort of, understand what I mean.
Now, if I don’t say to you, “What do I mean?,” you and I will go gaily off in the assumption that we understand each other. But, if I say to you, “Did you understand what I said then?” You say: ‘Yes. You meant that you don’t want to sit with Harry and Sally because their pending divorce makes you uncomfortable.“ So, "No, that’s not what I meant .” So there’s a misunderstanding because the dictionaries are not matched.
Now, notice what’s happening with the octopi – there is no dictionary. Both parties are seeing the same thing because my body is my meaning. I become my meaning, and you behold the meaning I have become. I am like a naked thought. Not even a naked nervous system. More naked than that! I am like a naked thought, in aqueous space, unfolding in time. I maintain, this is why octopi eject clouds of ink, it’s so they can have private thoughts! Because, if you can be seen, you can be understood! Well, this is a perfect model condoned by nature for the kind of transformation that we want to lead our culture toward. And I don’t think it’s that outlandish."
