The first thing that you must keep in mind if you have purchased this game ( or got for free ) is that you didn't spend a whole lot of money for it. For this, you will be Thankful ; you do get what you pay for. Don't expect a Burnout Series game level of development and gameplay. If you want a ' quality ' game, be prepared to pay the premium and scroll past Crash Time 2.
The game is based on a German TV show called ' Alarm für Cobra 11 – Die Autobahnpolizei Ausfahrt ', a TV show that I cannot figure out as to whether or not is a serious crime drama or a German spoof take on the 80's series, Miami Vice. If you are from an English speaking country, the TV show that it is based on looks really really bad ( I did some youtube research by watching a couple of episodes to try and better understand what this game is based on )
Graphics :  I haven't seen a PC game since that late 90's that has such a short draw distance and pop in. You can actually see the grass grow as you drive by embankments. The developers must have heard ' Bloom ' and ' HDR  ' and thought ' you mean ' Glare ' as that is what you get. Glare then translates to making the screen bright white in some areas. The plus to this level of techincal wizardry is that you don't need an i7 and a pair of Titans to play this game. The specs required to play this game are from around 2003 i.e. if you are reading this review, your computer can run the game. Yes there are some slow downs, but in general, it's not a bad frame rate for a 2003 standard driving game. Unlicensed cars which are very obviously actual BMW, Mercedes, VW's, etc. The cars are not bad at all, hence why you can actually tell what they are based on ( or not badged as ). The city is well, German ( industrial, efficient and logically laid out but a little bland  ; mostly built in the last 70 years onwards due a disagreement with a couple of countries a number of years ago ).  Graphics wise, not the worst - not the best - kinda ' Eh ' if you can forgive the HDR ( or lack of ) and pop in that is.
Gameplay : Hmmm. You have a car and can drive around - really enough said. The ' handling ' is an arcade racer, not a sim. Don't expect fantastic drifts, just understeer and poor brakes. I tend to use the handbrake instead of the normal brakes for stopping. The nearest driving experience would be if CrazyTaxi had a love child with an early TOCA game. The story is as deep as a standard cup of water but hey, you either paid $0.99 or got this game for free right?
Voice acting : Voice acting needs a special mention all of it's own. You need to play the game to understand where I am coming from around this. I have NEVER heard such bad voice acting from ANY game, TV show, telemarketing scammer, etc. When I first heard the characters, it was quite amusing. As the game went on, it becomes, well a little bit creepy. Ever heard a 6 year old in a school play? Well it's a bit like that but spoken by a 40 plus year old guy.  Why really bad English accents? Why not German's speaking English? I think this would have worked better ( and they could have slipped in the word Squirrel for bonus points ) .... You have been warned.
Controls :  I have read some reviews on this game that say that the controls are difficult. I did not experience this problem as I plugged in my generic USB gamepad AKA PS2 copy and configured to suit a PS2 layout. You MUST use the D Pad to control the menu up and down then use the top button to select ( Triangle for PS2 ) and circle equivalent ( PS2 ) to go back. If you use the keyboard at any point on the menu, the game pad will be disabled. It's really not very hard to figure out though. To configure, enter the control lay out menu and set the control for the button of your choice ( press enter on the keyboard, then the button on the game pad that you want to use for that control ). For those that have configured a DOS / Windows 95/98 game pad, it's back to those days. Once configured, controls were responsive and worked as you want them to.
Conclusion :  Reading the above you are probably wondering why I am recommending this game? The fact remains that it is a very cheap ( or Free )  FULL game with graphics that exceed homebrew games. Buy it, but don't expect Burnout Paradise for $0.99c or Free. If you want Burnout Paradise, then don't be so cheap and buy it ( or wait for a Steam Sale 75% off ).
Note that support for the game was ditched after about a year from release, but likely not for the reason that Apple use to ditch support to sell you another product ( though we are upto Crash time 5 according to the interweb )

Holy fetch quest!  No, but really it doesn't seem like there are a lot in the beginning (because most of them seem important to the story), but later on some of them are a bit irritating.
Despite that though, the survival, crafting, exploring and killing zombies parts of the game are really fun.
The survival: you have to eat drink and sleep, and the game is good about showing you about it (kovacs inperson npc tutorial) and showing you the resources you need. Everything you pick up has a purpose with something else.
You can also carry water and food with you for later, and any bottles you drink out of gives you the empty containers to reuse.
The crafting: it's amazing, you don't even need the recipes to craft (the recipes are just there for a cookbook-like guide for putting which parts together).
* warning slight crafting spoilers ahead:*
For example, I had a handmade handgun and found this long tube thing and thought 'what if I uncombined my gun and recombined with the longer tube, would it make a rifle-like gun?' And yes, yes it did.
Or crafting an inventory bag out of reel string and animal skin, it just makes sense, you know?
*End slight crafting spoilers*
The zombies do respawn after a while, but killing them is fun, and they drop ammo or arrows you fired at them (you can go pick up your arrows you shot, even if you accidently fired an arrow into a wall, it will probably still be in the wall) and other things.
And if you're interested in even more realism, kovacs way dlc difficulty makes survival even more intense and realistic (but irritating in my point of view).
It's adds more animals/armor types, makes your water well ground supply run out after a few uses, fires expire when it rains, you need to light fires with flint (which you have to find), resources are harder to get, and your flashlight needs to be charged over time. Changes the game quite a bit, I recommend trying it at least once to see.
End note:
I was really surprised at how good this game was, and at how realistic some of the crafting and other things were (since I just picked it up on sale at a whim because I was slightly interested before),
but yeah it's a fun and surprisingly realistic survival/crafting game. And plus zombies, always fun.

I've been a huge fan of Scott Benson's work as an animator and an illustrator/designer for years now, and I was super hyped when I heard he was working on his own game! Because of school, I didn't have the chance to play it until now, and boy did it exceeded my expectations!
Right off the bat, the art direction is simply beautiful! Simple yet complex. The game is essentially an interactive Benson illustration that tells an autobiographical story of growing up in a lively, small mining town where weird♥♥♥♥♥♥happens.
NITW gets waaay too real for comfort, specifically with interactions with Bea and Mae's mother. The way the cast reacts to everything happening around them is extremely believable. There's definitely no shortage of 3-dimensional characters, aside from maybe a couple random NPCs... That changes after the ending though (no spoilers, but you'll know what I mean).
Speaking of NPCs, I'm one of those people who has to talk to every NPC I come in contact with. Luckily, NITW features a lively town full of a diverse cast of folks who all have interesting, funny, and/or important things to say. Each new in-game day I looked forward to revisiting each of them to see what else they had to say.
My only complaint is that I wish the dialogue options had a bigger impact on the actual plot. They are mostly there for your own enjoyment, and each option still creates different minor story outcomes. And its worth replaying to see all of the different hilarious and dramatic differences you can do. Yet, you have no long lasting affect on the plot itself, which could have been interesting. There are, however, different routes you can take depending on which of the characters you decide to spend more time with, which reveal various things about the characters themselves and their motivations, issues, relationships, etc. Regardless, I still see lots of replay value.
My favorite aspect was the feeling of ambiguity and uncertainty at the end. It made the characters feel even more real then they already did, and like.... damn... its not a perfect game, but boy does it make you think about life n♥♥♥♥♥♥..

Pros:
Fast paced action
Great movement mechanics
Fun cartoon gore
Raunchy humor
Extensive weapon building/customization
Great character customization
PLAY to win!
Nice graphics
Good map design
Solid gameplay
Cons:
Some customization items are a bit pricey, and you could easily spend $100+ getting all the cool gear that you want.  Luckily, these are all purely cosmetic.  Still, prices feel a bit high.
Suggestion:
The store could benefit from more purchase options.  I would like to see some more bundle options for customization packs and in-game money deals.
Summary:
Don't be turned off by F2P just because some games didn't do it right in the past.  Game developers learn from mistakes like these, and Loadout has done just that.  It's free and it's fun, so try it out!

I waited a while to purchase Stellaris due to the reviews I read and the price so my review is based off of the version available about September 20th, 2016.
This game is at first difficult to understand because of the depth. Much like the very good Crusader Kings II. Though Stellaris is not as complicated, it has a lot of room for expansions and sufficiently complicated on its own. For CKII I had to watch a bunch of youtube videos and read a few forum posts so I could learn how to play. Stellaris so far has only required a portion of one youtube video and reading of the wiki and a few forum posts. So not as complicated, but still engaging.
The beginning gives you a lot do do and as far as I can tell you still have a lot to do until the mid game which I believe a lot of people complain about. I'm guessing I will enjoy that part of the game as well by keeping the game speed set to very fast(you can pause whenever you want).
The race creation is very good. I was able to create The Deep Ones(lovecraft mythos) with its own personality. There seems to be a lot of depth in this. Diplomacy is much simpler which is a bit disappointing. It does suffice though, but could be improved a lot.
Creating your own ship designs is a bit too simple for me, but its acceptable.
Research seems like it will be varied later on in the game, but in the beginning it's just the basics.
Space battles aren't very entertaining so far as I've researched only lasers. So lots of ships swimming around and a red line comes out of it and touches an enemy.
I can't not say how great the AI is, I'll update this later.
Stellaris seems to have enough depth to be interesting, but casual enough for people who do not want to take a lot of time to learn a game. I'm enjoying it and am looking forward to expansions.

Spiders are a weird company. They are one of the few game makers that try to break free of the 'norm' when it comes to fantasy RPG's and occasionally try things that are little bit different than the "Tolkien tropes" of other games.
Unfortunately, they also always seem to lose interest in FINISHING any of the ideas they come up with, leaving each game half baked and not quite finished (it was the same with Mars War Logs as well).
This game is no exception. There are some GREAT ideas in this game (the fae setting is a really brilliant idea and the way you develop and upgrade your character and have it physically affect your appearance is very interesting) but again - everything feels unpolished and not quite thought through completely. It's short, ends at a cliffhanger that will probably never be resolved and with a not particularly interesting main story.
That said, there's enough there to make it entertaining for a few hours. Providing you grab it at a discount during a steam sale then I don't think you'd be TOO disappointed. It might actually work quite well as an entry-level RPG for a younger gamer if you drop the difficulty level down to easy. It also lacks the casual mysogyny of their newer stuff like Bound By Flame.
If Spiders took what they learned from this game and put it into a sequel or another game in the same world I think they could come up with something really fun...but as with their other games, instead of building on and fleshing out the game systems they create, they seem to just get bored and move on to ANOTHER short RPG with fancier graphics, a completely different setting and a whole NEW set of half-baked mechanics and they end up right back at square one again. Weird.

Want to form a Federation and win that way? Well, getting the other civs to the happiness levels required means you have to form alliances with them, and inevitably they'll take you with them into some endless war. If this game gets a Victory overhaul, then I can reccomend it wholeheartedly. But as is, it always feels like you're spinning your wheels, waiting for the end game galactic destruction alarm to go off. It just doesn't feel like you're really progressing towards a win.

This is another one of those games where I wish I had an option between thumbs-up and thumbs-down. It's definitely not the worse game I've ever played but I don't know if I would recommend purchasing unless it was discounted, even if it's already cheap to begin with.
There are definitely positives with this game, don't get me wrong. For several of the quests you're given the option to solve them without having to fight which is a nice change from most games in this genre. So if you find the turn-based fights getting a little repetitive and boring like I did, you have the option to skip some of them by solving your problems non-violently. And the side quests are actually pretty entertaining. Most of them tie in well with the main quests and you usually only have to go out of your way to solve them if you forgot to get them in the first place.
The character designer is pretty awesome. You get to shade your character the way you like and pick from a few specific features and then fine tune them which I liked. I also liked the way you leveled up and aquired different designs and body modifications for your character (though I wish you could have picked the way they looked a little more).
Some of the NPCs you interact with are just gorgeously designed. Oberon is a pretty amazing looking character and your companions are all very fleshed out and look amazing. At the same time it's clear that they copied and pasted a lot of the character designs and that can get a little confusing. In the last mirror world it gets a little confusing to remember which little bearded man is which and on The Flying Dutchman all the Korrigans pretty much look the same. They're still nice to look at though.
My biggest problem with the game though were the two middle levels, the Tree World and The Flying Dutchman. The environment is just not player friendly. In the Tree World you're trying to find stuff amongst the branches and the leaves constantly block the camera so you keep having to go back and forth, round and round to find a character or a nest in order to complete a quest. It's frustrating and I had to keep turning the game off to keep myself from hitting the screen. The Flying Dutchman level does it with darkness and the holds of the ship. It's almost impossible to see where you're going and you have to hunt down three monsters on sound alone.
There is no voice acting which is fine, better no voice-acting than bad voice-acting. But there are weird parts where characters are "talking" and pointing to things and you literally have no idea what's going on. "Over there" amounts to nothing when you don't show what "over there" means.
Of course there's no real ending. Apparently there was supposed to be a sequel that never got made and it's a little bit frustrating that you don't really get a reward or even just a feeling of sastifaction from all that you did.
And a little pet peeve of mine is with the dialogue. You're allowed to choose the gender of the character but there are quite a few times where it's clear that the game was made with a male main character in mind because the pronouns get confused. I don't mind playing a male character, heck half the time I choose to do so when given the option, but if you're going to let me pick a female character make an effort to get it right.

Probably the most replayable game of all time, Binding of Isaac utilizes it's roguelike elements in a way that makes you want to keep playing over and over. All of the issues I have with the game can be attributed to the fact that it was made in flash. If you can learn to overlook any of the occasional glitches this game has due to flash, it is insanely good. The learning curve for the game is perfect, something McMillen achieved in SMB as well. It kicks your♥♥♥♥♥over and over again, but encourages you to keep trying. This makes the first time you defeat mom feel incredibly satisfying. The game will reward your progress by adding more items into the item pool, most of which are not dependent on weather or not you complete a run. The controls are simple, the storyline is good for what it's trying to do while also having a final ending that adds to the mystery of the plot. Despite the fact that this game only was initially an experiment, it evolved into so much more. Isaac is in all honesty one of the best games I have ever played.

An open world game about European Police. Well, A European city with british coppers. With stock sounds, laughable voice acting and a physics engine that doesn't quite understand mass you'll definately have a strange, yet somewhat enjoyable experience playing this game.
The voice acting in this game is quite bad. However if you pair that with the terrible jokes slipped in, it actually becomes
quite humourous, for the wrong reasons of course. The sound effects are stock sounds and the soundtrack is mediocre but expected for this type of game. You can put your own music in the game which will help you play for a little bit longer. Although the process of putting your music in could be tedious if you're not familiar with file explorers.
The graphics are actually quite good. There are great lighting and shadow effects and the textures are high resolution. The models of the vehicles are quite reasonable and there is a lot of detail in the damage of the cars. Realistic or not, it definately brings the game up.
Now, talking of the damage of the cars, there is definately a lot of detail put in and the damage is local to where you hit. Parts of the vehicle will hang off and debris will come from the vehicles. The vehicles also stop break down if you sustain too much damage to the engine area, though this can be annoying.
However, the vehicles do not crumple and wheels fly off at almost all high speed crashes. NPC vehicles explode with little damage, with their explosions causing no damage to surrounding vehicles. Also if you're travelling at ~90mph or above, most vehicles will just be smashed out of the way with little effect on your speed, which brings me on to the physics engine.
Vehicles that are part of the missions are better at taking collisions. But the physics are inconsistent. You can spin out a vehicle with a slight tap, yet if you shunt them from behind they experience next to no loss of control. This is quite annoying when you have to take down a vehicle as you have to wait for them to turn a corner so you can smash them in the side at high speed if you want to do any damage.
The handling of the vehicles isn't the best. But it's not quite the worst. It's easy to slalom and weave through traffic but if you want to turn a corner at high speed, you're gonna have a bad time. You need to slow down to near stopping point if you want to turn the corner without completely missing it or smashing into a wall and have a wheel fly off.

It's rare that I'll say a game is terrible, but this game has the least intuitive UI in any title I've ever played, and that's enough to result in a terrible game. You have no warning when you're being attacked at the other side of the map, you have no way of knowing which weapon you have equipped unless you know the ammo quantities and which weapon "model" is which. The tutorial is a single level with a half a dozen sign posts to tell you how to play on a game with considerable depth as this, that is not enough. The floor seems to melt away as you're walking on it resulting in getting stuck in the floor. There is no progression to show you which weapons are better than other or which bodies are more capable than others. You get given a list of several hundred buyable items and get no indication on which ones are worth buying. The campaign is simply a series of skirmishes with a shared resource pool. The graphics are mediocre, looking almost as though the whole game and all the assets are developed to play in 640 X 480, aiming is terrible and unintuitive, sometimes working and sometimes not, can we have an Aim button so we know when we're aiming or otherwise. Why can I not see any range of distance when aiming, often having to approximate the thing I'm aiming at but I can somehow see anywhere on the map when I'm choosing my delivery locations?
Personally I think the game would have had a lot of potential, but in it's current state it almost seems like the thing is having an identity crisis, it's like the game doesn't know if it want's to be a strategy game or a 2d action platformer. I think I would prefer it if it was played entirely like an RTS game and I could just pause the action issue commands to my troops where to move and which direction to cover etc. For a game which has been in development for such a long time, it seems that the developers have had no clear direction and rather than ending up with a solid game, have instead ended up with a digital identity crisis.

I finally got around to spending some time with Nex Machina and you know what, I wanted to like this as I had a great time with Super Stardust on PS3, PSP and Vita. But for the life of me Nex Machina just isn't fun. I think the problem is it tries to do too much in a very chaotic game. You have weapon power ups, ability power ups, stage secrets to find, humans to collect, secret humans to find, stages to navigate, obstacles to avoid all while legions of enemies are rushing at you with projectiles flying everywhere. What makes it worse is the dash sucks as it doesn't travel far enough (like in Super Stardust) and it isn't quite as responsive as one would expect (like in Super Stardust). I died so many times because I pressed the button to dash but apparently I was too close to an enemy when I did it because before the dash activated the enemy killed me. This happened with obstacles too. I approached a laser, dashed just as I got close to it but died anyway as if the dash invulnerability doesn't activate the moment you press the dash button. It sucks and feels like cheap deaths.
It's a shame really because I like the graphics and sound in Nex Machina but it plays like a dog's dinner because of the mentioned issues. Nex Machina just isn't much fun to play. It's not a difficult "rise to the challenge" type of game like Dark Souls, it's an annoying "this is some frustrating BS I don't need to be playing" type of game. I would enjoy it a lot more if the dash was more responsive and traveled a bit further, simplify the weapons and power ups making those that remain more effective (example, the smartbomb is a joke in this game and almost totally useless and a rocket launcher? Why?) and remember why Super Stardust is such a more enjoyable twin stick shooter. KISD Keep It Simple Dumba@@.

I always wanted to pick this up back in the day but never did.  Was suprised to see it released today and for that price said what the hell.  Upon starting it I saw the spiders (the developer's logo) and instantly knew it was the right decision.  After playing Mars War Logs last year, Bound by Flame, and then Of Orcs and Men (Co-developed by them I belive) I have come to the realization that they are probably my favourite RPG developer of the last couple of years.
So this game has a great atmosphere, and art style.  The music hasn't blown me away, whereas some of there other games have some great, sometimes, stuff.  No voice acting at all in this game FYI though that's ok.  The writing is not quite as smooth as some of their latest effforts but still humourous and charming.  All the NPCs have been entertaining so far, and the turn based combat is enjoyable.
Two of its strong points are the flying as a fairy which is a blast ziping across the map, hovering etc, all done very effortlessly by a couple of different ways either with the keys or mouse.  Also the character customization is unique and meaningful which really I believe is where Spiders are at the top of their game in all these RPGs.  The skill points you allocate are slotted at different body parts which both affect the way your fairy looks, male or female, and different skills like fire spells or lighting etc.  these then will branch and allow for other exclusive powers and then you can increase the level of each of these.
So yeah great spiders RPG character customization, engaging turn based combat, full flying exploration of the different levels, and a charming story about faerys and the dying of magic which lots of recognizable lore like Pan, mermaids, and the tree of the world.

Alright, so let's face it. A lot of the people who downloaded this game were looking to get a taste of FPS MOBA after Overwatch was released and became relevant - not a bad thing, really! Despite Paladins and Overwatch being in the similar genre, there are some mechanics which differentiate the games entirely. So let's get to it so that you can get a feel for the game before you try it out.
- Card System: Loadouts are combinations of 5 different cards that alter the champion's basic stats or alter their primary skills.
- Item System (during matches only): Similar to the card system, you buy items which alter your basic stats. These items can really determine your survival in a match or your effectiveness. [Quick Note: There are a handful of items, it might take a few games to learn the different effects of each item, read their descriptions before buying them]
- Lots of Champions: There are a variety of playstyles within each champion, therefore lots of people can find champions that suit what they want to do (whether it's throwing game changing ultimates, being at the enemy's face and play aggresively, or stand in the middle of the fight and take in damage for your team, etc).
- Champion Purchasing: Champions can be bought with gold aka the free in-game currency that one obtains via matches played or quests.
- Different Game Modes: There are three different game modes currently that have different paces.
- Game is in beta still after about a year and a half, so they might not feel rushed to fix certain bugs or server issues - it is very likely that you might experience a match crash and it will boot you to main menu... it is something you'll have to bear with. Sometimes this occurs frequently in a matter of a few games, and some times it won't happen at all.
Most matches tend to last 20-30 minutes. The least I've seen has been 10, and the most has been 40. This community is not as toxic either, but you might encounter a tryhard every fifteen games or so haha. Remember, it's a team game - therefore communication in your team is key. Use the chat system in matches to switch strategies and suggest items or priority targets.

1 – GENERAL
How to Survive is a Zombie Survival with crafting elements. When I've bought the game I thought it was more like a RPG, but now I think that is more like an hack and slash action game. That's immediate fun in my book.
Graphics are interesting for a top down game. We can clearly identify different classes of zombies. They are not the best I've seen, but they are quite good. All other elements are just ok, and I have some issues with some of the landscape that sometimes doesn't allow me to see my player.
Sounds are the worst thing of the game IMO, zombies sound like Muttley,♥♥♥♥♥♥Dastardly's dog in Wacky Races. Monkeys are simply annoying and parrots are just bad.
But we forget about that when we meet Kovac. The best character in the game. Badass as hell. Great voice acting from him.

2 – GAMEPLAY
I have some issues with mouse and keyboard controls, but they are completely ok when you get used to them, and after that I admit is not a bad PC port.
The game is a simple go there, and do that. Freedom of choice is not big, you have to follow the rules here.
Crafting is quite easy. Blueprints can give you a hand, but most of the time you can just press "combine" in your inventory and you will craft something useful. I could use more spots to collect since is hard to understand what is useful or not.
I've never felt that feeling of toughness in the game. You have to eat, drink and sleep, but every island provides you enough stuff for you to survive with small effort. Ofc I've only reached half way in the game, so this can be worse with progression.
It seems to me that the game has some replay value. It has different characters, different modes, different options to follow with skill tree.

3 – CONCLUSION
It was hard for me to get in the game. First 2 hours where a mess, but now I just want to keep going. The game is very interesting and fun. OFC it's not a AAA game, but is very common to be on sale, so is very cheap. Go for it!

Stellaris is a game that I really want to like but ultimately it comes up short. What we have here is an interesting game engine without much substance. All the game features are too generic. I don't find myself caring about any other factions. There's nothing that immerses me in the universe. I'm just playing around with generic templates with no real end game (there are late game "mega events" to try and mix things up but they are also rather bland).
Having played and loved EUIV I can sort of see how they might have ended making Stellaris like this. There are similarly generic mechanisms in EUIV but the trick is that the terrain (i.e. Earth) and the real world history behind each nation provides enough flavor and differentiates the otherwise generic cookie-cutter nations. In Stellaris, there's no terrain, just a big open space with stars scattered around, and the other races have nothing to make them stand out as memorable in any way.
At best this feels like a proof of concept for a game engine that could be used to make a compelling game. Whether they knew that and are relying on modders and/or DLC or if they just didn't realize the shortcomings is unclear to me.

Make no mistake, this game is still an early access product. In its current state, it is unfinished, poorly documented, and counterintuitive.
At first glance it seems like it stays true to the classix 4x formula of master of orion and others like it. Then it goes beyond handholding and straight into handcuffing the player. You are initially limited to direct control of 5 planets. Any more than that and you are required to assign them to an AI managed sector, in which you have precisely zero control over building or upgrading. While this is nice as an option for those who prefer a macromanagement approach to such games, forcing people to use it is inexcusable and a slap in the face to players who prefer to micro, or even those who want to step in during a crisis that would be easily solved with a few timely building upgrades. Adding insult to injury is that calling the sector management AI such things as "unoptimized" is being diplomatic at best. Options are a good thing. But force a player to use a tool, and it is no longer a tool but a constraint.
Then we get to stations. The most common station you will be building in this game is a mining station, armed with a single weapon that on paper upgrades as you research new tech in that weapons category. In practice, that only applies so far up the tech tree as the newer weapon types fall into different categories, so the automatic upgrade doesnt apply to the stations default weapons. This would be fine if you were allowed any kind of control over the design of your most commonly built installation, but you arent. By midgame you are stuck with systems full of outdated, vulnerable resource production stations that are the backbone of your economy and research, critical to your survival, and yet completely impossible to update to current tech! Paradox could learn a thing or two about proper unit design options from Malfador Machinations and thier Space Empires series.
So if the main focus of the game is on macro level strategy, wars must be really spectacular, right? Well, not so much. You cannot simply declare war on another race or empire, you must declare war goals, and good old fashioned extermination is not an available choice. In fact, depending on your peoples ethical traits, you may not even be able to destroy an empire at all, even one that has sworn itself to your extinction. Instead you may make them a vassal empire, which has all the management issues of a sector with the added bonus of being full of a people that likely despise you and can rebel against you at any moment. There is, as far as I can find, no way to alter or sidestep these ethical traits mid-game. so much for the hard choices and social and political evolution that make up a big part of what "space opera" means.
Graphically the game is pretty. I would not call it impressive, but the graphics do the job. Sure its cool to see a mass of ships in realtime slinging an amount of missiles at the enemy that would give a Robotech pilot pause, but that only goes so far and gets old fairly quick. Whats left is a game that is cumbersome to play, and seems to want to handicap and cut off the players options at every possible turn. Its playable, but only just, and doesnt really live up to the spirit of its predecessors. Longtime fans of the genre would be better served to look elsewhere.

The bad: This game has terrible tutorial, the controls feel awkward, for the life of me I can't find a website that explains what each tool / weapon does (How do I use the constructor? Why can't I cancel already given commands? Why does AI place blocks and not let me control them when I switch to other bots?) Maybe there's an answer for all of these, but the fact it's so insanely hard to find is what my main complaint is.
The menu doesn't explain much, the entire game feels like a beta (or alpha?)
The good: Great concept. Some game modes are very fun. Plenty of options to choose from for tools and weapons (if only I knew what each did or was.)
Overall: For the price of $2 it's not a waste of money for sure. But I'll be waiting for content / patches / wiki to come out before I can play any more. For now, it's a waste of time.

This is a bizarre game. I recommend it 100%. The weird thing is, I just can't play it for very long at a time, but I don't see that as a negative. It was the same with really good arcade machines back in the 80s, and this is like an 80s arcade machine from Heaven. The pace is just right, and when you get into the hypnotic flow it starts to feel like you're reacting before you even decided to respond.
You beat blocks of levels which are collected as "worlds". I couldn't tell you how many levels are in one world: 15? 20? 30? I have no idea; they whip by so fast. If I tell you that a world takes an average 8.5 minutes to beat, even when you hunt for full completion of secrets, that's going to sound bad. But so much happens in those minutes!
I bought this, Jydge and Neon Chrome on the same day. I've put far more time into the latter two, and I really couldn't pick a favourite. Jydge and Neon Chrome have more hours in them, and they're easier to sit and play for a long session. Nex Machina is something I only want to play for about 30 minutes max, but I enjoy my time with it immensely. Of the three, it has the best action, the best graphics, the best design. But if you want hours per £/$/Euro, you might prefer another twin-stick shooter.
But sooner or later, you have to buy this as well. Of all the top-down shooters I've played, I consider this to be the best in its genre -- just highly concentrated.

You were not forced to make any decision, not missions, tasks, not even whether or not you should kill a boss. How many games give you such options? The game is a simple go there, and do that. Freedom of choice is not big, you have to follow the rules here.
Crafting is quite easy. Blueprints can give you a hand, but most of the time you can just press "combine" in your inventory and you will craft something useful. I could use more spots to collect since is hard to understand what is useful or not.
I've never felt that feeling of toughness in the game. You have to eat, drink and sleep, but every island provides you enough stuff for you to survive with small effort. Ofc I've only reached half way in the game, so this can be worse with progression.
It seems to me that the game has some replay value. It has different characters, different modes, different options to follow with skill tree.

3 – CONCLUSION
It was hard for me to get in the game. First 2 hours where a mess, but now I just want to keep going. The game is very interesting and fun. OFC it's not a AAA game, but is very common to be on sale, so is very cheap. Go for it!

Zombies on the other hand isn’t too bad, though it’s very limited as well. The packaged maps Kino der Toten and Five are both enjoyable, but with only two maps (not including the arcade mode) and little variation in enemy types, the mode becomes boring very quick. Yes, another game about zombies. But this one has different concept.
Basically you wake up on island full of zombies after crash and your goal is to survive.
You need to craft items, and manage hunger, thirst, and exhaustion, all while fending off the limitless hordes of bloody, brain-eating monsters hell-bent on your death.
For the first few hours of story mode, you're introduced to the core mechanics of the game like combat, crafting new items, gaining experience, leveling up, and all of the other basics of survival.
These strategies are communicated to you by tutorials left behind by a mysterious man named Kovac.
If you're hungry, you can kill animals for meat, which will rapidly fill you up. However, all meat must be cooked because the animals of the islands contain deadly parasites. Fresh meat also attracts zombies and places you at additional risk until you can pop it on a fire.
There are plenty of ways for the island to kill you, and you need to stave them all off at once.
Then night falls, and you start to have to use your flashlight to chase away even nastier horrors.
There’s a talent/skill tree you can fill in as you progress up through levels, and there’s a fairly wide-open crafting mechanic, where junk can be taped together into guns and so on.
You are fairly vulnerable, and can reduce incoming damage with various bit of armour.
Combat is fairly simple but requires reflexes and a bit of forethought when taking down large groups of zombies, else you're likely to get munched on. The left mouse button is a basic attack, while you use the right mouse button to aim more precisely with both melee and ranged weapons.
Missions begin simply: find a jerry can, fill it with gasoline, and seek out other objects that might help you leave the archipelago.
Small rowboats allow you to get between the various islands, but you need a more permanent and long-distance solution if you’re to escape entirely.
Crafting is the game's strongest point. Testing out which items can be combined often yields unexpected but strangely logical results and turning your home-made pistol into a shotgun or machine-gun.
While the game map is static, the appearance of most of the zombies is random.
There are challenge modes to help extend the experience a bit, each of which involves starting with an empty inventory and trying to reach an escape plane before you die.

As far as 4x games go, Stellaris is one of the best I've ever played.

Deus Ex is considered a groundbreaking game of it's time that explored new ways of immersing a player into its carefully crafted world.
Many of its gameplay elements have been implemented into modern day games; like health stats for individual body parts and how they impact your character (Fallout 3); and multiple pathways and class options like stealth, democracy, guns-blazing, to complete a level (BioShock, Mass Effect, Alpha Protocol to name a few).
Though the graphics are dated and some of the gameplay elements may be hard to get peoples heads around, the story is full of daunting politics and conspiracy theories that infatuate our culture, along with an atmospheric soundtrack composed to underline the dystopian-future theme.
I'd give the game on it's own a 8/10, but for how it broke new ground and made an impact on game development, it's a solid 10.
P.S: Don't let the first level give a bad impression of the rest of the game.

A golden age game with some typical golden age flaws:
- the lack of a decent map - a staple in modern games - makes some parts very frustrating, the aerial photos and blueprints you get in your quest notes are hardly an alternative.
- you actually have to look through your quest information and type passwords and codes, where modern games would just fill those out for you if you already know them.
- there are some balancing and learning curve issues.
but that shouldn't stop anyone from playing this game, in fact, some of them give it a flair that modern games don't have.
On the other hand:
- It has a really solid storyline, right up until the end.
- It has fantastic level design that encourages players to imagine wild strategies to advance, and there are always several solutions to a given problem.
- You have tons of great gadgets and cyberpowers.
- It's an RPG that's better than most stealth games and a very good first person shooter too (this depends on how you want to build your character).
To me this is still easily the best cyberpunk RPG ever made. Better than its sequels, better than the System Shocks that inspired it, and vastly superior to the Bioshocks that should have picked up the batton, but turned out to be surprisingly easy linear first person shooters with some tiny RPG elements.

The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings Enhanced Edition
Summary: The second installment in the RPG saga about the Witcher, Geralt of Rivia, features a thoroughly engrossing, mature storyline defining new standards for thought-provoking, non-linear game narration. In addition to an epic story, the game features an original, brutal combat system that uniquely combines tactical elements with dynamic action. A new, modern game engine, responsible for beautiful visuals and sophisticated game mechanics puts players in the most lively and believable world ever created in an RPG game. A captivating story, dynamic combat system, beautiful graphics, and everything else that made the original Witcher such a great game are now executed in a much more advanced and sophisticated way.
Great story, great gameplay, and a great soundtrack, something you find rarely in current games. This game sets an example for any Role-Playing Games out there. It has a nice, flowing combat system with exciting gameplay. The story is very interesting, well written, and very mature. This game is not like many other competitors, in that it is very non-linear. Many current Role-Playing Games, to date, have a very linear and boring story line. I have not encountered any flaws with this game and recommend it to anyone who is interested in a mature, compelling game
Combat is just as important as story in an RPG, and it is here that The Witcher 2 breaks from convention. Fighting is slightly free-form, so you can unleash sword and magic combos similar to Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning. You can focus on one enemy at a time, but you can also move from one enemy to another without breaking stride. Even though you can't dual-wield, your two sword types are important; silver swords are only effective against monsters while basic steel is good for everything else. Unless you're playing the game on easy, blocking is an important part of the combat system, whether it's straight parrying or unleashing counterattacks. Disposable items, such as bombs and traps, can help you handle large crowds.
What makes this different from other combat systems is the emphasis on preparation. Going into the quick menus only slows down time, not freezes it, so enemies can hurt you badly if you sit there and try to decide on your weapon loadout. The same goes for potion use, since you need to enter a meditative state to conjure and drink potions. The use of potions is also limited since everything you make has a toxicity level that must be purged from your body before you can drink again. Especially in higher difficulty levels, preparing your arsenal is the best defense against seeing "game over" screens.
In between the combat, cut scenes and side-quests, you can partake in a few minigames, though most are only available at certain points and locations in the story. In arm wrestling, you try to keep your cursor in an ever-shrinking area to best your opponent. Fist fights are controlled by Quick Time Events (QTEs) instead of normal combat, so there's little to no say over whether you're unleashing an attack or performing a counterattack until you hit the button and see a cut scene. Both give you the opportunity to earn more money, but since they both fail to be exciting, you'll likely skip these events. A more interesting minigame is dice poker, which can also be played for money. Played with five standard dice, your objective is to roll a better hand than your opponent with a hand system similar to regular poker. Though the game is based more on luck than skill, it is more engaging.
Then there's the Arena, a side game mode where you face off against wave after wave of enemies in an enclosed area. The waves increase in variety and difficulty, forcing you to apply some tactics instead of relying solely on brute force. Alas, you can't take your current character into this mode, nor can you take this version of Gerald into the story, but you level up quickly enough that you can use this as a "preview" of your upgrades prior to continuing to the main story. Between rounds, you can buy items and potions and hire others like a dwarf, knight or sorceress to help keep enemies under control. Considering that it comes with online leaderboards, it makes for an interesting diversion if you're hungry for combat.
Of the minigames and side modes, the most surprising one is the tutorial. Unlike most games, the tutorial in The Witcher 2 places you on a separate mission instead of the first mission, so those who skip it won't miss anything crucial to the story. The tutorial is quite lengthy and necessary if you want to learn the ins and outs of the controls and battle system, but it is flawed. First, the tutorials don't let you perform any actions in a timely manner. The game gives you the instructions on-screen, but you have to wait a few seconds before you can perform the action, creating a disconnect due to the mandatory waiting period. Second, no matter how well you perform in this section of the game, continuing on to the story will always place you on Easy. Even though you can change this to anything but the two highest difficulty levels, it feels demeaning that anyone who tries the tutorial always gets placed at the lowest difficulty level.
On a side note, the game package is rather impressive. For the price of the standard game, you're given a soundtrack and paper map of the land. You're also given a quest handbook that tracks down the main quests from every chapter as well as all of the side-quests. It's useful stuff, and considering that most of this would have been locked away with pre-orders or through a special edition (though one still exists with even more physical goodies), it shows that the developers appreciate their fans.
The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings - Enhanced Edition is a game that lives up to the hype. The story and game come off as more mature than other similarly rated games. The combat is rewarding, and the completely alternate paths and side-quests provide more than enough incentive to replay the game once you finish it. The sound is masterfully done, and the graphics show that, even with a few flaws, developers can pull off some magic with this old hardware. Both RPG and action lovers will be more than satisfied with this very entertaining title.

TLDR: Super fun game, played with 3 other buddies so we had a fuill game. There are a decent amount of characters to choose from with unique skills. Also character had some type of chemistry with one another if using their skills correctly. We got super competitive, brought out some booze and had a great night. Played for 4 1/2 hours straight.
Real review:
I've had this game for super long and my friends and I haven't had the time to come together to try it out until recently. We were able to pick it up very quickly as the concept of the games and skills/items were very straight forward. Every game led to finding something new about the characters or the pairs of them together. The versatility of what type of fighter you want to be was easy to switch around through skill orders and the items you bought. The full potential of the game definitely came in when we had 4 players (2v2). My friends and I were communicating throughout, calling out objective or to focus down the enemy and so on. The game is quite simple but complex at the same time which made the replay value so high.
I understand this game is still under early access but the balancing of this game defintely needs to be reworked though. We ran into characters (mainly albert) that was completely useless in all situations of the games, and found that freya was super overpowered if you max out here trees first, which could be maxed averaged at round 3. We found counters for the over powered skills and combos in the game, but it soon became a rock paper scissor match, which definitely showed the imbalance imbetween characters, damage scaling or items.
Theses games are definitely made strictly for a team game, because when we tried 1v1, we found that it didn't take as much skill or just seemed very dull in the 1v1 aspect. (Race is the best example of that) Along with that, race just didn't seem like a good game mode, maybe it has to be reworked to make it less one tracked mind?'
Aside from all that, I really hope the game is still under works and does come out with patches and releases with in the 1 - 2 months time as it says.

2v2 Tournament (League) mode is highly strategic and seems to be the core of the game. It basically blends elements from a variety of genres into a round-based competive party game. Unfortunately, 1v1 means you miss out on the team based strategy elements and didn't seem quite as interesting. 1v1v1 (and presumably 1v1v1v1) was a bit more interesting, but can't really compare to 2v2.
I've only played a small amount of Survival mode so far. My gut feel is that it won't ever measure up to 2v2 League mode (which sets the bar pretty high), but should be interesting enough, particularly if you don't have enough players or just want to play co-op.
With the right marketing (and perhaps a bit of luck) I can definitely see 2v2 League mode becoming an extremely popular e-sport - get on it now!

The cut and bruised woman was begging for help telling them that she had been in a car accident and that her husband and son, a new born baby, were still inside the car which was in a deep ditch. She told them that the husband was already dead but that her baby seemed to still be alive.
The husband that was traveling decided to get down and try to rescue the baby and he asked the hurt woman to stay with his wife inside the their car. When he got down he noticed two people in the front seats of the car but he didn't pay any attention to it and took out the baby quickly and got up to take the baby to it's mother. When he got up, he didn't see the mother anywhere so he asked his wife where she had gone. She told him that the woman followed him back to the crashed car.

That said. I did originally buy this game thinking I'd get to play as a dinosaur in a meaningful way.
The modes where you can are not very interesting and seem unfinished.

You don't have to agree with the pricing of the cosmetic DLCs but the content updates so far have been fantastic and the upcoming patch looks like it will catapult the game even higher on the awesomeness-scale.
I couldn't help but nominate this for the "Just 5 more minutes" award and am looking forward to my December vacation to spend even more time conquering the galaxy.

TLDR: If you love The Witcher series, even if you only played The Witcher 3, then I recommend you buy this game. I give it a 6.5/10 by 2017 standards, but by 2011 standards this must be a 9/10
As someone who (maybe unfortunately) started at the end of the series by playing The Witcher 3 first, I can say that this game is a considerable leap backwards. The controls are clunky and sometimes annoying, the swordplay is vastly inferior, there's this annoying thing where walking through doors is a cutscene, and for whatever reason I have no desire to keep scrolling through the poorly designed menus in this game.
That said, however, this game really is gorgeous to look at (as long as you bear its age in mind) and so far has me hooked into the story and right back into the world that I fell in love with in The Witcher 3. The storytelling of The Witcher series is somewhat legendary and this game is no exception. I am constantly having to keep myself from Googling the characters in case I spoil something for myself.
At the end of the day, all of the shortfalls of this game are very easy to overlook, and none are gamebreaking in any way, just mildly annoying at first. I definitely recommend that you buy this game if you are debating it. Even if, like me, you started with The Witcher 3 and are worried about going backwards, trust me that you will not lose any love you have for the series. If this game is on special like it was when I bought it, then this is an absolute no-brainer. The value for money is insane.

: A key for this game was provided by the developer for the purpose of writing an unbiased, informative review. No other compensation was given.
==========
Dungeon League is a hack n' slash co-op dungeon crawler in the theme of a TV show. Your goal is to fight through seemingly endless hordes of monsters all the way down to the bottom level of the dungeon and defeat the Dungeon Master. So far, the game only has Local Co-op, which is somewhat of a letdown, but there is a chance online multiplayer will be added at a later date. Fans are certainly rallying for the devs to add it!
==========
There are several game modes for Dungeon League: Tournament, Gauntlet, Survival, Dungeon Ball, and Free Play. Tournment is the standard mode, pitting 2-4 players against a series of random objectives in a monster filled dungeon. Gauntlet is similarly for 1-4 players, throwing waves of monsters at players. Survival is described as endless waves of monsters....simply last as long as you can! Dungeon Ball is a sport of sorts, where the objective is to defeat monsters and get the ball to the endzone. Lastly, Free Play is simply....you and your friends in a room with monsters spawning every so often. Only Tournament and Free Play are available for play now, with the rest of the modes coming soon.
When you choose a mode, you get to choose from 4 teams. They all have a name, but they simply assign your heroes a color. Once a team is chosen, you have 6 All-Stars (Champions) to choose from. Each All-Star has their own unique abilities and playstyle. For example, Reginald is a sword and shield bearing knight, whose shield occasionally blocks frontal attacks.
Each All-Star has their own unique skill set, each assigned to a key or button. These skills are obtained by obtaining Skill Points, which are earned by leveling up. As you clear stages of the dungeon, you earn experience for all of your kills. You can spend your skills points any way you wish, up to 3 per skill (this i sthe maximum rank). The more points you invest in each skill, the more powerful or useful that skill becomes. This is extremely important for survival, so make sure you spend those points!
Lastly, there is a shop. As you battle your way through the dungeon you will pick up loads of gold. This gold can be spent in the shop between matches. The shopkeeper typically keeps several items up for you to purchase, but you can bribe the NPC to change the pool of items you can choose from. The more you bribe, the more it costs. Each All-Star can equip up to 2 items. Item have different effects, such as increasing HP or movement speed, or something more substantial such as giving a chance for a lightning attack when struck in combat.
==========
Everything is pixel-based. Not a ton of effort was put into the look of the game, but it still looks good. The characters have simple animations, and enemies are distinguishable enough. Attacks have some animation as well as All-Star abilities. Not much though. The general look and feel of the game is pretty good, but everything else can use a little bit more work. It's Early Access for a reason I suppose!
==========
The game's soundtrack is pretty pumped up for what it is. Like the look of the game, the music can use a little bit of work as well. Sound effects are pretty good, as well as the limited voice work each All-Star has. An example would be Reginald's cyclone attack, where he might say "Helicopter!", which is hilarious. Enemies also have limited voice work, like Minotaurs saying "Mooooooo!" when damaged or dying.
==========
Dungeon League ran extremely well on my mid-tier rig. 60+ FPS was observed constantly. The game also has full controller support, which is a plus in my book! No stuttering, lag, slowdown, or random crashes were observed.
==========
Dungeon League is a fun co-op game that can use some extra features and polish. It's fun, but lacks online multiplayer. Once online multiplayer is added, it'll be one heck of a party dungeon crawler game. Hopefully more time in Early Access will see this feature added at a later date!

Petrichor is one of those Rpg-maker games that make all Rpg-maker games look terrible and lazy. I'm actually a fan of Rpg-maker and I still can't figure out how this has positive reviews overall.
The game is about three minutes long for one playthrough and twenty minutes for all of them. In its short time, Petrichor frequently crashes and glitches. On top of that, it has abysmal writing. The dialogue feels childish and emotionless. The game is also filled with typos. It seems like almost every other sentence had a typo. Not to mention you can choose to date a man but the dev never changed the dialogue so you are constantly calling your boyfriend "she" and "her."
The story is about the protagonist recalling his life to his new therapist. The multiple endings are based on the choices you make throughout the game. Of course, this leads to an uninspired and cliche 3 minute playthrough.
If you are looking for a +1 in your library then this is the game for you. If you are looking for a good story, realistic characters, serviceable dialogue, or overall entertainment, then I'd avoid this one.

This game has a lot of potential, it looks great and the gameplay is fluid and fun. As it is at the moment you will need to have friends to play with locally otherwise you likely wont get much playtime out of it, it currently has very limited single player and no online multiplayer. Also I would reccommend you use a controller if you can as I'm not so sure about the keyboard support at this time.
The positives:
The current playable characters are awesome and fairly well balanced, plus the developer has stated that he has plans to add more and more characters as the game progresses.
The multiplayer is quite competitive and loads of fun, game modes such as 'capture the flag' and 'capture the point' aren't too common in RPG style games but they work extremely well here.
The art style and animation is very well done, pixel art isn't for everyone but this game does it well and if you give it a chance I'm sure you'll come to like it.
A few things I noticed which need some attention:
First up - ONLINE MULTIPLAYER, this is a big one, this is a great game which could really strive but in my opinion a game like this NEEDS online multiplayer otherwise it could potentially die off very early. If this game incorperates some sort of online matchmaking/lobby system where you can play with your friends and/or randoms it could really take off.
Next up, the keyboard supports feels a bit weird, I almost immediately switched to controller. Giving access to the options so we can remap keys will mostly fix this I imagine however my biggest problem is that it just doesn't feel right, the menu scrolling can be laggy and sometimes pauses if you scroll too fast, i.e. you can't mash up or down to quickly select things because it will stop registering key presses or something. This isn't noticable while using a controller as far as I could tell.
Another thing that I noticed is the free play mode could do with a bit of work, I tried playing on level 1 and was just getting mauled and dying instantly as soon as I respawned because it seems like the monsters don't scale to your level or anything like that. Free play isn't a big focus of the game and you can set your level higher to make yourself stronger so this is a minor issue but more options such as difficulty or number of enemies couldn't hurt.
Hopefully I can improve this review over time but overall I'm really liking the game so far, I just hope that online multiplayer is implemented soon, the developer said he's open to it just as long as there is a demand, so get on it people, let him know you want it!

I don't normally review games unless I wanna give my two cents but this game? I have to, it's mixed review rate just isn't right. That being said, let's actually review this game and the whole one hour I put into it.
I know one hour doesn't seem like much but to me it was enough to review most of this game.
This game is like a weird mix of Burnout and GTA without being able to get out of your vehicles, it's a lot like Starsky and Hutch for the PS2 minus the guns, that game was a blast with a steering wheel and light gun. c:
I bought this game for $0.99 and just recently saw it was a giveaway by Bundle Stars so I put it on my family account as well so my family could play it and it also reminded me that I should give it a try and I did.
The actual review:
Pros:
+Semi-realistic vehicle handling and physics.
+Ability to use warning indicators and turn signals as well as your siren and lights and silent police lights(No siren.).
+Decent damage system.
+You can pretty much destroy everything on a city wide rampage in the semi with a trailer.
+Cheesy voice acting.
+Great looking for being 6-7 years old.
+Tons of video options and resolutions.
+Great input support, works with all my gamepads and of course an X360 pad and I believe it has steering wheel support.
+Stable, never crashed on me once and it runs great.
+Splitscreen racing.
+Manual and Automatic settings, gear shifting and more.
+Fun to slam AI around during missions that warrant it.
Cons:
-Sometimes terrible AI and the AI spawn system is completely borked, AI will spawn miles away from you sometimes in a mission where you have to be within a few metres of them and thus causes you to fail and must restart the mission from the beginning, there are no checkpoints but most missions are pretty short. So try not to flip AI vehicles as a sort of fix.
-Cheesy voice acting, not completely a negative, it's sometimes pretty hilarious listening to the voice actors putting on fake accents and faking feeling and integrity in their lines.
-Not much depth to the game or story, but this game isn't really about story as it is gameplay.
-Some AI is incredibly difficult to take down and may take up to twenty minutes to take down a single car smaller and slower than your vehicle which is kind of realistic but also kind of annoying if you just want to be done with the mission.
-No online multiplayer and no splitscreen/online free roam/co-op.
Overall, my final verdict would be 7/10, the game has bad voice acting and poopy AI at times but the game is still rather fun especially to go on a rampage and destroy anything and everything. This game has been so far extremely solid for me, no FPS drops, no crashing and everything is maxed on my system while maintaining at least 60FPS at all times.
My suggestion: Wait until this game is like $3 or cheaper to purchase. It's mostly just one of those fun games to go back to and basically drive around destroying everything, taking out bad guys or leisurely strolling around and going with the flow of traffic and following road signs, etc.
It's like wine, gets better and better by time.

TLDR: If you love The Witcher series, even if you only played The Witcher 3, then I recommend you buy this game. I give it a 6.5/10 by 2017 standards, but by 2011 standards this must be a 9/10
As someone who (maybe unfortunately) started at the end of the series by playing The Witcher 3 first, I can say that this game is a considerable leap backwards. The controls are clunky and sometimes annoying, the swordplay is vastly inferior, there's this annoying thing where walking through doors is a cutscene, and for whatever reason I have no desire to keep scrolling through the poorly designed menus in this game.
That said, however, this game really is gorgeous to look at (as long as you bear its age in mind) and so far has me hooked into the story and right back into the world that I fell in love with in The Witcher 3. The storytelling of The Witcher series is somewhat legendary and this game is no exception. I am constantly having to keep myself from Googling the characters in case I spoil something for myself.
At the end of the day, all of the shortfalls of this game are very easy to overlook, and none are gamebreaking in any way, just mildly annoying at first. I definitely recommend that you buy this game if you are debating it. Even if, like me, you started with The Witcher 3 and are worried about going backwards, trust me that you will not lose any love you have for the series. If this game is on special like it was when I bought it, then this is an absolute no-brainer. The value for money is insane.

The grandfather of American arcade shooters, Eugene Jarvis, helped with development of this game. Imagine if Robo-Tron and Geometry Wars had a baby... and it came out looking like Resogun(PS4)...
Nex Machina is a fast-paced, twin-stick, shooter.  There are plenty of games like this on Steam.  However, this one stands in a leauge of its own.  It is a complete and well crafted package that, in my opinion, was worth every penny.
All the bells and whistles you'd want from a game like this are included; Online leaderboards, replays, unlockable modes and cosmetics.  There are tons of hidden secrets and power-ups.
The gameplay loop encourages experimenting to find the most optimal path through each level/enemy wave for maximum speed and scoring opportunites. So far, there appears to be 3 different worlds that consist of 20 or so "levels/waves", with a boss encounter at the end of each.
The worlds seem to be designed in a manner to be replayed multiple times with various modifiers/difficutlies.  It felt a little like a puzzle when trying to find the best way to approch each level/wave.  I actually enjoyed manually restarting the entire world if I died or failed to rescue a human.  It reminded me of doing time-trial laps in a racing game, with each subsequent attempt around the track I'd tighten-up my manuvers and find my ideal route.
I think this is one of the best "highscore" action/shooter games on Steam, and probably Housemarque's best work to date.  It's a shame that according to a recent public statement, they don't plan to continue making these types of smaller games in the future...

Unbalanced progression. I don't mind difficulty, infact I do like hard games, but there's usually a balancing act. When things get harder, there's things to mitigate the suffering; like better gear, better gold gain and better exp. Better gear is mostly drops, and the drop rate isn't particularly uncommon for gear. Gold gain does increase, but from like 10 to 20 (note that when you CAN buy gear again it's nearly 10k), and exp...oh boy.
Prepare to grind. Forever. Grind grind grind. That's the focus of this game. Your solution to everything is grind. Feel walled off? Grind. Want some of those better companions that some speak highly about? Grind reputation. Need certain drops? Farm to go with your grinding.
Now I don't mind some grinding, I can walk back and forth, get into battle and mash some hotkeys while I watch something; but the sheer amount of it is pretty ridiculous. Levels 1-12 is pretty fair and steady and then the exp towards next level spikes intensely, and it gets worse from there. Then it becomes some weird balancing act of what enemies you can handle vs exp gain. Even if the level cap is 30 or 32 or something, this can still be alleviated with some adjustments to the curve, or go the more modern mmo route and mask your exp grind with a quest grind so people feel like they're doing something while they gain exp.
Now I'm sure this was balanced more around the mmo aspect of teaming up with other players and using the market place to buy and sell stuff, but since the community is largely dead/small (you can see the occasional person on the main servers, or just go to devil's incarnate server) you can't rely on that. And even then, having the right party seems super important, so even if you rangle some buddies you can't really play what you want if you want to have a successful time.
That said I don't entirely hate this game. If it's every finished and/or has its amibitions realized, it can be a lot better. But from what I understand, the creator is preoccupied with health and life, which is perfectly understandable, but this also means any improvements are far over the horizon. So I can't really recommend it in its current state.
HOWEVER, if you get it on sale, give it a go. It's fine enough to get your money's worth off a sale price.

"YOU WERE WARNED"
...is what i'm saying to myself as I approach my 20th hour of playing this game. Because I read reviews explaining some of the game's many shortcomings and thought: "It looks fun. How bad can it really be? I'll cope."
To be clear: it's not that I feel I didn't get a good value for my money. On the contrary, for my ~$5, I got more "gameplay" than I can stand.
Lordy, this game drags on!
In most indidvidual aspects, it's of good quality. But, to the extent that "overall design" is an important aspect of a game's overall "quality", I am starting to feel that "overall" it's actually not great.
------------------------
FWIW I played "Iron Man" skill, (level 2 of 3, i.e. "Hard"), and played as Jack. (What follows may be spoilery, depending on your definition.)
First ~5 hours:
-- intriguing and captivating. "Yeah, this is going to be fun!"
-- Game teaches you its basic mechanics, you find/earn some basic weapons.
-- Don't have enough inventory space to pick up all the "cool" stuff I'm sure will come in handy, later.
5-10 hours:
-- "Phase II", the fun mid-game stretch where you are starting to feel more hunter than hunted, learning the maps/environments, getting good weapons, advancing the quests.
-- Exposure to new mechanics is starting to drop off but you don't care cuz you're "doing good".
-- Way more pick-ups than can be kept in inventory, so I resort to having gigantic stashes on the ground at a couple memorable locations. Game is starting to turn into "inventory administrator simulation". :|
10+ hours:
-- Urge to even play is already waning, mainly because I know the first thing I have to do next session is go round up the stuff I (think* I) need, from various locations, to advance my gear and quests. (In due fairness, it's not like I don't have a ton of other, better games to play -- and I have been! -- but... I was definitely fired up about this game when it was fresh, and I'm sad that the freshness wore off so fast.)  *but yeah, as it turns out, I may not have needed any of that stuff after all, as I explain below. But additionally there is one specific weapon they hint at which I have been expecting to craft for my last 3-4 play sessions, which .... I must have missed a lynchpin component somewhere along the line because no matter how many items I find along this certain "theme" and optimistically combine together hoping for a breakthrough that will let me build the weapon, nothing works. as I now near the end of the game, it's starting to look like I don't even need it anyway. :|
-- Sadly realize that the overall level of "depth" implied in the early stages of the game is not going to be borne out in the endgame.
-- Began one play session with the obligatory "character sheet check" to see how far I have to level up. (At least /that's/ something to be fired up about, right?) Bummed and surprised to find out I was at the level cap already, when plot-wise it felt like I was barely 1/2-way through. And the game is still throwing me more and "better" XP. I'd probably be 4-5 levels over the cap at this point. (Which coincidentally is right about what I'd need to max the skill tree. Not that I really care about the 80% of the skills anyway. No time for anything but passives. Early on, the game sets up this mentality of "scarcity" of materials, as well as scarcity of inventory. As such, I find the crafting-heavy skills in my character's skill tree totally unappealing. Not that I wouldn't relent and use them anyway, if the game required it of me, but it doesn't. I kill almost every single thing with my one wicked gun. I've thrown 2-3 molotovs out of boredom. And one explosive molotov I threw at a big pack cuz I thought it was going to kill everything and launch chunks everywhere. It didn't.)
-- No incentive to use or try new weapons or mechanics. The hardest boss enemies in the game are pretty easy to kill w/ my min/maxed build, and can also be glitched and killed harmlessly at least 25% of the time ... probably more if I really chose to refine my technique. (Are they really glitched or just stun-locked due, again, to my min/maxed build? IDK... IDRC.) Everything else is cake except the annoying electrical guys which can basically just be ignored if it comes down to it. Zero desire to carry around -- much less carry around the mats for, and actually craft -- any of the "advanced" items such as buff potions, quality food items, advanced ammunition, alternative weapons, etc. And for what it's worth, I can't see how, mechanically, playing on the hardest skill could really change things within the game's established framework in such a way to make me change my mind about the preceding choices ... at least not in a fun way. If the hardest skill means "you must use all this stuff constantly", well, that would just be nightmarish from a QoL standpoint. Pass.
-- Oh but wait! On the final 2 (extremely tedious) maps of the game, the designers decide to actually require you to pay attention to the basic biological survival-type needs that have been little more than a trivial annoyance through the whole game until now. But then they also throw you a couple bones to keep you from /being/ boned -- in a real "oops ruined my one-and-only checkpoint savegame" sense. (P.S., unrelated: sure glad I crafted this hazmat helm which says it's supposed to protect you in toxic gas environments, but doesn't actually seem to do so.)
--Start looking at the achievement list for spoilery indications on how to "best" proceed, cuz I surely don't want to have to play through this again if I miss anything. There appear to be two possible endings, and I'm also definitely going to look up if this is real or illusion, and if real, which one is preferable. Kinda sad. Again, if I could save/load on demand, I wouldn't have to worry about this.
-- At the moment, I'm more entertained by writing this review than by continuing to play. What more really needs to be said?
------------------------
A couple "positives":
-- After reviewing the achievements I see most of the ones I haven't earned yet concern other play modes/environments. Thankfully there is no "beat the story mode with all four characters" or whatever, cuz I couldn't deal with that. As it is, I'm hoping that beating the story on "Iron Man" will qualify me for the "Normal" achievement -- which is how any game designer who isn't a criminal against humanity does things.
-- The overall whole "fetch quest" design of the game doesn't really bother me. I mean .. what else is there? When you distill almost any game down to its raw elements, "fetch quests" are basically the way 99% of games add a strategic layer to whatever their core gameplay is. I mean .. I guess some "morality" quests with some actual RP would be OK, but ... probably not a big deal. Let's face it: most of the time those types of quests are trivial anyway, usually due to uninspired concepts/writing. Additionally, having a branching storyline would make it that much more often that I have to worry about "am I going to regret going through with this and be stuck with a f'ed up game because all I have is one stupid checkpoint save?!" So yeah, NTY I think.
------------------------
Finally, I have to explain that, with the caveats and cautionary anecdotes expressed above, I still *do* recommend this game. However, with Steam's messed-up review system, I feel compelled to choose "not recommended" because it is the only response that has a chance of moving the game's overall review score in the direction of "average" (or, actually "mostly positive") which is what it truly deserves. "Very positive" is going a bit overboard and anything above that is a pipe dream. Final score: "Worth $5 I guess, but could have been a masterpiece with more playtesting and dev love." (And on that note, I have to say: all the industry reviews are, as usual, totally suspect. They sound way too excited about a game that is, in actuality, pretty basic.)
