This game has potential but I am a little disappointed.
It's a space version of Civilization or a new take on Galactic Civilization. The game is a typical Paradox game, very complex with a cluttered UI, and I had to read a few guides online before figuring things out to really play it. The tutorial is somewhat helpful but if you just go by it, you'll miss a lot.
The start of the game, like any 4X, is interesting and you have to build up your home planet and search for others to colonize. This works reasonably well and you have to balance building mines/research stations with your ability to pay for them.
I quite like the upgrade system for buildings. I much prefer this to just having a new building that does a little bit more than the previous one. BE suffered from this. There were multitudes of buildings to construct, each with a different name and only small incremental benefits. Paradox fortunately didn't go this way - just upgrade your hydroponics farm for more food. Easy.
I'm not sure how I feel about research. You can't pick any technology you want or b-line for one. They are presented to you to choose from randomly. Some may only appear once and you may not see it again. Miss taking Cruisers, you may not get them again. It's a novel way to do things but I'd like the option to at least generally guide towards a technology. For example, if I'm going to war or am at war, you'd like to be able to get more military techs rather than just have them pop up randomly (get food tech when you need railguns). I'm reserving judgement on this one because it's not game breaking - I don't think.
Where Stellaris fails for me is at times it's like a Seinfeld episode - nothing happens. You just put it to fast/faster and wait for long periods. Sure you'll discover a new technology at first but a lot of them don't really convey a benefit other than being able to research the next technology. This compounds things as there's nothing to do. It's not like when you get a new technology you can do something with it (upgrade ships/buildings). Often, there's no immediate benefit and thus you wait. After a while, it takes a long time to get new technologies so again you wait. Diplomacy is pretty bland. The other races rarely contact you and I found not need to contact them as I had ample resources. I wish they were a little more interactive - ala Civ V. Sure Civ V's diplomacy was weak but they'd contact the player to ask for trades, open borders, etc and they had personality at least (if they were angry, you'd know). I really hope that Paradox can liven this up a little. It would make the dry periods in the game more interesting. Also, there's no really easy way to tell who's allied with who. I wish that these games would take a page out of Civ IV's book and have a screen that shows all the relationships - it did this really well. Also, like Civ V, Stellaris also doesn't give enough information in the diplomacy screen to evaluate offers. If a race is offering a defensive pact or non-aggression treaty I'd like to be able to easily see who they're allied with, who I'm allied with and if that will conflict with things. Again, Civ IV did this perfectly.
TL:DR/Conclusion: I think Stellaris has potential but as it stands now it's flaws (sometimes it's boring (nothing happens for good chunks of the game) – which is not a good thing in any game, researching technologies is sometimes frustrating, diplomacy is quite poor and has no personality) are significant enough that I can't recommend it. I hope that with some patches/DLC/expansions the game will evolve to become great.
Addenum: After the new patch and playing the game more, I recommend the game. It's come quite a ways in a little bit. The new Leviathains DLC is out (terrible timing - the same day as Civ VI - who's gonna buy the DLC or play Stellaris in the next month) but I haven't purchased it. Once I'm bored of Civ VI, in 6 months, may pick it up. From what I've read, it's adds a nice piece of gameplay/story to the game.
Would definitely recommend picking Stellaris up if your into spac 4X. If you just want 4X though, you have to consider Civ VI (the definitive Civ version) or pick up V if it's on sale.
That being said, Stellaris is probably the first 4X space game that has come closest to drawing me in like the Civ series has. Endless space was good too but it wasn't as approachable as Stellaris.

At first glance, this game may seem simple; however, it's anything but.
You start off with simple levels and enemies, collecting items that will help (or sometimes harm) you, getting you ready to fight progressively tougher enemies. Each time you go to the next level, you are met with different enemies, and all new opportunities to get items. And just when you think you've beat the game...you haven't. I'll let you figure out what that means.
The items, enemies, rooms, and level layouts are completely random, so you will likely never have the same exact experience in this game twice. Unlocking new characters adds to the experience, as each one has its own benefits and setbacks, making the game easier in some ways and harder in others. Because of the overwhelming amount of items and enemies, I'd always recommend playing with the wiki for the game open, just so that you never make a bad decision when it comes to picking up items. Still, some things in this game come with a learning curve and you'll just have to find out what items you like to use and which ones will make you rage.
It'll be frustrating at first, but once you unlock more items and beat your own personal records, you'll be addicted. Buying the Wrath of the Lamb DLC makes the game even tougher (so I suggest buying it after you have a good feel for the base game), but adds loads of new content, including enemies, items, levels, and more.
Honestly, I'd recommend this game to anyone I knew, even with all of the dark humor and blasphemous jokes. When you look past all of that, it's a great game with excellent replay value.

I recieved this for free from a site I found on reddit. While I of course like free games, I don't often also like playing them. As far as this title goes, I don't find anything special about this game, and in my opinion it is quite... uncomplete.
The graphics are decent at least, not great, but not bad either, and while they paid less attention to environment, cars are as shiny as they can be, which would make sense in a car game.
However the gameplay is where it takes a turn for the worse. The only storyline I've been able to gather is that you and a friend of yours are some sort of undercover cops who use a civilian car to catch. While there is no continuos gameplay, at least you have freeroam, and you can get random missions from the dispatch.
But let's see what the actual missions are about... well, chasing criminals, smashing their car until they come to a full stop. I have so many pet peeves when it comes to realism in this game that I can barely make myself write this review. Firstly, there are absolutely NO human animations. If the scenario makes your partner jump into a truck while you keep steady near it.... he just stays in the car, even though supposedly he is driving a truck now, even though he is still riding shotgun with you. Turning the wheel? No animation. Crashing recklessly in everything? No animations. The evil guy whos car you just totaled with nothing left other than the wireframe? No animation. What's more, you don't even arrest him. You just wreck his car (which takes a ridiculous ammount of bumping into) and then.. leave. And I guess he will just sit patiently idling (not like he has animations to begin with) in his carwreck until your fellow police officers arrive.
About the sound, not great either. The radio consists in a few metal instrumentals, which I can't say I dislike, but that's about it. No radio control, you always listen to the same tracks over. However that shouldn't be bugging you more than the total lack of talent in voiceacting. I'm not trying to bash the developer here. I didn't do my research, might as well be some guys in a basement, struggling to make their dream game but still... the voice acting is terrible. TERRIBLE.
All this being said, if you get the game from free from some random humblebudle-esque deal on the internet, go ahead and at least waste some time with this, however I would never recommend anyone actually paying money for.

Being honest with you, I bought this game 2 days ago. We are halfway in 2016 and the Call of Duty franchise is way past the point where I just stopped caring and I pretty much ignore the series after the Modern Warfare trilogy (Advanced Warfare was good though because of Kevin Spacey). Even back when Black Ops was new, I didn't care at all. Now, I say that I was right back then, but Black Ops is most certainly a game to play today, if you can pick it up for cheap.
I wanted a one day blast of a campign, that is linear, full of scripts and eyecandy, has a medicore story where the evil, evil, evil everyone in the world vs the good, good, good americans have a nonstop firefight until we kill some generic random russian (it always has to be russian, right?) bad guy.
Did it deliver? Absolutely. And I must say, even if the scripted scenes weren't anything special, the game had it's own great moments with adrenaline pumping, surprisingly modern drum n' base / rock music and good places to shoot bad guys on. The story's twist while after a point was easy to figure out and even after that it was explained like 5 to 10 times so every 13 year old can understand it, I must say was surprisingly good. Not that it is anything special, but it's nice to see that the franchise still can deliver something new storywise, even if it always comes down to USA propaganda and russians trying to destroy half the world.
The graphics definitly aged, some places badly, some still keep up with today's COD titles but even those are somewhat old even when they are new. The music was great, definitly lower the Effects volume and increase your master volume to have loud firefights and have loud music for them too, otherwise the music really gets lost behind effect sounds and it would be a shame because a lot of the cool-factor comes from it.
What else to say about singleplayer? Yes, it's still fully linear, yes, I died about 5 times trying to go back for a weapon left on the ground just to blow up for appearantly no reason (Vietnam parts mostly) after clearing the area. Did I have fun? Yes. It was well worth 5 euro for me.

Nex Machina is a very fun game, but if you use a mouse and keyboard, the unconventional aim system will take some time to get used to.
Instead of having crosshairs that the character aims at, there is an arrow which points in the direction in which the mouse was last moving. I don't think I've ever heard of any other game that does this. It feels like an unnecessary burden, and it takes a few hours to grow accustomed to.
Other than that, Nex Machina is an excellent game. The enemies feel more like a swarm than like bullet sponges; I'm a big fan of this decision. It just feels better to cut through clouds of 1-HP mobs than it does to take down a few larger ones.
None of the levels are randomly generated. I hadn't expected this at first, but I don't view it as a negative. The hidden levels and "beacons" take a few runs to find if you look for them on your own; I have no doubt that it would be extremely difficult to find all of them consistently in randomly generated levels. Even so, a random mode could be something I'd look forward to in a future update/DLC. There is a minor random enemy that appears every few levels to prevent automated play.
Levels are small, not taking more than a minute or two each to complete. Constantly being thrown into new levels gives the game a fast-paced feel.
The scoreboards allow viewing replays of top runs, and since the levels are pre-set, you can use these to help improve your own play.
The die-and-respawn system feels fair if you don't die too many times all at once. You gain five upgrades as drops as you kill a specific number of enemies, and you lose one as a drop when you die; if you can make your way back to it in time, you can reclaim it.
Overall I would rate Nex Machina 8/10. If there were a "normal" mouse aim mode, I'd increase this to 9-9.5/10.

I love this game, I really do. But it's not because of the awesome ship designs(which still REQUIRE a coloring feature) and the various species you can play as, but rather because of the little ways it brings the immersive part of your brain to life. If you try to play this in a roleplaying fashion, and not in the 'I named my plant species The Weed Bros lol' fashion, then you'll quickly find yourself coming up with snippets of everyday life in your homegrown empire. You'll think of all the conspiracy theorists on that frontier planet after your leader is mysteriously reelected for the fifth time(even if you just really need his fleet-building trait), you'll picture grand parades as your rookie admiral(who has the arm-chair commander trait) leads your fleet to victory and you'll be thrusted into a darkened conference room next to your fellow alien peers as they whisper about 'purging' those troublesome fanatical spiritualists who have been protesting on a planet rich in minerals vital to your fleet construction(causing literally no gameplay hindering effects other than a differently colored happiness bar).
I've never actually finished a game, my computer can't handle the armadas that everyone has towards the endgame, but I still keep making new games because I love the immersive value. There's more to just a game grid with a galaxy color scheme, there's more to planets than their sizes. The game doesn't pull you into an immersive experience, you won't even notice the transition.
For example, on my first playthrough I had a mining station on an asteroid in a middle of nowhere system. As I researched more and more, that asteroid turned out to hold a bunch of strategic resources. Lucky me, right? Then my neighbors, peace loving tapeworms, colonized a nearby planet and suddenly I no longer owned that asteroid. By this time I had found another exo-planet with equal value, but I went to war over this asteroid. The game refused to let me name the war, but I always refer to it as the 'War of the Rock'. The War of the Rock took twenty years, and saw the tapeworms lose twelve admirals before sneaking a fleet by my lines and bombarding my home planet. My population enraged and my key fleet-building station compromised, I gave my last admiral the divine blessings and ordered him to punch right into the tapeworm home system and lay waste. The War of the Rock resulted in a single asteroid's mining rights return to its previous owners and a Democratic Utopia crumble under the weight of rampant genoicde carried out by my vengeaful populace.
This is one possibility of interactions with an empire you encounter on the playing field. Gameplay wise, I could have conceded for economic reasons but I didn't. It wasn't a game then, and I still had 22 more Empires to interact with while the crime of genoicde hung over my empire. That's 22 potential space epics for you as well. And Paradox is doing all it can to help you make even more, because YOU'RE the storyteller in this one.
9/10, needs ship coloring and war naming. Oh wait; 11/10, makes up for it in endless entertainment derived from just staring at a planet grow and thinking of the horse colonists working side by side with robots and tentacled neighbors.

I've tried coming back to this game a few times over the years, starting way back when it first got mentioned in our little BYOND community. Each time I've been dissapointed.
-The player-base is small, with at most 10 people online at any given time. This means that many things you need for progression are simply impossible to get without devoting your own time and energy into crafting (in a poor crafting system) for hundreds of hours. The in-game economy is completely crippled because of this.
-The few players that do still play are either Admins or long-time players, none of which are friendly or willing to spend time playing with you.
-The admins can be outright abusive. Name-calling is common, as well as being banned for setting a server (hosted on your own computer) to private after banning individuals from joining. You need to hope that the person banned wasn't an alt account of an Admin, because you WILL become permabanned from all public servers, as well as having your account banned from logging in (and stopping your ability from hosting your own server.
-The last update was over nine months ago. What did it add? Alleged FPS improvements, which are not noticeable considering the immense lag (mentioned numerous times in other reviews) and DLC in the form of a soundtrack. Silk Games essentially only updated the game to milk a few bucks from their player-base, versus actually doing anything substantial to their MMO.
-The game lags heavily, regardless of your PC's specs or connection. It's an engine problem, and it hasn't been fixed in years. Even with 10 people on a server, or by yourself on a private server, you will suffer immense lag spikes and random freezes during encounters, rending it unplayable.
-The developer picks apart negative reviews without fixing the issues posted, many of which have been problems since release. I wouldn't be surprised if the same happens to my review.
-The game has effectively been abandoned. The last posted update was in September of 2016, and that was only to push a soundtrack DLC. The developer's Reddit account, Steam account, Facebook page, Twitter, BYOND account, blog and even website have all been abandoned since last year, with no updates posted or even responses sent to messages from customers.
It may be tempting to buy this on sale, but please don't. Your time is worth far more than that.
And let me respond to the developer, who elected to pretend problems don't exist instead of actually addressing issues:
"-"Crafting" is currently limited to creating simple weapon damage enchants, and isn't required for progression at all."
It's still an inaccessible part of the game, which means anyone who wants to min-max simply can't.
"-The Admins are not abusive, and are rarely even present on the official server. No one has been banned from the official servers since well before the game was released on Steam. Also, we don't care and don't pay attention to what happens on other public/private servers."
This is simply not true. Going through Steam reviews, BYOND forums and even the official forums confirms this.
"-Any online game will occasionally experience lag, but what you're describing here is a complete fabrication. The game is usually lag free and runs at 40 fps with no problems."
It is a legitimate issue that does happen. It's confirmed not just by me, but by other reviewers and people seeking technical support in the official forums.
"-The only time we've had players unable to login is when they've forgotten their account name or password, both problems that we're happy to help with."
Again, this is untrue, and again has been brought up in other reviews and the official forums.
"I'm not sure why you've taken the time to make this stuff up, but I've long given up trying to unpack the motives and actions of angry people and trolls on the internet."
The developer has been inactive on Steam and social media since the soundtrack update over nine months ago, and only came back to respond to my review. No word on updates, and no contact asking if these issues could be resolved. This game had the capacity to be great, and at one point was. Instead, legitimate issues with the game remain unfixed. The response by the developer wasn't, "here's a problem, how do I fix it." The response was, "I'm infallible so anyone who critiques my game is a troll." The very nature of an online game requires that it has an active developer, but the only action this game has seen in the past nine months is a developer calling their customers trolls.
I'm not sure why the developer continues to attack users with legitimate issues, especially considering that these problems have been happening for years. The developer can claim that there are regular updates and no server issues, but their own community as well as unofficial Discord, both of which have players who have struggled through the bulk of the game's lifespan, have complaints about the game's instability and the developer's dishonesty. There are a lot of 'Boo-hooers' and 'nay-sayers' in the review section because of a number of reasons over the course of this game's development. I won't say they're wrong to hold those opinions but I will say they're wrong for trying to sink this game when it needed their support the most. The game is fun, no one will deny that. I would even say $19.99 fun. I spent a lot of time messing with the engine, the scenarios and conquest modes and that was even before it was on steam. There's plenty to do and you can even do it with couch co-op. That comes standard. Then there's the modding and that takes you to a whole new level with added mechanics, ships, characters, factions. I highly recommend the game despite the rocky development due to a miscommunication between data realms and the consumers.
This was one of Steam's first Early Access titles as the video tries to describe. It wasn't a good move and many people starting blasting the game with negative reviews which hindered the game's development. Data Realms is a business and it costs money to run it so when the cash flow slows it becomes a vicious cycle of bad reviews, slow profit and slow development. I've been following the game since way back in early stages of development. I know about all the promises that couldn't be kept and sure it's a bummer, but at it's core it's still a great standalone game. The modding community is solid, the local play is solid. You're going to have fun and, since nothing can be done about the fanbase drama, that's all that matters at this point. Who knows with a resurgence of interest Data Realms could finally give this game the TLC it deserved Don't let the reviews sway you from a unique experience that no other game hits quite like Cortex Command. Enjoy the features it has now, then get pleasantly surprised if new stuff comes down the line.

If you get Monsti, you will see everything the game has to offer within the first 5 minutes. Then you might grind for a few hours to collect enough eggs to unlock all the characters, or just leave the game open to get all of the card drops. And then there is no reason to play Monsti ever again. The visual style and the music are very likeable (although there is only one music track on a loop, so beware when purchasing the soundtrack), which is why it is a shame that there is no game here. If Monsti was free, or a mobile game, it would be a great timesink for when you are at the doctor's office, but I see no reason to pay for this or to play it on a PC. There are only 2 levels, and the only difference between the two is the backdrop and the insane scroll speed on the Insane level. You get a highscore based on how far you fly before dying, but there are no leaderboards, and the game seems to encourage collecting eggs over surviving by constantly dumping piles of them in places that guarantee death. As far as I can tell, the Insane level is all but unplayable, which is also true for some of the characters which greatly speed up horizontal scrolling without adjusting the vertical speed of the character. This means that obstacles approach faster than the player can gain or lose altitude, and many of the obstacles become unpassable. The Normal level with the default character is at least playable, but there are constant audio glitches where some sound effects do not play at all, the obstacles are inconsistent in their design and it is not always obvious whether something will kill you or not, and the egg spawns are totally random, which means that they are often inside walls or in other unreachable places. As a result, Monsti just feels like an unfinished free game that the developer decided to charge money for.

The Binding Of Isaac is an flash indie game developed by Edmund McMillen and Florian Himsl. The game’s storyline and name are both a reference to the Biblical story known also as Binding of Isaac. In the game, the player controls Isaac, a child that seeks safety in the basement after his mother is given a message of God commanding her to sacrifice her own son in order to proof her faith. In the basement Isaac starts going through dungeons located in the basement having to face his nightmares in form of monsters, in order to escape.
The style and game’s gameplay are inspired by Legend of Zelda series and similar to roguelike, where the rooms of all dungeons are randomly generated, being different each time you play, and this is what makes it so special because every gameplay is totally different. On each floor of the basement, the player must kill monsters in order to proceed to the next room. Along the way, it will be possible to collect keys weapons and power-ups which will increase your chance of surviving because each item has a special effect and you can also pick up coins which are used to buy items in shops spread all over each floor, but need a key to be opened.
Each floor of the dungeon ends with a boss room, where a boss must be defeated in order to proceed to the next floor. Each time the bosses are different. At loading screens between floors, Isaac remembers scenarios, of his childhood while crying in fetal position, from rejection of his mother, unlucky moments and even bullying from his friends, some can even be Isaac’s own fears, but you’ll never know.
The gameplay is easy to master since does not require very buttons and the soundtrack is not diverse, but it does fit very well the atmosphere of the game.
One of the most awesome features of this game, in my opinion, and because due to flash limitation, it’s not possible to save, all your unlockables will stay unlocked and such, but you cannot save mid-game, so you will have to start over every time you go back to main menu, every time you lose and every time you close the game. And that is what makes it so hard and enjoyable since you will not get bored because every time all will be different and new!
A DLC to the game was also released, “Wrath of the Lambs”, also a religious reference, and it adds all new content including new items, new rooms, new enemies, new bosses and its totally worth it!
This game has me craving for more every time I play it, the creativity of it is amazing and it will make you spend some good long hours playing it. I totally recommend you to get it.
~ 9/10

Being honest with you, I bought this game 2 days ago. We are halfway in 2016 and the Call of Duty franchise is way past the point where I just stopped caring and I pretty much ignore the series after the Modern Warfare trilogy (Advanced Warfare was good though because of Kevin Spacey). Even back when Black Ops was new, I didn't care at all. Now, I say that I was right back then, but Black Ops is most certainly a game to play today, if you can pick it up for cheap.
I wanted a one day blast of a campign, that is linear, full of scripts and eyecandy, has a medicore story where the evil, evil, evil everyone in the world vs the good, good, good americans have a nonstop firefight until we kill some generic random russian (it always has to be russian, right?) bad guy.
Did it deliver? Absolutely. And I must say, even if the scripted scenes weren't anything special, the game had it's own great moments with adrenaline pumping, surprisingly modern drum n' base / rock music and good places to shoot bad guys on. The story's twist while after a point was easy to figure out and even after that it was explained like 5 to 10 times so every 13 year old can understand it, I must say was surprisingly good. Not that it is anything special, but it's nice to see that the franchise still can deliver something new storywise, even if it always comes down to USA propaganda and russians trying to destroy half the world.
The graphics definitly aged, some places badly, some still keep up with today's COD titles but even those are somewhat old even when they are new. The music was great, definitly lower the Effects volume and increase your master volume to have loud firefights and have loud music for them too, otherwise the music really gets lost behind effect sounds and it would be a shame because a lot of the cool-factor comes from it.
What else to say about singleplayer? Yes, it's still fully linear, yes, I died about 5 times trying to go back for a weapon left on the ground just to blow up for appearantly no reason (Vietnam parts mostly) after clearing the area. Did I have fun? Yes. It was well worth 5 euro for me.
I do not care about zombies or the traditional multiplayer, but since it is exactly the same since Modern Warfare 1, you know what you are getting if you buy it for competitive.
It's okay I guess.

Very good Dinosaur Horde game even though there are other modes most players choose to play either survival or conquest. There are three classes in the game and each has a special ability the Assault class has a jet pack that allows him to go reach higher areas easier than other classes, the Support class has a healing gun that should be self explanitory although with a certain upgrade it can damage enemies and repair turrets, vehicles, and generators, and the Recon class can go you guessed it invisible. Gameplay is nice no glitches unless you have a bad internet connection so check your connection before you play any mode. Weapon choice is decent in this game with one assault rifles, two sub machine guns, two light machine guns, two shotguns, two melee weapons, three sniper rifles, and a plethora of pistols which can be bought in temporarily in any game mode and if you die you lose them but if you remember where you died or you use a custom made loadout from the weapons you've unlocked. Now onto the special weapons better known as (to seasoned players at least) adrenaline weapons which can be unlocked each class has two and a universal adrenaline weapon that can be used by all three classes which is a bow yeah a bow what are the odds; The assualt can use a grenade launcher and a rocket launcher, support can use a flamethrower and a chain gun, and the recon can use a laser rifle and a energy carbine. Customization is really the only low point in the game unless you have money with the choice to only change the skin of a weapon when you start the game you have two armor and weapon skin colors black or purple you have to buy more aromor and weapons skins except for one for that one you just have to get 75 achievements for it. There are helmets in the game with one being unlocked after getting 50 achievements but like the armor and weapon skins they have to be bought as well. Taunts are in the same boat as weapon and armor colors so yeah it's more of a pay to look good kind of game. The community in the game is also very quiet not many will use the in game chat function but no one will randomly start insulting someone so it's about 50/50. Final Verdict a 7/10 for hours of fun in survival and conquest, decent weapon choice, and the fact that when a class reaches level 60 that class has unlocked every weapon that is best suited to them do this for every class and you will have 10 weapons unlocked and ready to use for any class it loses points for mediocre community, low customization, no story what so ever, and the fact that you can't unlock every weapon

Probably the finest game ever created.  Deus Ex is a conspiracy-driven, atmospheric first-person RPG title with remarkable story across a stunning array of locations from New York to Hong Kong. You play JC Denton; an American Special Agent stuck in a corrupt world of terrorists, disease and economic carnage. The game introduces itself in Liberty Island, New York where the city has been infected by a man-made virus set to wipe out the underclasses. Terrorists have hijacked a shipment of highly sought-after vaccine which has sent Manhattan into meltdown as people drop dead as they surrender their lives to the virus. As you begin your quest to restore order; you have to find the people who were behind the attack but also determine who and what caused the disease and more importantly why...
13 years on; this game outshines even the most ambitious modern day titles. The script is phenomenal, the characters are memorable and intriguing and the music is some of the best seen in a videogame. This is not a linear title either; you have considerable control in your actions with many various ways to complete objectives and affect outcomes.  This concept is largely unseen in today's bland offerings.
The inventory system is simple but smart and ensures tough decisions on what you can carry. The XP points and augmentations can improve your character's abilities from hacking computers to general combat and movement. The RPG elements are extremely well implemented in this game and the interface is very user friendly.  The combat mechanics may feel a little ropey and dated but the positives outweigh anything negative you may notice.
At any price; this game is worth getting as it stands tall against even the most elite games of this generation.  One of the finest titles in living memory and Deus Ex will live on for decades to come.

Assassins of Kings does everything a good sequel should do: improve on just about every aspect of the original. Combat is streamlined, doing away with the specific light/heavy/group enemy attacks, instead going for a combo of light and heavy attacks along with an adrenaline bar for group attacks, supplemented by rolling, parrying, and the full complement of signs (spells, magic) available from the very start of the prologue. What makes it really work is that it's skill based; if you don't learn to dodge and when to get your hits in between theirs, you will die. A lot. On normal. Even in the prologue. ESPECIALLY in the prologue. The good news is that once you learn the basics of combat, as well as pick up a few skill points, the game becomes significantly easier.
Outside of combat, level progression is fantastic as ~90% of the xp earned in the game comes from quests, with the quests making sense without holding your hand the whole way. For example, in Chapter 1 you get a contract to kill nekkers, where you have to go kill nekkers to learn how to dispose of them more permanently, and then craft bombs to drop at certain points in the environment to block tunnels so that they stop spawning. It takes simple "go kill this" quests and adds organic layers so that you actually get to go do some real monster hunting!
As for the story, it continues slightly after Witcher 1 and gets super heavy into politics pretty quickly. It is on rails for almost the entire thing, with a hub town/area for each Act, a handful of people to talk to, and a handful of areas to explore. Nothing super spectacular, similar to the first game, and it leads to the plot advancing fairly quickly. The plot itself picks up a lot of speed towards the end of the game and really brings everything together to make the world and a lot of events more understandable.
It's a small thing, but money is relatively scarce in this game, which is absolutely fantastic, as opposed to most RPGs where you end the game with 100x more money than you could ever find a use for. I believe it can be a pain for crafting the best of the best items on the hardest difficulties, which is where careful planning beforehand can be required for money allocation.
All in all, Witcher 2 improves on the interesting topic that was the original Witcher, and is a fantastic game in it's own right. Combat is fun and rewarding, but can be a stiff wall to climb in order to progress. I would give it a 8.5/10, definitely worth buying right away and that $2.49 price tag on sale is perfect for buying it and forgetting it exists for the next 5 years.

I love this game, I really do. But it's not because of the awesome ship designs(which still REQUIRE a coloring feature) and the various species you can play as, but rather because of the little ways it brings the immersive part of your brain to life. If you try to play this in a roleplaying fashion, and not in the 'I named my plant species The Weed Bros lol' fashion, then you'll quickly find yourself coming up with snippets of everyday life in your homegrown empire. You'll think of all the conspiracy theorists on that frontier planet after your leader is mysteriously reelected for the fifth time(even if you just really need his fleet-building trait), you'll picture grand parades as your rookie admiral(who has the arm-chair commander trait) leads your fleet to victory and you'll be thrusted into a darkened conference room next to your fellow alien peers as they whisper about 'purging' those troublesome fanatical spiritualists who have been protesting on a planet rich in minerals vital to your fleet construction(causing literally no gameplay hindering effects other than a differently colored happiness bar).
I've never actually finished a game, my computer can't handle the armadas that everyone has towards the endgame, but I still keep making new games because I love the immersive value. There's more to just a game grid with a galaxy color scheme, there's more to planets than their sizes. The game doesn't pull you into an immersive experience, you won't even notice the transition.
For example, on my first playthrough I had a mining station on an asteroid in a middle of nowhere system. As I researched more and more, that asteroid turned out to hold a bunch of strategic resources. Lucky me, right? Then my neighbors, peace loving tapeworms, colonized a nearby planet and suddenly I no longer owned that asteroid. By this time I had found another exo-planet with equal value, but I went to war over this asteroid. The game refused to let me name the war, but I always refer to it as the 'War of the Rock'. The War of the Rock took twenty years, and saw the tapeworms lose twelve admirals before sneaking a fleet by my lines and bombarding my home planet. My population enraged and my key fleet-building station compromised, I gave my last admiral the divine blessings and ordered him to punch right into the tapeworm home system and lay waste. The War of the Rock resulted in a single asteroid's mining rights return to its previous owners and a Democratic Utopia crumble under the weight of rampant genoicde carried out by my vengeaful populace.
This is one possibility of interactions with an empire you encounter on the playing field. Gameplay wise, I could have conceded for economic reasons but I didn't. It wasn't a game then, and I still had 22 more Empires to interact with while the crime of genoicde hung over my empire. That's 22 potential space epics for you as well. And Paradox is doing all it can to help you make even more, because YOU'RE the storyteller in this one.

The Binding Of Isaac is an flash indie game developed by Edmund McMillen and Florian Himsl. The game’s storyline and name are both a reference to the Biblical story known also as Binding of Isaac. In the game, the player controls Isaac, a child that seeks safety in the basement after his mother is given a message of God commanding her to sacrifice her own son in order to proof her faith. In the basement Isaac starts going through dungeons located in the basement having to face his nightmares in form of monsters, in order to escape.
The style and game’s gameplay are inspired by Legend of Zelda series and similar to roguelike, where the rooms of all dungeons are randomly generated, being different each time you play, and this is what makes it so special because every gameplay is totally different. On each floor of the basement, the player must kill monsters in order to proceed to the next room. Along the way, it will be possible to collect keys weapons and power-ups which will increase your chance of surviving because each item has a special effect and you can also pick up coins which are used to buy items in shops spread all over each floor, but need a key to be opened.
Each floor of the dungeon ends with a boss room, where a boss must be defeated in order to proceed to the next floor. Each time the bosses are different. At loading screens between floors, Isaac remembers scenarios, of his childhood while crying in fetal position, from rejection of his mother, unlucky moments and even bullying from his friends, some can even be Isaac’s own fears, but you’ll never know.
The gameplay is easy to master since does not require very buttons and the soundtrack is not diverse, but it does fit very well the atmosphere of the game.
One of the most awesome features of this game, in my opinion, and because due to flash limitation, it’s not possible to save, all your unlockables will stay unlocked and such, but you cannot save mid-game, so you will have to start over every time you go back to main menu, every time you lose and every time you close the game. And that is what makes it so hard and enjoyable since you will not get bored because every time all will be different and new!
A DLC to the game was also released, “Wrath of the Lambs”, also a religious reference, and it adds all new content including new items, new rooms, new enemies, new bosses and its totally worth it!
This game has me craving for more every time I play it, the creativity of it is amazing and it will make you spend some good long hours playing it. I totally recommend you to get it.
~ 9/10

Cortex command is a two-dimensional strategic and action game that requires the player to make decisive decisions in building a better offense and defense. The goal of the game is to keep your brain alive as this brain is the control center for all the robots and AI that work around it. The brain is either in a mobile suit or is hidden away in a cavern inside a base. There are a few game modes in Cortex Command such as skirmish/mission battles and campaign. Skirmish you can set your own conditions whereas mission battles have objectives (such as retrieve the chip and put it on a rocket then fly it away). The campaign is pretty cool and interesting as it let's you build up a base, conquer and expand your empire. The campaign starts with a few selected places where gold deposits are found. Upon finding these deposits, the player is asked to choose where to go. You may only go at one place at a time but can manage multiple places given you own more.
Once the player has chosen a location, the player can blindly jump into the area (which a fog of war will be on) or can actively scan and place their ship as they are scanning to try and get a better location (for defense or for more gold). Players should be wary how much they plan to spend on their expedition though. The one resource that runs this world is gold. Gold is used for everything so your job is to make sure it's distributed evenly. Going on an expedition will cost as well as scanning the surface. If you didn't allow for enough money to start-up, you could be very well losing land quite quickly. Overspend and leave future endeavors and other locations without a defense budget. The computer may attack two locations (as in one may be  your base and another may be a location you're looking to acquire). It is important to leave some money for base development in places you have settled. This lets the AI portion of the game take over and build for you. If you do like building yourself, this is also possible as well as placing objects and especially other units. Having more units will make your location a lot more secure. Just don't forget to arm them! To dig or construct, players need those specific tools to do the job. AI can be assigned to automatically do tasks if you tell them to by holding the right mouse button (which brings up a wheel) and choosing with the left. Players can build in-game and with the designer out of a mission. On the battle-field, the player orders new units or supplies by buying them and shipping them in VIA rocket. These rockets can also be controlled and can be used to blow up other units after dropping yours off.
Movement and
in the game are decent. The movement is a bit weird as the terrain will rip away slowly whether you walk, fly or jump on it which makes moving itself a little weird if you're on the ground. The "loose-body" impact is pretty cool but fly to quick and land with a crash can take some hit points away from a unit (and possibly make him drop his weapon). You can crouch and fly but there are no other action movements or dodges to perform. The point of the game is to make a nice balance between units that mine for gold, that attack and that defend (the brain). You can do this all manually yourself and even form squads or assign certain tasks for individual units. The brain unit (if in a mobile suit) can also perform these tasks. Careful though as I failed some missions due to my brain guy digging outside of the map area and killing himself. This has only happened on scenario maps not campaign maps as they do a full circle (meaning the player can attack from the left or the right).
The
are decent and are mostly pixelated. This is not too much of an issue if you've played games like Terraria, Nidhogg, Soldat or Liero. I personally like the theme chosen as it suits the environment well. The
are varied but can become very familiar after playing a few games.
Overall, not a bad game and worthy of a purchase on sale therefore I will recommend it within those conditions. For full price, it's a little steep I'd say unless it really appeals to you. If you have friends, I'm sure you'll find it worth it. Playing solo and finishing the campaign will leave you wanting more. Problem is, you'll have to restart the whole process again. For some players (especially ones that like to build-up like in Terraria), this may turn you off. Good concept, just needs a variable X to make it that much better.
RATING : 6.85/10

This is a great arcade style twin stick shooter. In particular, if you liked Housemarque's previous games like Resogun and Super Stardust, Nex Machina will certainly scratch that itch. The way it is structured and how you can earn extra points by saving humans, finding secret levels, and so on can give you more things to improve upon in addition to mastering later difficulties.
That said, your mileage may vary depending on how much you want to chase high scores or beat different difficulties. I personally got the most enjoyment out of Super Stardust and Resogun's endless modes, which were added later as DLC. Likewise, Nex Machina would likely benefit from an endless mode or something that is more repeatable than playing through the campaign again and again, but unfortunately this mode doesn't exist yet.
That said, Nex Machina is an incredibly fun game with great particle effects and an amazing soundtrack. As a fan of various twin stick shooters over the years, Nex Machina is one of the more fun games like this I've played.

I love this game, I really do. But it's not because of the awesome ship designs(which still REQUIRE a coloring feature) and the various species you can play as, but rather because of the little ways it brings the immersive part of your brain to life. If you try to play this in a roleplaying fashion, and not in the 'I named my plant species The Weed Bros lol' fashion, then you'll quickly find yourself coming up with snippets of everyday life in your homegrown empire. You'll think of all the conspiracy theorists on that frontier planet after your leader is mysteriously reelected for the fifth time(even if you just really need his fleet-building trait), you'll picture grand parades as your rookie admiral(who has the arm-chair commander trait) leads your fleet to victory and you'll be thrusted into a darkened conference room next to your fellow alien peers as they whisper about 'purging' those troublesome fanatical spiritualists who have been protesting on a planet rich in minerals vital to your fleet construction(causing literally no gameplay hindering effects other than a differently colored happiness bar).
I've never actually finished a game, my computer can't handle the armadas that everyone has towards the endgame, but I still keep making new games because I love the immersive value. There's more to just a game grid with a galaxy color scheme, there's more to planets than their sizes. The game doesn't pull you into an immersive experience, you won't even notice the transition.
For example, on my first playthrough I had a mining station on an asteroid in a middle of nowhere system. As I researched more and more, that asteroid turned out to hold a bunch of strategic resources. Lucky me, right? Then my neighbors, peace loving tapeworms, colonized a nearby planet and suddenly I no longer owned that asteroid. By this time I had found another exo-planet with equal value, but I went to war over this asteroid. The game refused to let me name the war, but I always refer to it as the 'War of the Rock'. The War of the Rock took twenty years, and saw the tapeworms lose twelve admirals before sneaking a fleet by my lines and bombarding my home planet. My population enraged and my key fleet-building station compromised, I gave my last admiral the divine blessings and ordered him to punch right into the tapeworm home system and lay waste. The War of the Rock resulted in a single asteroid's mining rights return to its previous owners and a Democratic Utopia crumble under the weight of rampant genoicde carried out by my vengeaful populace.
This is one possibility of interactions with an empire you encounter on the playing field. Gameplay wise, I could have conceded for economic reasons but I didn't. It wasn't a game then, and I still had 22 more Empires to interact with while the crime of genoicde hung over my empire. That's 22 potential space epics for you as well. And Paradox is doing all it can to help you make even more, because YOU'RE the storyteller in this one.
9/10, needs ship coloring and war naming. Oh wait; 11/10, makes up for it in endless entertainment derived from just staring at a planet grow and thinking of the horse colonists working side by side with robots and tentacled neighbors.

A mediocre trip down memory lane, if you are old enough to remember such games.
A mediocre waste of time for everyone else however.
See, unlike shovel knight which took the charm of 8 and 16bit games while adding an interesting game, NEStalgia used the 8 and 16bit games layer to hide a bland grindfest of a mostly dull game.
At first I enjoyed it since it reminded me of RPGs of old and then the grind began.
Almost immediately infact.
The second quest, "Kill a mouse", sounds simple enough but the mouse is the first boss of the game and you need to be around level 6 to beat it. No problem right? Weeeell you need about 600 exp and you gain about 3 a fight with the local slimes outside. Thats about 200 fights, by the way, of doing nothing except pressing 1 to pick attack and then 1 to select your target.
The game adds skills and magic but MP doesn't recharge so thats a rest at the inn for you. That will be 3 gold. Not bad except the slimes only drop 2 gold and your first armor can cost as much as 450 gold if you picked warrior.
It gets really dull, really quickly and this is only the first town! Theres a whole world out there to explore chump! So mouse is dead, move onto bandits and...I'm dead again. Bandits require you to be about level 9 and that armor you saved up for? Not as useful as you might have hoped now that enemies come in waves of 5 so you guessed it, back to grinding for you.
The game isn't all bad, for example you can recruit some of the monsters and they make pretty decent party members and what a good job too because outside of other players, they are the only party members you get! They also don't get to wear equipment so you decide if thats a positive (less gold grinding) or a negative (less overall stats).
And finally don't bot. Or appear to be botting at least. If the idea of pressing A,D,1,1 for 50 hours sounds a bit dull for you then I have bad news for you, it is dull. It was dull back then and its dull today. Old NES RPGs had something though, first of all they were all we had unless you owned a PC and second of all while the grind was a way to pad the game out, they normally had a story and events going on that should make you want to play on. Not everything was gated behind a grindfest at every turn, just to pad out the game. Here, grinding is the game and just like being in detention, you are expected to sit and do it and don't complain.
When I played, there were no more than 10 people on at ANY given time and while I think the game isn't terrible, I do feel it deserves better than 10 people playing but I can also accept that it probably did have more than 10 people at one time and the refusal to either make the story captivating or to reduce/remove the grind is what lead to the husk we have today.
Just as a final note, you can download the game for free outside of Steam although that is probably level capped or something.

To anyone who hasn't already played this game or at least heard about it (who are you?) take the time to read this review as I have personally never written a review before for a game.
There's a reason I am finally doing this.
The Binding of Isaac is not just a run-of-the-mill roguelike with randomly generated dungeons. This game is a wealth of replayability. If you enjoy games that are extremely challenging, this is the one for you. The great thing about this games devilish difficulty is that winning an instance of this game is overwhelmingly rewarding.
The gameplay is basic and easy to get the hang of.
The music is perfect.
The art, well, it is dark but expertly well-crafted.
The replayability is infinite.
I will say one important thing. If you do not like challenging, unforgiving games, this is not for you. This game will take you to the brink of your frustrations. This also happens to be the perfect formula for people who do enjoy a challenge. I personally have not gotten as much enjoyment from any other game.
Go ahead, indulge. You'll be glad you did.

Magicka: Brilliantly Ludicrous
I’m just going to get it out of the way: if you haven’t played Magicka, go buy it right now.
It’s only $10 dollars, has a very unique combat system, and is the perfect combination of self aware, stupid, and high concept rigamarole. PLUS, the sequel will be released on May 26th!
Now, if that doesn't interest you… Well, uh… GTAV is out on PC… Or something…
When people ask me why Magika is so good, the first thing I think of is its sense of humor.
“Oh no. Not a ‘funny’ game.”
Yeah, yeah, I know. We've all been burned by one of those in the past. But this one is different. Magicka is just stupid... but In the best way!
The main plot device used to get the story rolling is: a powerful wizard, Grimnir, wanted to harness the power of all magick and use it to bring peace and prosperity to all the lands. But his peers were intimidated by his ambition and had him exiled from the order and imprisoned at the end of the world for all eternity!
Seems reasonable...
And thus the world was saved... “aside from the increased numbers of monsters attacking the villagers”  and “The Orc warlord Khan, who united the orc tribes, and now threatens the great city of Havindir!”
Now it’s your job to fix everything!
Okay, yeah it’s pretty stupid. But give it a chance. Most of the humor in this game is self aware, even though it isn’t always presented with ‘a wink and a nod’. Magicka likes to play around with clichés from popular genres—Fantasy, RPG, Video Game, even some Sci-Fi—and everything is presented at face value. I appreciate that.
But humor isn’t the only thing Magicka has going for it. It has a decidedly unique spell system, which breaks down like this:
You have eight elements mapped to the QWER and ASDF keys.
You can combine any and all of the eight elements up to five times to create a myriad of different spells to fight with. In addition to the vast amount of possible combinations (something like 32,768),  many of the elements will actually interact. Some elemental pairs combine into entirely new elements! Like Water and Cold, which combine to create Ice. Water and Fire will create steam. Additionally certain elements will also cancel each other out, like Lightning and Earth, adding another layer of complexity.
But variety is pointless if the different elements don’t mean anything by themselves. That’s where the Magicka’s combat really shines.
Each element is unique and has it’s own rules and status effects. Straight forward, right? If something is wet, Fire will dry it off and Cold will freeze it. Lightning, by itself, electrocutes dudes. But! If they’re wet it will also deal far more damage! Not good enough for you? Well, If you’re feeling frisky, you can combine Fire and Arcane and make a fire-laser beam that not only ignites your foes in fiery anguish, but also causes them to explode upon death at no extra charge.
If that wasn’t enough for you, there are also three different ways to cast each spell:
Normally. (Need a group of people on fire? This is your best bet.)
Area of Effect. (Need a circle of fiery death around you? Look no further.)
And On Self. (This only goes bad about 98% of the time.)
Are you frozen solid? Better light yourself on fire to thaw the ice!
No seriously...
Let me give you an example of some of the possible interactions:
Scene: There are a bunch of Goblins, lets say twelve, running at you. They are trying to make your insides your outsides.
So, like any normal person, you conjure up a super awesome Water and Earth projectile spell, and shoot it towards them at high speed. The magical projectile splatters about 6 or 7 goblins into a smear of red paste and gracefully cover the survivors in water. Now would be a great time to electrocute them!
*A-A-A-A* “WHY AM I DEAD?!” - You, probably.
You were wet, that’s why. The water from your spell accidentally drenched you.
Anything you can do to the enemies, can be done to you.
The combat in Magicka is very interesting, and also quite hard. Sometimes annoyingly so. But it’s never impossible or cheap. From my perspective, each combat situation is a puzzle that needs to be solved via different spells. You just have to make sure not to rain down lightning from the heavens if your  Wizard Robe is sopping wet.
And the developers were not afraid of altering how you think about your spell combinations. During a specific chapter the Life element, the only way to heal, becomes one of the best ways to output damage. Which completely alters how you go about choosing your spells.
Side Note: that was also one of my favorite chapters in Magicka.
I have spent just shy of 40 hours with the game, and I’ve enjoyed every second of it. The game has a pretty lengthy story, filled to the brim with genuinely enjoyable referential humor. You might groan a few times, but that’s half the fun anyway.
I’ll leave you with one last comment. Messing around with your buds adds a great deal of enjoyment Magicka. The game is wonderful on it’s own, but adding friends makes all those interactions come into even greater effect: one mage is trouble. Two mages, a disaster. Three or more? Chaos. Utter chaos.
Just remember: Do. Not. Cross. The streams.
Trust me.

Cory in the House is a television show, which aired on the Disney Channel from January 12, 2007 to September 12, 2008 and was a spin-off from the Disney show That's So Raven. The show focuses on Cory Baxter, who moves from San Francisco, California to Washington, D.C. with his father, after Victor Baxter gets a new job in the White House as the official head chef. The series marks a Disney Channel first, as it is the channel's first spin-off. This is also the only Disney Channel spin-off series to be broadcast in standard definition for the entire length of the show. Reruns of the series have not been produced on Disney Channel, or on Disney XD; however they continue to air on the Family channel in Canada. Raven-Symoné guest-starred, reprising her role as Raven Baxter in one episode. In 2014 Disney Channel started airing a weekly block called Disney Replay on Wednesdays nights, during which episodes of Cory in the House air alongside That's So Raven and Kim Possible, among others.

Orion: Prelude is... Well it's a lot of things. It's a single player FPS, co-op FPS, PVP FPS, and a PVE FPS. Since it just became free, I wanted to review it. Please excuse me if I misspelled anything.
I cranked everything up to the highest it will go, and honestly, they're a mixed bag. Some maps look great, while others look like they came from the Xbox 360. A lot of the textures are bad too. The effects look nice though.
Again, another mixed bag. The music ic great. A lot of it is an epic orchestrated soundtrack which fits the game pretty well. There is basicly almost no voice other than the soldiers yelling out lines every once and a while. Sound effects are really what get me though. Some guns sound great, while others sound like peashooters. Explosions also don't sound beefy enough. The rest of the sounds are decent though.
*Edit: If you want to see what the music sounds like, then check out this video:
I only really got to test the single-player and co-op modes. So I can't review the PVE and PVP aspect just yet. When I do get to test them, I'll update my review. Anyways, the modes I did get to try out were called Survival and Conquest. they both are pretty much the same, only one is a lot bigger in scale. The general goal of each mode is to survive as long as possible against waves of dinosaurs. Of course, just like every horde mode, each wave gets more difficult than the last. There are always two buildings in each map. One supplies you with weapons, ammo, and other items, while the other gives you perks and upgrades. For every dino you kill, it earns you CR or credits. You can spend those credits on more weapons, items and perks. From what I could understand, if your power station in the map gets destroyed, you fail the match. also if you and your team runs out of lives then you fail the match as well. There are occasional objectives which task you to secure objectives. So, yeah. This mode has a lot going for it. And it is very fun to play. Like I said, it can be played in single player or co-op, and there are tons of cusomization options for the match so you can cusomize it to your liking. Speaking of customization, there is also character custiomization in the game too. As you level up you unlock new items to customize you character with. None of it is locked behind a paywall like most free-to-play games as well!

If you've played any of Housemarque's other games then you know exactly what to expect from Nex Machina.
Like Super Stardust HD, Dead Nation, and Resogun, Nex Machina is a twin-stick shooter that harkens back to Robotron--or if you grew up in US arcades in the 90's, Smash T.V.
In each level you move and shoot enemies coming from all directions while weaving through their attacks in bullet hell fashion. Each level is made of stages and each stage features any combination of level objective, powerup, or secret. Clearing the current stage moves you to the next one. If you don't find the secret you were looking for or save the human wandering around the stage then you miss out on that pickup and move on through the level.
The kinetic nature of the game provides plenty of depth and challenge. Every downed enemy inches you forward through the level. It requires critical thinking and quick decision-making skills to make it through a level without dying. But that score counter and leaderboard really make the whole experience worth it.
Visually, the game looks great and runs well on my i7-6700, 32 GB DDR4, GTX 1080. The game supports 21:9 aspect ratio natively and runs at 3440x1440/60 FPS at all settings maxed without issue. I enabled 2xDSR and encountered no issues either. I'm given to understand that the game runs well on mid and lower range gaming machines, too.
There are some quirks; like the lack of graphics options overall. Or the odd control-mapping system and the way that mouse/keyboard binding looks a little weird (possibly due to my somewhat unconventional aspect ratio). My game also refuses to run in an actual borderless window. Both windowed mode and borderless window mode feature a titlebar and borders. None of these issues are dealbreakers but they are worth mentioning.
The soundtrack is great because it fades into the background. But in those moments when you have a moment to think about the music and you listen to it you'll find a well-composed video game soundtrack that compliments the overall presentation well. I typically turn off game music when I get the chance but in Nex Machina I find the music essential. The driving beats alone helped me keep up the pace of the game and kept me on my toes.
Nex Machina is a definite buy if you are looking for a rewarding arcade-style experience.

A potentially fun game spoiled by a number of factors (including a lack of playerbase, Hope you enjoy only 8-10 people tops during peak hours when you want to party!) And I believe that may be hiding a lack of content through punishing difficulty under the guise of being "hardcore"
I've played plenty of RPGs old and new from console to PC. From JRPG to WRPG- And to compare this to any of them is a disservice to those games.
The game isn't hard. The game is unbalanced. You lose half of all any money you are holding if you die- Requiring constant bank trips in order to save up for anything least a mini boss way over your level pops out of nowhere
(And I do mean out of nowhere... The second town you can be walkign along or trying to do the catacombs quest and BAM mindflayer with 300 HP at a time you're only able to crank out 30 damage. Who does enough damage to party wipe you in 3-4 turns. Unavoidable RNG and he can appear in THREE DIFFERENT AREAS WHICH ARE YOU REQUIRED TO GO TO TO QUEST!)
Havign an easy breezy difficulty curve up to a set point where in you are deadlocked and unable to progress and run entirely out of quests and things to do besides run around the beginner continient and butt your head against the grind wall- And you think, but why do I have to do this?
Because past level 15 content is gated behind an immunity gimmick AOE spamming boss who can heal his immunity gimmick AOE helpers that will absolutely demolish you regardless of the arrangement of companions or party members unless you just plain get lucky and all have an inventory full of healing items and use them willy nilly and hope they land on someone who needs it due to the way the turns play out.
That is, if the AI doesn't arbitrarily burst damage one of you down before you can make any headway. And even if you do squeak past this? And even if you are so strong you can one shot the previous area's monsters- Now the next area's enemies are mini boss tough by comparison right out of the gate and you will absolutely require a perfect monster companion makeup or party with healing and endurance to make any progress further.
A few people or die hard fans might tell me. "Just get good!" I am, I did. Just the game itself got worse instead of better. I don't mind a challenge, I do mind when a game is holding me back at every turn for a lack of being able to make a proper challenge or difficulty curve.
Or when it's making me waste time because it's afraid of me getting anywhere or finding out there's nothing more to it than a tiny handful of areas disguised and gated by massive grind.

The game for me is both a hit and miss.
The beginning aka the exploration phase is great. It really gives you the feel of exploring the galaxy.
Then you start the colonization race, trying to colonize the best planets before the ai does and claim critical systems with outposts is fun.
And then after that is over, the game starts to become less fun.
The game has arrived on the grand strategy part of the game and that part is shallow at best.
The diplomacy is just bad, war is doomstackvsdoomstack and the largest/best equipped fleet wins.
Ethos barely make difference in how you play the game.
But worst of all, the a.i. empires are devoid of any personality.
When you meet a.i. empires, you only need to check their ethos(something like personality traits) and you know everything about them.
Worse is that many empires share the exact same ethos, which makes them all cheap copies.
When you make contact with other empires in mid to late game you usually just click the popup away. they are generally too far away too bother paying attention to it, and their is extremely high chance that the empire you made contact with has the exact same ethos(personality) as already discovered.
Generally people dont remember even one name of the many a.i. species, they are generallly remembered as generic democratic crusaders number 4 or federation builder number 6.
The game has a lot of potential, the game will be slowly improved but if you want to enjoy those improvements you will need to pay for the dozens of dlc paradox will sell.

Magicka: Brilliantly Ludicrous
I’m just going to get it out of the way: if you haven’t played Magicka, go buy it right now.
It’s only $10 dollars, has a very unique combat system, and is the perfect combination of self aware, stupid, and high concept rigamarole. PLUS, the sequel will be released on May 26th!
Now, if that doesn't interest you… Well, uh… GTAV is out on PC… Or something…
When people ask me why Magika is so good, the first thing I think of is its sense of humor.
“Oh no. Not a ‘funny’ game.”
Yeah, yeah, I know. We've all been burned by one of those in the past. But this one is different. Magicka is just stupid... but In the best way!
The main plot device used to get the story rolling is: a powerful wizard, Grimnir, wanted to harness the power of all magick and use it to bring peace and prosperity to all the lands. But his peers were intimidated by his ambition and had him exiled from the order and imprisoned at the end of the world for all eternity!
Seems reasonable...
And thus the world was saved... “aside from the increased numbers of monsters attacking the villagers”  and “The Orc warlord Khan, who united the orc tribes, and now threatens the great city of Havindir!”
Now it’s your job to fix everything!
Okay, yeah it’s pretty stupid. But give it a chance. Most of the humor in this game is self aware, even though it isn’t always presented with ‘a wink and a nod’. Magicka likes to play around with clichés from popular genres—Fantasy, RPG, Video Game, even some Sci-Fi—and everything is presented at face value. I appreciate that.
But humor isn’t the only thing Magicka has going for it. It has a decidedly unique spell system, which breaks down like this:
You have eight elements mapped to the QWER and ASDF keys.
You can combine any and all of the eight elements up to five times to create a myriad of different spells to fight with. In addition to the vast amount of possible combinations (something like 32,768),  many of the elements will actually interact. Some elemental pairs combine into entirely new elements! Like Water and Cold, which combine to create Ice. Water and Fire will create steam. Additionally certain elements will also cancel each other out, like Lightning and Earth, adding another layer of complexity.
But variety is pointless if the different elements don’t mean anything by themselves. That’s where the Magicka’s combat really shines.
Each element is unique and has it’s own rules and status effects. Straight forward, right? If something is wet, Fire will dry it off and Cold will freeze it. Lightning, by itself, electrocutes dudes. But! If they’re wet it will also deal far more damage! Not good enough for you? Well, If you’re feeling frisky, you can combine Fire and Arcane and make a fire-laser beam that not only ignites your foes in fiery anguish, but also causes them to explode upon death at no extra charge.
If that wasn’t enough for you, there are also three different ways to cast each spell:
Normally. (Need a group of people on fire? This is your best bet.)
Area of Effect. (Need a circle of fiery death around you? Look no further.)
And On Self. (This only goes bad about 98% of the time.)
Are you frozen solid? Better light yourself on fire to thaw the ice!
No seriously...
Let me give you an example of some of the possible interactions:
Scene: There are a bunch of Goblins, lets say twelve, running at you. They are trying to make your insides your outsides.
So, like any normal person, you conjure up a super awesome Water and Earth projectile spell, and shoot it towards them at high speed. The magical projectile splatters about 6 or 7 goblins into a smear of red paste and gracefully cover the survivors in water. Now would be a great time to electrocute them!
*A-A-A-A* “WHY AM I DEAD?!” - You, probably.
You were wet, that’s why. The water from your spell accidentally drenched you.
Anything you can do to the enemies, can be done to you.
The combat in Magicka is very interesting, and also quite hard. Sometimes annoyingly so. But it’s never impossible or cheap. From my perspective, each combat situation is a puzzle that needs to be solved via different spells. You just have to make sure not to rain down lightning from the heavens if your  Wizard Robe is sopping wet.
And the developers were not afraid of altering how you think about your spell combinations. During a specific chapter the Life element, the only way to heal, becomes one of the best ways to output damage. Which completely alters how you go about choosing your spells.
Side Note: that was also one of my favorite chapters in Magicka.
I have spent just shy of 40 hours with the game, and I’ve enjoyed every second of it. The game has a pretty lengthy story, filled to the brim with genuinely enjoyable referential humor. You might groan a few times, but that’s half the fun anyway.
I’ll leave you with one last comment. Messing around with your buds adds a great deal of enjoyment Magicka. The game is wonderful on it’s own, but adding friends makes all those interactions come into even greater effect: one mage is trouble. Two mages, a disaster. Three or more? Chaos. Utter chaos.
Just remember: Do. Not. Cross. The streams.
Trust me.
